contentHtml:
Baker Heritage Museum tells the story of Baker County inside the historic 1920 Natatorium in Baker City. Once known as the Oregon Trail Regional Museum, it fills about 33,000 square feet with permanent and changing exhibits.

Collections cover the industries that built the region, including mining, timber, ranching and agriculture, along with early Baker City life, Chinese culture and local wildlife. Visitors can spend anywhere from an hour to a full day exploring.

title: National Historic Oregon Trail Interpretive Center
imageAlt: Covered wagon among sagebrush with distant mountains at sunset

banner.alt: Covered wagon among sagebrush with distant mountains at sunset

contentHtml:
The National Historic Oregon Trail Interpretive Center, run by the Bureau of Land Management, brings 19th- century Oregon Trail migration to life on a 500-acre hillside near Baker City. Hands-on exhibits, life-size displays and a replica wagon camp show the daily lives of pioneers, the landscapes they crossed, and their encounters with Native Americans.

Outside, original Oregon Trail wagon ruts and the remains of the Flagstaff Gold Mine are still on site. About 2 miles of paved trails start from the back patio, including the easy half-mile Flagstaff Hill Loop and the Panorama Point Trail past a lode mine and stamp mill. Ranger programs, living history demonstrations and Oregon Trail Days run through the year.

note: Fee April-October: $8 adults, $6 seniors

title: Eastern Oregon Museum
imageAlt: Front entrance of the Eastern Oregon Museum

banner.alt: Front entrance of the Eastern Oregon Museum

contentHtml:
The Eastern Oregon Museum in historic Haines, on the Elkhorn Drive Scenic Byway, tells more than 150 years of community history. It began as a grange hobby show and now holds thousands of artifacts from the upper Baker and Powder valleys, housed in a former school gym.

Exhibits focus on western memorabilia and pioneer life, with a blacksmith shop, a carriage wing, antique washing machines, a telephone exhibit and a quilt show. Groups, organizations and reunions are welcome, and appointments are available outside regular hours.
excerpt: The Eastern Oregon Museum in historic Haines, on the Elkhorn Drive Scenic Byway, tells more than 150 years of community history. It began as a grange hobby show
note: Open Memorial Day to Labor Day; call 24 hours ahead for appointments

title: Malheur National Forest
contentHtml:
The Malheur National Forest covers 1.7 million acres of the Blue Mountains in eastern Oregon, from high desert grasslands of sage and juniper to pine and fir forests, hidden alpine lakes and meadows. Elevations run from 4,000 feet to 9,038 feet at Strawberry Mountain, whose range runs through the center of the forest.

The forest holds 88,350 acres of wilderness and the headwaters of the John Day River, the only tributary of the Columbia with no dams. The Malheur and Silvies rivers have Wild and Scenic stretches, and four former guard stations and a lookout can be rented for overnight stays.

title: Wallowa-Whitman National Forest
contentHtml:
The Wallowa-Whitman National Forest covers 2.4 million acres of northeastern Oregon and western Idaho. Elevations range from 9,843 feet in the alpine peaks of the Elkhorn, Wallowa and Seven Devils mountains down to 875 feet along the Snake River, with grasslands, canyons, rangelands and conifer forests in between.

The forest includes ten Wild and Scenic Rivers, four wilderness areas and the 652,488-acre Hells Canyon National Recreation Area. Visitors come for hiking, fly fishing, camping, ATV and OHV trails, and snowmobiling in winter.

title: Eagle Cap Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Eagle Cap Wilderness covers 359,991 acres in the heart of the Wallowa Mountains, with high alpine lakes and meadows, bare granite peaks and ridges, and U-shaped glaciated valleys. It became a primitive area in 1930 and a designated wilderness in 1940, making it one of Oregon's oldest.

About 535 miles of trails serve hikers and horseback riders, with trailheads on all sides from Wallowa, Union and Baker counties. The Lakes Basin is the most popular area. The land was home to ancestors of the Nez Perce from about 1400 A.D., and was the summer home of the Joseph Band of the Nez Perce.

title: Monument Rock Wilderness
imageAlt: Lupine blooming along the trail to Monument Rock

banner.alt: Lupine blooming along the trail to Monument Rock

contentHtml:
Monument Rock Wilderness protects 19,800 acres of the southern Blue Mountains, where the headwaters of the Little Malheur River and the upper South Fork Burnt River begin. Designated by Congress in 1984, it rises from 5,120 feet to 7,815 feet at Table Rock, which still has a fire lookout, along with Monument Rock and Bullrun Rock.

Subalpine fir covers the high ground, with ponderosa pine, Douglas fir, lodgepole pine, aspen and grassy meadows below. About 15 miles of relatively easy trails cross the area, and black bears, deer, elk, badgers, hawks and grouse live here. Snow usually falls by December and melts by the end of March.

title: Spring Recreation Site

gallery.alt: Boat launch at Spring Recreation Site
Spring Recreation Site on Brownlee Reservoir

contentHtml:
Spring Recreation Site sits on the banks of Brownlee Reservoir, a 52-mile-long reservoir on the Snake River near Huntington. Anglers come for big channel catfish, plentiful crappie and good bass fishing.

The site has a boat launch with a boarding dock, a fish cleaning station, drinking water, accessible vault toilets, and campsites with picnic tables and grills (no hookups). Apricot trees and grapevines planted by homesteaders still grow here, and a turnout overlooks the campground and water. Farewell Bend State Recreation Area is nearby.

title: Copper Creek Campground

gallery.alt: Morning light in Hells Canyon Wilderness
Mule deer buck in Hells Canyon Wilderness

contentHtml:
Copper Creek is a primitive campground and trailhead about nine miles north of Oxbow on the Oregon side of Hells Canyon, giving access to the southern part of the Hells Canyon Wilderness. Congress designated the 217,927-acre wilderness in 1975, and the Wild and Scenic Snake River splits it between Oregon and Idaho.

Lower down, grassland benches give way to steep, isolated canyons, while the high country has rocky slopes, grasslands and groves of Douglas fir and ponderosa pine. Rocky Mountain elk, bighorn sheep, mule deer and chukar live here. Trail junctions are mostly unsigned, so carry a map and compass.

imageAlt: Farewell Bend State Park sign with a covered wagon

banner.alt: Farewell Bend State Park sign with a covered wagon

contentHtml:
Farewell Bend State Recreation Area sits on the Snake River, where Oregon Trail travelers said goodbye to the river before heading northwest, and historic markers tell that story. Day use is open all year, with a paved boat ramp, a viewing deck, picnic areas, horseshoe pits, sand volleyball and a basketball court.

The campground has 91 electrical sites with water, 23 tent sites and two accessible log cabins, plus hot showers, flush toilets, an RV dump station, a fish cleaning station and a fenced off-leash pet area. Fishing, boating, water skiing, wildlife viewing and Snake River Water Trail access are all close at hand.

title: Sumpter Valley Dredge State Heritage Area
imageAlt: Aerial view of the Sumpter Valley Dredge floating in its pond

banner.alt: Aerial view of the Sumpter Valley Dredge floating in its pond

gallery.alt: Old mining machinery with the dredge behind
Dredge with its large rusty crane
The stacker at the back of the dredge
Old machinery by the river with mountains behind
"Floating in its own pond" interpretive sign

contentHtml:
The Sumpter Valley Dredge is a giant gold dredge that worked the valley floor nearly nonstop from 1935 to 1954, recovering an estimated $4 million in gold. It was the last of three dredges built here, and it worked like a floating ship on dry land. Piles of rock it left behind, called tailings, still line parts of the valley.

Gold was first found in the area in 1862. The dredge was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971 and opened to the public in 1994. About 1.5 miles of trails and viewing platforms wind through the park's wetlands, showing how nature has reclaimed the land.

imageAlt: Mountain road through pine forest in the Unity area

banner.alt: Mountain road through pine forest in the Unity area

contentHtml:
Unity Forest State Scenic Corridor protects a stretch of ponderosa pine forest along Highway 26 in the Blue Mountains near Unity. Managed by Oregon Parks and Recreation, it is a shaded place for travelers to stop and picnic beneath the pines.

Elk and mule deer are often seen at dawn and dusk. Unity Reservoir, a few miles away, offers trout, bass and crappie fishing.

contentHtml:
Unity Lake State Recreation Site is a high-desert park built around Unity Lake, formed when the Bureau of Reclamation dammed the Burnt River for irrigation. A boat ramp, trailer parking, a large shaded lawn and picnic tables make it a favorite day-use stop, and anglers fish here in spring and fall and ice fish in winter.

The campground has 35 electrical sites with water, two reservable cabins (one pet-friendly), a hiker and biker camp, hot showers, flush toilets and an accessible RV dump station. Firewood and ice are sold on site.

title: Anthony Lake
contentHtml:
Anthony Lake Campground is the largest of three campgrounds in the Anthony Lakes Recreation Area, set right beside Anthony Lake in the Elkhorn Mountains with views of Gunsight Peak. The main campground sits on the east side of the lake.

Only electric motorboats and non-motorized craft such as canoes, kayaks and rowboats are allowed on the lake, which makes it a quiet spot for fishing, paddling, day hiking and photography. Sites include tent and RV spots (no hookups), a group site and yurts, with vault toilets on site. The Anthony Lakes picnic area and boat launch are close by.

title: Anthony Lake Tent
contentHtml:
Anthony Lake Tent Campground offers walk-in tent sites on the southern end of Anthony Lake in the Elkhorn Mountains, reached by the lakeshore trail. No vehicles are allowed near the sites, which look out on Gunsight Peak and the surrounding mountains.

The lake allows only electric motorboats and non-motorized craft such as canoes, kayaks, rowboats and float tubes, so it stays quiet for fishing, paddling, day hiking and photography. Parking is limited near the boat launch and trailhead.

title: Boulder Park
contentHtml:
Boulder Park Campground sits at the end of a narrow, winding forest road beside Wild and Scenic Eagle Creek, with views of the Eagle Cap Wilderness and the Wallowa Mountains. It is set up for pack and riding stock, with a loading ramp, bunk feeders and trailer parking.

The seven sites each have a fire ring, picnic table and parking. The Main Eagle Trailhead into the Eagle Cap Wilderness is nearby, and the cool creekside setting is popular in summer heat. Campers without stock can use Two Color Campground about three miles down the road.

title: Eagle Forks
contentHtml:
Eagle Forks Campground sits where Little Eagle Creek meets Wild and Scenic Eagle Creek, with seven shady creekside sites, one of them accessible. It is popular and often full, especially on holiday weekends.

Visitors come to picnic and fish the creek, and the Eagle Forks Trailhead is close by. The last stretch of road is mostly single-lane gravel.

title: Elk Creek
contentHtml:
Elk Creek Campground is a small, rustic camp on Forest Road 6005 in the Burnt River country southwest of Unity, along the same road as South Fork and Stevens campgrounds. It offers basic tent and RV sites with vault toilets.

It makes a quiet base for exploring the forest, and off-road riders use the area's OHV routes. There is no water on site and reservations are not accepted.

title: Fish Lake
contentHtml:
Fish Lake Campground is a high-elevation camp beside Fish Lake in the Wallowa Mountains, with wilderness and non-wilderness trailheads close by. It has 21 tent and trailer sites, each with a picnic table, fire ring and parking.

Six sites are built for campers with disabilities, and six upper-loop sites fit RVs longer than 20 feet. Visitors come to fish, hike, watch wildlife and enjoy the water. The last stretch of road is mostly single-lane gravel.

title: Lake Fork
contentHtml:
Lake Fork Campground sits along North Pine Creek on the Hells Canyon Scenic Byway. It is popular from late spring through fall and makes a good base for day hikes and for exploring the byway and the Hells Canyon National Recreation Area.

Campsites have picnic tables, with vault toilets on site. Visitors fish the creek and picnic in the shade. The byway is usually closed by snow from late October to late May or early June.

title: McBride
contentHtml:
McBride Campground is a small camp along Brooks Ditch, shaded by a mixed pine and fir forest north of Halfway. In summer it is popular with local campers and berry pickers, and in fall with hunters.

Sites have picnic tables and vault toilets are on site. Parts of the access road are single-lane, steep gravel.

title: McCully Forks
contentHtml:
McCully Forks Campground sits beside a small stream in a forested setting on the Elkhorn Drive Scenic Byway, just past the historic town of Sumpter. Sites line both sides of the road and the creek.

It is an easy base for visiting the Sumpter Valley Dredge, exploring Sumpter and the byway, picnicking and day hiking.

title: Millers Lane
contentHtml:
Millers Lane Campground sits on the south shore of Phillips Lake in an open ponderosa pine forest. It is the smallest of the three campgrounds on the lake and a warm, sunny spot, with 11 tent and trailer sites and 4 tent-only sites.

Campers come for fishing, non-motorized boating, mountain biking, day hikes and wildlife watching, and for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing in winter. Lake levels change through the season, so the water can be a short walk away.

title: Oregon Campground
contentHtml:
Oregon Campground sits along Highway 26, part of the Journey Through Time Scenic Byway, with eight sites for tents and small trailers. Each has a picnic table, fire ring and parking.

It is right next to the Oregon OHV Trailhead of the Blue Mountain OHV Trail System, so it is popular with off- road riders, and also suits picnicking, hiking, wildlife viewing and photography.

title: South Fork
contentHtml:
South Fork Campground sits along the South Fork of the Burnt River, with 12 tent and trailer sites and 2 tent- only sites tucked among pine and fir trees. Each site has a picnic table, fire ring and parking space.

It is popular from late spring through fall for fishing, hiking, picnicking and wildlife viewing, and as a base for hunting. Off-road riders use the nearby Blue Mountain OHV Trails.

title: Southwest Shore
contentHtml:
Southwest Shore Campground is one of three campgrounds around Phillips Lake, set in a warm, open pine forest. It is usually the first of the three to open in spring.

Campers come to fish, paddle, picnic, mountain bike and watch wildlife, and the Phillips Lake South Shoreline Trail starts nearby. In winter the area is used for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Lake levels change through the season, so the water can be a short walk away.

title: Stevens Creek
contentHtml:
Stevens Creek Campground is a small tent-only camp on Forest Road 6005 in the South Fork Burnt River area southwest of Unity, near South Fork and Elk Creek campgrounds.

Visitors use it as a base for fishing, hiking, hunting and riding the area's OHV routes. Vault toilets are on site, but there is no water, and reservations are not accepted.

title: Tamarack
contentHtml:
Tamarack Campground is a small, open and sunny campground on Wild and Scenic Eagle Creek in the southern Wallowa Mountains. It has 12 tent and trailer sites, three of them fully accessible.

A short accessible path leads down to the creek, where two fishing platforms make it easy to cast a line. Visitors also come for hiking, bird watching and picnicking. Access roads are narrow gravel or dirt, and the campground fills up on holiday weekends.

title: Twin Lakes
contentHtml:
Twin Lakes Campground is a small, minimally developed camp on the southern edge of the Hells Canyon National Recreation Area and the southeast edge of the Eagle Cap Wilderness. Its five sites each have a picnic table, fire ring and parking.

Anglers fish from boardwalks along Twin Lakes, and Trail 1874 leads from camp into the wilderness through the remains of an old burn. It is a quiet base for hiking, backpacking and wildlife viewing.

title: Two Color
contentHtml:
Two Color Campground sits along Wild and Scenic Eagle Creek, where tall pine and spruce trees keep the nine sites cool and shady in summer. Each site has a picnic table, fire ring and parking.

The Eagle Cap Wilderness is about 3 miles up the road, and fishing and day hikes are popular nearby. The Two Color Guard Station, a historic cabin, can be rented through Recreation.gov.

title: Union Creek
contentHtml:
Union Creek Campground is one of the largest Forest Service campgrounds in eastern Oregon, set on the northern shore of Phillips Lake amid mature ponderosa pine forest, about 18 miles south of Baker City.

Campers can choose basic sites or sites with electric, water and sewer hookups, plus a group site. The Union Creek boat launch, picnic area and swimming are right at hand, and visitors come for fishing, boating, water skiing, mountain biking and day hikes.

title: Wetmore
contentHtml:
Wetmore Campground is one of three Wallowa-Whitman campgrounds along Highway 26, part of the Journey Through Time Scenic Byway. It has 11 sites for tents and small trailers, three of them accessible, each with a picnic table, fire ring and parking.

An accessible, barrier-free trail connects to nearby Yellow Pine Campground, and large tables by the upper spring have hosted group picnics. It is an easy stop for camping, hiking, wildlife viewing and photography.

title: Yellow Pine
contentHtml:
Yellow Pine Campground is the largest of three Wallowa-Whitman campgrounds along Highway 26, part of the Journey Through Time Scenic Byway, and a handy stop for travelers crossing the state. It has sites for tents and small trailers, including five accessible sites.

An accessible, barrier-free trail leads to nearby Wetmore Campground, passing wildflowers, birds and large old-growth ponderosa pines.

title: Anthony Lake
contentHtml:
Anthony Lake is a compact high-elevation mountain lake in the Elkhorn Mountains, ringed by conifer forest, rocky peaks and alpine terrain, with Gunsight Peak rising above it. Its small size suits relaxed shoreline exploring by kayak, canoe or stand-up paddleboard rather than long crossings.

Only electric motorboats and non-motorized craft are allowed, so the water stays calm and quiet. The boat launch, campgrounds and picnic area sit beside the lake, and hiking trails and a scenic drive are close by. The water stays cold even on warm afternoons, and mountain weather can change quickly.

title: Phillips Reservoir
contentHtml:
Phillips Reservoir, also known as Phillips Lake, sits on the Powder River about 17 miles from Baker City. Mason Dam, built between 1965 and 1968, holds back the water, and the lake covers 2,235 acres at an elevation of about 4,060 feet.

Most visitors start at the Union Creek Boat Launch on the north shore. It sits in open ponderosa pine forest, with a two-lane ramp, a large parking area for trailers and a small snack and bait shack. Kayaks, canoes and stand-up paddleboards share the lake with motorboats and water skiers, and anglers fish from boats and the shore. Next door, Union Creek Campground is one of the largest Forest Service campgrounds in eastern Oregon, and the Phillips Lake Shoreline Trail is open to walkers and mountain bikers.

Paddlers need an Oregon Waterway Access Permit, and there is a day-use fee per vehicle at Union Creek.

title: Unity Reservoir

gallery.alt: Two people in a small boat on Unity Lake
Stairs leading down to the lake
Unity Lake State Park entrance sign

contentHtml:
Unity Reservoir is an irrigation reservoir on the Burnt River in the high desert near Unity, with broad open views and good wildlife watching. Paddlers launch kayaks, canoes and stand-up paddleboards from the boat ramp at Unity Lake State Recreation Site, which also has restrooms, drinking water, picnic tables and a shaded lawn.

Motorboats share the water, so watch for wakes, and boats are not allowed past the buoy line near the dam spillway. The water level drops a lot during irrigation season, and at low water you may need to carry your boat to the shore. The area is exposed to wind, so check the forecast before heading out.

title: Red Mountain
contentHtml:
Red Mountain is the highest point in Baker County. At about 9,555 feet it is the 14th highest peak in Oregon, rising in the southern Wallowa Mountains inside the Eagle Cap Wilderness of the Wallowa-Whitman National Forest.

There is no maintained trail to the top. Climbers usually leave the Cliff Creek Trail in the meadows south of Crater Lake and follow one of the tree lines up toward the summit ridge, crossing 800 to 1,000 feet of scree. From the ridge it is an easy walk to the summit, with wide views over Truax Mountain, Crater Lake and Krag Peak. A summit register waits at the top.

title: Elkhorn Crest National Recreation Trail
contentHtml:
The Elkhorn Crest National Recreation Trail runs 23 miles along the spine of the Elkhorn Mountains from Anthony Lake to Marble Pass. It is the highest trail in the Blue Mountains, topping out above 8,000 feet in alpine and subalpine country.

Six lakes are visible from the crest, and five more can be reached by spur trails. Views stretch east over Baker Valley to the Wallowa Mountains and south and west across the Blue Mountains. The first 2 miles from Anthony Lake climb about 1,000 feet; after that the crest is easy going. Deer, elk, mountain goats and birds of prey are often seen.

title: National Historic Oregon Trail Interpretive Center Trails
imageAlt: Covered wagon among sagebrush with distant mountains at sunset

banner.alt: Covered wagon among sagebrush with distant mountains at sunset

contentHtml:
About 2 miles of paved, accessible trails leave the back patio of the National Historic Oregon Trail Interpretive Center on Flagstaff Hill, near Baker City. The easy half-mile Flagstaff Hill Loop circles the hilltop, and the Panorama Point Trail, about three-quarters of a mile, passes a lode mine and stamp mill on the way to wide views of the Baker Valley and the Elkhorn Mountains.

Another 1.6 miles of dirt trails lead down to original Oregon Trail wagon ruts, still visible in the sagebrush. Interpretive signs along the way explain the pioneers' journey and the area's mining history.

contentHtml:
Big Huckleberry is a 48-mile gravel loop near Baker City that climbs about 5,000 feet through remote northeast Oregon backcountry. The route is about 80% gravel, 15% single-track and 5% pavement, and is rated demanding.

There are no services along the way, so carry everything you need. Wide tires of 45mm or more are recommended. It is listed as a development route that has not yet been fully ridden and vetted by the route builders.

contentHtml:
The Dooley Mountain Climb is a 17-mile loop, half gravel and half paved, that follows the old Dooley Mountain Road used by gold miners in the late 1800s. It gains about 2,300 feet in 5.5 miles, averaging just over 8%.

Much of the ride passes through forest burned in the 2015 Cornet-Windy Ridge Fire, the largest in Baker County history, where about 1.4 million seedlings have since been planted. Views take in the Elkhorn, Burnt River and Wallowa mountains, and the return is a paved descent with light traffic.

title: Grande Tour Scenic Bikeway
imageAlt: Cyclists on a mountain road beside a river

banner.alt: Cyclists on a mountain road beside a river

contentHtml:
The Grande Tour Scenic Bikeway is a challenging 134-mile figure-eight ride on paved roads, starting and finishing in La Grande and passing through Union, Baker City and North Powder. It follows part of the historic Oregon Trail, with Baker City at the halfway point offering lodging, food, bike shops and a local brew.

Riders take in the Elkhorn Range, the Blue Mountains and the Eagle Caps of the Wallowas, and may see elk, bald eagles and pronghorn. Roads are wide with little traffic, and the route can be split into shorter sections. Catherine Creek and Hilgard Junction state parks offer camping along the way.

title: Halfway to New Bridge
contentHtml:
Halfway to New Bridge is a 42-mile loop of gravel and pavement with about 4,300 feet of climbing. It opens with a paved climb up Richland Grade, drops into Halfway, a town that grew out of the 1860s gold rush, and rolls through the ranches and farms of Pine Valley.

The gravel section enters the Wallowa-Whitman National Forest and follows Ethel Creek and Eagle Creek past rock outcrops and ponderosa pine, then passes the old settlement of New Bridge on the way back to Richland. Cafes, a bar and grill and a grocery store in Richland and Halfway make good stops.

title: Hell of Hess
imageAlt: Snake River in Hells Canyon, along the route

banner.alt: Snake River in Hells Canyon, along the route

Oxbow Fish Hatchery, along the route

contentHtml:
Hell of Hess is a very demanding 46-mile loop with about 5,200 feet of climbing, mostly on pavement with a tough gravel climb up Hess Road: roughly 7 miles at an average near 10%, with pitches over 15%.

Along the way riders follow an old railway grade beside the Snake River, past old train tunnels and the Oxbow fish hatchery, with Hells Canyon, North America's deepest river gorge, close by. A paved side trip leads to the Hells Canyon Overlook, and the ride finishes with a fast descent along North Pine Creek.

imageAlt: Riders leading out on the route

banner.alt: Riders leading out on the route

contentHtml:
Keating with Love & Virtue is a 46-mile gravel loop with about 2,700 feet of climbing, starting at the Oregon Trail Interpretive Center. It passes the Virtue Mine district, where gold and silver were mined in the late 1800s and early 1900s, then rolls through the farming and ranching valley of Keating.

Highlights include Love Reservoir, built around 1900 for irrigation, and big views of the Wallowa Mountains, the Alps of Oregon. The longest climb is about 4 miles and 900 feet. Water and flush toilets are available at the start.

imageAlt: Riders leading out on the route

contentHtml:
Keating with Love is a moderate 30-mile gravel loop with about 1,800 feet of climbing through the farm and ranch country around Keating, with rolling hills and views of the Wallowa Mountains. It crosses the Powder River twice and passes the Widman Access Area and Love Reservoir, built around 1900 for irrigation.

The middle section is the toughest, with exposed ground, loose river rock and a 4-mile, 900-foot climb, before a 6-mile downhill on hard-packed road through the short canyon at Ruckles Creek. The Oregon Trail Interpretive Center is about 7 miles from the start.

contentHtml:
The Oxbow ride is an easy 18-mile out-and-back, mostly gravel, along an old railroad grade beside the Snake River in Hells Canyon, North America's deepest river gorge. Because it follows the rail grade, it stays nearly level the whole way.

The route passes the site of Copperfield, a rough 1890s boomtown that was put under martial law in 1914, along with the Oxbow Dam and fish hatchery. The ghost town of Homestead lies about 4 miles north of Oxbow. Restrooms and picnic tables are at the Copper Creek Trailhead, about 9 miles in.

title: Sparta
contentHtml:
The Sparta loop is a moderate 35-mile ride, about 60% gravel, with 2,900 feet of climbing. It runs past the remains of the 1984 Hole in the Wall landslide on the Powder River and outcrops of Columbia River basalt, with views of the granite Wallowa Mountains.

Sparta was a late-1800s gold mining town with a large Chinese community, and its 1872 general store still stands. The route also passes the 32-mile Sparta Ditch, hand-dug largely by Chinese laborers, and the old trading post of New Bridge. Richland, about halfway, has a cafe, a bar and a grocery.

title: The Dirty Eagle

gallery.alt: Two-state view of Oregon and Idaho peaks

contentHtml:
The Dirty Eagle is a 51-mile, almost all-gravel loop with about 5,700 feet of climbing, which can be split into a two-day bikepacking trip with a night at Eagle Forks Campground. It passes the old gold town of Sparta, founded in the early 1870s, its 1872 general store, and the 1878 settlement of New Bridge.

Riders follow Eagle Creek into remote national forest, with two-state views of Oregon and Idaho peaks and the Elkhorn Mountains. Part of the route crosses the area burned in the 2024 Town Gulch Fire. Expect open cattle range and plenty of sun exposure.

title: The Dredge

gallery.alt: Gravel road on The Dredge route

contentHtml:
The Dredge is a very demanding 48-mile loop of gravel and pavement with about 4,000 feet of climbing, starting at the Sumpter Valley Dredge, where there are restrooms and water. A 32-mile shortcut is also available.

The route climbs Sawmill Gulch on a winding road, passes the 1908 Fremont Powerhouse, once fed by an eight-mile pipeline from Olive Lake, and reaches the ghost town of Granite, which has a general store and lodge. Along Bull Run Creek, active mining claims and old settling ponds show the area's gold-mining past.

title: Tony!
contentHtml:
Tony! is a 40-mile loop, about two-thirds gravel, with 4,300 feet of climbing, starting from the Elkhorn Wildlife Area, where elk herds are often seen. It climbs Tucker Flat through open grassland, then about 2,500 feet through forest, with one pitch reaching 15%.

Highlights include a viewpoint at mile 17.5 and a short spur to Grande Ronde Lake, the source of the Grande Ronde River, followed by an 11-mile paved descent of the Anthony Lakes Highway that drops about 3,600 feet. The finish runs on flat gravel past ranches and farms.

title: Wallowas Tour
contentHtml:
The Wallowas Tour is a 300-mile, five-day bikepacking loop from Baker City around the Wallowa Mountains, sometimes called the Alps of Oregon, with about 21,000 feet of climbing on a mix of pavement and gravel. Overnights are at campgrounds, with meals in towns along the way.

The route passes the old gold town of Sparta, crosses the Zumwalt Prairie, a Nez Perce homeland, and tackles Old Imnaha Road with about 8 miles of steep grades. Stops include Richland, Halfway, Imnaha, Enterprise, Wallowa, Cove and Union. Several gravel sections have no cell service.

title: Washington Gulch
contentHtml:
Washington Gulch is a moderate 25-mile loop from Baker City with about 2,100 feet of climbing, 60% gravel. It follows the historic Washington Gulch Road, which around 1865 linked Baker City with the gold-mining boomtown of Auburn.

The ride crosses rolling farmland at each end, with a steeper, rougher stretch of national forest road in the middle. Near mile 13 a high point by an old water tank gives views of the Wallowa Mountains. It starts at the 1926 Churchill School, now an arts hub and bike hostel.

title: Whiskey & Gold 20
contentHtml:
Whiskey & Gold 20 is an easy 19-mile loop from Haines, half gravel and half pavement, with only 750 feet of climbing across flat farmland and views of the Wallowa and Elkhorn mountains. The name comes from a 1980 Haines mayor's joke: "We've got whiskey in our water and gold in our streets."

The ride passes Wingville Cemetery, started in 1878, Kerns Rainbow Ranch, and Rock Creek Cemetery near a town wiped out by a 1917 dam failure. Back in Haines, the Eastern Oregon Museum is worth a stop. Restrooms are at the start.

Whiskey & Gold 40 is an easy 40-mile loop from Haines, about 40% gravel, with roughly 1,100 feet of climbing across flat farmland framed by the Elkhorn Mountains. It passes three historic cemeteries: Wingville, Rock Creek and Haines.

title: Eagle Creek (Wallowa-Whitman National Forest)
contentHtml:
Eagle Creek was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, from below Eagle Lake to the Wallowa-Whitman National Forest boundary at Skull Creek. It begins in a glacial cirque in the Eagle Cap Wilderness and tumbles through waterfalls and rapids, a U-shaped glacial valley, a narrow canyon with towering rock formations, and finally basalt plateaus with ponderosa pine and deep pools.

The creek is known for excellent trout fishing and native bull trout, and for its gold rush history, including the Sparta Ditch. The oldest vertebrate fossil found in Oregon came from this corridor. Visitors come year-round for fishing, hunting, camping, hiking, gold panning and winter sports, and Eagle Forks Campground is a popular access point.

title: North Fork Malheur River
contentHtml:
The North Fork Malheur River was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 25.5 scenic miles from its headwaters to the Malheur National Forest boundary. It links the Blue Mountains with the Great Basin, flowing through a broad, glacially carved valley in the north and a canyon 250 to 750 feet deep in the south, past columnar basalt, talus slopes and large old ponderosa pines.

The river is an important fishery for native redband trout, bull trout and mountain whitefish. Elk, mule deer, black bear, osprey and bald eagles live along the corridor. Camping, fishing, hiking and hunting are popular, with North Fork Malheur Campground and Trail 381 as the main access.

title: North Powder River
contentHtml:
The North Powder River starts high on Elkhorn Ridge at nearly 7,900 feet, fed by Meadow, Little Summit and Summit lakes. Its upper 6.4 miles, from the headwaters to the Wallowa-Whitman National Forest boundary, were designated a scenic Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988.

The corridor has jagged peaks, cirque basins, subalpine lakes and glaciated valleys with almost no sign of development. It lies within the ceded lands of the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation, and a primitive road beside the river follows an 1864 wagon route to early mining camps. Visitors come for hunting, fishing, camping, hiking, backpacking, horseback riding and mountain biking. The river is too small for boating.

title: Powder River
contentHtml:
An 11.7-mile stretch of the Powder River, from Thief Valley Dam to the Highway 203 bridge, was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988. Here the river cuts a steep-walled canyon up to about 500 feet deep, with bunchgrass and sage hillsides above a green riverside corridor.

The river holds native rainbow trout that can grow to record size, along with catfish and crappie. Mule deer, river otters, chukars and rattlesnakes live in the canyon, golden eagles and prairie falcons nest on the cliffs, and bald eagles visit in winter. Fishing, hunting and sightseeing are the main activities. Kayaking is possible only during spring runoff, and only for highly skilled paddlers.

title: Elkhorn Drive Scenic Byway
imageAlt: North Fork John Day River along the Elkhorn Drive

banner.alt: North Fork John Day River along the Elkhorn Drive

gallery.alt: Chandler Cabin near Haines, the first building in Baker County

contentHtml:
The Elkhorn Drive Scenic Byway is a 106-mile loop through the Elkhorn Mountains that starts and ends in Baker City, taking about 3 to 5 hours to drive. It follows the Powder River past Phillips Lake to Sumpter, with its 1935 gold dredge and narrow-gauge Sumpter Valley Railroad, then climbs over Blue Springs Summit to the old gold town of Granite.

From Granite the byway heads north to Elkhorn Summit at 7,392 feet, the highest point on the loop, then drops past Anthony Lake and Grande Ronde Lake into the Baker Valley and the town of Haines, home of the Eastern Oregon Museum. Fill up with gas in Granite: there are no services from there until Baker City.

title: Hells Canyon Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Hells Canyon Scenic Byway route map

contentHtml:
The Hells Canyon Scenic Byway, an All-American Road, is a 218-mile loop around the Wallowa Mountains that meets Interstate 84 at Baker City and La Grande. From Baker City it follows Highway 86 east through Richland, Halfway, Pine and Copperfield to the Snake River at the southern end of Hells Canyon, North America's deepest gorge.

A spur leads to the Hells Canyon Overlook at 5,400 feet. The byway then runs north on Forest Road 39 to Joseph and Wallowa Lake, and west through Enterprise, Wallowa and Elgin to La Grande. Allow 8 to 10 hours, or better, several days. Some stretches run more than 80 miles without services, so refuel whenever you can.

title: Journey Through Time Scenic Byway
imageAlt: Painted Hills on the Journey Through Time Scenic Byway

banner.alt: Painted Hills on the Journey Through Time Scenic Byway

contentHtml:
The Journey Through Time Scenic Byway runs 286 miles from the Columbia River at Biggs to Baker City, tracing Oregon's story through fossil beds, ghost towns, mining camps and ranch country. It takes 8 to 10 hours to drive, and is open year-round.

Highlights include the old wool-shipping town of Shaniko, the Clarno, Painted Hills and Sheep Rock units of John Day Fossil Beds National Monument, the Wild and Scenic John Day River, Kam Wah Chung State Heritage Site in John Day, and the ghost town of Whitney. The byway joins the Elkhorn Drive at Sumpter and ends in Baker City, the "Queen City of the Mines."

title: Snake River–Mormon Basin Back Country Byway
imageAlt: Entering Public Lands sign along the byway

banner.alt: Entering Public Lands sign along the byway

gallery.alt: Pair of chukars crossing the byway

contentHtml:
The Snake River-Mormon Basin Back Country Byway is a 150-mile drive on paved, gravel and dirt roads through the ranch and canyon country of Baker and Malheur counties, between Baker City and Huntington. Allow at least five hours of driving, not counting stops; the route suits high-clearance two-wheel-drive vehicles.

It follows the Snake River above Brownlee Reservoir, past colorful basalt cliffs and spring wildflowers, then climbs into Mormon Basin, where gold diggings, homesteads and old mines date from the 1860s. Along the way are fishing and boating on Brownlee Reservoir, the Spring Recreation Site near Huntington, and stories of outlaws, moonshiners and counterfeiters. Services are sparse, so carry what you need.

note: No fee; take care after storms and in winter

title: Clear Creek
contentHtml:
Clear Creek Sno-Park sits beside Clear Creek in mature ponderosa pine forest at 3,720 feet, linking the south end of the Wallowa Mountains with Hells Canyon National Recreation Area. It is a hub for about 87 miles of groomed snowmobile trails, kept up with local clubs, and 19 miles of ungroomed cross-country ski trails on six loops from easy to most difficult.

Facilities include two vault toilets, a three-sided log shelter with picnic tables and a loop parking area for RVs and trailers. There is no drinking water. Wilderness areas are closed to snowmobiles. From Halfway, take Main Street north to Fish Lake Road, turn right for 3.3 miles, then left on Clear Creek Road for 3.1 miles.

contentHtml:
Anthony Lakes Mountain Resort is a nonprofit, family-friendly ski area in the Elkhorn Mountains, with Oregon's highest ski-area base elevation at 7,100 feet and a reputation for some of the best powder in the Northwest. One triple chairlift serves 21 runs.

Beyond downhill skiing, the resort offers Nordic trails, guided cat-skiing, a ski school, rentals and overnight yurts. In summer, visitors come for mountain biking, yurt stays and camping at the nearby Anthony Lakes and Union Creek recreation areas, and the Starbottle restaurant is open in the lodge.

title: Armstrong Nugget

gallery.alt: Baker Heritage Museum sign in front of the brick Natatorium building

contentHtml:
The Armstrong Nugget is the largest gold nugget ever found in Oregon that still exists. George Armstrong and Dick Stewart pulled the fist-sized, 80.4-troy-ounce nugget from Buck Gulch near Susanville, in Grant County, on June 19, 1913. Larger Oregon nuggets were melted down, but this one survived.

For decades the nugget sat in the gold display at the U.S. Bank branch on Main Street. The bank donated the whole display to Baker County in 2023, and since July 2025 the nugget has been the centerpiece of "Echoes of the Rush: Relics of Eastern Oregon's Golden Age" at the Baker Heritage Museum, alongside about 1,000 ounces of gold flakes and small nuggets.

note: On display at the Baker Heritage Museum

Anthony Lakes Mountain Resort is a stop on the Historic Oregon Film Trail for Paint Your Wagon (1969), the musical western starring Lee Marvin, Clint Eastwood and Jean Seberg that was filmed in the mountains of Baker County in 1968.

Inside the resort lodge is the Starbottle Saloon, named for "Starbottle's Hotel," the prop building raised nearby when the film crew worked in the Elkhorn Mountains. The resort itself sits at 7,100 feet, Oregon's highest ski-area base, with skiing in winter and mountain biking and camping in summer.

contentHtml:
Baker Heritage Museum is a stop on the Historic Oregon Film Trail for Paint Your Wagon (1969). Baker City was the production's base during filming in 1968, when Paramount brought about 400 cast and crew to town and hired hundreds of local residents as extras.

The museum displays Paramount's large-scale model of the film's "No Name City" set, along with costumes, props and photographs from the shoot. The full-size set was built on Eagle Creek, in a remote valley about 42 miles northeast of Baker City. The museum's other exhibits cover Baker County's mining, timber and ranching history.

contentHtml:
The Historic Oregon Film Trail marker for Paint Your Wagon (1969) is mounted on the north wall of the Geiser Grand Hotel in downtown Baker City. It honors the film and the many Baker County residents who crewed and appeared in it when it was shot in the county's mountains in 1968.

The hotel itself opened in 1889 and was known in the gold rush days as "the Queen of the Mines." The Italianate Victorian building closed in 1968, was restored and reopened in 1993, and is part of the Baker Historic District on the National Register of Historic Places.

Richland's Historic Oregon Film Trail marker honors Paint Your Wagon (1969), the musical western starring Lee Marvin, Clint Eastwood and Jean Seberg. Its "No Name City" set rose on Eagle Creek in the Wallowa Mountains northeast of town, where filming ran from June to December 1968.

Hundreds of local people were hired as extras to play miners, camping on the set and earning $20 a day. The marker stands at Richland City Hall and is slated to move to the town's future playground.

title: Sumpter Valley Railroad
contentHtml:
The Sumpter Valley Railroad is Oregon's only narrow-gauge, steam-powered railroad. Trains run between the McEwen depot, 23 miles southwest of Baker City on Highway 7, and the Sumpter station at 211 Austin Street, on the edge of the Sumpter Valley Dredge State Heritage Area, 5.5 miles away.

Most trips leaving McEwen are round trips through the Sumpter Valley, past the tailings left by gold dredging. The McEwen site also has the railroad's yards and back shops and the Baker County Day Park. During moderate to high fire danger, a diesel locomotive may pull the train instead of steam.

Barley Brown's is a family-owned brewery and restaurant in downtown Baker City, serving pub food and small-batch, hand-crafted beers. Founded in 1998, it is best known for its flagship Pallet Jack IPA.

contentHtml:
North Seven Brewing is a small, family-run neighborhood brewery and taproom in downtown Baker City, opened in 2021. Its seven taps focus on balanced, approachable ales and lagers, and its beer is sold only at the taproom.

Wine, cider and non-alcoholic drinks are also on offer, with snacks like hot soft pretzels and chips with nacho cheese. The taproom is family friendly, and guests are welcome to bring in pizza or takeout from local restaurants.

title: Copper Belt Wines
contentHtml:
Copper Belt Wines is Baker County's only winery, a Cook family operation founded in 2010 with winemaker Travis Cook. Its grapes grow at high elevation in the Snake River Valley AVA, on land the family homesteaded in the 1890s in the Keating Valley east of Baker City, where Travis planted the first vines in 2004.

The downtown tasting room sits across from the Geiser Grand Hotel and shares space with The Cheese Fairy cheese shop. Wines include Merlot, Syrah and Riesling, along with a Pinot Noir from the Willamette Valley.

title: Baker Sports Complex
contentHtml:
The Baker Sports Complex disc golf course is a free, 9-hole course in Baker City, established in 2020. It plays at par 27 over about 2,700 feet, with rubber tees and home-made targets.

The course is flat with few obstacles, which makes it a good place to learn the game or play with friends. It is cart, stroller and wheelchair friendly, and dogs are allowed. There are no restrooms or drinking water on the course.

title: Corvallis Museum
contentHtml:
The Corvallis Museum is the flagship of the Benton County Historical Society. It opened in 2021 in downtown Corvallis, a short walk from Riverfront Park, shops and restaurants.

Permanent exhibits trace the history of Benton County and Oregon State University, alongside changing exhibitions drawn from the society's collections. The Konick Family Museum Store is on site.

title: Philomath Museum

The Philomath Museum is the Benton County Historical Society's original museum, open since 1980 inside the 1867 Philomath College building, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

The museum sits on Main Street in Philomath, five miles west of Corvallis, and hosts regional history exhibits that change through the year.

title: Siuslaw National Forest
contentHtml:
The Siuslaw National Forest covers more than 630,000 acres of the Oregon coast and Coast Range, and is one of only two national forests in the lower 48 states with oceanfront land. Its landscapes run from mossy coastal mountain forests to sand dunes and Pacific beaches.

Highlights include Cape Perpetua Scenic Area with its rocky headlands, Cascade Head with native prairie and rare wildflowers, the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, and Marys Peak, the highest point in the Coast Range, just west of Corvallis. Visitors come for old-growth forest, waterfalls, camping and off-highway vehicle riding on the dunes.

contentHtml:
Alsea Falls Recreation Site sits in the Oregon Coast Range along the South Fork Alsea River Back Country Byway, where the South Fork of the Alsea River drops about 30 feet over rocks to form Alsea Falls. Trails link the falls, the picnic grounds and the river, which offers a cool place to wade on warm days.

The campground has 16 reservable sites, some fitting RVs and trailers up to 32 feet, with drinking water and vault toilets. In winter, anglers fish the South Fork for salmon and steelhead. There is no cell reception in the drainage.

title: Marys Peak Campground
contentHtml:
Marys Peak Campground is a small, first-come, first-served campground near the top of Marys Peak, the highest peak in the Oregon Coast Range. Sites sit among Douglas fir, noble fir and western red cedar, a short drive from the day-use area and its views from the Cascades to the Pacific.

Each site has a picnic table and fire ring, with vault toilets but no drinking water. The Meadowedge Trail starts nearby. Camping is allowed only in the campground, since the peak is a protected Scenic Botanical Special Interest Area.

title: William L. Finley
imageAlt: McFadden Marsh at William L. Finley NWR

Black bear in a grove of Oregon white oak

contentHtml:
William L. Finley National Wildlife Refuge lies about ten miles south of Corvallis. It was established in 1964 to give wintering habitat to dusky Canada geese, and it protects the largest remaining tract of native Willamette Valley wet prairie along with oak savanna, bottomland forest, marshes and seasonal wetlands.

More than 260 bird species have been recorded here, and the refuge is home to Roosevelt elk, black-tailed deer, black bear, beaver and river otter, plus six threatened or endangered species including Fender's blue butterfly and Kincaid's lupine.

Over 12 miles of trails include the Woodpecker Loop, the Mill Hill loop and the Homer Campbell Memorial Boardwalk to an observation blind. The boardwalk starts by the historic 1855 Fiechter House, the oldest building in Benton County.

contentHtml:
E.E. Wilson Wildlife Area covers about 1,788 acres of the Willamette Valley floor, 10 miles north of Corvallis on the site of the World War II training base Camp Adair. A grid of old paved and gravel roads, reached from five parking lots on Camp Adair Road, makes it easy to explore on foot, by bike or on horseback.

It is popular for bird-watching from April to August, and has a stocked fishing pond open year-round, an archery park, an accessible shotgun range and a memorial garden honoring the four divisions that trained here. Hunting is shotgun and archery only.

contentHtml:
Green Peak Falls is a 45-foot waterfall where Peak Creek slides down a mossy rock wall into a small pool framed by tall maples. It sits in the Alsea River watershed, just upstream from Alsea Falls.

An easy, maintained trail of about half a mile leads from the signed Green Peak Falls parking lot in Hubert K. McBee Memorial Park, along and above the creek, to the base of the falls. In high water, getting a full view may mean getting wet.

title: Corvallis to Albany
imageAlt: Michael's Landing on the Willamette River, Corvallis

banner.alt: Michael's Landing on the Willamette River, Corvallis

gallery.alt: Kayaking the Willamette River near Corvallis

contentHtml:
This 9.5-mile point-to-point paddle on the Willamette River runs from Michael's Landing, next to downtown Corvallis, down to Hyak County Park near Albany. Expect about 3 hours 45 minutes of paddling at summer water levels.

The river makes broad bends between wooded banks and gravel bars, and motorboats are rare. Watch for strainers (downed trees), arrange a shuttle between the launch and take-out, and note that the Hyak take-out is not suitable in high water.

Paddle craft 10 feet and longer need an Oregon State Marine Board Waterway Access Permit, and children 12 and under must wear a life jacket while under way.

title: Marys Peak

gallery.alt: Noble fir forest on Marys Peak

contentHtml:
At 4,097 feet, Marys Peak is the highest point in the Oregon Coast Range and Benton County's high point. On clear days the summit looks out over the Willamette Valley to Mt. Hood, Mt. Jefferson and Mt. St. Helens, and west to the Pacific Ocean.

The peak is a Scenic Botanical Area known for its summit wildflower meadows and its old-growth noble fir forest. It is sacred to the Kalapuya people, who call it chatímanwi.

From the day use area near the top, the Summit Trail is a short climb to the highest point. The North Ridge, East Ridge and Meadow Edge trails also start on the mountain.

contentHtml:
The Corvallis-to-the-Sea Trail (C2C) runs about 60 miles from downtown Corvallis, over the Coast Range, to Ona Beach on the Pacific. It is one of 15 Oregon Signature Trails and is open to hikers and cyclists.

Much of the route crosses public forest and private timberland. Hikers need a free permit for three sections, including a current-year Starker Forests permit, and should sign in at each of the 11 trail kiosks.

Camping is allowed only on U.S. Forest Service land, and campfires only in public campgrounds.

title: Alder & Iron
contentHtml:
Alder & Iron is a 17-mile out-and-back gravel ride with about 850 feet of climbing, roughly half gravel and half pavement. It is rated easier, rides almost year-round and starts at Fort Hoskins Historic Park.

The route follows the Luckiamute River through the ghost town of Hoskins and along Red Alder Alley, a shaded logging road, to a remnant of the Valley & Siletz Railroad grade (1912 to 1978). Fort Hoskins (1856 to 1865) and its Commander's Residence, one of only two surviving pre-Civil War military buildings in Oregon, are at the start.

Spring and fall are best; avoid it right after heavy rain. A shorter 14.5-mile option turns at the mile 7.2 bridge, and a 47-mile option continues to Valsetz.

title: C2C (Corvallis to Coast) Trail
contentHtml:
The C2C gravel route is a 65-mile point-to-point ride from the Benton County Fairgrounds in Corvallis to Newport on the coast, with about 5,700 feet of climbing on roughly 70% gravel. It is rated moderate, with challenging navigation through remote country.

It follows the Corvallis-to-the-Sea Trail, one of 15 Oregon Signature Trails, passing Starker Forests timberland, the flanks of Marys Peak and the Sugar Bowl Creek singletrack before dropping toward Yaquina Bay.

Free permits are required for the Starker Forests and Emery Investments sections. Big Elk Campground (about mile 33) is the only water stop, and the Northwest Connector bus can bring riders back from Newport.

contentHtml:
Tum Tum is a 39-mile loop from Corvallis with about 3,800 feet of climbing, mixing gravel, paved road and a little singletrack. It is rated moderate and is one of Dirty Freehub's five-star premier routes.

Along the way riders cross the Marys River, pass Cardwell Hill Cellars and the Harris Covered Bridge, climb about five miles up Tum Tum, and ride part of the Corvallis-to-the-Sea Trail before refueling in Philomath. Tumtum is a Chinook Jargon word for the heart, the will and the mind.

A Starker Forests permit is required. The Mulkey Ridge section is closed to bikes from October 31 to April 15, when the Cardwell Hill Wagon Road option is used instead.

title: Marys Peak to Pacific Scenic Byway

contentHtml:
The Marys Peak to Pacific Scenic Byway is a 72-mile Oregon State Scenic Byway from the farmland near Tangent, through Corvallis and Philomath, over the Coast Range on OR-34 and down the Alsea River valley to Waldport on the coast. Allow 3 to 5 hours.

Stops include William L. Finley National Wildlife Refuge, the Philomath Museum in its 1867 college building, Marys Peak (4,097 ft), Alsea Falls, the Hayden Covered Bridge, the Oregon Hatchery Research Center, the Alsea Bay estuary and Seal Rock State Recreation Site.

contentHtml:
The Mid-Willamette Valley Food Trail is a self-guided route through more than 50 farms, eateries, bakeries, farmers markets, wineries, breweries and distilleries in Albany, Corvallis, Philomath, Lebanon, Sweet Home, Brownsville, Monroe and Alsea.

It is arranged as four themed routes: Family Fun For All, A Taster's Tour, Makers and Innovators, and Flora and Fauna. Stops include Lumos Wine Co., Thompson's Mills State Heritage Site, the Alsea Trout Hatchery, Sky High Brewing and Midway Farms, a celiac-safe farm with a red-barn farm market.

A free Digital Passport offers deals and free tastings at selected stops.

The South Willamette Valley Food Trail is a self-guided journey of 53 stops through Oregon's agricultural heartland: bakeries, restaurants, farms, growers markets, breweries, wineries and food-focused lodges.

It centers on Eugene and Springfield and reaches Veneta, Junction City, Coburg, Creswell, Cottage Grove, the McKenzie River and Oakridge, with stops across the county line in Monroe (Benton County) and Harrisburg (Linn County).

Highlights include King Estate Winery, North America's largest Demeter-certified Biodynamic vineyard, Alesong Brewing & Blending, the Lane County Farmers Market and seasonal berry, lavender, apple and truffle harvests.

contentHtml:
The South Fork Alsea River Back Country Byway is an 11-mile paved and gravel route between Alsea and Alpine, the shortest Back Country Byway in Oregon and a designated BLM National Back Country Byway.

Its signature stop is Alsea Falls, where the South Fork of the Alsea River drops about 30 feet beside the road. Trails lead from the falls to the picnic grounds and on to 45-foot Green Peak Falls, and old-growth Douglas fir and western red cedar line the nearby ridges.

The Fall Creek trailhead nearby has more than 12 miles of mountain bike trails. There is no cell reception in the drainage.

title: Harris Covered Bridge
imageAlt: Harris Covered Bridge over the Marys River

banner.alt: Harris Covered Bridge over the Marys River

contentHtml:
The Harris Covered Bridge carries Harris Road over the Marys River near Wren. Benton County records date the 75-foot Howe truss bridge to 1936, though some locals say it may date to 1929. H. W. Fiedler built it to replace an earlier covered bridge on the same site.

It has rounded portals, narrow daylighting windows below the roofline, board-and-batten siding and a shingled roof. Several wineries are nearby, and the bridge is a highlight of the Tum Tum gravel ride.

title: Hayden Covered Bridge
imageAlt: Hayden Covered Bridge over the Alsea River

banner.alt: Hayden Covered Bridge over the Alsea River

contentHtml:
Built in 1918, the 91-foot Hayden Covered Bridge crosses the Alsea River just west of Alsea. It is one of only seven Oregon covered bridges built before 1920 still standing.

It was partly rebuilt in 1945, when its rounded portals were enlarged for heavier loads. The Howe truss bridge has board-and-batten siding that flares at the base and daylighting windows along both sides. It is the last of several covered bridges that once crossed the Alsea River and its tributaries.

title: Irish Bend Covered Bridge

contentHtml:
The Irish Bend Covered Bridge was built in 1954 to carry Irish Bend Road over a Willamette River slough near Monroe. It was dismantled in 1988 and rebuilt on Oregon State University land, where it now crosses Oak Creek on the Campus Way bike and pedestrian path.

The 60-foot Howe truss bridge is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is maintained by Benton County Parks. It is an easy walk or ride from the Benton County Fairgrounds parking area on 53rd Street.

title: Graand Kinetic Challenge
imageAlt: Graand Kinetic racer at da Vinci Days

banner.alt: Graand Kinetic racer at da Vinci Days

contentHtml:
The Graand Kinetic Challenge is Oregon's longest-running kinetic sculpture race. Since 1993, human-powered art machines have raced over 20-plus miles of Corvallis streets, across a man-made sand dune, through about 200 feet of mud and 1.6 miles down the Willamette River, all under their own pedal power.

Raan Young founded the race as part of the da Vinci Days festival; the 'Graand' spelling, adopted in 2008, honors his name. Teams compete for prizes in speed, engineering, art and pageantry, and every team that finishes under its own power earns the Leo medallion.

Saturday opens with pageantry and the race start, then the Sand Dune Challenge at the Benton County Fairgrounds. Sunday brings the Mud Bog Challenge at Crystal Lake Park, the river leg and the finish downtown. The event is free for spectators.

contentHtml:
Founded in 1987 by Jerry and Nancy Shadomy, Oregon Trail Brewery is one of the pioneering Oregon craft breweries. It brews in a three-story, gravity-fed brewhouse inside the historic Old World Center, which also holds the Old World Deli and a live music venue.

The brewery still uses one of the oldest brew kettles in service, bought from Hart Brewing. Dave Wills ran it from 1993, and since 2021 it has been owned by the Pickett family. Flagships include a Wit, an IPA, Mosaic Red and Ginseng Porter.

Lumos Wine Co. is a family winery founded in 2000, now two generations making wine from a three- generation vineyard. All of its grapes come from certified organic vineyards, and the winemaking is natural and minimal-intervention.

The tasting room is a 1938 barn on the family farm at Wren, about 16 miles west of Corvallis, once part of the H Bar H Dude Ranch. It looks over the 15-acre Wren Vineyard (Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Chardonnay, planted 1985) toward Marys Peak. An original guest cabin above the vineyard is available as an overnight rental.

The vineyard has no tasting room or website of its own. Its fruit is bottled by Compton Family Wines as a vineyard-designate Mary's Peak Vineyard Pinot Noir.

contentHtml:
Adair Park is an 18-hole disc golf course established in 2001, with a main layout of 5,312 feet and par 54. The hilly course mixes open shots and wooded holes, and several holes have par 4 options.

Tees are concrete, gravel and turf, with DISCatcher Pro and Mach New II baskets. From about December 1 to March a winter layout avoids the old oak grove on the west side of the park. Dogs are allowed and a restroom is available, but there is no drinking water.

contentHtml:
The Museum of the Oregon Territory is the Clackamas County Historical Society's main history museum. It sits on the second floor of the Wallace B. Caufield Memorial Building on Highway 99E, overlooking Willamette Falls.

Exhibits trace the falls from their geological origins, through the Native peoples who traded here for thousands of years, to the hydropower that lit Portland. Highlights include petroglyphs and Columbia River basketry, a full-size farm wagon, the last surviving copy of the original 1850 plat map of San Francisco, the PGE power-station gallery and the antique Kaegi Pharmacy.

The newest permanent exhibit, Land & People of the Willamette Valley, opened in 2025. The museum is wheelchair accessible by elevator.

title: Stevens-Crawford Heritage House
contentHtml:
The Stevens-Crawford Heritage House is an American Foursquare home built in 1908 by Mary Elizabeth Crawford Stevens, who lived here with her husband Harley and their daughter Mertie. The family was active in Oregon City real estate, and the house stayed in the family until Mertie bequeathed it to the Clackamas County Historical Society in 1968.

Restored with period furnishings, its three stories hold 15 furnished rooms, including the dining room, kitchen, office, sewing room and nursery, along with a large toy collection and rotating seasonal displays. It is Clackamas County's only Edwardian house museum, and guided tours are offered.

contentHtml:
The End of the Oregon Trail Interpretive Center stands at the official end of the Oregon Trail in Oregon City, marked by three 50-foot wagon frames. It is run by a nonprofit that preserves and interprets Oregon Trail, Clackamas County and Oregon City history.

Admission includes costumed interpreters, historic artifacts and wagons, a research room, a theater and hands-on activities such as candle dipping and doll making. The center reopened in July 2022 with the film Oregon's First People, made with the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde.

The Miniature Overland Trail, the pioneer garden, outdoor displays and Abernathy Green park are free to visit.

contentHtml:
The Mt. Hood Cultural Center & Museum is the mountain's own award-winning museum in Government Camp, and it doubles as the Mt. Hood visitor information center.

Its galleries cover the Barlow Road, Western ski heritage and the natural and human history of Mount Hood, with a 3-D model of the mountain. The museum also cares for the historic Steiner Cabins.

title: Philip Foster Farm
contentHtml:
Philip Foster Farm is a living-history museum on Philip Foster's original donation land claim at Eagle Creek, right on the Barlow Road section of the Oregon Trail. It is kept by the Jacknife-Zion-Horseheaven Historical Society.

Guided tours visit the 1883 farmhouse, the 1860s barn and the blacksmith shop, and the country store is a replica of Foster's original, stocked with goods from the 1800s to the early 1900s. The Fall Cider Squeeze is the farm's signature event.

title: Fort Vancouver National Historic Site — McLoughlin House Unit

gallery.alt: Side view of the McLoughlin House

contentHtml:
The McLoughlin House is the Oregon City unit of Fort Vancouver National Historic Site. It was the retirement home of Dr. John McLoughlin (1784-1857), Chief Factor of the Hudson's Bay Company at Fort Vancouver, who extended credit to struggling Oregon Trail emigrants and lost his post for it.

McLoughlin and his wife settled here in 1846. He became a U.S. citizen in 1851, founded Oregon City and donated land for schools and churches, and in 1957 the Oregon legislature named him the Father of Oregon.

The house opened as a museum in 1910 and is restored to tell his story. Free guided tours of about an hour start next door at the historic Barclay House.

title: Mount Hood National Forest
contentHtml:
Mt. Hood National Forest covers about 1.1 million acres just 50 miles east of Portland, stretching more than 60 miles south from the Columbia River Gorge to the Olallie Scenic Area near Mt. Jefferson.

It has about 80 campgrounds, 20 sno-parks, part of the Pacific Crest Trail and several ski areas, including historic Timberline Lodge. About a third of the forest is designated wilderness, and the forest supplies about a third of Oregon's drinking and irrigation water.

The forest is managed through four ranger districts: Barlow, Clackamas River, Hood River and Zigzag.

title: Willamette National Forest

It holds eight wilderness areas and seven major volcanic peaks, and offers year-round hiking, backpacking, camping, fishing, waterfalls and skiing.

contentHtml:
Bull of the Woods Wilderness was designated by Congress in 1984 and enlarged in 2009. It is a remote, roadless basin of old-growth Douglas fir and western hemlock that feeds the Collawash, Breitenbush and Little North Santiam rivers, and it is home to the northern spotted owl.

About a dozen trout-filled lakes sit between high ridges, and a 68-mile trail system includes several loops. Bull of the Woods Peak (5,523 ft) has a historic fire lookout with views to Mt. Jefferson; the Pansy Lake Trail is an easy 1.2 miles to Pansy Lake, and the Hot Springs Trail leads 1.5 miles to Bagby Hot Springs.

Old mine shafts and equipment remain from early mining days. Twin Lakes and Elk Lake are the most popular spots.

title: Clackamas Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Clackamas Wilderness was designated in 2009 and covers 9,470 acres in five separate roadless tracts spread over about 50 miles on both sides of the Clackamas River: Big Bottom, Clackamas Canyon, Memaloose Lake, Sisi Butte and South Fork Clackamas.

It protects some of the largest trees in northwest Oregon and clean drinking water for many Oregonians. The most popular hike climbs 1.4 miles through old growth to Memaloose Lake, then about a mile more to the viewpoint on South Fork Mountain.

title: Mount Hood Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mount Hood Wilderness was one of the original wildernesses designated in 1964 and now covers about 67,000 acres around Oregon's highest peak (11,249 ft). The dormant volcano carries 11 active glaciers above alpine meadows and old-growth forest, with more than a dozen waterfalls on its lower slopes.

The 38-mile Timberline Trail circles the mountain and links with more than 20 other trails. Unbridged glacial streams can be dangerous during snowmelt or heavy rain, so plan a backup route.

Most of the wilderness lies in Hood River and Clackamas counties; the area gets about 150 inches of precipitation a year, mostly as snow from October to April.

title: Opal Creek Wilderness
imageAlt: Opal Creek cascades through old-growth forest

banner.alt: Opal Creek cascades through old-growth forest

gallery.alt: Hiker on a forest trail at Opal Creek

contentHtml:
Opal Creek Wilderness protects 20,454 acres around the largest uncut watershed in Oregon. Congress designated it, with the adjoining Scenic Recreation Area, in 1996, after decades of mining ended and the land passed to conservation.

Battle Axe and Opal creeks join here to form the Little North Santiam River, flowing through ancient Douglas fir, western hemlock and western red cedar. Jawbone Flats, a 1929 mining camp of about two dozen rustic buildings, is run by the Opal Creek Ancient Forest Center. Eight trails total 36 miles.

Much of the valley burned in the 2020 Beachie Creek Fire, and access has been limited since. Check current closures with the Detroit Ranger Station before you go.

title: Roaring River Wilderness
contentHtml:
Roaring River Wilderness was designated in 2009 and covers 36,550 acres, the largest block of new wilderness created in Oregon that year. It protects the roadless valley of the Roaring River, a tributary of the Clackamas River where salmon and steelhead spawn.

Black bear, cougar, mule deer, elk, spotted owls and pileated woodpeckers live here. Five trails, including Shining Lake, Serene Lake, Grouse Point and Dry Ridge, reach Rock Lakes, Serene Lake and alpine meadows such as Cache Meadow.

title: Salmon–Huckleberry Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Salmon-Huckleberry Wilderness was created by the 1984 Oregon Wilderness Act and enlarged in 2009 to about 61,000 acres. Its centerpiece is the Salmon River, the only river in the Lower 48 designated Wild and Scenic along its entire length, with runs of steelhead and chinook and coho salmon.

Dense forests of Douglas fir, western red cedar and hemlock fill the drainages, and volcanic plugs, pinnacles and cliffs line the ridges. About 70 miles of trail include the Salmon River National Recreation Trail and climbs to Salmon Butte (4,877 ft) and Wildcat Mountain.

Despite being close to Portland, much of the wilderness sees little use.

title: Table Rock Wilderness
contentHtml:
Table Rock Wilderness is an unusual BLM-managed wilderness of more than 5,700 acres in the western Cascade foothills, designated by Congress in 1984. Its namesake, Table Rock, is a columnar-basalt remnant of an ancient lava flow rising to 4,881 feet.

Steep slopes hold Douglas fir, western hemlock, noble fir and rhododendron, and two rare plants, Oregon sullivantia and Gorman's aster, bloom here. Deer and elk winter in the area.

Recent fires damaged parts of the trail system; trails start from the Old Bridge and Table Rock trailheads. Turn back if a trail becomes hard to follow.

title: Aquila Vista Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Aquila Vista is a forested, reservation-only group campsite beside a spring-fed wetland in the Molalla River corridor, good for birding, hiking and a small waterfall. It holds up to 20 people and 8 vehicles.

It has a vault toilet, two group picnic shelters and fire rings, and is close to the 20-plus-mile Molalla River Trail System for hikers, bikers and riders. There is no water, firewood or trash service. The site was closed by the 2020 Labor Day fires and reopened June 26, 2026.

title: Cedar Grove Campground
contentHtml:
Cedar Grove Campground has 10 walk-in tent sites in a grove of western red cedar along the Wild and Scenic Molalla River, with swimming, fishing, wildlife viewing and the nearby Hardy Creek Trailhead.

Each site has a tent pad, fire ring, grill and picnic table. There is a hand-pump water supply and vault toilets. Bring your own firewood; there is no cell service in the corridor.

title: Three Bears Campground
contentHtml:
Three Bears Campground has 15 tent sites in a grove of western red cedar on the Wild and Scenic Molalla River, with a cobble beach and swimming hole. Fishing, hiking and biking are close at hand, and the Hardy Creek Trailhead is nearest.

Each site has a tent pad, fire ring, grill and picnic table. Vault toilets are on site; drinking water is at Cedar Grove, about a mile east. Bring your own firewood.

title: Bonnie Lure State Recreation Area
contentHtml:
Bonnie Lure State Recreation Area is a quiet, off-the-beaten-path day-use park along Eagle Creek, close to Portland. Pileated woodpeckers live in the woods, and steelhead pass the park on their way back to the hatchery upstream.

The state bought the land from The Nature Conservancy in 1976 with help from the federal Land and Water Conservation Fund.

title: Milo McIver State Park
imageAlt: Clackamas River valley at Milo McIver

banner.alt: Clackamas River valley at Milo McIver

gallery.alt: Walking a dog under fall color

contentHtml:
Milo McIver State Park stretches along the Clackamas River near Estacada, with river, forest and meadow to explore. Rafting, canoeing, kayaking and fishing for steelhead and Chinook are popular, with a boat ramp and ADA fishing dock.

The park has a 27-hole disc golf course at the Riverbend day-use area, trails for hiking and horseback riding, and self-guided tours of the Clackamas Fish Hatchery.

The campground has 44 electrical sites, 9 tent sites, 3 group tent areas and hiker/biker sites, with hot showers, flush toilets and an RV dump station.

title: Molalla River State Park
contentHtml:
Molalla River State Park sits where the Willamette, Molalla and Pudding rivers meet, on floodplain habitat for waterfowl, wading birds and deer. It has one of the largest great blue heron rookeries in the Willamette Valley.

Visitors come for picnicking on grassy fields, fishing, boating from the ramp, hiking and wildlife watching, and there is a pet exercise area. The Canby Ferry crosses the Willamette a quarter mile downstream.

title: Alpine Campground
contentHtml:
Alpine Campground is the highest campground on Mt. Hood National Forest, near the headwaters of the Salmon River on the slopes of Mount Hood. Snow can linger into midsummer, so the season is short.

It is close to Timberline Lodge, Government Camp and hiking and mountain bike trails. Facilities include vault toilets and drinking water; vehicles are limited to 16 feet.

Armstrong Campground is a small campground on the edge of the Wild and Scenic Clackamas River, with roomy, family-friendly sites and easy river access for fishing, boating and hiking.

It was damaged in the 2020 Riverside Fire; watch for burned trees, eroded slopes and flash floods. Vault toilets and picnic tables; no drinking water.

title: Bagby Campground
contentHtml:
Bagby Campground sits beside the Hot Springs Fork of the Collawash River among cedar and old-growth Douglas fir, at the trailhead for Bagby Hot Springs and the Bull of the Woods Wilderness.

Sites have picnic tables and fire rings, with vault toilets and no drinking water. The hot springs are a 1.5-mile walk up the trail (separate $5 soaking pass).

title: Camp Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Camp Creek Campground is a shady, quiet campground on a bench above Camp Creek, among mature Douglas fir and cedar. It was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1936, and its stone fireplaces date from that era.

About 24 sites take tents and RVs, each with a table and fire ring with grill. Drinking water and accessible vault toilets are provided, and a dump station is nearby. Elevation is about 2,200 feet.

title: Carter Bridge Campground
contentHtml:
Carter Bridge Campground has about 15 sites along the Wild and Scenic Clackamas River. It was heavily damaged in the 2020 Riverside Fire, and recovery work is ongoing.

In 2026 it opens only after nearby Lockaby Campground, a quarter mile up the road, is full.

title: Clackamas Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Clackamas Lake Campground sits by a small, shallow lake near Timothy Lake, with fishing, swimming and non- motorized boating, plus trails and historic sites nearby. It is a good choice when Timothy Lake sites are full.

It has drinking water, vault toilets and horse corrals built by Oregon Equestrian Trails volunteers. Vehicles up to 32 feet.

title: Fish Creek Campground

Fish Creek Campground is a heavily forested campground beside the Wild and Scenic Clackamas River, known for steelhead and salmon fishing and whitewater rafting. Nearby trails follow the river.

It has vault toilets and no drinking water, and vehicles are limited to 16 feet.

Gone Creek Campground has 49 forested sites on the south shore of Timothy Lake, many overlooking the water, at 3,400 feet. It is popular for fishing, boating and the 12-mile trail around the lake.

Drinking water, vault toilets and barrier-free sites are provided.

Green Canyon Campground sits among old-growth trees in the canyon carved by the Wild and Scenic Salmon River, near Welches. Trails lead into the Salmon-Huckleberry Wilderness, and the river offers fishing.

Facilities include vault toilets and picnic tables; there is no drinking water, and vehicles are limited to 22 feet.

Hideaway Lake Campground is a primitive single-loop campground of about 10 sites above Hideaway Lake, at the edge of the Roaring River Wilderness. Sites sit well apart under Douglas fir, hemlock and rhododendron.

There is a vault toilet but no drinking water, and vehicles are limited to 16 feet. The road in is rough but drivable.

Indian Henry Campground sits along the Clackamas River in mixed conifer and hardwood forest, with ferns between sites; some sites overlook the river and others sit by a mountain creek.

Joe Graham Horse Campground is built for riders, with horse corrals and tie rails at each of its 13 sites at about 3,350 feet. Clackamas Lake is less than a mile away.

The 1-mile Joe Graham Trail connects to the Pacific Crest Trail. Hand-pump drinking water, vault toilets, picnic tables and fire rings are provided.

contentHtml:
Little Crater Lake Campground has about 15 sites in evergreen forest beside Little Crater Lake, a cold, spring- fed, turquoise pond. Swimming is not allowed, to protect the lake.

A short viewing trail leads to the lake and connects to the Pacific Crest Trail. Hand-pump water and accessible vault toilets are provided; RVs up to 26 feet.

Each site has a table and fire ring; drinking water and accessible vault toilets are provided.

title: Lost Creek Campground

Lost Creek Campground is a barrier-free campground in the Old Maid Flat area, on a volcanic mudflow from Mt. Hood's eruption in the 1700s, shaded by evergreens and moss. It has 10 standard sites, 4 walk-to sites and 2 yurts.

The paved, accessible Lost Creek Nature Trail explains the area's volcanic geology, and the Ramona Falls trailhead is nearby. Hand-pump water and vault toilets are provided.

Vault toilets are provided but there is no drinking water. Vehicles up to 22 feet.

Oak Fork Campground sits on the southeastern shore of Timothy Lake, a 1,400-acre reservoir at 3,400 feet. It has 36 standard sites, 6 rustic sleeping cabins and 8 hike-to tent sites.

A boat ramp, hand-pump water, vault toilets, picnic tables and fire rings are provided, and the 12-mile lake trail is nearby.

Raab Group Campground sits along the Collawash River in dense old-growth Douglas fir. It has 6 group sites only, each for 30 to 60 people, with picnic tables and fire rings with grills.

Vault toilets are provided but there is no drinking water, so bring your own. RVs and trailers up to 24 feet; the access road has tight turns.

Rainbow Campground has 16 tent sites on the Oak Grove Fork near the Wild and Scenic Clackamas River, under Douglas fir and big-leaf maple. It sits in the 2020 Riverside Fire burn scar and reopened in September 2024 after restoration.

The 3.7-mile Riverside Trail starts next to the campground. Accessible vault toilets are provided; there is no drinking water. Vehicles up to 24 feet.

contentHtml:
Riley Horse Campground is built for riders, with 14 sites that have horse corrals or hitching rails, beside Lost Creek near the Wild and Scenic Sandy River, northwest of Mount Hood. Non-riders may camp too.

The Cast Creek (5.3 mi), Horseshoe Ridge (4.9 mi) and Sandy River (3 mi) trails start nearby; the first two make a loop of nearly 14 miles. Vault toilets; no drinking water.

Boating, swimming and trout fishing are popular. Hand-pump water and accessible vault toilets are provided. In winter, the road to the lake becomes a Sno-Park trail.

It flows best after rain in winter and spring and may dry up in late summer.
