The Cast Creek Trail climbs the ridge above the creek from Riley Horse Campground.

Little Zigzag Falls is a 41-foot, two-tier cascade on the Little Zigzag River, near the old Mount Hood Highway. The water steps down two rounded, channeled ledges before flowing through a dark forest glade.

The river is fed by springs and Mount Hood snowmelt, so it flows year-round, strongest in late spring. An easy, well-graded trail of about a third of a mile starts beside the old bridge at the end of Kiwanis Camp Road.

title: Pup Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Pup Creek Falls is a 237-foot, two-tier waterfall in a lush side canyon of the Clackamas River. The upper drop plunges about 203 feet over an undercut ledge of layered basalt, then veils down a second tier of about 34 feet.

Moss, ferns and clover keep the canyon green most of the year. At least six smaller falls are reported upstream.

From Estacada, drive 15 miles east on OR-224 to Fish Creek Road, cross the river and park at the trailhead. Hike the Clackamas River Trail about 3.5 miles to a spur just before Pup Creek, which leads about 500 feet to the base of the falls.

title: Willamette Falls
imageAlt: Willamette Falls (Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde)

banner.alt: Willamette Falls (Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde)

gallery.alt: Willamette Falls from the I-205 viewpoint (Bryan Swan)

contentHtml:
Willamette Falls is the largest waterfall by volume in the Northwest: the Willamette River pours over a 1,500- foot-wide, horseshoe-shaped basalt ledge about 42 feet high between Oregon City and West Linn. Flow ranges from about 52,000 cubic feet per second in winter to about 1,200 in August.

The falls, called tumwata by the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde, were a village and salmon and lamprey fishing site for their Clackamas and Clowewalla ancestors. In 2019 the tribe bought the former Blue Heron Paper Mill site at the falls, and restoration and a planned riverwalk aim to reopen public access.

Today the falls are best seen from the OR-99E viewpoint, the I-205 northbound wayside and the Oregon City Bridge.

It is low-volume and may be seasonal, flowing best during summer snowmelt.

contentHtml:
Estacada Lake is a narrow, forested reservoir on the Clackamas River at Estacada, good for kayaks, stand-up paddleboards and canoes. It follows the river corridor, with coves, calmer stretches and foothill scenery.

Milo McIver State Park has a boat ramp, a dedicated ADA kayak launch, an ADA fishing dock and a life-jacket loaner station, with picnic areas, trails and the town of Estacada close by.

Motorboats are allowed, and water levels can change because the lake is a managed hydroelectric reservoir. The water stays cold even in summer.

title: Sandy River Water Trail
contentHtml:
The Sandy River Water Trail covers the lower 38 miles of the Sandy River, from its confluence with the Salmon River near Brightwood down to the Columbia River. It was Oregon's eighth designated water trail, created by the City of Sandy with the BLM and Oregon State Parks.

Signs mark public put-ins and take-outs, and the trail guide suggests six one-day float trips rated beginner to advanced, passing seven public parks including Dodge Park, Oxbow Regional Park and Dabney Park.

The river runs from Mount Hood's glaciers through a deep, forested canyon close to Portland, with salmon and steelhead runs; parts are Wild and Scenic and include Class II-III whitewater.

title: The Narrows
contentHtml:
The Narrows is a 4.8-mile flatwater loop on the Willamette River from Willamette Park in West Linn, rated beginner to moderate and taking about 2.5 hours of paddling.

The route heads upriver into The Narrows, a maze of exposed rock formations, islands and narrow passages that looks different at every river level. Expect motorboat traffic near the launch, watch for strainers along the shore, and allow for wind on the return.

Timothy Lake is a 1,400-acre forested mountain reservoir south of Mount Hood at 3,400 feet, with broad lake views of the mountain. Paddlers launch from Pine Point, West Shore and several campground ramps.

title: Trillium Lake
contentHtml:
Trillium Lake is a compact, motor-free lake beneath Mount Hood, famous for the mountain's reflection on calm mornings. Its forested shoreline makes it a quiet place for kayaks, paddleboards and canoes.

Paddlers launch from the day-use area beside the campground, with picnicking, hiking and Government Camp close by. Road and facility access is seasonal.

contentHtml:

It is ideal for new paddlers, with barely noticeable current through most of the summer, little development and natural and historic points of interest along the way. Tualatin Riverkeepers manage the trail and publish a map and safe-paddling guide.

title: Mount Hood
imageAlt: Timberline Lodge on the slopes of Mount Hood

banner.alt: Timberline Lodge on the slopes of Mount Hood

gallery.alt: Hiking above Timberline Lodge below Mt. Hood

contentHtml:
Mount Hood is Oregon's highest peak at 11,249 feet, a glacier-clad volcano in the Cascade Range whose summit sits on the Clackamas-Hood River county line.

The summit is a serious mountaineering objective, not a hike. Every route climbs snow and ice; the standard south-side route from Timberline Lodge crosses the Palmer Snowfield and climbs the Hogsback to the Pearly Gates, exposed to crevasses, rockfall and fast-changing weather.

Most visitors experience the mountain without the summit: historic Timberline Lodge on the south flank anchors year-round skiing, and the Timberline Trail circles the whole mountain in about 40 miles.

title: Wildwood Recreation Site - Cascade Streamwatch Trail
contentHtml:
Wildwood Recreation Site is a 550-acre BLM day-use area of old-growth forest beside the Wild and Scenic Salmon River, about 39 miles east of Portland on Highway 26.

The Cascade Streamwatch Trail is an accessible, paved three-quarter-mile loop with educational displays, river views and an underwater fish-viewing chamber where visitors can watch native fish, including salmon in the fall. The accessible Wetlands Trail adds a three-quarter-mile boardwalk loop with tactile plaques.

The site also has picnic areas and reservable group shelters, playing fields, a playground, flush toilets and drinking water, with swimming and fishing in the river.

contentHtml:
Lost Creek Campground was built by the Forest Service to be entirely barrier-free, in old-growth forest beside Lost Creek and the Sandy River above Zigzag.

Its nature trail is a flat, paved loop of about 0.3 mile through the campground, and the campground also has accessible campsites, accessible vault toilets and an accessible fishing platform on the river.

title: Cascading Rivers Scenic Bikeway
imageAlt: Cyclists on a forest road beside the river

banner.alt: Cyclists on a forest road beside the river

Bikes leaning against a tree at camp

contentHtml:
The Cascading Rivers Scenic Bikeway is a 70-mile, one-way road ride from Estacada to Detroit that follows the Wild and Scenic Clackamas River and then the Breitenbush River through ancient forest on quiet, remote roads. It was designated an Oregon Scenic Bikeway in 2014.

Riders get views of Mount Hood and Mount Jefferson, salmon and steelhead runs, elk and grouse, hot springs and swimming holes along the way. Ripplebrook, about 26 miles from Estacada, is the only community on the route, with restrooms, water, a camp store and a campground.

The ride is rated challenging, climbing about 3,125 feet from Estacada (1,985 feet from Detroit), and can be ridden in either direction. Camping is at Milo McIver State Park, with hiker-biker sites, and Detroit Lake State Recreation Area.

title: Cazadero Trail
contentHtml:
The Cazadero Trail is a 6.66-mile gravel rail-trail on the former Oregon Water Power and Railway Company corridor in the southeastern outskirts of the Portland area. It is planned to extend southeast through Eagle Creek to Estacada.

It is currently three separate segments: about 2.8 miles from Boring to Barton through shady woods along North Fork Deep Creek, about 1.6 miles from Bakers Ferry Road in Barton toward Goose Creek beside Highway 224, and about 2.2 miles through Eagle Creek.

title: Springwater Corridor
contentHtml:
The Springwater Corridor is a 21-mile paved rail-trail from the Willamette River in southeast Portland through Gresham to Boring, built on a 1903 electric interurban railroad line. Portland bought the corridor in 1990 and the trail opened in 1996; it is a Rail-Trail Hall of Fame inductee.

The trail follows Johnson Creek past wetlands, Oaks Bottom Wildlife Refuge, Tideman Johnson Park and Powell Butte, and is a key piece of Portland's 40-Mile Loop. Boring Station Trailhead Park at the eastern end has parking and restrooms.

title: T2T (Timberline to Town)
imageAlt: West Leg Road up to Timberline Lodge

banner.alt: West Leg Road up to Timberline Lodge

contentHtml:
T2T (Timberline to Town) is a 12 to 13-mile gravel-bike and mountain-bike loop from Government Camp: a 6- mile paved climb up the quiet, one-way West Leg Road to historic Timberline Lodge, then a 6-mile single-track descent on the Timberline to Town Trail back to town.

It gains about 2,100 feet and runs between 4,000 and 6,000 feet, half paved and half single-track, with Mount Hood views and food and water at Timberline Lodge at about mile 6. The descent is flowing but technical and sometimes rocky, so the route is rated very demanding.

title: Trolley Trail (OR)
contentHtml:
The Trolley Trail is a 6.9-mile paved multi-use path between Milwaukie and Gladstone on the former Portland Traction Company streetcar line to Oregon City, which ran from 1893 to 1968. Metro and North Clackamas Parks & Recreation District acquired the corridor in 2001 and the trail opened in 2012.

It passes through Oak Grove's neighborhoods with river views at both ends: the Willamette to the north and the Clackamas to the south. Milwaukie Bay Park is the best place to start, with parking and restrooms, and Stringfield Family Park in Oak Grove has parking, a playground and restrooms.

title: Clackamas River
contentHtml:
The Clackamas River flows northwest from the high Cascades through Mt. Hood National Forest to Big Cliff, just south of Estacada. Its 47-mile Wild and Scenic segment (20 miles scenic, 27 recreational) was designated on October 28, 1988, and passes forests, wetlands and rock cliffs.

The river holds the last significant wild late-winter coho run in the Columbia Basin and one of two remaining spring chinook runs in the Willamette Basin, plus winter steelhead and cutthroat trout. Old-growth Douglas-fir lines its banks, and bald eagles and northern spotted owls live in the corridor.

Close to Portland, it is popular for fishing, whitewater boating, hiking and mountain and wildflower views, with campgrounds along Highway 224. Human use here dates back about 10,000 years.

title: Collawash River
contentHtml:
The Collawash River is a major tributary of the Clackamas River on the west slope of the Cascades. Its 17.8- mile Wild and Scenic segment (11 miles scenic, 6.8 recreational) was designated on March 30, 2009.

The scenic segment runs through a narrow, steep, deeply cut canyon of cliffs and talus slopes, with rocks, pools and a waterfall of about 20 feet. It is excellent spawning habitat for spring chinook, steelhead and a rare native stock of winter-run coho, and the recreational segment holds a textbook example of an active earth flow.

title: Eagle Creek (Mt. Hood National Forest)
contentHtml:
This Eagle Creek is a tributary of the Clackamas River that joins it north of Estacada. Its 8.3-mile wild segment, from the headwaters to the Mt. Hood National Forest boundary, was designated on March 30, 2009, and lies entirely within the Salmon-Huckleberry Wilderness.

The creek runs from a cirque-shaped headwater basin through a steep, V-shaped valley of old Douglas-fir and hemlock, with riffles, downed logs and pools. Hiking, horseback riding, dispersed camping and trout fishing come with real solitude, and the corridor is northern spotted owl nesting habitat and big-game winter range.

title: Fish Creek
contentHtml:
Fish Creek is a 13.5-mile recreational Wild and Scenic river on the western slope of the Cascades, designated on March 30, 2009, from its headwaters to its confluence with the Clackamas River.

It runs through a narrow canyon near its headwaters, then widens as it approaches the Clackamas; the final four miles suit experienced whitewater paddlers. It is important habitat for spring chinook, steelhead and winter-run coho, and an ambitious restoration effort is underway after past flooding.

title: Molalla River
contentHtml:
The Molalla River rises in the Oregon Cascades and flows to the Willamette, about an hour from Portland and Salem. On March 12, 2019, 21.3 miles were designated a recreational Wild and Scenic river: 15.1 miles of the mainstem and 6.2 miles of the Table Rock Fork. It is also an Oregon State Scenic Waterway.

The BLM-managed corridor is popular for tubing, swimming, fishing, whitewater boating and camping, with more than 30 miles of non-motorized trails. Clear pools, whitewater and unusual horizontal columnar basalt "rosettes" make it scenic, and it is critical habitat for spring chinook and winter steelhead. It also supplies drinking water to Molalla and Canby.

title: Roaring River
contentHtml:
The Roaring River was designated Wild and Scenic on October 28, 1988, for 13.7 miles from its headwaters to the Clackamas River (13.5 miles wild). Its upper drainage is a broad glacial valley rising to sharp ridges and lake basins, and its lowest four miles form a narrow gorge with steep basalt cliffs.

The remote, primitive river has log jams, waterfalls and pools, with two large falls below the South Fork confluence. Its native late-run coho is considered the last self-sustaining native run in the Columbia Basin, and its clear, cold water is a regional baseline for water quality.

title: Salmon River
contentHtml:
The Salmon River runs 33.5 miles from Mount Hood near Timberline Lodge to the Sandy River, all of it designated Wild and Scenic on October 28, 1988 (15 miles wild, 4.8 scenic, 13.7 recreational). It is about an hour from Portland.

Six waterfalls from 15 to 75 feet drop within three miles in the Salmon-Huckleberry Wilderness, a rarity in Oregon. The river is key spawning habitat for steelhead, coho and spring chinook, and supports Roosevelt elk and Oregon's northernmost breeding sandhill cranes.

Visitors hike, camp and ski in the watershed, and BLM's Wildwood Recreation Site has the Cascade Streamwatch underwater fish-viewing window.

title: Sandy River
contentHtml:
The Sandy River starts in Mount Hood's glaciers and was designated Wild and Scenic on October 28, 1988, for 24.9 miles: 12.4 miles from the headwaters managed by the Forest Service, and 12.5 miles from Dodge Park to Dabney Park managed by the BLM.

Near Portland the lower river runs through a deep, winding forested gorge known for fish runs, plant diversity, boating and parks, including the last low-elevation old-growth stand of its type in the Willamette Valley. At least eight runs of salmon and steelhead use it.

Visitors hike (including the popular Ramona Falls Trail), fish, backpack, camp, kayak and raft, with Mount Hood's volcanic history exposed along the canyon.

title: South Fork Clackamas River
contentHtml:
The South Fork Clackamas River is a 4.2-mile wild river, designated on March 30, 2009, that flows through a narrow canyon of rock outcrops and cliffs to the Clackamas River, less than an hour's drive from Portland.

It has a 100-foot waterfall in its lower segment and old-growth Douglas-fir, with spring chinook, steelhead and a rare late-winter coho run below the falls. It is one of the most remote large streams in the state, with hiking, mountain biking, backpacking, whitewater boating and catch-and-release fishing.

title: South Fork Roaring River
contentHtml:
The South Fork Roaring River is a 4.6-mile wild river, designated on March 30, 2009, that runs from the Rock Lakes Basin in the Roaring River Wilderness to the main Roaring River.

It flows through a steep, narrow canyon of rock outcrops and cliffs, with log jams, landslides and waterfalls alternating with large pools. Old-growth trees line the banks, northern spotted owls nest here, and the rare cold-water corydalis wildflower grows along the stream. Development is almost nonexistent.

title: Zig Zag River
contentHtml:
The Zigzag River begins at the base of Zigzag Glacier at about 5,000 feet on Mount Hood. Its 4.3 miles from the headwaters to the Mt. Hood Wilderness boundary were designated a wild river on March 30, 2009.

The river drops steeply through a narrow, sparsely vegetated canyon over old mud and pyroclastic flows, with a forested rim and two waterfalls. The Pacific Crest Trail and Timberline Trail cross Zigzag Canyon, drawing hikers for wildflowers and mountain views.

contentHtml:
The Mount Hood Scenic Byway is a National Scenic Byway of roughly 100 miles that loops around Mount Hood between Troutdale and Hood River, following US-26 through Sandy and Government Camp and OR-35 through the Hood River Valley.

In Clackamas County the route climbs past Brightwood, Welches, Zigzag and Rhododendron to Government Camp, with the Cascade Streamwatch at Wildwood Recreation Site, Sandy's Jonsrud Viewpoint and the 6-mile spur up to 1937 Timberline Lodge at 6,000 feet.

Beyond the pass are the Barlow Road and Pioneer Woman's Grave, the Hood River Valley's Fruit Loop orchards, farm stands and wineries, and Hood River's waterfront.

title: West Cascades Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Along the West Cascades Scenic Byway

contentHtml:
The West Cascades Scenic Byway is a 220-mile National Scenic Byway along the northern half of Oregon's Cascade Range, from Estacada, about 25 miles from Portland, south to Westfir near Oakridge.

From Estacada it follows the Clackamas River on OR-224 and Forest Road 46 to Detroit Lake, then the McKenzie River past Clear Lake and 100-foot Sahalie Falls, ending on the Aufderheide road (Forest Road 19) at the Office Covered Bridge, Oregon's longest at 180 feet.

Along the way are old-growth groves such as the Delta Old Growth Trail, three National Recreation Trails, Olallie Lakes and the PGE powerhouse at Estacada. The full drive takes 7 to 9 hours, or sections can be driven on their own.

title: Farmlandia Farm Loop

gallery.alt: Rogerson Clematis Garden at Luscher Farm

contentHtml:
The Farmlandia Farm Loop is a self-guided farm trail of about 17 stops at the northern edge of the Willamette Valley, from Milwaukie and Oregon City through Stafford, West Linn and Wilsonville and out toward Boring. It is part of the Oregon Farm Loop program.

More than a dozen stops are working farms, joined by vineyards, nurseries, farm stores, farmers markets and a farm-to-table restaurant. Favorites include Lee Farms, a seventh-generation farm since 1869 with a store and bakery; Barn Owl Nursery's nearly 100 lavender varieties; Frog Pond Farm's animals and pumpkin patch; Triskelee Farm; Tollen Farm's miniature donkeys; and Terra Vina Wines.

Lavender peaks in June and July, fall brings pumpkins, and the holidays bring Christmas trees.

title: South Clackamas Farm Loop

contentHtml:
The South Clackamas Farm Loop gathers about 20 farms and farm businesses across the Canby and Molalla countryside, entirely within Clackamas County. It combines the former Canby Area Farm Loop and Molalla Country Farm Loop, names that still circulate.

Its best-known stop is Swan Island Dahlias in Canby, the nation's largest dahlia grower, family-run since 1927, whose fields bloom with about 500,000 plants during its free Dahlia Festival in August and September. Other stops include TMK Creamery, Lady Lane Farm in Mulino, Puddin' River Chocolates and Union Mills Feed.

Timberline Ski Area surrounds historic Timberline Lodge on Mount Hood's south face, with 1,685 acres of terrain and 4,540 feet of vertical, the longest in the United States, from the top of the Palmer Snowfield at 8,540 feet down to Summit Pass in Government Camp.

Six high-speed quads, two doubles and a surface lift serve groomed runs, tree skiing and terrain parks, and Palmer Snowcats carry ticket holders to 8,540 feet. Thanks to the Palmer Snowfield, Timberline offers summer skiing and the longest season in North America.

Lessons, rentals and programs are offered for all levels, and the lodge has dining and lodging on the mountain.

title: Bagby Hot Springs
contentHtml:
Bagby Hot Springs is a developed public hot spring in old-growth forest beside a tributary of the Clackamas River, reached by a walk of about 1.5 miles on Bagby Hot Springs Trail #544.

Hand-hewn cedar log tubs sit in rustic bathhouses: the lower bathhouse has three log tubs and a 6-foot round tub, and the upper bathhouse has a round tub on an open deck. The main spring flows at 138°F and is blended with cold water.

Hunter and prospector Bob Bagby found the springs in 1880, and Forest Service guard Phil Putz built a cabin here in 1913. Today the springs are run by Bagby Preservation.

contentHtml:
Oregon City's Municipal Elevator is one of only four municipal elevators in the world and the only outdoor municipal elevator in the United States. Its 130-foot tower carries riders up the bluff in about 15 seconds, and Elevator Street is the only "vertical street" in North America.

The first, water-powered elevator opened in 1915; the current one was dedicated in 1955. The upper level has an observation deck with views of downtown, the Willamette River and Willamette Falls, plus murals of historic Oregon City, and opens onto the McLoughlin Promenade.

title: Timberline Lodge & Ski Area
imageAlt: Timberline Lodge on Mount Hood at sunrise

banner.alt: Timberline Lodge on Mount Hood at sunrise

Hiking behind the lodge in summer

contentHtml:
Timberline Lodge was built in 1937 at 6,000 feet on Mount Hood's south slope by more than 500 Works Progress Administration workers in 18 months, using local volcanic stone, massive timbers and hand-forged iron. President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated it on September 28, 1937, and it became a National Historic Landmark in 1977.

Its ski area runs the longest season in North America and is the only one on the continent with lift-served skiing twelve months a year, thanks to the Palmer Snowfield.

The lodge offers rooms, fine dining and the Ram's Head Bar, with summer hiking, mountain biking and the Magic Mile Sky Ride, and draws nearly two million visitors a year.

title: Canby Ferry
imageAlt: Canby Ferry crossing the Willamette River

banner.alt: Canby Ferry crossing the Willamette River

contentHtml:
The Canby Ferry is one of only three car ferries still crossing the Willamette River. Clackamas County has run a ferry between Canby and Wilsonville since 1914, when the first boat was pushed by the current and guided by cable.

Today's ferry, the M.J. Lee II, entered service in 1997 and carries up to six cars and 43 people on a five-minute crossing, with no set schedule. It is named for Millard Jerome Lee, the first child born in Canby, and the ferry appeared on the cover of Sunset magazine in 1961.
excerpt: The Canby Ferry is one of only three car ferries still crossing the Willamette River. Clackamas County has run a ferry between Canby and Wilsonville since 1914,
note: One-way fares: $5 per car, $3 for walk-ons, bicycles and motorcycles; larger vehicles more. Cash or check only on board; punch passes online. Closed on major holidays and when the river reaches 70 feet. Email: roadconcerns@clackamas.us
address: Willamette River crossing between Canby and Wilsonville (follow signs to the Canby Ferry)

title: Haggart Observatory
contentHtml:
Haggart Observatory, at Clackamas Community College's Environmental Learning Center, opened in 1989 and was built with donated materials, gifts and many volunteer hours.

Its dome houses a 24-inch Newtonian reflector, and on public viewing nights Rose City Astronomers volunteers also set up portable telescopes on the deck to show the Moon, planets and star clusters. The college also hosts an annual Star Party in late August.
excerpt: Haggart Observatory, at Clackamas Community College's Environmental Learning Center, opened in 1989 and was built with donated materials, gifts and many volunte
note: Free; first come, first served, no registration. Check rosecityastronomers.net or call for cloudy-night cancellations.
address: Environmental Learning Center, Clackamas Community College, 19600 Molalla Ave, Oregon City, OR 97045 (enter off Beavercreek Rd, park past the ELC entrance)

title: Eco Park, Canby
imageAlt: City of Canby officials with the Oregon Film Trail sign

banner.alt: City of Canby officials with the Oregon Film Trail sign

contentHtml:
Canby's Eco Park is a city park and trailhead on the Molalla Forest Road. In early 2014 it doubled as a European forest for the "Synchronicity" episode of NBC's Grimm, the fantasy series filmed around Portland from 2011 to 2017.

In October 2021 the park became the 36th stop on the Oregon Film Trail, with a marker unveiled by the City of Canby and the Oregon Made Creative Foundation. It was the second Clackamas County location on the trail, after Oregon City.
excerpt: Canby's Eco Park is a city park and trailhead on the Molalla Forest Road. In early 2014 it doubled as a European forest for the "Synchronicity" episode of NBC's
note: Oregon Film Trail sign in the park.
address: Eco Park, Molalla Forest Rd just off S Territorial Rd, Canby

title: McLoughlin Promenade, Oregon City
contentHtml:
The McLoughlin Promenade is a 7.8-acre linear park along the bluff above downtown Oregon City, built around 1937 by the Works Progress Administration, with views of the Willamette River, Willamette Falls and downtown.

Its Oregon Film Trail marker overlooks the former Blue Heron paper mill, which played the "Grisham Mill" in Twilight's (2008) security-guard chase scene; The Hunted also filmed at the mill. The Municipal Elevator and the McLoughlin House are steps away.
excerpt: The McLoughlin Promenade is a 7.8-acre linear park along the bluff above downtown Oregon City, built around 1937 by the Works Progress Administration, with view
note: Benches and a walking path; parking at the south end near Tumwater Ave.
address: 300 Promenade Street, Oregon City, OR 97045

title: Molalla Train Park
imageAlt: Miniature train at Shady Dell Train Park

banner.alt: Miniature train at Shady Dell Train Park

contentHtml:
Molalla Train Park, also called Shady Dell Train Park, is run by volunteers of the nonprofit Pacific Northwest Live Steamers, who give free rides on miniature steam and diesel trains.

About 4,200 feet of 7.5-inch-gauge track winds through a 4-acre park of ponds, bridges and trees, on 7 to 10- minute rides open to all ages. A snack stand opens at noon.
excerpt: Molalla Train Park, also called Shady Dell Train Park, is run by volunteers of the nonprofit Pacific Northwest Live Steamers, who give free rides on miniature s
note: Free entry and rides; donations welcome. Extra open days on Memorial Day weekend, Founders Day weekend in July and Train Fest weekend in September. Email: harryharvey@shadydell.org
address: Shady Dell Train Park, 31803 S Shady Dell Rd, Molalla, OR

title: Willamette Shore Trolley
imageAlt: Willamette Shore Trolley at Elk Rock Tunnel

banner.alt: Willamette Shore Trolley at Elk Rock Tunnel

contentHtml:
The Willamette Shore Trolley is a heritage trolley run by Oregon Electric Railway Historical Society volunteers on about 6 miles of the old Southern Pacific Jefferson Street line, along the Willamette River between Lake Oswego and Portland's South Waterfront.

The ride crosses trestles and passes through the dark 1921 Elk Rock Tunnel, with river views and upscale riverside neighborhoods. The line opened in 1887 and carried Red Electric interurbans from 1914 to 1929; the trolley is a replica of Portland's Council Crest cars.

December Christmas Ships rides are the most popular event, and trolleys can be chartered.
excerpt: The Willamette Shore Trolley is a heritage trolley run by Oregon Electric Railway Historical Society volunteers on about 6 miles of the old Southern Pacific Jef
note: Check the schedule and buy tickets online. Email: mark@oerhs.org
address: Lake Oswego depot, 311 N State St, Lake Oswego, OR 97034

title: Bent Shovel Brewing
imageAlt: Bent Shovel beer garden in Estacada

banner.alt: Bent Shovel beer garden in Estacada

gallery.alt: Bent Shovel pub and beer garden

contentHtml:
Bent Shovel Brewing was founded in 2015 in Oregon City by Rick and Shelly Strauss, brewing a wide range of styles on a 10-barrel system in a retrofitted red barn along the Clackamas River.

Its pub and tree-lined beer garden sit on Springwater Road near the entrance to Milo McIver State Park outside Estacada, with parking and views of Mount Hood. The Strausses also bought the neighboring Viewpoint Restaurant & Lounge and McIver Outpost store in 2021.
excerpt: Bent Shovel Brewing was founded in 2015 in Oregon City by Rick and Shelly Strauss, brewing a wide range of styles on a 10-barrel system in a retrofitted red bar
note: Email: info@bentshovelbrewing.com. Pub open year-round.
address: 20189 S Springwater Rd, Estacada, OR 97023
photoCredit: New School Beer + Cider / Bent Shovel Brewing

title: Boring Brewing Company
contentHtml:
Boring Brewing is a family-friendly nano brewery in downtown Sandy on the way to Mount Hood. It began as a father-and-son homebrewing project; the owners took it over in 2017 and moved it to Sandy in 2018.

Everything is brewed in-house on a two-barrel system, including Big Yawn IPA, Boring Brown, Honey Ginger Rye and Hot Scotch plus about ten seasonals, with wine, local ciders, homemade root beer and pub snacks. Weekly game night, open mic, trivia, vinyl night and live music fill the calendar.
excerpt: Boring Brewing is a family-friendly nano brewery in downtown Sandy on the way to Mount Hood. It began as a father-and-son homebrewing project; the owners took i
note: Kids, dogs and outside food welcome. Call or text.
address: Corner of Bluff Rd and Pioneer Blvd, Sandy, OR

title: Breakside Brewery
contentHtml:
Breakside Brewery opened in 2010 in Northeast Portland and has grown into one of Oregon's most decorated breweries, named Oregon Beer Awards Brewery of the Year six times. It became employee-owned in 2019.

Its production brewery and taproom opened in Milwaukie in 2013, and a Lake Oswego taproom is also in Clackamas County. Breakside is known for a broad, inventive lineup led by West Coast IPAs such as Wanderjack and Cowboys and Poets, plus lagers and seasonal releases.
excerpt: Breakside Brewery opened in 2010 in Northeast Portland and has grown into one of Oregon's most decorated breweries, named Oregon Beer Awards Brewery of the Year
note: Lake Oswego hours: Sunday to Thursday 12 to 9 PM, Friday and Saturday 12 to 10 PM.
address: 5821 SE International Way, Milwaukie, OR 97222 (also 120 A Ave, Lake Oswego, (503) 344- 4164)

title: Little Beast Brewing

gallery.alt: Owners Charles Porter and Brenda Crow in the Clackamas tasting room

contentHtml:
Little Beast Brewing was founded in 2017 by brewer Charles Porter, formerly of Logsdon Farmhouse Ales, and Brenda Crow. It is known for mixed-culture, farmhouse and fruited sour ales, plus a can series from Helles lagers to hazy IPAs and imperial stouts.

Its production brewery is in Clackamas, where a casual, all-ages tasting room with dog-friendly outdoor seating opened in 2021. The Portland beer garden on SE Division serves the full lineup with pizza.
excerpt: Little Beast Brewing was founded in 2017 by brewer Charles Porter, formerly of Logsdon Farmhouse Ales, and Brenda Crow. It is known for mixed-culture, farmhouse
note: Check the website for current Clackamas tasting room days. Portland beer garden: Monday to Thursday 2 to 9 PM, Friday 2 to 10 PM, Saturday 12 to 10 PM, Sunday 12 to 9 PM.
address: 11517 SE Highway 212, Clackamas, OR (Cumberland Business Center); beer garden at 3412 SE Division St, Portland
photoCredit: New School Beer + Cider / Little Beast Brewing

title: Molalla River Brewing
contentHtml:
Molalla River Brewing Company is a family-owned, community-driven taphouse in Molalla, pouring beer, wine, cider, kombucha, boba teas and sodas.

Local food trucks serve on site, and its 18-hole mini golf course, classic cars and welcoming atmosphere make it a stop for the whole family.
excerpt: Molalla River Brewing Company is a family-owned, community-driven taphouse in Molalla, pouring beer, wine, cider, kombucha, boba teas and sodas.
note: Mini golf keeps the same hours. Food truck hours vary.
address: 180 Industrial Way, Molalla, OR 97038

title: Mt. Hood Brewing

gallery.alt: Beer and food at the brewpub

contentHtml:
Mt. Hood Brewing Co. opened in January 1991 in Government Camp, at the gateway to Mount Hood, and is a sister company of Timberline Lodge. Its ales are brewed with glacial Mt. Hood water and Pacific Northwest barley and hops, including the well-known Ice Axe IPA.

The family-friendly brewpub serves hearty après-ski pub fare, Oregon comfort food, cocktails and vegetarian options, and its beer is poured throughout Timberline Lodge. Sister locations are Tilikum Station in Portland and the Rainbow Tavern in Maupin.

note: Open daily.
address: 87304 E Government Camp Loop, Government Camp, OR 97028

title: Oregon City Brewing Company
contentHtml:
Oregon City Brewing Company opened in downtown Oregon City in the mid-2010s with the slogan "pioneering beer for the pioneer city." It brews its own house ales and IPAs, from a mild blonde and ESB to a rich triple chocolate porter.

The modern, lively taproom pours dozens of taps of house beers and regional favorites, with a rotating lineup of food carts, games and big-screen sports, making it a community gathering spot.
excerpt: Oregon City Brewing Company opened in downtown Oregon City in the mid-2010s with the slogan "pioneering beer for the pioneer city." It brews its own house ales
note: Food carts on site.
address: 1401 Washington St, Oregon City, OR 97045
photoCredit: Downtown Oregon City Association / Willamette Week

title: RAM Restaurant & Brewery
contentHtml:
The RAM Restaurant & Brewery in Wilsonville is a brewpub of the Northwest-based RAM chain, which has brewed its own beer since 1995 and has more than thirty locations.

It pours house-brewed beers such as Buttface Amber, Big Red's IPA and Big Horn Hefeweizen alongside seasonal lagers, with a full menu including beer-crust pizza and daily specials.

note: Online ordering and takeout available.
address: 29800 SW Boones Ferry Rd, Wilsonville, OR 97070

title: Vanguard Brewing Company
imageAlt: Couple with beers at an outdoor table at Vanguard Brewing

banner.alt: Couple with beers at an outdoor table at Vanguard Brewing

contentHtml:
Vanguard Brewing Company is an independent, veteran family-owned brewery, taproom and beer garden in Wilsonville, founded in 2015 by Don and Lin Anderson and now owned by Ted and Silvia Minshall.

It brews small batches of classic-style craft beers, especially pilsners and lagers, with locally grown ingredients, and has indoor and outdoor seating. It celebrated its 10th anniversary in September 2025.

address: 27501 SW 95th Ave, Suite 945, Wilsonville, OR 97070

title: Vision Brewing
contentHtml:
Vision Brewing is a small independent brewery and cidery from the Aurora area with a production address in Canby.

It has no public taproom; its beers and ciders appear at area taprooms and festivals, including a 2026 collaboration poured at Canby's FOB Taproom.
excerpt: Vision Brewing is a small independent brewery and cidery from the Aurora area with a production address in Canby.
note: No public taproom. Look for its beers and ciders at local taprooms and events.
address: Canby production address; based in Aurora area

title: Forest Edge Vineyard
contentHtml:
Forest Edge Vineyard is a small family winery in the Cascade foothills outside Oregon City, where about 7 acres of vines meet 36 acres of sustainably managed forest. Licensed in 2009, it is solar-powered and farmed with permaculture principles.

Its wines draw on the Burgundian tradition, and the relaxed tasting room sits right in the forest vineyard, with complimentary tastings and winemaker stories. Look for the winery at the Oregon City Farmers Market too.
excerpt: Forest Edge Vineyard is a small family winery in the Cascade foothills outside Oregon City, where about 7 acres of vines meet 36 acres of sustainably managed fo
note: Complimentary tastings. Wine pickup any day by appointment. Email: info@forestedgevineyard.com
address: 15640 S Spangler Rd, Oregon City, OR

title: Oswego Hills Winery
contentHtml:
Oswego Hills Vineyard and Winery is a West Linn winery and vineyard in the Willamette Valley, billed as the winery closest to downtown Portland.

Its tasting room showcases the latest vintages and new releases, and the estate is a popular wedding venue with indoor event spaces and landscaped grounds for outdoor ceremonies and dinners.
excerpt: Oswego Hills Vineyard and Winery is a West Linn winery and vineyard in the Willamette Valley, billed as the winery closest to downtown Portland.
note: Extended hours some summer weekends and in December, and on Memorial Day, Labor Day and Thanksgiving weekends. Call ahead for groups of 10 or more. Email: Help@OswegoHills.com
address: 450 S Rosemont Rd, West Linn, OR 97068

title: St. Josef's Winery
contentHtml:
St. Josef's Winery is a family-owned winery and vineyard near Canby and one of Oregon's original wine pioneers: its vines were planted in 1978 and its first vintage came in 1983.

It grows its own fruit on LIVE and Salmon-Safe certified vineyards, without irrigation or harsh chemicals, for wines including Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Syrah and Gewürztraminer, with the motto "Serious Wines for the Not So Serious."

Events include second-Sunday food and music, summer music on the pond, winemaker dinners and a fall grape-stomping festival, and the grounds host weddings.

address: 28836 S Barlow Rd, Canby, OR 97013

title: Terra Vina Wines
contentHtml:
Terra Vina Wines is a small family-owned winery with an estate vineyard of nearly 17 acres on Parrett Mountain above Wilsonville, in the Chehalem Mountains AVA, growing Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc.

Known for big, bold reds since its first release in 2004, winemaker Karl Dinger makes the estate La Famiglia label and Terra Vina reds from Eastern Oregon and Washington fruit. Wines are sold only through the tasting rooms, online and the wine club.
excerpt: Terra Vina Wines is a small family-owned winery with an estate vineyard of nearly 17 acres on Parrett Mountain above Wilsonville, in the Chehalem Mountains AVA,
note: Picnics welcome; tours, weddings and outdoor seating. Email: Info@TerraVinaWines.com
address: 33750 SW Ladd Hill Rd, Wilsonville, OR 97070 (second tasting room in downtown McMinnville)

title: Wooden Shoe Tulip Farm & Vineyard

Wooden Shoe Tulip Farm has been family-owned and operated since 1950 and grows more than 100 crops. It is best known for its spring Tulip Festival, with millions of tulips blooming across 40 acres plus the 4-acre Wooden Shoe Gardens.

title: Clark Park
contentHtml:
Clark Park's disc golf course is a technical, challenging 9-hole layout through a thickly wooded city park in Molalla, designed by Jerry Miller of Disc Golf Depot.

It mixes right-handed backhand and forehand lines with a couple of ace runs and two longer holes of 320 to 350 feet, on concrete tees with Bentley baskets. The course is mostly flat and free to play.

note: Free. Shared park: watch for dogs, kids and other park users. Parking on the north and south sides (the south lot serves hole 6).
address: Clark Park, 704 N Cole Ave, Molalla, OR 97038

title: Eco Park
contentHtml:
Eco Park in Canby has a short, technical 12-hole disc golf course, established in 2012 and designed by Steve Carson. All holes are par 3 (par 36) over about 2,950 feet, from 132 to 365 feet.

The course is mostly wooded with a few open-field holes; a creek crosses hole 4 and holes 5 through 9 run along the river. Rubber tees and DISCatcher baskets; a round takes about an hour.

note: Free. Watch for poison oak and thick rough along fairways.
address: Eco Park, Molalla Forest Rd off S Territorial Rd, Canby (first tee about 75 yards down the paved path)

title: Memorial Park
contentHtml:
Memorial Park in Wilsonville has a popular all-par-3 disc golf course, established in 2016 and redesigned in 2025, combining 10 original holes with an expansion section reached by a bridge behind hole 13's tee.

The 19-hole short layout plays to par 57 over about 4,300 feet on concrete and turf tees with Mach X baskets. It is mostly flat and easy, suited to all skill levels, and takes about 1 to 1.5 hours.

note: Free. Restrooms near the tennis courts and dog park; no drinking water. Dogs allowed; cart and stroller friendly.
address: Memorial Park, Wilsonville, OR

title: Metzler County Park
contentHtml:
Metzler County Park, a Clackamas County park near Estacada, has an 18-hole, all-par-3 disc golf course (par 54) on hilly, forested ground with concrete tees and DISCatcher baskets.

The short front nine has interesting elevation changes and tree-lined fairways, and the longer, more challenging back nine is heavily wooded. The park also has restrooms, drinking water and camping.
excerpt: Metzler County Park, a Clackamas County park near Estacada, has an 18-hole, all-par-3 disc golf course (par 54) on hilly, forested ground with concrete tees and
note: Disc golf is free; day-use parking $9 per vehicle (Clackamas County annual pass accepted). Front 9 open year-round; back 9 open October 1 to April 30. Dogs allowed.
address: Metzler County Park, Estacada, OR

title: Milo McIver State Park
contentHtml:
Milo McIver State Park has two disc golf courses with 27 baskets in all, and its Riverbend East course is rated the No. 1 course in Oregon and among the top 100 in the world on UDisc (2026). It was established in 1996.

The heavily wooded, hilly course is known for its scenery, elevation and technical shots, with concrete tees and DISCatcher and Mach X baskets. A round takes about 1.5 to 2.5 hours.
excerpt: Milo McIver State Park has two disc golf courses with 27 baskets in all, and its Riverbend East course is rated the No. 1 course in Oregon and among the top 100
note: Disc golf is free; state park day-use parking $10 per vehicle. Restrooms and drinking water; dogs allowed.
address: Milo McIver State Park, along the Clackamas River near Estacada

title: Singer Creek Park
contentHtml:
Singer Creek Park in Oregon City has a short 9-hole, par-27 disc golf course of about 1,850 feet, with holes from 149 to 245 feet that use the park's steep elevation well.

The hilly, wooded course has asphalt tees and Mach V baskets, takes about 45 minutes and is rated easy.
excerpt: Singer Creek Park in Oregon City has a short 9-hole, par-27 disc golf course of about 1,850 feet, with holes from 149 to 245 feet that use the park's steep elev
note: Free. No restrooms or drinking water. Dogs allowed. Very steep slopes. Respect neighbors and other park users.
address: Singer Creek Park, Oregon City, OR

title: Timber Park
contentHtml:
Timber Park in Estacada has a 21-hole disc golf course, established in 1996, set apart from the park's main public area. Most holes have at least one alternate basket position, on concrete tees with Mach III baskets.

The mostly flat, moderate course covers about 2.2 miles and takes 1.5 to 2 hours. Hole 12 runs beside a deep creek, and holes 19 and 20 border a road and a fenced quarry. The park also has a practice basket, restrooms, ball fields, picnic areas and an off-leash dog park.
excerpt: Timber Park in Estacada has a 21-hole disc golf course, established in 1996, set apart from the park's main public area. Most holes have at least one alternate
note: Parking $10 per vehicle per day (credit card at the lot kiosks) or $50 annual pass. Phone is for annual passes.

contentHtml:
This 9-hole, par-27 disc golf course on the grounds of Willamette Christian Church in West Linn was established in 2014: a short, technical layout of about 1,950 feet through big trees with elevation changes.

UDisc now lists the course as permanently closed; a posted sign said it lacked operating permits from Clackamas County and Clackamas Fire.

title: Xerox/Parkworks DGC
contentHtml:
The Xerox disc golf course is a flat 9-hole, par-27 course of about 2,250 feet on the former Xerox campus in Wilsonville, private property that is open to the public.

Established in 2017 and redesigned in 2022 by Jerry Miller, it has natural tees, Mach V baskets and good signage, and plays in about 30 minutes to an hour.

note: Free. No restrooms or drinking water. Dogs allowed; cart and stroller friendly.

title: Flavel House Museum

gallery.alt: Architect's drawing of the Flavel House

contentHtml:
The Flavel House Museum is one of the best-preserved examples of Queen Anne architecture in the Northwest, completed in 1886 as the retirement home of Captain George Flavel, a Columbia River bar pilot and businessman. It was designed by German-born architect Carl W. Leick.

The 11,600-square-foot mansion has a four-story tower, six fireplaces with exotic hardwood mantels, original woodwork and period furnishings that show late Victorian life, set on grounds planted with trees the captain collected on his travels.

Self-guided tours start at the 1887 Carriage House, now the visitor center, exhibit hall and museum store. The house has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1951 and is run by the Clatsop County Historical Society.
excerpt: The Flavel House Museum is one of the best-preserved examples of Queen Anne architecture in the Northwest, completed in 1886 as the retirement home of Captain G
note: Admission: adults $7, seniors $6, youth $2. Email: info@astoriamuseums.org
address: 714 Exchange St, Astoria, OR 97103

title: Heritage Museum (Clatsop County Historical Society)

gallery.alt: Exhibit on the Great Astoria Fire of 1922
Celebrating 100 Years of the Astoria Column

contentHtml:
The Heritage Museum is the Clatsop County Historical Society's regional history museum, in Astoria's Neo- Classical former City Hall, built in 1904-1905 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Two floors hold six permanent exhibits on the area's Native American tribes, Astoria's founding, immigration, local natural resources and the city's history of vice and virtue, plus rotating temporary exhibits. The Liisa Penner Research Center & Archives is in the same building.

The building later served as a USO dormitory and club and housed the Columbia River Maritime Museum for about twenty years before the Historical Society took it over in 1982.

title: Columbia River Maritime Museum
imageAlt: Cargo ship crossing the Columbia River bar

banner.alt: Cargo ship crossing the Columbia River bar

gallery.alt: Indigenous mask in the Cedar and Sea gallery

contentHtml:
The Columbia River Maritime Museum is Oregon's official state maritime museum, on the Astoria waterfront where the Columbia River meets the Pacific at the Graveyard of the Pacific.

Galleries include Crossing the Bar on the treacherous Columbia River entrance and the Coast Guard and bar pilots who work it, Shipwrecks!, Cedar and Sea on Indigenous maritime culture, and an exhibit made with the Chinook Indian Nation. A 3D theater, model boat pond and woodworking shop add hands-on fun.

Admission includes the Lightship Columbia, a floating lighthouse moored outside, with engine room tours most afternoons.

title: Oregon Film Museum
imageAlt: The old Clatsop County Jail, home of the Oregon Film Museum

banner.alt: The old Clatsop County Jail, home of the Oregon Film Museum

contentHtml:
The Oregon Film Museum celebrates the more than 400 major films and TV shows made in Oregon, housed in the old Clatsop County Jail, which held prisoners from 1914 to 1976 and is the jail in the opening jailbreak of The Goonies.

The Hot Set gallery shows how productions are made, with three sets, props and touch screens where visitors can film their own short movie on green screens. The jail cells are devoted to The Goonies, with memorabilia, a mug-shot station and a wall of fan notes.

Clatsop County movies featured include The Goonies, Short Circuit, Free Willy and Kindergarten Cop. Oregon Film Trail sign No. 1 stands outside.

title: Seaside Museum & Historical Society
contentHtml:
The Seaside Museum & Historical Society tells the story of Oregon's first seaside resort town, from about 2,000 years of Native heritage through the 1912 fire to the Prom.

On the same grounds is the 1893 Butterfield Cottage, the only beach cottage museum in Oregon, open for tours during museum hours and home to a holiday tea each November.

title: Cannon Beach History Center & Museum
imageAlt: Cannon Beach History Center and Museum

banner.alt: Cannon Beach History Center and Museum

contentHtml:
The Cannon Beach History Center & Museum shares the history of Cannon Beach and Arch Cape. Its centerpiece is the original cannon that gave the town its name, along with its capstan, conserved at Texas A&M University.

A permanent exhibit on Cannon Beach history, a replica Native American longhouse and changing temporary exhibits are joined by free lectures, oral histories, a museum store and the annual Cannon Beach Cottage Tour.

title: Lewis and Clark National Historical Park — Fort Clatsop
imageAlt: Fort Clatsop replica in the forest

banner.alt: Fort Clatsop replica in the forest

Kayak tour on a river side channel
Bridge over the river on the Netul River Trail

contentHtml:
Fort Clatsop is the main Oregon unit of Lewis and Clark National Historical Park, where the Corps of Discovery spent the winter of 1805-1806. A replica of the 50-foot-square log fort stands in the forest near the visitor center.

Rangers lead programs at the fort, and in summer offer free guided canoe and kayak tours on the Lewis and Clark River (reservations required). The Netul River Trail follows the river for 1.25 miles, and a Junior Ranger program serves kids. The park's other units are across the river in Washington.

title: Oregon Islands Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Oregon Islands Wilderness covers the rocks, reefs and islands of Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, some 1,853 of them strung along about 320 miles of coastline from Tillamook Head near Seaside to the California border.

The islands are breeding and resting grounds for most of Oregon's estimated 1.2 million nesting seabirds, including tufted puffins and cormorants, and for seals and sea lions that haul out and give birth there.

In Clatsop County the best-known wilderness rock is Haystack Rock at Cannon Beach, added in 1968 and made wilderness in 1978. The islands are closed to public entry; bring binoculars or a spotting scope and watch from shore.

title: Arcadia Beach State Recreation Site

gallery.alt: Rock formations and waves at Arcadia Beach

contentHtml:
Arcadia Beach State Recreation Site is a shady grove just off the highway, a few feet above a sandy ocean beach about a mile south of Cannon Beach.

The beach runs more than a mile between two headlands: Humbug Point to the north, which can only be passed at low tide, and Hug Point to the south. Visitors picnic, walk the beach, explore tidepools to the north and south, and watch surfers.

The sandstone bluffs were uplifted from the sea floor and show tilted, twisted rock layers. Watch the ocean and check the tide before heading out.
excerpt: Arcadia Beach State Recreation Site is a shady grove just off the highway, a few feet above a sandy ocean beach about a mile south of Cannon Beach.
note: Day-use area. Drones are not allowed.

title: Del Rey Beach State Recreation Site

gallery.alt: Dunes and mountains beyond the beach
Horseback riding on Del Rey Beach

contentHtml:
The ocean is just a short walk from Del Rey Beach's quiet, secluded parking area north of Gearhart.

It is a place to play on the wide beach, fly kites, build sandcastles or picnic, and the sunsets can be spectacular.
excerpt: The ocean is just a short walk from Del Rey Beach's quiet, secluded parking area north of Gearhart.
address: Near Gearhart, OR

title: Ecola State Park
imageAlt: Surfboards by a bench above the ocean

banner.alt: Surfboards by a bench above the ocean

gallery.alt: Ocean view with headlands and sea stacks

contentHtml:
Ecola State Park wraps around Tillamook Head between Seaside and Cannon Beach, with about 9 miles of coastline, a Sitka spruce entrance road, a grassy bluff over the Pacific and views tied to the 1806 travels of the Lewis and Clark Corps of Discovery.

About 8 miles of the Oregon Coast Trail cross the park, along with the 2.5-mile Clatsop Loop Trail and the Tillamook Head Trail, a National Recreation Trail. A primitive hike-in camp for coast trail hikers has three Adirondack-style shelters that sleep four each (no water).

Indian Beach is a secluded sandy beach popular with surfers, with tidepools nearby. Watch for deer, elk, eagles and, in winter and spring, migrating gray whales. Offshore stands Tillamook Rock Lighthouse.

note: Day-use parking permit required (sold on site). No overnight parking; drones prohibited; pets on a 6- foot leash. The west section of the Clatsop Loop Trail is closed by an active landslide.
address: Between Seaside and Cannon Beach, OR

title: Fort Stevens State Park
imageAlt: Rusty bow of the Peter Iredale shipwreck

banner.alt: Rusty bow of the Peter Iredale shipwreck

gallery.alt: Battery bunker with the ocean beyond

contentHtml:
Fort Stevens State Park was the main defense post in a three-fort harbor defense system at the mouth of the Columbia River, in service for 84 years from the Civil War to World War II. Today the park covers about 4,300 acres of beach, forest, wetland and dune.

Visitors tour the military museum, a Civil War-era earthen fort and concrete artillery batteries, and in summer the underground gun battery. The wreck of the Peter Iredale sits on the beach. Coffenbury Lake has swimming areas, picnic areas, restrooms, a boat ramp and a 2-mile lake trail, with summer ranger-guided kayak tours.

Paved bike trails and hiking trails wind through spruce and hemlock forest. The park is the northern trailhead of the Oregon Coast Trail, has the Columbia Shore disc golf course and seasonal bike rentals.

One of the nation's largest public campgrounds, it has 174 full-hookup sites, 302 electrical sites with water, 6 tent sites, 15 yurts, 11 deluxe cabins, primitive hike-in sites and a hiker/biker camp, with flush toilets and hot showers. Some yurts and cabins are pet-friendly and accessible.

note: Day-use parking permit required for all day-use areas (sold at kiosks, the visitor center or the ranger station). Camping reservations: (800) 452-5687, up to 6 months ahead.

title: Hug Point State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Hug Point State Recreation Site is a small wayside with forested picnic areas, a restroom and a short walkway down to a sandy cove beach between Austin Point and Hug Point.

A short walk north leads to a seasonal waterfall, caves in the sandstone cliffs and tidepools reachable at low tide, with Haystack Rock in view to the north.

Before the highway, the beach was the only road along this coast. At low tide you can walk the old stagecoach road north of the parking area, where wheel ruts are still carved into the rock; the point is named for travelers who had to hug the headland to get around it.

title: Saddle Mountain State Natural Area
contentHtml:
Saddle Mountain State Natural Area is known for wildflowers, mature forest, open grassy balds and a rocky summit. The 2.5-mile summit trail climbs about 1,640 feet from the parking lot to a viewing platform near 3,290 feet; it is steep and difficult in spots, so wear proper footwear.

On clear days the summit takes in the Columbia River meeting the sea, the Pacific shoreline and the Cascade Mountains. A shorter side trail branching off a quarter mile from the trailhead reaches a viewpoint in about 10 minutes.

The park has a day-use picnic area and a small seasonal campground with 10 primitive sites at the base of the mountain.

note: Weather changes quickly, with wind and rain year-round and snow in winter. Dogs must be leashed.

title: Sunset Beach State Recreation Site
imageAlt: Beach path leading to the ocean

banner.alt: Beach path leading to the ocean

contentHtml:
Sunset Beach State Recreation Site is a 120-acre park with direct access to the Pacific and wide views north to Cape Disappointment and south toward Ecola State Park.

It is the west trailhead of the Fort-to-Sea Trail, a 6.5-mile route that retraces the path the Lewis and Clark Corps of Discovery took between Fort Clatsop and the ocean in the winter of 1805-06.

Facilities include paved parking for 21 vehicles, an information station and an ADA-accessible boardwalk to the beach.
excerpt: Sunset Beach State Recreation Site is a 120-acre park with direct access to the Pacific and wide views north to Cape Disappointment and south toward Ecola State
address: Near Warrenton, OR

title: Tolovana Beach State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Tolovana Beach State Recreation Site is an oceanfront park at the south end of Cannon Beach, a place to play, fly kites, build sandcastles, picnic and watch the sunset.

Haystack Rock, the 235-foot basalt sea stack that is the town's landmark, is less than a mile north, home to tidepool life and nesting seabirds including tufted puffins. Please respect the protected area.

A playground sits on the north side of the parking lot, and a seasonal Mobi-Mat gives wheeled access across the sand.

title: Lewis and Clark
contentHtml:
Lewis and Clark National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1972, protects about 20 islands of Sitka spruce swamp, riparian forest, tidal marsh, mudflat and sandbar spread along roughly 27 miles of the Columbia River estuary, a landscape little changed in 200 years.

Its 12,167 acres are a wintering and resting ground for tundra swans, geese and ducks, hold 30 to 35 active bald eagle nests and give young salmon vital rearing water.

The refuge is reached only by boat. Day-use hours, hiking and hunting are regulated.

title: Oregon Islands

gallery.alt: Refuge staff with a puffin decoy on an offshore rock

contentHtml:
Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1935, is not one place but 1,853 rocks, reefs and islands plus two headlands, running from Tillamook Head near Seaside to the California border.

Most of Oregon's estimated 1.2 million nesting seabirds raise their young here, and seals and sea lions haul out and give birth on the rocks. All the rocks and islands except 1-acre Tillamook Rock are designated wilderness.

The islands are closed to entry, so watch from shore with binoculars or a spotting scope. In Clatsop County, Haystack Rock at Cannon Beach and Tillamook Rock off Ecola State Park are part of the refuge.

title: Julia Butler Hansen
contentHtml:
The Julia Butler Hansen Refuge for the Columbian White-tailed Deer was established in 1971 to protect the then-endangered Columbian white-tailed deer. Its more than 6,000 acres of pasture, forested tidal swamp, woodlot, marsh and slough lie on both the Washington and Oregon sides of the Columbia.

On the Oregon side, Tenasillahe Island is ringed by a 6.5-mile levee trail and reached only by boat or kayak; the Westport unit is on the mainland shore. Roosevelt elk, river otters, wintering birds and nesting bald eagles, great horned owls and osprey share the refuge.

Day-use hours, hiking and hunting are regulated. There is no camping on the refuge.

title: Jewell Meadows Wildlife Area
imageAlt: Feeding tour wagon among the elk

banner.alt: Feeding tour wagon among the elk

contentHtml:
Jewell Meadows Wildlife Area, established in 1969, covers 1,114 acres of the Coast Range and is managed as winter habitat for Roosevelt elk, to reduce elk damage on neighboring land and to let the public watch wildlife.

From November through April, up to 200 elk can be seen in the open pastures along Highway 202 from two paved parking areas and four viewing areas. The main meadow is a year-round refuge with no hunting or public access.

From December through February, ODFW runs free hour-long wagon tours where visitors help feed the elk, generally Thursday through Tuesday. Reservations open December 1 at 8 AM by phone.

title: Fishhawk Falls
contentHtml:
Fishhawk Falls drops 72 feet in two steps: Fishhawk Creek slides about 62 feet down a moss-covered bedrock face, then falls roughly 10 more feet over a wall of columnar basalt.

The falls are in Lee Wooden County Park, about 25.5 miles southeast of Astoria. Park improvements added a larger parking area and lengthened the trail to the falls by about a quarter mile. Small trees partly block the view from the trail's end; for a closer look you can wade or climb the hill beside the falls.

Jewell Meadows Wildlife Area, known for its elk herds, is about a mile downstream and makes a good second stop.

title: Plympton Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Plympton Creek Falls is a 53-foot waterfall on Plympton Creek in northeastern Clatsop County, dropping in three steps of 8, 30 and 15 feet according to Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife data.

The name is unofficial, and no directions or public trail information are published for the falls.

title: Youngs River Falls
imageAlt: Youngs River Falls with afternoon sun through the mist

banner.alt: Youngs River Falls with afternoon sun through the mist

contentHtml:
Youngs River Falls drops about 54 feet over a broad wall into a pool bordered by gravel bars. It flows year- round and is a popular local swimming spot close to Astoria.

Patrick Gass of the Lewis and Clark expedition recorded the falls in his journal on March 1, 1806. They appear in the films Free Willy 2 and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III.

The parking area is just off Youngs River Road before the bridge over the river. The falls are visible almost at once, and a short trail leads down to a rocky beach at their base.

title: Coffenbury Lake
contentHtml:
Coffenbury Lake is a freshwater lake inside Fort Stevens State Park near the mouth of the Columbia, with a forested shoreline suited to kayaks, stand-up paddleboards and canoes.

Launch from the boat ramp. The lake also has two picnic areas, restrooms, designated swimming areas and a roughly 2-mile trail around the shore. Motorboats are allowed at 10 mph.

note: State park day-use parking permit required (campers may use their camping receipt). Oregon boating rules apply, including Waterway Access Permits and life jackets.

title: Cullaby Lake
contentHtml:
Cullaby Lake is a flatwater lake on the Clatsop Plains between Astoria and Seaside, the centerpiece of 165- acre Cullaby Lake County Park, home of the Finnish-American Lindgren Cabin.

A 2.9-mile out-and-back easy paddle from the boat ramp crosses the open lake into narrowing water, wetland edges and a quiet wooded channel into Cullaby Slough, about 1.5 to 2 hours. Paddle in the morning, as afternoon winds pick up. Motorboats are allowed with no posted speed limit, and boat traffic can be heavy on some days.

The park has a boat launch and docks, flush restrooms, picnic shelters, play areas, fishing and swimming. Watch for beavers, bald eagles, deer and waterfowl. Best season April to October.

title: Lower Columbia River Water Trail
contentHtml:
The Lower Columbia River Water Trail runs 146 river miles from Bonneville Dam to the Pacific Ocean, along both the Oregon and Washington shores. Since 2000 the Lower Columbia Estuary Partnership has maintained the trail's launch points, camping and lodging, services and points of interest for non-motorized boats.

Paddlers pass bird-filled wetlands, island beaches and working marine parks, alongside barges, sailboats and cruise ships. Clatsop County holds the trail's lower end near Astoria.

The water is tidal flatwater with no whitewater, but tides, currents, wind and shipping traffic all need attention; the partnership's safety guide covers tides, weather and hazards.

address: Columbia River from Bonneville Dam to the Pacific Ocean; downstream end near Astoria

title: Neawanna Creek

gallery.alt: Red kayak passing under a low bridge
Kayaks on calm water between grassy banks

contentHtml:
Neawanna Creek is a quiet tidal waterway that shows a more natural side of Seaside, flowing into the Necanicum Estuary.

The easy 4.6-mile out-and-back route starts at the Broadway Park boat ramp and heads toward the estuary, taking about 1.5 to 2.5 hours. It is tidal, so go at high tide. Best season May to October.

The ADA-accessible kayak and canoe launch opened in 2015, and an osprey nest sits more than 70 feet above it.
excerpt: Neawanna Creek is a quiet tidal waterway that shows a more natural side of Seaside, flowing into the Necanicum Estuary.
address: Broadway Park boat ramp, Seaside, OR

title: Sunset Lake
contentHtml:
Sunset Lake is an easy-access freshwater paddle just outside Warrenton, mixing open-water views with quiet shoreline, lily pads and a narrow passage under a bridge.

The easy 2.4-mile out-and-back route from the Sunset Lake Park boat ramp takes about 1 to 1.5 hours. Paddle in the morning, as afternoon winds pick up. Motorboats are allowed at 10 mph, and boat traffic is generally light. Best season April to October.
excerpt: Sunset Lake is an easy-access freshwater paddle just outside Warrenton, mixing open-water views with quiet shoreline, lily pads and a narrow passage under a bri
address: Sunset Lake Park boat ramp, Warrenton, OR

title: Saddle Mountain
contentHtml:
At 3,288 feet, Saddle Mountain is the highest point in Clatsop County, with 2,323 feet of prominence. It formed about 15 million years ago when lava flowing down the ancient Columbia River valley met water and shattered into volcanic breccia.

A 2.5-mile trail in Saddle Mountain State Natural Area climbs about 1,640 feet to the summit through forest and wildflower balds. It is steep and slick in places.

The 360-degree summit view takes in the Pacific Ocean and, on clear days, Mount Hood, Mount St. Helens, Mount Rainier and Mount Adams.

note: Wind and rain year-round; snow in winter.

title: Oregon Coast Trail
imageAlt: Oregon Coast Trail sign along a forested trail

banner.alt: Oregon Coast Trail sign along a forested trail

contentHtml:
The Oregon Coast Trail follows Oregon's coastline from the Columbia River to the California border, about 382 miles by the official guide and about 425 miles if no ferries are used around the estuaries. It passes through 28 coastal towns.

Most of the route is on the beach, with other sections through state parks and public lands, on private land under trail easements, and on road shoulders. Clatsop County holds the northern end, starting at Fort Stevens State Park and crossing Tillamook Head in Ecola State Park.

Hiker/biker tent sites, first-come first-served, are at nearly every coastal state park. Check tide times, as some areas are passable only at low tide. During western snowy plover nesting season (March 15 to September 15), walk on wet sand in protected areas, where dogs, camping and beach fires are not allowed.
excerpt: The Oregon Coast Trail follows Oregon's coastline from the Columbia River to the California border, about 382 miles by the official guide and about 425 miles if
note: Trail conditions change quickly; check Oregon State Parks notices and Trailkeepers of Oregon alerts before you go.
address: Northern trailhead: Fort Stevens State Park, near Hammond, OR

title: Astoria Riverwalk
contentHtml:
The Astoria Riverwalk runs 6.4 flat miles of asphalt and boardwalk along the Columbia River on the old Burlington Northern rail corridor, from Pier 1 at the Port of Astoria east to the lagoons near Tongue Point.

It passes the working waterfront, where fishing boats unload beside cruise ships, the Columbia River Maritime Museum and the foot of the Astoria-Megler Bridge, with shops, dining and historic sites along the way. Lewis and Clark's party camped at nearby Tongue Point in March 1806.

The path is accessible and dog friendly. Cross the trolley tracks at a right angle, as they are slippery when wet. Parking is at the Maritime Memorial (200 W Marine Dr), Pier 1, the Port of Astoria, the Maritime Museum and the east-end lot on Lagoon Road.

note: The Astoria Riverfront Trolley shares the corridor; it has no wheelchair lift.
address: Astoria waterfront; main trailhead and parking at the Columbia River Maritime Museum, 1792 Marine Dr, Astoria, OR

title: Seaside Promenade
contentHtml:
The Seaside Promenade, known as the Prom, is a flat, paved, car-free walkway about 1.5 miles long and 15 feet wide along the Pacific, from Avenue U at the south end of town to 12th Avenue at the north. Built in 1920 and dedicated in 1921, it replaced an earlier wooden boardwalk.

At the Turnaround, where Broadway meets the ocean, a Lewis and Clark statue marks the end of the trail. Benches, close parking and a swing set line the way, with views of Tillamook Head, kites and sunsets.

The Prom brings people with limited mobility close to the beach, and Seaside's Mobi-Mat beach accesses at 12th Avenue and Avenue U reach the sand from it in season.

address: Seaside oceanfront, from Avenue U to 12th Avenue, Seaside, OR

title: David's Chair - Seaside
imageAlt: David's Chair track chair on the beach

banner.alt: David's Chair track chair on the beach

contentHtml:
David's Chair is a nonprofit that lends free, powered all-terrain track chairs to people with mobility challenges, in memory of Medford outdoorsman David Hartrick.

A chair is stationed at the Seaside Elks Lodge on Avenue A, about two and a half blocks from the Promenade, and is used on the beach off Avenue A. The chairs run by joystick, with a second joystick in back for a companion, and tilt so the rider sits upright while moving.

Sessions are about two hours, usually Thursday to Sunday. Reserve online at davidschair.org; a volunteer confirms by phone or text, and requests made less than 72 hours ahead may not be filled.

note: Free. Reserve at davidschair.org/request-fixed-location-chair/

title: Mobi-Mat - Seaside
imageAlt: Mobi-Mat across the sand in Seaside

banner.alt: Mobi-Mat across the sand in Seaside

contentHtml:
Seaside has two Mobi-Mat beach accesses, at 12th Avenue on the north side and Avenue U on the south, both reached from the Promenade. The sturdy, electric-blue mats are made of recycled polyester and anchored into the sand through the dunes.

They give a firm, flat, non-slip surface for wheelchairs, canes, strollers and wagons. Their length changes with ocean and tide conditions. The 12th Avenue entrance has a public parking lot and ramped restrooms.

note: Free, no booking. Mats are in place seasonally, roughly late May to early September, as conditions allow.

title: Mobi-Mat - Cannon Beach (Tolovana)
contentHtml:
A seasonal Mobi-Mat at Tolovana Beach State Recreation Site, at the south end of Cannon Beach, gives a firm, non-slip surface across the sand for wheelchair users, strollers and wagons.

From the beach, Haystack Rock is less than a mile north. The park also has parking and a playground on the north side of the lot.

contentHtml:
The Sunset Empire Park & Recreation District lends balloon-tire beach wheelchairs, the manual kind a companion pushes, free of charge from the Bob Chisholm Community Center.

Chairs are first-come, first-served with a 4-hour maximum, and reservations are encouraged, especially at busy times. Seaside also has a David's Chair track chair and Mobi-Mat beach accesses.

title: Beach Wheelchair Loan - Cannon Beach
contentHtml:
Free sand wheelchairs are checked out at Cannon Beach City Hall under a program run with the Haystack Rock Awareness Program.

The program began in 2017 so children and visitors with limited mobility could join the tidepool programs at Haystack Rock. A Mobi-Mat is also installed at Tolovana Beach at the south end of town.

title: Terrible Tilly
imageAlt: Ecola State Park coastline, on the route

banner.alt: Ecola State Park coastline, on the route

contentHtml:
Terrible Tilly is a 31-mile gravel bike loop from Cannon Beach with about 4,000 feet of climbing, roughly three-quarters gravel and one-quarter pavement. It is rated demanding, with grades up to 15 percent; 45 mm or wider tires are recommended.

The route climbs through Ecola State Park past the Ecola Point viewpoint, the best view of Tillamook Rock Lighthouse (the 'Terrible Tilly' of its name), and Indian Beach, then crosses Lewis & Clark Timberlands, Klootchy Creek County Park and the Necanicum River before returning through the Ecola Creek Forest Reserve, Cannon Beach's drinking water source.

Expect elk, logging trucks and an open ford of Ecola Creek near mile 28.5; walk your bike through if the water is high. Free parking and restrooms are near the start.

title: Pacific Coast Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway
Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway
Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway

contentHtml:
The Pacific Coast Scenic Byway, an All-American Road, follows US 101 for 363 miles along the whole Oregon coast, from Astoria at the Washington border to Brookings at the California border.

In Clatsop County the byway starts at the Astoria-Megler Bridge and passes Astoria's waterfront, Fort Stevens, Seaside and Cannon Beach. Farther south, highlights include clamming on Tillamook Bay, kayaking Alsea Bay, the dramatic rocks and islands of the south coast and jet boat trips up the Rogue River at Gold Beach.

EV charging stations are spaced along the route, making an electric road trip from Astoria to Brookings possible.

title: North Coast Food Trail
contentHtml:
The North Coast Food Trail is a culinary route along Oregon's north coast, from Astoria, Seaside and Cannon Beach through the Tillamook Coast to Lincoln City, billed as 85 miles and 60 stops to savor.

Stops include restaurants, beer and wine tastings, farm tours, bakeries, markets and lodging, built around wild seafood, artisan cheese and craft brews. It won a 2018 Travel Oregon award.

The month-long Crave the Coast festival runs along the trail each October.

title: Tillamook Rock Lighthouse
contentHtml:
Tillamook Rock Lighthouse was first lit on January 21, 1881, to guide ships toward the Columbia River. Quarrymen landed on the basalt rock in October 1879 and built the station over more than 200 days of work; its light stood 133 feet above the sea.

Nicknamed 'Terrible Tilly' for its storm-battered exposure, it was closed by the Coast Guard on September 1, 1957. The privately owned rock is part of Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, and the lighthouse is on the National Register of Historic Places.

There is no public access. The best view is from Ecola Point in Ecola State Park.

address: Tillamook Rock, about 1.2 miles off Tillamook Head; viewed from Ecola State Park

title: Astoria-Megler Bridge

gallery.alt: Traffic on the bridge, looking north

contentHtml:
The Astoria-Megler Bridge carries US 101 4.1 miles across the mouth of the Columbia River from Astoria to Point Ellice, Washington. Opened in 1966, it is the longest continuous truss bridge in North America, with 140 spans in the water.

More than 9,000 vehicles cross it on an average day. Pedestrians may cross only once a year, during the Great Columbia Crossing 10K. Good views are from the Astoria Riverwalk and the Maritime Memorial at the bridge's foot.

address: US 101 across the Columbia River, from Astoria, OR to Point Ellice, WA

title: Tillamook Rock Lighthouse
contentHtml:
After the light was closed in 1957, Tillamook Rock Lighthouse became the only lighthouse ever converted into a columbarium. A real estate developer bought it in 1980, gutted the interior and opened the Eternity at Sea Columbarium, where ashes were interred for $1,000 to $5,000.

The columbarium lost its license in 1999 over inaccurate recordkeeping. The rock remains privately owned and closed to the public, and is viewed from Ecola State Park.

address: Tillamook Rock, about a mile off Tillamook Head; viewed from Ecola State Park

title: Wreck of the Peter Iredale
contentHtml:
The Peter Iredale, a four-masted steel bark built in Maryport, England, in 1890, ran aground on Clatsop Spit on October 25, 1906, bound for Portland to load wheat for the United Kingdom. A squall and a strong current drove it ashore while it waited to cross the Columbia River bar; all 27 aboard, including two stowaways, reached shore safely.

The ship was a total loss. Its rusting bow and ribs still rise from the sand at Fort Stevens State Park, where visitors walk around them at low tide. It is one of the most photographed spots on the Oregon coast, in the waters sailors call the Graveyard of the Pacific.

title: Astoria Riverfront Trolley
imageAlt: Astoria Riverfront Trolley at a stop

banner.alt: Astoria Riverfront Trolley at a stop

contentHtml:
The Astoria Riverfront Trolley is a volunteer-run heritage streetcar along about 3 miles of former freight track on the Columbia River waterfront, from Basin Street to 39th Street, with narration that changes on the return trip. A round trip takes about an hour.

Its car, Old 300, was built in 1913 by the American Car Company of St. Louis for the San Antonio Traction Company in Texas. It was restored by volunteers and began Astoria service in 1999, and the Astoria Riverfront Trolley Association bought it in 2005.

Board at any of 12 stops or flag the car down anywhere along the line. The trolley does not run in the rain.

note: Season runs about March 20 to November 1. Fare $1 per boarding or $2 all-day pass (cash or Venmo). Charters $200 per hour: (503) 325-8790. Email: AstoriaTrolley@gmail.com. Pets allowed.

title: Astoria Brewing Company
imageAlt: Astoria Brewing and the Wet Dog Cafe

banner.alt: Astoria Brewing and the Wet Dog Cafe

contentHtml:
Astoria Brewing Company is Astoria's oldest microbrewery, overlooking the Columbia River since 1997. It began as a small brewery at the Wet Dog Cafe, first called Pacific Rim Brewery, and took the Astoria Brewing name in 2005 to honor the city's first brewery of 1872.

Its best-known beer is the Bitter Bitch Imperial IPA, whose success funded a 2012 expansion with a new taproom and a larger brewhouse for canning. In 2018 the brewpub dropped the Wet Dog Cafe name and became Astoria Brewing Company, now run by the founding Allen family and longtime manager Matthew McClure.

title: Bill's Tavern & Brewhouse
contentHtml:
Bill's Tavern & Brewhouse is Cannon Beach's original brewery, a locally owned, family-run tavern that has brewed its own ales on site since 1997. The founders of Astoria's Fort George Brewery got their start brewing here.

The handcrafted ales change over time, from Duck Dive Pale Ale to old-school English styles; check the board or ask your server. The kitchen serves coastal tavern fare such as fish and chips and burgers in a wooden, dimly lit pub.

title: Buoy Beer Company
contentHtml:
Buoy Beer Company was founded in Astoria in 2014, drawing its inspiration from the salt air and history of the place where the Columbia River meets the coast. After its original pier brewpub partially collapsed in 2022, the taproom moved to Duane Street downtown.

Year-round beers include its well-known Czech Pilsner and NW Red Ale, plus an IPA, Cream Ale, Pacific Pale Ale and Helles Lager, with rotating lager, benefit and barrel series. The taproom has three food trucks and cocktails made with Pilot House Distilling spirits.
