title: Fort George Brewery
contentHtml:
Fort George Brewery opened in 2007 and is credited with helping revive downtown Astoria. It has grown from a single brewpub into a city block of restaurants, tasting rooms, breweries, community spaces and music venues, including the 1922 Lovell building, a former auto dealership that survived the 1923 downtown fire.

Known for Vortex IPA and Cavatica Stout, it also pours pilsners, tree beers and many collaborations. Eat at the Downstairs Pub, Fort George Pizza upstairs or weekend brunch in the Lovell Taproom.

Fort George hosts talks, benefit nights, Sunday music and the Festival of Dark Arts each February.

title: Obelisk Beer Co.
contentHtml:
Obelisk Beer Co. opened in Astoria in 2022, started by former Fort George brewers. It honors tradition while embracing innovation, rooted in slow beer and good times.

The small-batch lineup runs from light, approachable lagers and ales to barrel-aged brews, such as the Sun Shrine German-style ale, Automagically hazy double IPA and collaborations with other Northwest breweries.

title: Public Coast Brewing Company
contentHtml:
Public Coast Brewing Co. opened in June 2016 as a brewery, restaurant and bar in Cannon Beach. It is named for Governor Tom McCall's landmark 1967 law that keeps Oregon's coastline open to the public.

Its flagship '67 Blonde Ale won gold at the 2018 Oregon Beer Awards. Alongside limited releases it makes seltzers, sodas and cold-brewed teas, some using blueberries, peaches, lavender, hops and mushrooms from its own Public Coast Farm. The family-friendly menu runs to burgers, fish and chips and chili.

The brewery celebrated its 10th anniversary in 2026.

title: Seaside Brewing Company
contentHtml:
Seaside Brewery opened in 2011 in Seaside's historic City Hall and City Jail, built from 1912 to 1914 after a fire destroyed much of downtown. The bar is built around the original jail cell, the old drunk tank, which now holds the keg cooler, with taps coming out of its wall.

The building sat mostly empty after city offices left in 1989 and was restored from 2011 with mostly locally reclaimed wood. Beers include Sneaker Wave IPA, a Marionberry Hefeweizen and a Belgian tripel, served with BBQ from two 1,000-gallon smokers: brisket, pulled pork, ribs, fish and more.

title: Columbia Shore DGC
contentHtml:
Columbia Shore DGC is set in the Fort Stevens historic area next to the Columbia River. Established in 2019 and designed by Chad McHugh, it has 23 holes on hilly ground, rated easy to moderate, with asphalt, rubber and concrete tees.

The full course is about 2.7 miles and takes around 2 hours 10 minutes. It is rated 4.6 out of 5 by more than 2,100 players, with top marks for scenery, and ranks among Oregon's best courses.

Play in the morning to avoid the wind and keep dogs on a leash. Discs are sold at the fort museum. Restrooms, drinking water and cart-friendly paths are available.

title: Columbia County Museum
contentHtml:
The Columbia County Museum is run by the volunteer Columbia County Museum Association, which preserves and shares the history of the county's towns, schools, cemeteries and people.

In 2025 the museum moved into the newly renovated John Gumm Building and Civic Center in St. Helens. Volunteers there help with research requests, and the association publishes local histories and runs programs on more than 35 topics.

title: Vernonia Pioneer Museum
contentHtml:
The Vernonia Pioneer Museum holds artifacts, pictures and stories of the Nehalem Valley's logging and pioneer past.

It is housed in the Oregon-American Lumber Company Mill Office, a Craftsman bungalow built around 1924 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2002.
excerpt: The Vernonia Pioneer Museum holds artifacts, pictures and stories of the Nehalem Valley's logging and pioneer past.
note: Free admission. Also open by appointment.
address: 511 E Bridge St, Vernonia, OR 97064

title: Caples House Museum
contentHtml:
The Caples House Museum is the 1870 home of Dr. Charles Green Caples, who came over the Oregon Trail as a child in 1844 and was for years the only doctor in Columbia County. He saw patients and performed surgery in the house, and his wife Lucinda worked as a midwife. His father founded Columbia City in 1852.

In 1959 the family's daughter left the property to the Oregon State Society, Daughters of the American Revolution, which runs it as a museum. It is on the National Register of Historic Places.

The hillside grounds overlook the Columbia River and include the barn, pioneer tool shed, a children's toy museum, the Tea Cottage and gazebo, the Knapp Social Center, a medicinal herb garden and a heritage apple and pear orchard.

title: Watts House Pioneer Museum
contentHtml:
The Watts House Pioneer Museum is the 1902 Queen Anne home of James Grant Watts, a founder of Scappoose and its first mayor, listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The Scappoose Historical Society, founded in 1974, preserves and runs it.

The lower level is a children's museum that recreates an 1888 pioneer mercantile. The house opens for society events through the year, including holiday tours.

title: Banks–Vernonia State Trail

gallery.alt: Cyclists on a wooden bridge over a stream
Cyclists on the paved path through the forest

contentHtml:
The Banks-Vernonia State Trail is Oregon's first rails-to-trails park, 21 miles on an abandoned railroad bed between Banks and Vernonia. An 8-foot paved path for walkers and cyclists runs beside a gravel horse trail about 4 feet wide.

Highlights include 13 bridges and the 733-foot Buxton Trestle, 80 feet high. The trailheads at Vernonia, Beaver Creek, Tophill, Buxton, Manning and Banks have parking and restrooms.

The grade is gentle, averaging about 2.5 percent, and the trail is classed as accessible. Short highway-crossing sections reach about 11 percent and one short stretch near the Buxton Trestle is unpaved, so it is not barrier- free end to end. The flattest stretches are Banks to Buxton and Beaver Creek to Vernonia. The Tualatin Valley Scenic Bikeway follows the trail.

note: Day-use parking permit required (buy on site); no overnight parking. E-bikes allowed. Pets on a 6-foot leash. Bridge decks can be uneven and slippery.

title: Julia Butler Hansen
contentHtml:
The Julia Butler Hansen Refuge for the Columbian White-tailed Deer was established in 1971 to protect the then-endangered Columbian white-tailed deer. Its more than 6,000 acres of pasture, tidal swamp, woodlot, marsh and slough lie on both the Washington and Oregon sides of the Columbia.

In Columbia County the refuge holds Crims Island and Wallace Island, river islands reached only by boat and open to foot traffic only. Their shorelines open seasonally for waterfowl hunting. Roosevelt elk, river otters, wintering birds and nesting bald eagles, great horned owls and osprey share the refuge.

There is no camping on the refuge.

title: Beaver Falls

gallery.alt: Beaver Falls at high flow from Old Route 30

contentHtml:
Beaver Falls drops 48 feet in a broad curtain from a shelf about 50 feet wide into an amphitheater of columnar basalt on Beaver Creek, near Clatskanie. In the wet season a small side stream adds a second falls.

A formal trail, a relatively easy quarter mile, leads from a large gravel pullout on Delena Road down to the base, so the falls can be visited year-round. It is a popular local swimming spot.

From the Lewis and Clark Bridge junction, drive west on US 30 for 5 miles, bear right onto Delena Road (Old Route 30) and go 3.8 miles to the pullout.

note: The last few hundred feet of trail are prone to slides and occasionally close.
address: Delena Rd (Old Route 30), about 3.8 miles off US 30, near Clatskanie, OR

title: Jack Falls
contentHtml:
Jack Falls is a 70-foot horsetail on tiny Jack Falls Creek, once a popular stop on the old Columbia River Highway near Rainier and now easy to miss since the road was realigned.

The small creek dries up in summer; in winter it sprays down the hillside and strikes a few rocks before running under the old roadbed.

note: No developed or officially sanctioned access. Nettles and blackberries cover the old roadbed.
address: Old Columbia River Highway (US 30) near Rainier, OR

title: Lower Columbia River Water Trail
contentHtml:
The Lower Columbia River Water Trail runs 146 river miles from Bonneville Dam to the Pacific Ocean, along both the Oregon and Washington shores. Since 2000 the Lower Columbia Estuary Partnership has maintained the trail's launch points, camping and lodging, services and points of interest for non-motorized boats.

Paddlers pass bird-filled wetlands, island beaches and working marine parks, alongside barges, sailboats and cruise ships. In Columbia County, Scappoose Bay Marine Park at river mile 89 has a boat launch and paddlers' dock.

The water is tidal flatwater with no whitewater, but tides, currents, wind and shipping traffic all need attention; the partnership's safety guide covers tides, weather and hazards.

address: Columbia River from Bonneville Dam to the Pacific; Columbia County launches include Scappoose Bay Marine Park, Warren, OR

title: Long Mountain
contentHtml:
At 2,265 feet, Long Mountain in the Oregon Coast Range is the highest point in Columbia County and the lowest county high point in Oregon.

The summit lies in Weyerhaeuser's Columbia-Washington Counties recreational permit area, where the logging-road approaches are gated. The long way in is a logging-road hike of about 12 miles round trip under a Weyerhaeuser recreation permit; a shorter foot approach of about 1.5 miles each way reaches the peak over BLM land from the southeast, by way of Bacona and Hoffman Roads.
excerpt: At 2,265 feet, Long Mountain in the Oregon Coast Range is the highest point in Columbia County and the lowest county high point in Oregon.
note: Sources differ on whether the summit needs a permit; check Weyerhaeuser's recreation access rules before going.
address: Coast Range, west of Scappoose; approached by logging roads near Bacona

title: Banks-Vernonia State Trail

gallery.alt: Cyclists on a wooden bridge over a stream
Cyclists on the paved path through the forest

contentHtml:
The Banks-Vernonia State Trail is Oregon's first rails-to-trails park, 21 miles on an abandoned railroad bed between Banks and Vernonia. An 8-foot paved path for walkers and cyclists runs beside a gravel horse trail about 4 feet wide.

Highlights include 13 bridges and the 733-foot Buxton Trestle, 80 feet high. The trailheads at Vernonia, Beaver Creek, Tophill, Buxton, Manning and Banks have parking and restrooms.

The grade is gentle, averaging about 2.5 percent, and the trail is classed as accessible. Short highway-crossing sections reach about 11 percent and one short stretch near the Buxton Trestle is unpaved, so it is not barrier- free end to end. The flattest stretches are Banks to Buxton and Beaver Creek to Vernonia. The Tualatin Valley Scenic Bikeway follows the trail.

note: Day-use parking permit required (buy on site); no overnight parking. E-bikes allowed. Pets on a 6-foot leash. Bridge decks can be uneven and slippery.
address: Banks Trailhead, NW Banks Rd and NW Sellers Rd, Banks, OR; northern end at Anderson Park, Vernonia

title: Crown Zellerbach Trail
contentHtml:
The Crown Zellerbach (CZ) Trail is a 23.4-mile rail-trail across Columbia County from Vernonia to Scappoose on the former Portland and Southwestern Railroad, later a logging road. It reopened to the public in 2014 and is a National Recreation Trail.

More than half is gravel, some of it loose, with grades near 20 percent in places, so wide tires help. The western end climbs from Vernonia through shaded forest along the Nehalem River and Scappoose Creek; the eastern end past Ruley is mostly flat through wetlands to Chapman Landing on Multnomah Channel. Highlights include Bonnie Falls and a 1920 railroad tunnel.

About ten trailheads, including Holce, Floeter, Ruley, Trtek and Chapman Landing, offer restrooms, picnic areas and repair stations. Horses are allowed along the whole trail, the Trtek to Chapman Landing section is ADA compliant, and at Vernonia Lake Park it connects to the Banks-Vernonia State Trail.
excerpt: The Crown Zellerbach (CZ) Trail is a 23.4-mile rail-trail across Columbia County from Vernonia to Scappoose on the former Portland and Southwestern Railroad, la
note: Open dawn to dusk; leashed pets allowed. The trail crosses US 30 at a signaled intersection.
address: Holce Trailhead, 1780 E Knott St, Vernonia, OR to Chapman Landing, Scappoose, OR

title: Tualatin Valley Scenic Bikeway
contentHtml:
The Tualatin Valley Scenic Bikeway runs about 50 miles one way from Rood Bridge Park in Hillsboro through Forest Grove and Banks to Anderson Park in Vernonia. It was designated an Oregon Scenic Bikeway in 2013.

The first half winds along valley back roads past dairy farms, vineyards, farm stands and the Tualatin River's wetlands. The second half follows the car-free Banks-Vernonia State Trail over trestles and through forest, climbing about 600 feet at gentle grades into Columbia County.

It is rated moderate: fine for regular riders, with some traffic and hills. Both ends are parks with parking, restrooms and water, and riders can camp at L.L. Stub Stewart State Park.
excerpt: The Tualatin Valley Scenic Bikeway runs about 50 miles one way from Rood Bridge Park in Hillsboro through Forest Grove and Banks to Anderson Park in Vernonia. I
address: Rood Bridge Park, Hillsboro, OR to Anderson Park, Vernonia, OR

title: North Coast Food Trail
contentHtml:
The North Coast Food Trail is a culinary route along Oregon's north coast, from Astoria, Seaside and Cannon Beach through the Tillamook Coast to Lincoln City, billed as 85 miles and 60 stops to savor.

Stops include restaurants, beer and wine tastings, farm tours, bakeries, markets and lodging, built around wild seafood, artisan cheese and craft brews. It won a 2018 Travel Oregon award.

Columbia County's stop on the trail is in Clatskanie. The month-long Crave the Coast festival runs along the trail each October.

address: Astoria, Seaside and Cannon Beach south through the Tillamook Coast to Lincoln City

title: Warrior Rock Lighthouse
contentHtml:
Warrior Rock Lighthouse is Oregon's smallest lighthouse, a 28-foot octagonal concrete tower built in 1930 on the sandstone base of the original 1889 light. It guards a bedrock reef at the tip of Sauvie Island and is one of only two working Oregon lighthouses not on the ocean, the last on the Columbia River.

Reach it by an easy, nearly flat 3-mile trail (6 miles round trip) through the Sauvie Island Wildlife Area from the north end of Reeder Road, or by a short boat ride from St. Helens. The exterior is open to the public.

Its 1855 fog bell, the Northwest's oldest, was cracked when a barge struck the tower in 1969. It now stands outside the Columbia County Courthouse in St. Helens beside a half-scale replica of the lighthouse.

address: Northeast tip of Sauvie Island, across Multnomah Channel from St. Helens, OR

title: St. Helens Riverfront District
contentHtml:
St. Helens' Riverfront District, a 10-block National Register historic district on the Columbia, is an Oregon Film Trail stop. Most of Disney's Halloweentown (1998) was filmed here, and the town played Port Angeles for the first Twilight movie (2008), including Bella's house, the bookstore and the dress shop.

Every fall since 1998 the Spirit of Halloweentown festival turns the district into a Halloween destination with a giant pumpkin in the plaza, costume contests, a parade, a haunted house and themed weekends, drawing tens of thousands of visitors.

The district also has views of the Columbia River, Mount Hood and Mount St. Helens.
excerpt: St. Helens' Riverfront District, a 10-block National Register historic district on the Columbia, is an Oregon Film Trail stop. Most of Disney's Halloweentown (1
note: Festival details: spiritofhalloweentown.com
address: St. Helens Riverfront District, along S 1st St, St. Helens, OR

title: Crooked Creek Brewery
contentHtml:
Crooked Creek Brewery brews rustic ales and lagers inspired by Belgian traditions and Northwest ingredients in a converted pole barn beside a creek in rural Columbia County, using Warren's well-regarded water.

Its taproom on the St. Helens riverfront is kid-friendly, with a dog-friendly patio, cider, Northwest wines and Oregon-spirit cocktails. Chef Jill Ramseier runs a full kitchen of seasonal comfort food and pub favorites, including a house-made sourdough pretzel with beer-cheese sauce.

Events include trivia, cribbage, live music and Pints for Nonprofits on the first Thursday of each month.

note: Email: hello@crookedcreekbrewery.com
address: 343 S 1st St, St. Helens, OR 97051

title: McCormick Park
contentHtml:
McCormick Park is a technical wooded 18-hole course in St. Helens with mostly natural boundaries, multiple pin placements on 11 holes, concrete tees and DISCatcher Pro baskets. It is about 2.5 miles long.

The hilly course is rated hard to very hard, with tight paths and elevation changes over rocky ground; blackberries or high water can make some holes tough going. Par runs from about 58 to 64 depending on the layout (59 for the winter layout).

It is rated 4.3 out of 5 by more than 1,800 players. Drinking water and a restroom are available, and dogs are allowed.
excerpt: McCormick Park is a technical wooded 18-hole course in St. Helens with mostly natural boundaries, multiple pin placements on 11 holes, concrete tees and DISCatc
note: Free to play. Not cart- or stroller-friendly.
address: McCormick Park, St. Helens, OR

title: Riverfront Park
contentHtml:
Riverfront Park in Rainier has a 9-hole introductory, family-friendly course in a multi-use park on the Columbia, with concrete tees, metal baskets and holes from 150 to 430 feet. A few holes have out-of-bounds.

Please respect other park users and pack out your trash. The park is drug and alcohol free.
excerpt: Riverfront Park in Rainier has a 9-hole introductory, family-friendly course in a multi-use park on the Columbia, with concrete tees, metal baskets and holes fr
note: Free to play.
address: Rainier City Park (Riverfront Park), Rainier, OR 97048

title: Trojan Park
contentHtml:
Trojan Park is a competitive 18-hole course set around a lake fed by the Columbia River, on the site of the former Trojan Nuclear Power Plant. It is about 3.2 miles long, par 63, with water and thick vegetation as natural out-of-bounds.

The ground is mostly flat but the course is rated very hard. Watch for bald eagles, turtles and geese around the lake. It is rated 4.1 out of 5 by more than 800 players.
excerpt: Trojan Park is a competitive 18-hole course set around a lake fed by the Columbia River, on the site of the former Trojan Nuclear Power Plant. It is about 3.2 m
note: Free to play. Restroom buildings open in summer; portable toilets year-round.
address: Trojan Park, near Rainier (Prescott), OR

title: Yankton Community Fellowship Church
contentHtml:
Yankton Community Fellowship's short recreational course has 9 tee pads and 5 baskets that some holes share, set among light woods with moderate elevation changes. It plays differently in leafy spring and summer than in fall and winter.

Established in 2012, it is a good warm-up before Trojan Park or McCormick Park.
excerpt: Yankton Community Fellowship's short recreational course has 9 tee pads and 5 baskets that some holes share, set among light woods with moderate elevation chang
note: Free to play. Closed on Sundays and during church functions; check in at the office if unsure. Park only in the signed disc golf area. Recent players report missing baskets.
address: Yankton Community Fellowship, 33579 Pittsburg Rd, St. Helens, OR 97051

title: Coos History Museum
imageAlt: Coos History Museum building with flag and boat display

banner.alt: Coos History Museum building with flag and boat display

contentHtml:
The Coos History Museum & Maritime Collection overlooks Coos Bay along Highway 101. It is run by the Coos County Historical Society, founded in 1891 and one of Oregon's oldest continuously operating local historical societies.

The community-built museum opened in 2015 with support from more than 550 donors. Its collection of more than 250,000 historic photographs and objects covers the region's Native nations, coal mining, logging, ranching, fishing, shipbuilding and local shipwrecks.

Rotating exhibits, a museum shop, event space and a bayfront plaza round out the visit.
excerpt: The Coos History Museum & Maritime Collection overlooks Coos Bay along Highway 101. It is run by the Coos County Historical Society, founded in 1891 and one of
note: Closed on major holidays. Email: info@cooshistory.org
address: 1210 N Front St, Coos Bay, OR 97420

title: Marshfield Sun Printing Museum
imageAlt: Marshfield Sun Printing Museum sign, established 1891

banner.alt: Marshfield Sun Printing Museum sign, established 1891

contentHtml:
The Marshfield Sun Printing Museum preserves the original shop and equipment of The Sun, a Marshfield (now Coos Bay) newspaper printed here from 1891 to 1944, with its working presses and type.

Exhibits cover the history of printing and of the local community.
excerpt: The Marshfield Sun Printing Museum preserves the original shop and equipment of The Sun, a Marshfield (now Coos Bay) newspaper printed here from 1891 to 1944, w
note: Open Memorial Day to Labor Day. Off-season and group tours by appointment: (541) 266-0901.
address: 1049 N Front St, Coos Bay, OR 97420

title: Bandon Historical Society Museum
contentHtml:
The Bandon Historical Society Museum, run by the Bandon Historical Society since 1976, tells the story of a town "blessed by water and cursed by fire." It is housed in Bandon's former City Hall, the second building raised after the 1936 fire that leveled the town.

Exhibits run from the Native peoples of the Coquille River mouth and their basketry through shipbuilding, shipwrecks and beach life, the Coast Guard, fires and floods, gold, wind and golf, and cheese, trees and cranberries.

The gift shop sells books, jewelry and myrtlewood items.

note: Admission: adults $3; members and children free. Hours: Monday to Saturday 10 AM - 4 PM most of the year; daily 10 AM - 4 PM June to September; closed in January. Email: bandonhistoricalmuseum@yahoo.com
address: 270 Fillmore Ave (Highway 101 and Fillmore), Bandon, OR 97411

title: Charleston Marine Life Center
imageAlt: A child at the tidepool touch tank

banner.alt: A child at the tidepool touch tank

contentHtml:
The Charleston Marine Life Center is the University of Oregon's public aquarium and museum at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology, opened in 2016 on the Charleston harbor.

Five galleries cover Oregon marine life from shore to deep sea. Gray and killer whale skeletons hang above the lobby, visitors can reach into a sperm whale skull, and a tidepool touch tank, aquaria with a giant Pacific octopus and sea slugs, and deep-sea specimens collected by the submersible Alvin fill the rest.

An open-air deck looks over the working harbor, where fishing boats unload and seals and sea lions swim. Microscopes, binoculars and loaner macro lenses invite a closer look.
excerpt: The Charleston Marine Life Center is the University of Oregon's public aquarium and museum at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology, opened in 2016 on the Char
note: Admission: adults $8; seniors 62+, active military and AAA $6; children and students free. Closed November 26 and December 24-25. Email: cmlc@uoregon.edu
address: 63466 Boat Basin Rd, Charleston, OR 97420

title: Coquille Valley Museum
imageAlt: Exterior of the Coquille Valley Museum

banner.alt: Exterior of the Coquille Valley Museum

contentHtml:
The Coquille Valley Museum, run by the Coquille Valley Historical Society since 2005, is in downtown Coquille near the county courthouse.

Exhibits cover the Coquel people, the wood products industry, dairy farming, coal mining and the Coquille River as the valley's 'river highway', along with a genealogy library.
excerpt: The Coquille Valley Museum, run by the Coquille Valley Historical Society since 2005, is in downtown Coquille near the county courthouse.
note: Volunteer-run; hours can change, so call ahead.
address: 153 N Central Blvd, Coquille, OR 97423

title: Coos County Logging Museum
imageAlt: Entrance to the Coos County Logging Museum

banner.alt: Entrance to the Coos County Logging Museum

contentHtml:
The Coos County Logging Museum tells the story of South Coast timber in a cedar-shingled, onion-domed building begun in 1910 for the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints and modeled on the Mormon Tabernacle. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979 and opened as a museum in 1987.

Inside are antique logging equipment, rare photographs, a scale model of the Gardiner sawmill and nine large hand-carved myrtlewood panels by Alexander Benjamin Warnock showing the timber industry's heyday.
excerpt: The Coos County Logging Museum tells the story of South Coast timber in a cedar-shingled, onion-domed building begun in 1910 for the Reorganized Church of Jesus
note: Free admission (donations welcome). Open Memorial Day to Labor Day; for tours at other times, leave a message.
address: 705 Maple St, Myrtle Point, OR 97458

title: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest
contentHtml:
The Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest covers about 1.8 million acres of southwest Oregon, from the Cascades to the coast, managed through five ranger districts: High Cascades, Siskiyou Mountains, Wild Rivers, Gold Beach and Powers.

In Coos County the forest's Powers Ranger District takes in the South Fork Coquille River country with its waterfalls and small campgrounds. Across the forest, highlights include Applegate Lake, Mount McLoughlin and the Siskiyou and Sky Lakes wilderness areas.
excerpt: The Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest covers about 1.8 million acres of southwest Oregon, from the Cascades to the coast, managed through five ranger distric
note: Forest headquarters is in Medford. Powers Ranger District: (541) 439-6200.
address: 3040 Biddle Rd, Medford, OR 97504

title: Siuslaw National Forest
contentHtml:
The Siuslaw National Forest covers more than 630,000 acres of the Oregon coast and Coast Range, and is one of only two national forests in the lower 48 states with oceanfront land. Its landscapes run from mossy coastal mountain forests to sand dunes and Pacific beaches.

Highlights include Cape Perpetua Scenic Area with its rocky headlands, Cascade Head with native prairie and rare wildflowers, the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, and Marys Peak, the highest point in the Coast Range, just west of Corvallis. Visitors come for old-growth forest, waterfalls, camping and off-highway vehicle riding on the dunes.

note: Forest headquarters is in Corvallis

title: Oregon Islands Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Oregon Islands Wilderness covers the rocks, reefs and islands of Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, some 1,853 of them strung along about 320 miles of coastline from Tillamook Head near Seaside to the California border.

The islands are breeding and resting grounds for most of Oregon's estimated 1.2 million nesting seabirds, including tufted puffins and cormorants, and for seals and sea lions that haul out and give birth there.

In Coos County, Coquille Point in Bandon is the refuge's mainland unit and a good place to look out over the wilderness rocks. The islands are closed to public entry; bring binoculars or a spotting scope and watch from shore.
excerpt: The Oregon Islands Wilderness covers the rocks, reefs and islands of Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, some 1,853 of them strung along about 320 miles of
note: All rocks and islands are closed to the public. Email: Oregoncoast@fws.gov
address: Offshore rocks and islands along the Oregon coast; Coquille Point in Bandon is the mainland viewing area

title: Wild Rogue Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Wild Rogue Wilderness protects 36,453 acres of rugged canyon country along the Rogue River in Curry and Coos counties. Designated in 1978, it is managed jointly by the U.S. Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management.

The year-round, hiker-only Rogue River National Recreation Trail #1160 follows about 15 of its 40 miles through the wilderness between Graves Creek and Illahe. Other trails include Panther Ridge #1253, Mule Creek #1159 and the Mount Bolivar Trail #1259 to the 4,319-foot summit.

The river itself is famous for rafting and for salmon and steelhead fishing. Under Wild and Scenic River rules, motorboats and riverside lodges are allowed on the river.

note: No motorized or mechanical transport in the wilderness. Group size limit: 12 people and 9 head of stock.

title: Park Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Park Creek is a quiet Bureau of Land Management campground in the forested Coast Range east of Coquille, with 15 first-come, first-served sites and no camping fee.

To get there from Coquille, take Fairview Road 9 miles, then Lone Pine Road 4 miles, and turn left on Middle Creek Road. Bear right at the Y at milepost 8, cross the bridge and continue 2 more miles.
excerpt: Park Creek is a quiet Bureau of Land Management campground in the forested Coast Range east of Coquille, with 15 first-come, first-served sites and no camping f
note: Vault toilet; no drinking water. Open fires banned July 1 - September 30. 14-day stay limit. Email: BLM_OR_CB_Mail@blm.gov
address: Middle Creek Rd, east of Coquille, OR (BLM Coos Bay District)

title: Bandon State Natural Area
imageAlt: Sunset over the beach and sea stacks

banner.alt: Sunset over the beach and sea stacks

gallery.alt: Seals resting on a rocky shore
Aerial view of forest and sandy path

contentHtml:
Bandon State Natural Area stretches along Bandon's Beach Loop Road, with several beach access points, picnic spots and wide ocean views over Bandon's sea stacks. "Bandon awaits the beachcomber, the explorer, the artist and the dreamer."

Parking is ample at every access point.
excerpt: Bandon State Natural Area stretches along Bandon's Beach Loop Road, with several beach access points, picnic spots and wide ocean views over Bandon's sea stacks
note: No beach camping from Bandon to Floras Lake.
address: Beach Loop Rd, Bandon, OR 97411

title: Bullards Beach State Park
contentHtml:
Bullards Beach is a large, family-friendly park two miles north of Bandon, with campsites tucked among shore pines and sheltered from ocean winds.

A paved path of just over a mile winds through grassy fields and forest to the dunes, with views of the Coquille River. The historic Coquille River Lighthouse stands at the end of the beach access road, with about 4.5 miles of open beach beyond it. The boat launch is popular for fishing and crabbing on the river.
excerpt: Bullards Beach is a large, family-friendly park two miles north of Bandon, with campsites tucked among shore pines and sheltered from ocean winds.
note: Camping: about 100 full-hookup sites, 82+ electrical sites with water, 13 yurts (6 pet-friendly), a horse camp with 8 primitive sites, a hiker/biker camp and an RV dump station. Six campsites and three yurts are accessible.
address: Two miles north of Bandon on US 101, Bandon, OR 97411

title: Cape Arago State Park
imageAlt: Rocky cliffs and ocean at Cape Arago

banner.alt: Rocky cliffs and ocean at Cape Arago

gallery.alt: Storm waves on the cliffs with a lighthouse

contentHtml:
Cape Arago is a scenic headland jutting into the Pacific at the end of the road out of Coos Bay. It is a fine spot to watch for migrating whales, marine mammals and ships entering Coos Bay.

The south cove trail leads to a sandy beach and tidepools (look, but don't touch). The north cove trail offers fishing, beachcombing and views of the seal and sea lion colonies on Shell Island, part of a National Wildlife Refuge.
excerpt: Cape Arago is a scenic headland jutting into the Pacific at the end of the road out of Coos Bay. It is a fine spot to watch for migrating whales, marine mammals
note: North cove trail closed March 1 - June 30 to protect seal pups. Picnic tables, restrooms and a day-use gazebo shelter.
address: End of Cape Arago Hwy, about 15 miles southwest of Coos Bay, OR

title: Coquille Myrtle Grove State Natural Site
contentHtml:
Coquille Myrtle Grove is a secluded swimming hole along the Powers Highway that "will bring out the Huckleberry Finn in you." A shaded grove of Oregon myrtlewood sits near the parking area.

A short walk downhill leads to a sandy beach on the Coquille River. Bring an inner tube and float with the river's gentle current.
excerpt: Coquille Myrtle Grove is a secluded swimming hole along the Powers Highway that "will bring out the Huckleberry Finn in you." A shaded grove of Oregon myrtlewoo
note: No drinking water on site.
address: Powers Hwy (OR 242), near Powers, OR 97466

title: Golden and Silver Falls State Natural Area
contentHtml:
Golden and Silver Falls State Natural Area is a hidden gem in the dense coastal forests of southwest Oregon. Trails wind through canyons to two waterfalls that drop over sheer rock cliffs onto moss-covered boulders about 100 feet below.

A 1.4-mile hike leads to the top of Golden Falls, with views of the falls and of old-growth firs and cedars. A small parking area and picnic area sit along Glenn and Silver Creeks, shaded by maple, alder and Oregon myrtle.
excerpt: Golden and Silver Falls State Natural Area is a hidden gem in the dense coastal forests of southwest Oregon. Trails wind through canyons to two waterfalls that
note: About a 24-mile drive from Highway 101; the last 3 miles are a one-lane gravel road.
address: East Fork Millicoma Rd via Allegany, about 24 miles from US 101 near Coos Bay, OR

title: Seven Devils State Recreation Site
imageAlt: Rocky beach with a cliff and driftwood

banner.alt: Rocky beach with a cliff and driftwood

contentHtml:
"Seven Devils Wayside is the jumping-off point for sandy beach adventure." From this out-of-the-way spot you can walk several miles up and down the open beach.

Agates are often the beachcombing goal of visitors here.
excerpt: "Seven Devils Wayside is the jumping-off point for sandy beach adventure." From this out-of-the-way spot you can walk several miles up and down the open beach.
address: Seven Devils Rd, Bandon, OR 97411

title: Shore Acres State Park

gallery.alt: Japanese-style garden with pond and stone lantern

contentHtml:
Shore Acres was once the estate of timber baron Louis Simpson, set on sandstone cliffs above the ocean. Its gardens hold plants from around the world, with something in bloom nearly every day of the year: a formal garden, a Japanese-style garden with a lily pond, and two rose gardens, one an All-America Rose Selections display.

Trails lead to Simpson Beach and along the cliff edge, where storm waves and migrating gray whales can be seen. An enclosed observation building on the site of Simpson's mansion tells the estate's history, and a 95- foot Monterey pine from the Simpson era is on the national Big Tree Register.

Holiday lights decorate the gardens from Thanksgiving through New Year's Eve.
excerpt: Shore Acres was once the estate of timber baron Louis Simpson, set on sandstone cliffs above the ocean. Its gardens hold plants from around the world, with some
note: Daily vehicle parking fee; annual permits, the Oregon Pacific Coast Passport or a Sunset Bay camping receipt are accepted. No animals outside vehicles except service animals. Friends of Shore Acres: shoreacres.net
address: Cape Arago Hwy, Charleston, OR 97420 (13 miles southwest of Coos Bay)

title: Sunset Bay State Park
contentHtml:
Sunset Bay is a sandy beach sheltered by tall sea cliffs, on one of the most scenic stretches of the Oregon coast. The campground is a short walk from the beach, and the day-use area along the bay is good for beachcombing, fishing, swimming and boating.

Trails link the park to Shore Acres and Cape Arago state parks, with views of Gregory Point and the Cape Arago Lighthouse. A public golf course is next door, and the fishing village of Charleston nearby offers crabbing, clamming and fishing.
excerpt: Sunset Bay is a sandy beach sheltered by tall sea cliffs, on one of the most scenic stretches of the Oregon coast. The campground is a short walk from the beach
note: Camping: about 30 full-hookup sites, 35 electrical sites, 65+ tent sites, 8 yurts (4 pet-friendly), 2 group tent areas and a hiker/biker camp. Flush toilets, hot showers, firewood for sale.
address: 89748 Cape Arago Hwy, Coos Bay, OR 97420

title: William M. Tugman State Park
imageAlt: Eel Lake dock in fall mist

banner.alt: Eel Lake dock in fall mist

gallery.alt: Yurt with picnic table and ramp

contentHtml:
William M. Tugman State Park sits on Eel Lake near Lakeside, close to Highway 101 but less busy than most coast parks. Campsites lie among shore pines, and the day-use area has wide lawns, a gazebo-style shelter and a fully accessible fishing dock by the boat ramp.

Eel Lake is good for fishing, swimming, canoeing, sailing and boating, with largemouth bass, crappie, stocked rainbow trout, steelhead and coho salmon (all coho must be released). A trail around the south end of the lake explores inlets and forests of spruce, cedar, fir and alder, and the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area is less than a mile away.

title: Bluebill Campground
contentHtml:
Bluebill Campground sits beside Bluebill Lake in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area north of North Bend, with 19 reservable sites.

A 1-mile loop trail circles Bluebill Lake. From North Bend, go 1.5 miles north to Transpacific Lane, follow it 1 mile, then turn right onto Horsfall Beach Road for 1 3/8 miles.
excerpt: Bluebill Campground sits beside Bluebill Lake in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area north of North Bend, with 19 reservable sites.

title: Buck Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Buck Creek is a tiny two-site campground on the Powers to Glendale Bike Route in the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest, about 6 miles from Panther Ridge Trail #1253, which leads to Hanging Rock.

From Gold Beach, drive north on US 101 to Agness Road (Forest Road 33) and continue about 32 miles to Forest Road 3348. Turn right; the campground is on the left about 9 miles from the junction.

note: Picnic tables and fire rings. No restrooms, no drinking water and no garbage service; pack out trash. 14-day stay limit.

title: Daphne Grove Campground
contentHtml:
Daphne Grove Campground lies along the South Fork Coquille River near Coquille River Falls Trail #1257, 15 miles south of Powers on Forest Road 33.

It has 14 campsites plus a group shelter for up to 25 people.

contentHtml: Eden Valley Campground has 11 sites on the Glendale-Powers Bicycle Route, about 33 miles southeast of Powers via Forest Road 33 and Forest Road 3348.

title: Horsfall Beach Campground
contentHtml:
Horsfall Beach Campground sits at the end of Horsfall Beach Road in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, about 2 miles north of North Bend. Its 34 sites serve mainly as a base for off-highway vehicle riding on the dunes, with the Horsfall Beach Day Use OHV Staging Area on site.

An accessible beach viewing platform and paved day-use parking give walkers access to the beach. From North Bend, go north 1.5 miles to Transpacific Lane, turn left and go 1 mile, bearing right across the railroad tracks, then turn right onto Horsfall Beach Road and continue 3 miles.

note: $25 per night; reservations required at Recreation.gov. Drinking water and restrooms; no hookups or dump station. State of Oregon OHV permit required for riding. No horses. Snowy plover beach restrictions March 15 - September 15.

Horsfall Campground is a year-round off-highway vehicle base camp in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area just north of North Bend, with a day-use OHV staging area next door.

Each site has a picnic table and fire ring, and the campground has flush toilets, drinking water and showers.

title: Bandon Marsh
imageAlt: Ni-les'tun Marsh flooded by winter high tides

banner.alt: Ni-les'tun Marsh flooded by winter high tides

contentHtml:
Bandon Marsh National Wildlife Refuge is where the winding Coquille River meets the Pacific. Established in 1983, it protects 889 acres of mudflats, salt marsh and forested wetland, the largest tidal salt marsh in the Coquille River estuary.

The refuge has two units, Bandon Marsh and Ni-les'tun Marsh, plus the Myrtlewood Grove Nature Trail. It is a famous shorebird stopover where rarities such as ruff and Hudsonian godwit turn up among the regular migrants.

Two public trails and viewing platforms offer year-round wildlife viewing, and hunting and fishing are allowed.

title: Oregon Islands

gallery.alt: Refuge staff with a puffin decoy on an offshore rock

contentHtml:
Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1935, is not one place but 1,853 rocks, reefs and islands plus two headlands, running from Tillamook Head near Seaside to the California border.

Most of Oregon's estimated 1.2 million nesting seabirds raise their young here, and seals and sea lions haul out and give birth on the rocks. All the rocks and islands except 1-acre Tillamook Rock are designated wilderness.

The islands are closed to entry, so watch from shore with binoculars or a spotting scope. In Coos County, Coquille Point in Bandon is the refuge's mainland unit.

title: Coquille Valley Wildlife Area
imageAlt: Ducks at Coquille Valley Wildlife Area

banner.alt: Ducks at Coquille Valley Wildlife Area

contentHtml:
Established in 2013, the Coquille Valley Wildlife Area protects Coquille River floodplain habitat for migrating and nesting waterfowl and native fish. Its Winter Lake and Beaver Slough tracts lie between Coquille and Bandon.

Walk-in waterfowl hunting, fishing and paddling in small boats are popular. Wildlife watchers may see hawks, warblers, herons, waterfowl, western pond turtles, beaver and river otter; spring and fall are best.

From Hwy 42, turn onto North Bank Lane; the parking area is about 0.6 mile on the right. From Hwy 101, turn onto East Beaver Hill Road (8.5 miles north of Bandon), then left onto North Bank Lane.
excerpt: Established in 2013, the Coquille Valley Wildlife Area protects Coquille River floodplain habitat for migrating and nesting waterfowl and native fish. Its Winte
note: A free access permit from the kiosk in the North Bank Lane parking lot is required; all access goes through this point. September 1 - January 31: Winter Lake Tract open Wednesdays, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays only; Beaver Slough Tract open daily. February 1 - August 31: both tracts open daily. Managed from the ODFW Charleston Field Office, 63538 Boat Basin Dr, Charleston.

title: Cawrses Falls
contentHtml:
Cawrses Falls drops 46 feet in two tiers on Hidden Creek, a small seasonal stream that falls into Upper Rock Creek near the old Cawrses Log Pond. In higher flow the lower tier spreads into a veil.

From Remote, follow Highway 42 east 2 miles and turn left onto Upper Rock Creek Road, just east of the bridge over the Middle Fork Coquille River. Cross the Upper Rock Creek bridge and continue about 0.8 mile to a large gravel pit on the right. Circle the pit; the falls are near its southern end.

title: Coquille River Falls
contentHtml:
Coquille River Falls drops 115 feet in two steps on the South Fork Coquille River, just off the Rogue-Coquille Scenic Byway south of Powers. The upper falls plunges about 50 feet over a broad, horseshoe-shaped cliff; 180 feet downstream the lower falls splits into two parallel horsetails for another 65 feet.

From Highway 42 east of Myrtle Point, take the Powers Highway (Route 542) south about 38 miles, bear right onto Forest Road 3348 (signed for Eden Valley and Sru Lake) and drive 1.5 miles to the trailhead on the left, just past the Sru Creek bridge. Coquille River Falls Trail #1257 descends half a mile, steep near the end.

note: Rock steps can be slick. Crossing Drowned Out Creek to reach the upper tier is hazardous; do not scramble up the cliff in winter.

Drowned Out Creek Falls tumbles 65 feet in four steep tiers into the South Fork Coquille River, right beside the larger Coquille River Falls. Three of the four drops can be seen from the viewpoint at the end of the Coquille River Falls trail.

Follow the directions to Coquille River Falls: Powers Highway (Route 542) south about 38 miles from Highway 42, then right on Forest Road 3348 for 1.5 miles to the trailhead just past the Sru Creek bridge. The trail descends about half a mile.

title: Elk Creek Falls
imageAlt: Heavy winter flow at Elk Creek Falls

banner.alt: Heavy winter flow at Elk Creek Falls

contentHtml:
This Elk Creek Falls, just off the Rogue-Coquille Scenic Byway south of Powers, drops 191 feet in a series of tiered horsetails, the tallest about 83 feet. It flows strongly about nine months of the year.

From Highway 42, take the Powers Highway (Route 542) south about 24.5 miles to the Elk Creek bridge and park in the large signed pull-off on the left. An easy trail reaches a viewpoint with a picnic table in under five minutes. The nearby Big Tree Trail climbs to old-growth trees, including a giant Port Orford cedar.

title: Elk Creek Falls
contentHtml:
This Elk Creek Falls is the lower of two large waterfalls on the headwaters of Elk Creek northeast of Allegany: a 150-foot veiling horsetail that cascades through thick brush toward the road.

From Coos Bay, follow the Coos River road past Allegany to the road marked for the Millicoma Tree Farm. Follow Weyerhaeuser Road #100 for 9.5 miles, turn right for 1.6 miles, right again for 2.8 miles to a fork, then right for 0.7 mile. The falls are above the road at the Elk Creek crossing; the best view is about 500 feet farther down the road.

title: Hewett Falls

From Coos Bay, follow the Coos River road past Allegany to the road marked for the Millicoma Tree Farm. Sru Creek keeps moderate flow from October through May and runs much lower in summer.

title: Eel Lake
imageAlt: Eel Lake dock in fall mist

banner.alt: Eel Lake dock in fall mist

contentHtml:
Eel Lake is a freshwater coastal lake with a winding, forest-lined shoreline at William M. Tugman State Park near Lakeside. The park has a dedicated kayak launch next to the regular boat ramp, plus restrooms, an open lawn, picnic space and an accessible fishing dock.

Motorboats are allowed with a 10 mph speed limit, so keep an eye on boat traffic and give anglers room. Wind can make small craft harder to handle, and the water stays cold even on warm days.

title: Powers Pond
contentHtml:
Powers Pond is a man-made pond of more than 30 acres at the south end of Powers County Park, set in the wooded Coast Range in the small town of Powers. It is limited to nonmotorized craft, which makes it a relaxed spot for kayaks, canoes and stand-up paddleboards, with a dedicated kayak launch.

The pond is stocked with trout, bass, catfish and crappie. The park around it is open year-round, with 40 RV sites, 30 tent sites, 3 cabins, restrooms with showers, a picnic shelter, playground and sports courts, a steam donkey logging yarder on display and a hand-carved 20-foot totem pole.

note: Oregon Waterway Access Permit required for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). Check Oregon Health Authority algae advisories. Clean, drain and dry your boat after use. Park reservations: 541-396-7755, Monday - Friday 10 AM - 5 PM.

title: Tenmile Lakes
imageAlt: Map of Tenmile Lake County Park

banner.alt: Map of Tenmile Lake County Park

contentHtml:
Tenmile Lake and North Tenmile Lake, joined by the narrow North Lake Canal, cover roughly 2,000 acres near Lakeside. Together they are the most heavily used body of water in Coos County, popular for fishing, waterskiing, wakeboarding, swimming, sailing and boating.

Tenmile Lakes County Park has an accessible kayak launch separate from its four powerboat ramps, plus three accessible docks, a fishing dock, picnic tables, a swimming and wading area, restrooms and a reservable gazebo. The adjoining campground has 45 RV sites with hookups and showers.

Expect boat traffic and wakes in summer, and wind on open crossings. Anglers catch steelhead, rainbow and cutthroat trout, largemouth bass, catfish, bluegill and brown bullhead.

note: Slow-no-wake in the North Lake Canal and Tenmile Creek. Oregon Waterway Access Permit required for paddlecraft. Check Oregon Health Authority algae advisories. RV park: 170 S 12th St.

title: Mount Bolivar
contentHtml:
At 4,319 feet, Mount Bolivar is the highest point in Coos County. The Mount Bolivar Trail #1259 in the Wild Rogue Wilderness climbs about 1,200 feet in roughly 1.4 miles, with nearly two dozen switchbacks, to a rocky, meadowed summit.

On a clear day the view reaches north to Mount Hood and south to Mount Shasta, over the Rogue River valley, the Coast Range and the Siskiyous. Three fire lookouts once stood on top; only concrete footings remain. A plaque from the people of Venezuela honors Simón Bolívar, for whom surveyor Simón Bolívar Cathcart named the peak in 1900.

From Powers, follow Forest Road 33 south, then turn east on paved Forest Road 3348 (signed for Glendale). The road becomes BLM Road 32-8-3.1 (Kelsey Mule Road); the trailhead is on this road.

note: Best hiked spring through fall. Coastal fog and smoke can limit views. Powers Ranger District: (541) 439-6200.
address: Mount Bolivar Trailhead, Forest Road 3348 (Kelsey Mule Rd), southeast of Powers, OR

title: Oregon Coast Trail
imageAlt: Oregon Coast Trail sign along a forested trail

banner.alt: Oregon Coast Trail sign along a forested trail

contentHtml:
The Oregon Coast Trail follows Oregon's coastline from the Columbia River to the California border, about 382 miles by the official guide and about 425 miles if no ferries are used around the estuaries. It passes through 28 coastal towns.

Most of the route is on the beach, with other sections through state parks and public lands, on private land under trail easements, and on road shoulders.

Hiker/biker tent sites, first-come first-served, are at nearly every coastal state park. Check tide times, as some areas are passable only at low tide. During western snowy plover nesting season (March 15 to September 15), walk on wet sand in protected areas, where dogs, camping and beach fires are not allowed.
excerpt: The Oregon Coast Trail follows Oregon's coastline from the Columbia River to the California border, about 382 miles by the official guide and about 425 miles if
note: Trail conditions change quickly; check Oregon State Parks notices and Trailkeepers of Oregon alerts before you go.
address: Runs the length of the Oregon coast, including Coos County

title: David's Chair - Coos Bay (Tow 'N Go)
imageAlt: All-terrain wheelchair on a sandy beach

banner.alt: All-terrain wheelchair on a sandy beach

contentHtml:
David's Chair Outdoor Mobility Systems is a White City nonprofit, founded in memory of Medford outdoorsman David Hartrick, that lends powered, tracked all-terrain wheelchairs at no cost. Its tank-like tracks cross beaches and trails that ordinary wheelchairs can't.

The Coos Bay chair is a Tow 'N Go location: the Action Trackchair and its enclosed trailer are kept at the Coos Bay Visitor Center. You tow the trailer (the rear door becomes the ramp) to a destination of your choice, for up to 7 days.
excerpt: David's Chair Outdoor Mobility Systems is a White City nonprofit, founded in memory of Medford outdoorsman David Hartrick, that lends powered, tracked all-terra
note: Free. Book at davidschair.org, ideally two or more weeks ahead; requests made less than 72 hours ahead may not be filled. A volunteer confirms by phone or text. Towing needs a 2-inch ball, a 4-prong trailer hookup, working trailer lights, a driver's license and $100,000 liability insurance. Phone is the Coos Bay visitor bureau.
address: Coos Bay Visitor Center, 50 Central Ave, Coos Bay, OR 97420
photoCredit: Nicole O'Brien / Travel Oregon; David's Chair

title: Agness Went Rogue
contentHtml:
Agness Went Rogue is a 75-mile out-and-back gravel ride with about 6,400 feet of climbing, roughly 35% gravel and 65% paved. From Powers it climbs through old-growth hardwood and conifer forest and follows about 7 miles of the Rogue River, including a 3-mile Wild and Scenic stretch, to a turnaround at Singing Springs Resort in Curry County.

Water, flush toilets and camping are at the start; food and water at Singing Springs Resort, about mile 37. The route runs each June as an organized ride by Tour de Frond.
excerpt: Agness Went Rogue is a 75-mile out-and-back gravel ride with about 6,400 feet of climbing, roughly 35% gravel and 65% paved. From Powers it climbs through old-g
note: Development route not fully vetted; navigation needs attention. Come well prepared.
address: Start: Powers County Park, Hwy 242, Powers, OR 97466

title: Catching Blue
contentHtml:
Catching Blue is a 23-mile lollipop (28-mile option) with about 2,300 feet of climbing, 90% paved. The first 9 miles run flat and fast beside Catching Slough on quiet roads with no shoulder.

At about mile 9 "The Wall" climbs half a mile at up to 20%, and the climb continues to the crest of Blue Ridge, with peekaboo views of Coos Bay and the Pacific. The descent passes forests and hobby farms back to the slough.

note: Rated easier technically, effort 2 of 5. Rideable most of the year.
address: Start: gravel lot at Coos River Hwy and Catching Slough Rd (south side of the Catching Slough bridge), near Coos Bay, OR

title: Double Go!
contentHtml:
Double Go! is an easy 19-mile out-and-back, about 60% gravel, along the East Fork Millicoma River and Glenn Creek to Golden and Silver Falls, finishing with a short hike (about 1.2 miles total) to both falls.

Along the way: Steamboat Landing, where "mosquito fleet" boats once ran upriver; myrtlewood trees and the story of myrtlewood money in the Great Depression; the C.A. Smith Logging Camp; and the historic Allegany- Scottsburg Pack Trail.
excerpt: Double Go! is an easy 19-mile out-and-back, about 60% gravel, along the East Fork Millicoma River and Glenn Creek to Golden and Silver Falls, finishing with a s
note: About 953 feet of climbing. Best in spring for the falls and fall for color. Don't ride when wet; the hike gets muddy. No food or water on route. Don't block Weyerhaeuser Lane when parking.
address: Start: pullouts by the Kruse Road bridge, off East Millicoma Rd (County Road 241) near Allegany, OR

title: Milli-Mania
contentHtml:
Milli-Mania is a 34-mile loop (62-mile option) with about 3,900 feet of climbing, 80% gravel, through the remote Coast Range. Long, steep climbs and descents pass moss-draped trees under a high canopy, flowing creeks and some recently harvested timberland.

Most of the route is in the Elliott State Forest, which has no trail system and offers real solitude.

note: Moderate difficulty; extremely remote. Tires 45 mm or wider suggested. No restrooms, food or water. Best in spring before mid-May; also a summer heat escape.
address: Start: Allegany Community Center and Post Office parking lot, Allegany, OR

title: Charleston to Bandon Tour Route
contentHtml:
The Charleston to Bandon Tour Route is a 41-mile drive off the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway that packs a lot of natural wonders into a small stretch of coast. Allow 2 to 3 hours; spring through fall is best.

From the fishing port of Charleston it runs out to Sunset Bay, Shore Acres and Cape Arago state parks, with views of the Cape Arago Lighthouse and the sea lions and seals at Simpson Reef. It then heads south on Seven Devils Road past the Charleston Marine Life Center, the South Slough Reserve, cranberry bogs and Bandon Dunes Golf Course to the Coquille River Lighthouse and Bandon's sea-stack beaches.

address: Cape Arago Hwy (OR 540) from Charleston to Seven Devils Rd and Bandon, OR

title: Pacific Coast Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway
Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway
Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway

contentHtml:
The Pacific Coast Scenic Byway, an All-American Road, follows US 101 for 363 miles along the whole Oregon coast, from Astoria at the Washington border to Brookings at the California border.

In Coos County the byway runs through North Bend, Coos Bay and Bandon. Highlights along the whole route include clamming on Tillamook Bay, kayaking Alsea Bay, the dramatic rocks and islands of the south coast and jet boat trips up the Rogue River at Gold Beach.

EV charging stations are spaced along the route, making an electric road trip from Astoria to Brookings possible.

address: US 101 from Astoria to Brookings, OR

title: Wild Rivers Coast Food Trail

gallery.alt: Fresh catch and Oregon pinot gris

contentHtml:
The Wild Rivers Coast Food Trail is a self-guided guide to berries, seafood and scenic landscapes on Oregon's South Coast. It links farms and ranches, eateries, seafood sellers, markets, craft beverage makers, artisans and experiences along Highway 101, with Coos County stops in Bandon, Charleston, Coos Bay, North Bend and Myrtle Point.

Add the Digital Passport to your phone and check in at members to earn discounts and prizes. Themed itineraries and a printable brochure are on the trail website.

High season runs June through November: blueberries in July and August, pumpkin patches late September through October, cranberries mid-October to early December, and Dungeness crab late December through August.

note: Open year-round; check each stop's hours. Cell service is spotty in remote areas. Email: wrcfoodtrail@gmail.com
address: Highway 101 from Reedsport and Coquille to Gold Beach and Brookings, OR

title: Sandy Creek (Remote) Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1921, the 60-foot Sandy Creek Covered Bridge carried Highway 42 traffic until a bypass opened in 1949. It is the only remaining covered bridge in Coos County and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.

Unusually for so short a bridge, it is reinforced with two crossed Howe truss members on each chord, and large windows on both sides let in light. In the early 1980s the Myrtle Point Lions Club restored it as a covered picnic site; the park was dedicated in 1984 and includes a tourist information center.
excerpt: Built in 1921, the 60-foot Sandy Creek Covered Bridge carried Highway 42 traffic until a bypass opened in 1949. It is the only remaining covered bridge in Coos
note: From Roseburg, drive west on Highway 42 about 31 miles to Remote. The bridge is on the north side of the highway.

title: Cape Arago Lighthouse

gallery.alt: Stormy waves and the lighthouse from Cape Arago
The 1909 Cape Arago Lighthouse (U.S. Coast Guard)
The 1866 Cape Arago Lighthouse (U.S. Coast Guard)

contentHtml:
Cape Arago Lighthouse stands on Chiefs Island just south of the entrance to Coos Bay. The first tower was lit in 1866, a second followed in 1909, and the current 44-foot reinforced-concrete tower was built in 1934 when erosion threatened the second. Its light shone 100 feet above the ocean.

The light was automated in 1966 and switched off in 2006; its original Fresnel lens is on loan to the Coos History Museum. In 2013 the lighthouse, island and about 24 acres were transferred to the Confederated Tribes of the Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indians.
excerpt: Cape Arago Lighthouse stands on Chiefs Island just south of the entrance to Coos Bay. The first tower was lit in 1866, a second followed in 1909, and the curren
note: The lighthouse and grounds are closed to the public. Best view: from the shore a quarter mile south of the Sunset Bay campground entrance.
address: Chiefs Island off Gregory Point, near Sunset Bay State Park, Charleston, OR

title: Coquille River Lighthouse
contentHtml:
The Coquille River Lighthouse was first lit on February 29, 1896, on Rackliff Rock at the mouth of the Coquille River, to guide ships across the dangerous river bar. Its stucco-covered brick tower, with an elongated octagonal shape and arched windows, is unique among West Coast lighthouses.

Decommissioned in 1939 and later abandoned, it became part of Bullards Beach State Park and was restored and opened to the public in 1979, with another restoration in 2007 that returned it to its original tan with a red base.
excerpt: The Coquille River Lighthouse was first lit on February 29, 1896, on Rackliff Rock at the mouth of the Coquille River, to guide ships across the dangerous river
note: Interpretive center open daily 11 AM - 5 PM, May through September, with park hosts. The tower itself is closed to the public.
address: End of the beach access road, Bullards Beach State Park, 2 miles north of Bandon, OR

title: North Bend Ice Skating Rink
contentHtml:
North Bend's seasonal ice rink is a 3,250-square-foot synthetic ice surface inside a 5,000-square-foot holiday tent downtown. Four polar bear push aids help young and new skaters keep their balance, and theme nights add to the fun.

Skating is free with your own skates; rentals are $5.

note: 2026-27 season: November 21, 2026 - February 14, 2027. Up to 70 skaters. Children under 14 need a guardian; waivers required. Dress in layers. Parking on Union Ave or the municipal lot at Virginia and McPherson Aves.

title: Doerner Fir
contentHtml:
The Doerner Fir, a roughly 450-year-old giant above East Fork Brummit Creek in the Coast Range, was for decades the world's tallest measured Douglas-fir and Oregon's tallest tree, at 327 feet in 1991.

In August 2025 a mysterious single-tree fire burned away about 50 feet of its crown. Climbers saved the tree, but the height record has passed on. A half-mile trail through old-growth forest leads to the tree.

note: Trail closed until further notice. Vault toilet; no drinking water. Roads are narrow and winding with frequent slides. BLM Coos Bay District, 1300 Airport Lane, North Bend. Email: blm_or_cb_mail@blm.gov

title: South Slough National Estuarine Research Reserve

gallery.alt: A boy touches the water at South Slough

contentHtml:
South Slough was the nation's first National Estuarine Research Reserve, designated in 1974. Managed by the Oregon Department of State Lands with NOAA, it protects tidal marsh, estuary channels, wetlands and forest in the South Slough of Coos Bay.

An interpretive center on Seven Devils Road, boardwalk trails and water trails lead into the slough. The reserve's signs pair Miluk with English, developed with the Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indians and the Coquille Indian Tribe.

The 0.25-mile Big Cedar Trail is wheelchair accessible with assistance from the lower parking lot to the marsh observation deck.

note: Free to visit; some classes have fees. Trails and waterways open daily dawn to dusk. Dogs on leash. No camping. Cell service may be nonexistent.

title: Bald Knob Lookout
contentHtml:
Bald Knob Lookout is a 16 x 16-foot flat-top cab on a 20-foot tower, perched at 3,630 feet in the Rogue River- Siskiyou National Forest and rented for overnight stays. The site was first developed in 1931, served as an Aircraft Warning Service post in 1942-44, and got its present tower in 1963.

The cab looks north over Eden Valley and south to the Rogue River, and the Panther Ridge Trail starts here. Inside are a single bed, a small table and chairs; outside, a picnic table, fire ring and vault toilet.

From Powers, drive south on Forest Road 33 about 11.5 miles to FR 3348, go about 2 miles to FR 5520 and turn right for 2 miles, then right on FR 5520-020 about 2 miles through two gates to the end of the road.
excerpt: Bald Knob Lookout is a 16 x 16-foot flat-top cab on a 20-foot tower, perched at 3,630 feet in the Rogue River- Siskiyou National Forest and rented for overnight
note: Reserve at Recreation.gov. Up to 4 people; no pets; no smoking. No water: bring all drinking, cooking and washing water. No propane heat, stove, refrigerator or lights until the 2026 season after storm damage. FR 5520 needs a high-clearance 4x4. Powers Ranger District: (541) 439-6200.
address: Forest Road 5520-020, Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest, south of Powers, OR

title: 7 Devils Brewing Company
contentHtml:
7 Devils Brewing Co., founded in Coos Bay in 2013, pours handmade ales in a public house filled with work by local artists. Watch the brewers at work, catch live music, or sit by the patio fire pit; the menu includes wraps, tacos and homemade ice cream.

Beers include Endless Summer blonde ale, Spindrift juicy ale and Arago amber. Brewery tours and event space are available.

title: Bandon Brewing
contentHtml:
Bandon Brewing Company opened in 2017 at the entrance to Old Town Bandon. The brewpub pairs Oregon craft beer with pizza from a wood-fired oven, plus cider from Bandon Rain, and has a family-friendly patio.

House beers include One Eyed Jack IPA and Pacific Puffin Porter.

title: Bandon City Park
contentHtml:
The Bandon disc golf course winds through Bandon City Park next to town, mixing long open throws across the park with wooded doglegs. UDisc lists 21 holes, with a 30-hole "Bandon 30" layout (8,324 feet, par 95).

Tees are a mix of pavers, grass, concrete and gravel. The ground is flat, and standing water can collect in the wet season.

title: Ferry Road Park

gallery.alt: North Bend bridge from Ferry Road Park

contentHtml: Ferry Road Park's 9-hole course (par 27, about 2,200 feet) plays through a flat park forest of big trees, with longer open holes and concrete tees. From the parking lot, head east toward the restroom and playground; hole 1 starts by the picnic bench.

title: Mingus Park
contentHtml:
Established in 1993, the Mingus Park course climbs into the wooded hills behind the park: 9 baskets with two tees each for an 18-hole, par-54 layout of about 2,975 feet. It is short but very hilly and demands accurate lines, with elevated pins and a "top of the world" shot on hole 6.

Tees are concrete and the bright yellow baskets are well marked.

title: Winsor Park
contentHtml:
Winsor Park has 9 baskets with two tees each, played as an 18-hole, par-54 crossover layout of about 4,264 feet. The holes are short with some elevation change and plenty of trees; holes 1, 2, 10 and 11 are mostly open.

Some holes overlap and a few baskets are blind, so watch for other players and walk up to check holes 5, 6 and 14.

title: A. R. Bowman Memorial Museum
contentHtml:
The A.R. Bowman Memorial Museum has preserved and shared the history of Crook County and Central Oregon since 1971. It is housed in a restored 1911 bank building listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Its collection of artifacts, photographs and personal stories is shown in exhibits, hands-on programs, lectures and field trips. In 1996 it hosted the first Smithsonian exhibit in Central Oregon. The Crook County History Center, added in 2012, expanded the museum to the Belknap Exhibit Center (136 NE 3rd St) and Caboose Park.
excerpt: The A.R. Bowman Memorial Museum has preserved and shared the history of Crook County and Central Oregon since 1971. It is housed in a restored 1911 bank buildin
note: Free admission; donations welcome. Closed major holidays and all of January. Research library by appointment. Email: bowmanmuseum@gmail.com

title: Malheur National Forest
contentHtml:
The Malheur National Forest covers 1.7 million acres of the Blue Mountains in eastern Oregon, from high desert grasslands of sage and juniper to pine and fir forests, hidden alpine lakes and meadows. Elevations run from 4,000 feet to 9,038 feet at Strawberry Mountain, whose range runs through the center of the forest.

The forest holds 88,350 acres of wilderness and the headwaters of the John Day River, the only tributary of the Columbia with no dams. The Malheur and Silvies rivers have Wild and Scenic stretches, and four former guard stations and a lookout can be rented for overnight stays.

note: Check forest alerts and closures before visiting

title: Ochoco National Forest
contentHtml:
The Ochoco National Forest and Crooked River National Grassland cover nearly one million acres of Central Oregon, a landscape of forests, grasslands and rocky river canyons. The Ochoco Mountains rise east of Prineville, with ponderosa pine forest, volcanic spires such as Steins Pillar and Twin Pillars, and the Mill Creek Wilderness.

Visitors come for hiking, camping, horseback riding, fishing at Walton Lake, rockhounding at the forest's agate beds, and winter snow play at the sno-parks along Highway 26.

note: Winter range closures December 1 - May 1 prohibit motorized vehicles in some areas to protect deer and elk. Supervisor's Office open Monday - Friday 8:00 AM - 4:30 PM.

title: Mill Creek Wilderness
imageAlt: Steins Pillar in the Ochoco National Forest

gallery.alt: Steins Pillar in the Ochoco National Forest

contentHtml:
The Mill Creek Wilderness protects about 17,400 acres of the Ochoco Mountains inside the 40-million-year- old Wildcat Mountain Caldera, at elevations from 3,700 to 6,200 feet. Mill and Marks creeks drain it and hold small trout.

Its best-known landmark is Twin Pillars, eroded volcanic spires with walls rising about 200 feet above the forest. Steins Pillar stands just outside the southwest boundary, and remote Desolation Canyon lies to the north. A lightning fire in 2000 burned over half the wilderness, and the forest is recovering.

About 18 miles of trail, including Twin Pillars Trail #832 and Wildcat Trail #833, start from four trailheads, each next to a small rustic campground. From Prineville, drive 9 miles east on US 26, then turn left on Mill Creek Road (FR 33) for 9 miles to Wildcat Campground.

note: No motorized equipment, bicycles or mechanical transport. Certified weed-free feed required for stock.

title: Oregon Badlands Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Oregon Badlands Wilderness protects 29,180 acres of rugged lava country east of Bend, with its eastern part in Crook County. Most of it is the Badlands volcano, a rootless shield volcano whose lava formed castle- like rocks, cracked pressure ridges called tumuli and narrow moat-like cracks. Ancient western junipers grow from the rock.

About 50 miles of trails, open to hikers and horse riders, start from five trailheads. Watch for yellow-bellied marmots, bobcat, mule deer, elk, pronghorn, prairie falcons and golden eagles. Fall, winter and spring are the most popular seasons.

From Highway 20 and 3rd Street in Bend, drive east 17.9 miles to the wilderness sign, then turn left and go 1 mile to the Badlands Rock Trailhead.

note: No fee. No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles. 14-day stay limit. Email: BLM_OR_PR_Mail@blm.gov

banner.alt: The bend in the Crooked River at Big Bend

The Powderhouse Cove boat ramp on Prineville Reservoir is 1.6 miles away.

note: $8 per night; group site $16; extra vehicle $2. First-come, first-served; 14-day limit. Drinking water in spring and summer. No cell service. Watch for cyclists: Highway 27 between Prineville and Bowman Dam is the Crooked River Canyon Scenic Bikeway. Email: BLM_OR_PR_Mail@blm.gov

It has individual and group sites, an accessible fishing platform, a riverside group picnic area and interpretive panels. Fly-fishing, wildlife viewing and picnicking are popular.

note: $8 per night; extra vehicle $2. First-come, first-served; 14-day limit. Accessible vault toilet; no drinking water; no cell service. Watch for cyclists: Highway 27 between Prineville and Bowman Dam is the Crooked River Canyon Scenic Bikeway. Email: BLM_OR_PR_Mail@blm.gov
address: Highway 27, 13.9 miles south of Prineville, OR

title: Jasper Point Campground
contentHtml:
Jasper Point is the quieter of the two developed campgrounds at Prineville Reservoir State Park, with 27 first- come, first-served sites with electricity and water, some looking over the water and all a short walk from the lake.

It has a two-lane boat ramp and courtesy dock, a trailhead into the State Wildlife Area, and a 1.75-mile lakeside trail to the park's main campground. One small pet-friendly deluxe cabin sleeps up to three.

note: Flush toilets, hot showers and an RV dump station. Two sites are accessible.

title: Prineville Reservoir State Park
contentHtml:
Prineville Reservoir State Park sits on a 15-mile, 3,000-acre reservoir in the high desert juniper and sage south of Prineville, formed where Bowman Dam holds back the Crooked River. Its 43 miles of shoreline draw anglers after rainbow trout, bass, catfish and crappie, along with waterskiers, wakeboarders, windsurfers, paddleboarders and kayakers.

In 2021 it became Oregon's first International Dark Sky Park, and its clear skies make for exceptional stargazing. Deer and bald eagles are often seen.

Camping includes about 22 full-hookup sites, 20+ electrical sites, 20+ tent sites, primitive drive-in and boat-in sites and 5 deluxe log cabins (one pet-friendly), plus 32 summer boat moorages.
excerpt: Prineville Reservoir State Park sits on a 15-mile, 3,000-acre reservoir in the high desert juniper and sage south of Prineville, formed where Bowman Dam holds b
note: Flush toilets, hot showers and an amphitheater. Two campsites and two cabins are accessible.
address: 19020 SE Parkland Dr, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Allen Creek Horse Camp
contentHtml:
Allen Creek Horse Camp has five campsites and several corrals among large ponderosa pines south of the Bridge Creek Wilderness. A stream on the east side of camp can water stock.

From Prineville, drive about 27 miles east on US 26, turn right on FR 2630 for 3 miles, right on FR 2210 for 2 miles, then left on FR 22 for about 12 miles. The camp is on the right.
excerpt: Allen Creek Horse Camp has five campsites and several corrals among large ponderosa pines south of the Bridge Creek Wilderness. A stream on the east side of cam
note: Free. Vault toilets; no drinking water; no manure pits, so pack out horse waste. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Antelope Flat Reservoir Campground and Day Use
imageAlt: Antelope Flat Reservoir Campground and Day Use
contentHtml:
Antelope Flat Reservoir Campground sits among large ponderosa pines above the reservoir's day-use area and boat ramp in the Maury Mountains. A few sites overlook the water, which is less than a 10-minute walk away, for swimming and fishing. Large birds of prey sometimes nest on the east shore.

From Prineville, drive 30 miles southeast on Highway 380 to FR 17, turn right and follow it about 12 miles to FR 1700-600.
excerpt: Antelope Flat Reservoir Campground sits among large ponderosa pines above the reservoir's day-use area and boat ramp in the Maury Mountains. A few sites overloo
note: $8 per night; extra vehicle $3 - $4 (fees not collected while water is unavailable). Vault toilet and fire rings in the day-use area; no hookups. Don't park in the boat ramp loop. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Big Spring Campground
contentHtml:
Big Spring is a free, primitive campground in open ponderosa pine forest along a creek. Ranchers graze cattle nearby, so you may see or hear cows in camp.

From Prineville, take US 26 east 16 miles to FR 42 and follow it about 31 miles past the Ochoco Ranger Station and Deep Creek Campground. About 5 miles past Deep Creek, turn left on FR 4270 for 1.5 miles.
excerpt: Big Spring is a free, primitive campground in open ponderosa pine forest along a creek. Ranchers graze cattle nearby, so you may see or hear cows in camp.
note: Free. Vault toilets; no drinking water. Trailer sites are limited. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Biggs Springs Campground
contentHtml:
Biggs Springs is a tiny free campground across the meadow from Lytle Prairie. The headwaters of the Wild and Scenic North Fork Crooked River, with trout fishing, are a short drive away.

From Prineville, go east on Hwy 126 about 13 miles, right on County Road 123 for 7 miles, stay right on FR 42 for about 15 miles, right on FR 4215 for 5 miles, then right on FR 150.
excerpt: Biggs Springs is a tiny free campground across the meadow from Lytle Prairie. The headwaters of the Wild and Scenic North Fork Crooked River, with trout fishing
note: Free. Vault toilet; no drinking water. The spring's water is untreated and not safe to drink. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Bingham Springs Campground
contentHtml:
Bingham Springs is a tiny, rustic campground beside a meadow and small pond in the northwest Ochoco National Forest, ringed by ponderosa and lodgepole pines. It sits next to the Twin Pillars North Trailhead into the Mill Creek Wilderness.

The open meadow is a fine spot for stargazing on warm summer nights.
