address: Twin Pillars North Trailhead, Ochoco National Forest, northeast of Prineville, OR

title: Deep Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Deep Creek Campground lies along the North Fork Crooked River among ponderosa pine and western larch, with about 15 drive-in sites and river fishing. Nearby spur roads make for informal hikes.

From Prineville, take US 26 east 15 miles, turn right on County Road 123 for 8 miles, then continue on FR 42 for 23 miles. The campground is on the right.
excerpt: Deep Creek Campground lies along the North Fork Crooked River among ponderosa pine and western larch, with about 15 drive-in sites and river fishing. Nearby spu
note: $8 per night; extra vehicle $3. Vault toilets; no drinking water. Often full during hunting season and holidays. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Dry Creek Horse Camp
contentHtml:
Dry Creek Horse Camp is a free, rustic equestrian camp in ponderosa pine forest along Dry Creek, directly across the road from the Giddy-Up Go Trailhead and its horse trails. Each site has a corral with two or four stalls, and stock can drink from the creek when it runs.

From Prineville, drive about 7 miles east on US 26, turn left on Mill Creek Road (FR 33) for about 5 miles, turn left at the end of the pavement on FR 3370 for 3 miles, then left on FR 3370-200.
excerpt: Dry Creek Horse Camp is a free, rustic equestrian camp in ponderosa pine forest along Dry Creek, directly across the road from the Giddy-Up Go Trailhead and its
note: Free; first-come, first-served. Vault toilet; no drinking water. Trailers up to 20 feet. No cell service. 14- day stay limit.
address: FR 3370-200, off Mill Creek Rd (FR 33), northeast of Prineville, OR

title: Elkhorn Campground
contentHtml:
Elkhorn is a free primitive campground in the Maury Mountains, near the Maury Mountain agate beds, just inside the National Forest boundary.

From Prineville, drive southeast on Highway 380 about 32 miles, then south on FR 16 about 5 miles. The campground is on the left.
excerpt: Elkhorn is a free primitive campground in the Maury Mountains, near the Maury Mountain agate beds, just inside the National Forest boundary.
note: Free. Vault toilets; no drinking water. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Mud Springs Horse Camp
contentHtml:
Mud Springs Horse Camp has 6 campsites and 9 corrals on the southeast flank of Wolf Mountain, just outside the Black Canyon Wilderness.

From Paulina, go east on Hwy 112 about 3.5 miles, left on County Road 113 for 1.5 miles, right on County Road 135 for 9 miles, right on FR 58 for 4 miles, left on FR 5840 for 7 miles, then right on FR 800.
excerpt: Mud Springs Horse Camp has 6 campsites and 9 corrals on the southeast flank of Wolf Mountain, just outside the Black Canyon Wilderness.
note: Free. Vault toilets; no drinking water. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Ochoco Divide Campground
contentHtml: Ochoco Divide Campground has 25 first-come, first-served sites in ponderosa pine forest at 4,700 feet on the Ochoco Divide, about 30 miles east of Prineville on US 26, just past the Ochoco Divide Sno-Park and just below the summit. It is popular with touring cyclists, and trailheads start at Bandit Springs about a mile away.
excerpt: Ochoco Divide Campground has 25 first-come, first-served sites in ponderosa pine forest at 4,700 feet on the Ochoco Divide, about 30 miles east of Prineville on
note: Closed for the rest of the 2026 season because of a wildfire in the area. Single site $20 - $25; extra vehicle $10; day use $5 - $7 (the Forest Service lists both rates). Vault toilets. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Ochoco Divide Group Site
contentHtml:
The Ochoco Divide Group Site sits on a hill above the road within Ochoco Divide Campground, at 4,700 feet on the divide. It comfortably fits about 12 people (35 maximum) and is mostly used by touring cyclists crossing US 26.

It has a large group fire ring, with drinking water near the site. Campers park at the base of the hill and walk up. Trailheads start at Bandit Springs about a mile away.

note: Reserve at Recreation.gov. Closed for the rest of the 2026 season because of a wildfire in the area. Group site $75 weekdays, $125 weekends. Not accessible. Check-in 2 PM, check-out noon.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Ochoco Forest Camp
contentHtml:
Ochoco Forest Camp sits in the Ochoco Mountains near 6,926-foot Lookout Mountain, known for its unusual rock formations. Besides several first-come, first-served campsites, it has a large reservable picnic pavilion for up to 125 people and a small meadow with a group fire ring and barbecue, popular for weddings and reunions.

The Lookout Mountain Trail is open to hikers, mountain bikers and riders, and nearby Walton Lake has a swimming beach, fishing pier and boat ramp. Elk, mule deer and sometimes wild horses are seen nearby.

From Prineville, take US 26 for 16 miles, turn right on Ochoco Ranger Station Road for 9 miles, then left on FR 2610 across the small bridge to the fee station.
excerpt: Ochoco Forest Camp sits in the Ochoco Mountains near 6,926-foot Lookout Mountain, known for its unusual rock formations. Besides several first-come, first-serve
note: Drinking water and vault toilets. Electricity at the pavilion only (no RV hookups). No horses or OHVs at the pavilion or campground. Pavilion reservations at Recreation.gov.
address: FR 2610 at the Ochoco Ranger Station, about 25 miles east of Prineville, OR

title: Salters Cabin Horse Camp
contentHtml:
Salters Cabin Horse Camp is a free, primitive equestrian camp in shaded second-growth ponderosa pine in the Paulina area, cool in summer heat. It has one large corral, and a preserved historic cabin stands on site (closed to entry).

From Prineville, follow Highway 380 east about 53 miles to County Road 112, turn left on County Road 113 (Beaver Creek Rd) for 2 miles, stay left onto FR 42 for 5 miles, then stay left at the FR 58 junction for 1 more mile.
excerpt: Salters Cabin Horse Camp is a free, primitive equestrian camp in shaded second-growth ponderosa pine in the Paulina area, cool in summer heat. It has one large
note: Free; first-come, first-served. Vault toilets and picnic tables; no drinking water. Pack out all trash and horse waste. No cell service. 14-day stay limit.
address: FR 42, about 1 mile past the FR 58 junction, east of Paulina, OR

title: Scotts Campground
contentHtml:
Scotts Campground is a small free camp at the junction of FR 22 and FR 3010, north of Big Summit Prairie and south of the Bridge Creek Wilderness.

From Prineville, take US 26 east about 27 miles, right on FR 2630 for 3 miles, right on FR 2210 for 2 miles, left on FR 22 for about 13 miles, then bear sharply left to stay on FR 22 for 2 miles. The camp is across from a gravel pit.
excerpt: Scotts Campground is a small free camp at the junction of FR 22 and FR 3010, north of Big Summit Prairie and south of the Bridge Creek Wilderness.
note: Free. Vault toilets; no drinking water. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Sugar Creek Campground and Day Use Area
contentHtml:
Sugar Creek Campground and Day Use Area sits on Sugar Creek about 12 miles from Paulina, with three moderately accessible campsites, a group picnic area and the short Sugar Creek Trail for wildlife viewing and creek fishing.

From Prineville, take Highway 380 southeast about 55 miles, turn left on County Road 112 for 3.5 miles, left on County Road 113 for 7.5 miles, then FR 58 for 2.25 miles.
excerpt: Sugar Creek Campground and Day Use Area sits on Sugar Creek about 12 miles from Paulina, with three moderately accessible campsites, a group picnic area and the
note: $8 per night; extra vehicle $3. Vault toilets; no drinking water. Access may close December 1 - May 1 to protect bald eagles. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Walton Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Walton Lake Campground sits among old-growth ponderosa pine and mountain meadows beside Walton Lake, and most sites have lake views. The lake is stocked with rainbow trout and catfish and is open to swimming and non-motorized paddling.

The 1-mile Walton Lake Trail #809 circles the lake, and the 7.5-mile Round Mountain Trail starts nearby. From Prineville, drive about 15 miles east on US 26, turn right on County Road 123 for 8 miles, then left on FR 22 for about 7 miles.
excerpt: Walton Lake Campground sits among old-growth ponderosa pine and mountain meadows beside Walton Lake, and most sites have lake views. The lake is stocked with ra
note: $20 per night; extra vehicle $10; day use $7. Boat ramp, fire rings, garbage service, vault toilets and a hand pump. No horses, ATVs or firearms. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Walton Lake Group Campsites
contentHtml: Walton Lake Campground has two reservable group campsites for 15 to 35 campers each, set among old- growth ponderosa pine beside Walton Lake. The lake offers trout fishing, swimming and non-motorized paddling, and the 1-mile Walton Lake Trail circles it.
excerpt: Walton Lake Campground has two reservable group campsites for 15 to 35 campers each, set among old- growth ponderosa pine beside Walton Lake. The lake offers tr
note: Group site $75 weekdays, $125 weekends. Reserve at Recreation.gov. Vault toilets and a hand pump. No horses, ATVs or firearms. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Whistler Campground
contentHtml:
Whistler Campground is a free camp off FR 27 on the edge of the Mill Creek Wilderness, near the Wildcat North Trailhead. The Whistler Springs rockhounding site is in the campground, just downhill from the restroom.

From Prineville, go north on Main Street about 11 miles to the forest boundary, where it becomes FR 27. Continue about 12 miles, stay right on FR 27 at the FR 2745 junction for 4 miles, then turn right on FR 200 past the trailhead into camp.
excerpt: Whistler Campground is a free camp off FR 27 on the edge of the Mill Creek Wilderness, near the Wildcat North Trailhead. The Whistler Springs rockhounding site
note: Free. No drinking water. Unpaved roads are very rough: 4WD or AWD recommended; no RVs or trailers. Many standing dead trees, so choose sites carefully. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: White Rock Campground
contentHtml:
White Rock is a free campground at the dead end of FR 300 on the southeast edge of the Mill Creek Wilderness, near the White Fir Springs agate beds.

From Prineville, drive east on US 26 about 19 miles, turn left on Wildcat Mountain Road (FR 3350) for 6 miles, then right on FR 300 for 2 miles.
excerpt: White Rock is a free campground at the dead end of FR 300 on the southeast edge of the Mill Creek Wilderness, near the White Fir Springs agate beds.
note: Free. Vault toilets; no drinking water. The final mile is rough; high-clearance 4WD recommended. 14- day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Wildcat Campground and Day Use Area
imageAlt: Wildcat Campground and Day Use Area
contentHtml:
Wildcat Campground and Day Use Area has 17 sites at the southwest corner of the Mill Creek Wilderness, next to the Twin Pillars Trailhead.

From Prineville, take US 26 east about 7 miles past Ochoco Reservoir, turn left on Mill Creek Road (FR 33) for about 10 miles, and go straight where the road makes a sharp left.
excerpt: Wildcat Campground and Day Use Area has 17 sites at the southwest corner of the Mill Creek Wilderness, next to the Twin Pillars Trailhead.
note: Temporarily closed; check with the Forest Service before visiting. $20 per site; extra vehicle $10; group site $50. Vault toilets; no drinking water. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Wiley Flat Campground
contentHtml: Wiley Flat is a free campground in the Maury Mountains. From Prineville, take Highway 380 southeast about 32 miles to the third bridge, turn south on FR 16 for about 12 miles, right on FR 16-400, stay left at the large ponderosa pine in the road and go under half a mile.
excerpt: Wiley Flat is a free campground in the Maury Mountains. From Prineville, take Highway 380 southeast about 32 miles to the third bridge, turn south on FR 16 for
note: Free. Vault toilets; no drinking water. Previously closed after the 2024 Wiley Flat Fire; the Forest Service now lists it as open. Check fire danger before visiting. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Wolf Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Wolf Creek Campground lies in shaded ponderosa pine forest beside Wolf Creek, about 12 miles from Paulina. Wolf Creek Industrial Campground is now run as part of it; a bridge splits the campground into two sections.

From Prineville, take Highway 380 southeast about 55 miles, turn left on County Road 112 for 3.5 miles, left on County Road 113 for about 6 miles, then FR 42 for 2 miles.
excerpt: Wolf Creek Campground lies in shaded ponderosa pine forest beside Wolf Creek, about 12 miles from Paulina. Wolf Creek Industrial Campground is now run as part o
note: $6 per night; extra vehicle $3. Vault toilets; no drinking water. Trailers up to 20 feet; narrow roads with tight corners. 14-day stay limit.
address: Ochoco National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Prineville Reservoir
contentHtml:
Prineville Reservoir stretches about 15 miles through the high desert south of Prineville, with five boat ramps. Kayaks, canoes and paddleboards launch from the state park's main day-use boat ramp.

The reservoir is shared with motorboats, jet skis and sailboats, and afternoon wind can raise waves, so paddlers often go out early and stay near shore.

note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for paddlecraft. Check for algae advisories before you go.
address: Prineville Reservoir State Park, 19020 SE Parkland Dr, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Walton Lake
contentHtml:
Walton Lake is a small mountain lake in the Ochoco National Forest, ringed by ponderosa pine. Paddlers launch from the small-craft boat ramp at the campground and day-use area.

Gas motors are not allowed (electric motors are), so the water stays calm and wake-free. The area also has a fishing pier, a swimming beach and a 1-mile loop trail around the lake.

note: Day-use fee.
address: Walton Lake Campground & Day Use, FR 22, Ochoco National Forest, OR

title: Lookout Mountain
contentHtml:
At 6,926 feet, Lookout Mountain is the highest point in Crook County and in the Ochoco Mountains. A 7-mile loop climbs about 1,300 feet to the summit, roughly 3.5 miles in, past ridgetop sagebrush, ancient junipers and seasonal wildflowers. On clear days the view reaches from Mount Shasta to Mount Rainier.

From Prineville, drive US 26 east 13 miles, take County Road 123 for 7.5 miles, stay right onto FR 42 for 7 miles, then turn right on FR 4205 and go 1.5 miles past the Round Mountain Trailhead to the Independent Mine Trailhead.
excerpt: At 6,926 feet, Lookout Mountain is the highest point in Crook County and in the Ochoco Mountains. A 7-mile loop climbs about 1,300 feet to the summit, roughly 3
note: Difficult hike.
address: Independent Mine Trailhead (Trail 808), FR 4205, Ochoco National Forest, OR

title: Big Summit Prairie
imageAlt: Cyclists leaving the Ochoco Ranger Station

banner.alt: Cyclists leaving the Ochoco Ranger Station

contentHtml:
Big Summit Prairie is a 50-mile loop (30- and 71-mile options) with about 4,000 feet of climbing, 45% gravel, around Big Summit Prairie in the Ochoco National Forest. Climbs are moderate at 4 to 6%.

Look for wildflowers, including more than a hundred native species such as the rare Peck's mariposa lily, wild horses, pronghorn, historic wagon roads, the Walton Lake area, and old mining sites such as the Four Horsemen hotel and the Independent and Mother Lode mines.
excerpt: Big Summit Prairie is a 50-mile loop (30- and 71-mile options) with about 4,000 feet of climbing, 45% gravel, around Big Summit Prairie in the Ochoco National F
note: Rated easier; remote. Tires 45 mm+. Pit toilets and a yard hydrant at the start; no other food or water. Best mid-spring to mid-summer.
address: Start: Old Ochoco Ranger Station parking lot, about 24 miles east of Prineville, OR

title: Bonanaza
contentHtml:
Bonanaza is a 51-mile, 100% gravel lollipop with about 3,200 feet of climbing through ranch country, rolling hills and wide views, with very little traffic.

It follows part of the 1845 Meek's Lost Wagon Train trail past the Coffelt Barn site and the legend of the Lost Blue Bucket Gold Mine.
excerpt: Bonanaza is a 51-mile, 100% gravel lollipop with about 3,200 feet of climbing through ranch country, rolling hills and wide views, with very little traffic.
note: Rated demanding. Tires 40 mm. No water or food: carry everything. Best in spring. Roberts Road is closed November 15 - April 15, and the clay roads clog bikes when wet.
address: Start: end of pavement at Camp Creek Rd and Merrill Rd, about 12 miles northeast of Brothers, OR

title: Crooked River Canyon Scenic Bikeway
contentHtml:
The Crooked River Canyon Scenic Bikeway is a 37-mile paved out-and-back (18.4 miles each way) of moderate difficulty. It follows the Crooked River south from Prineville past llama farms and cattle ranches into the Crooked River Canyon, with gentle curves and climbs between basalt cliffs.

Stop at the viewpoint near Palisades Campground or at Chimney Rock Recreation Site, a favorite picnic spot where anglers fly fish the river. Watch for deer, great blue herons and golden eagles. The turnaround is at Big Bend Campground below Bowman Dam.
excerpt: The Crooked River Canyon Scenic Bikeway is a 37-mile paved out-and-back (18.4 miles each way) of moderate difficulty. It follows the Crooked River south from Pr
note: Most day-use sites have restrooms; two have water. Big Bend Campground has parking, restrooms, water and power. Best in spring and fall; clear winter days are rideable.
address: Start: Rimrock City Park, Prineville, OR; end: Big Bend Campground

title: Dreamliner
contentHtml:
Dreamliner is a 38-mile loop with about 3,600 feet of climbing, 75% gravel, in the remote Ochoco National Forest. It visits Boeing Field, a grassy meadow that fills with spring flowers and is named for a 1942 B-18A bomber crash nearby, then crosses Little Summit Prairie.

It finishes on the Dreamliner descent, a single-lane paved road that drops about 1,600 feet over roughly 6 miles. "Brakes are (almost) optional."
excerpt: Dreamliner is a 38-mile loop with about 3,600 feet of climbing, 75% gravel, in the remote Ochoco National Forest. It visits Boeing Field, a grassy meadow that f
note: Rated demanding. Tires 40 mm. No services. Best mid-spring to mid-summer.
address: Start: Salters Cabin Horse Camp, FR 42, east of Paulina, OR

title: Kloochman
contentHtml:
Kloochman is a 92-mile mixed gravel near-century with about 4,400 feet of climbing, 40% gravel. It links the Crooked River Canyon Scenic Bikeway and the Post-Paulina road with gravel through ranch and farm country and over the Maury Mountains, topping out at 5,300 feet.

The only resupply is the Post General Store around mile 65, known for its milkshakes and meatloaf sandwiches.
excerpt: Kloochman is a 92-mile mixed gravel near-century with about 4,400 feet of climbing, 40% gravel. It links the Crooked River Canyon Scenic Bikeway and the Post-Pa
note: Rated very demanding. Very limited cell service: be self-sufficient. Best in spring; summer can be hot and fall overlaps hunting season. Check current conditions first: the route was damaged by the 2026 fires and Forest Service road closures change often.
address: Start: Good Bike Co, downtown Prineville, OR

title: Little Brother
contentHtml:
Little Brother is a 37-mile, 100% gravel loop with about 1,700 feet of climbing along the southern edge of Crook County, skirting the Maury Mountains. It passes rolling farmland, desert sage, rhyolite and basalt cliffs and flowing creeks, near the Crooked River Caldera and John Day Formation.

Expect free-grazing cattle on the ranch roads; pass calmly.
excerpt: Little Brother is a 37-mile, 100% gravel loop with about 1,700 feet of climbing along the southern edge of Crook County, skirting the Maury Mountains. It passes
note: Moderate; tires 45 mm+. Best late spring to early summer; rideable mid-April to early November. Little shade: ride early in July and August, and avoid windy days.
address: Start: Camp Creek Rd and Merrill Rd, about 12 miles northeast of Brothers, OR (roadside parking)

title: Lush!
imageAlt: Cyclist on gravel in the Ochoco National Forest

banner.alt: Cyclist on gravel in the Ochoco National Forest

contentHtml:
Lush! is a 31-mile loop with about 3,300 feet of climbing, 93% gravel, through lush meadows, big ponderosa pines and wildflowers in the Ochoco Mountains. A steady climb near mile 8 has views of Lookout and Round mountains, and pronghorn and the Big Summit wild horse herd have been seen nearby.

Miles 19 to 21 are a boggy, technical primitive section, and the final 850-foot climb looks over the 2014 Bailey Butte fire scar.
excerpt: Lush! is a 31-mile loop with about 3,300 feet of climbing, 93% gravel, through lush meadows, big ponderosa pines and wildflowers in the Ochoco Mountains. A stea
note: Moderate; remote. Tires 45 mm+. Pit toilets at the start; no water or food. Ride from late June or early July until the first fall rains, and only when dry.
address: Start: Bandit Springs Sno-Park, north side of US 26, east of Prineville, OR

title: Major Enoch
contentHtml:
Major Enoch is a 54-mile loop with about 5,900 feet of climbing, 85% gravel and primitive road, around the Wildcat Mountain Caldera past Twin Pillars and Steins Pillar. It climbs to Harvey Gap, follows the historic Summit Trail through prairie and forest, and drops about 1,800 feet in 7 miles.

Watch for the Big Summit wild horse herd and signs for the Lucky Strike Mine, a thunderegg collecting site. A decommissioned road section has soft ground, downed trees and short pitches up to 15%.
excerpt: Major Enoch is a 54-mile loop with about 5,900 feet of climbing, 85% gravel and primitive road, around the Wildcat Mountain Caldera past Twin Pillars and Steins
note: Moderate; remote. Tires 40 mm+. Potable water by detour at the Old Ochoco Ranger Station around mile 35. Best late spring to early summer. Check current conditions first: the route was damaged by the 2026 fires and Forest Service road closures change often.
address: Start: Steins Pillar viewpoint parking area (dirt lot), FR 3300-500, Ochoco National Forest, OR

title: McKay Creek Lollipop
contentHtml:
McKay Creek Lollipop is a 38-mile ride (33-mile option) with about 3,700 feet of climbing, 55% gravel. It starts in farm country, climbs to Harvey Gap and follows a ridge with views into the Ochoco National Forest and Steins Pillar, then a fast paved descent leads into rollers deeper in the Ochocos.

An easier final climb is followed by a long gravel descent back to pavement. Late-afternoon headwinds are common.
excerpt: McKay Creek Lollipop is a 38-mile ride (33-mile option) with about 3,700 feet of climbing, 55% gravel. It starts in farm country, climbs to Harvey Gap and follo
note: Moderate; remote. No water or food. Ride late spring through late October; check hunting season dates.
address: Start: McKay Creek Rd and Allen Creek Rd (north-side dirt shoulder), northeast of Prineville, OR

title: Meatloaf
imageAlt: Leading out from Post along the Crooked River

banner.alt: Leading out from Post along the Crooked River

contentHtml:
Meatloaf is a 36-mile loop with about 3,200 feet of climbing, 85% gravel, mixing farmland and ponderosa forest with views of the Ochoco Mountains. One long climb leads to a winding traverse past big mossy trees and a long gravel descent.

The Post General Store at the start and finish sells drinks and food.
excerpt: Meatloaf is a 36-mile loop with about 3,200 feet of climbing, 85% gravel, mixing farmland and ponderosa forest with views of the Ochoco Mountains. One long clim
note: Moderate. Ask the store's permission before parking at the far east end of its lot. Best late spring to mid-summer or fall; wear bright colors in hunting season. Check current conditions first: the route was damaged by the 2026 fires and Forest Service road closures change often.
address: Start: Post General Store, Highway 380, Post, OR (25 miles southeast of Prineville)

title: Mitch & Walt
imageAlt: Cyclists on the Old Ochoco Highway

banner.alt: Cyclists on the Old Ochoco Highway

contentHtml:
Mitch & Walt is a 64-mile lollipop with about 5,600 feet of climbing, 55% gravel. It climbs through Ochoco forest to the Old Ochoco Highway, descends about 6 miles to US 26 and the town of Mitchell, then tackles a 26-mile gravel stretch to the high alpine Big Summit Prairie.

The return is mostly downhill on pavement.
excerpt: Mitch & Walt is a 64-mile lollipop with about 5,600 feet of climbing, 55% gravel. It climbs through Ochoco forest to the Old Ochoco Highway, descends about 6 mi
note: Very demanding; remote. Tires 40 mm+. Kiosk, pit toilets and water at the start; grocery and small stores in Mitchell. Best late spring through fall.
address: Start: Old Ochoco Ranger Station parking lot, about 24 miles east of Prineville, OR

title: Opal

gallery.alt: Fire area in the Mill Creek Wilderness

contentHtml:
Opal is a 38-mile loop with about 4,200 feet of climbing, 75% gravel, through mature ponderosa forest with views of the Ochocos, Mount Jefferson and Mount Hood. It follows the historic Summit Trail, a former stock driveway, past the Mill Creek Wilderness.

An optional 1.5-mile detour near mile 29 reaches the Lucky Strike Mine, a fee thunderegg dig. The last climb gains about 1,400 feet at 6 to 8%.
excerpt: Opal is a 38-mile loop with about 4,200 feet of climbing, 75% gravel, through mature ponderosa forest with views of the Ochocos, Mount Jefferson and Mount Hood.
note: Moderate; remote. Tires 45 - 50 mm+. Pit toilets at the start; no water. Open cattle grazing on Summit Road. Check current conditions first: the route was damaged by the 2026 fires and Forest Service road closures change often.
address: Start: Bandit Springs Rest Area, US 26, east of Prineville, OR

title: Reuben
contentHtml:
Reuben is a 56-mile loop with about 5,100 feet of climbing, 80% gravel. It climbs about 2,500 feet in 11.5 miles into the Maury Mountains, traverses the range for about 22 view-filled miles, then makes a long descent back to Post.

Bail-outs to Highway 380 are via FR 17 at mile 26.2 and FR 16 at mile 34.9.
excerpt: Reuben is a 56-mile loop with about 5,100 feet of climbing, 80% gravel. It climbs about 2,500 feet in 11.5 miles into the Maury Mountains, traverses the range f
note: Very demanding; challenging navigation. Tires 45 mm+. Ask the store's permission before parking. Best late spring to early fall; wear bright colors in hunting season. Check current conditions first: the route was damaged by the 2026 fires and Forest Service road closures change often.
address: Start: Post General Store, Highway 380, Post, OR

title: Skydog
contentHtml:
Skydog is a 47-mile lollipop with about 3,400 feet of climbing, 80% gravel. It descends from Taylor Butte into a ranch valley, runs six miles on OR 27 and then fast gravel on Bear Creek Road.

The toughest part is Little Bear Creek and Roberts Road (miles 24.5 to 38), with rutted clay, short 10% climbs and Cascade views. Horses from the Skydog Ranch sanctuary may appear: slow down and don't stop or feed them. It finishes with an 800-foot paved climb back to Taylor Butte.
excerpt: Skydog is a 47-mile lollipop with about 3,400 feet of climbing, 80% gravel. It descends from Taylor Butte into a ranch valley, runs six miles on OR 27 and then
note: Moderate; remote. Tires 40 mm. No water or food. Best mid-May through July. Seasonal road closure November 15 - April 15.
address: Start: dirt pull-out on the west side of OR 27 near Taylor Butte, south of Prineville

title: Wolf & Bear
contentHtml:
Wolf & Bear is a 52-mile loop with about 3,200 feet of climbing, 75% gravel. It climbs through ponderosa forest along Wolf Creek into the shadow of Bear Mountain, crosses Little Summit Prairie, a high meadow known for wildflowers, and ends with a long descent into Paulina Valley.

The first 12 miles are paved; expect a rugged, rocky section around mile 37.5.
excerpt: Wolf & Bear is a 52-mile loop with about 3,200 feet of climbing, 75% gravel. It climbs through ponderosa forest along Wolf Creek into the shadow of Bear Mountai
note: Moderate; extremely remote. Tires 40 mm+. No water or food on route; the Paulina General Store is across from the start. Best mid-spring to mid-summer.
address: Start: dirt pullout at Hwy 380 and Paulina Valley Rd, Paulina, OR

title: Wolf Mountain Lookout
contentHtml:
Wolf Mountain Lookout is a 37-mile lollipop with about 3,100 feet of climbing, 70% gravel, through ponderosa forest, streams and meadows. It climbs to the 1947 Wolf Mountain Lookout, which you may climb, for views over the Black Canyon Wilderness.

It also passes the old Rager Ranger Station and "Flower Power Alley." Expect free-ranging cattle.
excerpt: Wolf Mountain Lookout is a 37-mile lollipop with about 3,100 feet of climbing, 70% gravel, through ponderosa forest, streams and meadows. It climbs to the 1947
note: Moderate; extremely remote. Tires 40 mm+. Pit toilets at the start; no food or water on route. Best mid-spring to mid-summer.
address: Start: Sugar Creek Day Use Area, east of Paulina, OR

title: Crooked River

gallery.alt: Crooked River canyon along the byway

contentHtml:
The Crooked River was designated a National Wild and Scenic River in 1988. Its 14.8 recreational miles run from just below Bowman Dam to Dry Creek, and from the National Grassland boundary to a point south of Opal Springs.

The river is valued for its botany, geology, hydrology, recreation, scenery and wildlife. It holds steelhead, brown trout and redband trout, and in spring offers Class IV-V whitewater.

note: Managed by the Bureau of Land Management, Prineville District.
address: BLM Prineville District, 3050 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754
photoCredit: Bob Wick/BLM; Bureau of Land Management

title: North Fork Crooked River
contentHtml:
The North Fork Crooked River is a National Wild and Scenic River for 33.7 miles, from its source at Williams Prairie to one mile above its meeting with the Crooked River: 12.2 miles wild, 8.2 scenic and 13.3 recreational.

It runs through old-growth ponderosa pine, holds redband trout and draws bald eagles in winter.
excerpt: The North Fork Crooked River is a National Wild and Scenic River for 33.7 miles, from its source at Williams Prairie to one mile above its meeting with the Croo
note: Managed by the Bureau of Land Management and the Ochoco National Forest.
address: Near Deep Creek Campground, near Paulina, OR

title: High Desert Food Trail

gallery.alt: Pumpkins on the High Desert Food Trail

contentHtml:
The High Desert Food Trail is a self-guided farm and food trail run by the High Desert Food & Farm Alliance. Stops include farms, ranches and food businesses in Bend, Redmond, Sisters, La Pine, Prineville, Madras and Warm Springs.

Visitors can follow one of the trail's itineraries or build their own route to buy produce, meat and other foods directly from local growers.
excerpt: The High Desert Food Trail is a self-guided farm and food trail run by the High Desert Food & Farm Alliance. Stops include farms, ranches and food businesses in
note: Email: info@hdffa.org. Check each stop's own hours before visiting.
address: Farms and food stops across Crook, Deschutes and Jefferson counties, OR

title: Lower Crooked River Back Country Byway
contentHtml:
The Lower Crooked River Back Country Byway follows OR 27 for about 43 miles through the Crooked River canyon, from Prineville south to US 20, 33.3 miles east of Bend. The southern 18 miles are graded gravel.

Along the river are nine campgrounds open year-round and the 1.3-mile Chimney Rock Trail. The river below the road is known for fly fishing and bald eagles.
excerpt: The Lower Crooked River Back Country Byway follows OR 27 for about 43 miles through the Crooked River canyon, from Prineville south to US 20, 33.3 miles east of
note: Open range: watch for livestock. Cell service is limited; services are in Prineville only.
address: OR 27 (Crooked River Hwy), from Prineville south to US 20, OR

title: Bandit Springs
contentHtml:
Bandit Springs Sno-Park has the most varied trail network in the Ochoco National Forest, with trails rated from easy to most difficult. In winter it is used for cross-country skiing, snowshoeing and snowmobiling; in summer, for hiking, mountain biking and picnicking.

From Prineville, drive east on US 26 about 27 miles. The sno-park is on the left, one mile west of Ochoco Divide summit.
excerpt: Bandit Springs Sno-Park has the most varied trail network in the Ochoco National Forest, with trails rated from easy to most difficult. In winter it is used for
note: Two vault toilets and picnic tables; no drinking water. An Oregon Sno-Park Permit is required November 15 - April 30 (sold at the Prineville DMV and Bi-Mart; Idaho, Washington and California permits are honored). Display it on the dashboard.
address: US 26, about 27-30 miles east of Prineville, Ochoco National Forest, OR

title: Ochoco Divide
contentHtml:
Ochoco Divide Sno-Park is a snowmobiling base on US 26. Snowmobile Trail #1 starts at the parking area and heads east into the trail network around Walton Lake Sno-Park, on well-kept winter roads in a less crowded area.

From Prineville, drive east on US 26 about 30 miles. The sno-park is on the right, just past Bandit Springs Sno- Park.
excerpt: Ochoco Divide Sno-Park is a snowmobiling base on US 26. Snowmobile Trail #1 starts at the parking area and heads east into the trail network around Walton Lake
note: Vault toilets; no drinking water. Large parking area for all vehicle sizes. An Oregon Sno-Park Permit is required November 15 - April 30 (sold at the Prineville DMV and Bi-Mart; Idaho, Washington and California permits are honored). Display it on the dashboard.
address: US 26, about 30 miles east of Prineville, Ochoco National Forest, OR

title: Sled Hill/Marks Creek
contentHtml: Sled Hill at Marks Creek is a sledding and snow play area on US 26, 28 miles east of Prineville, about half a mile south of Bandit Springs Sno-Park.
excerpt: Sled Hill at Marks Creek is a sledding and snow play area on US 26, 28 miles east of Prineville, about half a mile south of Bandit Springs Sno-Park.
note: An Oregon Sno-Park Permit is required November 15 - April 30 (sold at the Prineville DMV and Bi- Mart; Idaho, Washington and California permits are honored). Display it on the dashboard.
address: US 26, 28 miles east of Prineville, Ochoco National Forest, OR

title: Walton Lake
contentHtml: Walton Lake Sno-Park, near Walton Lake on FR 22, is used for cross-country skiing and snowmobiling, and is a hub of the snowmobile trail network that runs from Ochoco Divide.
excerpt: Walton Lake Sno-Park, near Walton Lake on FR 22, is used for cross-country skiing and snowmobiling, and is a hub of the snowmobile trail network that runs from
note: An Oregon Sno-Park Permit is required November 15 - April 30 (sold at the Prineville DMV and Bi- Mart; Idaho, Washington and California permits are honored). Display it on the dashboard.
address: FR 22, 16 miles east of Prineville, Ochoco National Forest, OR

title: Crooked River Wetlands Complex
contentHtml:
The Crooked River Wetlands Complex is a 120-acre City of Prineville site, completed in 2017, where treated wastewater flows through 15 ponds built to be bird-friendly. It has become one of Central Oregon's best- known birding spots, with 5.4 miles of trails (3.25 miles paved), viewing platforms and pollinator gardens.

Shorebirds and waterfowl are the main attractions, and rare visitors have included Tundra Bean-Goose, Ruddy Turnstone, Red Knot and Little Gull. Guided bird walks run monthly from March through October.
excerpt: The Crooked River Wetlands Complex is a 120-acre City of Prineville site, completed in 2017, where treated wastewater flows through 15 ponds built to be bird-fr
note: A city facility and wildlife habitat, not a state or federal refuge.
address: 4035 NW Rimrock Acres Loop, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Eagle Rock
contentHtml:
Eagle Rock is an ash-flow tuff monolith shaped like a perched eagle, standing over the Paulina Highway southeast of Prineville. The Bureau of Land Management has set aside about 150 acres here as a public rockhounding site, where collectors dig for Eagle Rock plume agate along with moss, botryoidal and angel wing agate.

A rough gravel road leaves the highway between mileposts 14 and 15 and climbs to a trailhead. A steep trail of about 0.7 mile, gaining some 500 feet, reaches the collecting ground.
excerpt: Eagle Rock is an ash-flow tuff monolith shaped like a perched eagle, standing over the Paulina Highway southeast of Prineville. The Bureau of Land Management ha
note: High-clearance vehicle recommended. Private mining claims are nearby: collect only on BLM land, under BLM rules.
address: Paulina Hwy (OR 380) between mileposts 14 and 15, southeast of Prineville, OR

title: Oregon Badlands
contentHtml:
The Oregon Badlands Wilderness protects 29,180 acres of rugged lava country east of Bend, with its eastern part in Crook County. Most of it is the Badlands volcano, a rootless shield volcano whose lava formed castle- like rocks, cracked pressure ridges called tumuli and narrow moat-like cracks. Ancient western junipers grow from the rock.

About 50 miles of trails, open to hikers and horse riders, start from five trailheads. Watch for yellow-bellied marmots, bobcat, mule deer, elk, pronghorn, prairie falcons and golden eagles. Fall, winter and spring are the most popular seasons.

From Highway 20 and 3rd Street in Bend, drive east 17.9 miles to the wilderness sign, then turn left and go 1 mile to the Badlands Rock Trailhead.
excerpt: The Oregon Badlands Wilderness protects 29,180 acres of rugged lava country east of Bend, with its eastern part in Crook County. Most of it is the Badlands volc
note: No fee. No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles. 14-day stay limit. Email: BLM_OR_PR_Mail@blm.gov
address: Badlands Rock Trailhead, off US 20 near milepost 15, about 18 miles east of Bend, OR

title: Steins Pillar
imageAlt: Steins Pillar in the Ochoco National Forest

gallery.alt: Steins Pillar in the Ochoco National Forest

contentHtml:
Steins Pillar is a 350-foot monolith of welded tuff, left standing when the Wildcat Caldera collapsed about 40 million years ago. It rises above Mill Creek in the Ochoco National Forest, south of the Mill Creek Wilderness, and is named for Maj. Enoch Steen, whose name was misspelled on maps.

Steins Pillar Trail #837 reaches the base in about 4 miles round trip. The pillar can also be seen from a viewing area on Mill Creek Road. From Prineville, drive US 26 east about 7 miles past Ochoco Reservoir, turn north on Mill Creek Road for 6 miles, then take FR 3300-500 for 2 miles to the trailhead.
excerpt: Steins Pillar is a 350-foot monolith of welded tuff, left standing when the Wildcat Caldera collapsed about 40 million years ago. It rises above Mill Creek in t
note: Temporarily closed. Free; day use only; no restrooms.
address: Steins Pillar Trailhead, FR 3300-500, Ochoco National Forest, OR

title: Rimrock Park
contentHtml:
Rimrock Park has a free 9-hole disc golf course along the Crooked River, across from the Crook County RV Park. All holes are par 3, for par 27 over 2,318 feet, on flat, mostly manicured ground with some rough. Holes 1 and 6 need about 150 feet of power to carry the water.

The course was cleared and redesigned in 2024, with rubber tees and new signs added in 2025. There is a practice basket near the first tee, and the park also has a fishing pond.
excerpt: Rimrock Park has a free 9-hole disc golf course along the Crooked River, across from the Crook County RV Park. All holes are par 3, for par 27 over 2,318 feet,
note: Free. Porta-potty and drinking water. Dogs allowed. Run by Crook County Parks and Recreation District.
address: 843 S Main St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Curry Historical Society Museum
contentHtml:
The Curry Historical Society Museum, in the Alice Wakeman Memorial Building on Highway 101 in Gold Beach, studies and shares the history of Curry County.

The society also points visitors to the county's other historic sites, including the Chetco Valley Museum, Agness-Illahe Museum, Port Orford Lifeboat Station, Historic Hughes House and Cape Blanco Lighthouse.
excerpt: The Curry Historical Society Museum, in the Alice Wakeman Memorial Building on Highway 101 in Gold Beach, studies and shares the history of Curry County.
note: Adults $5; children under 12 free. Closed January, February, holidays and Christmas week. For visits outside open hours, call and leave a message. Email: info@curryhistory.com
address: 29419 Ellensburg Ave, Gold Beach, OR 97444

title: Chetco Valley Historical Society Museum
contentHtml:
The Chetco Valley Museum, just south of Brookings in Harbor, is housed in the Blake House, built in 1857 and the oldest house still standing in the Chetco Valley. It was once a stagecoach stop, trading post and the valley's first post office, on a hill overlooking the valley and the Pacific.

Rooms show Chetco-area photos, old books and cameras, World War II items, antique sewing machines, vintage clothing and quilts (one dated 1844), and an early-1900s kitchen. Monterey cypresses planted on the grounds in the 1860s include the largest Monterey cypress in Oregon.
excerpt: The Chetco Valley Museum, just south of Brookings in Harbor, is housed in the Blake House, built in 1857 and the oldest house still standing in the Chetco Valle
note: Open mid-May through the end of October. Phone is for tours.
address: 15461 Museum Rd, Harbor, OR 97415

title: Port Orford Lifeboat Station Museum
contentHtml:
The Port Orford Lifeboat Station Museum is in the 1934 Coast Guard lifeboat station on Coast Guard Hill in Port Orford Heads State Park. For 36 years, until 1970, its surfmen launched through the surf to rescue mariners along this coast.

Run by the Cape Blanco Heritage Society since 2000, the museum keeps a restored 36-foot motor lifeboat of the kind used on those rescues.
excerpt: The Port Orford Lifeboat Station Museum is in the 1934 Coast Guard lifeboat station on Coast Guard Hill in Port Orford Heads State Park. For 36 years, until 197
note: Free admission. Open seasonally, late May through September. Email: Info@CapeBlancoHeritageSociety.com
address: Coast Guard Hill, Port Orford Heads State Park, Port Orford, OR 97476

title: Hughes House
contentHtml:
The Hughes House is a restored Victorian farmhouse built in 1898 for dairyman Patrick Hughes and his wife Jane, designed by pioneer builder Pehr Johan Lindberg and framed in old-growth Port Orford cedar. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

The Hughes ranch, worked from 1860 and grown past 2,000 acres, is now the heart of Cape Blanco State Park. Exhibits in the house and around the grounds tell of ranch life a century ago and the couple's seven children, one of whom was a longtime keeper at Cape Blanco Light Station.

From Highway 101, 4.5 miles north of Port Orford, drive west on Cape Blanco Road; the house entrance is on the right after the road climbs.
excerpt: The Hughes House is a restored Victorian farmhouse built in 1898 for dairyman Patrick Hughes and his wife Jane, designed by pioneer builder Pehr Johan Lindberg
note: Free tours by the Cape Blanco Heritage Society, May 1 to September 30. The ground floor and grounds are wheelchair accessible; the second floor is not. Email: Info@CapeBlancoHeritageSociety.com
address: 91814 Cape Blanco Rd, Sixes, OR 97476 (Cape Blanco State Park)

title: Rogue River Ranch

gallery.alt: Inside the Rogue River Ranch museum

contentHtml:
Rogue River Ranch sits at the mouth of Mule Creek on the wild section of the Rogue River. The Billings family built the main house in 1903, packing its windows 21 miles by mule from Galice, and ran a mining claim, general store and hotel here; their daughter Marial gave the settlement its name.

The ranch was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975, and the Bureau of Land Management remodeled the main house in 2017-2019 as a museum with exhibits and signs. A BLM caretaker lives on site.

Reach it by the Grave Creek to Marial Back Country Byway, by boat, or on foot via the Rogue River National Recreation Trail. Roads are narrow and winding, with no fuel or services.
excerpt: Rogue River Ranch sits at the mouth of Mule Creek on the wild section of the Rogue River. The Billings family built the main house in 1903, packing its windows
note: Free. Day use only. No accessible facilities. Primitive camping nearby at Tucker Flat Campground. Email: BLM_OR_MD_Mail@blm.gov
address: Marial, OR (Rogue River, mouth of Mule Creek)

title: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest
contentHtml:
The Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest covers about 1.8 million acres of southwest Oregon, from the Cascades to the coast, managed through five ranger districts: High Cascades, Siskiyou Mountains, Wild Rivers, Gold Beach and Powers.

In Curry County, the forest's Gold Beach Ranger District takes in the lower Rogue River country and the coastal mountains. Across the forest, highlights include Applegate Lake, Mount McLoughlin and the Siskiyou and Sky Lakes wilderness areas.
excerpt: The Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest covers about 1.8 million acres of southwest Oregon, from the Cascades to the coast, managed through five ranger distric
note: Forest headquarters is in Medford. Gold Beach Ranger District: 29279 Ellensburg Ave, Gold Beach, OR 97444, (541) 247-3600.
address: 3040 Biddle Rd, Medford, OR 97504

title: Copper Salmon Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Copper Salmon Wilderness protects 13,757 acres about 11 miles east of Port Orford, taking in the North and South Forks of the Elk River and the upper Middle Fork of the Sixes River. It holds one of the nation's largest remaining stands of low-elevation old-growth forest, with Douglas-fir up to 10 feet across and 300 feet tall, and healthy Port Orford cedar.

The North Fork Elk River has one of the healthiest salmon, steelhead and cutthroat trout runs in the lower 48 states. Wildlife includes marbled murrelets, northern spotted owls, Roosevelt elk, mountain lions and black bears. Barklow Mountain Trail #1258 is reached from the Barklow Mountain West and Northeast trailheads.

note: No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles. No caching of equipment or supplies; no hay or unprocessed grain.
address: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3040 Biddle Rd, Medford, OR 97504

title: Grassy Knob Wilderness
contentHtml:
Grassy Knob Wilderness, designated in 1984, covers 17,159 acres of steep, rugged coastal rain forest with a thick understory. Elevations run from near sea level to 2,342-foot Grassy Knob on the western edge, and the Wild and Scenic Elk River forms the southern boundary.

It shelters old-growth Port Orford cedar over six feet across, and salmon spawn in Dry Creek. Small streams and waterfalls run through shaded ravines, and vine maples turn red in autumn. Grassy Knob Trail #1241 starts at the Grassy Knob Trailhead; off-trail travel is very difficult.
excerpt: Grassy Knob Wilderness, designated in 1984, covers 17,159 acres of steep, rugged coastal rain forest with a thick understory. Elevations run from near sea level
note: No restrooms or drinking water. Wet winters, about 130 inches of rain a year; weather changes quickly. Overnight groups limited to 12 people and 9 pack animals. No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles. No caching of equipment or supplies; no hay or unprocessed grain.
address: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest Supervisor's Office: 3040 Biddle Rd, Medford, OR 97504

title: Kalmiopsis Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Kalmiopsis Wilderness, designated in 1964, covers 180,095 acres of deep canyons, sharp rock ridges and clear, fast streams, including the headwaters of the Chetco and North Fork Smith rivers and part of the Illinois River canyon. Elevations run from 500 feet to 5,098 feet at Pearsoll Peak.

Its serpentine soils support many rare plants, including the namesake shrub Kalmiopsis leachiana, found in 1930 in the Gold Basin area. Trailheads include Babyfoot Lake, Vulcan Lake/Johnson Butte, Chetco Divide/Vulcan Peak, Upper Chetco, Tincup, Illinois River and Kalmiopsis Rim.
excerpt: The Kalmiopsis Wilderness, designated in 1964, covers 180,095 acres of deep canyons, sharp rock ridges and clear, fast streams, including the headwaters of the
note: No drinking water: treat surface water. Trails damaged by past fires are being repaired; watch for dead trees, high winds and fast-changing weather. Overnight groups limited to 12 people and 9 pack animals. Boating permits required. No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles. No caching of equipment or supplies; no hay or unprocessed grain.
address: Wild Rivers Ranger District, Grants Pass Interagency Office: 2164 NE Spalding Ave, Grants Pass, OR 97526
photoCredit: USDA Forest Service; Adobe Stock; Oregon Flora

title: Oregon Islands Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Oregon Islands Wilderness covers the rocks, reefs and islands of Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, some 1,853 of them strung along about 320 miles of coastline from Tillamook Head near Seaside to the California border.

The islands are breeding and resting grounds for most of Oregon's estimated 1.2 million nesting seabirds, including tufted puffins and cormorants, and for seals and sea lions that haul out and give birth there.

The islands are closed to public entry; bring binoculars or a spotting scope and watch from shore.
excerpt: The Oregon Islands Wilderness covers the rocks, reefs and islands of Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, some 1,853 of them strung along about 320 miles of
note: All rocks and islands are closed to the public. Email: Oregoncoast@fws.gov
address: Offshore rocks and islands along the whole Oregon coast, including Curry County

title: Wild Rogue Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Wild Rogue Wilderness protects 36,453 acres of rugged canyon country along the Rogue River in Curry and Coos counties. Designated in 1978, it is managed jointly by the U.S. Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management.

The year-round, hiker-only Rogue River National Recreation Trail #1160 follows about 15 of its 40 miles through the wilderness between Graves Creek and Illahe. Other trails include Panther Ridge #1253, Mule Creek #1159 and the Mount Bolivar Trail #1259 to the 4,319-foot summit.

The river itself is famous for rafting and for salmon and steelhead fishing. Under Wild and Scenic River rules, motorboats and riverside lodges are allowed on the river.

note: No motorized or mechanical transport in the wilderness. Group size limit: 12 people and 9 head of stock.
address: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest, 3040 Biddle Rd, Medford, OR 97504

title: Edson Creek Campground (OR)

gallery.alt: Day use area and boat ramp

contentHtml:
Edson Creek Campground is an open meadow beside a creek that flows into the Sixes River, with 27 individual sites and 5 group sites. Group sites B-E are across the creek, reached by a seasonal bridge from June to late September.

A day-use area and boat ramp are across the road, and the area is popular for fishing, boating and water play. From US 101 between Bandon and Port Orford, turn east on Sixes River Road, go about 4 miles and turn left just before the Edson Creek Bridge.
excerpt: Edson Creek Campground is an open meadow beside a creek that flows into the Sixes River, with 27 individual sites and 5 group sites. Group sites B-E are across
note: $16 single site; $32 double; $40 group; $8 extra vehicle. Reserve at Recreation.gov or pay with Scan & Pay. Picnic tables, fire rings, vault toilets and water spigot. Sites 20-24 are accessible. Poor cell coverage. Email: BLM_OR_CB_Mail@blm.gov
address: Sixes River Rd, about 4 miles east of US 101, near Port Orford, OR

title: Sixes River Campground
contentHtml:
Sixes River Campground has 19 sites on the Sixes River, shaded by bigleaf maple, oak and Douglas-fir. It is a good spot for picnicking, swimming, fishing, gold panning and wildlife viewing.

From US 101 about 5 miles north of Port Orford, turn east on Sixes River Road and follow it about 11 miles.
excerpt: Sixes River Campground has 19 sites on the Sixes River, shaded by bigleaf maple, oak and Douglas-fir. It is a good spot for picnicking, swimming, fishing, gold
note: $16 per site; $8 extra vehicle; day use $6. Reserve online or pay on arrival with Scan & Pay in the Recreation.gov app.
address: Sixes River Rd, about 11 miles east of US 101, near Port Orford, OR

title: Tucker Flat Campground
contentHtml:
Tucker Flat is a small no-host campground with six first-come, first-served sites on Mule Creek near Rogue River Ranch, along the Grave Creek to Marial Back Country Byway. It is open year-round.

The Mule Creek Trail starts at the back of the campground and climbs about 3,000 feet over 6.5 miles along bluffs above Mule Creek into the Wild Rogue Wilderness. The 40-mile Rogue River National Recreation Trail is also close by.

From I-5, take the Merlin exit and drive west on Merlin-Galice Road about 23 miles, cross the Grave Creek Bridge onto Mt. Reuben Road, turn left at Kelsey Mule Road, then left at Marial Saddle on Marial Road and follow the signs.
excerpt: Tucker Flat is a small no-host campground with six first-come, first-served sites on Mule Creek near Rogue River Ranch, along the Grave Creek to Marial Back Cou
note: No fees. Pit toilets and picnic tables; no hookups. Water is not safe to drink: bring your own. 14-day stay limit. Email: BLM_OR_MD_Mail@blm.gov
address: Marial Rd (BLM Rd 32-9-14.2), near Rogue River Ranch, Marial, OR

title: Alfred A. Loeb State Park
contentHtml:
Alfred A. Loeb State Park sits in a grove of myrtlewood trees, many over 200 years old, along the clear Chetco River. Several campsites and three rental log cabins look over the river.

Visitors fish, swim, raft and walk the self-guided Riverview nature trail. The Chetco is known for strong fall and winter salmon and steelhead runs, fished from the bank or a drift boat. At the end of the Riverview Trail, cross North Bank Road to the 1-mile Forest Service Redwood loop through the northernmost redwood grove in the U.S.
excerpt: Alfred A. Loeb State Park sits in a grove of myrtlewood trees, many over 200 years old, along the clear Chetco River. Several campsites and three rental log cab
note: 47 first-come, first-served electrical sites with water; 3 reservable log cabins (1 pet-friendly; reservations 800-452-5687). Flush toilets, hot showers, firewood for sale; no dump station.
address: Chetco River, Brookings, OR

title: Arizona Beach State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Arizona Beach is a two-thirds-mile stretch of sand between two rocky headlands that shelter it from prevailing winds, keeping it mild enough to earn its name. Mussel and Myrtle creeks run through the park east of US 101, and the wetlands draw elk and waterfowl.

Arizona Pond, stocked with rainbow trout, is reserved for young anglers 17 and under, and is used for school groups and park fishing and education programs.
excerpt: Arizona Beach is a two-thirds-mile stretch of sand between two rocky headlands that shelter it from prevailing winds, keeping it mild enough to earn its name. M
note: Youth fishing only at Arizona Pond (licenses required ages 14-17). Arizona Beach Group Camp is nearby.
address: US 101, Ophir, OR

title: Cape Blanco State Park
contentHtml:
Cape Blanco State Park sits on Oregon's westernmost point, beside Cape Blanco Lighthouse. Proposed in 1864, the lighthouse became the first in Oregon fitted with a first-order Fresnel lens in 1870; a second-order lens replaced it in 1936.

The lighthouse and the historic Hughes House are open for tours April through October. The park has more than eight miles of hiking trails through coastal, woodland and wetland settings, seven miles of horse trails, and headland beaches known for sunset walks.
excerpt: Cape Blanco State Park sits on Oregon's westernmost point, beside Cape Blanco Lighthouse. Proposed in 1864, the lighthouse became the first in Oregon fitted wit
note: About 50 electrical sites with water, 4 reservable cabins (2 pet-friendly), an 8-site horse camp, a group camp for up to 50 people and a hiker/biker camp. Flush toilets, hot showers, firewood for sale. 7 accessible campsites and 1 accessible cabin.
address: Cape Blanco Rd, Sixes, OR

title: Cape Sebastian State Scenic Corridor

gallery.alt: Walking the beach below the cape

contentHtml:
Cape Sebastian was named for Saint Sebastian by Spanish navigator Sebastian Vizcaino in 1603. Two parking areas sit more than 200 feet above the sea: from the south vista you can see 43 miles north to Humbug Mountain, and nearly 50 miles south toward Crescent City, California, and Point St. George Lighthouse.

A Sitka spruce forest covers most of the park. A 1.5-mile trail leads down to the lower levels of the cape, with chances to spot gray whales during their migrations.
excerpt: Cape Sebastian was named for Saint Sebastian by Spanish navigator Sebastian Vizcaino in 1603. Two parking areas sit more than 200 feet above the sea: from the s
address: US 101, Gold Beach, OR

title: Crissey Field State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Crissey Field is a 40-acre park between the California border and the Winchuck River, with a sandy beach, wetlands and a small stand of mature trees. It is a popular beach access for residents from Gold Beach to Crescent City.

Its 4,500-square-foot Welcome Center shows off green building: solar panels generate up to 20,000 kWh a year, and the building is heated and cooled by the earth around it. Inside are travel brochures, an information kiosk and a solar energy dashboard.
excerpt: Crissey Field is a 40-acre park between the California border and the Winchuck River, with a sandy beach, wetlands and a small stand of mature trees. It is a po
note: Picnic table under a gazebo; beach access and walking paths.
address: US 101, Brookings, OR (at the California border)

title: Geisel Monument State Heritage Site
contentHtml:
Geisel Monument State Heritage Site marks the scene of a skirmish in the Rogue Indian War and holds the graves of the Geisel family.

Today it is a quiet, secluded picnic area beside Highway 101, among tall trees and ferns.
excerpt: Geisel Monument State Heritage Site marks the scene of a skirmish in the Rogue Indian War and holds the graves of the Geisel family.
address: US 101, near Gold Beach, OR

title: Harris Beach State Park
contentHtml:
Harris Beach State Park is named for Scottish pioneer George Harris, who settled here in the 1880s to raise sheep and cattle. Offshore is Bird Island (also called Goat Island), the largest island off the Oregon coast and a National Wildlife Sanctuary where tufted puffins breed.

The shore mixes sandy beaches, rocky outcrops, tidepools and sea stacks. Watch for gray whales during winter and spring migrations, plus harbor seals, California sea lions and seabirds.
excerpt: Harris Beach State Park is named for Scottish pioneer George Harris, who settled here in the 1880s to raise sheep and cattle. Offshore is Bird Island (also call
note: About 35 full-hookup sites, about 50 electrical sites, more than 60 tent sites, 6 yurts (3 pet-friendly) and a hiker/biker camp. Flush toilets, hot showers, playground, RV dump station, firewood for sale. 1 accessible campsite and 1 accessible yurt.
address: US 101, Brookings, OR

title: Humbug Mountain State Park
contentHtml:
Humbug Mountain State Park is dominated by 1,756-foot Humbug Mountain and ringed by forested hills. The mountains block cool ocean breezes, giving the campground some of the warmest weather on the Oregon coast.

The hike to the top of Humbug Mountain is the park's main draw, and visitors also windsurf and scuba dive off the beach.
excerpt: Humbug Mountain State Park is dominated by 1,756-foot Humbug Mountain and ringed by forested hills. The mountains block cool ocean breezes, giving the campgroun
note: About 40 electrical sites with water, more than 55 tent sites and a hiker/biker camp; 2 accessible electrical sites. Hot showers, flush toilets, firewood for sale.
address: US 101, Port Orford, OR

title: McVay Rock State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
McVay Rock State Recreation Site is a hidden park on a bluff above the ocean near Brookings, where seabirds riding the updrafts often fly at eye level. Below is plenty of beach for walking, surf fishing and clamming, and the bluff is a good whale-watching spot.

A large lawn suits picnics and disc golf, and the park has the Brookings area's only off-leash dog park, built by local scouts with State Parks oversight.
excerpt: McVay Rock State Recreation Site is a hidden park on a bluff above the ocean near Brookings, where seabirds riding the updrafts often fly at eye level. Below is
address: Brookings, OR

title: Otter Point State Recreation Site
contentHtml: Otter Point is a bluff-top day-use site just north of Gold Beach, with walking and hiking trails overlooking pristine beaches and unusual sandstone rock formations sculpted by wind and waves.
excerpt: Otter Point is a bluff-top day-use site just north of Gold Beach, with walking and hiking trails overlooking pristine beaches and unusual sandstone rock formati
address: US 101, just north of Gold Beach, OR

title: Paradise Point State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Paradise Point is a beach access just off US 101 at Port Orford. Its parking area has a wide coastal view from Port Orford Heads and the offshore reef to distant Cape Blanco and its lighthouse.

The beach is good for beachcombing; floats and agates are often found here.
excerpt: Paradise Point is a beach access just off US 101 at Port Orford. Its parking area has a wide coastal view from Port Orford Heads and the offshore reef to distan
address: US 101, just south of Port Orford, OR

title: Port Orford Heads State Park
contentHtml:
Port Orford Heads State Park sits on the headland above Port Orford, with hiking trails that look up and down the Pacific coast. The Coast Guard built the Port Orford Lifeboat Station here in 1934 and it served the southern Oregon coast until 1970.

The station is now a free museum run by the Cape Blanco Heritage Society, with a 36-foot motor lifeboat from the station on the grounds. A large herd of blacktail deer lives in the park; treat them as wild animals.
excerpt: Port Orford Heads State Park sits on the headland above Port Orford, with hiking trails that look up and down the Pacific coast. The Coast Guard built the Port
note: Museum admission free (donations welcome).
address: Coast Guard Hill, Port Orford, OR

title: Samuel H. Boardman State Scenic Corridor
contentHtml:
The Samuel H. Boardman State Scenic Corridor is a 12-mile forested park along a steep, rugged stretch of coast between Brookings and Gold Beach, named for Samuel H. Boardman, the first Oregon State Parks superintendent.

It has old-growth Sitka spruce, seaside prairies, small cove beaches, cliffs and forested sea stacks. Highlights include Arch Rock, Natural Bridges and Secret Beach, linked by about 27 miles of the Oregon Coast Trail.
excerpt: The Samuel H. Boardman State Scenic Corridor is a 12-mile forested park along a steep, rugged stretch of coast between Brookings and Gold Beach, named for Samue
address: US 101 between Brookings and Gold Beach, OR

title: Tseriadun State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Tseriadun (pronounced serry-AH-dun) is a long beach in Port Orford that locals call Agate Beach for the agates found here. Visitors walk the shore and photograph the offshore rocks and headlands.

Native Americans once lived here in cedar plank houses, hunting and fishing in the nearby mountains and rivers. Nearby Garrison Lake has rainbow and native cutthroat trout.
excerpt: Tseriadun (pronounced serry-AH-dun) is a long beach in Port Orford that locals call Agate Beach for the agates found here. Visitors walk the shore and photograp
address: Agate Beach Rd, Port Orford, OR

title: Winchuck State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Winchuck State Recreation Site has a parking area with access to the Winchuck River and an ocean beach, for fishing, clamming, walking, photography and watching marine life.

A multi-agency project is restoring a 1.2-acre estuary at the river's mouth on the 6.8-acre site, to improve habitat, open more beach and add viewpoints.
excerpt: Winchuck State Recreation Site has a parking area with access to the Winchuck River and an ocean beach, for fishing, clamming, walking, photography and watching
note: Trail improvements and more landscaping are planned.
address: US 101, Brookings, OR

title: Butler Bar Campground
contentHtml:
Butler Bar is a 7-site primitive campground on the Wild and Scenic Elk River, bordering the Copper Salmon and Grassy Knob wilderness areas and along the Wild Rivers Coast Scenic Bikeway. Visitors hike, swim, picnic, cycle and watch for wildlife.

From Port Orford, drive north on Highway 101 to Forest Road 5325, turn right and continue 22 miles.

note: Vault toilet, picnic tables and fire rings. No drinking water and no garbage service: pack out your trash. Quiet hours 10 PM - 6 AM; campfires in fire pits only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; no OHV/ATV use in the campground; 14-day stay limit.

title: Elko Campground
contentHtml: Elko is a primitive campground in the Gold Beach Ranger District of the Siskiyou National Forest, with three tent sites and one outhouse, first come, first served.
excerpt: Elko is a primitive campground in the Gold Beach Ranger District of the Siskiyou National Forest, with three tent sites and one outhouse, first come, first serv

title: Foster Bar Campground
contentHtml:
Foster Bar Campground sits at the edge of a large meadow beside the Wild and Scenic Rogue River, site of the last battle of the Rogue River Indian Wars. A boat ramp just downstream serves rafters and anglers on a stretch known for its fishing.

The Lower Rogue River Trail #1168 is about half a mile away from the Foster Bar Trailhead. From Gold Beach, take Jerry's Flat Road (County Road 595) and Agness Road (FR 3300) 27 miles to the mouth of the Illinois River, then Agness-Illahe Road (County Road 375) 7.5 miles to the campground.

note: 8 first-come, first-served sites (4 tent-only, 4 tent or trailer). $15 per night; $5 extra vehicle. contentHtml: Game Lake is a primitive campground with three tent sites and an outhouse on the edge of the Kalmiopsis Wilderness. The Game Lake Trailhead nearby leads onto Horse Sign Butte Way Trail #1175.

title: Laird Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Laird Lake Campground has 4 first-come, first-served sites near Laird Lake at the headwaters of the Wild and Scenic Elk River, along the Wild Rivers Coast Scenic Bikeway. The lake is stocked each year with catchable rainbow trout.

From Port Orford, drive north on Highway 101 to Forest Road 5325, turn right and continue 28 miles.

contentHtml: Little Redwood is a small first-come, first-served campground on North Bank Chetco River Road near Brookings, with 12 to 15 sites, picnic tables, fire pits and vault toilets.

title: Lobster Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Lobster Creek Campground has seven sites among the trees near the Wild and Scenic Lower Rogue River, with a boat launch and a gravel bar for day use. Nearby trails include Frances Shrader Old Growth Trail #1172, Myrtle Tree Trail #1163 and Lower Rogue River Trail #1168.

From Gold Beach, drive 10 miles east on County Road 595, then continue on Forest Road 33.

title: Oak Flat Campground
contentHtml:
Oak Flat Campground has 15 sites for tents and small trailers along the Wild and Scenic Illinois River near its mouth, close to the Illinois River West Trailhead. The area is good for hiking, horse riding, swimming, non- motorized boating and river fishing.

From Gold Beach, take County Road 595 and Forest Road 33 east along the Rogue River about 29 miles to County Road 450, then follow it south 4 miles.

title: Quosatana Campground
contentHtml:
Quosatana Campground covers 15 acres on a large river bar along the Wild and Scenic Lower Rogue River, with room for camping, boating and shore fishing. It has a day-use area with a play area, a boat launch and a fish cleaning station.

From Gold Beach, travel 14 miles east on County Road 595 and Forest Road 33.

title: Sunshine Bar Campground
contentHtml:
Sunshine Bar is a free campground with six sites on the Wild and Scenic Elk River, along the Wild Rivers Coast Scenic Bikeway. Visitors hike, swim, picnic, cycle and watch for wildlife.

From Port Orford, drive north on Highway 101 to Forest Road 5325, turn right and continue 19 miles; the campground is on the left.

title: Wildhorse Campground
contentHtml:
Wildhorse Campground is a free, primitive tent campground in the Siskiyou National Forest outside Gold Beach, with pit toilets, fire rings and tables.

From Gold Beach, take County Road 595 for 10 miles, continue on Forest Road 33 east along the Rogue River to Forest Road 3318, turn right and drive about 12 miles to the campground.
excerpt: Wildhorse Campground is a free, primitive tent campground in the Siskiyou National Forest outside Gold Beach, with pit toilets, fire rings and tables.

title: Winchuck Campground
contentHtml: Winchuck is a Forest Service site on the Winchuck River near Brookings. The Forest Service now lists it as Winchuck Day Use.
excerpt: Winchuck is a Forest Service site on the Winchuck River near Brookings. The Forest Service now lists it as Winchuck Day Use.
