note: Reservation only. No recreation pass needed for the boat-in parking lot. No drinking water.
address: Deschutes National Forest Supervisor's Office: 63095 Deschutes Market Rd, Bend, OR 97701

title: West South Twin Campground
contentHtml:
West South Twin Campground has 23 sites on the shore of Wickiup Reservoir, between South Twin Lake and the reservoir, for tents, trailers and RVs along the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway.

From Bend, drive 26.8 miles south on Highway 97 to Wickiup Junction, then 11 miles west on County Road 43, 4.6 miles west on FR 42 and 2 miles south on FR 4260.
excerpt: West South Twin Campground has 23 sites on the shore of Wickiup Reservoir, between South Twin Lake and the reservoir, for tents, trailers and RVs along the Casc
note: Flush toilets and a boat launch to Wickiup Reservoir. Extra vehicles pay a nightly fee at the campground. Reserve at Recreation.gov.
address: Deschutes National Forest Supervisor's Office: 63095 Deschutes Market Rd, Bend, OR 97701

title: Whispering Pines Horse Camp
contentHtml:
Whispering Pines Horse Camp is a rustic horse camp under ponderosa pine west of Sisters, with 9 sites that each hold up to 4 horses. It offers early-season access to trails, including routes into the Three Sisters Wilderness.

From Sisters, drive west on Highway 242 (McKenzie Pass Highway) and follow the signs to the camp.
excerpt: Whispering Pines Horse Camp is a rustic horse camp under ponderosa pine west of Sisters, with 9 sites that each hold up to 4 horses. It offers early-season acce
note: Livestock water and vault toilets. No drinking water: bring your own. Extra vehicles pay a nightly fee at the campground. Reserve at Recreation.gov.
address: Deschutes National Forest Supervisor's Office: 63095 Deschutes Market Rd, Bend, OR 97701

title: Wyeth Campground
contentHtml:
Wyeth Campground is a small campground in mixed conifer forest on the Deschutes River just downstream from Wickiup Reservoir, popular for paddling and fishing. It has 5 sites, one of them tent-only, and a boat ramp.

From Bend, drive about 27 miles south on Highway 97, then 8 miles west on County Road 43. Look for the sign on County Road 43.
excerpt: Wyeth Campground is a small campground in mixed conifer forest on the Deschutes River just downstream from Wickiup Reservoir, popular for paddling and fishing.
note: Picnic tables, fire pits and vault toilets. No water or hookups: bring your own water. Extra vehicles pay a nightly fee at the campground. Reserve at Recreation.gov.
address: Deschutes National Forest Supervisor's Office: 63095 Deschutes Market Rd, Bend, OR 97701

title: Chush Falls
contentHtml:
Chush Falls is the most powerful of the many waterfalls in the upper Whychus Creek basin on the north side of Broken Top, and the only one with a maintained trail. Whychus Creek drops 67 feet in a single veiling plunge about 75 feet wide, bulging outward as it falls, and its spray keeps the base green with moss. The flow is strongest early in the season.

From Highway 242 in downtown Sisters, turn south on FR 16 (signed for Three Creek Lake; not FR 15). After about 7 miles turn right on FR 1514 for just under 5 miles, then left on FR 1514-600 just before the concrete bridge over Whychus Creek. This very rough road (passable for passenger cars with decent clearance) runs just under a mile to the Chush Falls Trailhead. The falls are about 2.25 miles up a moderate trail, at its official end.
excerpt: Chush Falls is the most powerful of the many waterfalls in the upper Whychus Creek basin on the north side of Broken Top, and the only one with a maintained tra
note: Formerly called Lower Squaw Creek Falls; the Forest Service renamed it in 2005. Chush is a Sahaptin word for water.
address: Three Sisters Wilderness, Chush Falls Trailhead off FR 1514-600, south of Sisters, OR (44.14975, -121.68298)
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Cline Falls
imageAlt: The Deschutes River at Cline Falls (area photo)

banner.alt: The Deschutes River at Cline Falls (area photo)

contentHtml:
Cline Falls is a 20-foot segmented cascade where the Deschutes River pours through several channels cut into basalt, with sagebrush along the banks. It is named for Dr. Cass A. Cline, a Redmond dentist who homesteaded across the river.

The falls are just north of the Highway 126 bridge over the Deschutes. Exit onto 74th Street and turn left; a long pullout by a fence gives views. Closer views are reported from the far side of the river, walking downstream from Cline Falls State Scenic Viewpoint.
excerpt: Cline Falls is a 20-foot segmented cascade where the Deschutes River pours through several channels cut into basalt, with sagebrush along the banks. It is named
note: Much of the river is diverted upstream for irrigation and power, so flow can be low, and the falls may run dry in dry years.
address: Off OR 126 at the Deschutes River bridge, about 4 miles west of Redmond, OR (44.27688, -121.25845)

title: Columnar Canyon Falls
contentHtml: Columnar Canyon Falls is the major waterfall on the South Fork of Whychus Creek, plunging 125 feet in two drops (the tallest 100 feet) into a gaping canyon lined for several hundred feet with columnar basalt.
excerpt: Columnar Canyon Falls is the major waterfall on the South Fork of Whychus Creek, plunging 125 feet in two drops (the tallest 100 feet) into a gaping canyon line
note: Also called Upper South Fork Falls. The waterfall survey calls it one of the more precarious falls in the drainage to view and does not recommend visiting. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.
address: South Fork Whychus Creek, Three Sisters Wilderness, south of Sisters, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Crater Creek Cascades
contentHtml: Crater Creek Cascades is a 67-foot series of six cascades between two larger falls on Crater Creek. The upper part is a run of bedrock slides and shallow punchbowls; the last is a 17-foot twisting horsetail about 100 feet above Lower Crater Creek Falls. The creek bed is heavily scoured from a 1966 flood, when a glacier calved into Moraine Lake on Broken Top and the wave breached the lake's natural dam.
excerpt: Crater Creek Cascades is a 67-foot series of six cascades between two larger falls on Crater Creek. The upper part is a run of bedrock slides and shallow punchb
note: The canyon is too steep to approach the upper slides closely. Flows year-round, but a ditch diverts part of Crater Creek upstream, so late-summer flow can be much lower. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.
address: Crater Creek, below Broken Top, west of Bend, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Crater Creek Falls
contentHtml: Crater Creek Falls drops 81 feet in two tiers in the canyon of Crater Creek: a 9-foot plunge over a low ledge, then a 72-foot curtain-style plunge into a deeper part of the chasm. It is most powerful in early summer, and in autumn the water spreads into lacy rivulets. The creek bed is heavily scoured from a 1966 flood, when a glacier calved into Moraine Lake on Broken Top and the wave breached the lake's natural dam.

note: Flows year-round, but a ditch diverts part of Crater Creek upstream, so late-summer flow can be much lower. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.

title: Demaris Falls
contentHtml: Demaris Falls is a 65-foot horsetail on South Fork Whychus Creek at about 6,145 feet, its height measured from lidar data.
excerpt: Demaris Falls is a 65-foot horsetail on South Fork Whychus Creek at about 6,145 feet, its height measured from lidar data.
note: Unofficial name. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.
address: South Fork Whychus Creek, south of Sisters, OR (44.13441, -121.73248)

title: Double Falls
imageAlt: The namesake double of Double Falls

banner.alt: The namesake double of Double Falls

contentHtml:
Double Falls is really a triple waterfall on Tumalo Creek beneath Broken Top, 89 feet in all: a 37-foot slide over a two-step cascade, a quick S-bend, a 23-foot fanning veil and a final 29-foot plunge. The third drop is just out of sight from the main viewpoint.

From Highway 97 in Bend, go west on Franklin Street, then right on Galveston Street across the Deschutes River. Galveston becomes Skyliners Road after Century Drive; follow it about 10.5 miles and turn left on FR 4601 (signed for Tumalo Falls) just after crossing Tumalo Creek. The gravel road ends 2.5 miles later at the Tumalo Falls Trailhead. Hike past the top of Tumalo Falls and about a mile upstream to the first viewpoint; trailside views are 300 feet farther.

note: The trail runs along a sheer cliff about 125 feet above the canyon floor; keep children close.
address: Tumalo Creek, about 10 miles west of Bend, OR (44.04165, -121.57837)

title: Howlaak Falls
contentHtml: Howlaak Falls is a 70-foot veiling horsetail, about 90 feet wide, near the head of a deep canyon on Park Creek close to where it joins Whychus Creek. It is the second largest waterfall in the Park Creek drainage and flows well year-round.

note: Also called Park Creek Falls. The creek confluence makes the falls hard to reach and hard to see clearly. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.

title: Island Falls
imageAlt: The upper tier of Island Falls

banner.alt: The upper tier of Island Falls

contentHtml:
Island Falls drops 53 feet in two tiers on Paulina Creek, which drains the Newberry Volcano caldera. The upper tier spreads over a broad ledge and may split around a small rock; the lower tier, about 75 feet downstream, is a narrower horsetail. Snowmelt filtered through lava keeps it flowing fairly steadily all year.

From the Ten Mile Sno-Park on Paulina-East Lake Road, take the bike trails that fork left from the top of the lot to a dirt road (about a third of a mile). Turn left and go downhill about half a mile, then right on a narrower trail; the top of the falls is about 0.1 mile on. For the lower tier, cross the footbridge and go about a quarter mile downstream on the Peter Skene Ogden Trail.
excerpt: Island Falls drops 53 feet in two tiers on Paulina Creek, which drains the Newberry Volcano caldera. The upper tier spreads over a broad ledge and may split aro
note: Trees and fallen boulders partly block the views.

title: Kaluwas Falls
imageAlt: Kaluwas Falls from just beyond the end of the trail

banner.alt: Kaluwas Falls from just beyond the end of the trail

contentHtml:
Kaluwas Falls drops about 230 feet in two tiers on Whychus Creek on the north side of Broken Top: a 45-foot chute, then a broad 185-foot veil framed by volcanic cliffs. Fed by the Bend Glacier on Broken Top, it keeps a healthy flow through much of the summer.

From Highway 242 in downtown Sisters, turn south on FR 16 (signed for Three Creek Lake; not FR 15). After about 7 miles turn right on FR 1514 for just under 5 miles, then left on FR 1514-600 just before the concrete bridge over Whychus Creek. This very rough road (passable for passenger cars with decent clearance) runs just under a mile to the Chush Falls Trailhead. The falls are about 2.75 miles from the trailhead, about half a mile past the end of the maintained trail at Chush Falls.

The creek bed is heavily scoured from a 1966 flood, when a glacier calved into Moraine Lake on Broken Top and the wave breached the lake's natural dam.

title: Lower North Fork Tumalo Falls
contentHtml: Lower North Fork Tumalo Falls is the last of four major falls on North Fork Tumalo Creek, a 43-foot plunge into an azure pool. It flows year-round.

title: Middle Crater Creek Falls
contentHtml: Middle Crater Creek Falls is a 52-foot horsetail, the third of several falls on Crater Creek below the Soda Creek meadows. Unlike the falls upstream, it slides over a rounded ledge of bright red rock. The creek bed is heavily scoured from a 1966 flood, when a glacier calved into Moraine Lake on Broken Top and the wave breached the lake's natural dam.

title: Middle Fork Tumalo Falls
imageAlt: Both tiers of Middle Fork Tumalo Falls

banner.alt: Both tiers of Middle Fork Tumalo Falls

contentHtml:
Middle Fork Tumalo Falls drops 53 feet in two tiers (44 and 9 feet) over a broad, undercut basalt ledge up to 65 feet wide. Water diverted from Crater Creek keeps it flowing year-round.

From Highway 97 in Bend, go west on Franklin Street, then right on Galveston Street across the Deschutes River. Galveston becomes Skyliners Road after Century Drive; follow it about 10.5 miles and turn left on FR 4601 (signed for Tumalo Falls) just after crossing Tumalo Creek. The gravel road ends 2.5 miles later at the Tumalo Falls Trailhead. Hike upstream just over 3.1 miles, past Double Falls and Middle Tumalo Falls, to a large wooden post marking the spur to the viewpoint below the falls.

photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Middle Tumalo Falls
contentHtml: Middle Tumalo Falls is a 43-foot vertical drop into a small gorge on Tumalo Creek, the uppermost mapped falls on the creek. Hikers pass Tumalo Falls and Double Falls on the way, and it flows year-round.
excerpt: Middle Tumalo Falls is a 43-foot vertical drop into a small gorge on Tumalo Creek, the uppermost mapped falls on the creek. Hikers pass Tumalo Falls and Double
note: Reached by the Tumalo Creek trail from the Tumalo Falls Trailhead, with an official viewpoint just off the trail. Trees block much of the view; seeing it in full means scrambling down the slopes.
address: Tumalo Creek, west of Bend, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: North Fork Tumalo Falls
contentHtml: North Fork Tumalo Falls drops 84 feet in three tiers, the second of four falls on North Fork Tumalo Creek: a 5- foot sluice, a 38-foot curtain and a final 41-foot chute through a narrow crack in the wall of a broad canyon more than 150 feet deep. It flows year-round.
excerpt: North Fork Tumalo Falls drops 84 feet in three tiers, the second of four falls on North Fork Tumalo Creek: a 5- foot sluice, a 38-foot curtain and a final 41-fo
note: The canyon slopes are crumbly. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.
address: North Fork Tumalo Creek, west of Bend, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Paulina Creek Falls
imageAlt: Paulina Creek Falls from the trail to its base

banner.alt: Paulina Creek Falls from the trail to its base

gallery.alt: Paulina Creek Falls from the top

contentHtml:
Paulina Creek Falls is a pair of side-by-side 78-foot falls where a horseshoe-shaped cliff splits Paulina Creek, about a quarter mile below the outlet of Paulina Lake in Newberry National Volcanic Monument. The south channel falls freely; the north one hits a ledge that throws the water outward. Fed by Paulina and East lakes, it flows fairly steadily all year.

From Bend, drive about 21 miles south on Highway 97 to Paulina Lake Road, then about 12.5 miles to the signed parking lot. A 200-foot trail leads to the viewpoint above the falls, and a quarter-mile trail winds down to the base.
excerpt: Paulina Creek Falls is a pair of side-by-side 78-foot falls where a horseshoe-shaped cliff splits Paulina Creek, about a quarter mile below the outlet of Paulin
address: Paulina Lake Road, Newberry National Volcanic Monument, OR (43.71225, -121.28239)
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Phoenix Falls
contentHtml: Phoenix Falls is a 115-foot spreading veil, about 70 feet wide, flanked by basalt cliffs on East Fork Park Creek, with a meadow-lined stream below. It is the uppermost of nine waterfalls in the Whychus Creek basin north of Broken Top and the second largest. Springs keep it flowing year-round.
excerpt: Phoenix Falls is a 115-foot spreading veil, about 70 feet wide, flanked by basalt cliffs on East Fork Park Creek, with a meadow-lined stream below. It is the up
note: Informal name, after the burned forest around it. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.
address: East Fork Park Creek, north of Broken Top, south of Sisters, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Tumalo Falls
imageAlt: Morning light on Tumalo Falls from the lower viewpoint

banner.alt: Morning light on Tumalo Falls from the lower viewpoint

gallery.alt: Looking down on Tumalo Falls from above

contentHtml:
Tumalo Falls is the tallest and most impressive waterfall on Tumalo Creek, an 89-foot vertical curtain beneath Broken Top. A 1979 fire burned the valley, which is now regrowing with young firs.

From Highway 97 in Bend, go west on Franklin Street, then right on Galveston Street across the Deschutes River. Galveston becomes Skyliners Road after Century Drive; follow it about 10.5 miles and turn left on FR 4601 (signed for Tumalo Falls) just after crossing Tumalo Creek. The gravel road ends 2.5 miles later at the Tumalo Falls Trailhead. The lower viewpoint is about 50 feet from the parking lot, and an easy trail zigzags up to the top of the falls.
excerpt: Tumalo Falls is the tallest and most impressive waterfall on Tumalo Creek, an 89-foot vertical curtain beneath Broken Top. A 1979 fire burned the valley, which
note: Flows year-round.
address: Tumalo Falls Trailhead, end of FR 4601, about 10 miles west of Bend, OR (44.03378, -121.5669)
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Crane Prairie Reservoir

gallery.alt: Rock Creek on Crane Prairie Reservoir

contentHtml:
Crane Prairie Reservoir is a large high-country reservoir in the Cascade Lakes area, where wetlands, standing timber and shallow water draw many kinds of birds. Browns Mountain is an unimproved launch with a gentle slope and calmer water; Crane Prairie Day Use and Rock Creek are developed alternatives.

Motorboats share the reservoir under a 10 mph speed limit. Water levels change through the season, and wind builds quickly on open water.
excerpt: Crane Prairie Reservoir is a large high-country reservoir in the Cascade Lakes area, where wetlands, standing timber and shallow water draw many kinds of birds.
note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). Keep away from nesting areas and follow posted closures. Check Oregon Health Authority algae advisories before you go.
address: Browns Mountain launch, Crane Prairie Reservoir, Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway, Deschutes National Forest, OR

title: Deschutes Paddle Trail
contentHtml:
The Deschutes Paddle Trail takes in the navigable stretches of the Deschutes and Little Deschutes rivers in Deschutes County plus nine of the county's largest Cascade lakes. The river trail covers 121 miles: 95 miles of the Deschutes from Wickiup Reservoir north to Lower Bridge, and 26 miles of the Little Deschutes from La Pine to where it joins the Deschutes near Sunriver.

Water ranges from easy Class I to expert-only Class V. Flows are managed for irrigation, so sections south of north Bend are generally paddleable April to October and sections north of Bend October to April. The Bend Paddle Trail Alliance offers downloadable river and lake maps.
excerpt: The Deschutes Paddle Trail takes in the navigable stretches of the Deschutes and Little Deschutes rivers in Deschutes County plus nine of the county's largest C
note: The hardest sections are dangerous; know your section before you launch. The Little Deschutes has little flow in winter.
address: Riverbend Park, 799 SW Columbia St, Bend, OR (one access point)

title: Deschutes River: Big River to Harper Bridge
contentHtml:
This easy 7.5-mile one-way float on the Deschutes River runs from Big River Boating Site to Harper Bridge River Access, about 2 to 3 hours on gentle current past ponderosa pine forest, open meadows and river bends. Watch for osprey, deer, otters, kingfishers and herons.

It is part of the Deschutes Paddle Trail. Motorboats are allowed, but traffic is usually light.
excerpt: This easy 7.5-mile one-way float on the Deschutes River runs from Big River Boating Site to Harper Bridge River Access, about 2 to 3 hours on gentle current pas
note: Shuttle required: arrange a pickup or leave a second vehicle at Harper Bridge.
address: Big River Boating Site, South Century Drive (FR 4205), south of Sunriver, OR

title: Deschutes River: La Pine State Park to Big River
imageAlt: Deschutes River from the La Pine State Park viewpoint

banner.alt: Deschutes River from the La Pine State Park viewpoint

contentHtml:
This easy 10.6-mile one-way float on the Deschutes River runs from the La Pine State Park bridge launch to Big River Boating Site, about 3 to 4 hours on flatwater with a gentle current. The wide river passes pine forest, grassy meadows and volcanic rock.

It is part of the Deschutes Paddle Trail. Motorboats are allowed, but traffic is usually light.
excerpt: This easy 10.6-mile one-way float on the Deschutes River runs from the La Pine State Park bridge launch to Big River Boating Site, about 3 to 4 hours on flatwat
note: Shuttle required: arrange a pickup or leave a second vehicle at Big River.
address: La Pine State Park Bridge Boat Launch, La Pine State Park, OR

title: East Lake
contentHtml:
East Lake covers about 1,044 acres inside the Newberry Volcano caldera south of Bend, sharing the caldera with Paulina Lake. Paddlers launch from the boat ramp at East Lake Campground, which has day-use parking, flush toilets and drinking water.

Motorboats and anglers share the lake under a 10 mph speed limit.
excerpt: East Lake covers about 1,044 acres inside the Newberry Volcano caldera south of Bend, sharing the caldera with Paulina Lake. Paddlers launch from the boat ramp
note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). A recreation pass or day-use fee is required at the boat launch. Check algae advisories. Water stays cold even in summer and wind can rise quickly; wear a life jacket. Clean, drain and dry your boat to stop invasive species.
address: East Lake Campground boat ramp, Newberry National Volcanic Monument, OR

title: Hosmer Lake
contentHtml:
Hosmer Lake is a shallow, clear mountain lake lined with marsh and reeds, with views of Mt. Bachelor, South Sister and Broken Top. Brook and rainbow trout can be seen in the water, and the lake is fly-fishing only, so give anglers room.

The Hosmer Lake Boating Site has a small ramp, gravel parking and vault toilets but no drinking water. Only electric motors are allowed, so there are no wakes.
excerpt: Hosmer Lake is a shallow, clear mountain lake lined with marsh and reeds, with views of Mt. Bachelor, South Sister and Broken Top. Brook and rainbow trout can b
note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). Recreation pass or $5 per vehicle per day to park. Move carefully through shallow water and thick vegetation. Water stays cold even in summer and wind can rise quickly; wear a life jacket. Clean, drain and dry your boat to stop invasive species.
address: Hosmer Lake Boating Site, FR 4625 off the Cascade Lakes Highway, west of Bend, OR

title: Little Deschutes River: Thousand Trails to Harper Bridge
imageAlt: Little Deschutes River: Thousand Trails to Harper Bridge
contentHtml:
This easy 5.3-mile one-way paddle on the Little Deschutes River takes about 1.5 to 2 hours, following a narrow, winding channel through pine forest, grassy banks and open meadows with occasional Cascade views. It launches at the Thousand Trails Sunriver boat ramp and takes out at Harper Bridge River Access.

It is part of the Deschutes Paddle Trail.
excerpt: This easy 5.3-mile one-way paddle on the Little Deschutes River takes about 1.5 to 2 hours, following a narrow, winding channel through pine forest, grassy bank
note: Shuttle required. The launch ramp is inside the Thousand Trails campground. The route passes through Crosswater Golf Course, which is private property: stay on the water.
address: Thousand Trails Bend-Sunriver boat ramp, Little Deschutes River, Sunriver, OR

title: Little Lava Lake
contentHtml:
Little Lava Lake is a forested mountain lake at about 4,740 feet on the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway, considered the source of the Deschutes River. The Little Lava Lake Boating Site has a gravel ramp and limited parking, with no fee listed by the Forest Service.

Motorboats share the lake, so stay visible.
excerpt: Little Lava Lake is a forested mountain lake at about 4,740 feet on the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway, considered the source of the Deschutes River. The Little Lav
note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). No drinking water. Water stays cold even in summer and wind can rise quickly; wear a life jacket. Clean, drain and dry your boat to stop invasive species.
address: Little Lava Lake Boating Site, FR 4600-500 and 4600-520 off the Cascade Lakes Highway, OR

title: Paulina Lake
contentHtml:
Paulina Lake is a high volcanic lake inside Newberry National Volcanic Monument south of Bend, with several Forest Service boat launches and a resort with boating access. Kayaks and paddleboards can also launch from the day-use area next to Paulina Lake Campground.

Motorboats share the lake under a 10 mph speed limit. Open water can get rough in wind.
excerpt: Paulina Lake is a high volcanic lake inside Newberry National Volcanic Monument south of Bend, with several Forest Service boat launches and a resort with boati
note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). A recreation pass is required at Forest Service boat launches. Roads, docks and facilities are seasonal. Water stays cold even in summer and wind can rise quickly; wear a life jacket. Clean, drain and dry your boat to stop invasive species.
address: Paulina Lake Campground boat launch, Newberry National Volcanic Monument, OR

title: South Twin Lake
contentHtml: South Twin Lake is a volcanic crater lake of about 99 acres in the Deschutes National Forest, averaging about 33 feet deep. Motorboats are not allowed, so it is a quiet lake for kayaks, canoes and paddleboards, launched from the ramp at the South Twin Day Use Area.
excerpt: South Twin Lake is a volcanic crater lake of about 99 acres in the Deschutes National Forest, averaging about 33 feet deep. Motorboats are not allowed, so it is
note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). $5 day-use fee or recreation pass to park. No drinking water. Water stays cold even in summer and wind can rise quickly; wear a life jacket. Clean, drain and dry your boat to stop invasive species.
address: South Twin Day Use Area, FR 4260 off FR 42, near Wickiup Reservoir, OR

title: Sparks Lake
contentHtml:
Sparks Lake sits along the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway, fed by streams off Broken Top, with a boat launch, parking and picnic area at the Sparks Lake Day Use Area. Shallow, rocky areas call for care.

The 10 mph speed limit for boats is strictly enforced.
excerpt: Sparks Lake sits along the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway, fed by streams off Broken Top, with a boat launch, parking and picnic area at the Sparks Lake Day Use Are
note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). $5 day-use fee or recreation pass to park. No drinking water and no camping at the ramp or day-use area. Water stays cold even in summer and wind can rise quickly; wear a life jacket. Clean, drain and dry your boat to stop invasive species.
address: Sparks Lake Day Use Area, off the Cascade Lakes Highway, about 26 miles west of Bend, OR

title: Three Creek Lake
contentHtml: Three Creek Lake is a high mountain lake south of Sisters near the Three Sisters Wilderness. Motorboats are not allowed, and paddlers launch from a primitive ramp on the east shore near Driftwood Campground. Vault toilets are near the campgrounds, but there is no drinking water.
excerpt: Three Creek Lake is a high mountain lake south of Sisters near the Three Sisters Wilderness. Motorboats are not allowed, and paddlers launch from a primitive ra
note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). Snow can delay access into summer. Water stays cold even in summer and wind can rise quickly; wear a life jacket. Clean, drain and dry your boat to stop invasive species.
address: East-shore boat ramp near Driftwood Campground, FR 16, about 16 miles south of Sisters, OR

title: South Sister
contentHtml: South Sister is a 10,358-foot volcano in the Three Sisters Wilderness, its summit on the Lane-Deschutes county line. The standard route, the South Sister Climber Trail from Devils Lake Trailhead, is about 12 miles round trip with about 4,900 feet of gain: no technical climbing, but very demanding. The Green Lakes/Soda Creek Trailhead is a longer alternative.
excerpt: South Sister is a 10,358-foot volcano in the Three Sisters Wilderness, its summit on the Lane-Deschutes county line. The standard route, the South Sister Climbe
note: From June 15 to October 15 a reserved Central Cascades Wilderness day-use permit is needed at the Devils Lake and Green Lakes trailheads, and an overnight permit for any night in the wilderness; book on Recreation.gov. A federal recreation pass is needed to park.
address: Devils Lake Trailhead, Cascade Lakes Highway (46), west of Bend, OR

title: Metolius–Windigo Trail
contentHtml:
The Metolius-Windigo Trail (Trail #99) runs roughly 150 miles through the Deschutes National Forest, from the Metolius Basin near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness west of Sisters south to Windigo Pass near Crescent Lake. Created around 1980 as a lower-elevation alternative to the Pacific Crest Trail, it connects to the PCT at both ends and is popular with horse riders.

Todd Creek Horse Camp and the Todd Lake Trailhead, off the Cascade Lakes Highway west of Bend, are official access points.
excerpt: The Metolius-Windigo Trail (Trail #99) runs roughly 150 miles through the Deschutes National Forest, from the Metolius Basin near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness
note: Published lengths vary from about 120 to 152 miles.
address: Deschutes National Forest Supervisor's Office: 63095 Deschutes Market Rd, Bend, OR 97701

title: Oregon Desert Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Desert Trail is a 750-mile route across Oregon's high desert, created and managed by the Oregon Natural Desert Association (ONDA). It starts in the Oregon Badlands Wilderness outside Bend and ends at Lake Owyhee State Park near the Idaho border, linking Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, Steens Mountain, the Pueblo and Trout Creek mountains and the Owyhee Canyonlands.

It strings together hiking trails, old jeep tracks and wagon roads with long cross-country stretches. All of it is open to hiking, and some sections suit horseback, boat, bike or skis.
excerpt: The Oregon Desert Trail is a 750-mile route across Oregon's high desert, created and managed by the Oregon Natural Desert Association (ONDA). It starts in the O
note: Some sections are easy, marked walks; many need GPS navigation, real backcountry experience and careful planning, because water can be very limited. ONDA offers maps, a guidebook and GPS waypoints.
address: Western terminus: Oregon Badlands Wilderness, outside Bend, OR

title: Oregon Timber Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Timber Trail is a 670-mile mountain bike and bikepacking route from the California border near Lakeview north to Hood River on the Columbia, managed by the nonprofit Oregon Timber Trail Alliance. It is split into four tiers: Fremont, Willamette, Deschutes and Hood.

The Deschutes Tier runs from Waldo Lake to Sisters. Riders can take on the whole route or ride a shorter piece.
excerpt: The Oregon Timber Trail is a 670-mile mountain bike and bikepacking route from the California border near Lakeview north to Hood River on the Columbia, managed
address: Deschutes Tier: Waldo Lake to Sisters, OR

title: Pacific Crest Trail
contentHtml:
The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail runs 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada through California, Oregon and Washington, managed by the Forest Service with the Pacific Crest Trail Association. Its roughly 455-mile Oregon section is the shortest and easiest on the trail, from near Siskiyou Summit to the Bridge of the Gods over the Columbia River.

In Deschutes County the trail passes small lakes in the Three Sisters Wilderness beneath the Three Sisters volcanoes.
excerpt: The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail runs 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada through California, Oregon and Washington, managed by the Forest Service with the
note: Central Cascades Wilderness permits apply in the Three Sisters Wilderness from June 15 to October 15.
address: Oregon section: California border near Ashland to the Bridge of the Gods, Cascade Locks, OR

title: 4 Boys
contentHtml:
4 Boys is a 36-mile loop with about 2,100 feet of climbing: 35% gravel, 25% singletrack and the rest paved path and road. It rides Ben's Trail and the West Bend forest-thinning area, then follows the Wild and Scenic Deschutes River past Benham Falls and a Ryan Ranch wetland, along an old logging haul road and over a lava flow to Sunriver and Tetherow.

The singletrack is easy to low-intermediate mountain bike terrain with only short hike-a-bike sections. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: 4 Boys is a 36-mile loop with about 2,100 feet of climbing: 35% gravel, 25% singletrack and the rest paved path and road. It rides Ben's Trail and the West Bend
note: Rideable most of the year; late fall and early spring are best, as summer trails are busy. Food and water at Sunriver Marketplace near mile 18 (about a 1-mile detour). The GPX file has no turn-by-turn cues.
address: Start: Phil's Trailhead, west of Bend, OR

title: Alpaca
contentHtml:
Alpaca is a 36-mile loop with about 1,400 feet of climbing, 60% gravel, through alpaca farms, ranches and juniper high desert with views of Mt. Bachelor, the Three Sisters and Mt. Jefferson. It crosses the Deschutes River twice and passes some of Central Oregon's oldest junipers.

The roughest part is about 4 miles of rocky, rolling 'pump and chunk' on Barr Road. Tires of 50 mm or wider are recommended.
excerpt: Alpaca is a 36-mile loop with about 1,400 feet of climbing, 60% gravel, through alpaca farms, ranches and juniper high desert with views of Mt. Bachelor, the Th
note: Best late fall to mid-spring on a sunny day; summer dust makes the rough section very hard. A wastewater plant construction closure between miles 13 and 17 is expected to last until fall 2027: use the posted bypass route. No food or water on the route. Use a rear light on busier road sections.
address: Start: Maston Trailhead parking area, between Bend and Redmond, OR (pit toilets)

title: Big Red

gallery.alt: Big Red, the giant ponderosa pine

contentHtml:
Big Red is an easy 17-mile loop with about 500 feet of climbing on mostly shaded, smooth gravel roads and trails, visiting Big Red, a ponderosa pine estimated at more than 500 years old and about 162 feet tall. It also stops at Fall River Falls and follows the Deschutes River through La Pine State Park.

Dead Slough along the way is habitat for the Oregon spotted frog. For families, an out-and-back to Fall River Falls can start at the Big Red trailhead.
excerpt: Big Red is an easy 17-mile loop with about 500 feet of climbing on mostly shaded, smooth gravel roads and trails, visiting Big Red, a ponderosa pine estimated a
note: Late spring to late fall, once the ground is dry. Many turns are unsigned, so follow the GPS track closely. Water at a campground around mile 8.6. No parking permit needed.
address: Start: Big River Boat Launch, South Century Drive at the Deschutes River, south of Sunriver, OR

title: Big, Big Red
contentHtml:
Big, Big Red is a 48-mile loop with about 1,500 feet of climbing that circles the Deschutes River through big ponderosa pines: 35% gravel, 25% singletrack, 10% bike path and 30% paved road. It visits Big Red, the more than 500-year-old ponderosa, plus Fall River Falls, McGregor Viewpoint and Benham Falls, and rolls through Sunriver's bike paths.

A shorter 29-mile option starts in Sunriver and skips the sandy sections. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: Big, Big Red is a 48-mile loop with about 1,500 feet of climbing that circles the Deschutes River through big ponderosa pines: 35% gravel, 25% singletrack, 10%
note: Best before Memorial Day or after Labor Day: summer brings sand and heavy Sunriver traffic. Navigation is tricky, especially the Sunriver roundabouts. Food and water at La Pine State Park (mile 22, detour), Sunriver Village (mile 37, detour) and Sunriver Marketplace (mile 42). No parking permit needed.
address: Start: gravel lot just before Conklin Road (FS 41) and Benham Falls Road (FS 400), south of Bend, OR

title: Black Butte Loop
contentHtml:
Black Butte Loop is a 33-mile lollipop from Sisters, about 60% singletrack, 35% gravel road and 5% paved. Fast, flat singletrack winds through big ponderosa pines beside creeks and marshes, and double-track on Black Butte's west side gives views of the Three Sisters, Mt. Washington, Three Fingered Jack and Mt. Jefferson.

The middle technical section suits an intermediate gravel rider. Part of the route crosses into Jefferson County.
excerpt: Black Butte Loop is a 33-mile lollipop from Sisters, about 60% singletrack, 35% gravel road and 5% paved. Fast, flat singletrack winds through big ponderosa pin
note: Best in late spring and fall; it can get soft in summer, especially on trails shared with horses. Slow down for horses and ask riders how they want to be passed. No fees or permits.
address: Start: Village Green City Park, downtown Sisters, OR (free parking, restrooms, showers, water)

title: Brooks-Scanlon Rail Trail
contentHtml: The Brooks-Scanlon Rail Trail is a 27.3-mile gravel trail between Bend and Sisters through the Deschutes National Forest, following a former logging road. Parts are hilly and best for mountain bikes, and there is camping nearby.
excerpt: The Brooks-Scanlon Rail Trail is a 27.3-mile gravel trail between Bend and Sisters through the Deschutes National Forest, following a former logging road. Parts
note: A Deschutes National Forest day or annual pass is required to park.
address: Southern end: Brooks Scanlon Logging Rd at Skyliners Rd, Bend, OR (nearest parking: Phil's Trailhead)

title: Bust Your Butte
imageAlt: Red cinder road near China Hat

banner.alt: Red cinder road near China Hat

contentHtml: Bust Your Butte is a 50-mile lollipop with about 2,400 feet of climbing, about 85% gravel and 15% singletrack, following the 2018 gravel race course around China Hat and Horse Butte. Expect a mix of smooth gravel, loose red cinder, thick pumice sand and washboard, with big views.
excerpt: Bust Your Butte is a 50-mile lollipop with about 2,400 feet of climbing, about 85% gravel and 15% singletrack, following the 2018 gravel race course around Chin
note: Best in early spring or late fall, when there is less washboard. No food or water on the route. This is a development route not fully checked by Dirty Freehub, and the GPX file has no turn-by-turn cues.
address: Start: Horse Butte Trailhead parking area, southeast of Bend, OR

title: Coffee Run!

gallery.alt: Bull Creek dam and bridge at the start

contentHtml: Coffee Run! is a 31-mile out-and-back with about 1,200 feet of climbing (65% gravel, 15% singletrack, 20% paved) that ends with coffee in Sisters. It has big views of the Cascades and the Three Sisters, passes Tumalo Reservoir, a failed irrigation project with a colorful history, and rides part of the Peterson Ridge singletrack. Low climbing makes it a good cold-weather ride.
excerpt: Coffee Run! is a 31-mile out-and-back with about 1,200 feet of climbing (65% gravel, 15% singletrack, 20% paved) that ends with coffee in Sisters. It has big vi
note: Mule deer and elk winter range December 1 to March 31: keep groups to 4 riders or fewer. Watch for Peck's milkvetch, a threatened plant, near Bull Flat. The only stop is Sisters at mile 16 (Village Green Park). Use a rear light and radar on Sisemore Road.
address: Start: dirt pull-off just before the old Tumalo Reservoir bridge, Tumalo Reservoir Rd at Sisemore Rd, northwest of Bend, OR

title: Cowboy Preacher
contentHtml:
Cowboy Preacher is a 38-mile loop with about 2,100 feet of climbing, 40% gravel and 60% paved, circling Whychus Canyon. It passes historic Camp Polk Meadow and its pioneer cemetery, crosses Whychus Creek, tackles the roughest dirt roads in the Crooked River National Grassland with Cascade views, and finishes on fast gravel past hobby farms.

Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: Cowboy Preacher is a 38-mile loop with about 2,100 feet of climbing, 40% gravel and 60% paved, circling Whychus Canyon. It passes historic Camp Polk Meadow and
note: The area was burned in the 2026 Akawa Butte Fire; watch for falling burned trees and report conditions. Riders are asked to stay off the route December 1 to March 31 for mule deer migration. Check the Whychus Creek gauge before you go: above 200 cfs the crossing can't be ridden. No food or water on the route.
address: Start: Cliff Clemens Park, Sisters, OR (water and flush toilets)

title: Creek to Peak
imageAlt: Riding the road to Paulina Peak

banner.alt: Riding the road to Paulina Peak

contentHtml:
Creek to Peak is a 32-mile ride with about 3,800 feet of climbing (25% gravel, 25% singletrack, 50% paved) in Newberry National Volcanic Monument. It climbs the one-way-uphill Peter Skene Ogden singletrack along Paulina Creek past Island Falls and other waterfalls, passes Paulina Lake, grinds up gravel to Paulina Peak near 8,000 feet and returns on a long paved descent.

The singletrack has technical spots where you may need to walk.
excerpt: Creek to Peak is a 32-mile ride with about 3,800 feet of climbing (25% gravel, 25% singletrack, 50% paved) in Newberry National Volcanic Monument. It climbs the
note: Best in late spring and early summer after snowmelt, or mid-fall; the trail gets dusty and loose when dry. Ride on a weekday, as the summit road gets busy with cars. Seasonal services only at Paulina Lake Lodge (about mile 11; call ahead). The summit is much colder than the start.
address: Start: paved lot at the northeast corner of Highway 97 and Paulina Lake Road (FR 21), north of La Pine, OR

title: Dark Skies
contentHtml:
Dark Skies is a gravel loop that climbs FR 2017 through ponderosa forest to Pine Mountain Observatory at about 6,200 feet, home to several research telescopes under the high desert's dark skies, then returns along Pine Mountain Ridge. The main climb is about 4 miles at around 6%, with a 300-yard walk through deep sand.

Tires of 45 mm or wider are recommended.
excerpt: Dark Skies is a gravel loop that climbs FR 2017 through ponderosa forest to Pine Mountain Observatory at about 6,200 feet, home to several research telescopes u
note: Season mid-April to late November; late spring or fall is best, as deep summer sand makes it hard going. The summit is colder and windier. On night rides skip the ridge and use red light only. Expect cattle on open range.
address: Start: dirt parking off FR 2017 near Highway 20, Millican area, east of Bend, OR

title: Deschutes River Rambler (DR2)
imageAlt: Headwaters of the Deschutes at Little Lava Lake

banner.alt: Headwaters of the Deschutes at Little Lava Lake

gallery.alt: Deschutes River canyon near Mecca Flats

contentHtml:
The Deschutes River Rambler (DR2) is a 305-mile point-to-point bikepacking route with about 14,000 feet of climbing, 47% gravel, that follows the Deschutes River from its headwaters at Little Lava Lake to the Columbia River. It passes Cascade forests, volcanic plateaus and river canyons, climbs into the dry Oregon Outback and ends on a gravel rail-trail with seven trestle-gully hike-a-bike crossings.

It continues through Jefferson and Wasco counties. Miles 165 to 252 leave the river because of private land.
excerpt: The Deschutes River Rambler (DR2) is a 305-mile point-to-point bikepacking route with about 14,000 feet of climbing, 47% gravel, that follows the Deschutes Rive
note: A very demanding, remote development route affected by the 2026 fires. Water is scarce: carry at least 4 liters and refill at La Pine State Park, Bend, Tumalo, The Cove Palisades, Warm Springs, Trout Creek, Ashwood, Antelope and Maupin. Watch for rattlesnakes and goatheads on the trestle section. Many state park campgrounds need reservations.
address: Start: Little Lava Lake Campground, Cascade Lakes Highway; finish: Deschutes River State Recreation Area at the Columbia River

title: Devil's Dilemma
contentHtml:
Devil's Dilemma is a 76-mile loop around Mt. Bachelor with about 6,100 feet of climbing, about 70% unpaved, including some 17 miles of high alpine dirt roads, big mountain views and a creek crossing or two. The steep, rugged middle section from around mile 10 is the crux.

After that, a long, mostly downhill paved stretch passes the Deschutes River headwaters and several alpine lakes, and the ride ends on the old railroad grade along the river. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: Devil's Dilemma is a 76-mile loop around Mt. Bachelor with about 6,100 feet of climbing, about 70% unpaved, including some 17 miles of high alpine dirt roads, b
note: Best from mid-to-late June, after snowmelt, until about August 1, when the road beyond Todd Lake opens to vehicles; rideable until the first fall snow. Miles 27 to 45 are paved and busy on summer weekends. Food and water at Elk Lake Resort (mile 36) and Lava Lake Resort (mile 42, short detour). No parking permit needed.
address: Start: Cascade Lakes Welcome Station, Cascade Lakes Highway, southwest of Bend, OR (pit toilets)

title: Discovery

gallery.alt: The Flaming Chicken sculpture on Phil's Trail

contentHtml: Discovery is a 20-mile loop with about 1,000 feet of climbing, mostly fast, flowing singletrack (65%) in Bend's Phil's Trail network, plus gravel and paved path. Look for hidden gnomes along the E.L.V. trail, the Flaming Chicken sculpture near Phil's Trailhead and a mural on the way back.
excerpt: Discovery is a 20-mile loop with about 1,000 feet of climbing, mostly fast, flowing singletrack (65%) in Bend's Phil's Trail network, plus gravel and paved path
note: Best mid-spring to late fall; spring and fall give the best grip, and summer dirt gets loose. Water only at the start. Many trails are multi-use: yield to walkers, and uphill riders have the right of way. Check bendtrails.org for conditions.
address: Start: Discovery Park pavilion, NorthWest Crossing, Bend, OR (on-street parking; restrooms and water nearby)

title: Dropbar
contentHtml:
Dropbar is a 28-mile loop with about 1,800 feet of climbing (40% gravel, 40% singletrack) that links Ben's Trail with forest roads and trails up to Tumalo Falls, then a flowing descent on Mrazek. It passes through the West Bend forest thinning and burn project and the historic Skyliners Lodge area.

Much of the singletrack can be ridden without putting a foot down, with a few technical spots. Many bail-out points lead to Skyliners Road and back to Bend.
excerpt: Dropbar is a 28-mile loop with about 1,800 feet of climbing (40% gravel, 40% singletrack) that links Ben's Trail with forest roads and trails up to Tumalo Falls
note: Spring to late fall. The aspen connector near mile 14.3 can be wet in spring and fall; stay on the main gravel road to Tumalo Falls to skip it. No food or water on the route.
address: Start: Ben's Trail, Phil's Trail network, west of Bend, OR

title: Fifty 50

gallery.alt: Haul roads and rail spurs, Bend

contentHtml: Fifty 50 is a short 21-mile loop from near central Bend with about 1,200 feet of climbing: about 65% gravel, plus a little singletrack, bike path and pavement. It is good for building technical and navigation skills and for short or cold days. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: Fifty 50 is a short 21-mile loop from near central Bend with about 1,200 feet of climbing: about 65% gravel, plus a little singletrack, bike path and pavement.
note: Best in early spring and late fall; summer is busy, dusty and sandy. Keep your speed down on the busy paved path.
address: Start: NorthWest Crossing roundabout at The Grove Market Hall, Bend, OR

title: GravelCracker (The Classic)
imageAlt: Gravel road just out of Sisters

banner.alt: Gravel road just out of Sisters

contentHtml:
GravelCracker (The Classic) is a 42-mile loop from Sisters with at least 2,100 feet of climbing (35% gravel, 45% singletrack, 20% paved), past the Metolius River and Camp Sherman, behind Black Butte Ranch and around Suttle Lake, with mountain views and big ponderosa pines. It includes fast, flat drop-bar singletrack and an underpass beneath Highway 20.

It rides well in either direction and crosses into Jefferson County.
excerpt: GravelCracker (The Classic) is a 42-mile loop from Sisters with at least 2,100 feet of climbing (35% gravel, 45% singletrack, 20% paved), past the Metolius Rive
note: Best early spring to mid-summer and late fall; in summer expect deep loose dirt on GravelCracker Hill (miles 31 to 32). The route is near the 2026 fire closures (in effect until December 31, 2026), which Dirty Freehub says should not affect it. Seasonal food and water at Camp Sherman Store (mile 19), Suttle Lake Lodge (mile 23) and Cold Springs Campground (mile 38).
address: Start: Village Green City Park, Sisters, OR (restrooms, water, showers)

title: GravelCracker (The Overlander)
contentHtml:
GravelCracker (The Overlander) is a 77-mile loop from Sisters with about 4,800 feet of climbing (50% gravel and dirt, 20% singletrack, 30% paved). It rides the flanks of Black Butte, follows the Metolius River for about 10 miles, climbs through the 2003 B&B Complex fire area and passes Round Lake, Suttle Lake and Black Butte Ranch.

It crosses into Jefferson County. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: GravelCracker (The Overlander) is a 77-mile loop from Sisters with about 4,800 feet of climbing (50% gravel and dirt, 20% singletrack, 30% paved). It rides the
note: Best in spring, early summer or late fall, midweek. Nearby 2026 fire road closures (until December 31, 2026) should not include this route. Food and water at Camp Sherman (mile 26); water at Wizard Falls Fish Hatchery (mile 31), Suttle Lake Lodge (mile 62) and Cold Springs Campground.
address: Start: Village Green City Park, Sisters, OR (restrooms, water, showers)

title: H2O
imageAlt: Riding a gravel trail in the forest west of Bend

banner.alt: Riding a gravel trail in the forest west of Bend

contentHtml: H2O is a quick, fairly easy 20-mile loop just west of Bend with about 1,300 feet of climbing, about 70% gravel, one or two small hills and a short stretch of rarely ridden singletrack. Its many unmarked turns make it good navigation practice. Tires of 40 to 45 mm are suggested.
excerpt: H2O is a quick, fairly easy 20-mile loop just west of Bend with about 1,300 feet of climbing, about 70% gravel, one or two small hills and a short stretch of ra
note: Late spring through fall. A development route updated in 2026 after Forest Service closures. Around mile 10.9 a green gate leads past a cinder pit: bikes are allowed, but expect heavy trucks when the gate is open. No food or water on the route.
address: Start: The Grove (Market Hall), NorthWest Crossing, Bend, OR

title: Haul Road Trail
imageAlt: Old logging haul road near Bend (area photo)

banner.alt: Old logging haul road near Bend (area photo)

contentHtml: The Haul Road Trail is a 5-mile paved path on the route of an old railroad line that hauled lumber for Bend's mills. It runs southwest along Century Drive from near the Skyline Sports Complex, past Bend's neighborhoods and shops, to the edge of the Deschutes National Forest, and connects with the Colorado Trail and the Deschutes River Trail for longer rides.
excerpt: The Haul Road Trail is a 5-mile paved path on the route of an old railroad line that hauled lumber for Bend's mills. It runs southwest along Century Drive from
note: Parking at Skyline Sports Complex (19617 Mountaineer Way) and the Cascade Lakes Welcome Station.
address: SW Reed Market Rd, Bend, to the Cascade Lakes Welcome Station, 18500 Cascade Lakes Hwy, OR

title: Hauling Lava
imageAlt: Entering singletrack on a gravel bike

banner.alt: Entering singletrack on a gravel bike

contentHtml:
Hauling Lava is an easy 18-mile out-and-back with about 800 feet of climbing, about 55% gravel, designed with adaptive riders (trikes and quads) in mind. It follows the Old Haul Road, a former logging railroad bed, then the Upper Deschutes River past Benham Falls and ancient lava flows to the Lava Lands Visitor Center, a good turnaround and rest stop.

The haul road section is closed to cars; the paved path is shared with hikers. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: Hauling Lava is an easy 18-mile out-and-back with about 800 feet of climbing, about 55% gravel, designed with adaptive riders (trikes and quads) in mind. It fol
note: Spring through late fall; snow can linger in spring, and summer is busy. A Forest Service recreation pass is required to park and is not sold on site. A tight gate near mile 1 may need a helper for adaptive riders. Food and water only at Lava Lands Visitor Center (mile 9, seasonal).
address: Start: Aspen Day Use Area on the Deschutes River, south of Bend, OR (pit toilets)

title: Haystack
contentHtml:
Haystack is a 20-mile lollipop with about 1,500 feet of climbing, about 45% gravel, through the Crooked River National Grassland, with some of the best Cascade views in Central Oregon. It mixes gravel and BLM dirt roads, pavement, juniper country and farmland, and starts by crossing the Crooked River High Bridge.

It crosses into Jefferson County. Tires of about 40 mm are suggested.
excerpt: Haystack is a 20-mile lollipop with about 1,500 feet of climbing, about 45% gravel, through the Crooked River National Grassland, with some of the best Cascade
note: Don't ride when wet. The BLM dirt roads are the hardest part, with chunky, rutted sections. The start is the trickiest navigation: cross the High Bridge, follow the paved path to Highway 97, cross and go north 20 to 40 yards to the old Culver Highway. No food or water.
address: Start: Peter Skene Ogden State Scenic Viewpoint, Highway 97 north of Terrebonne, OR (pit toilets)

title: Haystacks & Skulls
contentHtml:
Haystacks & Skulls is a 35-mile loop with about 2,300 feet of climbing (35% gravel, 65% paved) that combines the Haystack and Skull Hollow routes: big mountain views, fast, quiet paved riding and steep gravel climbs.

It crosses into Jefferson County. Tires of about 40 mm are suggested.
excerpt: Haystacks & Skulls is a 35-mile loop with about 2,300 feet of climbing (35% gravel, 65% paved) that combines the Haystack and Skull Hollow routes: big mountain
note: Best in spring and fall. Don't ride when wet: the mud can force you to walk. Use a rear light on roads with traffic. No food or water.
address: Start: 16th Street in Terrebonne, OR, across from La Catrina Chingona (public parking; don't use the restaurant lot)

title: In Plain View

gallery.alt: Log truck on the Brooks-Scanlon logging road

contentHtml:
In Plain View is an easy 23-mile loop with about 850 feet of climbing, 90% unpaved, with views of the Three Sisters, Mt. Washington, Mt. Jefferson and Black Butte and no big climbs or descents. It passes the Skyline Forest, the failed Tumalo Reservoir and Bull Flat, and finishes over the 1914 Bull Creek (Sisemore) Bridge.

A 9.5-mile Snow Creek Shortcut is an option. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: In Plain View is an easy 23-mile loop with about 850 feet of climbing, 90% unpaved, with views of the Three Sisters, Mt. Washington, Mt. Jefferson and Black But
note: Best in spring and fall. Riding is discouraged December 1 to March 15 (mule deer winter range, closed to vehicles), and summer fire closures are possible. Some rough sections on the Brooks-Scanlon road and late-season sand. No food or water.
address: Start: dirt lot at Tumalo Reservoir Rd and Sisemore Rd, northwest of Bend, OR

title: Lower Bridge
imageAlt: The pump-and-chunk section of Barr Road, near Tumalo

banner.alt: The pump-and-chunk section of Barr Road, near Tumalo

contentHtml: Lower Bridge is a 76-mile loop with about 3,100 feet of climbing (40% gravel, 60% paved) through farm and ranch country northwest of Bend, borrowing parts of the Alpaca, Westside and H2O routes. Barr Road has a 3-mile stretch of rough 'pump and chunk', and miles 56 to 59 are the hardest, with sand, rollers and rocks. Tires of 38 mm or wider are recommended.
excerpt: Lower Bridge is a 76-mile loop with about 3,100 feet of climbing (40% gravel, 60% paved) through farm and ranch country northwest of Bend, borrowing parts of th
note: Best late fall to early spring; dry 'moon dust' on Barr Road is very rough. Rainshadow Organics (around mile 35, seasonal) sells snacks and has water. Use a rear light on paved sections. A development route not fully checked by Dirty Freehub; the GPX has no turn-by-turn cues.
address: Start: NorthWest Crossing roundabout, Bend, OR

title: McCool
contentHtml:
McCool is a 39-mile loop with about 2,000 feet of climbing on about 90% gravel and dirt road. It follows Davis Creek, skirts Davis Mountain and crosses the Black Rock lava flow through pine forest and a 2003 burn, past Davis Lake. Riders often see wildlife, including a wolf pack, white pelicans, bald eagles and osprey.

It crosses into Klamath County. Tires of 50 mm or wider are suggested; a Davis Creek bypass cuts about 4 miles.
excerpt: McCool is a 39-mile loop with about 2,000 feet of climbing on about 90% gravel and dirt road. It follows Davis Creek, skirts Davis Mountain and crosses the Blac
note: Late spring to early summer, and fall: the route tops out near 5,300 feet, so wait for snowmelt, and ride when the ground is damp to avoid soft sand. Miles 9.2 to 9.8 use a road missing from some maps.
address: Start: roadside pullout on the Cascade Lakes Highway just past Davis Creek (from the north), near Davis Lake, OR

title: McKenzie Pass Scenic Bikeway

gallery.alt: Reaching the top of the pass

contentHtml:
The McKenzie Pass Scenic Bikeway is an epic one-way road ride of about 35 miles from Sisters west over McKenzie Pass on Highway 242, which follows an 1860s wagon route. After an easy first 8 miles, a climb of about 5 miles starts at McGregor's Curve and passes Windy Point, with views of Mt. Washington, and lava- rock walls to the summit.

At the top, a lava 'moonscape' surrounds the Dee Wright Observatory, whose windows frame 360-degree views. The 25-mile descent drops about 4,000 feet through switchbacks into the wetter McKenzie River forests to Highway 126.
excerpt: The McKenzie Pass Scenic Bikeway is an epic one-way road ride of about 35 miles from Sisters west over McKenzie Pass on Highway 242, which follows an 1860s wago
note: Rated extreme; requires top fitness. Restrooms and water at Village Green Park, the summit and the McKenzie General Store. Highway 242 closes seasonally: check TripCheck.com or ODOT District 10 in Bend (541-388-6169) for conditions. Published lengths range from 35 to 38 miles.
address: Start: Village Green Park, Sisters, OR

title: McKenzie Tough!
imageAlt: The roll out from Cold Springs Campground

banner.alt: The roll out from Cold Springs Campground

contentHtml:
McKenzie Tough! is a 77-mile loop with about 7,400 feet of climbing (40% gravel and dirt, 10% singletrack, 50% paved), with views of Mt. Washington, Three Fingered Jack and Hayrick Butte. It rides 7.5 miles of the historic Santiam Wagon Road, passes Clear Lake, follows the McKenzie River for about 17 miles and finishes with a long paved climb over Old McKenzie Pass (Highway 242) to Dee Wright Observatory and back down to the start.

It crosses Linn and Lane counties. Wide tires (50 mm) are almost a must, and the ride can be split over 2 or 3 days.
excerpt: McKenzie Tough! is a 77-mile loop with about 7,400 feet of climbing (40% gravel and dirt, 10% singletrack, 50% paved), with views of Mt. Washington, Three Finge
note: Short riding window: mid-May to June or, best, October, a few days after high snow, in the morning. Highway 242 is sometimes closed to cars; check ODOT. Watch for downed trees after mile 21.5. Water at the start; Clear Lake Resort (about mile 27) is seasonal. Use a rear light from mile 45.
address: Start: Cold Springs Campground, Highway 242, west of Sisters, OR

title: Metolius Weekender

gallery.alt: Dispersed camping on a Metolius bend

contentHtml:
The Metolius Weekender is a 105-mile bikepacking loop with about 7,100 feet of climbing that circles the Metolius River basin, with views of the snow-capped Cascades. Green Ridge has open scenery and many dispersed campsites, and the main test is about a mile of hike-a-bike through old-growth forest along the river.

It uses gravel, singletrack, hiking trail and pavement in and out of Sisters, and crosses into Jefferson County. Gravel or hybrid bikes with 40 mm+ tires and low gearing are recommended.
excerpt: The Metolius Weekender is a 105-mile bikepacking loop with about 7,100 feet of climbing that circles the Metolius River basin, with views of the snow-capped Cas
note: Demanding and remote; affected by the 2026 fires. Expect self-contained wild camping. No water after Sisters until a pump at the Perry Campground boat ramp past mile 24 (river water can be treated). No cell service on the northern Metolius; carry a satellite beacon. Watch for black bears and ticks.
address: Start: Village Green City Park, Sisters, OR (overnight parking allowed; no camping)

title: Oktoberfest
contentHtml: Oktoberfest is a 29-mile loop with about 1,800 feet of climbing, 80% gravel and dirt road. It crosses Tumalo Creek, climbs through the Two Bulls burn, turns around at Tumalo Falls, descends 3 miles of the easy Tumalo Creek Trail singletrack and passes through a Forest Service thinning project. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: Oktoberfest is a 29-mile loop with about 1,800 feet of climbing, 80% gravel and dirt road. It crosses Tumalo Creek, climbs through the Two Bulls burn, turns aro
note: Spring or fall, not summer, when the dust is brutal. Closed December 1 to March 31 for wildlife migration. With the Skyline Forest closed, the route now uses steeper Jack Pine Road. No water on the route.
address: Start: Phil's Trailhead parking area, west of Bend, OR (pit toilets)
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Quick & Dirty
contentHtml: Quick & Dirty was a 20-mile, 90% gravel loop of moderate difficulty in the Skyline Forest northwest of Bend.
excerpt: Quick & Dirty was a 20-mile, 90% gravel loop of moderate difficulty in the Skyline Forest northwest of Bend.
note: Dirty Freehub removed this guide in February 2024 after the Skyline Forest closed to the public; the route may no longer be rideable as described. The Skyline Forest is private land closed to public recreation since fall 2022.
address: Skyline Forest, northwest of Bend, OR

title: Railbed Spurs
contentHtml: Railbed Spurs was an easy 23-mile lollipop, all gravel and dirt, in the Skyline Forest northwest of Bend.
excerpt: Railbed Spurs was an easy 23-mile lollipop, all gravel and dirt, in the Skyline Forest northwest of Bend.
note: Dirty Freehub removed this guide in February 2024 after the Skyline Forest closed to the public; the route may no longer be rideable as described. The Skyline Forest is private land closed to public recreation since fall 2022.
address: Skyline Forest, northwest of Bend, OR

title: Ringo
contentHtml: Ringo is a remote 20-mile loop with about 1,500 feet of climbing on about 85% gravel and dirt. It follows Wickiup Reservoir, skirts Davis Mountain and drops to Davis Lake, with views of Maiden Peak and lava flows. Bald eagles and osprey are common, and the shoreline changes with the water level. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: Ringo is a remote 20-mile loop with about 1,500 feet of climbing on about 85% gravel and dirt. It follows Wickiup Reservoir, skirts Davis Mountain and drops to
note: Late spring to early summer, and fall; wait for snowmelt and ride when the ground is damp. Part of the lava-flow area east of Davis Lake closes January 1 to August 31 for nesting eagles: if the gate at mile 15.3 is shut, return by the Cascade Lakes Highway. No food or water.
address: Start: roadside pullout on the Cascade Lakes Highway just past Davis Creek (from the north), near Davis Lake, OR

title: Sisters to Smith Rock Scenic Bikeway
imageAlt: Riding below the cliffs of Smith Rock

banner.alt: Riding below the cliffs of Smith Rock

contentHtml:
The Sisters to Smith Rock Scenic Bikeway is a moderate 37-mile one-way road ride from Sisters, past alpaca pastures with the snow-covered Cascades behind them, through Terrebonne to the multicolored volcanic cliffs and rock climbers of Smith Rock State Park. It passes forest, farm valleys, streams, historic sites and the Deschutes River.

It is mostly downhill from Sisters (about 711 feet up and 1,074 feet down), including almost 6 miles of unbroken descent. Ride it with a shuttle, or as a round trip with a break at the turnaround.
excerpt: The Sisters to Smith Rock Scenic Bikeway is a moderate 37-mile one-way road ride from Sisters, past alpaca pastures with the snow-covered Cascades behind them,
note: Parks at both ends have free parking, restrooms and drinking water (summer and early fall). Food in Sisters and Terrebonne. Check TripCheck.com or ODOT District 10 (541-388-6169) for road conditions.
address: Start: Village Green City Park, Sisters, OR; finish: Smith Rock State Park, Terrebonne, OR

title: Skull Hollow
contentHtml:
Skull Hollow is a 28-mile loop with about 1,900 feet of climbing (70% paved, 30% gravel). It crosses the historic Crooked River High Bridge over the gorge, passes a railroad bridge and an old homestead, and gives views of the Cascades and Smith Rock. Skull Hollow takes its grim name from wagon remains found there in 1864.

It crosses into Jefferson County. A detour of about a mile reaches Smith Rock State Park near mile 24.
excerpt: Skull Hollow is a 28-mile loop with about 1,900 feet of climbing (70% paved, 30% gravel). It crosses the historic Crooked River High Bridge over the gorge, pass
note: Best in spring and fall. Don't ride when wet: the mud can force you to walk. Expect cattle on open range. Navigation at mile 5.5, crossing the gorge and Highway 97, is tricky. Food at the start; none on the route.
address: Start: dirt road (16th St) across from the Terrebonne Depot restaurant, Terrebonne, OR (don't use the restaurant lot)

title: The Bishop
contentHtml: The Bishop was a very demanding 100-mile loop from Sisters, about 65% gravel and 20% singletrack, crossing into Jefferson County.
excerpt: The Bishop was a very demanding 100-mile loop from Sisters, about 65% gravel and 20% singletrack, crossing into Jefferson County.
note: Dirty Freehub removed this guide in February 2024 after the Skyline Forest closed to the public; the route may no longer be rideable as described.
address: Start: Village Green City Park, Sisters, OR

title: The Pawn
contentHtml:
The Pawn is a 42-mile loop with about 3,300 feet of climbing (80% gravel, 15% singletrack) with big views of volcanic craters, peaks and long ridgelines, including Tam McArthur Rim and North Sister. Terrain shifts from gravel to rugged forest tracks to flowing singletrack, through regrowing burn areas and across Whychus Creek, the site of a major restoration project since 2016.

A 32-mile Espresso Option and a Less Rugged Option are available. Tires of 45 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: The Pawn is a 42-mile loop with about 3,300 feet of climbing (80% gravel, 15% singletrack) with big views of volcanic craters, peaks and long ridgelines, includ
note: Best late spring to early June; rougher and sandier after mid-June. Dirty Freehub is checking private- property issues on part of the route and recommends the Espresso Option for now. Mule deer and elk winter range December 1 to March 31: keep groups to 4 or fewer. No food or water.
address: Start: Sisters City Park, Sisters, OR (restrooms, picnic area, gazebo)

title: Townie
imageAlt: Greetings from mural, Old Mill District

banner.alt: Greetings from mural, Old Mill District

gallery.alt: The Deschutes River filled with logs

contentHtml: Townie is an easy 17-mile loop with about 1,000 feet of climbing through Bend's older neighborhoods, canal roads and riverfront, with a climb up Pilot Butte for views and geology kiosks. Along the way are murals, logging-era sculptures and local history; ride slowly to take them in. Skip the Pilot Butte climb to cut the gain to about 600 feet.
excerpt: Townie is an easy 17-mile loop with about 1,000 feet of climbing through Bend's older neighborhoods, canal roads and riverfront, with a climb up Pilot Butte for
note: Rideable most of the year unless there is snow in town; in summer start before 8 AM. Water and toilets at Larkspur Center (mile 4.7), toilets on Pilot Butte (mile 8.5). Keep groups to 4 or fewer on shared paths and expect city traffic.
address: Start: wooden footbridge in the Old Mill District, Bend, OR

title: Twin Bridges Loop Scenic Bikeway

gallery.alt: Wooden bridge over the Deschutes River

contentHtml:
The Twin Bridges Scenic Bikeway is a moderate 36-mile road loop from Drake Park in Bend, past Mirror Pond and Shevlin Park, through the village of Tumalo and back, crossing the Deschutes River twice on the bridges that give it its name. Expect Cascade views, high desert, hobby farms, hay fields, wildlife, Tumalo State Park and the river's wetlands.

Ride it clockwise only, as it uses a short stretch of Highway 20 with a bike lane. It was designated in 2012.
excerpt: The Twin Bridges Scenic Bikeway is a moderate 36-mile road loop from Drake Park in Bend, past Mirror Pond and Shevlin Park, through the village of Tumalo and ba
note: Usually rideable late February through November. Restrooms and water at Shevlin Park; camping, hiker-biker sites and showers at Tumalo State Park; food in Tumalo. Check TripCheck.com or ODOT District 10 (541-388-6169).
address: Start and finish: Drake Park, downtown Bend, OR

title: Two Bulls, One Coffee
contentHtml: Two Bulls, One Coffee was a demanding 58-mile loop from Shevlin Park, half gravel road and half paved.
excerpt: Two Bulls, One Coffee was a demanding 58-mile loop from Shevlin Park, half gravel road and half paved.
note: Dirty Freehub removed this guide in February 2024 after the Skyline Forest closed to the public; the route may no longer be rideable as described.
address: Start: Shevlin Park, Bend, OR

title: Water & Lava

gallery.alt: Shevlin-Hixon mill site, west bank of the Deschutes

contentHtml: Water & Lava is an easy 31-mile loop with about 1,400 feet of climbing (45% gravel, 20% singletrack, 35% paved) and a popular first gravel ride close to town. It follows the Deschutes River past Benham Falls, with an optional climb up Lava Butte for views over the lava fields. Tires of 40 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: Water & Lava is an easy 31-mile loop with about 1,400 feet of climbing (45% gravel, 20% singletrack, 35% paved) and a popular first gravel ride close to town. I
note: Best in spring and fall; summer paths are busier and can be sandy. Seasonal food, water and flush toilets at Lava Lands Visitor Center (about mile 12). A family-friendly start at Aspen Day Use needs a Forest Service parking pass, sold at the Welcome Center. In Sunriver, stay on the bike paths.
address: Start: Cascade Lakes Welcome Center, Cascade Lakes Highway, south of Bend, OR (seasonal water and toilets)

title: Westside Tour
imageAlt: The high-wheel logging skidder at the start

banner.alt: The high-wheel logging skidder at the start

contentHtml: Westside Tour is an easy 25-mile urban gravel loop with about 1,300 feet of climbing that strings together the Deschutes River trails, Shevlin Park, Phil's Trails and Drake Park. It has river and mountain views, a short bit of singletrack, stops for Bend's logging and irrigation history, and sculptures and murals along the way. Tires of 40 mm or wider are suggested.
excerpt: Westside Tour is an easy 25-mile urban gravel loop with about 1,300 feet of climbing that strings together the Deschutes River trails, Shevlin Park, Phil's Trai
note: Rideable most of the year unless there is snow in town; in summer start before 8 AM. Food and water downtown (mile 0), at The Loge cafe (mile 20.5) and the Old Mill (mile 24). Yield to walkers on shared trails.
address: Start: Drake Park, by the historic logging wheel, downtown Bend, OR

title: Deschutes River
contentHtml:
The Deschutes River was designated a National Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 174.4 miles (143.4 recreational, 31 scenic) in three reaches: Wickiup Dam to Bend, Odin Falls to Lake Billy Chinook, and Pelton Reregulating Dam to the Columbia River. The upper and middle reaches are in Deschutes County.

Near Bend the upper river offers easy-to-reach brown trout fishing; the middle river has hiking and basalt canyon geology, rock art and spring-fed waters; the lower river is known for whitewater rafting, steelhead and trout fishing and camping, with about 300 kinds of wildlife in the canyon.
excerpt: The Deschutes River was designated a National Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 174.4 miles (143.4 recreational, 31 scenic) in three reaches: Wicki
note: Managed by the Deschutes National Forest ((541) 383-5300) and the BLM Prineville District ((541) 416- 6700).
address: Benham Falls Day Use Area (upper river), Deschutes National Forest, south of Bend, OR

title: Whychus Creek
contentHtml:
Whychus Creek was designated a National Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 54 miles (45.2 wild, 8.8 scenic), from its three forks in the Three Sisters Wilderness down the east slope of the Cascades. Its name means 'the place we cross the water.'

The creek is valued for native redband trout, glacial and volcanic canyons and waterfalls, a traditional Native American travel route to high Cascades obsidian, and wild scenery below the much-photographed Three Sisters glaciers.

note: Managed by the Deschutes National Forest.
address: Whychus Creek Overlook Trailhead, Three Creeks Lake Rd (FR 16), south of Sisters, OR

title: Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway
imageAlt: Sparks Lake, a favorite of photographer Ray Atkeson

contentHtml:
The Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway is a 66-mile National Scenic Byway from Bend past Mt. Bachelor and a chain of mountain lakes to Highway 58 near Crescent Lake. Stop at Sparks Lake for views of South Sister and Broken Top and the Ray Atkeson loop trail, shallow Devils Lake, crystal-clear Elk Lake and Hosmer Lake, Lava and Little Lava lakes with Three Sisters views, and Davis Lake's lava formations and fly fishing.

Hike-in lakes such as Green Lakes, Doris Lake and Lucky Lake, and the riverside Deschutes River Trail with two waterfalls, are along the way. Only the southern end crosses into Klamath County.

note: Check TripCheck.com for road conditions and wildfire alerts before you go.

title: McKenzie Pass-Santiam Pass Scenic Byway
imageAlt: Lava flow and peaks from Dee Wright Observatory

banner.alt: Lava flow and peaks from Dee Wright Observatory

contentHtml:
The McKenzie Pass-Santiam Pass Scenic Byway is an 82-mile loop from Sisters over two Cascade passes: Santiam Pass (4,817 feet), where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses, and McKenzie Pass (5,335 feet), crowned by the lava-rock Dee Wright Observatory with views over an ancient lava flow to 11 peaks.

Along the way are Suttle Lake, Scott Lake, Clear Lake Resort, the wild and scenic McKenzie River and historic stretches of the Santiam Wagon Road. Back in Sisters, browse downtown boutiques and galleries.

title: Oregon Outback Scenic Byway
contentHtml:
The Oregon Outback Scenic Byway runs 171 miles southeast from near La Pine on Highway 31, then south on US 395, a 4-to-6-hour drive across the high desert. Highlights include Fort Rock, a 325-foot volcanic crater with a state park and homestead museum; the Summer Lake Wildlife Area, with nearly 250 bird species; Paisley and its hot springs; Abert Rim, a 30-mile fault scarp popular for hang gliding; and Lakeview, Oregon's 'tallest town' at 4,800 feet.

Only the northern start near La Pine is in Deschutes County; most of the route is in Lake County.

title: High Desert Food Trail

contentHtml:
The High Desert Food Trail is a self-guided farm and food trail run by the High Desert Food & Farm Alliance. Stops include farms, ranches and food businesses in Bend, Redmond, Sisters, La Pine, Prineville, Madras and Warm Springs.

Visitors can follow one of the trail's itineraries or build their own route to buy produce, meat and other foods directly from local growers.

title: Lower Crooked River Back Country Byway
contentHtml:
The Lower Crooked River Back Country Byway follows OR 27 for about 43 miles through the Crooked River canyon, from Prineville south to US 20, 33.3 miles east of Bend. The southern 18 miles are graded gravel.

Along the river are nine campgrounds open year-round and the 1.3-mile Chimney Rock Trail. The river below the road is known for fly fishing and bald eagles.

title: Rock O' The Range Covered Bridge
imageAlt: Rock O' The Range Covered Bridge

banner.alt: Rock O' The Range Covered Bridge

contentHtml:
Rock O' The Range is Oregon's only covered bridge east of the Cascades, a 42-foot span carrying Bowery Lane over the Swalley Canal north of Bend. Developer William Bowen wanted a covered crossing to reach his land, inspired by Lane County's Goodpasture Bridge, and local contractor Maurice Olson built it in 1963 from a calendar photo, for about $4,500.

It has cedar siding, a shingle roof and windows on Douglas-fir timbers set on concrete piers, but no true truss. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

contentHtml: Dutchman Flat Sno-Park sits across from Mt. Bachelor and is a hub for cross-country skiing, snowmobiling and dog sledding, with access to Central Oregon's snowmobile and Nordic trail systems. Snowshoers climb about 1,400 feet up Tumalo Mountain, with views of Todd Lake and Broken Top.

note: An Oregon Sno-Park permit is required November 1 to April 30 (daily $4, 3-day $9, annual $25; sold at DMV offices, resorts and outdoor shops, and annual permits online at DMV2U.Oregon.gov). contentHtml:
Mt. Bachelor is a Cascade volcano west of Bend with about 4,300 acres of lift-served terrain, one of the biggest ski resorts in the U.S., with skiing and snowboarding off the 9,068-foot summit in every direction.

Non-skiers can ride a chairlift to Pine Marten Lodge for views over the Cascade Lakes, and in summer the mountain offers hiking and mountain biking.

From mid-April through September it becomes a roller rink, with open skate, roller hockey and skatepark sessions.
