imageAlt: The Umpqua River at the wayside

banner.alt: The Umpqua River at the wayside

contentHtml: Umpqua State Scenic Corridor (Umpqua Wayside) is a small day-use stop on the Umpqua River along OR 38, with a few picnic tables, a vault restroom and a short boat ramp.
excerpt: Umpqua State Scenic Corridor (Umpqua Wayside) is a small day-use stop on the Umpqua River along OR 38, with a few picnic tables, a vault restroom and a short bo
note: Free; boat launching permitted. Limited trailer parking; best for passenger vehicles.
address: OR 38 along the Umpqua River, near Reedsport, OR

title: Apple Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Apple Creek Campground has seven campsites on the bank of the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, where Apple and Panther creeks meet. Deep pools, steady riffles and wadeable stretches make it a good base for anglers.

It has vault toilets and picnic tables, run by a concessionaire under a Forest Service permit.
excerpt: Apple Creek Campground has seven campsites on the bank of the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, where Apple and Panther creeks meet. Deep pools, steady riffle
note: First come, first served. No drinking water. Closed for the 2026 summer season.
address: OR 138, about 28 miles east of the North Umpqua Ranger Station, OR

title: Ash Flat Campground
imageAlt: The South Umpqua River at Ash Flat

banner.alt: The South Umpqua River at Ash Flat

contentHtml:
Ash Flat Campground is a small campground at 1,500 feet with four shaded sites in mixed conifers and hardwoods, a few steps from the beaches of the South Umpqua River.

Each site has a picnic table and fire ring, with a vault toilet. It is a quiet spot for swimming, birding and stargazing.
excerpt: Ash Flat Campground is a small campground at 1,500 feet with four shaded sites in mixed conifers and hardwoods, a few steps from the beaches of the South Umpqua
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay (no cash). No drinking water or trash service. Fishing not allowed. No cell coverage for about 30 miles. From Canyonville, take OR 227 to Tiller, then County Rd 46 for 18 miles.
address: County Rd 46 (South Umpqua Rd), 18 miles from Tiller, OR

title: Bogus Creek Campground
imageAlt: The campground road through the forest

banner.alt: The campground road through the forest

contentHtml:
Bogus Creek Campground has 14 sites in old-growth Douglas fir and cedar near the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, with the Riverview Trail in the campground and a raft launch across the highway.

It has drinking water, accessible flush toilets and a campground host in peak season, close to the 79-mile North Umpqua Trail and the Rogue-Umpqua Scenic Byway.
excerpt: Bogus Creek Campground has 14 sites in old-growth Douglas fir and cedar near the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, with the Riverview Trail in the campground
note: Listed as closed due to fire damage; check before you go.
address: OR 138, 35 miles east of Roseburg, OR

title: Boulder Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Boulder Creek Campground sits on the South Umpqua River near the mouth of Boulder Creek, in shady, secluded mixed conifer forest. Its 7 sites have picnic tables, with vault toilets and drinking water from a hand pump.

Swimming and hiking are nearby.
excerpt: Boulder Creek Campground sits on the South Umpqua River near the mouth of Boulder Creek, in shady, secluded mixed conifer forest. Its 7 sites have picnic tables
note: $10 per night, $5 per extra vehicle; first come, first served. Fishing not allowed. Watch for poison oak. From Canyonville, take OR 227 to Tiller, then County Rd 46 for 14 miles.
address: County Rd 46 (South Umpqua Rd), 14 miles from Tiller, OR

title: Boulder Flat Campground
imageAlt: The North Umpqua River at Boulder Flat

banner.alt: The North Umpqua River at Boulder Flat

contentHtml:
Boulder Flat Campground sits on the upper Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River and is popular with whitewater rafters, with a concrete boat ramp and changing room.

Its nine sites each have a picnic table and fire ring, and all but one have river access. Hiking, mountain biking, the North Umpqua Trail and Toketee Falls are nearby.
excerpt: Boulder Flat Campground sits on the upper Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River and is popular with whitewater rafters, with a concrete boat ramp and changing room
note: No drinking water. Maximum vehicle length 24 ft. Run by a concessionaire in summer; Scan & Pay in the winter off-season.
address: OR 138, 53 miles east of Roseburg, OR

title: Briggs Forest Camp
contentHtml: Briggs Forest Camp is a small, primitive campground on the site of a late-1950s logging camp run by R.A. Briggs. Stump Lake and the Clearwater River are nearby.
excerpt: Briggs Forest Camp is a small, primitive campground on the site of a late-1950s logging camp run by R.A. Briggs. Stump Lake and the Clearwater River are nearby.
note: Free; first come, first served. Vault toilets; no drinking water or garbage service.
address: NF-4785 off NF-3701, about 50 miles east of Glide on OR 138, OR

title: Broken Arrow Campground
contentHtml:
Broken Arrow Campground is a large lodgepole pine campground at the south end of Diamond Lake, with views of Mount Bailey and Mount Thielsen. It has about 120 standard sites and group sites, set up for families and large groups.

Sites have picnic tables, fire rings and grills, with drinking water, flush toilets and campground hosts. Diamond Lake offers fishing, swimming and kayaking, with an 11-mile paved trail around the lake and the Pacific Crest Trail nearby.
excerpt: Broken Arrow Campground is a large lodgepole pine campground at the south end of Diamond Lake, with views of Mount Bailey and Mount Thielsen. It has about 120 s
note: Reservation only; extra vehicle $5 per night. Maximum vehicle length 32 ft. Seasonal.
address: Diamond Lake Loop (FR 4795), south end of Diamond Lake, OR

title: Buckhead Mountain Camping Area
contentHtml: Buckhead Mountain Camping Area is a rustic campground shaded by old trees on the border of the Tiller and Diamond Lake ranger districts, with nearby roads leading to other forest recreation sites.
excerpt: Buckhead Mountain Camping Area is a rustic campground shaded by old trees on the border of the Tiller and Diamond Lake ranger districts, with nearby roads leadi
note: Free; first come, first served. No restrooms or drinking water. Maximum vehicle length 22 ft. From Tiller, take FR 28 about 24 miles, then FS Rd 2814 about 8 miles to FS Rd 2715.
address: FS Rd 2715 at FS Rd 2814, off South Umpqua Rd (FR 28) from Tiller, OR

title: Bunker Hill Campground
contentHtml:
Bunker Hill Campground has five rustic sites on the northwest shore of Lemolo Lake, below wooded Bunker Hill. Bald eagles often soar over the lodgepole pine forest.

Lemolo Lake is used for boating, fishing (brown, brook and rainbow trout and kokanee), swimming and paddling, and the Lemolo Falls Trail leads into the North Umpqua canyon to a 150-foot waterfall.
excerpt: Bunker Hill Campground has five rustic sites on the northwest shore of Lemolo Lake, below wooded Bunker Hill. Bald eagles often soar over the lodgepole pine for
note: Reservation only; extra vehicle $5 per night. Vault toilets; no drinking water. Maximum vehicle length 22 ft. From Roseburg, take OR 138 east about 72 miles, FR 2610 across Lemolo Lake Dam, then FR 2612. Seasonal.
address: FR 2612, northwest shore of Lemolo Lake, OR

title: Camas Creek Camping Area
contentHtml:
Camas Creek Camping Area is a free, primitive campground in the Cascades near Soda Springs, with access to the North Umpqua Trail and the North Umpqua River.

It is a base for hiking, whitewater paddling, fishing and swimming.
excerpt: Camas Creek Camping Area is a free, primitive campground in the Cascades near Soda Springs, with access to the North Umpqua Trail and the North Umpqua River.
note: Free; first come, first served. No restrooms or drinking water. Maximum vehicle length 25 ft.
address: Near Soda Springs, North Umpqua River, OR

title: Canton Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Canton Creek Campground is a small campground on Steamboat Creek near the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, with five sites (three creekside), each with a picnic table and fire ring.

It has a day-use pavilion with grills, flush toilets and drinking water, close to hiking, mountain biking, rafting and the 79-mile North Umpqua Trail.
excerpt: Canton Creek Campground is a small campground on Steamboat Creek near the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, with five sites (three creekside), each with a pic
note: Fee paid at the fee board. Maximum vehicle length 24 ft. From Roseburg, take OR 138 east 39 miles, then left on Steamboat Creek Rd. Seasonal.
address: Steamboat Creek Rd (FR 38), 1/4 mile off OR 138, OR

title: Carter Lake Campground

gallery.alt: The south side of Carter Lake

contentHtml:
Carter Lake Campground sits on 28-acre Carter Lake in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, among shore pine, Sitka spruce, Douglas fir and rhododendron. The Carter Dunes Trailhead is inside the campground, and the ocean is a short drive away.

Its 21 sites have fire pits and picnic tables, with drinking water and flush toilets. The lake is stocked with rainbow trout and good for swimming, canoeing and kayaking, and the Siltcoos Lake and Threemile Creek trails are nearby.
excerpt: Carter Lake Campground sits on 28-acre Carter Lake in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, among shore pine, Sitka spruce, Douglas fir and rhododendron. T
note: Reserve on Recreation.gov or at 877-444-6777. Two vehicles per site. No off-road vehicles in the campground. Seasonal.
address: US 101, about 10 miles south of Florence, OR

title: Clearwater #1 Forebay Forest Camp
contentHtml: Clearwater #1 Forebay Forest Camp is a primitive forest camp of about 11 sites at the Clearwater #1 forebay, with vault toilets.
excerpt: Clearwater #1 Forebay Forest Camp is a primitive forest camp of about 11 sites at the Clearwater #1 forebay, with vault toilets.
note: Free; first come, first served.
address: Clearwater #1 Forebay, off OR 138, OR

title: Clearwater #2 Forebay Forest Camp
contentHtml:
Clearwater #2 Forebay Forest Camp sits in a grove of large old-growth trees beside the forebay, with a boat ramp for access to Lemolo Lake.

It is a base for hiking and lake and pond fishing.
excerpt: Clearwater #2 Forebay Forest Camp sits in a grove of large old-growth trees beside the forebay, with a boat ramp for access to Lemolo Lake.
note: Free; first come, first served. Vault toilets; no drinking water.
address: NF-252 off NF-4776, 44 miles east of Glide on OR 138, OR

title: Clearwater Falls Campground
contentHtml:
Clearwater Falls Campground sits beside the Clearwater River in old-growth Douglas fir along the Rogue- Umpqua Scenic Byway. Five lower sites overlook a 30-foot waterfall, and four secluded upper sites along the river are reached by a short trail.

Each of the nine sites has a picnic table and fire ring, with a vault toilet. It is a quiet spot for hiking, fishing and berry picking.
excerpt: Clearwater Falls Campground sits beside the Clearwater River in old-growth Douglas fir along the Rogue- Umpqua Scenic Byway. Five lower sites overlook a 30-foot
note: Pay on site with Scan & Pay. No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. Maximum trailer length 25 ft.
address: OR 138, about 70 miles east of Roseburg, OR

title: Coolwater Campground
contentHtml:
Coolwater Campground is a forested, 7-site campground in the Little River valley, used for fishing, swimming and quiet weekends. Grotto Falls and Taft and Lookout mountains are nearby.

It has vault toilets and picnic tables and is run by a concessionaire under a Forest Service permit.
excerpt: Coolwater Campground is a forested, 7-site campground in the Little River valley, used for fishing, swimming and quiet weekends. Grotto Falls and Taft and Looko
note: First come, first served. No drinking water. Closed for the 2026 summer season. From Roseburg, take OR 138 east about 16 miles, then Little River Rd 15.5 miles.
address: Little River Rd (#17), 15.5 miles from OR 138, OR

title: Deer Flat Group Site
imageAlt: A forested campsite at Deer Flat

banner.alt: A forested campsite at Deer Flat

contentHtml:
Deer Flat Group Site is a reserve-only group campground for up to 70 people, in old-growth Douglas fir and sugar pine within Horseshoe Bend Campground, a short walk from the North Umpqua River.

It has picnic tables, campfire rings, grills, flush toilets and drinking water.
excerpt: Deer Flat Group Site is a reserve-only group campground for up to 70 people, in old-growth Douglas fir and sugar pine within Horseshoe Bend Campground, a short
note: Group reservations only. Check in with the campground host, as the gate is closed. No amplified music after 10 PM.
address: FS Rd 4750 off OR 138, 48 miles east of Roseburg, OR

title: Devil's Flat Campground
contentHtml:
Devil's Flat Campground is a small, three-site campground under a bluff in the Cow Creek drainage, surrounded by cedar, pine and madrone. It is named for a tiki carving on site.

Historic features include a 1930s CCC stone water fixture, a 1915 ranger cabin and a 1920s horse barn, and several hiking trails start here.
excerpt: Devil's Flat Campground is a small, three-site campground under a bluff in the Cow Creek drainage, surrounded by cedar, pine and madrone. It is named for a tiki
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay (no cash). Extra vehicle $5. No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. Maximum vehicle length 22 ft.
address: County Rd 36, about 17 miles east of Azalea, OR

title: Diamond Lake Campground
imageAlt: A campsite looking at Mount Bailey

banner.alt: A campsite looking at Mount Bailey

contentHtml:
Diamond Lake Campground stretches along most of the east shore of Diamond Lake at about 5,183 feet, with views of Mount Bailey and Mount Thielsen. Its 238 sites have picnic tables, fire rings and grills, with drinking water and flush toilets.

There are boat ramps, fish cleaning stations and Saturday evening programs at the amphitheater. The lake is stocked with rainbow trout, and an 11-mile paved path circles it. A nearby resort rents bikes, boats and horses.
excerpt: Diamond Lake Campground stretches along most of the east shore of Diamond Lake at about 5,183 feet, with views of Mount Bailey and Mount Thielsen. Its 238 sites
note: Reservation only. Extra vehicle $5 per night. Maximum vehicle length 35 ft. The gatehouse is staffed daily 8 AM - 6 PM in season.
address: Diamond Lake Loop (FR 4795), east shore of Diamond Lake, OR

title: Dumont Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Dumont Creek Campground is a small, quiet, three-site campground where Dumont Creek meets the South Umpqua River, with a short trail to a rocky beach for wading.

Campbell Falls, Deer Lick Falls, South Umpqua Falls and Rogue-Umpqua Divide Wilderness trailheads are nearby.
excerpt: Dumont Creek Campground is a small, quiet, three-site campground where Dumont Creek meets the South Umpqua River, with a short trail to a rocky beach for wading
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay (no cash). No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. Trailers not recommended.
address: County Rd 46 (South Umpqua Rd), about 12 miles from Tiller, OR

title: Eagle Rock Campground
contentHtml:
Eagle Rock Campground is a riverside campground on the North Umpqua River, popular with fly anglers and whitewater rafters, in old-growth Douglas fir below the rocky butte it is named for.

Its 27 sites (16 reservable) have picnic tables and fire rings, and most have river access. The 79-mile North Umpqua Trail and Twin Lakes are nearby.
excerpt: Eagle Rock Campground is a riverside campground on the North Umpqua River, popular with fly anglers and whitewater rafters, in old-growth Douglas fir below the
note: No drinking water. Maximum vehicle length 30 ft. Run by a concessionaire.
address: OR 138, 50.5 miles east of Roseburg, OR

title: East Lemolo Campground
imageAlt: A campsite with Lemolo Lake behind

banner.alt: A campsite with Lemolo Lake behind

contentHtml:
East Lemolo Campground sits on the southeast shore of Lemolo Lake, the highest reservoir on the North Umpqua River at 4,150 feet. Its 15 sites each have a picnic table and campfire ring with grill, and there is a boat launch.

The lake is used for boating, fishing, swimming, paddling and water skiing, and the Lemolo Falls Trail leads to a 150-foot waterfall.
excerpt: East Lemolo Campground sits on the southeast shore of Lemolo Lake, the highest reservoir on the North Umpqua River at 4,150 feet. Its 15 sites each have a picni
note: Reservation only; extra vehicle $5 per night. Vault toilet; no drinking water. Maximum vehicle length 22 ft. Seasonal, about May 15 - Oct 31.
address: FR 430 off FR 2614, southeast shore of Lemolo Lake, OR

title: Eel Creek Campground
imageAlt: The dunes next to the campground

banner.alt: The dunes next to the campground

contentHtml:
Eel Creek Campground is a quiet campground among coastal shrubs on the edge of the dunes in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, popular with hikers and birders. The John Dellenback Dunes Trail runs 2.7 miles one way from the forest to the Pacific beach.

Its 51 sites are mostly screened by rhododendron and salal, and four sit on the dunes. There are flush toilets, drinking water, a campground host and an amphitheater.
excerpt: Eel Creek Campground is a quiet campground among coastal shrubs on the edge of the dunes in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, popular with hikers and b
note: $22 per night; reserve on Recreation.gov or at 877-444-6777. Two vehicles per site. Mosquitoes are common April - August.
address: US 101 near milepost 222, about 10 miles south of Reedsport, OR

title: Grassy Ranch Camping Area
contentHtml:
Grassy Ranch Camping Area is a free, quiet and secluded campground at the edge of the Boulder Creek Wilderness, with vault toilets.

It is a base for day hikes into the wilderness.
excerpt: Grassy Ranch Camping Area is a free, quiet and secluded campground at the edge of the Boulder Creek Wilderness, with vault toilets.
note: Free; first come, first served. No drinking water. Maximum vehicle length 25 ft. From Glide, take OR 138 east, Steamboat Creek Rd, then NFSR 3810.
address: NFSR 3810 off Steamboat Creek Rd, OR

title: Hemlock Lake Campground
imageAlt: Hemlock Lake from the lake trail

banner.alt: Hemlock Lake from the lake trail

gallery.alt: Meadow on the Yellow Jacket Trail

contentHtml:
Hemlock Lake Campground sits on Hemlock Lake, a 28-acre reservoir about 33 feet deep, surrounded by mixed conifers. The lake is stocked with trout for bank and boat fishing, with a boat ramp, picnic area and trails looping the lake.

Its 14 sites each have a picnic table and fire ring, with two vault toilets.
excerpt: Hemlock Lake Campground sits on Hemlock Lake, a 28-acre reservoir about 33 feet deep, surrounded by mixed conifers. The lake is stocked with trout for bank and
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay. No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. May not be reachable in winter.
address: Little River Rd (NF Rd 27), 32 miles from OR 138, OR

title: Hemlock Meadows Campground
imageAlt: Hemlock Lake from the boat ramp

banner.alt: Hemlock Lake from the boat ramp

contentHtml:
Hemlock Meadows Campground is a small, four-site campground on the east arm of Hemlock Lake, a 28-acre trout-stocked reservoir in mixed conifer forest.

It has a vault toilet and boat ramp, with a loop trail around the lake.
excerpt: Hemlock Meadows Campground is a small, four-site campground on the east arm of Hemlock Lake, a 28-acre trout-stocked reservoir in mixed conifer forest.
note: Pay with Scan & Pay. No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. May not be reachable in winter.
address: East arm of Hemlock Lake, Little River Rd (NF Rd 27), OR

title: Horseshoe Bend Campground
contentHtml:
Horseshoe Bend Campground sits in old-growth Douglas fir and sugar pine on the banks of the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, a base for fishing, whitewater rafting, hiking, mountain biking and swimming.

Its 25 reservable sites have picnic tables and fire rings, many with river access, plus drinking water, flush toilets and a campground host.
excerpt: Horseshoe Bend Campground sits in old-growth Douglas fir and sugar pine on the banks of the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, a base for fishing, whitewater r
note: Extra vehicle $5 per day. Maximum vehicle length 35 ft. Run by a concessionaire.
address: FSR 4750 off OR 138, about 51 miles east of Roseburg, OR

title: Inlet Campground
contentHtml:
Inlet Campground is a forested campground on the North Umpqua River where it enters Lemolo Lake, at 4,150 feet among lodgepole pine, mountain hemlock and Shasta red fir.

Its 13 sites each have a picnic table, campfire ring and grill. Boating, fishing, swimming, kayaking and the Lemolo Falls Trail are close by.
excerpt: Inlet Campground is a forested campground on the North Umpqua River where it enters Lemolo Lake, at 4,150 feet among lodgepole pine, mountain hemlock and Shasta
note: Reservation only; extra vehicle $5 per night. Vault toilets; no drinking water. Maximum vehicle length 25 ft.
address: FR 2614 off FR 2610, near Lemolo Lake, OR

title: Island Campground
contentHtml:
Island Campground is a small, seven-site campground right off Highway 138 beside the North Umpqua River, with hiking and mountain biking trails nearby.

Each site has a picnic table and fire ring, with a vault toilet.
excerpt: Island Campground is a small, seven-site campground right off Highway 138 beside the North Umpqua River, with hiking and mountain biking trails nearby.
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay. No drinking water or trash service; limited cell coverage. Maximum trailer length 24 ft.
address: OR 138, about 40 miles east of Roseburg, OR

title: Kelsay Valley Horse Campground
contentHtml:
Kelsay Valley Horse Camp is a campground and trailhead on the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River in high Cascade meadows, known for spring wildflowers. It has 10 equestrian sites with corrals and 5 standard sites, all with picnic tables and fire rings with grills.

Trails link to the North Umpqua Trail and Windigo Pass Trail, leading toward the Mount Thielsen Wilderness and the Pacific Crest Trail. Lemolo Lake is a short drive away.
excerpt: Kelsay Valley Horse Camp is a campground and trailhead on the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River in high Cascade meadows, known for spring wildflowers. It has 1
note: Equestrian sites are for visitors with horses. Vault toilets and manure bins; no drinking water. Maximum vehicle length 20 ft. From Roseburg, take OR 138 east about 74 miles, then Windigo Pass Rd 4.5 miles.
address: End of FR 6000-958 off Windigo Pass Rd (FR 60), OR

title: Lake in the Woods Campground
contentHtml:
Lake in the Woods Campground sits beside a 4-acre lake in mixed conifer forest, with a trail cabin built in 1907. Its 11 sites on a loop each have a picnic table and fire ring.

Fishing, birding and non-motorized boating are popular, and the Yakso Falls, Hemlock Falls and Hemlock Creek trails start nearby.
excerpt: Lake in the Woods Campground sits beside a 4-acre lake in mixed conifer forest, with a trail cabin built in 1907. Its 11 sites on a loop each have a picnic tabl
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay. No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. The last 7 miles are gravel. May not be reachable in winter.
address: Little River Rd (NF Rd 27), 27 miles from OR 138, OR

title: Lemolo 2 Forebay Forest Camp
contentHtml: Lemolo #2 Forebay Forest Camp is a quiet, secluded campground with pond-side sites. Toketee Falls, Umpqua Hot Springs and Watson Falls are nearby.
excerpt: Lemolo #2 Forebay Forest Camp is a quiet, secluded campground with pond-side sites. Toketee Falls, Umpqua Hot Springs and Watson Falls are nearby.
note: Free; first come, first served. Vault toilets; no drinking water or garbage service. Maximum vehicle length 25 ft.
address: NF-3402 off NF-34, 41 miles east of Glide on OR 138, OR

title: Poole Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Poole Creek Campground sits on the west shore of Lemolo Lake at 4,150 feet, in lodgepole pine, mountain hemlock and Shasta red fir. It has about 60 sites and a reservable group site, with drinking water, vault toilets and a boat ramp.

The lake has brown, brook and rainbow trout and kokanee, and is used for swimming, paddling and water skiing. The Lemolo Falls Trail drops into the North Umpqua canyon.
excerpt: Poole Creek Campground sits on the west shore of Lemolo Lake at 4,150 feet, in lodgepole pine, mountain hemlock and Shasta red fir. It has about 60 sites and a
note: The campground and boat ramp are reported closed for construction until the summer 2027 season. Reserve at least two days ahead; some sites are first come, first served. Extra vehicle $5 per night. Maximum vehicle length 35 ft.
address: FR 2610 (Bird's Point Rd), west shore of Lemolo Lake, OR

title: South Umpqua Falls Campground
contentHtml:
South Umpqua Falls Campground is an open meadow campground ringed by timber, with 20 sites. Across the road a picnic area overlooks a river cascade, where Chinook salmon and bald eagles can be seen.

It is a good spot for hiking, birding, picnicking and stargazing.
excerpt: South Umpqua Falls Campground is an open meadow campground ringed by timber, with 20 sites. Across the road a picnic area overlooks a river cascade, where Chino
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay (no cash). No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. Fishing not allowed.
address: County Rd 46 (South Umpqua Rd), 20 miles from Tiller, OR

title: Spinreel Campground
contentHtml:
Spinreel Campground is an off-highway vehicle hub in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area on Tenmile Creek, with access to open dunes, riding routes such as the Coast Guard Trail and nearby ocean beaches.

Its 37 sites have picnic tables and fire rings, with drinking water, flush toilets and a small boat ramp. Tenmile Creek and Tenmile Lake are good for fishing and boating.
excerpt: Spinreel Campground is an off-highway vehicle hub in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area on Tenmile Creek, with access to open dunes, riding routes such a
note: Reserve on Recreation.gov or at 877-444-6777. Two vehicles per site. An Oregon OHV permit is required for riding. No hookups or dump station.
address: Spinreel Rd off US 101, about 12 miles south of Reedsport, OR

title: Steamboat Ball Field Group Site
contentHtml:
Steamboat Ball Field Group Site is a reservation-only group site for up to 100 people and 20 vehicles, under forest cover near the North Umpqua River.

It has a ball field, picnic shelter, horseshoe pits, picnic tables, fire rings, grills and accessible vault toilets, with river access and trailheads nearby.
excerpt: Steamboat Ball Field Group Site is a reservation-only group site for up to 100 people and 20 vehicles, under forest cover near the North Umpqua River.
note: Group reservations only. Tents only; no trailers or long RVs. No drinking water. From Roseburg, take OR 138 east 39 miles to Mott Bridge (FSR 4712).
address: End of FSR 4712-009, across Mott Bridge from OR 138, OR

title: Steamboat Falls Campground
contentHtml:
Steamboat Falls Campground is a shaded, nine-site campground under towering firs across Steamboat Creek. In summer visitors swim at the falls, and during spawning runs steelhead can be seen leaping the falls beside a fish ladder.

The Mott segment of the North Umpqua Trail starts about 6 miles southwest, and the North Umpqua River offers fly fishing.
excerpt: Steamboat Falls Campground is a shaded, nine-site campground under towering firs across Steamboat Creek. In summer visitors swim at the falls, and during spawni
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay. No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. Steamboat Creek is closed to fishing.
address: FS Rd 3810 off Steamboat Creek Rd (FR 38), OR

title: Tahkenitch Campground
contentHtml:
Tahkenitch Campground is a coastal campground in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, with secluded, wooded sites and more open ones. Tahkenitch Lake is across the road, and the Tahkenitch Dunes and Threemile Lake trails start next to the campground.

Its sites have fire rings and picnic tables, with drinking water and flush toilets. The lake holds cutthroat and steelhead trout, largemouth bass and yellow perch.
excerpt: Tahkenitch Campground is a coastal campground in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, with secluded, wooded sites and more open ones. Tahkenitch Lake is a
note: $22 per night; reservation only. Mosquitoes are common April - August. Seasonal.
address: US 101, 8 miles north of Reedsport, OR

title: Tahkenitch Landing Campground
contentHtml:
Tahkenitch Landing is a grassy campground on the shore of 2,118-acre Tahkenitch Lake in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area. Smaller tent sites sit on the lake rim, with larger RV sites up the hill.

It has a boat ramp, vault toilets and a day-use picnic area. The Tahkenitch Dunes Trail across the highway leads to the Pacific.
excerpt: Tahkenitch Landing is a grassy campground on the shore of 2,118-acre Tahkenitch Lake in the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area. Smaller tent sites sit on the
note: Reserve on Recreation.gov. Two vehicles per site. No drinking water; bring your own. Mosquitoes are common April - August.
address: US 101, about 9 miles north of Reedsport, OR

title: Thielsen View Campground
contentHtml:
Thielsen View Campground sits on the west shore of Diamond Lake in the shadow of Mount Bailey, named for its view across the water to Mount Thielsen. Its 60 sites are mostly shaded and close to the lake, a favorite with families and anglers.

Campers can use the boat ramp free. Diamond Lake is stocked with rainbow trout, the 11-mile paved lake trail is good for biking, and trailheads for Mount Bailey and Rodney Butte are nearby.
excerpt: Thielsen View Campground sits on the west shore of Diamond Lake in the shadow of Mount Bailey, named for its view across the water to Mount Thielsen. Its 60 sit
note: Reservation only; extra vehicle $5 per night. Water spigots and vault toilets. Maximum vehicle length 35 ft.
address: Diamond Lake Loop (FR 4795), west shore of Diamond Lake, OR

title: Three C Rock Campground
imageAlt: Three C Rock picnic and fishing area

banner.alt: Three C Rock picnic and fishing area

gallery.alt: The South Umpqua River from site 5

contentHtml:
Three C Rock Campground has five sites on the South Umpqua River, under mixed conifers on the site of a late-1930s Civilian Conservation Corps camp. It is the only spot on the river where fishing is permitted.

It sits next to the Three C Rock picnic area, boat launch and swimming area.
excerpt: Three C Rock Campground has five sites on the South Umpqua River, under mixed conifers on the site of a late-1930s Civilian Conservation Corps camp. It is the o
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay (no cash). No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. Watch for poison oak.
address: County Rd 46 (South Umpqua Rd), 4 miles from Tiller, OR

title: Threehorn Campground
contentHtml:
Threehorn Campground is a primitive, five-site campground near the Rogue-Umpqua Divide, at 2,600 feet on the scenic road between Tiller and Trail, shaded by large pine and fir.

Rogue-Umpqua Divide Wilderness trailheads are nearby.
excerpt: Threehorn Campground is a primitive, five-site campground near the Rogue-Umpqua Divide, at 2,600 feet on the scenic road between Tiller and Trail, shaded by lar
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay (no cash). Vault toilet; no drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. Maximum trailer length 22 ft.
address: OR 227, about 36 miles from Canyonville, OR

title: Timpanogas Campground
contentHtml:
Timpanogas Campground is a small, 10-site campground at 5,300 feet in fir forest beside Timpanogas Lake, the headwaters of the Middle Fork Willamette River. The lake is open to non-motorized boating and fishing for cutthroat and brook trout.

The basin has 23 miles of trails, some open to mountain bikes and OHVs. It has vault toilets, drinking water and picnic tables.
excerpt: Timpanogas Campground is a small, 10-site campground at 5,300 feet in fir forest beside Timpanogas Lake, the headwaters of the Middle Fork Willamette River. The
note: $14 per night, $6 per extra vehicle, $5 day use; first come, first served. Be ready for mosquitoes June - August. The last 8 miles are past the end of pavement and rough. Middle Fork Ranger Station: (541) 782-2283.
address: FR 2154 off FR 21, about 42 miles southeast of Oakridge, OR

title: Toketee Group Site
contentHtml:
Toketee Group Site is a quiet group camp at Toketee Reservoir on the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, with a small pavilion, a large grass area for tents and gravel parking for RVs.

Beaver, otter, great blue herons and kingfishers live here, joined by ducks, geese and bald eagles in fall and winter. Watson Falls and Toketee Falls are each about five minutes away, and the North Umpqua Trail starts nearby.
excerpt: Toketee Group Site is a quiet group camp at Toketee Reservoir on the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River, with a small pavilion, a large grass area for tents and
note: Group reservations only. Dry site: bring your own water.
address: FR 34 off OR 138 at milepost 59, Toketee Reservoir, OR

title: Toketee Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Toketee Lake Campground is a quiet spot on the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River at Toketee Lake, shaded by willow, maple and alder. Beaver, otter, herons and kingfishers live here, joined by ducks, geese and bald eagles in fall and winter.

It is close to the North Umpqua Trail and to Watson and Toketee falls. The lake has German brown trout and is best for small non-powered boats.
excerpt: Toketee Lake Campground is a quiet spot on the Wild and Scenic North Umpqua River at Toketee Lake, shaded by willow, maple and alder. Beaver, otter, herons and
note: Dry campground: bring your own water. Vault toilets. Extra vehicle $5. Maximum vehicle length 30 ft. Run by a concessionaire in summer; Scan & Pay in the winter off-season.
address: FR 34 off OR 138 at milepost 59, Toketee Lake, OR

title: White Creek Campground
imageAlt: The Little River from White Creek Campground

banner.alt: The Little River from White Creek Campground

gallery.alt: The Little River at the campground

contentHtml:
White Creek Campground is a small campground on the Little River with a sandy beach and shallow water. Three of its four sites are walk-in only.

The Overhang Trail leads 1/4 mile downstream to a scenic cliff, and the Grotto Falls and Shadow Falls trails and Hemlock Lake are nearby.
excerpt: White Creek Campground is a small campground on the Little River with a sandy beach and shallow water. Three of its four sites are walk-in only.
note: First come, first served; pay with Scan & Pay. No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. Fishing not allowed. Run by a concessionaire in summer.
address: FS Rd 2792 (Red Butte Rd), off Little River Rd (#17), OR

title: Whitehorse Falls Campground
contentHtml:
Whitehorse Falls Campground is a small, quiet five-site campground under old-growth Douglas fir by the Clearwater River, along the Rogue-Umpqua Scenic Byway. A viewing platform at the day-use parking area looks out on Whitehorse Falls.

Lemolo Lake is about 10 miles away and Diamond Lake about 15 miles.
excerpt: Whitehorse Falls Campground is a small, quiet five-site campground under old-growth Douglas fir by the Clearwater River, along the Rogue-Umpqua Scenic Byway. A
note: Pay with Scan & Pay. No drinking water, trash service or cell coverage. Maximum trailer length 25 ft.
address: OR 138, 66 miles east of Roseburg, OR

title: Wolf Creek Group Site
imageAlt: The picnic shelter with its stone fireplace

banner.alt: The picnic shelter with its stone fireplace

contentHtml:
Wolf Creek Group Site is a reserve-only group campground for up to 150 people near the Little River, with a large open area ringed by forest, suited to family reunions and celebrations.

It has a shelter with a stone fireplace, picnic tables, fire rings, grills, drinking water, a ball field, volleyball court and horseshoe pits, with a campground host on site.
excerpt: Wolf Creek Group Site is a reserve-only group campground for up to 150 people near the Little River, with a large open area ringed by forest, suited to family r
note: Group reservations only. Maximum vehicle length 30 ft. No amplified music after 10 PM.
address: Little River Rd (#17), 12 miles from OR 138, OR

title: Alkali Falls
imageAlt: The upper drops of Alkali Falls

banner.alt: The upper drops of Alkali Falls

gallery.alt: The bottom cascades at the end of the trail

contentHtml:
Alkali Falls drops about 485 feet in six steep, tiered cascades down a long chute-like gully on Alkali Creek, starting with a near-vertical veil of about 130 feet. Below it the creek turns sharply and slides down a 120-foot incline before ending in a small rocky basin.

The creek is small, so the falls are tall but light in volume. The name recalls Alkali Meadows, a sheepherders' camp around 1900.
excerpt: Alkali Falls drops about 485 feet in six steep, tiered cascades down a long chute-like gully on Alkali Creek, starting with a near-vertical veil of about 130 fe
note: A short Forest Service trail ends at the creek less than 500 feet downstream of the base; seeing more takes a scramble. From the OR 62/230 junction at Union Creek, go north on OR 230 to the second FR 6540 junction (about 1/4 mile north of Highway Falls), follow 6540 for 1/2 mile, stay left on 6540-900, then left on 6540-950 to its end. Flows about 7 months a year.
address: End of FR 6540-950 off OR 230, north of Union Creek, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Bluff Falls
contentHtml: Bluff Falls is a 200-foot waterfall on Bluff Creek at about 2,750 feet elevation.
excerpt: Bluff Falls is a 200-foot waterfall on Bluff Creek at about 2,750 feet elevation.
note: Unofficial name. Detailed information and directions are not published.
address: Bluff Creek, Umpqua National Forest, OR (43.48701, -122.85235)

title: Burnt Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Burnt Creek Falls (also called Ramsay Falls, from a roadside sign) is a 125-foot horsetail on Burnt Creek. The low-volume falls drop over a cliff band, then cascade steeply down talus before the creek passes under a gravel road.

The basin is small and mostly above 3,000 feet, so flow drops to a trickle or dries up by midsummer.
excerpt: Burnt Creek Falls (also called Ramsay Falls, from a roadside sign) is a 125-foot horsetail on Burnt Creek. The low-volume falls drop over a cliff band, then cas
note: In 2019 the falls were partly visible from the road just downstream, with trees blocking the view; the 2020 Archie Creek Fire may have opened the view. Reaching the base takes a steep scramble. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.
address: Burnt Creek, Umpqua National Forest, OR (43.32313, -122.8636)
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Cascade Creek Falls

gallery.alt: The Cascade Creek canyon in the Mazama ash

contentHtml:
Cascade Creek Falls drops about 75 feet as a horsetail into a wide canyon carved into Mazama ash. The small creek starts at a spring just below the Rogue River Trail, so it is not expected to dry up during the year.

Walk about 200 feet along the canyon rim past where the trail turns south for the best views.
excerpt: Cascade Creek Falls drops about 75 feet as a horsetail into a wide canyon carved into Mazama ash. The small creek starts at a spring just below the Rogue River
note: From the Mazama trailhead on OR 230, drive about 1.5 miles west, park along the highway and walk through the woods to the Rogue River Trail, then hike about 3/4 mile east until the falls come into view.
address: Rogue River Trail, about 2.75 miles west of the Mazama viewpoint trailhead on OR 230, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Cedar Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Cedar Creek Falls plunges 140 feet off a high cliff in several columns, at about 2,780 feet elevation in the Umpqua River watershed.

The watershed is small: once snowmelt ends in summer, the falls shrink to a trickle or nearly dry up. They flow about 6 months a year.
excerpt: Cedar Creek Falls plunges 140 feet off a high cliff in several columns, at about 2,780 feet elevation in the Umpqua River watershed.
note: A Forest Service sign marks the falls, but they are not visible from the road in summer. Reaching the base takes a short scramble up a steep streambed. Watch for ticks. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.
address: Cedar Creek, Umpqua National Forest, OR (43.22135, -122.77345)

title: Conley Creek Falls
contentHtml: Conley Creek Falls is an 80-foot waterfall on Conley Creek at about 1,480 feet elevation.
excerpt: Conley Creek Falls is an 80-foot waterfall on Conley Creek at about 1,480 feet elevation.
note: Unofficial name. Detailed information and directions are not published.
address: Conley Creek, Umpqua National Forest, OR (43.35773, -122.95442)

title: Fall Creek Falls
imageAlt: Fall Creek Falls from the base

banner.alt: Fall Creek Falls from the base

contentHtml:
Fall Creek Falls drops about 120 feet in four tiers, spraying into a small amphitheater before cascading through a scenic gorge to the North Umpqua River. It is one of the more accessible waterfalls in the North Umpqua corridor.

An easy 3/4-mile trail from the Fall Creek picnic area passes several cascades and a rock outcrop called Jobs Garden.
excerpt: Fall Creek Falls drops about 120 feet in four tiers, spraying into a small amphitheater before cascading through a scenic gorge to the North Umpqua River. It is
note: Drive east from Glide to milepost 32 on OR 138, where the picnic area and trailhead are signed. The falls can also be reached from FR 4710.
address: Fall Creek Trailhead, OR 138 at milepost 32, east of Glide, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Grotto Falls

gallery.alt: Grotto Falls from the opposite side of the cliff

contentHtml:
Grotto Falls plunges 78 feet over a deeply undercut cliff that forms a nearly semicircular alcove, on a branch of Emile Creek in the Little River system. At high flow water spills through a notch about 25 feet across; at lower flow it splits into two side-by-side plunges.

An easy trail with a few switchbacks reaches the falls in about 1/3 mile, and you can walk behind the falls under the cliff.
excerpt: Grotto Falls plunges 78 feet over a deeply undercut cliff that forms a nearly semicircular alcove, on a branch of Emile Creek in the Little River system. At hig
note: From Glide, take Little River Rd south 16 miles, turn left on Road 2703 for 4.4 miles, then left on Road 2703-150 (signed for Grotto Falls) for 2.2 miles. The trailhead is just past the concrete bridge over Emile Creek.
address: Grotto Falls Trailhead, Road 2703-150 off Little River Rd, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Hemlock Falls
contentHtml:
Hemlock Falls drops about 45 feet down a rugged chasm into a gorge lined with moss, ferns and trees on Hemlock Creek.

A wide, well-graded but somewhat steep trail from Lake in the Woods Campground reaches the base in about 1/2 mile.
excerpt: Hemlock Falls drops about 45 feet down a rugged chasm into a gorge lined with moss, ferns and trees on Hemlock Creek.
note: From Glide, take Little River Rd south 25.8 miles to Lake in the Woods Campground. The trailhead is about a third of the way around the lake.
address: Lake in the Woods Campground, Little River Rd, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Huckleberry Creek Falls
contentHtml: Huckleberry Creek Falls is a steep, cascading waterfall that drops well over 200 feet (about 225 feet in total) on Huckleberry Creek, below a road that passes high above the creek.

title: Jack Falls
contentHtml:
Jack Falls drops about 200 feet in three or four horsetail tiers on Jack Creek, close to Highway 138. Dense foliage hides most of it from the road; the lowest tier, just upstream of the highway, is the easiest to see.

The creek is small and may run dry in summer, so the falls are best at higher flow.
excerpt: Jack Falls drops about 200 feet in three or four horsetail tiers on Jack Creek, close to Highway 138. Dense foliage hides most of it from the road; the lowest t
note: Reaching the upper tiers takes a difficult scramble up steep slopes, for experienced waterfall hunters only. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.
address: Jack Creek, beside OR 138, OR

title: Lemolo Falls
imageAlt: Lemolo Falls from the end of the trail

banner.alt: Lemolo Falls from the end of the trail

gallery.alt: First view of Lemolo Falls from the trail

contentHtml:
Lemolo Falls is the tallest and most powerful waterfall on the North Umpqua River, dropping about 165 feet over a contorted cliff of columnar basalt into a large pool. It flows year-round and is one of the most consistent falls in Oregon.

Lemolo Lake Dam diverts most of the river but keeps a fixed flow over the falls. At peak snowmelt the cliff can become a spray wall about 60 feet wide.
excerpt: Lemolo Falls is the tallest and most powerful waterfall on the North Umpqua River, dropping about 165 feet over a contorted cliff of columnar basalt into a larg
note: From OR 138, 11 miles east of Toketee, take FR 2610 (signed Lemolo Lake) 4.25 miles, turn left on Thorn Prairie Rd 3401 for 1/2 mile, then Road 3401-800 for 1.75 miles and Road 3401-840 to its end. The trail follows an old road 1/3 mile to the old trailhead, then 1 mile to the falls. The Forest Service lists the height as 102 feet; the USGS map shows 165 feet.
address: Lemolo Falls Trail #1468, end of Road 3401-840, near Lemolo Lake, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Lower Kentucky Falls
imageAlt: Lower Kentucky Falls at moderate flow

banner.alt: Lower Kentucky Falls at moderate flow

contentHtml:
Lower Kentucky Falls plunges 117 feet into a grotto framed by bigleaf maples, in the Kentucky Falls Natural Area. A small ledge three-quarters of the way down makes the water veil outward. North Fork Falls pours over the same cliff band on a neighboring stream and can often be seen from the same spots.

The trail passes the top of Upper Kentucky Falls, crosses some exposed, unguarded cliff sections, then switchbacks down to a viewing deck at the base, about 2 miles from the trailhead. The falls flow year-round.

note: From Reedsport, cross the Smith River bridge and take Lower Smith River Rd 11 miles, turn left on Road 48 before the North Fork Smith River bridge and go about 10.5 miles to FS Rd 23, then follow it 12.4 miles to the trailhead. From the north, take Sweet Creek Rd from OR 126 near Mapleton (it becomes FS Rd 48).
address: Kentucky Falls Trailhead, FS Rd 23, Siuslaw National Forest, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Middle Hemlock Falls
contentHtml:
Middle Hemlock Falls drops about 120 feet in three horsetail tiers on Hemlock Creek, and is the first falls you reach climbing the Hemlock Creek Trail from Lake in the Woods toward Hemlock Lake.

A 15-foot sliding upper tier is visible near a series of switchbacks, followed by a 25-foot drop over a wide block. The largest tier, an 80-foot plunge downstream, is not closely approached by the trail and is hard to see.
excerpt: Middle Hemlock Falls drops about 120 feet in three horsetail tiers on Hemlock Creek, and is the first falls you reach climbing the Hemlock Creek Trail from Lake
note: Lake in the Woods Campground is 25.8 miles up Little River Rd from Glide.

contentHtml: Middle Mountain Creek Falls is an 80-foot waterfall on Middle Mountain Creek at about 2,410 feet elevation.

title: North Fork Falls

gallery.alt: North Fork Falls from the riverbed

contentHtml:
North Fork Falls drops 145 feet on the North Fork Smith River in the Kentucky Falls Natural Area, right next to Lower Kentucky Falls. The water splits around a rock promontory and leaps 130 feet in two streams at right angles, merging into one broad veil at high flow.

It flows year-round but is usually a wispy mist by late July or August. From the viewing deck at Lower Kentucky Falls it is partly visible through the trees; for a clear view, take the steps down to the creek and rock- hop about 100 feet downstream.

note: The rocks are slick when wet, and in winter and spring you may get your feet wet. About 2 miles from the trailhead. From Reedsport, cross the Smith River bridge and take Lower Smith River Rd 11 miles, turn left on Road 48 before the North Fork Smith River bridge and go about 10.5 miles to FS Rd 23, then follow it 12.4 miles to the trailhead. From the north, take Sweet Creek Rd from OR 126 near Mapleton (it becomes FS Rd 48).

title: Platinum Falls
contentHtml: Platinum Falls (also called Bickford Falls) is a roughly 100-foot waterfall on Bickford Creek. Its name became official in 2013, chosen to contrast with nearby Golden and Silver Falls.
excerpt: Platinum Falls (also called Bickford Falls) is a roughly 100-foot waterfall on Bickford Creek. Its name became official in 2013, chosen to contrast with nearby

title: Shadow Falls
contentHtml:
Shadow Falls drops about 75 feet in three plunges where Cavitt Creek, after scouring potholes into the bedrock of a narrow gorge, pours into a dark chasm with a pool below. From some angles it seems to fall through a hole in the rock.

The name comes from the dark chasm, which rarely gets direct sun. The trail descends gradually to the creek and reaches the falls in about a mile.

note: From Glide, follow Little River Rd about 6.5 miles, turn right on Cavitt Creek Rd and go about 8 miles to a parking area on the right.

title: Slide Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Slide Creek Falls is a narrow, 137-foot plunge near the mouth of Slide Creek, in the Soda Springs reservoir area on the North Umpqua River. The water drops from a notch in the cliff into a small blue pool in a basalt grotto, with large mossy boulders below.

Flow is fairly low but steady most of the year, and the creek should not dry up even in late summer.

photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Toketee Falls
contentHtml:
Toketee Falls drops 89 feet in two steps from a narrow slot canyon cut into basalt with striking columnar jointing. The upper fall drops 19 feet into a small grotto, then the North Umpqua River leaps about 70 feet into a large blue-green pool.

A well-graded trail of about 1/3 mile leads to the viewpoint. A large wooden penstock near the trailhead carries water diverted for hydropower, and its leaky seams can spray visitors on hot days.

note: The turn is signed off OR 138, about 43 miles east of Glide or 16 miles west of Diamond Lake. The trail is not built for wheelchairs. The base of the falls is closed to the public.
address: Toketee Falls Trailhead, 1/2 mile north of OR 138 near Toketee Lake, OR

title: Upper Kentucky Falls
imageAlt: Upper Kentucky Falls from the trail

banner.alt: Upper Kentucky Falls from the trail

gallery.alt: Upper Kentucky Falls from its plunge pool

contentHtml:
Upper Kentucky Falls drops 88 feet in two steps where Kentucky Creek bends through a narrow gap: an 18- foot upper cascade, then a 69-foot free fall that splits into two or three channels at lower flow and becomes a wall of water up to 50 feet wide in high water.

The first 3/4 mile of the trail is easy and level to the top of the falls; the base is about a mile from the trailhead, on steeper trail cut into an unguarded cliff. The falls flow year-round.

note: From Reedsport, cross the Smith River bridge and take Lower Smith River Rd 11 miles, turn left on Road 48 before the North Fork Smith River bridge and go about 10.5 miles to FS Rd 23, then follow it 12.4 miles to the trailhead. From the north, take Sweet Creek Rd from OR 126 near Mapleton (it becomes FS Rd 48).

title: Warm Springs Falls
contentHtml:
Warm Springs Falls is a 60-foot curtain of water that pours over columnar basalt into a mossy amphitheater on Warm Springs Creek, near Lemolo and Diamond lakes.

A wheelchair-accessible trail of about 1/3 mile leads to a viewing deck, passing wild rhododendrons that usually bloom in June and early July.
excerpt: Warm Springs Falls is a 60-foot curtain of water that pours over columnar basalt into a mossy amphitheater on Warm Springs Creek, near Lemolo and Diamond lakes.
note: From OR 138, 11 miles east of Toketee, take FR 2610 (signed Lemolo Lake) 5.2 miles across Lemolo Dam, turn left on Road 600 for 3 miles, then left on Road 680 for 1.7 miles to the trailhead.
address: Warm Springs Falls Trail #1499, Road 680 near Lemolo Lake, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Watson Falls
imageAlt: Watson Falls and its amphitheater from below

banner.alt: Watson Falls and its amphitheater from below

gallery.alt: Watson Falls from the upper viewpoint

contentHtml:
Watson Falls is the tallest waterfall in the North Umpqua basin, plunging about 293 feet over a basalt amphitheater onto a talus slope covered in moss and vine maple. In late summer, gusts at the overhang can blow the water sideways or even upward.

The trail crosses Road 37 and climbs steadily about 1/3 mile to the base, with an upper viewpoint along the way.
excerpt: Watson Falls is the tallest waterfall in the North Umpqua basin, plunging about 293 feet over a basalt amphitheater onto a talus slope covered in moss and vine
note: Turn onto Fish Creek Rd #37 just over 2 miles east of Toketee Falls (about 43 miles east of Glide or 16 miles west of Diamond Lake). Parking is about 500 feet south of OR 138 on the right.
address: Watson Falls Trailhead, Fish Creek Rd (#37) just off OR 138, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Wolf Creek Falls
imageAlt: The upper visible tier of Wolf Creek Falls

banner.alt: The upper visible tier of Wolf Creek Falls

contentHtml:
Wolf Creek Falls is the largest accessible waterfall in the Little River area, falling about 175 feet in five tiers. The visible part is the final two steps: a 78-foot horsetail that spreads over a bulging, moss-covered cliff into a small pool, then a 30-foot drop into a deep pool ringed with logs.

The trail crosses the Little River on an arched metal bridge and reaches a viewpoint in about 1.2 miles. Flow drops in summer and fall and swells in winter.

note: From Glide, follow Little River Rd just over 10.5 miles to the signed trailhead; parking is across the road. The upper tiers sit in a gorge that cannot be reached without technical gear.
address: Wolf Creek Falls Trailhead, Little River Rd, 10.5 miles from Glide, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Yakso Falls
imageAlt: Yakso Falls from near its base

banner.alt: Yakso Falls from near its base

gallery.alt: Yakso Falls from the end of the trail

contentHtml:
Yakso Falls is a 60-foot fan-shaped veil on the Little River, falling over a bulging, sculpted cliff whose knobs split the water into smaller veils. Its name is a Chinook Jargon word for hair, describing the falls at lower flow.

An easy 0.7-mile trail winds through evergreens, vine maples and rhododendrons to the base. Spring snowmelt brings the biggest flow, and the falls stay attractive into late summer.

note: From Glide, take Little River Rd south 25.8 miles to Lake in the Woods Campground; the trailhead is across from the entrance.
address: Yakso Falls Trailhead, across from Lake in the Woods Campground, Little River Rd, OR

title: Diamond Lake

gallery.alt: A campsite looking at Mount Bailey

contentHtml:
Diamond Lake is a large, open mountain lake at about 5,183 feet in the Umpqua National Forest, with Mount Bailey rising to the west and Mount Thielsen to the east. It is good for kayaking, canoeing and paddleboarding, with Crater Lake National Park nearby.

The South Shore Boating Site has a boat ramp, flush toilets and picnic tables. Other launches include the Diamond Lake Campground ramps and Thielsen View Boat Ramp, and an 11-mile paved trail circles the lake.
excerpt: Diamond Lake is a large, open mountain lake at about 5,183 feet in the Umpqua National Forest, with Mount Bailey rising to the west and Mount Thielsen to the ea
note: Motorboats are allowed with a 10 mph lake-wide speed limit, and the lake can get windy. Day-use parking $5 per vehicle or a recreation pass. Kayaks, canoes and SUPs need an Oregon Waterway Access Permit. Check for blue-green algae advisories. Facilities are seasonal.
address: South Shore Boating Site, Diamond Lake, OR

title: Lemolo Lake
imageAlt: A campsite with Lemolo Lake behind

banner.alt: A campsite with Lemolo Lake behind

contentHtml:
Lemolo Lake is the highest reservoir on the North Umpqua River, at about 4,150 feet, with forested shores and a mountain backdrop. It reaches about 100 feet deep in places and is wide enough that wind and distance matter.

Paddlers launch from East Lemolo Campground, which has a vault toilet and picnic tables but no drinking water.
excerpt: Lemolo Lake is the highest reservoir on the North Umpqua River, at about 4,150 feet, with forested shores and a mountain backdrop. It reaches about 100 feet dee
note: Poole Creek Campground and Boat Ramp are closed for construction until the summer 2027 season. Motorboats and water skiing are allowed. Kayaks, canoes and SUPs need an Oregon Waterway Access Permit. The water is cold even in summer; check for blue-green algae advisories.
address: East Lemolo Campground, FR 430 off FR 2614, Lemolo Lake, OR

title: Loon Lake
imageAlt: Loon Lake from the day-use beach

banner.alt: Loon Lake from the day-use beach

contentHtml:
Loon Lake is a 260-acre, roughly two-mile-long lake in the Coast Range, formed when a large landslide blocked the valley, and unusually deep for its size. It has a forested shoreline, clear water and a warm sandy beach.

The BLM day-use area has a boat launch, fishing dock, swimming beach, picnic sites, restrooms and drinking water, and the campground has more than 50 sites. A short trail leads about 1/4 mile to a waterfall.

note: Day-use and launch fees apply. Motorboats and personal watercraft are allowed; mornings are calmer. Kayaks, canoes and SUPs need an Oregon Waterway Access Permit. No cell service. Seasonal.
address: Loon Lake Recreation Site, 7273 Loon Lake Rd, Reedsport, OR 97467

title: Mount Thielsen
contentHtml:
Mount Thielsen (9,182 ft) is Douglas County's highest point, a glacier-carved volcanic spire on the Douglas- Klamath county line north of Crater Lake, nicknamed the 'Lightning Rod of the Cascades.' Its summit is the highest point in the Umpqua National Forest.

Mountain hemlock and whitebark pine give way to steep, treeless rocky slopes. August is usually the best month for alpine wildflowers.
excerpt: Mount Thielsen (9,182 ft) is Douglas County's highest point, a glacier-carved volcanic spire on the Douglas- Klamath county line north of Crater Lake, nicknamed
note: A serious climb, not a hike: the strenuous 5-mile trail (#1456) has no markers above timberline and ends with a difficult 200-foot hand-over-hand scramble; ropes are advised for the summit.
address: Mount Thielsen Trailhead, OR 138 west of Diamond Lake, OR

title: Metolius–Windigo Trail
contentHtml:
The Metolius-Windigo Trail (Trail #99) runs roughly 150 miles through the Deschutes National Forest, from the Metolius Basin near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness west of Sisters south to Windigo Pass near Crescent Lake. Created around 1980 as a lower-elevation alternative to the Pacific Crest Trail, it connects to the PCT at both ends and is popular with horse riders.

Its southern end, Windigo Pass, sits on the Douglas-Klamath county line.
excerpt: The Metolius-Windigo Trail (Trail #99) runs roughly 150 miles through the Deschutes National Forest, from the Metolius Basin near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness
note: Published lengths vary from about 120 to 152 miles.
address: Southern terminus: Windigo Pass, on the Douglas-Klamath county line, OR

title: Oregon Coast Trail
imageAlt: Oregon Coast Trail sign along a forested trail

banner.alt: Oregon Coast Trail sign along a forested trail

contentHtml:
The Oregon Coast Trail follows Oregon's coastline from the Columbia River to the California border, about 382 miles by the official guide and about 425 miles if no ferries are used around the estuaries. It passes through 28 coastal towns.

Most of the route is on the beach, with other sections through state parks and public lands, on private land under trail easements, and on road shoulders.

Hiker/biker tent sites, first-come first-served, are at nearly every coastal state park. Check tide times, as some areas are passable only at low tide. During western snowy plover nesting season (March 15 to September 15), walk on wet sand in protected areas, where dogs, camping and beach fires are not allowed.
excerpt: The Oregon Coast Trail follows Oregon's coastline from the Columbia River to the California border, about 382 miles by the official guide and about 425 miles if
note: Trail conditions change quickly; check Oregon State Parks notices and Trailkeepers of Oregon alerts before you go.
address: Runs the length of the Oregon coast, including Douglas County

title: Oregon Timber Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Timber Trail is a 670-mile mountain bike and bikepacking route from the California border near Lakeview north to Hood River on the Columbia, managed by the nonprofit Oregon Timber Trail Alliance. It is split into four tiers: Fremont, Willamette, Deschutes and Hood.

Riders can take on the whole route or ride a shorter piece of any tier.

address: California border near Lakeview to Hood River, OR

title: Pacific Crest Trail
contentHtml:
The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail runs 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada through California, Oregon and Washington, managed by the Forest Service with the Pacific Crest Trail Association. Its roughly 455-mile Oregon section is the shortest and easiest on the trail, from near Siskiyou Summit to the Bridge of the Gods over the Columbia River.

In Douglas County, 26 miles of the trail cross the Mount Thielsen Wilderness.

address: Oregon section: California border near Ashland to the Bridge of the Gods, Cascade Locks, OR

title: Cowhorn
imageAlt: Lemolo Lake, near the start (area photo)

banner.alt: Lemolo Lake, near the start (area photo)

contentHtml:
Cowhorn is a 38-mile gravel lollipop with about 3,700 feet of climbing, roughly 60% gravel, 30% paved and 10% single track. It climbs past Diamond Peak, Hills Peak and Cowhorn Mountain, then descends a narrow paved road with views of Mount Thielsen.

The route also takes in a stretch of the North Umpqua Trail single track and a rough canal section along Lemolo Lake. Spring through fall, on a sunny day, gives the best views.
excerpt: Cowhorn is a 38-mile gravel lollipop with about 3,700 feet of climbing, roughly 60% gravel, 30% paved and 10% single track. It climbs past Diamond Peak, Hills P
note: Very demanding and remote, with challenging navigation. The opening climb has 10-15% grades for about a mile, and the North Umpqua Trail section is narrow and technical. Do not continue along the canal past the wooden bridge exit. No food or water on the route; 40 mm tires or wider are recommended.
address: Dirt pull-out on NF 2614 just before the Umpqua River bridge to Inlet Campground, Lemolo Lake, OR

title: Crosscut
imageAlt: Leading out on the Crosscut route

banner.alt: Leading out on the Crosscut route

contentHtml:
Crosscut is a 39-mile gravel lollipop near Reedsport with about 3,500 feet of climbing, 75% gravel and 25% paved. It passes Tahkenitch and Siltcoos lakes, with a timber-country section, farmland and a loop around Siltcoos Lake.

Park in a wide spot along Fivemile Road at the start.

note: Several steep pitches (up to 15%, including one 10%+ climb of 1.1 miles). Active logging may occur: log trucks have the right of way, so use lights and ride together. No food or water on the route; 45 mm tires or wider are suggested.
address: Highway 101 and Fivemile Rd, near Tahkenitch Lake, OR

title: Minnehaha Loop
imageAlt: Gravel climb through the burn zone up Minnehaha Ridge

banner.alt: Gravel climb through the burn zone up Minnehaha Ridge

contentHtml:
The Minnehaha Loop is a 24.1-mile lollipop of about 60% gravel and 40% pavement with about 2,900 feet of climbing. It climbs about 1,800 feet over 8 miles through fire-scarred forest up Minnehaha Ridge, with views of Mount Thielsen.

An optional short hike leads to National Falls.

title: Franklin Creek
contentHtml:
Franklin Creek was designated a Wild and Scenic River on March 12, 2019, for 4.5 wild miles from its headwaters to the private land boundary. It flows through the remote, steep Devils Staircase Wilderness in the Coast Range, between the Umpqua and Smith rivers.

Its nearly pristine water makes it a reference stream for scientific research. It is recognized for temperate rainforest ecology, high-quality habitat for threatened coho salmon, winter steelhead, fall Chinook and Pacific lamprey, old-growth scenery and regionally significant beaver habitat.

note: No trails or developed access. Managed by the Siuslaw National Forest.
address: Siuslaw National Forest: 3200 SW Jefferson Way, Corvallis, OR 97331

title: North Umpqua River
contentHtml:
The North Umpqua River was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 33.8 recreational miles from the Soda Springs Powerhouse to the confluence with Rock Creek. Its jade-green water runs past basalt cliffs and spires, meadows and hemlock forests along Highway 138.

It is known for one of the best summer steelhead fisheries on the West Coast, along with winter steelhead, Chinook, coho and sea-run cutthroat trout. People have lived along the river for at least 6,300 years, and the Mott Bridge, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1935-36, is an Oregon Historical Civil Engineering Landmark.

Recreation includes fly fishing, whitewater boating (best in May, June and early July), camping, swimming and the 79-mile North Umpqua Trail.
excerpt: The North Umpqua River was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 33.8 recreational miles from the Soda Springs Powerhouse to the confluenc
note: Fly fishing only in the designated section. Managed by the Umpqua National Forest and the BLM Roseburg District (541-440-4930).
address: 777 NW Garden Valley Blvd, Roseburg, OR 97471
photoCredit: Bob Wick, Bureau of Land Management

title: Rogue (Upper) River
contentHtml:
The Upper Rogue River was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 40.3 miles (6.1 wild, 34.2 scenic) from the Crater Lake National Park boundary to Prospect. About the first 13 miles are in Douglas County.

Fed by Cascade snowmelt and springs, the river runs through pumice flats, deep gorges and chutes; in one two-mile stretch it has cut more than 200 feet into Mazama pumice. It is a prized steelhead and salmon fishery, and the Upper Rogue River Trail, a National Recreation Trail, follows its full length.

At Natural Bridge the river flows through a lava tube.
excerpt: The Upper Rogue River was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 40.3 miles (6.1 wild, 34.2 scenic) from the Crater Lake National Park boun
note: Boating is for experienced paddlers only, and the wild section is generally not recommended for boating. Managed by the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest.
address: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest: 3040 Biddle Rd, Medford, OR 97504

title: Wasson Creek
contentHtml:
Wasson Creek was designated a Wild and Scenic River on March 12, 2019, for 10.1 wild miles through the Devils Staircase Wilderness in the Coast Range, between the Umpqua and Smith rivers. The BLM manages the 4.2-mile eastern segment and the Siuslaw National Forest the 5.9-mile western segment.

The remote, steep, densely vegetated drainage supports mammals, birds, amphibians and fish, and is recognized for its ecology, fish, recreation, scenery and high-quality beaver habitat.

note: No system trails or developed facilities, and few roads nearby. Siuslaw National Forest: (541) 750- 7000.
address: BLM Coos Bay District Office: 1300 Airport Ln, North Bend, OR 97459

title: Cow Creek Tour Route
contentHtml:
The Cow Creek Tour Route is about 45 miles of canyon driving through historic mining country, a 1-2 hour loop off I-5 from Riddle to Glendale. It follows Cow Creek and the 1870s Oregon and California railroad route, past historic railroad structures including Tunnel Number One.

Riddle shows remnants of a nickel mine among lumber mills, ranches and farms, and local hardware stores sell gold pans. Past the tunnel, the Cow Creek Recreational Gold Panning Area invites visitors to try their luck. In Glendale, volunteers are restoring the 1901 Springer Martin House.

Spring brings waterfalls and wildflowers, and autumn turns the hardwoods gold and red.
excerpt: The Cow Creek Tour Route is about 45 miles of canyon driving through historic mining country, a 1-2 hour loop off I-5 from Riddle to Glendale. It follows Cow Cr
note: Exit 103 is the only place to fuel up on the route. The gold panning area includes private mining claims; check boundaries with the BLM Roseburg District (541-440-4930) before panning.
address: I-5 exit 103 near Riddle to I-5 exit 80 near Glendale, OR

title: Myrtle Creek-Canyonville Tour Route
contentHtml:
The Myrtle Creek-Canyonville Tour Route is a 68-mile, 3-4 hour loop through the southern Cascade foothills, following the South Umpqua River past small towns, clear streams, farms and forest. Spring and fall are the best times to drive it.

Stops include the Milo Academy Covered Bridge and the Tiller Ranger Station, a 1930s Civilian Conservation Corps complex on the National Register of Historic Places with a cupola-style fire lookout open to the public. The route then climbs through old-growth Douglas fir and mountain hemlock in the Umpqua National Forest to Red Top Pond, popular for fishing and picnics.

It returns along South Myrtle Creek to Millsite Park in Myrtle Creek, home of the re-created Horse Creek Covered Bridge.

note: The forest road section is steep and narrow and not suitable for motor homes or trailers. The route may be closed in winter.
address: Canyonville (I-5 exit 98) to Myrtle Creek, OR

title: Pacific Coast Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway
Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway
Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway

contentHtml:
The Pacific Coast Scenic Byway, an All-American Road, follows US 101 for 363 miles along the whole Oregon coast, from Astoria at the Washington border to Brookings at the California border.

In Douglas County the byway passes Winchester Bay and Reedsport. Highlights along the whole route include clamming on Tillamook Bay, kayaking Alsea Bay, the dramatic rocks and islands of the south coast and jet boat trips up the Rogue River at Gold Beach.

EV charging stations are spaced along the route, making an electric road trip from Astoria to Brookings possible.
excerpt: The Pacific Coast Scenic Byway, an All-American Road, follows US 101 for 363 miles along the whole Oregon coast, from Astoria at the Washington border to Brooki
address: US 101 from Astoria to Brookings, OR

title: Rogue-Umpqua Scenic Byway
contentHtml:
The Rogue-Umpqua Scenic Byway, a National Scenic Byway, runs 172 miles (5-7 hours) from Roseburg up the North Umpqua River, past Diamond Lake, and down the Upper Rogue River to Gold Hill. The North Umpqua stretch is called the Highway of Waterfalls, with more than 15 cascades.

Highlights include the Winchester Dam fish ladder viewing window, the Douglas County Museum, Colliding Rivers near Glide, the 79-mile North Umpqua Trail, Toketee Falls, 272-foot Watson Falls, Lemolo Lake and Diamond Lake. On the Rogue side are Rogue Gorge, Natural Bridge, Lost Creek Lake and Cole Rivers Hatchery.

June through October brings clear roads, fair weather and long days.
excerpt: The Rogue-Umpqua Scenic Byway, a National Scenic Byway, runs 172 miles (5-7 hours) from Roseburg up the North Umpqua River, past Diamond Lake, and down the Uppe
note: Check wildfire and road conditions before you go.
address: Roseburg (I-5 and OR 138) to Gold Hill (I-5 and OR 234), OR

title: Umpqua River Scenic Byway
contentHtml:
The Umpqua River Scenic Byway runs 66 miles (3-5 hours) from Oakland to Reedsport, following OR 138 and OR 38 along the Umpqua River to the coast. It is open year-round.

Oakland's historic downtown is a National Historic Landmark. Past Sutherlin, a roughly 100-foot walnut tree estimated at over 250 years old stands beside the highway. Elkton has its own wine region, a butterfly house and hummingbird garden, and Fort Umpqua, a replica Hudson's Bay Company trading post.

Scottsburg Park has a riverside picnic area. Near Reedsport, Dean Creek Elk Viewing Area often shows Roosevelt elk in the morning and evening, and the Umpqua Discovery Center covers regional history. The river is known for Chinook salmon, sturgeon, steelhead and smallmouth bass.

address: Oakland (I-5) to Reedsport (US 101), OR

title: Great Umpqua Food Trail
imageAlt: Steamboat Inn breakfast overlooking the Umpqua River

banner.alt: Steamboat Inn breakfast overlooking the Umpqua River

contentHtml:
The Great Umpqua Food Trail links about 40 stops across Douglas County: wineries, breweries, farm-to-table restaurants, farmers markets, farm stands, u-pick farms, bakeries, cafes and a historic country store.

Three itineraries guide the way: Rambling Rivers (Roseburg to Idleyld Park on the North Umpqua Highway), Old Wagon Roads (Canyonville to Lookingglass) and Sip to the Sea (Elkton to Reedsport).

The trail is open year-round, with high season June through October: cherries June through August, blueberries and peaches in July and August, and pumpkin patches in September and October.
excerpt: The Great Umpqua Food Trail links about 40 stops across Douglas County: wineries, breweries, farm-to-table restaurants, farmers markets, farm stands, u-pick far
note: Cell service is limited in remote areas, so map your route before you go, and confirm each stop's hours.
address: Throughout Douglas County, OR

title: Wild Rivers Coast Food Trail

gallery.alt: Fresh catch and Oregon pinot gris

contentHtml:
The Wild Rivers Coast Food Trail is a self-guided guide to berries, seafood and scenic landscapes on Oregon's South Coast. It links farms and ranches, eateries, seafood sellers, markets, craft beverage makers, artisans and experiences along Highway 101, with Douglas County stops in Winchester Bay and Reedsport.

Add the Digital Passport to your phone and check in at members to earn discounts and prizes. Themed itineraries and a printable brochure are on the trail website.

High season runs June through November: blueberries in July and August, pumpkin patches late September through October, cranberries mid-October to early December, and Dungeness crab late December through August.

note: Open year-round; check each stop's hours. Cell service is spotty in remote areas. Email: wrcfoodtrail@gmail.com
address: Highway 101 from Reedsport and Coquille to Gold Beach and Brookings, OR

title: Cavitt Creek Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1943 by Floyd C. Frear, the Cavitt Creek Covered Bridge is a 70-foot Howe truss carrying Cavitt Creek Road over the Little River where it meets Cavitt Creek. Its Tudor arch portals were shaped to let log trucks through, and its upper chords are unhewn logs.

The area was settled in the early 1880s and named for Robert Cavitt, who settled on a Little River tributary.
excerpt: Built in 1943 by Floyd C. Frear, the Cavitt Creek Covered Bridge is a 70-foot Howe truss carrying Cavitt Creek Road over the Little River where it meets Cavitt
note: From Roseburg, take OR 138 east toward Glide; just before Glide turn right onto Little River Rd, go about 7 miles, then turn right onto Cavitt Creek Rd.
address: Cavitt Creek Rd at Little River Rd, near Glide, OR

title: Horse Creek Covered Bridge
imageAlt: Horse Creek Covered Bridge in Millsite Park

banner.alt: Horse Creek Covered Bridge in Millsite Park

gallery.alt: Horse Creek Covered Bridge in Millsite Park

contentHtml:
The Horse Creek Covered Bridge was built in 1930 as a Howe truss over Horse Creek near McKenzie Bridge in Lane County. It was bypassed in 1968 and dismantled in 1987, and its timbers were given to the City of Myrtle Creek in 1990.

Rebuilt over Myrtle Creek, it now serves as a pedestrian bridge linking a parking lot to Millsite Park.

note: From I-5 exit 108, continue on Old Highway 99 (Main Street) for one mile; the bridge is to the west in Millsite Park.
address: Millsite Park, Myrtle Creek, OR

title: Milo Academy Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1962, the 100-foot Milo Academy Covered Bridge spans the South Umpqua River and is Oregon's only steel bridge housed in wood. It replaced a 1920 wooden covered bridge on the same site; residents wanted stronger materials that kept the same look.

It is privately owned by Milo Adventist Academy, provides access to the school, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.
excerpt: Built in 1962, the 100-foot Milo Academy Covered Bridge spans the South Umpqua River and is Oregon's only steel bridge housed in wood. It replaced a 1920 wooden
note: From I-5 exit 98, go through Canyonville and continue on 3rd Street (toward Days Creek) for 17 miles, then turn right onto Milo Drive at the bridge.
address: Milo Dr at Milo Adventist Academy, Milo, OR

title: Neal Lane Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
The Neal Lane Covered Bridge over South Myrtle Creek is one of Oregon's shortest covered bridges and the only one in the state using a kingpost truss. Built for $1,000, it has arched portals, narrow window openings and plank flooring.

It was renovated in 2015.

note: Five-ton weight limit. From I-5 exit 108, go south on Old Highway 99 (Main Street) half a mile, turn left onto Riverside Drive just after the bridge, then right onto Days Creek Cutoff Rd; the bridge is on the left.

title: Pass Creek Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
The 61-foot Pass Creek Covered Bridge is a Howe truss that once carried traffic over Pass Creek in Drain. It is officially dated 1925, though local historians argue it is older.

Bypassed and closed to vehicles in 1981, it was moved one block in 1987 and reassembled in a park behind the Drain Civic Center, where it now serves pedestrians.

note: From I-5 exit 150 toward Yoncalla/Drain, keep left, turn right onto W A Avenue, then make a sharp right to stay on W A Avenue toward the bridge.

title: Rochester Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1933 by Floyd Frear, the 80-foot Rochester Covered Bridge is a Howe truss carrying Rochester Road over Calapooya Creek. Its design is unique among Oregon covered bridges, with four curved-top windows on each side.

In the late 1950s, after a county crew burned a nearby covered bridge, local residents guarded this one overnight with rifles.
