note: From I-5 exit 136 (Sutherlin/Elkton), turn left onto OR 138 (Central Avenue), right onto Stearns Lane, then left onto Rochester Bridge Rd.
address: Rochester Rd over Calapooya Creek, about 3 miles west of Sutherlin, OR

title: Umpqua River Lighthouse
contentHtml:
First lit in 1894 to mark the entrance to the Umpqua River, the 65-foot Umpqua River Lighthouse stands beside the site of the Oregon coast's first lighthouse, built in 1857 and lost to erosion in 1861. It is nearly identical to Heceta Head's, but its lens flashes a distinctive red and white.

The tower, built with 240,000 bricks, is part of the adjoining U.S. Coast Guard base. Tours start at the Umpqua River Lighthouse Museum, about half a mile from Umpqua Lighthouse State Park.

note: Tour schedule is posted at umpquavalleymuseums.org; tours cannot be booked at the state park. Mention the 240,000 bricks for a tour discount.
address: 1020 Lighthouse Rd, Winchester Bay, OR 97467

title: Cinnamon Butte
contentHtml:
Cinnamon Butte Sno-Park, at 4,820 feet in the Umpqua National Forest, is recommended for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. The trail climbs 3 miles to the 6,417-foot summit of Cinnamon Butte, topped by a 41- foot fire lookout tower built in 1955, with views of Mount Thielsen, Sawtooth Ridge, Lemolo Lake and the North Umpqua canyon.

Skiing to the top of the ridge also brings views of Mt. Bachelor and the Three Sisters, and the downhill runs on both trails are a highlight. Restrooms are available; no drinking water.

note: An Oregon Sno-Park permit is required November 1 to April 30 (daily $4, 3-day $9, annual $25). Camping at trailheads is prohibited.

excerpt: Claude Lewis Trailhead Sno-Park, in the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest, is a winter staging area for cross-country skiing and snowmobiling.

title: Mt. Thielsen
contentHtml:
Mount Thielsen Sno-Park, at 5,300 feet, is the trailhead for the most direct route up Mount Thielsen, and in winter it is popular for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. The Mount Thielsen Trail, the Pacific Crest Trail and the Spruce Ridge Trail start here.

Vault toilets and picnic tables; no drinking water or garbage service. The lot is on the east side of OR 138.

title: North Crater Lake
contentHtml:
North Crater Sno-Park sits just north of Crater Lake National Park, with access to the Pacific Crest Trail (which enters the Mount Thielsen Wilderness to the north) and the North Crater Trail. It is used for snowshoeing, cross-country skiing and snowmobiling.

Vault toilet; no drinking water.

title: South Diamond
contentHtml:
South Diamond Sno-Park, at 5,200 feet near the junction of OR 230 and OR 138, serves cross-country skiers, snowshoers, snowmobilers and dog sledders. Nordic trails include Pizza Connect, Horse-N-Teal, Outback, Diamond Lake West, Silent Creek and North Crater.

No restrooms, drinking water or picnic tables.

note: An Oregon Sno-Park permit is required November 1 to April 30 (daily $4, 3-day $9, annual $25). Camping at trailheads is prohibited.
address: OR 230 at FR 6592, 0.2 mile from OR 138, OR

title: Three Lakes (West Diamond Lake)
contentHtml:
Three Lakes Sno-Park (West Diamond Lake) offers downhill and cross-country skiing, snowshoeing and snowmobiling. Nordic trails include the 2.3-mile Silent Creek Trail and the 3.6-mile Hemlock Butte Trail, whose first two miles are shared with snowmobiles.

Vault toilets; no drinking water or picnic tables.

note: An Oregon Sno-Park permit is required November 1 to April 30 (daily $4, 3-day $9, annual $25). Camping at trailheads is prohibited.
address: OR 230, 2.7 miles west of the OR 138 junction, OR

title: Umpqua Hot Springs (Toketee Hot Springs)
contentHtml:
Umpqua Hot Springs is a natural stone tub carved from travertine on a bare rock face about 150 feet above the North Umpqua Wild and Scenic River, sheltered by an open-air roof. Water seeping through an active fault runs 100 to 115°F, and Surprise Falls is visible across the river.

From the trailhead, cross the footbridge over the river and climb a steep, narrow trail (Trail #1444) of about a third of a mile to the springs. A vault toilet is at the trailhead; there is no drinking water. Toketee Lake Campground is the nearest overnight site.
excerpt: Umpqua Hot Springs is a natural stone tub carved from travertine on a bare rock face about 150 feet above the North Umpqua Wild and Scenic River, sheltered by a
note: Day use only, sunrise to sunset. Trailhead day-use fee $5 per vehicle or a Northwest Forest Pass; no cash or checks. Expect crowds and nudity, and pack out all trash. The road usually closes in winter, leaving a 2.5-mile hike, ski or snowshoe in.
address: Umpqua Hot Springs Trailhead, off OR 138 near Toketee Lake, OR

title: Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area
contentHtml:
The Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area protects about 31,500 acres of the Siuslaw National Forest, stretching some 40 miles along the coast from Florence to Coos Bay. It is the largest expanse of coastal sand dunes in North America, with dunes rising as high as 500 feet, and was designated by Congress in 1972.

Dunes, forest and ocean meet here, for off-highway vehicle riding, hiking, paddling, wildlife viewing, birding, camping, picnicking and sand play. Reedsport's Oregon Dunes Visitor Center is a good place to start.

note: Western snowy plovers, a threatened species, nest March 15 to September 15; follow nesting-season restrictions on the beach.
address: Oregon Dunes Visitor Center, Reedsport, OR

title: Acker Rock Lookout

gallery.alt: Acker Rock Lookout and access stairs

contentHtml:
Acker Rock Lookout is a 12-by-12-foot cab set by helicopter in 1964 on the edge of a thin volcanic ridge at about 4,000 feet, with part of the floor hanging over several hundred feet of open air. Sheer cliffs drop on two sides, the views take in the South Umpqua watershed, and on a clear day the rim of Crater Lake shows from the catwalk. It is still used for active fire detection.

The one-room lookout sleeps up to four and has a single bed, table and chair, propane heater, lanterns, stove with oven and refrigerator, plus a composting toilet. Everything is packed in on the steep 0.4-mile Acker Rock Trail (#1585) from the gated spur road.
excerpt: Acker Rock Lookout is a 12-by-12-foot cab set by helicopter in 1964 on the edge of a thin volcanic ridge at about 4,000 feet, with part of the floor hanging ove
note: Reservable August 1 to November 15, depending on snow. No water on site; the nearest spigot is at the Tiller Ranger Station, about 45 minutes away. High-clearance 4WD or AWD recommended; follow the printed directions, not GPS. No smoking in the tower; pack out all trash; no cash accepted.
address: Tiller Ranger Station: 27812 Tiller Trail Hwy, Tiller, OR 97484

title: Pickett Butte Lookout
contentHtml:
Pickett Butte Lookout is a one-room flat-top lookout on Pickett Butte at 3,200 feet, reached by a steep, narrow 40-foot stairway, with panoramic views of the Jackson Creek drainage and the country around Tiller. The original 1934 lookout was replaced by the current structure in 1948.

It sleeps up to four, with a single bed, table and chair, propane heater, lanterns, stove with oven and refrigerator, a vault toilet and a pulley for hauling gear up.
excerpt: Pickett Butte Lookout is a one-room flat-top lookout on Pickett Butte at 3,200 feet, reached by a steep, narrow 40-foot stairway, with panoramic views of the Ja
note: Reservable October 15 to July 15; used for fire detection in summer. No water on site; the nearest spigot is at the Tiller Ranger Station, about 20 minutes away. Roads are not plowed, so winter guests may need to ski, snowshoe or snowmobile the last few miles. Not recommended for families with small children. No smoking.
address: Tiller Ranger Station: 27812 Tiller Trail Hwy, Tiller, OR 97484

title: Backside Brewing Co.
contentHtml:
Founded in 2012, Backside Brewing serves craft beer, wood-fired pizza and cocktails in a rustic, industrial taproom it shares with a bike shop. There is indoor seating, a covered patio with picnic tables and a fire pit, and a very long shuffleboard table, and families, groups and pets are welcome.

Beers include How Now Brown Ale and Twin Sisters Stout. The brewery hosts trivia nights and charity events, and has a second location in Sutherlin at 105 W Central Ave.

address: 1640 NE Odell Ave, Roseburg, OR 97470

title: Draper Brewing
contentHtml:
Draper Brewing is a small brewery in Tenmile, with its tasting room, the Draper Draft House, in downtown Roseburg. It brews porters, IPAs, farmhouse ales and sours, along with its signature Draper Lager and seasonal beers.

The casual, rustic Draft House serves pub food such as burgers, sandwiches and appetizers, and has shuffleboard, trivia nights and live music.

address: Draper Draft House: 640 SE Jackson St, Roseburg, OR 97470

title: Lookingglass
contentHtml:
Lookingglass Brewery moved from Lookingglass to downtown Winston in 2016 and brews on a 10-barrel system, pouring IPAs, stouts and seasonal beers. It bills itself as the only brewery between Roseburg and Grants Pass.

The taproom has exposed brick and wooden beams, 18 taps, a small stage and two patios with covered seating, and hosts trivia, live music and community fundraisers.

note: The brewery and building are listed for sale but still operating; check before visiting.

title: North Forty Beer
contentHtml:
North Forty Beer's downtown Roseburg taproom pours rotating beers from hop-forward IPAs to rich stouts.

Regulars include Fireline, a coppery red with caramel notes; True North, an IPA with six hops giving citrus, tropical fruit and pine flavors; and Black Forest, a roasty stout with cherry and coffee notes.
excerpt: North Forty Beer's downtown Roseburg taproom pours rotating beers from hop-forward IPAs to rich stouts.
address: 435 SE Jackson St, Roseburg, OR 97470

title: Two Shy Brewing
imageAlt: A pour on the taproom bar

banner.alt: A pour on the taproom bar

contentHtml:
Two Shy Brewing started as a garage batch in 2009, and Lyle and Danielle Hruda have run its Park Street taproom since 2012. Up to 25 rotating taps range from hazy and cold IPAs to pilsner, amber, cream porter and barrel-aged stouts; the Belgian-style quad Olaf's Warm Hugs won silver at the 2024 Oregon Beer Awards.

The dog-friendly taproom and patio host rotating food trucks, live music and trivia nights. A second taproom is in Reedsport at 473 Fir Ave.

title: Abacela Winery
imageAlt: Earl and Hilda Jones at Abacela

banner.alt: Earl and Hilda Jones at Abacela

contentHtml:
Abacela, founded in 1995 by Earl and Hilda Jones, is the pioneer of American Tempranillo and planted Oregon's first commercial Tempranillo. Earl chose the Umpqua Valley for its Rioja-like climate; the 76-acre estate, Fault Line Vineyards, has five soil types on slopes from flat to 46 degrees, and grows 17 varieties.

The estate Vine & Wine Center pours Tempranillo, Albariño, Malbec, Syrah, Grenache, Tannat, Touriga Nacional, sparkling and dessert wines, with vineyards a short walk from the tasting room. Food is available, and it is family and dog friendly.

title: Bradley Vineyards
contentHtml:
Bradley Vineyards is a second-generation, family-owned vineyard and winery established in 1983 by John Bradley, the largest grape producer in the Elkton Oregon AVA. It sells most of its fruit to other Oregon winemakers and keeps the best estate grapes for its own small-production label, made by John's son Tyler Bradley.

The tasting room pours Pinot Noir, Baco Noir, Gewürztraminer, Riesling and dry rosé. Picnics among the vines are welcome, and a guest yurt is available to rent.

title: Brandborg Vineyard & Winery
contentHtml:
Terry and Sue Brandborg searched for a cool, coastal-influenced site and settled in Elkton, about 36 miles inland, where they planted 5 acres of Pinot Noir on a site rising to 1,100 feet with views of the Umpqua River and Coast Range. The self-taught winemakers have made wine for 40 vintages, and the vineyard is certified Salmon-Safe and LIVE.

The downtown Elkton tasting room pours Pinot Noir and Alsace-inspired whites such as Gewürztraminer, Riesling and Pinot Gris, plus sparkling wine. Dogs are welcome on the patio, and there is an EV charger.

Cooper Ridge Vineyard is a family-owned winery on the North Umpqua River, where walnut orchards were converted to a 25-acre estate vineyard. It makes limited-production estate wines including Pinot Noir, Riesling, Chenin Blanc, Tempranillo, Grüner Veltliner, sparkling and dessert wines.

Since 2015 its tasting room and patio have offered panoramic vineyard and mountain views, with charcuterie plates, seasonal live music and a guest house.

title: Foon Estate
contentHtml:
FOON Estate Vineyard is a small-lot, family-owned and managed winery in the Umpqua Valley, making hand- crafted wines only from grapes grown on its own property.

It focuses on Spanish and French varieties such as Tempranillo, Malbec and Albariño, served with tapas in an 1850s timber barn tasting room.
excerpt: FOON Estate Vineyard is a small-lot, family-owned and managed winery in the Umpqua Valley, making hand- crafted wines only from grapes grown on its own property
note: Tastings by appointment; call to schedule.

title: River's Edge Winery
contentHtml:
Founded in 2000, River's Edge is Elkton's first winery, on the north bank of the Umpqua River. It makes sustainable wines sourced entirely from the Elkton AVA.

The tasting room pours unusual varieties such as Aligoté and Baco Noir alongside Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Sauvignon Blanc, rosé and port-style wines. It is dog and family friendly.
excerpt: Founded in 2000, River's Edge is Elkton's first winery, on the north bank of the Umpqua River. It makes sustainable wines sourced entirely from the Elkton AVA.
address: 1395 River Dr, Elkton, OR 97436

title: Trella Vineyards
contentHtml:
Trella Vineyards is a boutique, family-run winery founded in 2011 by Stephen and Susan Williams, with a 7- acre sustainably farmed estate at the base of the Callahan Mountains, near Oregon's first Pinot Noir plantings.

Its downtown Roseburg tasting room, in a restored 1908 building, has a cozy wine-bar feel with artisan pairings. Wines include Pinot Noir, Tempranillo, Barbera, Malbec, Baco Noir, Grüner Veltliner, Pinot Gris, rosé and sparkling.

note: Email: info@trellavineyards.com
address: 646 SE Jackson St, Roseburg, OR 97470

title: Triple Oak Vineyard
imageAlt: Triple Oak tasting room in Oakland

banner.alt: Triple Oak tasting room in Oakland

contentHtml:
Triple Oak Vineyard was planted in 2000 by Paul and Betty Tamm outside Oakland, making wine commercially since 2005, with labels celebrating the wildlife of the surrounding oak woodland. The house Tempranillo and Pinot Noir lead, with small releases of whites, rosé and blends.

The wines are poured at the Triple Oak Wine Vault, now Triple Oak Wine & Coffee, in a restored historic bank building in downtown Oakland, which also serves coffee and pastries and pours other Umpqua Valley wines.

address: 137 NW Locust St, Oakland, OR 97462

title: Whitetail Ridge Vineyard
contentHtml:
Whitetail Ridge Vineyard is a small, mountaintop boutique winery, vineyard and farm overlooking the Umpqua Valley nearly 1,000 feet below. First planted in 2010, with its first bottling in 2014, it now has 10 acres of grapes, hand-picked and processed the same day.

Its 'Wines of Elevation' include Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec, Merlot, Syrah, Riesling, Viognier and Grüner Veltliner. A cottage on the property is available to rent.
excerpt: Whitetail Ridge Vineyard is a small, mountaintop boutique winery, vineyard and farm overlooking the Umpqua Valley nearly 1,000 feet below. First planted in 2010
note: Tastings by appointment, Monday - Saturday; call to schedule.
address: 5920 Flournoy Valley Rd, Roseburg, OR 97471

title: Bicentennial Park
contentHtml:
Bicentennial Park has a free, moderate 10-hole course established in 2017, about a mile long on hilly, mixed- use park ground, with concrete and wood-chip tees and Mach V baskets. A 20-hole, par 60 layout plays to 4,083 feet, and one hole has an island green.

Local players hold random-flip doubles on Sundays at 2:00 and a singles league on Tuesdays at 5:30.
excerpt: Bicentennial Park has a free, moderate 10-hole course established in 2017, about a mile long on hilly, mixed- use park ground, with concrete and wood-chip tees
note: Free. Restrooms; no drinking water. Dogs allowed.
address: Bicentennial Park, Reedsport, OR

title: Glendale City Park
contentHtml:
Glendale City Park has a free, short, technical 18-hole, par 54 course of about 2,800 feet on wooded, hilly ground, established in 2010.

Tees are small rubber mats, and the custom chain-and-steel baskets are thought to have been made from scraps at the old lumber mill.
excerpt: Glendale City Park has a free, short, technical 18-hole, par 54 course of about 2,800 feet on wooded, hilly ground, established in 2010.
note: Free.
address: Glendale City Park, Glendale, OR

title: Lawson Bar
contentHtml:
Lawson Bar is an 11-hole course established in 1989, with some rough fairways along an old river bed, rolling terrain and a mix of trees and open ground. There are three sets of natural tees (red, white and blue) and tone-pole targets.

Take I-5 exit 102, go west about 100 feet, turn left on Lawson Bar Rd and drive about half a mile to the first tee on the right by the Lawson Bar sign.
excerpt: Lawson Bar is an 11-hole course established in 1989, with some rough fairways along an old river bed, rolling terrain and a mix of trees and open ground. There
note: A private course on private property, still a work in progress; check access before playing. No facilities or tee signs. Camping available.
address: Lawson Bar Rd, Riddle, OR 97457

title: Millsite Park
contentHtml:
Millsite Park has a free, moderate 9-hole, par 27 course of about 3,100 feet, established in 2014. The mostly flat holes run from about 270 to 410 feet, with concrete tees and Mach III baskets in several positions on each hole.

It is cart friendly.
excerpt: Millsite Park has a free, moderate 9-hole, par 27 course of about 3,100 feet, established in 2014. The mostly flat holes run from about 270 to 410 feet, with co
note: Free. Dogs allowed.
address: Back of Millsite Park, behind the railroad tracks by the RV area, Myrtle Creek, OR

title: Oakland DGC
contentHtml:
The Oakland Disc Golf Course is a free 9-hole, par 27 course of about 2,600 feet, established in 2015, set between two hills on very hilly ground. Holes run from 139 to 412 feet, with rubber mat tees and Mach III baskets.

It is in Mildred Kanipe City Park in town, not Mildred Kanipe County Park five miles northeast of Oakland.
excerpt: The Oakland Disc Golf Course is a free 9-hole, par 27 course of about 2,600 feet, established in 2015, set between two hills on very hilly ground. Holes run fro
note: Free.
address: Mildred Kanipe City Park, Oakland, OR

title: Riverfront Park
contentHtml:
Riverfront Park has a free, hilly 18-hole, par 54 course of about 4,600 feet, established in 1993, with concrete, paver and dirt tees and Prodigy T2 and Mach III baskets.

The mixed-use public park is cart and stroller friendly; avoid the hill between holes 2 and 3 with a stroller.
excerpt: Riverfront Park has a free, hilly 18-hole, par 54 course of about 4,600 feet, established in 1993, with concrete, paver and dirt tees and Prodigy T2 and Mach II
note: Free. Restrooms; no drinking water. Dogs allowed. Not recommended for limited mobility.
address: Riverfront Park, Roseburg, OR

title: Whistler's Bend County Park
imageAlt: Hole 15 long tee, the 'Edge of the World'

banner.alt: Hole 15 long tee, the 'Edge of the World'

contentHtml:
Whistler's Bend has a free 27-hole course, established in 1991 and rated 4.7 out of 5 by more than 1,900 players. The main layout is par 82 and about 8,500 feet over extremely hilly woods and rolling meadows, with the North Umpqua River wrapping around most of the park.

Tees are concrete with ChainStar baskets, and seven layouts are available. The park also has camping.
excerpt: Whistler's Bend has a free 27-hole course, established in 1991 and rated 4.7 out of 5 by more than 1,900 players. The main layout is par 82 and about 8,500 feet
note: Free. Restrooms; no drinking water. Dogs allowed. Not cart or stroller friendly. Road access may be behind a locked gate with restricted hours; check before you go.
address: Whistler's Bend County Park, northeast of Roseburg, OR

title: Gilliam County Historical Museum
contentHtml:
The Gilliam County Historical Museum is a complex of century-old buildings on Highway 19 next to Burns Park in Condon, including an 1884 homestead, a 1905 railroad depot, an authentic one-room schoolhouse, a church, agricultural exhibits and a building that was once a brothel and later a barbershop.

Its collections remember the pioneers whose wagons crossed the county on the Oregon Trail, and past residents including Tonight Show musician Doc Severinsen and Nobel Prize winners Linus Pauling and William Murphy.
excerpt: The Gilliam County Historical Museum is a complex of century-old buildings on Highway 19 next to Burns Park in Condon, including an 1884 homestead, a 1905 railr
note: Seasonal, May 1 to October 31.
address: 221 S Oregon St, Condon, OR 97823

title: John Day Crossing Historic Site
imageAlt: Sunset at the John Day Crossing Historic Site

banner.alt: Sunset at the John Day Crossing Historic Site

gallery.alt: The Oregon Trail's hillside descent to the crossing

contentHtml:
John Day Crossing Historic Site marks where two branches of the Oregon Trail met at the lower John Day River. White markers on the hillside show where the wagon routes descended, and an interpretive site about a quarter mile up the road overlooks the crossing. Emigrants who came down one branch reportedly joked that the other 'could not be worse than the one they descended.'

A small primitive campsite sits in a cottonwood grove, with picnic tables and a vault toilet, and a primitive boat launch is the last public takeout on the John Day Wild and Scenic River above Tumwater Falls.
excerpt: John Day Crossing Historic Site marks where two branches of the Oregon Trail met at the lower John Day River. White markers on the hillside show where the wagon
note: No fee; 14-day stay limit. No drinking water or garbage service; pack out trash. Fire closure June 1 to October 15. The last 2 miles of McDonald Ferry Rd are unmaintained and impassable when wet. From Arlington, take OR 19 south 6.7 miles, right on Cedar Springs Ln 9.2 miles, right on Lower Rock Creek Ln 5.5 miles, then right on McDonald Ferry Rd 2 miles.
address: End of McDonald Ferry Rd, east bank of the lower John Day River, OR

title: Thirtymile Recreation Area
contentHtml:
The Thirtymile Recreation Area is about 20,000 acres of BLM land on the east side of the John Day River, taking in parts of Armstrong Canyon, Thirtymile Creek and the river. It was acquired in 2018-19.

A primitive boat ramp just upriver from the mouth of Thirtymile Creek has trailer parking and a boating kiosk, and dispersed camping is allowed in the cleared field near the launch until a campground is built. Foot, bike and horse access continues up the old roads and Thirtymile Creek.
excerpt: The Thirtymile Recreation Area is about 20,000 acres of BLM land on the east side of the John Day River, taking in parts of Armstrong Canyon, Thirtymile Creek a
note: No fee. Armstrong Rd is unimproved dirt and rock, open to vehicles April 1 to December 14; high clearance recommended, and it can be impassable when wet. No toilet, drinking water, trash or cell service; pack out all waste. No campfires June 1 to October 15. A launch permit from Recreation.gov is required year-round to boat between Service Creek and Tumwater Falls.
address: End of Armstrong Rd at the John Day River, about 10 miles southwest of Condon, OR
photoCredit: Greg Shine, Bureau of Land Management

title: Willow Creek Wildlife Area
contentHtml:
Willow Creek Wildlife Area protects 646 acres at the mouth of Willow Creek on the Columbia River, one of four ODFW wildlife areas in the Columbia Basin. Its wetland, sagebrush-steppe and grassland habitat draws white pelicans, black-crowned night herons, great egrets, waterfowl, shorebirds, songbirds and California quail.

Visitors can fish, hunt, launch a boat and explore on foot from the parking lot.
excerpt: Willow Creek Wildlife Area protects 646 acres at the mouth of Willow Creek on the Columbia River, one of four ODFW wildlife areas in the Columbia Basin. Its wet
note: An ODFW Wildlife Area Parking Permit is required ($10/day, $30/year). No camping or open fires. From exit 151, head south on Threemile Canyon Rd about half a mile and turn right at the wildlife area sign; traffic passes a private-land security checkpoint, so say you are going to the wildlife area and follow the signed route.
address: I-84 exit 151, Threemile Canyon Rd, between Arlington and Boardman, OR

title: Northwest Discovery Water Trail
imageAlt: Earl Snell Memorial Park on the Columbia in Arlington (area photo)

banner.alt: Earl Snell Memorial Park on the Columbia in Arlington (area photo)

contentHtml:
The Northwest Discovery Water Trail is a 367-mile boating route from Canoe Camp on the Clearwater River in Idaho, down the Snake River and the Columbia to Bonneville Dam in the Columbia River Gorge. More than 150 sites along the way are for launching, picnicking or camping, for motorboats, canoes, sailboats and kayaks.

In Oregon it follows the Columbia's south shore through Umatilla, Morrow, Gilliam, Sherman, Wasco, Hood River and Multnomah counties. Much of it is flatwater behind eight dams, with locks to pass through or portage around.
excerpt: The Northwest Discovery Water Trail is a 367-mile boating route from Canoe Camp on the Clearwater River in Idaho, down the Snake River and the Columbia to Bonne
note: Always wear a life jacket. Check forecasts for high winds and storms, yield to commercial barges and their wakes, and watch for submerged stumps and debris. Plan each dam lock-through or portage before you go.
address: Columbia River south shore, including Arlington, OR

title: Unnamed Gilliam Co. High Point
contentHtml: Gilliam County's high point is an unnamed summit of 4,285 feet (1,306 m) on the South Columbia Plateau.
excerpt: Gilliam County's high point is an unnamed summit of 4,285 feet (1,306 m) on the South Columbia Plateau.
address: Southeastern Gilliam County, OR

title: Lost Valley of Condon
imageAlt: On the Lost Valley of Condon route

banner.alt: On the Lost Valley of Condon route

contentHtml:
Lost Valley of Condon is a 44-mile loop of about 60% gravel and dirt with about 3,500 feet of climbing, past farm fields, basalt canyons and cottonwoods. It heads south on a paved downhill past tall basalt cliffs, then climbs onto the plateaus to its high point near the southern tip.

Late spring brings green hills and late fall brings orange, yellow and taupe colors. The loop can be ridden in either direction.
excerpt: Lost Valley of Condon is a 44-mile loop of about 60% gravel and dirt with about 3,500 feet of climbing, past farm fields, basalt canyons and cottonwoods. It hea
note: Not fully vetted by Dirty Freehub. Little shade, so start early in summer, and expect wind on the final climb into Condon. Light ranch traffic; a red blinking light is recommended. 40 mm tires or wider are suggested.
address: Main St near Hotel Condon, Condon, OR

title: John Day River
contentHtml:
The John Day River is the longest undammed river in Oregon. Its 147.5-mile recreational section from Service Creek to Tumwater Falls was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, running through colorful canyons, broad valleys and high desert, with basalt cliffs over 1,000 feet high.

It holds one of the region's few remaining wild runs of summer steelhead and spring Chinook, plus prime smallmouth bass water, and the Oregon Trail crossed it at McDonald Ford. Boating is mostly calm with a few rapids; the corridor also offers camping, swimming and wildlife watching, including bald and golden eagles, bighorn sheep and elk.
excerpt: The John Day River is the longest undammed river in Oregon. Its 147.5-mile recreational section from Service Creek to Tumwater Falls was designated a Wild and S
note: A launch permit from Recreation.gov is required year-round to boat between Service Creek and Tumwater Falls. Managed by the BLM Prineville District.

photoCredit: Greg Shine, Bureau of Land Management

title: John Day River Farm Trail
contentHtml:
The John Day River Farm Trail is a food-focused drive along the John Day River, where small valleys hold lush grass, alfalfa, gardens and fruit orchards. More than 30 stops run from John Day through Kimberly, Spray, Fossil and Condon to Arlington: farms and orchards, farmers markets, breweries, ranch stays, outfitters and museums.

In Gilliam County, stops include the Gilliam County Museum, the Condon Community Summer Concert and Artisan Market, Cottonwood Canyon State Park and the Arlington Farmers Market.

note: Check each stop's hours before visiting; a couple of listed stops have closed.
address: Along OR 19, OR 402 and OR 206, from John Day to Arlington, OR
photoCredit: Alex Jordan / Eastern Oregon Visitors Association

title: Lonerock
contentHtml:
Lonerock, about 20 miles east of Condon, is one of the smallest incorporated cities in Oregon, with 25 residents at the 2020 census. It is named for a 35-foot rock that still stands beside the old Methodist church.

Platted in 1882 as Lone Rock, a service center for nearby ranches, it became one word because the post office preferred one-word names. It once had a jail, a school and a rodeo on Main Street, peaked at 82 residents in 1930 and never unincorporated. The white Methodist church, built in 1898, still stands and occasionally holds services.

title: Condon Wind Farm Viewpoint
imageAlt: Wind turbines above yellow fields near Arlington (area photo)

banner.alt: Wind turbines above yellow fields near Arlington (area photo)

contentHtml:
The Condon Wind Farm Viewpoint is a signed pullout on OR 206 just northwest of Condon, facing east to watch the turbines turn on the plateau skyline. Shepherds Flat, among the largest wind farms in the world, spreads across the Morrow County line northeast of town, with turbines rising more than 250 feet above the rangeland.

It is the nearer of two wind-farm viewpoints on the Condon highway.

address: OR 206, just northwest of Condon, OR

title: Wind Farm Viewpoint
imageAlt: Wind turbines above yellow fields near Arlington (area photo)

banner.alt: Wind turbines above yellow fields near Arlington (area photo)

contentHtml:
Wind Farm Viewpoint is the farther of two signed wind-farm viewpoints on OR 206 west of Condon. It carries a peak-identification board naming the Cascade peaks on the western skyline, with the plateau's turbines turning in the foreground.

Its companion, the Condon Wind Farm Viewpoint, is closer to town on the same highway.
excerpt: Wind Farm Viewpoint is the farther of two signed wind-farm viewpoints on OR 206 west of Condon. It carries a peak-identification board naming the Cascade peaks
address: OR 206, west of Condon, OR

title: Harney County Historical Museum
contentHtml: The Harney County Historical Museum in Burns is run by the Harney County Historical Society, whose mission is to promote the preservation and restoration of Harney County history.
excerpt: The Harney County Historical Museum in Burns is run by the Harney County Historical Society, whose mission is to promote the preservation and restoration of Har
note: Open from the first week of April through the last weekend of September; visits outside these hours by appointment.

title: George M. Benson Memorial Museum
imageAlt: Malheur National Wildlife Refuge at sunset (area photo)

banner.alt: Malheur National Wildlife Refuge at sunset (area photo)

contentHtml:
The George M. Benson Memorial Museum, inside the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge headquarters, displays nearly 200 mounted bird specimens in habitat dioramas and a large bird-egg collection, the life's work of George Benson, the refuge's warden from 1918.

The museum was dedicated to him in 1953 and is maintained by the Friends of Malheur NWR.
excerpt: The George M. Benson Memorial Museum, inside the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge headquarters, displays nearly 200 mounted bird specimens in habitat dioramas a
note: Free. The museum is open sunrise to sunset year-round; the visitor center and nature store keep shorter hours.
address: Malheur National Wildlife Refuge headquarters, 36391 Sodhouse Ln, Princeton, OR

title: Oard's Gallery & Museum
contentHtml:
Oard's Museum & Gallery is a free museum of Native American art about 23 miles east of Burns at the northern end of the Great Harney Basin, in a family business run for three generations. It grew from the family's own collection of Indian antiques, dishes, furnishings, clocks and dolls.

It shows art from nine tribes: pottery, jewelry, ceremonial sand paintings, scrimshaw, Navajo rugs and crafts from Southwest, Midwest and local Paiute tribes, including a noted collection of Paiute cradleboards.
excerpt: Oard's Museum & Gallery is a free museum of Native American art about 23 miles east of Burns at the northern end of the Great Harney Basin, in a family business
note: Free admission.
address: 42456 Hwy 20 East, Burns, OR 97720

title: Riddle Brothers Ranch

gallery.alt: Inside the Frederick Riddle ranch house

contentHtml:
The Riddle Brothers Ranch National Historic District is a preserved ranch on the Little Blitzen River, built by three bachelor brothers, Walter, Frederick and Benjamin Riddle, who came from western Oregon and built the ranch by gaining control of the area's water. They sold it in the late 1950s, and the BLM bought it in 1986.

Visitors can see Fred Riddle's house, which they may enter, the bunkhouse, blacksmith shop and corrals, a glimpse of ranch life on Oregon's last frontier.

note: No fee. Vault toilet; no drinking water, overnight use or cell service. High-clearance, four-wheel-drive vehicles recommended. From Burns, take OR 78 southeast about 2 miles, turn right on OR 205 and go 60 miles south to Frenchglen. Continue up 'P' Hill about 10 miles to the Steens Mountain Loop Road south entrance; the turnoff is about 20 miles from OR 205.
address: Off the Steens Mountain Loop Road (south entrance), on the Little Blitzen River, OR

title: Malheur National Forest
contentHtml:
The Malheur National Forest covers 1.7 million acres of the Blue Mountains in eastern Oregon, from high desert grasslands of sage and juniper to pine and fir forests, hidden alpine lakes and meadows. Elevations run from 4,000 feet to 9,038 feet at Strawberry Mountain, whose range runs through the center of the forest.

The forest holds 88,350 acres of wilderness and the headwaters of the John Day River, the only tributary of the Columbia with no dams. The Malheur and Silvies rivers have Wild and Scenic stretches, and four former guard stations and a lookout can be rented for overnight stays.
excerpt: The Malheur National Forest covers 1.7 million acres of the Blue Mountains in eastern Oregon, from high desert grasslands of sage and juniper to pine and fir fo
note: Check forest alerts and closures before visiting

title: Ochoco National Forest
contentHtml:
The Ochoco National Forest and Crooked River National Grassland cover nearly one million acres of Central Oregon, a landscape of forests, grasslands and rocky river canyons. The Ochoco Mountains rise east of Prineville, with ponderosa pine forest, volcanic spires such as Steins Pillar and Twin Pillars, and the Mill Creek Wilderness.

Visitors come for hiking, camping, horseback riding, fishing at Walton Lake, rockhounding at the forest's agate beds, and winter snow play at the sno-parks along Highway 26.
excerpt: The Ochoco National Forest and Crooked River National Grassland cover nearly one million acres of Central Oregon, a landscape of forests, grasslands and rocky r
note: Winter range closures December 1 - May 1 prohibit motorized vehicles in some areas to protect deer and elk. Supervisor's Office open Monday - Friday 8:00 AM - 4:30 PM.
address: Supervisor's Office: 3160 NE 3rd St, Prineville, OR 97754

title: Steens Mountain Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Steens Mountain Wilderness, designated in 2000, covers about 170,000 acres of a 70-mile fault block rising over 9,000 feet, with deep glacier-carved gorges, the Donner und Blitzen Wild and Scenic River and an alpine lake. Nearly 99,000 acres of the wilderness are free of cattle.

Deer, elk, pronghorn, wild horses and redband trout live here. Visitors come for camping, hiking, horseback riding, photography, trout fishing, hunting, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing.
excerpt: The Steens Mountain Wilderness, designated in 2000, covers about 170,000 acres of a 70-mile fault block rising over 9,000 feet, with deep glacier-carved gorges,
note: High-clearance or 4x4 vehicles recommended on primitive roads. Snow can fall any month and weather changes quickly. Fuel in Fields, Frenchglen, Crane or the Narrows. From Burns, take OR 78 southeast about 2 miles, turn right on OR 205 and go 60 miles south to Frenchglen. Turn left just past Frenchglen onto the Steens Mountain Loop Road.
address: Steens Mountain Loop Road, east of Frenchglen, OR

title: Chickahominy Recreation Site
imageAlt: Chickahominy Recreation Site on a summer afternoon

banner.alt: Chickahominy Recreation Site on a summer afternoon

contentHtml:
Chickahominy Recreation Site sits on Chickahominy Reservoir, a popular eastern Oregon fishery stocked with rainbow trout since 1967, ringed by foothills, buttes and high-desert ridges. Mule deer, pronghorn, jackrabbits, waterfowl and raptors are often seen.

There are 28 campsites, drinking water, vault restrooms, a fish cleaning station and a boat ramp.
excerpt: Chickahominy Recreation Site sits on Chickahominy Reservoir, a popular eastern Oregon fishery stocked with rainbow trout since 1967, ringed by foothills, buttes
note: $16 per vehicle per night, $5 per extra vehicle; first come, first served, no reservations. Pay at the entrance kiosk. 14-day stay limit. Fishing peaks in June and again in September, and ice fishing is popular December to late February. Limit five trout a day, 8 inches minimum.
address: US 20 at milepost 100, about 32 miles west of Burns, OR

title: Fish Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Fish Lake Campground sits at 7,400 feet on the flanks of Steens Mountain, beside a lake stocked with trout by ODFW. It has 23 campsites with picnic tables and fire grates, an accessible restroom and drinking water.

Fishing, hiking, swimming, boating and picnicking are popular.
excerpt: Fish Lake Campground sits at 7,400 feet on the flanks of Steens Mountain, beside a lake stocked with trout by ODFW. It has 23 campsites with picnic tables and f
note: $16 per vehicle per night, $5 per extra vehicle; first come, first served, no reservations. Pay at the entrance kiosk. 14-day stay limit. From Burns, take OR 78 southeast about 2 miles, turn right on OR 205 and go 60 miles south to Frenchglen. Continue a short distance, turn left on the Steens Mountain Loop Road and go about 17 miles.
address: Steens Mountain Loop Road, about 17 miles from Frenchglen, OR

title: Jackman Park Campground
imageAlt: Fall colors and snow on Steens Mountain

banner.alt: Fall colors and snow on Steens Mountain

contentHtml:
Jackman Park Campground sits at 7,800 feet among aspen stands on Steens Mountain, with some of the best fall color on the mountain. It has six campsites with picnic tables and fire grates and an accessible restroom.

Kiger Gorge Overlook, with views of a glacier-carved U-shaped valley and sometimes wild horses, is nearby.
excerpt: Jackman Park Campground sits at 7,800 feet among aspen stands on Steens Mountain, with some of the best fall color on the mountain. It has six campsites with pi
note: $16 per vehicle per night, $5 per extra vehicle; first come, first served, no reservations. Pay at the entrance kiosk. 14-day stay limit. High-clearance vehicles recommended on parts of the loop road. Nearest services in Fields, Frenchglen, Crane or the Narrows.
address: Steens Mountain Loop Road, about 2 miles past Fish Lake, OR

title: Mann Lake Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Mann Lake Recreation Site is a remote, rugged spot below the east face of Steens Mountain. The shallow 200- acre lake, named for an early rancher, is a premier fishery for Lahontan cutthroat trout, with weed beds and good wading shorelines.

Camping, hiking, wildlife viewing (pronghorn, quail, chukar) and rockhounding for thunder eggs and agates are popular. Two vault restrooms are the only facilities.
excerpt: Mann Lake Recreation Site is a remote, rugged spot below the east face of Steens Mountain. The shallow 200- acre lake, named for an early rancher, is a premier
note: No fee; primitive camping only. Bring shade, shelter and water, and secure gear against strong winds. Limit two trout a day, 8 inches minimum, artificial flies and lures only. From Burns, take OR 78 southeast about 72 miles, then East Steens Road southwest about 23 miles.
address: Off East Steens Road, about 23 miles southwest of OR 78, OR

title: Page Springs Campground
contentHtml:
Page Springs Campground sits at the base of Steens Mountain beside the Donner und Blitzen River, shaded by cottonwood and juniper, about 3 miles from Frenchglen. It has 36 campsites, a large covered day-use picnic area, vault restrooms, trash cans and drinking water.

The Blitzen River Trail follows the river about 4 miles, and the 1-mile Wilderness Nature Trail loops up to a bluff overlooking the valley.
excerpt: Page Springs Campground sits at the base of Steens Mountain beside the Donner und Blitzen River, shaded by cottonwood and juniper, about 3 miles from Frenchglen
note: $16 per vehicle per night, $5 per extra vehicle; first come, first served, no reservations. Pay at the entrance kiosk. 14-day stay limit.
address: Steens Mountain Loop Road, about 3 miles from Frenchglen, OR

title: South Steens Campground
contentHtml:
South Steens Campground sits in the heart of Steens Mountain among juniper and sage, with 36 family sites with picnic tables and grills and, next door, 15 equestrian sites with tie posts and small corrals. Vault restrooms and drinking water are provided.

Several hiking trails, the historic Riddle Brothers Ranch and the Little Blitzen and Big Indian gorges are nearby.
excerpt: South Steens Campground sits in the heart of Steens Mountain among juniper and sage, with 36 family sites with picnic tables and grills and, next door, 15 eques
note: $16 per vehicle per night, $5 per extra vehicle; first come, first served, no reservations. Pay at the entrance kiosk. 14-day stay limit. Stock not allowed in the family area; certified weed-free hay required. From Burns, take OR 78 southeast about 2 miles, turn right on OR 205 and go 60 miles south to Frenchglen. Continue up 'P' Hill about 9 miles to the Steens Mountain Loop Road south entrance.
address: Steens Mountain Loop Road (south entrance), about 18 miles from OR 205, OR

title: Frenchglen Hotel State Heritage Site
contentHtml:
The Frenchglen Hotel State Heritage Site is a small historic hotel built around 1917 at the gateway to Steens Mountain. Oregon State Parks acquired it in 1973 to preserve the hotel and its outbuildings.

Guests stay in rustic rooms with restrooms down the hall, or in the four rooms with private baths at the Drover's Inn on the same property, and gather in the dining room and lobby.
excerpt: The Frenchglen Hotel State Heritage Site is a small historic hotel built around 1917 at the gateway to Steens Mountain. Oregon State Parks acquired it in 1973 t
note: Breakfast daily 7:30 - 9:30 AM; picnic lunch and family-style dinner by reservation. Reserve rooms through the Frenchglen Hotel and Drover's Inn website.
address: Frenchglen, OR

title: Pete French Round Barn State Heritage Site
contentHtml:
The Pete French Round Barn State Heritage Site preserves a round barn built by cattle king Peter French, used to train wild horses through the winter to pull wagon trains of wool, hay and supplies to market. French arrived in 1872 and by the mid-1880s ran about 70,000 acres and 45,000 head of cattle; a land dispute ended in his murder in 1897.

The barn, 100 feet across with an umbrella roof carried on juniper posts, is the sole survivor of three French built and Oregon's largest historic round barn. Views take in the surrounding buttes and Steens Mountain.
excerpt: The Pete French Round Barn State Heritage Site preserves a round barn built by cattle king Peter French, used to train wild horses through the winter to pull wa
address: 52229 Lava Bed Road, near Diamond, OR

title: Buck Spring Campground
contentHtml: Buck Spring Campground is a wooded campground off the beaten path at 4,900 feet, with fishing a drive away at Delintment Lake or Chickahominy Reservoir. Trailers up to 20 feet; one vault toilet.
excerpt: Buck Spring Campground is a wooded campground off the beaten path at 4,900 feet, with fishing a drive away at Delintment Lake or Chickahominy Reservoir. Trailer
note: $6 per night, $3 per extra vehicle. No drinking water and no trash service; pack out all trash. From Riley, go east on US 20 about 2.1 miles to FR 45, follow it about 14.7 miles to FR 4540, about 8.2 miles to FR 4545, then about 1 mile.
address: FR 4545, off FR 4540, east of Riley, OR

title: Delintment Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Delintment Lake Campground is a family campground on a lake, with two loops and trails and fishing along the banks. It has 29 sites (16 pull-through, 8 back-in and 5 hike-in tent sites), a group camping area, a non- motorized boat launch, a beach, a fishing pier, 12 picnic sites and vault toilets.

Lake fishing, paddling, swimming, picnicking, wildlife viewing and hiking are popular. Hosts are on site in summer.
excerpt: Delintment Lake Campground is a family campground on a lake, with two loops and trails and fishing along the banks. It has 29 sites (16 pull-through, 8 back-in
note: $10 per night, $5 per extra vehicle. Check-in 2:00 PM, check-out 12:00 PM; quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM. Pack out all trash. Blue-green algae may bloom in warm weather. From Burns, take US 20 west to Burns-Izee Road (Road 127), go about 11 miles to FR 41, then about 31 miles; paved from Burns.
address: FR 41, about 42 miles northwest of Burns, OR

title: Emigrant Campground
contentHtml: Emigrant Campground is a quiet 7-site campground shaded by large ponderosa pines along Emigrant Creek, with trout fishing and wildlife viewing. It is a short drive to the top of Snow Mountain and the Snow Mountain Fire Lookout. Trailers up to 20 feet; vault toilets.
excerpt: Emigrant Campground is a quiet 7-site campground shaded by large ponderosa pines along Emigrant Creek, with trout fishing and wildlife viewing. It is a short dr
note: Temporarily closed (Falls Fire area closure). $8 per night, $4 per extra vehicle. No drinking water. From Burns, take US 20 west to County Road 127, go about 23 miles to FR 43, about 9.9 miles to FR 4340, then 0.3 mile.
address: FR 4340 off FR 43, northwest of Burns, OR

title: Falls Campground
contentHtml: Falls Campground sits on the banks of Emigrant Creek, with trout fishing right beside camp. Its picnic area suits family outings and rarely fills. Vault toilets.
excerpt: Falls Campground sits on the banks of Emigrant Creek, with trout fishing right beside camp. Its picnic area suits family outings and rarely fills. Vault toilets
note: $8 per night, $4 per extra vehicle. Check-in 2:00 PM, check-out 12:00 PM; quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM. Pack out all trash. Drinking water only in warmer months (off October to late May or early June). From Burns, take US 20 west to County Road 127, go about 23 miles to FR 43, then about 8.5 miles; the campground road is on the left.
address: FR 43, about 31 miles from Burns, OR

title: Idlewild Campground
contentHtml:
Idlewild Campground was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s just off US 395, a quiet stop for travelers that is lightly used except in fall hunting season. Trailers up to 20 feet; vault toilets.

An open-air wooden picnic pavilion can be reserved for groups, and the area offers mountain biking, day hiking, and cross-country skiing and snowshoeing in winter.
excerpt: Idlewild Campground was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s just off US 395, a quiet stop for travelers that is lightly used except in fall hu
note: $10 per night, $5 per extra vehicle. Pavilion $25 a day plus $9 reservation fee on Recreation.gov (1- 877-444-6777). Oregon Sno-Park permit required November 1 - April 30. Check-in 2:00 PM, check-out 12:00 PM; quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM. Pack out all trash. From Burns, go 2.8 miles on US 20 to US 395, north about 14.6 miles to FR 2820, 0.8 mile, then about 1 mile on Idlewild Campground Road.
address: Off US 395, about 17 miles north of Burns, OR

title: Joaquin Miller Horse Camp
contentHtml: Joaquin Miller Horse Camp is an 8-site campground on US 395 north of Burns, designed for stock users with two pipe corrals and hitching rails. It gets light use most of the year. Trailers up to 20 feet; vault toilet.
excerpt: Joaquin Miller Horse Camp is an 8-site campground on US 395 north of Burns, designed for stock users with two pipe corrals and hitching rails. It gets light use
note: $8 per night, $4 per extra vehicle. Check-in 2:00 PM, check-out 12:00 PM; quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM. Pack out all trash. Drinking water only in warmer months. Trails nearby have had little recent maintenance; expect down logs and brush after wildfires.
address: US 395, about 19 miles north of Burns, OR

title: Tip Top Campground
contentHtml: Tip Top Campground is a small, quiet 3-site campground near Delintment Lake, recently renovated with new restrooms, picnic tables and fire rings.
excerpt: Tip Top Campground is a small, quiet 3-site campground near Delintment Lake, recently renovated with new restrooms, picnic tables and fire rings.
note: $6 per night, $3 per extra vehicle. No drinking water and no trash service; pack out all trash. From Burns, take US 20 west to Burns-Izee Road, follow it about 11.8 miles, continue on FR 41 (about 32.8 miles in all), then left on FR 800 for 0.5 mile; the last mile is unpaved.
address: FR 800 off FR 41, near Delintment Lake, OR

title: Yellowjacket Campground
contentHtml: Yellowjacket Campground is a quiet lakeside campground with a small sand beach, easy shoreline fishing, non-motorized boating and a covered group picnic area. Eagles, ospreys and pronghorn may be seen. Vault toilets.
excerpt: Yellowjacket Campground is a quiet lakeside campground with a small sand beach, easy shoreline fishing, non-motorized boating and a covered group picnic area. E
note: Closed (Falls Fire area closure). $10 per night, $5 per extra vehicle. Blue-green algae may bloom in warm weather. From Burns, take US 20 west to County Road 127/FR 47, go about 30 miles to FR 37, right about 2.3 miles, then right on FR 3745 for 1 mile.
address: FR 3745 off FR 37, Yellowjacket Lake, OR

title: Malheur
contentHtml:
Malheur National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1908, covers more than 187,000 acres of high desert at the northern end of the Great Basin, including Malheur and Harney lakes and the Blitzen Valley. The Wild and Scenic Donner und Blitzen River flows from Steens Mountain into the refuge.

A key stop on the Pacific Flyway, it hosts hundreds of thousands of migratory birds, with up to 320 species recorded, among them avocets, stilts, pelicans, ibises, sandhill cranes, ducks and grebes. Visitors come for the Blitzen Valley auto tour, hiking trails, guided tours, hunting, fishing and the historic Sod House Ranch.
excerpt: Malheur National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1908, covers more than 187,000 acres of high desert at the northern end of the Great Basin, including Malheur a
note: Free. The visitor center and nature store at headquarters are open daily 8:00 AM - 4:00 PM when staff and volunteers are available.
address: Refuge headquarters, 36391 Sodhouse Ln, Princeton, OR (about 30 miles south of Burns)

title: Steens Mountain
contentHtml:
Steens Mountain, at 9,738 feet, is the high point of Harney County and the largest fault-block mountain in North America, rising about a mile above the Alvord Desert.

In summer the gravel Steens Mountain Loop Road climbs nearly to the top, and the Steens Mountain Summit trailhead and the Wildhorse Lake trail, down into a deep cirque, start near the summit.
excerpt: Steens Mountain, at 9,738 feet, is the high point of Harney County and the largest fault-block mountain in North America, rising about a mile above the Alvord D
note: Check road reports before going; the loop road is closed in winter. Carry at least a gallon of water per day and expect snow or intense heat. Best July through October.
address: Steens Mountain Summit trailhead, Steens Mountain Loop Road, OR

title: Oregon Desert Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Desert Trail is a 750-mile route across Oregon's high desert, from outside Bend to Lake Owyhee State Park, developed by the Oregon Natural Desert Association. It stitches together existing trails, old jeep tracks and historic wagon roads with long stretches of cross-country travel on public land.

It crosses the Oregon Badlands Wilderness, Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, the Steens Mountain Wilderness, the Pueblo and Trout Creek mountains and the Owyhee Canyonlands. All sections can be hiked, and some are open to horses, boats, bikes or skis.
excerpt: The Oregon Desert Trail is a 750-mile route across Oregon's high desert, from outside Bend to Lake Owyhee State Park, developed by the Oregon Natural Desert Ass
note: Water is very limited; careful water planning is essential.
address: Crosses Steens Mountain and the Alvord Desert in Harney County

title: Big Bird
imageAlt: Riding gravel at the Malheur refuge

banner.alt: Riding gravel at the Malheur refuge

gallery.alt: Crossing the Donner und Blitzen River

contentHtml:
Big Bird is a 24-mile all-gravel loop from the Malheur refuge visitor center, rated moderate with about 400 feet of gain. It starts on Big Bird Road, a ranch road that grows rougher and narrower through open cattle land, then returns on a straight refuge road with water on both sides.

Highlights include Steens Mountain views, pronghorn, eagles and hawks, the Donner und Blitzen River crossing, Rattlesnake Butte and Malheur Lake birdlife, with an optional longer route past the Malheur Field Station and Sod House Ranch.
excerpt: Big Bird is a 24-mile all-gravel loop from the Malheur refuge visitor center, rated moderate with about 400 feet of gain. It starts on Big Bird Road, a ranch ro
note: Phone is the refuge, for road conditions. No water on the route. Best spring to early summer, peaking mid-May to mid-June for birds. Center Patrol Road can be badly washboarded; tires 50 mm or wider suggested; bring bug spray.
address: Start: Malheur National Wildlife Refuge Visitor Center, OR

title: Bird Nerd
imageAlt: Riding gravel in the Malheur refuge

banner.alt: Riding gravel in the Malheur refuge

gallery.alt: Kiger Gorge from Buena Vista Overlook

contentHtml:
Bird Nerd is a 41-mile ride (90% gravel) south through the Malheur refuge, rated easier with about 400 feet of gain. It runs past ponds, canals and wetlands, crossing the Blitzen River several times, climbs briefly to Buena Vista Overlook with views toward Kiger Gorge, and returns on pavement.

Highlights include Malheur Lake, Rattlesnake Butte, Steens Mountain views and an optional detour to Sod House Ranch. Shorter 22-mile and 16-mile options are mapped.
excerpt: Bird Nerd is a 41-mile ride (90% gravel) south through the Malheur refuge, rated easier with about 400 feet of gain. It runs past ponds, canals and wetlands, cr
note: Phone is the refuge, for road conditions. No water on the route. Go early to beat strong winds; expect mosquitoes in birding season. Best spring to early summer.
address: Start: Malheur National Wildlife Refuge Visitor Center, OR

title: Egypt Canyon
contentHtml:
Egypt Canyon is a 44-mile loop (65% gravel) north of Riley, rated moderate with about 1,900 feet of gain. It follows paved Silver Creek Road, then gravel through Egypt Canyon and Dick Miller Canyon around Dry Mountain, past Silver Creek wetlands, ponderosa and juniper forest, limestone formations and open pasture.

A 36-mile shorter option is mapped.
excerpt: Egypt Canyon is a 44-mile loop (65% gravel) north of Riley, rated moderate with about 1,900 feet of gain. It follows paved Silver Creek Road, then gravel throug
note: No services. Rough gravel with shale and washboard; watch for rattlesnakes; poor cell coverage. Best mid-spring to mid-summer. The route was affected by the 2026 Egypt Canyon fire; check current closures.
address: Start: Miller Canyon Rd at Silver Creek Rd, about 1.6 miles north of US 20 near Riley, OR

title: Giants Throwing Stones
contentHtml: Giants Throwing Stones is a demanding 57-mile loop (60% gravel) with about 3,000 feet of gain. It follows Silver Creek and Sawmill Creek, crosses Corral Ridge among scattered boulders, runs about 21 miles of single- lane pavement on NF 41 past Delintment Lake through ponderosa and juniper, and returns through Egypt Canyon.
excerpt: Giants Throwing Stones is a demanding 57-mile loop (60% gravel) with about 3,000 feet of gain. It follows Silver Creek and Sawmill Creek, crosses Corral Ridge a
note: No services at the start; seasonal water at Delintment Lake Campground (about mile 24.5). Expect washboard on the gravel. Best mid-spring to early summer. The route was affected by 2026 fires; check current closures.
address: Start: Silver Creek Rd where pavement turns to gravel, south of Delintment Lake, OR

title: Happy Valley
contentHtml:
Happy Valley is a 44-mile lollipop ride (65% paved), rated easier with about 1,500 feet of gain. It passes through Diamond Craters Outstanding Natural Area, then follows Happy Valley Road past hay farms with Steens Mountain in the distance and crosses the Kiger Mustang viewing road, finishing with a downhill into Diamond.

Side trips reach the Pete French Round Barn and the historic Hotel Diamond, built in 1898. A shorter version starting at Hotel Diamond cuts about 13 miles.
excerpt: Happy Valley is a 44-mile lollipop ride (65% paved), rated easier with about 1,500 feet of gain. It passes through Diamond Craters Outstanding Natural Area, the
note: No food or water on the route; Hotel Diamond is closed November to the end of March. Best spring through fall.
address: Start: OR 205 at Diamond Lane, OR

title: Pink Lady
contentHtml:
Pink Lady is a remote 32-mile all-gravel loop, rated moderate with about 1,400 feet of gain. It follows Silver Creek and then Nicoll Creek for about 10 miles through canyon, rangeland and ponderosa forest, passes Buck Spring Campground, and descends along Dairy Creek through wetlands back to the start.

Highlights include rocky canyons, the meadows at Gravelly Flat, moss-draped pines and views of Dry Mountain.
excerpt: Pink Lady is a remote 32-mile all-gravel loop, rated moderate with about 1,400 feet of gain. It follows Silver Creek and then Nicoll Creek for about 10 miles th
note: No food or water. Rough roads with shale and washboard; 50 mm tubeless tires suggested. Best mid- spring to mid-summer.
address: Start: Silver Creek Rd where pavement turns to gravel, west of Riley, OR

title: Steens Mountain Loop Road
contentHtml:
The Steens Mountain Loop Road ride is a 72-mile loop (85% gravel) from Frenchglen, rated moderate, climbing steadily to about 9,700 feet near the summit of Steens Mountain, then descending about 4,100 feet on gravel and returning on OR 205.

Optional viewpoints include Kiger Gorge, the East Rim and the true summit with views of Wildhorse Lake and the Alvord Desert. Kiger mustangs, pronghorn and birds of prey may be seen.
excerpt: The Steens Mountain Loop Road ride is a 72-mile loop (85% gravel) from Frenchglen, rated moderate, climbing steadily to about 9,700 feet near the summit of Stee
note: Phone is the BLM Burns District, for road status. Water at Fish Lake (mile 16.5), Jackman Park (mile 18.5) and South Steens (mile 43) campgrounds. The road usually opens in early July and stays open until November. Little shade; the summit can be about 15°F cooler; no cell service on the back side.
address: Start: Frenchglen Hotel, Frenchglen, OR

title: Donner und Blitzen River
contentHtml:
The Donner und Blitzen River flows from Steens Mountain to the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge through glaciated canyons and marshland, with an exceptional wild trout fishery. Its name is German for 'thunder and lightning,' after a storm soldiers met while crossing it.

It was designated Wild and Scenic in 1988, with tributaries added in 2000, for 87.5 wild miles including the Little Blitzen and South Fork Blitzen rivers and several creeks. The Blitzen River Trail follows it from Page Springs Campground.
excerpt: The Donner und Blitzen River flows from Steens Mountain to the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge through glaciated canyons and marshland, with an exceptional wil
note: Managed by the BLM Burns District.
address: Page Springs Campground, near Frenchglen, OR

title: Wildhorse & Kiger Creeks
contentHtml:
Wildhorse, Little Wildhorse and Kiger creeks were designated Wild and Scenic in 2000, for 13.9 wild miles. Wildhorse and Little Wildhorse creeks flow from high lakes on Steens Mountain through canyons on the east face to the Alvord Valley, while Kiger Creek runs through glacier-carved Kiger Gorge toward the Malheur refuge.

The creeks support redband trout, bighorn sheep, elk and mule deer, with hiking, primitive camping, fishing and sightseeing.
excerpt: Wildhorse, Little Wildhorse and Kiger creeks were designated Wild and Scenic in 2000, for 13.9 wild miles. Wildhorse and Little Wildhorse creeks flow from high
note: Managed by the BLM Burns District.
address: Wildhorse Lake Overlook, Steens Mountain Loop Road, OR

title: Diamond Loop Tour Route
imageAlt: Peter French Round Barn, on the route

banner.alt: Peter French Round Barn, on the route

contentHtml:
The Diamond Loop Tour Route is a 69-mile drive of 3 to 5 hours. It heads east from OR 205 through the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge and Diamond Swamp, turns north on Lava Beds Road through Diamond Craters, with its craters, lava domes and tubes, and reaches the Peter French Round Barn about 3 miles beyond.

Return through the ranching town of Diamond to OR 205, or continue north through New Princeton to Crane to join the East Steens Tour Route. The Round Barn Visitor Center sits at the barn entrance.
excerpt: The Diamond Loop Tour Route is a 69-mile drive of 3 to 5 hours. It heads east from OR 205 through the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge and Diamond Swamp, turns
note: Best spring through fall.
address: Loop from OR 205 via Diamond Craters and Diamond, OR

title: East Steens Tour Route
contentHtml:
The East Steens Tour Route is a 143-mile drive of 4 to 7 hours from Fields, with its stone roadhouse dating to 1881, north past the Alvord Desert playa below Steens Mountain to Alvord Hot Springs, Mann Lake and Ten Cent Lake, then west on OR 78 past Crystal Crane Hot Springs to Burns.

Pronghorn are often seen, and Crane Union High School is one of the few public boarding schools in the Lower 48. Combine it with the High Desert Discovery Scenic Byway for a loop.
excerpt: The East Steens Tour Route is a 143-mile drive of 4 to 7 hours from Fields, with its stone roadhouse dating to 1881, north past the Alvord Desert playa below St
note: Fields-Denio Road is gravel and dirt, maintained for passenger cars. Supplies in Fields and full services in Burns. Best spring through fall.
address: Fields to Burns via Fields-Denio Road, East Steens Road and OR 78, OR

title: High Desert Discovery Scenic Byway
contentHtml:
The High Desert Discovery Scenic Byway runs 127 miles, 5 to 7 hours, from Burns south on OR 205 past the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge and Frenchglen, through Catlow Valley and over Long Hollow Summit to Fields. From Fields, the East Steens Tour Route loops back north to Burns.

Highlights include Steens Mountain, Diamond Craters, the refuge, the Peter French Round Barn, the Alvord Desert, the historic Frenchglen Hotel, Alvord Hot Springs, The Narrows between Malheur and Harney lakes, and redband trout fishing on the Donner und Blitzen River.
excerpt: The High Desert Discovery Scenic Byway runs 127 miles, 5 to 7 hours, from Burns south on OR 205 past the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge and Frenchglen, throug
note: Services are few and far between: lodging and meals in Frenchglen; food, gas and lodging in Fields. Passable year-round; best late spring through fall.
address: Burns to Fields via OR 205, OR

title: Steens Loop Tour Route
contentHtml:
The Steens Loop Tour Route is a 59-mile loop from Frenchglen to the top of Steens Mountain, near 10,000 feet, taking at least 3 to 5 hours. The East Rim overlook drops nearly a vertical mile to the Alvord Desert, and Kiger Gorge overlook sits at the head of a glacier-carved U-shaped canyon.

Bighorn sheep, pronghorn, mule deer, elk, golden eagles and the South Steens wild horse herd may be seen as the landscape climbs from sagebrush to juniper, aspen and mountain mahogany.
excerpt: The Steens Loop Tour Route is a 59-mile loop from Frenchglen to the top of Steens Mountain, near 10,000 feet, taking at least 3 to 5 hours. The East Rim overloo
note: Closed in winter; best July through October.
address: Steens Mountain Loop Road from Frenchglen, OR

title: Lakeview to Steens Mountain Back Country Byway
imageAlt: A paved stretch of the byway

banner.alt: A paved stretch of the byway

contentHtml:
The Lakeview to Steens Back Country Byway runs about 90 miles from OR 140 north of Lakeview across the Warner Mountains, Warner Valley and Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge to OR 205 south of Frenchglen. About 40 miles are paved and 50 graveled, suitable for passenger cars.

Highlights include waterfowl in the Warner Wetlands, rare lunate sand dunes, pronghorn, bighorn sheep, mule deer and golden eagles on Hart Mountain, and views east to Steens Mountain.
excerpt: The Lakeview to Steens Back Country Byway runs about 90 miles from OR 140 north of Lakeview across the Warner Mountains, Warner Valley and Hart Mountain Nationa
note: No fees; dispersed camping, 14-day limit. Winter storms can close the road briefly; refuge roads are primitive. Fuel and food only in Lakeview and Adel.
address: OR 140 north of Lakeview to OR 205 south of Frenchglen, via Plush, OR

title: Idlewild
contentHtml: Idlewild Sno-Park, about 15 miles north of Burns, is a day-use winter area for snowmobiling, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. It has a vault toilet.
excerpt: Idlewild Sno-Park, about 15 miles north of Burns, is a day-use winter area for snowmobiling, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. It has a vault toilet.
note: An Oregon Sno-Park permit is required November 1 - April 30 ($4 per day, $9 for three consecutive days, $25 annual). Pack out all trash.
address: US 395, about 15 miles north of Burns, OR

title: Alvord Hot Springs
contentHtml:
Alvord Hot Springs is a family-owned hot springs at the east base of Steens Mountain on the edge of the Alvord Desert. Twin concrete soaking pools date to the 1940s, fed by water that emerges at about 170°F and cools as it mixes into the pools.

There are bunkhouses sleeping up to four, campsites for tents and RVs (no hookups), a small store and restrooms, with caretakers on site.
excerpt: Alvord Hot Springs is a family-owned hot springs at the east base of Steens Mountain on the edge of the Alvord Desert. Twin concrete soaking pools date to the 1
note: Day visitors welcome during business hours; call ahead. Overnight guests can soak at any hour. Reservations recommended for lodging. Check in at the office for the lakebed gate code.
address: 36095 E Steens Road, Princeton, OR 97721

title: Crystal Crane Hot Springs
contentHtml:
Crane Hot Springs is a soaking resort in the high desert of Harney County. Its large spring-fed pond, about 5 feet deep in the center, averages around 101°F, and private cedar bathhouses have tubs with adjustable natural hot water.

Lodging includes teepees, a sheepherder's wagon, suites, cabins and inns, plus RV sites and dry camping.
excerpt: Crane Hot Springs is a soaking resort in the high desert of Harney County. Its large spring-fed pond, about 5 feet deep in the center, averages around 101°F, an
note: Day use needs no reservation. Overnight guests can use the pond 24 hours. The pond is cleaned 7 - 10 AM Monday, Wednesday and Friday and stays open.
address: 59315 Hwy 78, Burns, OR

title: Mickey Hot Springs
imageAlt: Winter steam at Mickey Hot Springs

banner.alt: Winter steam at Mickey Hot Springs

contentHtml:
Mickey Hot Springs is a geothermal area at the north end of the Alvord Desert. Usually there is a clear pool 15 to 20 feet across and over 10 feet deep with near-boiling water, along with hissing steam vents, gurgling mud pots and small streams up to about 180°F. The white crust is safe-to-touch sodium borate.

Activity varies with season and rainfall.
excerpt: Mickey Hot Springs is a geothermal area at the north end of the Alvord Desert. Usually there is a clear pool 15 to 20 feet across and over 10 feet deep with nea
note: All pools are too dangerously hot for soaking; viewing only. No fee. From Burns, take OR 78 southeast about 33 miles, East Steens Road south about 21 miles, then the signed access road about 6 miles. The road can be dusty or slick clay when wet.
address: Mickey Hot Springs access road off East Steens Road, OR

title: Willow Creek Hot Springs
contentHtml:
Willow Creek Hot Springs, also called Whitehorse Ranch Hot Springs, is a remote, primitive soak on BLM land at 4,495 feet. Water at about 110°F rises through the sandy bottom of a 14-foot pool kept around 100 - 105°F, with a larger, cooler pool beside it.

Wild horses, deer, coyotes and pronghorn may be seen, and a 5-mile trail offers longer hikes.
excerpt: Willow Creek Hot Springs, also called Whitehorse Ranch Hot Springs, is a remote, primitive soak on BLM land at 4,495 feet. Water at about 110°F rises through th
note: Free. Vault toilet only. Free camping on surrounding BLM land at least 100 feet from the springs. The last 2.5 miles are dirt and can be impassable when wet. From Fields, take OR 205 south 8 miles to Whitehorse Ranch Lane, go east 23 miles, then 2.5 miles south on the dirt road.
address: Off Whitehorse Ranch Lane, about 35 miles from Fields, OR

title: Mickey Geyser
imageAlt: Winter steam at Mickey Hot Springs

banner.alt: Winter steam at Mickey Hot Springs

contentHtml: Mickey Geyser, at Mickey Hot Springs, began in 1992 when a bubbling spot became a mini-geyser, erupting 6 to 8 feet high. It is the only known active natural geyser in the continental U.S. outside Yellowstone.
excerpt: Mickey Geyser, at Mickey Hot Springs, began in 1992 when a bubbling spot became a mini-geyser, erupting 6 to 8 feet high. It is the only known active natural ge
note: Viewing only; all pools are dangerously hot. No fee. The access road can be impassable when wet.
address: Mickey Hot Springs, north end of the Alvord Desert, OR

title: Pete French Round Barn
contentHtml:
The Pete French Round Barn State Heritage Site preserves a round barn built by cattle king Peter French, used to train wild horses through the winter to pull wagon trains of wool, hay and supplies to market. French arrived in 1872 and by the mid-1880s ran about 70,000 acres and 45,000 head of cattle; a land dispute ended in his murder in 1897.

The barn, 100 feet across with an umbrella roof carried on juniper posts, is the sole survivor of three French built and Oregon's largest historic round barn. Views take in the surrounding buttes and Steens Mountain.
excerpt: The Pete French Round Barn State Heritage Site preserves a round barn built by cattle king Peter French, used to train wild horses through the winter to pull wa
address: 52229 Lava Bed Road, near Diamond, OR

title: Steens Mountain
contentHtml:
Steens Mountain is the largest fault-block mountain in North America, a single mountain some 50 miles long whose 9,738-foot summit drops a vertical mile to the Alvord Desert. Glacier-carved gorges cut its north side, and Wildhorse Lake sits in a deep cirque near the top.

In summer the gravel Steens Mountain Loop Road reaches the top, with short walks to the Kiger Gorge and East Rim viewpoints. Hikes include Wildhorse Lake, the summit, Big Indian Gorge, Pike Creek and Little Blitzen Gorge.
excerpt: Steens Mountain is the largest fault-block mountain in North America, a single mountain some 50 miles long whose 9,738-foot summit drops a vertical mile to the
note: Check road reports before going. Carry at least a gallon of water per day and expect snow or intense heat. Primitive camping allowed on BLM land unless marked.
address: Steens Mountain Loop Road, east of Frenchglen, OR

title: Diamond Craters Outstanding Natural Area
imageAlt: Lava Pit Crater in early spring

banner.alt: Lava Pit Crater in early spring

contentHtml:
Diamond Craters Outstanding Natural Area covers about 17,000 acres of young basalt formed within the last 25,000 years: craters and vents, cinder and spatter cones, lava tubes, driblet spires, a graben and a water- filled maar. The BLM calls it some of the most diverse basaltic volcanic features in the nation, clustered in one small, accessible area.

A self-guided tour runs off the Diamond Loop on Lava Bed Road.
excerpt: Diamond Craters Outstanding Natural Area covers about 17,000 acres of young basalt formed within the last 25,000 years: craters and vents, cinder and spatter co
note: No fee and no facilities; bring water and shelter, and leave the rocks in place. From Burns, take OR 78 southeast about 2 miles, OR 205 south 46 miles to Diamond Junction, turn left about 6 miles, then left on Lava Bed Road.
address: Lava Bed Road, south of New Princeton, OR

title: Alvord Desert
contentHtml:
The Alvord Desert is Oregon's largest dry lakebed, a white, cracked playa about 12 miles long and 7 wide at around 4,000 feet in the rain shadow of Steens Mountain. In the dry season it can be driven on, and it is used for land sailing, off-highway riding, camping and stargazing.

It is a natural racetrack: in 1976 Kitty O'Neil set the women's land-speed record here at 512.710 mph, and in August 2019 Jessi Combs raised it to 522.783 mph in the run that took her life, a record Guinness certified the next year.
excerpt: The Alvord Desert is Oregon's largest dry lakebed, a white, cracked playa about 12 miles long and 7 wide at around 4,000 feet in the rain shadow of Steens Mount
note: Usually dry May to October; avoid wet areas and spring drainages. Free access and camping at Frog Springs (BLM). Strong winds, no cell service and long distances between services; high-clearance 4WD recommended. Gas, food and lodging in Fields.
address: Fields-Denio Road, about 22 miles north of Fields, OR

title: The History Museum of Hood River County
contentHtml:
The History Museum of Hood River County, on the Hood River waterfront, brings the county's history to life, with a focus on agriculture, timber, entrepreneurial spirit and the outdoors. It is run by Hood River County and the Hood River County Heritage Council, with roots in a historical society collecting since 1907; the current building opened in 1978.

Changing exhibitions are shown alongside the permanent collection.

title: Western Antique Aeroplane & Automobile Museum (WAAAM)
imageAlt: Antique biplane flying near Mount Hood

banner.alt: Antique biplane flying near Mount Hood

contentHtml:
The Western Antique Aeroplane & Automobile Museum (WAAAM) holds one of the largest collections in the country of antique aircraft and cars that still fly and drive, focused on the 1900s to 1930s. Exhibits include aircraft, automobiles, motorcycles, tractors, military jeeps and engines.

On the second Saturday of each month, 10 AM to 2 PM, volunteers open the hangar doors for antique car rides, takeoffs and landings, and living-history programs.

title: Cascade Locks Historical Museum
imageAlt: Bridge of the Gods centennial exhibit

banner.alt: Bridge of the Gods centennial exhibit

contentHtml:
The Cascade Locks Historical Museum fills the 1905 locktender's house in the Port of Cascade Locks Marine Park. It interprets the Cascade Locks and canal, the portage railroad and the sternwheeler era on the Columbia, and is home to the Oregon Pony, the Oregon Territory's first locomotive.

Its current exhibit, Riveting History, marks 100 years of the Bridge of the Gods.

note: Open seasonally, March through October; closed in winter.

title: Hutson Museum
contentHtml:
The Hutson Museum in Parkdale tells the deep history of the upper Hood River Valley through artifacts and geology. It opened in 1993 beside the Ries-Thompson House (about 1900), Parkdale's oldest residence, around the rock and mineral collection Jesse and Winifred Hutson left to the town.

The collection holds thousands of rough specimens, polished slabs, cabochons, spheres and eggs, plus Native tools of obsidian, agate and basalt. There is also a logging-history exhibit, a historic Parkdale train layout visitors can run, and a gift shop.

note: Run by volunteers; hours vary.
address: 4967 Baseline Dr, Parkdale, OR 97041

title: Mount Hood National Forest
contentHtml:
Mt. Hood National Forest covers about 1.1 million acres just 50 miles east of Portland, stretching more than 60 miles south from the Columbia River Gorge to the Olallie Scenic Area near Mt. Jefferson.

It has about 80 campgrounds, 20 sno-parks, part of the Pacific Crest Trail and several ski areas, including historic Timberline Lodge. About a third of the forest is designated wilderness, and the forest supplies about a third of Oregon's drinking and irrigation water.

The forest is managed through four ranger districts: Barlow, Clackamas River, Hood River and Zigzag.

title: Badger Creek Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Badger Creek Wilderness, designated in 1984 and enlarged in 2009, lies on the dry east slope of the Cascades across OR 35 from the Mount Hood Wilderness. Lookout Mountain, at 6,525 feet, is its high point, and Badger, Little Badger and Tygh creeks drain its subalpine ridges and glacier-smoothed upper basins.

Its forests shift from mountain hemlock to ponderosa pine, Oregon white oak and grassland in the warm east. About 55 miles of trail include the 11.9-mile Badger Creek National Recreation Trail.

title: Mark O. Hatfield Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mark O. Hatfield Wilderness, designated in 1984 and enlarged in 2009, rises south of the Columbia River Gorge cliffs, from about 100 feet near the river to 4,900 feet on Mount Defiance. It is a land of basalt cliffs, talus slopes, a rolling plateau, lakes and old-growth forest.

About 200 miles of trail follow its drainages, including the Eagle Creek Trail with seven waterfalls and about 14 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail.
