title: Mount Hood Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mount Hood Wilderness was one of the original wildernesses designated in 1964 and now covers about 67,000 acres around Oregon's highest peak (11,249 ft). The dormant volcano carries 11 active glaciers above alpine meadows and old-growth forest, with more than a dozen waterfalls on its lower slopes.

The 38-mile Timberline Trail circles the mountain and links with more than 20 other trails. Unbridged glacial streams can be dangerous during snowmelt or heavy rain, so plan a backup route.

Most of the wilderness lies in Hood River and Clackamas counties; the area gets about 150 inches of precipitation a year, mostly as snow from October to April.

title: Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail
imageAlt: Cycling through the Mosier Twin Tunnels

banner.alt: Cycling through the Mosier Twin Tunnels

gallery.alt: Walking and biking through a tunnel

contentHtml:
The Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail turns more than 12 miles of the historic highway into paved paths in three segments: John B. Yeon to Cascade Locks, Wyeth to Viento (about 6 miles, with the 500-foot Summit Creek Viaduct and four waterfalls), and Hood River to Mosier (about 4.5 miles).

On the Hood River-Mosier segment, the Mosier Twin Tunnels, filled with rock when I-84 opened, have been cleared and restored for walkers and cyclists.
excerpt: The Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail turns more than 12 miles of the historic highway into paved paths in three segments: John B. Yeon to Cascade Loc
note: A day-use parking permit is required (1-day permits sold on site). Dogs on leashes 6 feet or shorter. Eagle Creek parking needs a Northwest Forest Pass. E-bikes allowed; electric scooters not. Trail conditions: 541-374-8811.
address: Trailheads at Toothrock, Bridge of the Gods (Cascade Locks), Wyeth, Starvation Creek, Viento and Mark O. Hatfield West (Hood River) and East (Mosier), OR

title: Koberg Beach State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Koberg Beach State Recreation Site is a westbound I-84 wayside near Hood River with a short hiking trail and a beach on the Columbia River.

The Koberg family long owned and developed the beach, with a rustic dance hall popular with Hood River residents. The state bought the land in 1953, removed the hall and opened the entrance road and parking in 1962.
excerpt: Koberg Beach State Recreation Site is a westbound I-84 wayside near Hood River with a short hiking trail and a beach on the Columbia River.
note: Reached from westbound I-84 only.
address: I-84 westbound, near Hood River, OR

title: Mitchell Point Trailhead
contentHtml:
Mitchell Point Trailhead is the gateway to Wygant State Natural Area, with Gorge views and interpretive displays about the historic Mitchell Point Tunnel a short walk from the parking area. The tunnel, built in 1915 on the Historic Columbia River Highway, was destroyed in 1966 to widen I-84, and a new crossing is being built to link the state trail.

The Mitchell Point Trail climbs 2.6 miles round trip and about 1,300 feet to a crest with views of the Columbia; the Wygant Trail is 8 miles round trip with about 2,300 feet of gain.
excerpt: Mitchell Point Trailhead is the gateway to Wygant State Natural Area, with Gorge views and interpretive displays about the historic Mitchell Point Tunnel a shor
note: Dogs on leashes 6 feet or shorter. Winter storms often damage trails; check conditions before going.
address: Mitchell Point Trailhead, I-84 Exit 58, west of Hood River, OR

title: Seneca Fouts Memorial State Natural Area
imageAlt: Seneca Fouts Memorial State Natural Area
contentHtml: Seneca Fouts Memorial State Natural Area lies at Mitchell Point in the Columbia River Gorge just west of Hood River, next to an abandoned section of the Historic Columbia River Highway. With Vinzenz Lausmann and Wygant state natural areas it forms a trio of parks offering scenic hiking and views over the Gorge.
excerpt: Seneca Fouts Memorial State Natural Area lies at Mitchell Point in the Columbia River Gorge just west of Hood River, next to an abandoned section of the Histori
note: Reached from the Mitchell Point Trailhead.
address: Mitchell Point, off I-84 Exit 58, west of Hood River, OR

title: Sheridan State Scenic Corridor
contentHtml:
Sheridan State Scenic Corridor is an 11-acre stand of old-growth forest beside I-84 west of Cascade Locks, acquired in 1923 and named for Philip H. Sheridan. It was a wayside on the Historic Columbia River Highway until I-84 cut off car access in 1960.

Since 1998 it has been reached on foot or by bike on the Eagle Creek - Cascade Locks segment of the state trail, which passes under I-84 through a 150-foot tunnel just east of the park.
excerpt: Sheridan State Scenic Corridor is an 11-acre stand of old-growth forest beside I-84 west of Cascade Locks, acquired in 1923 and named for Philip H. Sheridan. It
note: No motor vehicle access.
address: Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail, west of Cascade Locks, OR

title: Starvation Creek State Park

gallery.alt: Starvation Creek and state trail signs

contentHtml:
Starvation Creek State Park is a small park at the foot of the Gorge walls along eastbound I-84. A short boardwalk leads about 50 feet from the parking area to Starvation Creek Falls, with picnic tables overlooking the falls.

It is a trailhead for the Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail, about 1 mile east to Viento and 4.6 miles west to Wyeth past several waterfalls. The Mount Defiance Trail starts near Hole-in-the-Wall Falls.
excerpt: Starvation Creek State Park is a small park at the foot of the Gorge walls along eastbound I-84. A short boardwalk leads about 50 feet from the parking area to
note: A day-use parking permit is required (1-day permits sold on site). Dogs on leashes 6 feet or shorter. The Starvation Ridge Cut-Off Trail is closed by a washout.
address: I-84 eastbound, west of Hood River, OR

title: Viento State Park
contentHtml:
Viento State Park sits on both sides of I-84 about 8 miles west of Hood River, with Columbia River access, windsurfing and a creekside picnic area. The campground has 56 electrical sites, 10 tent sites and 5 hiker/biker sites, with flush toilets and hot showers.

A 5.6-mile accessible section of the Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail runs west from the park to Wyeth.
excerpt: Viento State Park sits on both sides of I-84 about 8 miles west of Hood River, with Columbia River access, windsurfing and a creekside picnic area. The campgrou
note: Reserve up to 6 months ahead (800-452-5687). Non-campers need a day-use parking permit. Trains pass day and night.
address: I-84 Exit 56, about 8 miles west of Hood River, OR

title: Vinzenz Lausmann Memorial State Natural Area
imageAlt: Vinzenz Lausmann Memorial State Natural Area
contentHtml: Vinzenz Lausmann Memorial State Natural Area, entered through the Seven Streams Staging Area, is 126 acres of rugged land donated by the Lausmann family in his memory. It is the gateway to the Post Canyon Trail System, with hiking, horse, mountain bike and ATV trails across state, Forest Service and private land managed by Hood River County.
excerpt: Vinzenz Lausmann Memorial State Natural Area, entered through the Seven Streams Staging Area, is 126 acres of rugged land donated by the Lausmann family in his
note: Narrow entrance road; take care with trailers.
address: Seven Streams Staging Area, about 5 miles west of Hood River, OR

title: Wygant State Natural Area
contentHtml:
Wygant State Natural Area, about six miles west of Hood River, was given to Oregon in 1933 by the Winch family in honor of Theodore and Margaret Wygant, Oregon Trail pioneers of 1850, and its trails were built by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

The Wygant Trail starts on a paved section of the old highway, then follows a creek through dense forest, 8 miles round trip with about 2,300 feet of gain.
excerpt: Wygant State Natural Area, about six miles west of Hood River, was given to Oregon in 1933 by the Winch family in honor of Theodore and Margaret Wygant, Oregon
note: Reached from the Mitchell Point Trailhead. Check trail conditions after winter storms.
address: Mitchell Point Trailhead, I-84 Exit 58, about 6 miles west of Hood River, OR

contentHtml: Badger Lake Campground sits beside Badger Lake and is a main entry point to the Badger Creek Wilderness, with swimming, non-motorized boating, fishing, hiking and horseback riding on Badger Lake Trail #479A and Badger Creek Trail #479. Vault toilets; no drinking water; horses allowed.

title: Black Lake Campground
contentHtml: Black Lake Campground offers primitive tent camping on the east shore of Black Lake at 3,740 feet, with swimming and picnicking. The Black Lake Trail leads north into the Mark O. Hatfield Wilderness. Vault toilets; no drinking water.

contentHtml: Bonney Meadows Campground is a small, quiet campground with horse corrals on a high ridge near a lush meadow. Bonney Meadows Trail #471 is used by hikers, mountain bikers and riders. Vault toilets; no drinking water; vehicles up to 16 feet.

contentHtml: Boulder Lake Campground is a small Barlow Ranger District campground by Boulder Lake, near the Boulder Lake Trailhead with trails into the 44 Trails System and the Badger Creek Wilderness. The area burned in the 2023 Boulder Fire.

title: Cloud Cap Saddle Campground
contentHtml: Cloud Cap Saddle Campground is a small, high-elevation campground at about 5,900 feet on the north side of Mount Hood, home to the Cloud Cap Trailhead with access to the Timberline Trail and Tilly Jane Trail. Vault toilet; no drinking water.

contentHtml: Fifteenmile Campground is a small campground on Fifteenmile Creek near the Badger Creek Wilderness and Fifteenmile Trail #456, popular with hikers and bikers. Vault toilets; no drinking water; vehicles up to 16 feet.

title: Kinnikinnick Campground
contentHtml:
Kinnikinnick Campground sits on Laurance Lake north of Mount Hood, just outside Parkdale, with lake views and surrounding hills. It has 25 sites (19 tent-only, 6 RV), fire pits, picnic tables, vault toilets and a boat ramp nearby.

Non-motorized boating, fishing and mountain biking are popular, and bald eagles are often seen.

contentHtml: Knebal Springs Campground sits in open ponderosa pine beside the 10-mile Knebal Springs Trail loop, popular with mountain bikers and horseback riders. One vault toilet; no drinking water; vehicles up to 22 feet.

title: Lost Lake Resort and Campground
contentHtml:
Lost Lake Resort and Campground sits between Lost Lake and Mount Hood, with a full-service resort of cabins, yurts, lodge rooms and a general store beside group, family and single campsites. Lost Lake Butte offers views of Mount Hood, its glaciers and the lake, and an old-growth boardwalk trail winds through one of Oregon's large old-growth stands.

Kayaks, rowboats, fishing boats and paddleboards are rented; no motors on the lake. Fishing, swimming, biking, berry picking and trails from a quarter mile to over 100 miles are nearby.

note: Reserve campsites on Recreation.gov and cabins at lostlakeresort.org. Three-night minimum on weekends and holidays. Day use $15 per vehicle. Bears present; store food in closed containers.

title: Nottingham Campground
contentHtml:
Nottingham Campground sits right off OR 35 along the East Fork Hood River, where most sites have direct river access. It has 21 sites (14 RV, 7 tent-only), pit toilets and trash cans, with a camp host in peak season.

The Tamanawas Falls trailhead is next door, with hiking, biking and fishing nearby.

title: Polallie Campground
contentHtml: Polallie Campground, once a dispersed site, is a quiet campground beside the Polallie Trailhead on OR 35. East Fork Trail #650 starts at the pullout and meets Elk Meadows Trail #645 after 0.1 mile. No drinking water.

title: Rainy Lake Campground
contentHtml: Rainy Lake Campground sits on Rainy Lake with trailhead access to the Mark O. Hatfield Wilderness on Rainy Lake Trail #423A, Rainy Wahtum Trail #409 and North Lake Trail #423. It has 4 first-come sites and restrooms; no drinking water.

note: $20 per night, $10 per extra vehicle; day use $10. Bring cash or check. Free self-issued wilderness permits May 15 - October 15. From Hood River, take OR 281 about 11 miles to Dee, cross the East Fork, take Punchbowl Road 1.2 miles to Dead Point Road (FR 2820), then 11 miles.

title: Sherwood Campground
contentHtml:
Sherwood Campground is a small, easy-to-reach campground on the East Fork Hood River, with 16 sites (13 tent-only, 3 RV) on one loop; several sit right on the river, whose sound masks the highway.

The Tamanawas Falls trailhead is a short walk away, and Mount Hood is about 15 minutes by car. Pit toilets; camp host in peak season.

note: Reserve on Recreation.gov. No hookups.
address: OR 35, just past the Tamanawas Falls trailhead, OR

title: Tilly Jane Campground
contentHtml: Tilly Jane Campground sits on Tilly Jane Creek at the edge of the Mount Hood Wilderness, where Tilly Jane Trail #600A begins. Vault toilets; no drinking water; wheelchair-accessible.

title: Wahtum Lake Campground
contentHtml: Wahtum Lake Campground has five primitive, shaded sites with fire pits and picnic tables next to the Wahtum Lake Trailhead, just east of the Mark O. Hatfield Wilderness; the lake is a short, steep walk below. Day hiking, backpacking and fishing. Vault toilets; no drinking water.

note: Listed as closed; confirm before going. $30 per night, $10 per extra vehicle; day use $10 (Northwest Forest Pass accepted). FR 13 and FR 1310 are narrow with rockfall.

title: Herman Creek Campground/Horse Camp
contentHtml: Herman Creek Campground and Horse Camp is the trailhead for Herman Creek Trail #406 and the Pacific Crest Trail, a gateway to the Mark O. Hatfield Wilderness. Vault toilets; no drinking water; trailers up to 20 feet.
excerpt: Herman Creek Campground and Horse Camp is the trailhead for Herman Creek Trail #406 and the Pacific Crest Trail, a gateway to the Mark O. Hatfield Wilderness. V
note: Closed for reconstruction: the surrounding forest had laminated root rot, was treated and replanted with native hardwoods, and the campground is being redesigned. From Hood River, take I-84 west to exit 47, then 0.6 mile west on Forest Lane.

title: Wyeth Campground
contentHtml:
Wyeth Campground has 13 individual and 3 group sites under Douglas-fir and bigleaf maple just off I-84, with drinking water and flush toilets. The site was a Civilian Conservation Corps camp in the 1930s and a Conscientious Objector camp in the 1940s.

Gorge Trail #400 and Wyeth Trail #411 start nearby, and the restored state trail runs from Wyeth to Viento.

title: Cabin Creek Falls
imageAlt: The bottom of Cabin Creek Falls in May

banner.alt: The bottom of Cabin Creek Falls in May

gallery.alt: Cabin Creek Falls at high water from the Mount Defiance trail

contentHtml:
Cabin Creek Falls drops 220 feet in two tiered plunges, the tallest about 135 feet. The water pours from a narrow crack in the cliff and bounces once on a shelf before the final drop.

It is the first waterfall on the Mount Defiance trail. Two boulders about 75 feet tall block a full view of the falls, which are partly visible from I-84.

title: Camp Benson Falls
contentHtml: Camp Benson Falls, also called Lower Summit Creek Falls, is an 85-foot veiling horsetail on Summit Creek. It is partly visible from I-84 in winter.
excerpt: Camp Benson Falls, also called Lower Summit Creek Falls, is an 85-foot veiling horsetail on Summit Creek. It is partly visible from I-84 in winter.

title: Coe Falls
contentHtml: Coe Falls, also called Coe Branch Falls and West Coe Falls, drops 220 feet in tiered plunges (the tallest about 193 feet) on the Coe Branch of the Hood River, at about 4,960 feet elevation.
excerpt: Coe Falls, also called Coe Branch Falls and West Coe Falls, drops 220 feet in tiered plunges (the tallest about 193 feet) on the Coe Branch of the Hood River, a
note: Detailed information and directions are not published.

title: Dead Point Falls
contentHtml:
Dead Point Falls drops 75 feet in tiered horsetails and is viewed from the rim of the West Fork Hood River canyon. A fish hatchery diversion splits the upper tier into a reverse pitchfork shape.

The creek takes its name from its source in a stand of burnt timber.

note: From Hood River, take OR 35 south 7 miles, then the highway to Dee 9 miles. Follow Punchbowl Road about 1.5 miles to a gated gravel road just before the West Fork bridge, then walk about 1/5 mile.

photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Dry Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Dry Creek Falls plunges 74 feet out of a narrow canyon, with hidden upper drops bringing the total to 230 feet over five drops. It flows all year.

The creek is the water source for Cascade Locks; a small dam just below the falls diverts the water.
excerpt: Dry Creek Falls plunges 74 feet out of a narrow canyon, with hidden upper drops bringing the total to 230 feet over five drops. It flows all year.
note: Start at the Pacific Crest Trail trailhead at the Bridge of the Gods, go under I-84 and about 300 feet up the road to where the trail continues. At about 2 miles, just before the Dry Creek crossing, take a gravel road about 1/4 mile up to the falls.

title: Four Mile Falls
imageAlt: Loowit Falls on the Eagle Creek Trail (area photo)

banner.alt: Loowit Falls on the Eagle Creek Trail (area photo)

contentHtml: Four Mile Falls drops 95 feet in two horsetail tiers on Four Mile Creek, in an alcove across Eagle Creek from the trail. The lower tier is barely visible through the trees.
excerpt: Four Mile Falls drops 95 feet in two horsetail tiers on Four Mile Creek, in an alcove across Eagle Creek from the trail. The lower tier is barely visible throug

title: Gorton Creek Falls
contentHtml: Gorton Creek Falls drops 148 feet in two plunges of 49 and 99 feet at about 590 feet elevation. The upper tier is mostly hidden in its gorge and is best seen head-on. The creek flows all year.

note: A rough trail goes about two-thirds of the way. The final climb means scrambling up a mossy, boulder- strewn streambed or a steep, precarious herd path; in summer, when the creek is low, walking up the stream is easier. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.

title: Grand Union Falls
contentHtml:
Grand Union Falls is a 41-foot sliding punchbowl on Eagle Creek that rolls over columnar basalt into a large pool.

Near the falls the trail crosses The Potholes, where dripping water has shaped the columnar joints into bowls.
excerpt: Grand Union Falls is a 41-foot sliding punchbowl on Eagle Creek that rolls over columnar basalt into a large pool.
note: Visible through the trees from the Eagle Creek Trail, but hard to photograph unless the trees are bare; a clear view means climbing down to the creek.

title: Harrison Falls
contentHtml:
Harrison Falls is the lowest of several waterfalls on Lindsey Creek, which drops down the north side of Mount Defiance to the Columbia River. It falls 64 feet in four steps through a narrow, mossy canyon.

Vines and young alder and maple largely block the view, even up close. The falls sit in a high-voltage power line clearing along the Gorge.

title: Hole-In-The-Wall Falls
imageAlt: The upper tier emerging from the namesake hole

banner.alt: The upper tier emerging from the namesake hole

contentHtml:
Hole-In-The-Wall Falls was created in 1938. Floods on Warren Creek often washed out the original Columbia River Highway, so crews blasted a tunnel through the cliff and diverted the creek through it. The water now drops 96 feet in two tiers, the tallest 63 feet.

A wooden plank in the cliff above the tunnel opening marks the change. The old streambed, where Warren Falls once fell, is a couple hundred feet away.

title: Lancaster Falls
imageAlt: The upper tier of Lancaster Falls

banner.alt: The upper tier of Lancaster Falls

Looking up at Lancaster Falls from the Mount Defiance trail

contentHtml:
Lancaster Falls is one of three waterfalls on the Mount Defiance Trail. Wonder Creek starts from a spring high on the mountain and carries a small but very steady flow over a mossy cliff, through a narrow slot and down the final drop beside the trail, 410 feet in all.

The trail passes right below the last 35 feet. The upper tier can be seen from I-84 and from the Dog Mountain Trailhead across the river in Washington.

note: From the Starvation Creek State Park lot (reachable only from eastbound I-84; westbound drivers turn around at Exit 51, Wyeth, or use Viento State Park at Exit 56), take the signed Mt. Defiance trail beside the exit ramp. The trail parallels the freeway just under a mile to Wonder Creek. Poison oak is abundant near the falls. Reaching the upper falls means a very steep, crumbly climb; long pants are recommended.

title: Lindsey Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Lindsey Creek Falls is the only one of about a dozen known Lindsey Creek waterfalls shown on topographic maps. It sits in a narrow grotto about 0.4 mile upstream of the I-84 crossing and drops 53 feet in two plunges.

The main drop veils outward at higher flow as the creek pours over a choke stone. In summer, water passes over only one side of the boulder and the falls look much narrower.

title: Loowit Falls
contentHtml:
Loowit Falls is the first major side-stream waterfall seen clearly from the Eagle Creek Trail. It drops about 78 feet as a narrow horsetail, then slides about 10 feet out of a small pool into Eagle Creek, 88 feet in all.

The trail views it from a catwalk cut into the cliff, with only a cable handrail on the uphill side. Take care and keep children close.

Westbound drivers exit at Bonneville Dam and turn around. Follow the road about 1/2 mile to the trailhead. The viewpoint is about 3.2 miles along the trail, about 500 feet downstream of High Bridge.

title: Metlako Falls
imageAlt: Metlako Falls from the former main viewpoint

banner.alt: Metlako Falls from the former main viewpoint

gallery.alt: Metlako Falls seen from the top of Sorenson Falls

contentHtml:
Metlako Falls drops 82 feet from a calm, narrow pool into a long box canyon on Eagle Creek. Earlier estimates ranged from 100 to 150 feet.

In December 2016 a large section of the canyon wall collapsed and took the viewpoint with it. The falls are now effectively not accessible; partial views may be possible through the trees from a few spots on the trail.
excerpt: Metlako Falls drops 82 feet from a calm, narrow pool into a long box canyon on Eagle Creek. Earlier estimates ranged from 100 to 150 feet.
note: Eastbound on I-84, take the Eagle Creek exit (about one mile past the Bonneville Dam exit, just after a short tunnel); it is reachable only from eastbound lanes. Westbound drivers exit at Bonneville Dam and turn around. Follow the road about 1/2 mile to the trailhead. The falls are about 1.6 miles along the trail, but the old viewpoint trail is closed.
address: Eagle Creek Trail, Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area, near Bonneville Dam, OR

title: Punch Bowl Falls
imageAlt: Swimmers reaching the cove in front of Punch Bowl Falls

banner.alt: Swimmers reaching the cove in front of Punch Bowl Falls

contentHtml:
Punch Bowl Falls is a punchbowl waterfall about 35 feet tall on Eagle Creek. The creek squeezes through a narrow channel and shoots into a large, bowl-shaped basin deep in a lush, circular gorge.

In 2017 a cliff collapsed between Punch Bowl and Lower Punch Bowl Falls, and the debris changed the creek's flow between the two.
excerpt: Punch Bowl Falls is a punchbowl waterfall about 35 feet tall on Eagle Creek. The creek squeezes through a narrow channel and shoots into a large, bowl-shaped ba
note: The falls are reached on the first 1.5 miles of the Eagle Creek Trail, about 4 miles round trip depending on parking and viewpoints. Some sections have cliff exposure where the trail follows narrow ledges. Eastbound on I-84, take the Eagle Creek exit (about one mile past the Bonneville Dam exit, just after a short tunnel); it is reachable only from eastbound lanes. Westbound drivers exit at Bonneville Dam and turn around. Follow the road about 1/2 mile to the trailhead.
address: Eagle Creek Trail, Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area, near Bonneville Dam, OR

title: Ruckel Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Ruckel Creek Falls is a 46-foot horsetail, one of the least appreciated falls in the Gorge, known for its mossy cliffs and ornate bridge stonework. It is especially scenic in spring.

Flow is weaker later in summer, and the falls are visible from I-84 only when the trees are bare.

photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Sahale Falls
contentHtml:
Sahale Falls is the easiest to reach of the few waterfalls on the East Fork Hood River. The main drop of about 64 feet veils down the back of a green grotto, with smaller drops just downstream, 78 feet in all.

It is viewed from an arch bridge built in the 1930s for the original Mount Hood Scenic Byway, now closed to cars. The river flows all year, though late-summer flow can be much weaker. The name comes from a Chinook word meaning "high".
excerpt: Sahale Falls is the easiest to reach of the few waterfalls on the East Fork Hood River. The main drop of about 64 feet veils down the back of a green grotto, wi
note: From US 26, take OR 35 for 7.8 miles to the signed Hood River Meadows entrance and turn left. After 1/2 mile turn left on the Old Mount Hood Scenic Byway (signed for Sahale Falls) and follow it about 3/4 mile to its end, just before the bridge below the falls.
address: Old Mount Hood Scenic Byway, off Hood River Meadows entrance, OR 35, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Sevenmile Falls
contentHtml:
Sevenmile Falls is the uppermost of seven major waterfalls on Eagle Creek. It drops 52 feet over basalt into a pool beside the trail, which crosses a narrow ledge. Brush partly blocks the view, so there is no fully clear view.

Few hikers reach it, since most turn back at Tunnel or Twister Falls. The name comes from a nearby campground.

note: Eastbound on I-84, take the Eagle Creek exit (about one mile past the Bonneville Dam exit, just after a short tunnel); it is reachable only from eastbound lanes. Westbound drivers exit at Bonneville Dam and turn around. Follow the road about 1/2 mile to the trailhead. The falls are about 6.5 miles from the trailhead, less than 1/4 mile past Twister Falls.
address: Eagle Creek Trail, Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area, near Bonneville Dam, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Skoonichuk Falls
contentHtml:
Skoonichuk Falls is the fourth major waterfall hiking up the Eagle Creek Trail. It drops about 32 feet through a funnel-like channel into an alcove, then about 16 feet over a broad ledge into a large pool, 48 feet in all.

A cliff up to 400 feet tall shades the falls in the morning. A camp area near the top looks down the falls; the rocks are slick.

title: Sorenson Falls
contentHtml: Sorenson Falls is a sister waterfall to Metlako Falls on Eagle Creek. Sorenson Creek drops about 100 feet in two tiers into an alcove that cannot be seen from the Eagle Creek Trail.
excerpt: Sorenson Falls is a sister waterfall to Metlako Falls on Eagle Creek. Sorenson Creek drops about 100 feet in two tiers into an alcove that cannot be seen from t
note: Attempting to visit this waterfall is not recommended: it means rappelling into the canyon or swimming more than half a mile up Eagle Creek. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.

title: Starvation Creek Falls

gallery.alt: Starvation Creek Falls from the end of the paved trail
Near the base of Starvation Creek Falls

contentHtml:
Starvation Creek Falls drops 270 feet in three tiered horsetails, the tallest 141 feet, from a narrow channel into a natural bowl, then spills past a picnic area to the Columbia River.

At high water the lower falls split around a large rock, a tier hidden from the paved viewpoint by a boulder. The facilities are wheelchair accessible.
excerpt: Starvation Creek Falls drops 270 feet in three tiered horsetails, the tallest 141 feet, from a narrow channel into a natural bowl, then spills past a picnic are
note: The parking area is reachable only from eastbound I-84; westbound drivers turn around at Exit 51 (Wyeth) or use Viento State Park at Exit 56. From the lot, follow the paved walkway past the restrooms to the "Waterfall" sign; the falls are no more than 300 feet away. For better views, cross the creek and follow a dirt path upstream. Climbing to the base or onto the boulder is not recommended.
address: Starvation Creek State Park, off eastbound I-84 between Cascade Locks and Hood River, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Stranahan Falls
contentHtml:
Stranahan Falls is the major waterfall of the Eliot Branch of the Middle Fork Hood River. It drops 282 feet in three steps of 36, 20 and 226 feet into a deeply scoured canyon below Inspiration Point and Cloud Cap Inn.

It is named for Oscar L. Stranahan, who helped build the Cloud Cap Road, opened in 1885. USGS maps have long mislabeled it as Wallalute Falls.

note: Detailed information and directions are not published.
address: Mount Hood, Mt. Hood National Forest, OR (45.41083, -121.65611)

title: Tamanawas Falls
contentHtml:
Tamanawas Falls drops 111 feet over a broad, amphitheater-like cliff on Cold Spring Creek, on the east side of Mount Hood, spreading into a curtain up to about 45 feet wide. Springs and permanent snowfields feed the creek, so the falls flow all year.

The cliff is undercut, and visitors often scramble behind the falls on a boot path, though there is no formal trail. In winter, large icicles form on the cliffs. First called Gifford's Falls after photographer Benjamin A. Gifford, it took its current name in 1971.

note: From the parking area the trail crosses the Hood River, turns right at the first junction, climbs gradually, then drops to Cold Spring Creek. Keep left at later junctions. The falls come into view after about 1.75 miles of moderate hiking; the base is about 0.1 mile farther.

photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Tish Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Tish Creek Falls is among the tallest waterfalls in the Eagle Creek basin, a plunge of 196 feet over a cathedral- like cliff into a narrow canyon. It is rarely visited because it is off-trail.

Flow is strongest from November to June, drops considerably by July and may be a trickle by late August.

title: Tunnel Falls
imageAlt: Twister Falls, about 1/4 mile up the trail (area photo)

banner.alt: Twister Falls, about 1/4 mile up the trail (area photo)

contentHtml:
Tunnel Falls drops a nearly sheer 160 feet on the East Fork Eagle Creek into a bowl-shaped amphitheater of columnar basalt. The trail was blasted into the cliff, with a tunnel carved behind the falls, which gives them their name.

The East Fork, the largest tributary of Eagle Creek, rises at Wahtum Lake and flows strongly all year. Only a small cable guards a drop of about 80 feet, so take care.

note: Eastbound on I-84, take the Eagle Creek exit (about one mile past the Bonneville Dam exit, just after a short tunnel); it is reachable only from eastbound lanes. Westbound drivers exit at Bonneville Dam and turn around. Follow the road about 1/2 mile to the trailhead. Tunnel Falls is about 6 miles from the trailhead; Twister Falls is about 1/4 mile farther.

title: Twister Falls
imageAlt: The trailside view of Twister Falls

banner.alt: The trailside view of Twister Falls

contentHtml:
Twister Falls drops about 135 feet in three sections: a short sliding cascade, a 39-foot plunge where two carved channels split the water into crossing plumes in a bow-tie shape, and an 89-foot horsetail that strikes a rock before the pool below.

The trail approaches along a cliff, so seeing the whole falls is difficult. There are no railings near the top.

note: Eastbound on I-84, take the Eagle Creek exit (about one mile past the Bonneville Dam exit, just after a short tunnel); it is reachable only from eastbound lanes. Westbound drivers exit at Bonneville Dam and turn around. Follow the road about 1/2 mile to the trailhead. The falls are about 6.25 miles from the trailhead, just past Tunnel Falls. Reaching the base takes a steep scramble down loose rock.
address: Eagle Creek Trail, Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area, near Bonneville Dam, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Umbrella Falls
contentHtml:
Umbrella Falls is a 59-foot veiling horsetail near the headwaters of the East Fork Hood River, dropping over a rough wall of reddish bedrock in a forested meadow.

Snow lingers into July, and flow drops considerably by September.
excerpt: Umbrella Falls is a 59-foot veiling horsetail near the headwaters of the East Fork Hood River, dropping over a rough wall of reddish bedrock in a forested meado
note: From US 26, take OR 35 for 6.5 miles to the signed Mount Hood Meadows entrance. Drive about 1.5 miles uphill toward the ski area and look for the trail on the right (the sign may be missing). The gentle trail crosses meadows about 1/4 mile to a bridge at the base.
address: Umbrella Falls Trail, Mt. Hood Meadows access road, off OR 35, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Upper Loowit Falls
contentHtml:
Upper Loowit Falls drops 92 feet over basalt into a fern-carpeted gully framed by a long sheer cliff, about a quarter mile upstream of Loowit Falls. Fallen logs partly hide the base.

The flow is light and changes with the season, but the drainage gets heavy rain from October to June, so the falls should flow all year.

note: Seldom visited, as reaching it means a roundabout off-trail trek. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.

photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Upper Ruckel Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Upper Ruckel Creek Falls is the largest waterfall documented on Ruckel Creek, a 100-foot plunge over an undercut basalt cliff. A natural ledge about halfway up wraps around the alcove behind the falls.

Mining relics have been found near the falls. The name is unofficial.

note: The route to the base is precarious. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.

title: Wah Gwin Gwin Falls
imageAlt: Wah Gwin Gwin Falls from the hotel terrace

banner.alt: Wah Gwin Gwin Falls from the hotel terrace

contentHtml:
Wah Gwin Gwin Falls is a horsetail on Phelps Creek, which runs through the landscaped gardens of the Columbia Gorge Hotel before dropping toward the Columbia River. Listed at 207 feet, though the survey estimates the falls themselves at no more than about 120 feet, followed by steep cascades to the river.

Once called Lullaby Falls, its name is a Chinook term meaning "rushing waters".

note: Take I-84 Exit 62 (Westcliff Drive); the hotel is on the north side of the freeway. Park where permitted and follow the garden paths on the hotel's east side to overlooks above the falls. The hotel allows public access, but it is private land, so please be courteous and don't overstay.
address: Columbia Gorge Hotel, Westcliff Drive, Hood River, OR (I-84 Exit 62)
photoCredit: Bryan Swan / Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest

title: Wallalute Falls
contentHtml: Wallalute Falls is the major waterfall on Compass Creek, on the north side of Mount Hood: a 177-foot plunge at about 4,850 feet elevation that flows all year. Its name means "strong water" in Wasco; it is also called Compass Creek Falls, Branch Falls and Middle Fork Falls.

title: Wauna Falls
imageAlt: Loowit Falls on the Eagle Creek Trail (area photo)

banner.alt: Loowit Falls on the Eagle Creek Trail (area photo)

contentHtml:
Wauna Falls is the first major waterfall up the Eagle Creek drainage, dropping 150 feet in five plunges on an unnamed stream. It is almost entirely hidden from the trail; only slivers show through the trees.

Small streams spray down from the cliffs above the trail here, making a wall of showers along the route.

note: A good view requires fording Eagle Creek. No developed trail or official access; the waterfall survey does not publish directions.

title: Wy'east Falls
contentHtml: Wy'east Falls is perhaps the most impressive side-stream waterfall on the Eagle Creek Trail, a 157-foot plunge over basalt whose spray keeps the alcove wet and mossy most of the year. The spring-fed stream flows all year but loses most of its volume by late summer.

note: Visible from the Eagle Creek Trail, best before the trees leaf out. A clear view takes a short scramble upstream on a boot path, which may mean wet feet.

title: Lost Lake
imageAlt: Mount Hood seen from across Lost Lake

banner.alt: Mount Hood seen from across Lost Lake

contentHtml:
Lost Lake is a quiet, motor-free mountain lake in Mt. Hood National Forest, southwest of Hood River, with a forested shoreline and views of Mount Hood. It is good for kayaks, stand-up paddleboards and canoes.

The public boat launch is in the South Day Use Area. Rowboats, kayaks and paddleboards can be rented in season at the Boat House across from the General Store.

note: Motors are prohibited on the whole lake. The water stays cold even on warm days, and wind can build quickly. Oregon requires a Waterway Access Permit for each paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). A vehicle day-use fee applies. Summer weekends can be crowded.
address: Lost Lake Resort, 9000 Lost Lake Road, Hood River, OR 97031

title: Northwest Discovery Water Trail
contentHtml:
The Northwest Discovery Water Trail is a 367-mile boating route from Canoe Camp on the Clearwater River in Idaho, down the Snake River and the Columbia to Bonneville Dam in the Columbia River Gorge. More than 150 sites along the way are for launching, picnicking or camping, for motorboats, canoes, sailboats and kayaks.

In Oregon it follows the Columbia's south shore through Umatilla, Morrow, Gilliam, Sherman, Wasco, Hood River and Multnomah counties. Much of it is flatwater behind eight dams, with locks to pass through or portage around.
excerpt: The Northwest Discovery Water Trail is a 367-mile boating route from Canoe Camp on the Clearwater River in Idaho, down the Snake River and the Columbia to Bonne
note: Always wear a life jacket. Check forecasts for high winds and storms, yield to commercial barges and their wakes, and watch for submerged stumps and debris. Plan each dam lock-through or portage before you go.
address: Columbia River south shore, including Cascade Locks and Hood River, OR

title: Mount Hood
imageAlt: Timberline Lodge on the slopes of Mount Hood

banner.alt: Timberline Lodge on the slopes of Mount Hood

gallery.alt: Hiking above Timberline Lodge below Mt. Hood

contentHtml:
Mount Hood is Oregon's highest peak at 11,249 feet, a glacier-clad volcano in the Cascade Range whose summit sits on the Clackamas-Hood River county line.

The summit is a serious mountaineering objective, not a hike. Every route climbs snow and ice; the standard south-side route from Timberline Lodge crosses the Palmer Snowfield and climbs the Hogsback to the Pearly Gates, exposed to crevasses, rockfall and fast-changing weather.

Most visitors experience the mountain without the summit: historic Timberline Lodge on the south flank anchors year-round skiing, and the Timberline Trail circles the whole mountain in about 40 miles.
excerpt: Mount Hood is Oregon's highest peak at 11,249 feet, a glacier-clad volcano in the Cascade Range whose summit sits on the Clackamas-Hood River county line.
note: Summit climbs require mountaineering skills, equipment and experience.
address: Summit on the Clackamas-Hood River county line; south-side climbing routes start at Timberline Lodge, 27500 E Timberline Rd, Timberline Lodge, OR 97028

title: 7 Mile Hill
contentHtml:
7 Mile Hill is a 41-mile lollipop ride (3,600 feet of climbing, 93% paved) mixing the Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail, quiet farm roads through orchards, Mount Hood views and fast, curvy descents.

The first and last 6 miles use the car-free state trail through the Mosier Twin Tunnels. The route passes Mosier, Rowena Crest Viewpoint and The Dalles, then climbs treeless 7 Mile Hill Road and returns on fast gravel down Dry Creek Road.
excerpt: 7 Mile Hill is a 41-mile lollipop ride (3,600 feet of climbing, 93% paved) mixing the Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail, quiet farm roads through orch
note: Moderate difficulty. Food and water at the Mosier General Store (about miles 6.5 and 34.5) and in The Dalles (about mile 21). The exposed climb can be very hot, and wind can make it much harder; on windy days ride it in reverse. Watch for walkers, dogs and children on the trail. The route's GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; bike-computer auto-directions are often inaccurate.
address: Park and Ride at Highway 35 and Old Highway 30, Hood River, OR

title: Bennett Pass
contentHtml:
Bennett Pass is a very demanding 27-mile loop (3,600 feet of climbing, 60% gravel). It drops down Highway 35, climbs NF-44 and Lookout Mountain Road past Horkelia Meadow to the High Prairie, then returns on the rough, historic Bennett Pass Road, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the early 1930s.

Views take in Mount Hood, Mount St. Helens, Mount Adams, Mount Rainier, Mount Jefferson and the Three Sisters. The road passes Badger Lake and the cliffside Terrible Traverse.
excerpt: Bennett Pass is a very demanding 27-mile loop (3,600 feet of climbing, 60% gravel). It drops down Highway 35, climbs NF-44 and Lookout Mountain Road past Horkel
note: No food or water, limited cell service. North-facing slopes can hold snow into late June; ride after July 4 and avoid weekends and holidays. A bike closer to a mountain bike is recommended. Don't miss the hard right turn at about mile 22.5. The route's GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; bike-computer auto-directions are often inaccurate.
address: Bennett Pass Sno-Park, Highway 35, Mt. Hood National Forest, OR

title: Hood River Mountain Loop (Long)
contentHtml:
The long Hood River Mountain Loop is a 29-mile ride (3,400 feet of climbing, 40% gravel). It climbs from town onto the Historic Columbia River Highway, car-free for the first 6 miles with Gorge viewpoints and a tunnel, then turns south at Mosier for a sustained, shaded forest climb of more than 12 miles.

A gravel descent with breakout views turns to pavement for the run back to the start.

note: Moderate difficulty. A development route not yet fully vetted, so go prepared. Winter riding only if the snow line is above 3,000 feet. No food or water listed. The route's GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; bike-computer auto-directions are often inaccurate.
address: Park and Ride at Highway 35 and Old Highway 30, Hood River, OR

At the top, a gravel descent with breakout views turns to pavement for the return.

title: Laurance Lake
contentHtml:
Laurance Lake is a 20-mile out-and-back ride (2,200 feet of climbing, 30% gravel) from Parkdale. It climbs through orchards with constant Mount Hood views, winds up through forest on the Laurance Lake road and finishes on a gravel climb to a Mount Hood viewpoint on Pinnacle Ridge.

The return is a long downhill back to Parkdale, where Solera Brewery and Blue Canoe cafe are close by.

note: Easier difficulty, though one pitch is about 9% and the final gravel climb suits riders comfortable on gravel. Watch for farm trucks in the orchards. Water and flush toilets at Red Barn Park. The route's GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; bike-computer auto-directions are often inaccurate.

title: Lost!
contentHtml: Lost! is a 57-mile loop (5,800 feet of climbing) from Parkdale: about 14% gravel, 36% rough "Roubaix" pavement and 50% paved. It visits Lost Lake and its Mount Hood view, descends along Trout Creek, climbs through orchards to Vista Ridge's views of Mount Adams and Mount Hood, and drops about 1,700 feet down Red Hill past the Parkdale lava flow.
excerpt: Lost! is a 57-mile loop (5,800 feet of climbing) from Parkdale: about 14% gravel, 36% rough "Roubaix" pavement and 50% paved. It visits Lost Lake and its Mount
note: Closed: FS 13 (about miles 15 to 22) is under bridge and drainage reconstruction through December 31, 2026; check conditions before riding. Moderate difficulty. Food and water at the Lost Lake General Store (about mile 23); water and flush toilets at Red Barn Park. The route's GPX file has no turn-by- turn directions; bike-computer auto-directions are often inaccurate.
address: Red Barn Park, Clear Creek Road, Parkdale, OR

title: Punchbowl (Oregon)
contentHtml:
Punchbowl is an 18-mile loop (2,700 feet of climbing, 85% gravel). After a short paved warm-up it climbs about 2,500 feet on gravel past Dead Point Creek, with big views of the Hood River Valley and Mount Hood, then follows Larch Road, a steep paved descent and gravel Kingsley Road back toward the river.

It finishes at Punchbowl Falls, with a swimming hole where the river's branches meet.

note: Demanding. Active logging area: pull over and stop for logging trucks. The paved descent is steep with limited sight lines, and some gravel is coarse and chunky. No food or water. Bring a lock and a towel to explore the falls. The route's GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; bike-computer auto-directions are often inaccurate.
address: Punchbowl Road and Lost Lake Road, just past the West Fork Hood River bridge, near Dee, OR

title: Fifteenmile Creek
contentHtml:
Fifteenmile Creek rises at Senecal Springs on Lookout Mountain, the highest point in the Badger Creek Wilderness, and flows northeast to the Columbia below The Dalles Dam. An 11.1-mile stretch (10.5 miles wild, 0.6 scenic) was designated Wild and Scenic in 2009.

Braided, spring-fed channels give way to a steep creek through dense conifer forest, then waterfalls and a box canyon. The creek holds the easternmost wild winter steelhead run in the Columbia Basin, and the Fifteenmile Creek Trail follows it for 5.7 miles.

note: Managed by Mt. Hood National Forest.
address: Fifteenmile Creek Campground at the Badger Creek Wilderness boundary, Mt. Hood National Forest, OR

title: Hood River (East Fork)
contentHtml:
The East Fork Hood River flows from the Newton-Clark Glacier on Mount Hood, then turns north beside Highway 35 through a broad glacial valley and a steep, cliff-lined canyon. A 13.5-mile recreational stretch to the forest boundary was designated Wild and Scenic in 2009.

The corridor has Mount Hood's most popular groomed Nordic trails, riverside campgrounds, rock climbing on columnar basalt and fishing for steelhead and coho salmon. The Tamanawas Trailhead explains the glacial floods and debris flows that shaped the valley.
excerpt: The East Fork Hood River flows from the Newton-Clark Glacier on Mount Hood, then turns north beside Highway 35 through a broad glacial valley and a steep, cliff
note: Managed by Mt. Hood National Forest.
address: Tamanawas Falls Trailhead on OR 35, Mt. Hood National Forest, OR

title: Middle Fork Hood River
contentHtml:
The Middle Fork Hood River begins at glaciers on Mount Hood's north slope, where the Clear, Coe and Eliot Branches meet near the Parkdale Lava Beds. A 3.7-mile scenic stretch was designated Wild and Scenic in 2009.

The river runs the full length of the roughly 7,000-year-old Parkdale Lava Flow, the youngest in the Cascades between Mount Jefferson and Mount Adams and a textbook example of rough a'a lava. It also supports threatened bull trout and steelhead.

note: Recreation is limited to dispersed day and overnight use. Managed by Mt. Hood National Forest.
address: Middle Fork Hood River near Parkdale, Mt. Hood National Forest, OR

title: White River
contentHtml:
The White River runs about 53 miles from Mount Hood to the Deschutes River, and 46.8 miles of it (24.3 scenic, 22.5 recreational) were designated Wild and Scenic in 1988; the short stretch at White River Falls is excluded.

Glacial silt turns it milky in late summer. Along it are the Devil's Kitchen fumarole field, the Old Maid lava and mudflow deposits, the Barlow Road, Timberline Trail and historic Keeps Mill, with Nordic skiing, camping, hiking and wildlife watching.

title: Historic Columbia River Highway
imageAlt: Mosier Twin Tunnels on the state trail

banner.alt: Mosier Twin Tunnels on the state trail

contentHtml:
The Historic Columbia River Highway, "King of Roads," is America's first scenic highway: about 70 miles along the walls of the Columbia River Gorge. Designed by Samuel Lancaster and built from 1913 to 1922, its bridges and tunnels were made to complement the waterfalls and viewpoints. It is a National Historic Landmark.

I-84 replaced most of it by 1960, but restored sections now form the Historic Columbia River Highway State Trail. In Hood River County these include the Mitchell Point segment from Wyeth to Viento and the Twin Tunnels segment from Hood River to Mosier, with Starvation Creek Falls and Cascade Locks along the way.

note: The state trail segments are paved paths for walking, biking and e-bikes; the highway is owned and maintained by ODOT.
address: Troutdale to The Dalles; Hood River County sections between Cascade Locks, Hood River and Mosier, OR

contentHtml:
The Mount Hood Scenic Byway is a National Scenic Byway of roughly 100 miles that loops around Mount Hood between Troutdale and Hood River, following US-26 through Sandy and Government Camp and OR-35 through the Hood River Valley.

In Hood River County the byway follows OR-35 down the Hood River Valley past the Fruit Loop's orchards, farm stands and wineries, with Mount Hood in view, and ends at Hood River's waterfront on the Columbia.

note: Carry chains or traction tires in winter; Sno-Park permits are needed at winter pullouts November 1 to April 30.

title: Hood River Fruit Loop
contentHtml:
The Hood River Fruit Loop is a self-guided 35-mile drive on country roads through the Hood River Valley, with 32 on-the-farm stands: fruit stands, wineries, breweries, cideries, flower fields and farm markets, many with U-pick.

Fruit trees were first planted in the valley in 1855; today about 14,500 acres grow pears, apples and cherries beneath Mount Hood.

In heavy snow years, snowmobiles may not be able to reach the Terrible Traverse because of deep snow on its steep canyon walls.

Mt. Hood Meadows, on Mount Hood's southeast face, is the largest ski area on the mountain: 2,150 skiable acres, 11 chairlifts and 87 trails from a 4,523-foot base to 7,300 feet, with a longest run of 3 miles.

It offers alpine and Nordic skiing, night skiing, lessons and rentals, and in summer scenic chairlift rides, hiking and weekend events.

title: Cooper Spur Mountain Resort

Cooper Spur Mountain Resort is a family ski area on Mount Hood's north side, run by Mt. Hood Meadows. One double chairlift, a beginner rope tow and two tubing lifts serve ten ski runs and two tubing hills, with alpine touring, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing.

The resort also has a rustic lodge, log cabins and condos (pet-friendly cabins) and the farm-to-table Crooked Tree Tavern & Grill.

The Mount Hood Railroad is a century-old short line running scenic excursions up the Hood River Valley through orchards, vineyards and forest, with views of Mount Hood.

Seasonal trips include Spring, Summer and Fall trains, Easter and Oktoberfest trains and The Polar Express in winter, plus railbikes, the Fruit Valley Trolley, The Fruit Company orchard tour and e-bike rentals.

contentHtml:
Double Mountain has brewed in Hood River since 2007. The original taproom is a laid-back, living-room-style space with vinyl records, free live music weekly and trivia nights.

Food is for sharing: New Haven-style pizzas, sandwiches and salads, with nothing fried.

Ferment Brewing Company is an award-winning waterfront brewery and tasting room that pairs traditional farmhouse brewing with a modern, scientific approach, drawing on the Columbia River Gorge and foraged ingredients for its ales and lagers.

The kitchen menu is built around fermentation, from fermented ketchup to housemade kraut, with local sourcing.

contentHtml:
Kings & Daughters Brewing, founded in 2021 by brewer Kyle Larsen and artist Kacie McMackin and named for their children, is known for soft, balanced, hop-forward beers and hand-drawn labels. In 2025 it opened The Walled Garden public house in downtown Hood River.

The bright taproom and boutique market pours thirteen K&D beers plus cocktails and wine, with a French- inspired food truck on the covered patio.

Mt. View Brewing is the small-batch brewery of Mt. View Orchards, a fifth-generation family fruit farm on the north side of Mount Hood that also makes Grateful Vineyard wines and Golden Row cider, all poured in one tasting room.

The farm grows apples, pears, cherries and grapes, and the tasting room has a farm-to-table kitchen and a big lawn patio with mountain views. All ages and dogs welcome.

contentHtml: pFriem Family Brewers, founded in 2012, brews Belgian- and Northwest-inspired artisanal beers, with Pilsner as its flagship, at its waterfront tasting room in Hood River.

Solera Brewery has brewed in Parkdale, about 20 minutes south of Hood River, since 2012. The taproom fills a converted theater, with a back patio facing Mount Hood.

Small batches include sour and wild seasonals; Hedonist IPA is the only year-round draft, and the tap list changes often. Order food at the bar; no reservations.

Thunder Island Brewing Co. is a community-focused brewery celebrating outdoor adventure and the Columbia River Gorge, with distinctive small-batch beers sold across Oregon.

The family- and dog-friendly taproom has an outdoor patio and an Asian-fusion-inspired menu, plus local wines, ciders and kombucha.

Working Hands Fermentation, "The Lager Brewery of the Columbia River Gorge," is a brewery and cidery in Hood River's Heights neighborhood, a short walk south of downtown. It specializes in German-style lagers and ciders from local apples.

The taproom has seasonal outdoor seating, pub fare and cocktails, with pub trivia on Thursdays and open mic on Sundays.

Standard, reserve, library and barrel tastings are offered at the Hood River tasting room.

Mt. Hood Winery sits among century-old family orchards on the Hood River Fruit Loop, where volcanic soil, sun and alpine breezes meet generations of farming. The patio and tasting room look out on Mount Hood and Mount Adams.

Dog- and family-friendly, with a fireplace, charcuterie boxes and free live music on Thursdays, April through October.

title: Stave & Stone Winery
contentHtml:
Stave & Stone Winery is a family farm rooted in Hood River since 1919. Of its 50 acres, about 20 have been planted with grapes since 2012 and 3 with lavender.

The 21-and-over tasting room and the family-friendly Wine Garden both look out on volcanoes to the north and south. Wines include whites, reds and three Pinot Noir rosés.

title: Locks Approach DGC
contentHtml:
This 18-hole disc golf course in the Columbia Gorge at Cascade Locks, listed on UDisc as the Cascade Locks Disc Golf Course, runs 6,083 feet at par 56 over hilly terrain, with a good mix of shots, concrete tees and views of the river and mountains.

Established in 2013, it is rated hard; a round takes about 1 hour 40 minutes. Wind is a factor most days.

title: Hanley Farm
contentHtml:
Hanley Farm is a 37-acre working farm and museum just outside Jacksonville, established in 1857 and owned by the Southern Oregon Historical Society. It preserves the story of the people who settled the land and their part in Rogue Valley agriculture.

The Century Farm has a 19th-century farmhouse, barns, a water tower and historic outbuildings, and is listed on the National Register. Mary Hanley, a founder of the society, gave it to SOHS in 1982. Its vegetable gardens are no-till and chemical-free.

note: Visitors are welcome during Hanley Farm public events, including farmhouse tours and living-history programs on first Saturdays, June to September. Tours can be scheduled through SOHS.

imageAlt: Southern Oregon History Center (Southern Oregon Historical Society)

The Southern Oregon History Center in downtown Medford is the exhibit space and research library and archives of the Southern Oregon Historical Society, founded in 1946. Its collections hold an estimated one million artifacts documenting settlement in Southern Oregon.

The society also runs the free Windows in Time lunchtime lecture series with Jackson County Library Services.

title: Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument
contentHtml:
Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument protects some 113,500 acres where the Cascade, Siskiyou and Great Basin landscapes meet, a rare, diverse ecosystem of biological, geological and historic value. It was designated in 2000 and expanded in 2017, and is managed by the Bureau of Land Management.

It includes the Soda Mountain Wilderness, Jenny Creek country and Pilot Rock. Activities include hiking, backpacking, horseback riding, fat-tire biking, camping, picnicking, wildlife viewing, cross-country skiing and snowmobiling.

note: Fees apply at Hyatt Lake Campground, the monument's developed campground. The contact station is staffed on summer weekends. Email: BLM_OR_MD_Mail@blm.gov

title: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest
contentHtml:
The Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest covers about 1.8 million acres of southwest Oregon, from the Cascades to the coast, managed through five ranger districts: High Cascades, Siskiyou Mountains, Wild Rivers, Gold Beach and Powers.

Highlights across the forest include Applegate Lake, Mount McLoughlin and the Siskiyou and Sky Lakes wilderness areas. In Jackson County the High Cascades and Siskiyou Mountains ranger districts cover the Upper Rogue country around Prospect and Union Creek, Fish Lake and the Applegate Valley.

note: Forest headquarters is in Medford.

title: Umpqua National Forest
contentHtml:
The Umpqua National Forest covers about 983,000 acres on the western slopes of the Oregon Cascades in Douglas, Lane and Jackson counties. Its landscape was shaped by high Cascade glaciers, volcanic activity and whitewater rivers, and it is known for its biodiversity, recreation and scenery.

It is managed through four ranger districts: Cottage Grove, Diamond Lake, North Umpqua and Tiller. Highlights include Toketee Falls and the waterfalls of the North Umpqua corridor, Diamond Lake, and the Boulder Creek, Mount Thielsen and Rogue-Umpqua Divide wilderness areas.

note: Forest headquarters is in Roseburg.

title: Sky Lakes Wilderness
imageAlt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin (area photo)

banner.alt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin (area photo)

contentHtml:
The Sky Lakes Wilderness covers about 116,300 acres along the southern Oregon Cascades, about 27 miles long and 6 miles wide, from Crater Lake National Park to Highway 140. It was designated in 1984.

More than 200 lakes and pools dot the high country, including 900-acre Fourmile Lake and the pure waters of Alta and Natasha lakes. Elevations run from about 3,800 feet in the Middle Fork Rogue canyon to 9,495-foot Mount McLoughlin, and the Pacific Crest Trail crosses it for about 35 miles.

Elk, black bears, cougars, pine martens, fishers and pikas live here, and hundreds of thousands of migrating birds pass through in October and November.

The Soda Mountain Wilderness covers 24,100 acres of the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument near Ashland, along the California border, where the Cascade, Siskiyou and Great Basin landscapes meet. It was designated in 2009 and is managed by the Bureau of Land Management.

Its high country takes in Soda Mountain, Boccard Point and many other peaks.

title: Elderberry Flat Campground
contentHtml:
Elderberry Flat Campground has 11 campsites along the West Fork of Evans Creek, a Rogue River tributary. Creek access points, granite sandbars, calm water and gently sloping banks make it a family-friendly swimming spot.

Each site has a picnic table and grill, and there is a day-use area. Campsite 10 is accessible, with an accessible path and interpretive kiosk.

title: Hyatt Lake Recreation Area
contentHtml:
Hyatt Lake Recreation Area covers 745 acres at just over 5,000 feet in the northern corner of Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument, with views of Mount McLoughlin. It is a base for exploring the monument and the Pacific Crest Trail.

Hyatt Lake Campground has 44 sites with showers, flush toilets, a playground, dump station and two boat ramps; Wildcat Campground has 12 primitive sites, and the Equestrian Campground 5 sites with corrals and a spur to the PCT. Group sites include the Mountain View Group Shelter and Osprey Kitchen.

The lake is a 10 mph no-wake lake with trout and smallmouth bass fishing; in winter the area offers cross- country skiing, sledding and snowshoeing.
excerpt: Hyatt Lake Recreation Area covers 745 acres at just over 5,000 feet in the northern corner of Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument, with views of Mount McLoughlin
note: Hyatt Lake Campground $12 weekdays, $15 weekends (reservations required at Recreation.gov); Wildcat $7; Equestrian $10; group shelter $100 per day; Osprey Kitchen $95 per night. Day use first- come with self-service permits. From Ashland, take Highway 66 about 17 miles to the Green Springs Inn, then East Hyatt Lake Road about 3 miles.

title: Casey State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Casey State Recreation Site is a day-use park on the Rogue River, a popular spot for salmon, steelhead and trout fishing, picnics on shady lawns and rafting.

The land was leased in 1932, where James Allen Casey ran a small restaurant and auto camp, and bought in 1937; the Civilian Conservation Corps added the parking, tables, stoves and trails. A boat ramp gives access to the river.

title: TouVelle State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
TouVelle State Recreation Site is a day-use park on the Rogue River at the foot of Table Rock, next to the Denman Wildlife Area. Salmon and steelhead pass through in season.

Six reservable group picnic areas, two with shelters, plus horseshoe pits and volleyball courts are on the main side; the boat-ramp side has a ramp, a dog off-leash area and a life-jacket loaner station. A 2-mile nature trail, fishing and swimming round out the park. Frank L. Tou Velle gave the land in 1946.

title: Valley of the Rogue State Park
imageAlt: Valley of the Rogue State Park
contentHtml:
Valley of the Rogue State Park has a day-use picnic area and a year-round campground along three miles of Rogue River shoreline in the Rogue Valley.

The campground has 92 full-hookup sites, 58 electrical sites, 13 yurts (6 pet-friendly) and two group tent areas, with flush toilets, showers and a dump station. A 1.25-mile interpretive trail follows the river, and 4 miles of the Rogue River Greenway pass through the park. Fishing here was made famous by Zane Grey.

note: Reservations up to 6 months ahead (800-452-5687). Day-use parking permit required. Firewood $7. Dump station $10 for non-campers. Buy firewood locally (Emerald Ash Borer advisory).

title: Abbott Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Abbott Creek Campground is a remote, picturesque campground in old-growth forest beside Abbott Creek, with 25 sites, fishing, swimming and hiking.

Sites 1 to 5 allow OHVs and connect to the Prospect OHV Trail System, and the Upper Rogue River Trail is reached nearby at Woodruff Bridge Day Use Area.
