Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 68, about 3.5 miles off Highway 62, 6.5 miles north of Prospect, OR

title: Acorn Woman Lakes Campground
contentHtml:
Acorn Woman Lakes Campground has walk-in tent sites in mixed-conifer forest on the banks of the Acorn Woman Lakes, most at the water's edge: 10 individual sites, 5 group sites and 10 picnic sites, 0.25 to 1.5 miles from the parking area.

Drinking water, vault toilets, picnic tables and fire rings are provided. From Ruch, take Upper Applegate Road about 14 miles to Applegate Lake, then Forest Road 1075 8.5 miles.
excerpt: Acorn Woman Lakes Campground has walk-in tent sites in mixed-conifer forest on the banks of the Acorn Woman Lakes, most at the water's edge: 10 individual sites
note: $25 per night single site, $75 group site, $5 extra vehicle, $7 day use; fees early May to mid- September, free with no services November to mid-May. Vehicles stay in the lot; carry gear in. Lake levels are low after a record-low snowpack.
address: End of Forest Road 1075, 8.5 miles past Applegate Lake, Applegate Recreation Area, OR

title: Beaver Dam Group Campground
contentHtml:
Beaver Dam Group Campground is a rustic group site for up to 40 people along Beaver Creek in old-growth forest, with three tent sites and one small trailer site (28 feet maximum).

Wildflowers bloom along the creeks in early to mid-summer. Nearby trails include Brown Mountain, High Lakes, Mt. McLoughlin and Fish Lake.
excerpt: Beaver Dam Group Campground is a rustic group site for up to 40 people along Beaver Creek in old-growth forest, with three tent sites and one small trailer site
note: $40 per night; reserve at Recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777. No drinking water or garbage service; pack it out. Vault toilets. Check-in 2:00 PM, check-out 12:00 PM. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 37, 1 mile north of Dead Indian Memorial Highway, 22 miles east of Ashland, OR

title: Beaver Sulphur Group Campground
contentHtml:
Beaver Sulphur Group Campground has nine campsites in mixed-conifer shade beside Beaver Creek, reserved as one site for groups and large family gatherings.

The Mule Mountain Trail climbs the dry Siskiyou ridges above the Applegate Valley, with spring wildflowers, and Applegate Lake is nearby for swimming, boating and fishing.
excerpt: Beaver Sulphur Group Campground has nine campsites in mixed-conifer shade beside Beaver Creek, reserved as one site for groups and large family gatherings.
note: $75 per night; reserve at Recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777. No drinking water or garbage service; pack it out. Vault toilets. Store food properly (bears). Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 20, 3 miles off Upper Applegate Road, south of Ruch, OR

title: Bessie Shelter Horse Camp
contentHtml: Bessie Shelter Horse Camp is a primitive horse camp with a shelter, picnic tables and fire rings on the High Cascades Ranger District, near the Sky Lakes country.
excerpt: Bessie Shelter Horse Camp is a primitive horse camp with a shelter, picnic tables and fire rings on the High Cascades Ranger District, near the Sky Lakes countr
note: No fee. No water, toilet or garbage service; pack it out. From Prospect, take the Prospect-Butte Falls Highway about 3 miles to FR 37, FR 37 about 3 miles to FR 3795 (watch for log trucks), 4 miles to FR 600, then about 1 mile east. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 600, off FR 3795 and FR 37, east of Prospect, OR

title: Carberry Group Campground
contentHtml:
Carberry Group Campground is a large group campground along Cougar Creek near Applegate Lake, for tents and RVs: 10 sites with tables and fire pits, smaller tent sites beside the creek and a paved lot with room for up to 8 dry RV spots.

It suits hunting groups and large gatherings; single sites can be booked through the concessionaire when available.
excerpt: Carberry Group Campground is a large group campground along Cougar Creek near Applegate Lake, for tents and RVs: 10 sites with tables and fire pits, smaller ten
note: $75 per night for the whole campground or $40 per single site (concessionaire, 541-899-9220; key at the Hart-Tish store). Reserve at Recreation.gov. Bring drinking water; accessible vault toilets; garbage in season only. Locked gate. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: County Road 777, 0.3 mile off Upper Applegate Road, Applegate Lake, OR

title: Daley Creek Campground
contentHtml: Daley Creek Campground has 6 sites with picnic tables near the meeting of Beaver Dam and Daley creeks in old-growth forest, with hiking, fishing and swimming.
excerpt: Daley Creek Campground has 6 sites with picnic tables near the meeting of Beaver Dam and Daley creeks in old-growth forest, with hiking, fishing and swimming.
note: $8 per night, $4 extra vehicle. No drinking water or garbage service; pack it out. Vault toilet. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 37, 1 mile north of Dead Indian Memorial Highway, 22 miles east of Ashland, OR

title: Doe Point Campground
contentHtml:
Doe Point Campground sits in old-growth forest beside Fish Lake, with 30 sites for trailers, RVs and tents, 5 of them walk-to tent sites. Each has a picnic table and fire ring, with drinking water and flush toilets.

Fish Lake is a 483-acre reservoir at 4,639 feet, fed by more than 45 underground volcanic streams, with views of Mount McLoughlin and a lava flow from Brown Mountain about 2,000 years old along its shore. Fish Lake Resort's store, cafe and lodging are a short walk away.
excerpt: Doe Point Campground sits in old-growth forest beside Fish Lake, with 30 sites for trailers, RVs and tents, 5 of them walk-to tent sites. Each has a picnic tabl
note: Bears frequent the area: keep a clean camp and store food in closed containers. Fish Lake has a 10 mph speed limit. No off-road vehicles in the campground. Extra vehicles pay at the campground.
address: Fish Lake, off Highway 140, about 39 miles east of Medford, OR

title: Farewell Bend Campground
contentHtml:
Farewell Bend Campground, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1934, has 60 sites for trailers, RVs and tents in old-growth forest about 18 miles west of Crater Lake National Park. The Rogue River runs through it.

Fishing, swimming and hiking are close by, including the Rogue Gorge Trail, and Union Creek Resort is about a mile away. Drinking water, flush toilets, grills, a children's play area and garbage service are provided.
excerpt: Farewell Bend Campground, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1934, has 60 sites for trailers, RVs and tents in old-growth forest about 18 miles west of
note: Closed for the season (closed 10/7/2026). $22 per night, $44 group standard sites, $7 extra vehicle. Reserve at Recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 8:00 AM; no fireworks; dogs on leash.
address: Highway 62, 56.7 miles from Medford, near Union Creek, OR

title: Fish Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Fish Lake Campground sits in old-growth forest beside Fish Lake, a 483-acre reservoir at 4,639 feet, with 17 sites for trailers, RVs and tents and 3 tent-only sites. Fish Lake Resort, with a store, cafe and lodging, is a short walk away.

The lake has a 10 mph speed limit, fishing and swimming, and a day-use area with a historic picnic shelter. The Fish Lake, High Lakes and Brown Mountain trails and the Pacific Crest Trail are nearby.
excerpt: Fish Lake Campground sits in old-growth forest beside Fish Lake, a 483-acre reservoir at 4,639 feet, with 17 sites for trailers, RVs and tents and 3 tent-only s
note: Closed for the season (closed 10/13/2026). Fish Lake boat ramp closure in effect. $25 per night ($12.50 walk-in site), $7 extra vehicle. Reserve at Recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777. Drinking water, flush toilets, host. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14- day stay limit.
address: Fish Lake access road, 0.5 mile off Highway 140, about 39 miles east of Medford, OR
photoCredit: USDA Forest Service (Fish Lake: Sherri Camp, Adobe Stock)

title: Flumet Flat Group Campground
contentHtml:
Flumet Flat Group Campground is a large meadow for group events such as reunions, church and school camps and scouting, rented as a whole for up to 50 people. Swimming and fishing on the Applegate River are a short walk away.

Just south is the Gin Lin National Recreation Trail, a 3/4-mile self-guided loop through a 19th-century mining site. The Mule Mountain Trail and Applegate Lake are nearby.
excerpt: Flumet Flat Group Campground is a large meadow for group events such as reunions, church and school camps and scouting, rented as a whole for up to 50 people. S
note: $75 per night; reservation only at Recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777 (gate combination sent in the confirmation). No drinking water; vault toilet, garbage collection, paved parking. Horses allowed. Rattlesnakes, ticks and poison oak are common. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Palmer Creek Road, 0.5 mile off Upper Applegate Road, OR

title: Fourbit Ford Campground
contentHtml: Fourbit Ford Campground is a quiet, secluded campground of 7 sites by Fourbit Creek in pine forest, on the Old Military Road that once supplied Fort Klamath, a short distance from Willow Lake.
excerpt: Fourbit Ford Campground is a quiet, secluded campground of 7 sites by Fourbit Creek in pine forest, on the Old Military Road that once supplied Fort Klamath, a
note: $16 per night. Reserve at Recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777. No drinking water (treat surface water; water at nearby Whiskey Springs Campground). Vault toilet, garbage service. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 3065, 1.4 miles off County Road 821, 9 miles past Butte Falls, OR

title: Harr Point Campground
contentHtml: Harr Point Campground is a semi-primitive campground of five tent-only sites on the east shore of Applegate Lake, reached by a 0.25-mile walk on the Payette Trail or by boat.
excerpt: Harr Point Campground is a semi-primitive campground of five tent-only sites on the east shore of Applegate Lake, reached by a 0.25-mile walk on the Payette Tra
note: No fee. No drinking water or garbage service; pack it out. Vault toilet. Boaters should check lake levels. From Ruch, take Upper Applegate Road about 15 miles, cross the dam on County Road 959, go about 3 miles, then Forest Road 100 about 0.5 mile. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Payette Trail #970, 0.25 mile from the Teel Arm parking area, east shore of Applegate Lake, OR

title: Jackson Campground
contentHtml:
Jackson Campground sits on the Applegate River north of the Red Buttes Wilderness, with 8 tent-only sites, 3 dry RV sites and a group site beside a day-use area. Swimming, boating, fishing and hiking are close at hand, and a general store rents kayaks and paddleboards.

On the Collings Mountain Trail stands an inactive Bigfoot trap built in 1974; baited for six years, it caught only bears.
excerpt: Jackson Campground sits on the Applegate River north of the Red Buttes Wilderness, with 8 tent-only sites, 3 dry RV sites and a group site beside a day-use area
note: $30 per night, $75 group site, $5 extra vehicle. Reserve at Recreation.gov (two-night minimum on weekends). Drinking water, flush toilets, boat ramp. Trailers not recommended (tight corners, short spurs). Walkways are eroded and hard for mobility devices. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: 10250 Upper Applegate Rd, about 7 miles south of Ruch, OR

title: Mill Creek Campground
contentHtml: Mill Creek Campground has 10 shaded campsites beside Mill Creek, with fishing and swimming.
excerpt: Mill Creek Campground has 10 shaded campsites beside Mill Creek, with fishing and swimming.
note: $15 per night, $7 extra vehicle. No drinking water (treat surface water). Vault toilet, garbage service. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 030, about 1 mile off Highway 62, 2 miles north of Prospect, OR

title: Natural Bridge Campground
contentHtml: Natural Bridge Campground has 17 sites shaded by conifers along the Upper Rogue River, beside the Natural Bridge interpretive site, with fishing, swimming and hiking. The Rogue Gorge and Upper Rogue trails start from the campground.
excerpt: Natural Bridge Campground has 17 sites shaded by conifers along the Upper Rogue River, beside the Natural Bridge interpretive site, with fishing, swimming and h
note: First come, first served. $15 per night, $7 extra vehicle. No drinking water (treat surface water). Vault toilets, garbage service. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 8:00 AM; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Highway 62, about 11 miles north of Prospect, OR

title: North Fork Campground
contentHtml: North Fork Campground is a small campground of 9 sites in old-growth forest near Fish Lake, with fishing and swimming. The Fish Lake Trail starts across the road, and the Mt. McLoughlin, Brown Mountain and Pacific Crest trails are nearby.
excerpt: North Fork Campground is a small campground of 9 sites in old-growth forest near Fish Lake, with fishing and swimming. The Fish Lake Trail starts across the roa
note: First come, first served. $16 per night. Drinking water, vault toilets, garbage service. From Medford, take Highway 62 to Highway 140, then 28 miles east to FR 37. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 37, 1 mile south of Highway 140, near Fish Lake, OR

title: River Bridge Campground
contentHtml: River Bridge Campground has nine campsites beside the Upper Rogue River, two of them for OHV campers with access to the Prospect OHV trail system. The Upper Rogue River Trail starts from the parking lot, with sandy spots along the river nearby.
excerpt: River Bridge Campground has nine campsites beside the Upper Rogue River, two of them for OHV campers with access to the Prospect OHV trail system. The Upper Rog
note: $15 per night, $7 extra vehicle. No drinking water (treat surface water). Vault toilet, garbage service. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 8:00 AM; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 6210, 1 mile off Highway 62, about 4 miles north of Prospect, OR

title: Squaw Lakes Campground
contentHtml:
Acorn Woman Lakes Campground has walk-in tent sites in mixed-conifer forest on the banks of the Acorn Woman Lakes, most at the water's edge: 10 individual sites, 5 group sites and 10 picnic sites, 0.25 to 1.5 miles from the parking area.

Drinking water, vault toilets, picnic tables and fire rings are provided. From Ruch, take Upper Applegate Road about 14 miles to Applegate Lake, then Forest Road 1075 8.5 miles.
excerpt: Acorn Woman Lakes Campground has walk-in tent sites in mixed-conifer forest on the banks of the Acorn Woman Lakes, most at the water's edge: 10 individual sites
note: $25 per night single site, $75 group site, $5 extra vehicle, $7 day use; fees early May to mid- September, free with no services November to mid-May. Vehicles stay in the lot; carry gear in. Lake levels are low after a record-low snowpack.
address: End of Forest Road 1075, 8.5 miles past Applegate Lake, Applegate Recreation Area, OR

title: Union Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Union Creek Campground has 74 sites in old-growth forest in the Union Creek Historic District, where Union Creek runs through camp to meet the Rogue River. Three full-hookup RV sites sit outside the main loop.

Union Creek Resort, for snacks and a hot meal, is within walking distance, and the Union Creek and Upper Rogue River trails are nearby.
excerpt: Union Creek Campground has 74 sites in old-growth forest in the Union Creek Historic District, where Union Creek runs through camp to meet the Rogue River. Thre
note: Closed for the season. $22 per night, $35 with electric hookup, $5 extra vehicle. Reserve at Recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777. Drinking water, vault toilets, host, firewood for sale. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 8:00 AM; dogs on leash.
address: Highway 62, about 55.8 miles from Medford, through the Union Creek Wayside parking area, Union Creek, OR

title: Watkins Campground
contentHtml: Watkins Campground on Applegate Lake has 14 tent sites and a group site for 20 to 50 people, with wheelchair-accessible facilities.
excerpt: Watkins Campground on Applegate Lake has 14 tent sites and a group site for 20 to 50 people, with wheelchair-accessible facilities.
note: $20 per night in peak season (early May to mid-September), $5 extra vehicle; free off-season, when it is walk-in only with no services. No drinking water. Vault toilets; garbage in season only. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Upper Applegate Road, 18.5 miles south of Ruch, 3 miles past Hart-Tish Park, OR

title: Whiskey Springs Campground
contentHtml: Whiskey Springs Campground is a quiet, secluded campground of 34 sites on the Old Military Road that once supplied Fort Klamath, a short distance from Willow Lake. A one-mile interpretive loop trail circles through camp, and the Mt. McLoughlin Trail is nearby.
excerpt: Whiskey Springs Campground is a quiet, secluded campground of 34 sites on the Old Military Road that once supplied Fort Klamath, a short distance from Willow La
note: $16 per night, $5 extra vehicle. Reserve at Recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777. No drinking water (treat surface water). Vault toilets, garbage service. Trailers over 28 feet not recommended. Quiet hours 10:00 PM - 6:00 AM; fires in fire rings only; no fireworks; dogs on leash; 14-day stay limit.
address: Forest Road 3065, 0.3 mile off County Road 821, 9 miles past Butte Falls, OR

title: Willow Prairie Horse Campground
imageAlt: Saddle and horse at a corral

banner.alt: Saddle and horse at a corral

contentHtml:
Willow Prairie Horse Camp sits in tall timber at 4,400 feet just southwest of Mount McLoughlin, beside a meadow. Converted to a horse camp in 1990 with help from the Coalition of Equestrian Clubs, it has 19 miles of connected riding trails.

Its 11 large sites have corrals, picnic tables and fire rings with grills, with a vault toilet and a horse watering trough. A nearby wetland with beaver ponds draws sandhill cranes, geese, ducks, elk and deer, and the 1924 Willow Prairie Guard Station stands at the meadow's edge. Fish Lake is about 10 minutes away.
excerpt: Willow Prairie Horse Camp sits in tall timber at 4,400 feet just southwest of Mount McLoughlin, beside a meadow. Converted to a horse camp in 1990 with help fro
note: Reserve at Recreation.gov. Extra vehicles pay at the kiosk. Certified weed-free feed only. Manure trailer on site. From Highway 140, take County Road 821 about 2 miles to FR 3738, west 1.3 miles to FR 3735, then left.
address: Forest Road 3735, off FR 3738 and County Road 821, near Fish Lake, OR

title: Kenneth Denman Wildlife Area
contentHtml:
The Kenneth Denman Wildlife Area provides water developments for migrating and nesting waterfowl and habitat for upland birds. Kiosks offer maps and information, and the area is popular for wildlife viewing, fishing and hunting in season.

The 0.7-mile Denman Interpretive Trail loops through six ecosystems and can be reached from Tou Velle Road and neighboring Tou Velle State Park on the Rogue River. Wildlife includes red-tailed hawks, kestrels, osprey, otters, beavers, black-tailed deer, game birds, waterfowl and warm-water fish. The land was first home to the Takelma people, later served as a World War II training camp, and became a wildlife area in 1954.
excerpt: The Kenneth Denman Wildlife Area provides water developments for migrating and nesting waterfowl and habitat for upland birds. Kiosks offer maps and information
note: A Wildlife Area Parking Permit is required. Camp host and restrooms on site. From I-5 exit 33, go east on Pine Street, north on Table Rock Road, then left on E. Gregory Road at the headquarters sign.
address: 1495 E. Gregory Road, Central Point, OR 97502
photoCredit: Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife

title: Barr Creek Falls
imageAlt: Barr Creek Falls in early July

banner.alt: Barr Creek Falls in early July

contentHtml:
Barr Creek Falls is a 240-foot, three-tiered horsetail waterfall in the Rogue River Canyon just outside Prospect. Barr Creek drops over a mostly tree-hidden 60-foot fall, cascades 30 feet, then plunges 150 feet to the canyon floor.

The creek carries modest water, so the falls are most forceful in spring and thin to a veil by late summer. With enough flow, a second strand forms beside the final drop.
excerpt: Barr Creek Falls is a 240-foot, three-tiered horsetail waterfall in the Rogue River Canyon just outside Prospect. Barr Creek drops over a mostly tree-hidden 60-
note: From Highway 62, take Mill Creek Road through Prospect about 1.5 miles to the Mill Creek Falls Trailhead, then follow the trail downhill about 0.5 mile to an unguarded overlook at the canyon rim.
address: Mill Creek Falls Trailhead, Mill Creek Road, Prospect, OR

title: Bybee Falls
contentHtml: Bybee Falls, also known as Lost Falls and Secret Falls, is a 120-foot waterfall on Lost Creek in the Rogue River watershed. It drops in two tiers, the tallest about 80 feet, at an elevation of about 4,057 feet.
excerpt: Bybee Falls, also known as Lost Falls and Secret Falls, is a 120-foot waterfall on Lost Creek in the Rogue River watershed. It drops in two tiers, the tallest a
note: No published trail directions.
address: Lost Creek, near Grizzly Peak, Jackson County, OR

title: Mill Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Mill Creek Falls plunges 173 feet into the Rogue River Gorge and is the centerpiece of the Mill Creek Falls Scenic Area near the town of Prospect.

Mill Creek's flow changes with the seasons, but the falls look much the same year-round, making it a good destination at any time.
excerpt: Mill Creek Falls plunges 173 feet into the Rogue River Gorge and is the centerpiece of the Mill Creek Falls Scenic Area near the town of Prospect.
note: From Highway 62, turn east onto Mill Creek Road and follow it through Prospect 1.5 miles to the marked trailhead. The falls come into view after a hike of just under half a mile; the trail network can be confusing, so follow the old roadbed and listen for the falls.
address: Mill Creek Falls Trailhead, Mill Creek Road, Prospect, OR

title: Prospect Falls
contentHtml:
Prospect Falls is a 50-foot series of cascades on the Rogue River just outside Prospect, where the river works through a wall of block and slide rock, drops over small steps and spreads into a long boulder field.

A hydroelectric diversion just upstream usually reduces the flow, so the falls are best when the river is running high.
excerpt: Prospect Falls is a 50-foot series of cascades on the Rogue River just outside Prospect, where the river works through a wall of block and slide rock, drops ove
note: Follow Mill Creek Road through Prospect about one mile and park in the large turnout on the left before the Rogue River bridge. Walk about 100 feet through the woods to an old roadbed, then about 500 feet toward the river until the canyon comes into view.
address: Mill Creek Road at the Rogue River bridge, Prospect, OR

title: Agate Lake
contentHtml:
Agate Lake is a 216-acre Jackson County reservoir about 14 miles northeast of Medford, with roughly three miles of shoreline and wide views of the Rogue Valley and Mount McLoughlin. Kayaks, canoes and paddleboards share the water with electric-motor boats only, so it stays quiet with few wakes.

Its modest size suits a casual flatwater paddle, and the shallow, vegetated margins draw birds and other wildlife. Mornings are usually calmest, before afternoon breezes develop.
excerpt: Agate Lake is a 216-acre Jackson County reservoir about 14 miles northeast of Medford, with roughly three miles of shoreline and wide views of the Rogue Valley
note: Internal-combustion motors are prohibited. Day-use parking, boat ramp and vault toilets; no parking fee. No campground or services, so bring water and supplies. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Water levels change through the season and low water can close ramps, so check the Oregon State Marine Board access report before you go. Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Agate Lake County Park, Highway 140 near Eagle Point, OR

title: Applegate Lake
contentHtml:
Applegate Lake is a mountain reservoir with forested shorelines and views toward the Siskiyou Mountains. Its branching arms and coves invite exploring by kayak, paddleboard or canoe, and it feels quieter than the more developed reservoirs in Southern Oregon.

Hart-Tish Park offers a boat ramp, parking, restrooms, drinking water, a general store, seasonal kayak and SUP rentals, camping, swimming and picnic space. An 18.5-mile trail system circles the lake, including the Collins Mountain Trail near Hart-Tish.
excerpt: Applegate Lake is a mountain reservoir with forested shorelines and views toward the Siskiyou Mountains. Its branching arms and coves invite exploring by kayak,
note: Motorboats are limited to 10 mph. When other ramps no longer reach the water, use the French Gulch Boat Ramp. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Water levels change through the season and low water can close ramps, so check the Oregon State Marine Board access report before you go. Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Hart-Tish Park, Applegate Lake, near Jacksonville, OR

title: Emigrant Lake
contentHtml:
Emigrant Lake is a reservoir in the rolling hills just outside Ashland, offering kayaking, paddleboarding and canoeing without a long drive into the mountains. The open hillsides give it a different feel from Oregon's forested mountain lakes, and its arms and coves contrast with the larger open water.

Paddlers launch from the North and West launch areas, close to downtown Ashland, Rogue Valley wineries and hiking.
excerpt: Emigrant Lake is a reservoir in the rolling hills just outside Ashland, offering kayaking, paddleboarding and canoeing without a long drive into the mountains.
note: Motorboats share the lake; slow-no-wake zones are marked in parts of Hill Creek Arm, Emigrant Creek Arm and Spillway Cove. The open setting brings wind, sun and summer heat. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Water levels change through the season and low water can close ramps, so check the Oregon State Marine Board access report before you go. Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Emigrant Lake Recreation Area (Jackson County Parks), near Ashland, OR

title: Fish Lake
contentHtml:
Fish Lake is a 483-acre mountain reservoir at about 4,639 feet, between Mount McLoughlin and Brown Mountain. Old-growth forest surrounds much of the recreation area, and a roughly 2,000-year-old lava flow from Brown Mountain borders the southern shore.

A 10 mph limit on motorboats keeps it calmer than many mixed-use reservoirs. The Forest Service boating site has a ramp, parking, drinking water and restrooms in season, and Fish Lake Resort on the lake offers lodging, camping, a store, cafe and boating services.
excerpt: Fish Lake is a 483-acre mountain reservoir at about 4,639 feet, between Mount McLoughlin and Brown Mountain. Old-growth forest surrounds much of the recreation
note: Motorboats are limited to 10 mph. Water stays cold at this elevation and mountain weather changes quickly. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Water levels change through the season and low water can close ramps, so check the Oregon State Marine Board access report before you go. Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Fish Lake Boating Site, via Fish Lake Campground, Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest, OR

title: Howard Prairie Lake
contentHtml:
Howard Prairie Lake is a high-elevation reservoir in the Cascades east of Ashland, with broad open water, forested shorelines, coves and views toward Mount McLoughlin.

Klum Landing Park, a Jackson County park with a two-lane boat ramp, has day-use parking, picnic tables, restrooms, showers and seasonal camping. Howard Prairie Resort has a second ramp, marina, campground, store and cafe; Willow Point and Grizzly Park offer carry-in launching.
excerpt: Howard Prairie Lake is a high-elevation reservoir in the Cascades east of Ashland, with broad open water, forested shorelines, coves and views toward Mount McLo
note: Parking at Klum Landing is $6 per vehicle per day. Motorboats are allowed. Mornings are usually calmest; afternoon wind can make exposed water rough. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Water levels change through the season and low water can close ramps, so check the Oregon State Marine Board access report before you go. Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Klum Landing Park, about 28 miles east of Ashland, OR

title: Hyatt Lake
imageAlt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin

banner.alt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin

contentHtml:
Hyatt Lake is a reservoir at about 5,200 feet in the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument, with forested surroundings and views toward Mount McLoughlin. A 10 mph motorboat limit makes it pleasant for kayaks, paddleboards and canoes.

Hyatt Lake Campground has developed boat ramps and docks, and Wildcat Campground offers a more primitive launch. The area has restrooms, picnic areas and camping, and the Pacific Crest Trail passes through.
excerpt: Hyatt Lake is a reservoir at about 5,200 feet in the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument, with forested surroundings and views toward Mount McLoughlin. A 10 mph
note: Motorboats are limited to 10 mph. Day-use permits are sold at self-service pay stations. Ramps and campgrounds operate seasonally. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Water levels change through the season and low water can close ramps, so check the Oregon State Marine Board access report before you go. Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Hyatt Lake Recreation Area (BLM), about 20 miles east of Ashland, OR

title: Lost Creek Lake
contentHtml:
Lost Creek Lake is a large reservoir on the upper Rogue River ringed by forested hills, with open water, a branching shoreline and coves to explore close to shore.

Takelma Park has a paved boat ramp, day-use parking, restrooms, covered picnic tables and fishing access. Joseph Stewart County Park, on another part of the lake, has more than 200 campsites, a swim area, marina, playground and off-leash dog area, and more than 30 miles of trails surround the lake.
excerpt: Lost Creek Lake is a large reservoir on the upper Rogue River ringed by forested hills, with open water, a branching shoreline and coves to explore close to sho
note: Motorboats are allowed; no motors between the breakwaters at the Joseph Stewart swim area, and slow-no-wake in the marked Takelma ramp cove, the Lost Creek Arm above the narrows and upstream of Peyton Bridge. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Water levels change through the season and low water can close ramps, so check the Oregon State Marine Board access report before you go. Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Takelma Park (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers), near William L. Jess Dam, about 28 miles northeast of Medford, OR

title: Willow Lake
contentHtml:
Willow Lake is a wooded reservoir near Mount McLoughlin, about 7.5 miles east of Butte Falls, with open water, shallow edges and sheltered coves. The southwest cove is the most relaxed area to paddle.

The county park has picnic areas, restrooms, a playground, swimming, fishing and hiking, plus 63 campsites, cabins, yurts and a group camp. The campground typically runs mid-April into early October.
excerpt: Willow Lake is a wooded reservoir near Mount McLoughlin, about 7.5 miles east of Butte Falls, with open water, shallow edges and sheltered coves. The southwest
note: Motorboats are limited to 10 mph south of the marked buoy line, and the southwest cove is slow-no- wake. When the lake is low, carry down from the auxiliary-ramp area. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Water levels change through the season and low water can close ramps, so check the Oregon State Marine Board access report before you go. Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Willow Lake County Park, 7800 Fish Lake Road, near Butte Falls, OR

title: Mount McLoughlin
imageAlt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin (area photo)

banner.alt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin (area photo)

contentHtml:
Mount McLoughlin, 9,493 feet, is the highest point in Jackson County and a non-technical but arduous climb in the Sky Lakes Wilderness. The Mt. McLoughlin Trail gains about 4,000 feet from the trailhead to the summit, joining the Pacific Crest Trail for a stretch before climbing through boulder fields above timberline.

The trailhead has parking for 15-20 vehicles (no stock trailers), a vault toilet and picnic tables; camping is not allowed. Horses are not recommended above the Pacific Crest Trail junction.
excerpt: Mount McLoughlin, 9,493 feet, is the highest point in Jackson County and a non-technical but arduous climb in the Sky Lakes Wilderness. The Mt. McLoughlin Trail
note: Day use $5 per vehicle or $30 per year; recreation passes accepted. No water at the trailhead or on the trail. Summit weather can turn to cold wind, rain, lightning or snow. Hikers often get lost on the descent: avoid the sandy cinder slope on the south side, return along the ridge and keep the cairns or poles in sight. From Medford, take OR 62 to White City, then OR 140 east about 35.7 miles to Forest Road 3661.
address: Mt. McLoughlin Trailhead, Forest Road 3650 off Forest Road 3661 (Four Mile Lake Road), north of Highway 140, OR

title: Pacific Crest Trail
imageAlt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin, near the trail

banner.alt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin, near the trail

contentHtml:
The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail runs 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada through California, Oregon and Washington, managed by the Forest Service with the Pacific Crest Trail Association. Its roughly 455-mile Oregon section is the shortest and easiest on the trail, from near Siskiyou Summit to the Bridge of the Gods over the Columbia River.

In Jackson County the Oregon section begins at the California border near Siskiyou Summit, passes Hyatt Lake in the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument and runs north past Mount McLoughlin into the Sky Lakes Wilderness, which it crosses for about 35 miles.

address: Oregon section: California border near Ashland to the Bridge of the Gods, Cascade Locks, OR

title: Lithia Park
contentHtml:
Lithia Park, opened in 1916 on the site of a former mill, covers nearly 100 acres of hilly ground along Ashland Creek, next to downtown shops and the Oregon Shakespeare Festival grounds. Visitors come to relax, people- watch or sip from the lithium-rich fountains that gave the park its name.

A paved path follows the creek past the Lower Duck Pond, Lithia Rose Garden, Butler-Perozzi Fountain, Butler Bandshell, the Japanese Garden and the Upper Duck Pond, where deer often forage at dusk; narrower canyon trails continue beyond. A mile-long nature walk identifies dozens of tree species, and volunteer naturalists lead free guided walks at 10 a.m. several days a week.
excerpt: Lithia Park, opened in 1916 on the site of a former mill, covers nearly 100 acres of hilly ground along Ashland Creek, next to downtown shops and the Oregon Sha
note: Playground, sand volleyball, ice-skating rink, tennis and pickleball courts, restrooms, picnic sites and parking. A free David's Chair all-terrain track chair is available for the sloped and dirt paths. Granite Street Reservoir at the south end has a swimming lawn (no lifeguards).
address: Winburn Way, downtown Ashland, OR 97520
photoCredit: Carol Barrington; Sean Bagshaw, Outdoor Exposure Photography; Travel Oregon

title: Bear Creek Greenway
contentHtml:
The Bear Creek Greenway is a 20-mile paved, multi-use trail linking Ashland, Talent, Phoenix, Medford and Central Point along Bear Creek, running from the Ashland Dog Park to Dean Creek Frontage Road near the Seven Oaks Interchange north of Central Point.

Separated from car traffic except for two at-grade road crossings, it is popular for walking, cycling, bird watching and wildlife viewing. Parks along the route provide parking, restrooms and drinking water.

note: Paved and car-free, suitable for wheelchairs and strollers. Segments occasionally close for flooding or construction; Jackson County posts status on its Greenway pages.
address: Southern trailhead: W Nevada St at Almeda Dr (Ashland Dog Park), Ashland, OR

title: Cascade Siskiyou Scenic Bikeway
contentHtml:
The Cascade Siskiyou Scenic Bikeway is a 55-mile loop from Ashland with about 5,000 feet of steep, winding climbing, rated extreme. It rises from the Bear Creek Valley through oak savannah into fir and pine forest, past Emigrant Lake and through the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument to 4,551-foot Green Springs Summit.

Highlights include views of Pilot Rock, spring wildflowers, an optional out-and-back to Tub Springs State Wayside, Hyatt Reservoir with views of Mount McLoughlin, alpine meadows at Lily Glen and Buck Prairie, and a winding 13-mile descent back to Ashland. Campgrounds near Hyatt Reservoir and Howard Prairie Lake make it a two-day bike-camping trip.

note: Signed counter-clockwise only. Roads have narrow shoulders and farm equipment. Check road conditions on TripCheck.com or call ODOT District 8 at 541-774-6299.

title: Rabbit Ears

gallery.alt: Rabbit Ears seen through the woods

contentHtml:
Rabbit Ears is a 30-mile, all-gravel loop with about 4,000 feet of climbing through old-growth forest with huge trees, past the Rabbit Ears volcanic formation and up to Hershberger Lookout. Rhododendron forest, streams and wildflowers, including wild dogwoods, line the way.

Most roads are fast and in good shape, but about 8 miles are rugged and steep, and the final half mile to the lookout is rutted and loose at 10-15% grades. The opening climb gains about 2,800 feet over 10 miles; the last 8 miles roll.
excerpt: Rabbit Ears is a 30-mile, all-gravel loop with about 4,000 feet of climbing through old-growth forest with huge trees, past the Rabbit Ears volcanic formation a
note: Moderate difficulty, extremely remote; navigation requires attention. Tires 40mm or wider suggested. No food or water on the route; Union Creek Resort is about 2 miles from the start. Check for downed trees.
address: Dirt pullout off Highway 230 at the Rogue River bridge, near Union Creek, OR

title: Elk Creek
contentHtml:
Elk Creek is a major tributary of the Rogue River near Shady Cove, flowing about 18 miles from the high Cascades to the Rogue just below Lost Creek Dam. On March 12, 2019, 7.3 miles from the Flat Creek confluence to the Army Corps of Engineers boundary were designated Scenic.

An old road grade beside the creek is now a year-round day-use path for sightseeing, biking, hiking and running, and deep swimming holes draw visitors in summer. Since the Elk Creek Dam was notched in 2008, native chinook, coho, steelhead and lamprey move freely again, and the watershed supports Roosevelt elk winter range.

title: Jenny Creek
contentHtml:
Jenny Creek flows through the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument and the Soda Mountain Wilderness before joining the Klamath River in northern California. On March 12, 2019, 17.6 miles to the Oregon- California line were designated Scenic.

Lying where the Klamath, Cascade and Great Basin regions meet, the creek has remarkable biodiversity: scattered old growth, wetlands, two high waterfalls, the endemic Jenny Creek sucker and redband trout, and winter range for deer and elk. People have lived here for over 6,000 years, and part of the 1846 Applegate Trail crosses the watershed. Visitors come for hunting, fishing, camping, hiking and kayaking.

title: Rogue (Upper) River
contentHtml:
The Upper Rogue River was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 40.3 miles (6.1 wild, 34.2 scenic) from the Crater Lake National Park boundary to Prospect. About 27 miles, down to Prospect, are in Jackson County.

Fed by Cascade snowmelt and springs, the river runs through pumice flats, deep gorges and chutes; in one two-mile stretch it has cut more than 200 feet into Mazama pumice. It is a prized steelhead and salmon fishery, and the Upper Rogue River Trail, a National Recreation Trail, follows its full length.

At Natural Bridge the river flows through a lava tube.
excerpt: The Upper Rogue River was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 40.3 miles (6.1 wild, 34.2 scenic) from the Crater Lake National Park boun
note: Boating is for experienced paddlers only, and the wild section is generally not recommended for boating. Managed by the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest.
address: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest: 3040 Biddle Rd, Medford, OR 97504

title: Spring Creek
contentHtml:
Spring Creek runs 1.1 miles from its source at Shoat Springs to Jenny Creek in the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument, designated Scenic on March 12, 2019. Its cold, clear water supports an endemic population of redband trout.

Ponderosa pine and Douglas fir, grasslands and meadows frame the spring-fed stream, home to endemic snails, the northern Pacific pond turtle and diverse birdlife.

note: The creek is almost entirely on private land with no public access; please respect property boundaries. Managed by the BLM Medford District Office.
address: Shoat Springs to Jenny Creek, Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument, OR

title: Rogue-Umpqua Scenic Byway
contentHtml:
The Rogue-Umpqua Scenic Byway, a National Scenic Byway, runs 172 miles (5-7 hours) from Roseburg up the North Umpqua River, past Diamond Lake, and down the Upper Rogue River to Gold Hill. The North Umpqua stretch is called the Highway of Waterfalls, with more than 15 cascades.

Highlights include the Winchester Dam fish ladder viewing window, the Douglas County Museum, Colliding Rivers near Glide, the 79-mile North Umpqua Trail, Toketee Falls, 272-foot Watson Falls, Lemolo Lake and Diamond Lake. On the Rogue side are Rogue Gorge, Natural Bridge, Lost Creek Lake and Cole Rivers Hatchery.

June through October brings clear roads, fair weather and long days.

note: Check wildfire and road conditions before you go.
address: Roseburg (I-5 and OR 138) to Gold Hill (I-5 and OR 234), OR

title: Rogue Valley Food Trail
contentHtml:
The Rogue Valley Food Trail is a self-guided culinary journey through the valley's farmland, open year-round to explore at your own pace for a day or a week. Stops include farm stands, u-pick farms, farm-to-table restaurants, farmers' markets, craft beverage makers, chocolatiers, cheese makers, bakeries and cafes, all committed to sourcing products grown, raised or made in Southern Oregon.

Seasonal highlights include lavender (April to July), pears (July to September), apples (August to November) and year-round farmers' markets. Annual events include the Oregon Chocolate Festival, Oregon Cheese Festival, Rogue Valley Farm Tour and the Brine, Brew & Barrel Fermentation Festival.
excerpt: The Rogue Valley Food Trail is a self-guided culinary journey through the valley's farmland, open year-round to explore at your own pace for a day or a week. St
note: High season is typically April to November; check hours and seasons with each business. A downloadable brochure is available from Travel Southern Oregon.
address: Rogue Valley, Southern Oregon (start anywhere along the trail)

title: Antelope Creek Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
The Antelope Creek Covered Bridge is a 58-foot queenpost truss built in 1922, which originally spanned Antelope Creek about 10 miles southeast of Eagle Point. In August 1987 volunteers loaded it onto a makeshift trailer and hauled it into Eagle Point, where it now crosses Little Butte Creek as a pedestrian bridge.

During the rebuild, arched openings were cut into each side so schoolchildren could be watched crossing; the bridge has since been re-sided to match its original design, with ribbon openings under the eaves. Listed on the National Register in 1979 and removed after the move, it was relisted in 2012.

title: Lost Creek Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
At 39 feet, the Lost Creek Covered Bridge is the shortest covered bridge in Oregon. Its official construction date is 1919, but many locals believe it dates to 1878-1881, which would make it the state's oldest; a sign on the bridge reads "Lost Creek Bridge, built about 1881." It has a shingle roof, flying buttress braces, diagonal plank flooring and hand-hewn truss members.

Closed to vehicles in 1979, when a concrete span was built alongside, it is now pedestrian-only beside the Walch Memorial Wayside Park, with picnic tables, a bandstand and flower gardens. It nearly washed away in the 1964 Christmas flood; residents prayed through the night and the water receded by morning. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.

note: From Highway 140, take Lake Creek Loop Road and South Fork Little Butte Creek Road south through Lake Creek, then turn south on Lost Creek Road for about half a mile.

title: McKee Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
The McKee Covered Bridge is a 122-foot Howe truss over the Applegate River, built in 1917 by Jason Hartman and his son Wesley on land donated by Aldelbert "Deb" McKee. It carried mining and logging traffic and served as a rest stop roughly halfway between Jacksonville and the Blue Ledge Copper Mine.

Declared unsafe for vehicles in 1956, it has been pedestrian-only ever since, with flying buttresses, daylighting windows at the roofline and a shingle roof. Local groups and the McKee Committee have raised funds to preserve it, and the McKee Picnic Ground sits at its west end. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.

note: From Medford, take Highway 238 west through Jacksonville to Ruch, then go south on Applegate Road about 8.5 miles.

title: Wimer Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
The Wimer Covered Bridge carries East Evans Creek Road over Evans Creek in the rural community of Wimer. A first covered bridge was built here in 1892, replaced in 1927 by an 85-foot queenpost truss built by the Hartman Brothers of Jacksonville and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.

That bridge collapsed into the creek in 2003. Federal funds and local labor built a look-alike replacement, opened in February 2008, which carries one-way traffic with a 10-ton load limit.

contentHtml:
Buck Prairie Sno-Park is the main trailhead for the Buck Prairie Nordic Trail System in the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument: 32.8 miles of connected trails for cross-country skiing, snowshoeing and snowmobiling, some groomed by the Southern Oregon Nordic Club.

Trails range from easy runs like Bullwinkle's Run and Ryan's Trail to the difficult 9.6-mile Table Mountain loop, and Homer's Hide Away is a dog-friendly loop. The Table Mountain Winter Play Area has a sled hill for tubing, and clear days bring views of the Rogue Valley, the Cascades, Mount McLoughlin and Mount Shasta.

A warming shelter with a fireplace and firewood, picnic tables and vault toilets are on site.

title: Mt. Ashland Ski Area
contentHtml:
Mt. Ashland Ski Area sits at the highest point in the Siskiyou Mountains, at 7,533 feet, and has been run since 1964 by the Mt. Ashland Association, a community nonprofit. It offers 240 acres and 44 runs served by four chairlifts, with more than 265 inches of average snowfall.

A full rental and tuning shop, retail shop, ski and snowboard school and the historic lodge with the Gemütlichkeit Grill round out the mountain. In summer it hosts events, Alpine Adventure Camps, disc golf, hiking and running.

title: Jackson Wellsprings
contentHtml:
Jackson Wellsprings is a 30-plus-acre property with natural mineral hot springs, 2.5 miles from downtown Ashland. Its Olympic-sized swimming pool is fed by 80,000 gallons a day of naturally alkaline mineral water, alongside a warm soaking pool, private tubs, a steam room and a sauna.

The grounds include gardens, a temple and an events center, plus tent and car camping, tipis, glamping and an RV park. In 1862 Eugenia Jackson dedicated the waters to "natatorium and sanitarium purposes."

title: Lithia Springs Resort
contentHtml:
Lithia Springs Resort is a day spa and resort 3 miles from downtown Ashland, with 46 studios, bungalows and suites. Sulfur-rich mineral springs deep beneath the resort are piped to private soaking tubs and mineral showers, included for all resort guests.

The grounds hold a seasonal outdoor saline pool and Jacuzzi, koi ponds, gardens, a gazebo and aspen grove, a tea room, library and fire pit, cruiser bikes, the Waterstone Spa and a Wine Garden tasting room pouring Applegate Valley wines.

note: Mineral waters are an amenity for overnight guests.

title: Natural Bridge
contentHtml:
At Natural Bridge, the entire Rogue River plunges underground into an ancient lava tube and flows out of sight for about 250 feet before re-emerging downstream, beneath the natural bridge formed by the tube's roof.

An interpretive trail with signs explaining the area's natural history offers good views of the river. The flagstone overlook with its low basalt wall was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1933-34.

note: Part of the Upper Rogue Wild and Scenic River along Highway 62 between Farewell Bend and Natural Bridge. High Cascades Ranger District.
address: Natural Bridge Interpretive Site, off Highway 62 near Union Creek, OR 97536

title: Oregon Vortex
contentHtml:
The Oregon Vortex, open to the public since 1930, is an area of strange visual and perceptual phenomena on Sardine Creek outside Gold Hill, where objects seem to roll uphill and people appear to change height depending on where they stand.

At its heart is the House of Mystery, built in 1904 by the Old Grey Eagle Mining Company as an assay office, which later slid from its foundation and came to rest at an odd angle. Geologist and mining engineer John Litster developed the site and ran thousands of experiments there until his death in 1959.

title: Rogue Gorge Viewpoint
contentHtml:
At the Rogue Gorge, the young Rogue River funnels into a narrow, turbulent chasm of black lava, racing far below the rim.

An interpretive trail with signs explaining the gorge's natural history provides good views of the river. It is part of the Upper Rogue Wild and Scenic River, which runs beside Highway 62 between Farewell Bend and Natural Bridge.
excerpt: At the Rogue Gorge, the young Rogue River funnels into a narrow, turbulent chasm of black lava, racing far below the rim.
note: High Cascades Ranger District.
address: Rogue Gorge Interpretive Site, Highway 62 at Union Creek, OR

title: Acorn Woman (Squaw) Peak Lookout
contentHtml:
Acorn Woman Peak Lookout, formerly Squaw Peak Lookout, is a historic L-4 style cabin built in 1942 and listed on the National Historic Site Registry. Glass windows on all sides look out over the Siskiyou Mountains and steep drop-offs.

The 14 x 14-foot room sleeps one or two and is rented in the snow-free season. It holds a small table, a working Osborne Firefinder, a broom, mop and fire extinguisher, and maps of the area; a primitive vault toilet and fire pit are nearby.
excerpt: Acorn Woman Peak Lookout, formerly Squaw Peak Lookout, is a historic L-4 style cabin built in 1942 and listed on the National Historic Site Registry. Glass wind
note: Reservations on Recreation.gov; maximum stay 5 nights. No water: bring drinking and washing water, a stove, light, sleeping bag and pad. Pack it in, pack it out. The final mile is behind a locked gate (combination with your reservation); the access road is steep and winding and may not suit passenger cars or large trucks. From Ruch, take Upper Applegate Road 10.2 miles, Forest Road 20 for 4.1 miles, then Forest Road 2010 for 5.1 miles.
address: Forest Road 2010 (Hanley Gulch Road), Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest; ranger station: 6941 Upper Applegate Road, Jacksonville, OR 97530

title: Art Bop Beer Company
contentHtml:
Art Bop Beer Co is an independent, award-winning small-batch brewery and community hub with local art, live music, vinyl, games and events. Owner-brewers Dave and Kimber began homebrewing in 2013 for band rehearsals and went professional in 2018 in a converted 1960s auto garage.

In 2026 the brewery and beer garden moved to 102 Talent Ave in the historic district. Year-round flagship ales and rotating seasonals are joined by European-style eats, kombucha, wine and sodas, with indoor and outdoor seating, a gallery and a dog-friendly outdoor space.

title: Caldera

Caldera Brewing Company is an independent, locally owned production brewery and restaurant in Ashland, brewing award-winning craft beer since 1997. The name refers to the boiling kettle where beer takes shape.

Fifty taps pour house beers alongside hard seltzers, NA beers, craft sodas and waters, served with upscale pub food in a casual, family-friendly setting with a dog-friendly patio and private event space.

title: Ferment and Fire Restaurant and Brewery
contentHtml:
Ferment & Fire is a pizza and beer destination opened by four longtime friends after 15 years of planning. Beer is brewed on site over three to seven weeks with style-specific yeasts and hops for crisp, clean, drinkable pours.

New York-style pizzas use dough fermented for five days and baked in an oven with precise top and bottom heat control.

title: Walkabout Brewing Company
contentHtml:
Walkabout Brewing Company has brewed craft beer in Southern Oregon for over 20 years on its original, home-made 7-barrel system, making the beers its brewers love and sharing them with others.

Flagships include Worker's Pale Ale, Jabberwocky Strong Ale, Wallaby White and Platypus Porter, along with rotating IPAs, stouts and local collaborations, served in the tasting room and The Outback.

contentHtml: Celestina Vineyard is a Rogue Valley grape-growing vineyard in Medford owned by John and Sherry Pratt, who bought the property in 2004, planted vines in 2007 and brought in their first harvest in 2009. After a brief stint making wine, they chose to focus on growing grapes, including Early Muscat, for other wineries.

title: DANCIN Vineyards
contentHtml:
DANCIN Vineyards sits in the forested foothills above the Rogue Valley, minutes from Ashland, Medford and Jacksonville, with views of the Table Rocks and Mount McLoughlin and seating areas beside the vines. It makes Burgundian-style Pinot Noir and Chardonnay along with Barbera, Sangiovese, Syrah, Zinfandel and port-style wines.

The kitchen serves house-made pastas, seasonal soups and artisan pizzas from local farm ingredients, plus a three-course wine-paired menu and a rotating Sunday brunch.

title: Hummingbird Estate
contentHtml:
Hummingbird Estate is a winery, inn and event venue on a historic 1926 property just outside Jacksonville, overlooking the Rogue Valley. The tasting room pours the estate's wines seven days a week, with lawns for celebrations and a wine club with members-only events and early releases.

Upstairs in the 1926 home, the inn has five sunlit rooms, each with a king bed and private bath, handy for the Britt Festival and the Oregon Shakespeare Festival.

title: Irvine & Roberts Vineyards
contentHtml:
Irvine & Roberts is a family winery and high-elevation estate vineyard in the foothills where the Cascade and Siskiyou Mountains meet, 5 miles from downtown Ashland. Afternoon mountain breezes help preserve acidity in its estate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, along with Rosé, Pinot Meunier and traditional-method sparkling wines.

The vineyard is sustainably farmed, and the tasting room has been named one of USA Today's 10Best.

title: Kriselle Cellars
contentHtml:
Kriselle Cellars pours its wines in a hillside tasting room overlooking the estate vineyard, with shaded, misted patio seating in summer and an indoor fireplace, blankets and heaters in cooler weather.

The winery focuses on quality from the vineyard up, beginning with careful pruning and water management, and offers reds, whites, rosé and large formats.

note: Reservations encouraged, especially on weekends.

title: Naumes Crush and Fermentation

contentHtml:
Naumes Crush & Fermentation is a custom-crush winery offering "the complete winemaking experience" in a state-of-the-art facility: custom crush and fermentation, a full wine lab, storage, and beer and cider production for growers who want wines made to their specifications.

The Naumes family opened the 23,000-square-foot facility in 2015, with capacity for about 500 tons.

title: Quady North
contentHtml:
Quady North makes Rhône-style wines on a 100-acre estate in the Applegate Valley. Herb Quady founded it in 2005, clearing an old motocross track to plant Syrah, Viognier and Cabernet Franc, and today the winery makes more than thirty wines, including its signature GSM rosé, sparkling, dessert and single-vineyard bottlings.

The estate is certified LIVE sustainable, Bee Friendly and Salmon Safe, and the tasting room offers a casual, wine-centric experience with small bites and big views. Dogs and well-behaved children are welcome.

title: Schultz Glory Oaks
contentHtml:
Schultz Glory Oaks is the tasting room of Schultz Wines, established in 2010, at the Glory Oaks Vineyard and Farm in the Applegate Valley AVA. The property has been farmed organically since 2016.

Its small-lot wines, about 800 cases across 11 varietals, use native yeast and natural malolactic fermentation and are unfiltered: Tempranillo, Malbec, Viognier, Petit Verdot, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah from the lower vineyard, and Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Noir from the cooler upper vineyard.

title: Somar
contentHtml:
Somar Family Vineyards is a family winery in the Rogue Valley whose roots trace to a stone house in Portugal's Douro Valley. All fourteen of its varietals are estate grown by hand on vineyards on Griffin Creek Road and West Main Street.

Wines include sparkling Bubbly Rosé and Muscat, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, unoaked Chardonnay, Grenache, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon.

title: Troon Vineyards
contentHtml:
Troon Vineyard is a 100-acre biodynamic and organic farm and winery in the Applegate Valley, certified Demeter Biodynamic and Regenerative Organic (Gold). Alongside the vines are cider apples, a vegetable garden, hay fields, honeybees, sheep and chickens.

Wines are made minimally with native yeasts, no additives and no new oak, from the Druid's Red, White and Pink to Vermentino, amphora-aged wines, Tannat and Négrette. Troon has been nominated by Wine Enthusiast as American Winery of the Year and earns the Slow Wine Guide's Snail Award every year.

title: Upper Five Vineyard
contentHtml:
Upper Five Vineyard is an organic and biodynamic farm outside Talent, planted by Terry Sullivan and Molly Morison in 2003 on the "upper five" acres of a historic Bagley pear orchard at 1,920 feet. Sauvignon Blanc, Tempranillo and Syrah went in first, with Grenache added in 2006.

In 2005 it became the first certified organic vineyard in Southern Oregon, and it earned Demeter Biodynamic certification in 2018. Its old-world-style wines follow the motto "hands on in the vineyard, hands off in the winery."

title: Weisinger Family Winery
contentHtml:
Weisinger Family Winery is Ashland's original craft winery, making small-lot wines since 1988 exclusively from local fruit, each from a single vineyard on the estate or within 5 miles.

It specializes in Tempranillo, Syrah, Malbec, Pinot Noir, Viognier, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, heritage Gewürztraminer and signature Bordeaux-style blends, served on spacious outdoor seating with views of the hills, minutes from downtown.

title: Southern Oregon University
contentHtml: The Southern Oregon University disc golf course is a simple 9-hole, par-27 course on campus, about 2,071 feet long with holes from 188 to 300 feet. Most holes run across a sloping hillside, with Mach V baskets and dirt or mat tees.

title: The Cove @ Emigrant Lake
contentHtml:
The Emigrant Lake disc golf course is an 18-hole, par-54 course of about 5,230 feet, established in 2010, with mostly open fairways and baskets tucked among scattered oak trees. Most holes have some elevation change, and the wind is often a factor.

Rated moderate difficulty, it takes about an hour and a half to play. It is maintained by the Rogue Valley Disc Golf Club.

title: The Museum at Warm Springs
imageAlt: The Museum at Warm Springs entrance

banner.alt: The Museum at Warm Springs entrance

contentHtml:
The Museum at Warm Springs, Oregon's first tribal museum, is run by the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs and shares the traditions, cultural and artistic heritage of the Warm Springs, Wasco and Northern Paiute peoples. It opened on March 14, 1993, built to Smithsonian professional standards.

Collections highlight the mastery of traditional craftspeople, and changing exhibitions feature Native artists, such as Lillian Pitt's "Art, Memory, Home." A gift shop is on site.
excerpt: The Museum at Warm Springs, Oregon's first tribal museum, is run by the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs and shares the traditions, cultural and artistic her
note: Admission: adults $7, seniors (60+) $6, students 13-18 $4.50, children 5-12 $3.50, 4 and under and members free. Group rates at ext. 409.
address: 2189 Hwy 26, Warm Springs, OR

title: Erickson Aircraft Collection
imageAlt: Erickson Aircraft Collection hangar with Mount Jefferson

banner.alt: Erickson Aircraft Collection hangar with Mount Jefferson

gallery.alt: A vintage warbird over Central Oregon farmland

contentHtml:
The Erickson Aircraft Collection fills a 65,000-square-foot hangar at the Madras airport with more than 25 aircraft, most still in flying condition, which visitors can see up close without ropes or barriers. Jack Erickson started the collection in 1983.

Highlights include a P-38 Lightning, P-51 Mustang, Ki-43 Hayabusa, F4U Corsair, SBD Dauntless, Grumman Duck and B-17 Flying Fortress. Warbird rides can be booked.

title: Deschutes National Forest
contentHtml:
The Deschutes National Forest covers nearly 1.6 million acres on the eastern slopes of the Cascades in Central Oregon, with recreation year-round.

Highlights include Newberry National Volcanic Monument (Lava Lands Visitor Center, Lava River Cave, Lava Butte and the Newberry Caldera), the Cascade Lakes, and the Mount Jefferson, Mount Washington and Three Sisters wilderness areas.
excerpt: The Deschutes National Forest covers nearly 1.6 million acres on the eastern slopes of the Cascades in Central Oregon, with recreation year-round.
note: Some sites charge day-use fees. Central Cascades Wilderness permits are required at some trailheads in summer. Lava River Cave needs a timed-entry parking reservation.

title: Mount Hood National Forest
contentHtml:
Mt. Hood National Forest covers about 1.1 million acres just 50 miles east of Portland, stretching more than 60 miles south from the Columbia River Gorge to the Olallie Scenic Area near Mt. Jefferson.

It has about 80 campgrounds, 20 sno-parks, part of the Pacific Crest Trail and several ski areas, including historic Timberline Lodge. About a third of the forest is designated wilderness, and the forest supplies about a third of Oregon's drinking and irrigation water.

The forest is managed through four ranger districts: Barlow, Clackamas River, Hood River and Zigzag.

title: Willamette National Forest
contentHtml:
The Willamette National Forest runs about 110 miles along the western slopes of the Oregon Cascades and covers 1,675,407 acres of high mountains, narrow canyons, fast streams and wooded slopes. About 61% of it lies in Lane County, with a smaller share in Clackamas County.

It holds eight wilderness areas and seven major volcanic peaks, and offers year-round hiking, backpacking, camping, fishing, waterfalls and skiing.

title: Mount Jefferson Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mount Jefferson Wilderness, established in 1968, protects 111,177 acres in Linn, Jefferson and Marion counties and is Oregon's second most visited wilderness. At its heart is Mount Jefferson, 10,497 feet, the state's second-tallest peak, a stratovolcano with five glaciers; Three Fingered Jack (7,841 feet) anchors the south end.

More than 150 lakes, including Marion, Duffy, Santiam and Wasco lakes, dot the forests and alpine meadows, and about 190 miles of trails include 40 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail. Visitors hike, backpack, camp, ski and climb among Douglas-fir, mountain hemlock, rhododendron, bear grass and lupine, with deer, black bear and bald eagles.

title: Mecca Flat Campground
imageAlt: Overlook of the campground and the Deschutes Wild & Scenic River

banner.alt: Overlook of the campground and the Deschutes Wild & Scenic River

contentHtml:
Mecca Flat Campground sits on the banks of the Deschutes Wild and Scenic River below basalt rimrock, about 1.5 miles from Highway 26 near Warm Springs. It has 13 individual sites and a group area, open year-round on a first-come, first-served basis, with an accessible vault toilet.

The southern end of the 7-mile Trout Creek Trail starts here, and the campground is popular for fishing the "Lower D," hiking and paddling.

note: Individual sites $8 per night Sunday-Thursday, $12 Friday-Saturday; group sites $25/$35; $2 per extra vehicle. 14-day stay limit. No drinking water or cell service. Goatheads (puncturevine) are present, so protect pets and bike tires. The access road is narrow and single-lane with few pullouts; use caution towing. contentHtml:
Trout Creek Campground lies along the Lower Deschutes Wild and Scenic River, with 21 individual sites (some pull-through), 3 group sites, day-use parking, a boat launch, a seasonal ranger station and a trailhead.

The 7-mile Trout Creek Trail and the Trout Creek Climbing Area start at its south end, beneath towering columnar basalt cliffs.

note: Individual sites $8 per night Sunday-Thursday, $12 Friday-Saturday; group sites $25/$35; $2 per extra vehicle. 14-day stay limit. No drinking water or cell service. title: The Cove Palisades State Park
contentHtml:
The Cove Palisades State Park spreads across the Deschutes and Crooked River canyons on Lake Billy Chinook, among towering cliffs in Oregon's high desert. It is a year-round favorite for camping, boating and water sports, with nearly 10 miles of trails and the popular Eagle Watch event.

Crooked River Campground has 91 electric sites, Deschutes River Campground adds full-hookup and tent sites, and three deluxe lakeside cabins and group tent sites are available. Three day-use areas have swim beaches, and the Cove Palisades Resort and Marina rents boats, houseboats and moorage with a cafe and store. Trails include the Tam-a-láu Trail, climbing about 600 feet to canyon and Cascade views.

note: Reservations: 800-452-5687, up to 6 months ahead. Day-use parking permit required. Swim beaches have no lifeguards. Blue-green algae blooms can occur April through September. Cell service is unreliable.

title: Allen Springs Campground

The spring-fed Metolius River rises at the base of Black Butte and flows north through pine forest and volcanic country. It is famous for fly-fishing for rainbow trout, whitefish, bull trout and kokanee, and nearby are the Camp Sherman Fish Viewing Platform, the Wizard Falls and Metolius fish hatcheries and the Metolius- Windigo Trail.

The 240-acre reservoir, ringed by juniper and sagebrush, is stocked with largemouth bass, rainbow trout, kokanee, crappie and catfish, with paved boat ramps and swimming. Migrating loons and grebes stop here, and Smith Rock State Park is about 20 minutes south.

Shallow, clear Link Creek is a good place to watch spawning fish, and vine maples blaze orange and red in autumn. Summer brings boating, fishing, hiking and biking, including the 3.2-mile Suttle Lake Loop Trail; winter brings cross-country skiing and snowshoeing.

It is famous for fly-fishing for rainbow trout, whitefish, bull trout and kokanee, and nearby are the Camp Sherman Fish Viewing Platform, the Wizard Falls and Metolius fish hatcheries and the Metolius- Windigo Trail.

note: No drinking water; bring your own. No RVs or trailers. Reservations on Recreation.gov. One RV with tow vehicle or one vehicle per site; extra vehicles pay a nightly fee at the campground. No generators 10:00 PM - 7:00 AM. 14-day stay limit. Fire restrictions may apply in hot, dry weather.
address: Forest Road 1419, 1.5 miles north of Forest Road 14, Camp Sherman area, OR

title: Pioneer Ford Campground
contentHtml:
Pioneer Ford Campground is a popular, fairly quiet campground north of Camp Sherman, with 20 back-in and pull-through sites for tents, trailers and RVs, many right on the Metolius River and shaded by pine and cedar. It has drinking water, vault toilets and a picnic shelter beside site 8.

The spring-fed Metolius River rises at the base of Black Butte and flows north through pine forest and volcanic country. It is famous for fly-fishing for rainbow trout, whitefish, bull trout and kokanee, and nearby are the Camp Sherman Fish Viewing Platform, the Wizard Falls and Metolius fish hatcheries and the Metolius- Windigo Trail.

title: Riverside Campground
contentHtml:
Riverside Campground is a walk-in, tent-only campground on the upper Metolius River, with 16 walk-to sites, picnic tables, fire rings with grills and vault toilets.

The spring-fed Metolius River rises at the base of Black Butte and flows north through pine forest and volcanic country. It is famous for fly-fishing for rainbow trout, whitefish, bull trout and kokanee, and nearby are the Camp Sherman Fish Viewing Platform, the Wizard Falls and Metolius fish hatcheries and the Metolius- Windigo Trail.

title: Scout Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Scout Lake Group Campground sits near the shore of Scout Lake at 3,600 feet, in mixed conifer forest. Its 10 single, double and triple sites can host about 100 guests together, with three vault toilets, gravity-fed water, and a day-use area with 11 picnic tables and a large beach steps away.

Only non-motorized boats are allowed on Scout Lake; Suttle Lake, less than a mile away, has water skiing, fishing and boating.

note: Day-use parking $5. Pets on leash, but not in the day-use area or the lake. Reservations on Recreation.gov. One RV with tow vehicle or one vehicle per site; extra vehicles pay a nightly fee at the campground. No generators 10:00 PM - 7:00 AM. 14-day stay limit. Fire restrictions may apply in hot, dry weather.
address: Forest Road 2066, off Forest Road 2070 near Suttle Lake, OR

title: Sheep Springs Horse Camp
contentHtml:
Sheep Springs Horse Camp has 11 large equestrian sites, each with a 4-place box stall, picnic table, fire ring and room for trailers, plus drinking water and a vault toilet, among old-growth ponderosa pine, spruce and fir at about 3,200 feet.

A trailhead for the Metolius-Windigo Trail starts right in camp, and this lower-elevation route stays snow-free longer than nearby trails. Camp Sherman has basic supplies and restaurants.
