note: For equestrian camping only. Horses must stay in the stalls; certified weed-free hay required. Bears have been seen in the area. Reservations on Recreation.gov. One RV with tow vehicle or one vehicle per site; extra vehicles pay a nightly fee at the campground. No generators 10:00 PM - 7:00 AM. 14-day stay limit. Fire restrictions may apply in hot, dry weather.
address: Forest Road 1260/200, off Jack Lake Road (FS 12), about 6 miles north of Highway 20, OR

title: Skull Hollow Campground
contentHtml:
Skull Hollow Campground is a first-come, first-served campground southeast of Haystack Reservoir with views of Gray Butte, popular with climbers heading to nearby Smith Rock State Park. It has 70 sites with picnic tables and fire rings, three vault toilets and a campground host.

It gives access to the Skull Hollow and Gray Butte trailheads and the Cole Loop Trail for riding, hiking and mountain biking.
excerpt: Skull Hollow Campground is a first-come, first-served campground southeast of Haystack Reservoir with views of Gray Butte, popular with climbers heading to near
note: Single site $20, double $40 per night; extra vehicle $7; day use $7. Half-price single sites with senior and access passes. No drinking water, hookups or dump station. 14-day stay limit; no dispersed camping nearby.
address: Skull Hollow Road (County Road 5710), off Lone Pine Road, Crooked River National Grassland, OR

title: Smiling River Campground
contentHtml:
Smiling River Campground has 35 tent and RV sites (no hookups), many overlooking the Metolius River, with picnic areas, trails, scenic overlooks, firewood, drinking water and flush toilets.

The spring-fed Metolius River rises at the base of Black Butte and flows north through pine forest and volcanic country. It is famous for fly-fishing for rainbow trout, whitefish, bull trout and kokanee, and nearby are the Camp Sherman Fish Viewing Platform, the Wizard Falls and Metolius fish hatcheries and the Metolius- Windigo Trail.
excerpt: Smiling River Campground has 35 tent and RV sites (no hookups), many overlooking the Metolius River, with picnic areas, trails, scenic overlooks, firewood, drin
note: Reservations on Recreation.gov. One RV with tow vehicle or one vehicle per site; extra vehicles pay a nightly fee at the campground. No generators 10:00 PM - 7:00 AM. 14-day stay limit. Fire restrictions may apply in hot, dry weather.
address: Forest Road 1419/900 (SW Metolius River Rd), Camp Sherman, OR

title: South Shore Campground
contentHtml:
South Shore Campground sits along Suttle Lake at 3,400 feet, shaded by Douglas fir and ponderosa pine, with one section on the shoreline and another on a hillside; most of its 37 sites have lake views. Sites have gravel spurs, picnic tables and fire rings, with drinking water, vault toilets and dump stations.

The glacier-formed lake, with views of Mount Washington, offers power and paddle boating, sailing, water skiing and windsurfing, fishing for rainbow and brown trout and kokanee (with a fish cleaning station), and the 3.2-mile shoreline trail for hikers and mountain bikers.
excerpt: South Shore Campground sits along Suttle Lake at 3,400 feet, shaded by Douglas fir and ponderosa pine, with one section on the shoreline and another on a hillsi
note: Boat launch day-use parking requires a separate fee. Reservations on Recreation.gov. One RV with tow vehicle or one vehicle per site; extra vehicles pay a nightly fee at the campground. No generators 10:00 PM - 7:00 AM. 14-day stay limit. Fire restrictions may apply in hot, dry weather.
address: Forest Road 2070 off Highway 20/126, about 12 miles northwest of Sisters, OR

title: Billy Chinook Falls
imageAlt: Billy Chinook Falls in early July

banner.alt: Billy Chinook Falls in early July

contentHtml:
Billy Chinook Falls, also called Jordan Road Falls, plunges 160 feet off the rim of the Crooked River canyon toward Lake Billy Chinook in The Cove Palisades State Park. It is the more accessible of the park's two big falls.

Its small stream is fed mostly by irrigation runoff, so the falls are best in early to mid summer and may be dry much of the year. The main park road passes above and below the falls, with several viewpoints.
excerpt: Billy Chinook Falls, also called Jordan Road Falls, plunges 160 feet off the rim of the Crooked River canyon toward Lake Billy Chinook in The Cove Palisades Sta
note: From Highway 97 just south of Culver, follow signs to The Cove Palisades State Park; about 6.5 miles in, the road bends sharply right at a large pullout with views of the falls and lake.
address: Main park road, The Cove Palisades State Park, near Culver, OR

title: Round Butte Falls
contentHtml: Round Butte Falls is a mostly seasonal, 200-foot plunge into Lake Billy Chinook near Round Butte Dam. Its very small drainage depends heavily on irrigation runoff, so it can run one day and be dry the next, likely flowing best in late afternoon.
excerpt: Round Butte Falls is a mostly seasonal, 200-foot plunge into Lake Billy Chinook near Round Butte Dam. Its very small drainage depends heavily on irrigation runo
note: No established viewpoint or published directions.
address: Near Round Butte Dam, Lake Billy Chinook, OR

title: Haystack Reservoir
imageAlt: Haystack Reservoir with Mt. Jefferson (area photo)

banner.alt: Haystack Reservoir with Mt. Jefferson (area photo)

contentHtml:
Haystack Reservoir is a high-desert irrigation reservoir near Culver with open views and big skies instead of a forested shoreline, quieter than the region's better-known lakes. Kayaks, canoes and paddleboards share the water with motorboats.

Paddlers launch from Haystack South (day use and camping), the Haystack East campground boat ramp, or the West ramp when water levels allow. Smith Rock State Park and Lake Billy Chinook are nearby.
excerpt: Haystack Reservoir is a high-desert irrigation reservoir near Culver with open views and big skies instead of a forested shoreline, quieter than the region's be
note: Wind can make the exposed water rough, especially for paddleboards. Obey slow-no-wake zones. Water levels change during the irrigation season; check ramp status first. Check Oregon Health Authority algae advisories. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Haystack Reservoir, Crooked River National Grassland, near Culver, OR

title: Scout Lake
contentHtml:
Scout Lake is a small, quiet lake in mixed-conifer forest near Suttle Lake, suited to a relaxed paddle by kayak, canoe or paddleboard. Motors are prohibited, so the water stays calm.

The day-use area has parking, picnic tables and vault toilets.
excerpt: Scout Lake is a small, quiet lake in mixed-conifer forest near Suttle Lake, suited to a relaxed paddle by kayak, canoe or paddleboard. Motors are prohibited, so
note: No motors. Dogs are not allowed in the day-use area or on the lake. Mountain weather changes quickly and the water stays cold. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Scout Lake Campground and Day Use, off Forest Road 2066 near Suttle Lake, OR

title: Suttle Lake
imageAlt: Link Creek on Suttle Lake in fall

banner.alt: Link Creek on Suttle Lake in fall

contentHtml:
Suttle Lake is a forested Cascade mountain lake near Sisters with several public launches, including Link Creek, the Suttle Lake Day Use area, South Shore and Blue Bay, making it easy to explore by kayak, canoe or paddleboard.

Motorboats also use the lake. Sisters and the Metolius River area are close by for food and more recreation.
excerpt: Suttle Lake is a forested Cascade mountain lake near Sisters with several public launches, including Link Creek, the Suttle Lake Day Use area, South Shore and B
note: Traffic varies with season and time of day; wind can make open water hard for small boats; the water stays cold even on warm days. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Suttle Lake, off Highway 20/126 about 13 miles northwest of Sisters, OR

title: Mount Jefferson
imageAlt: Mt. Jefferson from the high desert near Haystack Reservoir

banner.alt: Mt. Jefferson from the high desert near Haystack Reservoir

contentHtml:
At 10,497 feet, Mount Jefferson is the second-highest mountain in Oregon after Mount Hood. It is a heavily glaciated stratovolcano of the Cascade Volcanic Arc, one of the most eroded in the state, whose last eruptive activity was about a thousand years ago.

Known as Seekseekqua to Native peoples, it was named for President Thomas Jefferson after Lewis and Clark saw it from the mouth of the Willamette River in 1806. It rises within the 111,177-acre Mount Jefferson Wilderness, which has more than 150 lakes and 190 miles of trails, including 40 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail; the eastern side lies within the Warm Springs Indian Reservation, so public access is limited to the western flanks.
excerpt: At 10,497 feet, Mount Jefferson is the second-highest mountain in Oregon after Mount Hood. It is a heavily glaciated stratovolcano of the Cascade Volcanic Arc,
note: The summit is a technical climb recommended only for experienced climbers; the first ascent was in 1888 via the south ridge.
address: Central Oregon Cascades, Mount Jefferson Wilderness (Jefferson, Linn and Marion counties), OR

title: Metolius–Windigo Trail
contentHtml:
The Metolius-Windigo Trail (Trail #99) runs roughly 150 miles through the Deschutes National Forest, from the Metolius Basin near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness west of Sisters south to Windigo Pass near Crescent Lake. Created around 1980 as a lower-elevation alternative to the Pacific Crest Trail, it connects to the PCT at both ends and is popular with horse riders.

In Jefferson County, the trail's northern end begins in the Metolius Basin near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness.
excerpt: The Metolius-Windigo Trail (Trail #99) runs roughly 150 miles through the Deschutes National Forest, from the Metolius Basin near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness
note: Published lengths vary from about 120 to 152 miles.
address: Deschutes National Forest Supervisor's Office: 63095 Deschutes Market Rd, Bend, OR 97701

title: Oregon Timber Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Timber Trail is a 670-mile mountain bike and bikepacking route from the California border near Lakeview north to Hood River on the Columbia, managed by the nonprofit Oregon Timber Trail Alliance. It is split into four tiers: Fremont, Willamette, Deschutes and Hood.

The Deschutes Tier runs from Waldo Lake to Sisters. Riders can take on the whole route or ride a shorter piece.

address: Deschutes Tier: Waldo Lake to Sisters, OR

title: Pacific Crest Trail
contentHtml:
The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail runs 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada through California, Oregon and Washington, managed by the Forest Service with the Pacific Crest Trail Association. Its roughly 455-mile Oregon section is the shortest and easiest on the trail, from near Siskiyou Summit to the Bridge of the Gods over the Columbia River.

In Jefferson County the trail crosses the Mount Jefferson Wilderness on the flanks of Mount Jefferson, Oregon's second-highest peak.

note: Central Cascades Wilderness permits apply in the Mount Jefferson Wilderness from June 15 to October 15.
address: Oregon section: California border near Ashland to the Bridge of the Gods, Cascade Locks, OR

title: Billy’s Playground
contentHtml:
Billy's Playground is a long, demanding 79-mile lollipop loop (5,600 feet of climbing, about half unpaved) along the southern edge of Lake Billy Chinook. It passes basalt cliffs, the Crooked and Deschutes river arms, Mount Jefferson views, the Crooked River National Grassland and the ghost towns of Geneva and Grandview.

Ponderosa forest and burn areas, bright with lupine in spring, line the route, which is named for Billy Chinook, a Wasco guide whose real name was Guygo.
excerpt: Billy's Playground is a long, demanding 79-mile lollipop loop (5,600 feet of climbing, about half unpaved) along the southern edge of Lake Billy Chinook. It pas
note: Day-use fee at the start, which has flush toilets and water. Lake Chinook Village Store, about a mile off route near mile 42, has food and water. Expect heat, washboard, chunky gravel and burn damage from the 2021 Grandview Fire; navigation requires attention. Tires 45mm or wider suggested.
address: Crooked River Day Use Area, The Cove Palisades State Park, OR

title: Donnybrook
contentHtml:
Donnybrook is a remote 54-mile loop (4,400 feet of climbing, 35% gravel) with a scenic canyon, big mountain views, the abandoned 1914 Donnybrook schoolhouse and the ghost town of Ashwood. Technically easier, it is still a climber's route.

Gravel begins after Ashwood with climbs up to 8%, rough cobblestone-like gravel near mile 21 and loose gravel past the Wasco County line, then pavement back past the Priday Ranch preserve.

note: Self-help kiosks at Ashwood (about mile 15) and Antelope Market (about mile 38). The final stretch on US 97 has traffic; use a rear light and radar. Ride on a sunny day with light winds.
address: Gravel lot on US 97 at Pony Butte Road, north of Madras, OR

title: Experimental Rattlesnake
contentHtml:
Experimental Rattlesnake is an easy 18-mile high desert loop (1,100 feet of climbing, about 75% gravel and dirt) past farms, ranchland, grassland and irrigation canals, with views of Mount Jefferson, Grizzly Mountain and Gray Butte.

It starts at Haystack Reservoir among basalt and rhyolite cliffs and follows mostly well-kept gravel roads, with a rougher dirt section through the National Grassland.
excerpt: Experimental Rattlesnake is an easy 18-mile high desert loop (1,100 feet of climbing, about 75% gravel and dirt) past farms, ranchland, grassland and irrigation
note: Day-use fee $7 April-October; pit toilets at the start. No food or water on the route. Yield to farm equipment, watch for free-range cattle and stay on the right side of the canal road (the left is private). Avoid when wet.
address: North Fishing Pier Day-Use Area, Haystack Reservoir, OR

title: Ghost of Ashwood
contentHtml:
Ghost of Ashwood is a demanding 60-mile lollipop loop (6,100 feet of climbing, about 60% gravel) across the Crooked River National Grassland, past basalt cliffs and painted hills, through the Baldwin Hills near historic Hay Creek Ranch and by the Polka Dot Agate Mine, with views of Mount Jefferson and Mount Hood.

The only settlement is the ghost town of Ashwood, which had a brief mining boom around 1901-1902. Shorter 44- and 40-mile options are available.

note: Start has parking, flush toilets and water. Ashwood's seasonal honor-system store (about mile 35) has snacks and drinks; bring small bills, and don't drink from the hydrants. The 3-mile descent into Ashwood is steep and can be rutted. Affected by the 2025 Cram Fire.
address: Juniper Hills Park, Madras, OR

title: Green Ridge Lookout
imageAlt: Single track out of Black Butte Trailhead

banner.alt: Single track out of Black Butte Trailhead

contentHtml:
The Green Ridge Lookout ride is a 32-mile loop (3,100 feet of climbing, about 80% unpaved) that climbs Green Ridge to a lookout with one of the few full panoramas of the Cascades: Mount St. Helens, Mount Hood, Mount Jefferson, Three Fingered Jack, Mount Washington and the Sisters.

Big ponderosa pines, red cinder roads, the Wizard Falls Fish Hatchery and the Camp Sherman store add to the ride, which passes through several burn areas.

note: Moderate difficulty; the main climb gains about 2,000 feet over 5.5 miles on loose cinder and rocky dirt. Camp Sherman Store at mile 3; Wizard Falls Hatchery at mile 8. The lookout is behind a locked gate and may be occupied by renters.
address: Black Butte Trailhead, near Camp Sherman, OR

title: Horn of the Metolius
contentHtml:
Horn of the Metolius is a premier, very demanding 53-mile gravel loop (4,600 feet of climbing, about 90% unpaved) around the "Horn," the forested land inside a U-shaped bend of the Metolius River, passing Lake Billy Chinook and a Wild and Scenic stretch of the river.

It climbs a red cinder road with Mount Jefferson views, drops to the lake shore over loose gravel and boulders, then follows primitive single track along the river. Most riders need 5 to 6 hours, longer than the numbers suggest.

note: Extremely remote with little cell service; carry a satellite messenger. Water at Perry South Campground (May-September) around mile 29. About a mile of hike-a-bike on the brushy Shut-In Trail. Black bear, cougar, elk and wolves live here. Two locked gates complicate rescue.

title: Larch Time
contentHtml:
Larch Time is a relaxed 23-mile loop (900 feet of climbing, about 85% unpaved, mostly single track) near Sisters, made for October when the western larches turn bright yellow. It winds through big ponderosa pines past Suttle Lake, Larch Creek and the historic Camp Allingham and Camp Sherman.

Short with little climbing, it is still slow going on flowy single track and a real navigation challenge; expect to miss a few turns the first time.
excerpt: Larch Time is a relaxed 23-mile loop (900 feet of climbing, about 85% unpaved, mostly single track) near Sisters, made for October when the western larches turn
note: Seasonal food and water at Suttle Lake Lodge (about mile 11) and Camp Sherman General Store (about mile 20.5). Horses and hikers have the right of way on multi-use trails. The Metolius Preserve loops (miles 14 to 19.5) are muddy early in the season. Tires 45mm or wider suggested.
address: Black Butte Lower Trailhead, near Camp Sherman, OR

title: Lost Wagon Train
contentHtml:
Lost Wagon Train is a 57-mile loop (4,600 feet of climbing, 40% unpaved) over land crossed by the lost 1845 Meek wagon train. It takes in the Baldwin Hills, Hay Creek, the Crooked River National Grassland, the farming community of Gateway, Lake Simtustus and Dry Canyon, with views of Mount Jefferson and Mount Hood.

Moderate distance, small climbs and plenty of pavement make it a good early-season training ride, with a flat stretch past halfway before the Pelton Hill climb near mile 45.

title: Madras Mountain Views Scenic Bikeway
contentHtml:
The Madras Mountain Views Scenic Bikeway is a 30-mile, fully paved loop through farmland and pastureland with views of the Cascade volcanoes and the basalt palisades above the Deschutes and Crooked rivers.

Gravel overlooks above The Cove Palisades State Park and Lake Billy Chinook (miles 15.2 to 17.4) offer chances to see eagles, raptors and deer. The route also passes Round Butte Overlook Park and the historic railroad depot in Metolius.

note: Moderate difficulty, with a very steep, long hill after the Cove Palisades State Park entrance. The park has camping, water and restrooms.

title: Metolius Preserve
contentHtml:
The Metolius Preserve ride is a relaxed 14-mile loop (800 feet of climbing, all gravel, double track and single track) through pine, larch and fir forest to an easy mountain bike area in the Metolius Preserve, land given to the Deschutes Land Trust. The larches turn yellow in fall and the shaded trails stay pleasant in summer.

Turkeys and grouse are common. Afterward, walk the Suttle Lake trail or stop at Suttle Lake Lodge.

note: Parking and restrooms at the lodge; no food or water on the route. Several tricky turns: easy to miss one, hard to get lost. One short climb near the end tops 9%. The Highway 26 underpass may need to be walked.
address: Suttle Lake Lodge, near Sisters, OR

title: Over the Rainbow
contentHtml:
Over the Rainbow is a 42-mile loop (1,900 feet of climbing, 45% unpaved) along Lake Simtustus and the Lower Deschutes River, following old railway grades from the early-1900s railroad wars, with an optional 7-mile out- and-back to Trout Creek Ranch.

About 10 miles of dirt road, single track and rail grade beside the river lead past cattle and eagles, then through a one-lane tunnel, up the Gateway Grade and back across farmland.

note: Park in the dirt lot north of the building; flush toilets and water, no fees. Seasonal Dockside Cafe and Grill near mile 10 and Rainbow Market near mile 16. Goat heads are common in late summer; tubeless tires recommended. Some rocky single track runs close to the water. Parts along Lake Simtustus were damaged by 2026 fires.

title: Path of Totality
contentHtml:
Path of Totality is a 42-mile lollipop (2,800 feet of climbing, about 25% unpaved) found during the 2017 total solar eclipse. It starts on the rocky shores of Lake Simtustus, climbs Willow Creek Canyon on the old Oregon Trunk railroad line, then tackles the paved "M" Hill at nearly 20%.

The middle crosses irrigated farmland near Madras and Culver, circles Round Butte and follows the rim above Lake Billy Chinook before a long, steep descent back to the lake. A 35-mile option skips the lake section.

title: Poke the Bear
contentHtml:
Poke the Bear is a showcase of Madras gravel: a 33-mile loop (2,400 feet of climbing, 86% gravel) on fast, hard-packed roads through the high desert. A paved climb over the Baldwin Hills leads to gravel past historic farms, creeks and ranches.

A long, gradual descent on the "Gravel Super Highway" brings views of Mount Jefferson and the Three Sisters, and the ride ends near the Poke the Bear roundabout sculptures, a 27-foot mother bear and three cubs.

note: Flush toilets at the start; no fee. No food or water on the route. Expect livestock guardian dogs near Hay Creek Ranch around mile 10, where the road gets primitive; turn around if it is muddy. Affected by the 2025 Cram Fire.
address: Juniper Hills Park, Madras, OR

title: Saxophone
contentHtml:
Saxophone (formerly Into the Horn) is a remote, very demanding 43-mile loop (3,500 feet of climbing) in the Horn of the Metolius area, split evenly between primitive Forest Service roads and hard-packed gravel, with big views and red-barked ponderosas.

Most of the ride is rolling: rocky roads with shale in the first half, then wide gravel with some washboard. A 24-mile shortcut uses Prairie Farm Road.

title: Sherman's Hard Rock
contentHtml:
Sherman's Hard Rock (formerly Sherman's Waltz) is a demanding 45-mile loop (3,300 feet of climbing, 65% unpaved) past Round Lake, Abbot Butte, the Metolius River, the Wizard Falls Fish Hatchery and Camp Sherman, with lake, river and mountain views.

The Round Lake climb and descent and the Abbot Butte section are rocky and rugged, close to mountain biking, while the paved stretches are fast. Shortcuts skip Round Lake (11 miles) or Abbot Butte (5 miles).

Suttle Wizard is a mellow 27-mile loop (1,600 feet of climbing, about 45% unpaved) through the Metolius Basin's ponderosa pines, following the clear Metolius River for about 7 miles with views of Mount Jefferson.

Highlights include the bridge over the Metolius and Wizard Falls Fish Hatchery's spawning ponds. The Lake Creek Trail passes under the highway to avoid a busy crossing.

title: The Big One6
contentHtml:
The Big One6 is a 31-mile out-and-back (2,500 feet of climbing, about 20% gravel) through the Warm Springs Indian Reservation, following the Deschutes River to Lake Simtustus. Rolling pavement passes farms, an abandoned church, basalt cliffs and open land where wild mustangs graze.

At about mile 13 a gravel road drops steeply to the lake past a "16% grade ahead" sign; the climb back is the hardest part of the ride.

title: Tripple Ripple
contentHtml:
Tripple Ripple (formerly Metolius Preserve + Bonus Lakes) is a demanding 28-mile loop (1,800 feet of climbing, 75% gravel and 25% single track) around Suttle and Round lakes with views of Three Fingered Jack, then through the Metolius Preserve's ponderosa, Douglas fir and western larch forest along Lake Creek.

It combines parts of the Metolius Preserve, Sherman's Hard Rock and Gravel Cracker 85 routes; finish at Suttle Lodge or the Boathouse.

title: Crooked River

gallery.alt: Crooked River canyon along the byway

contentHtml:
The Crooked River was designated a National Wild and Scenic River in 1988. Its 14.8 recreational miles run from just below Bowman Dam to Dry Creek, and from the National Grassland boundary to a point south of Opal Springs.

The river is valued for its botany, geology, hydrology, recreation, scenery and wildlife. It holds steelhead, brown trout and redband trout, and in spring offers Class IV-V whitewater.

title: Deschutes River
contentHtml:
The Deschutes River was designated a National Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, for 174.4 miles (143.4 recreational, 31 scenic) in three reaches: Wickiup Dam to Bend, Odin Falls to Lake Billy Chinook, and Pelton Reregulating Dam to the Columbia River. The middle and lower reaches flow through Jefferson County.

Near Bend the upper river offers easy-to-reach brown trout fishing; the middle river has hiking and basalt canyon geology, rock art and spring-fed waters; the lower river is known for whitewater rafting, steelhead and trout fishing and camping, with about 300 kinds of wildlife in the canyon.

note: Managed by the Deschutes National Forest ((541) 383-5300) and the BLM Prineville District ((541) 416- 6700).

title: John Day River
contentHtml:
The John Day River is the longest undammed river in Oregon. Its 147.5-mile recreational section from Service Creek to Tumwater Falls was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, running through colorful canyons, broad valleys and high desert, with basalt cliffs over 1,000 feet high.

It holds one of the region's few remaining wild runs of summer steelhead and spring Chinook, plus prime smallmouth bass water, and the Oregon Trail crossed it at McDonald Ford. Boating is mostly calm with a few rapids; the corridor also offers camping, swimming and wildlife watching, including bald and golden eagles, bighorn sheep and elk.

title: Metolius River
contentHtml:
The Metolius runs through a forested valley on the east side of the Cascades and is one of the largest spring- fed rivers in the United States. Its cold, steady, clear water supports renowned fly fishing for wild and hatchery rainbow trout and a recovering bull trout population, as well as whitewater boating.

Designated Wild and Scenic in 1988, 28.6 miles (11.5 recreational, 17.1 scenic) run from the Deschutes National Forest boundary to Lake Billy Chinook. Visitors camp, hike, hunt, mountain bike and sightsee along the developed upper 8 to 10 miles; the lower river, bordering the Warm Springs Reservation, is a primitive area with no motorized access.

title: McKenzie Pass-Santiam Pass Scenic Byway
imageAlt: Lava flow and peaks from Dee Wright Observatory

banner.alt: Lava flow and peaks from Dee Wright Observatory

contentHtml:
The McKenzie Pass-Santiam Pass Scenic Byway is an 82-mile loop from Sisters over two Cascade passes: Santiam Pass (4,817 feet), where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses, and McKenzie Pass (5,335 feet), crowned by the lava-rock Dee Wright Observatory with views over an ancient lava flow to 11 peaks.

Along the way are Suttle Lake, Scott Lake, Clear Lake Resort, the wild and scenic McKenzie River and historic stretches of the Santiam Wagon Road. Back in Sisters, browse downtown boutiques and galleries.

title: High Desert Food Trail

gallery.alt: Pumpkins on the High Desert Food Trail

contentHtml:
The High Desert Food Trail is a self-guided farm and food trail run by the High Desert Food & Farm Alliance. Stops include farms, ranches and food businesses in Bend, Redmond, Sisters, La Pine, Prineville, Madras and Warm Springs.

Visitors can follow one of the trail's itineraries or build their own route to buy produce, meat and other foods directly from local growers.

title: Balancing Rocks
contentHtml:
Balancing Rocks Overlook looks over more than 30 rock pillars, Oregon's "hoodoos," standing above the Metolius Arm of Lake Billy Chinook. The towering formations are more than 20,000 years old.

A short hike on an improved-access trail leads to the overlook. The site is managed by PGE and the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs with the U.S. Forest Service.

title: Head of the Metolius
contentHtml:
The Head of the Metolius is where the Metolius River emerges, fully formed, from cold springs at the foot of Black Butte, flowing at about 50,000 gallons per minute and 48°F. Two spring groups about 200 feet apart feed the headwaters, which run 29 miles through the Deschutes National Forest to Lake Billy Chinook.

A paved walkway with interpretive signs leads from the parking area to the viewing point. Lumber mill owner Sam Johnson, who kept the springs natural and open to the public, gave the viewing area to the Forest Service in 1965.

note: From Sisters, go northwest on Highway 20 for 9.6 miles, turn north onto Forest Road 14 and go 4.3 miles to the signed entrance. Three picnic tables and a vault toilet; no drinking water; no camping.

title: Peter Skene Ogden State Scenic Viewpoint
imageAlt: Peter Skene Ogden State Scenic Viewpoint

banner.alt: Peter Skene Ogden State Scenic Viewpoint

contentHtml:
Peter Skene Ogden State Scenic Viewpoint sits on the rim of the Crooked River Gorge, a basalt canyon roughly 300 feet deep on the Deschutes-Jefferson county line. From the rim you can see three bridges: the Crooked River Railroad Bridge, the historic Crooked River High Bridge (now pedestrian only) and the Rex T. Barber Veterans Memorial Bridge.

It is named for Peter Skene Ogden, who led a Hudson's Bay Company trapping party into the Crooked River Valley in 1825, and has a memorial to World War II flying ace Rex T. Barber. Restrooms and picnic tables are available, and the canyon views are popular with photographers.
excerpt: Peter Skene Ogden State Scenic Viewpoint sits on the rim of the Crooked River Gorge, a basalt canyon roughly 300 feet deep on the Deschutes-Jefferson county lin
note: Drive-through parking with a loop exit on the west side of US 97, reachable from both directions; limited parking for trucks and trailers. Pets on leash.
address: US 97, about 9 miles north of Redmond (near Terrebonne), OR
photoCredit: Another Believer, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

title: Green Ridge Lookout
contentHtml:
Green Ridge Lookout is a 1960s, 20-foot fire lookout on a ridge more than 2,000 feet above the Metolius River, with views of Mount Jefferson and the Metolius basin. Volunteers staff it in summer for fire detection; in spring and fall it is rented as a one-room cabin on a two-story tower, reached by a short boardwalk and steps to the catwalk.

It sleeps up to four (one futon) and has a table and chairs, a propane refrigerator, light, wall heater and four- burner stove with oven. Nearby are fly fishing on the Metolius, hiking on Black Butte and boating at Lake Billy Chinook.

note: Reservations through Recreation.gov. No water or kitchenware; bring all water, food, bedding, cookware, toilet paper and garbage bags. Call the Sisters Ranger District a week ahead for the lock code. Early and late season may require high-clearance 4WD. Check-in 3 p.m., check-out 11 a.m. Pets outside only; no smoking.
address: Spur Road 600 off Forest Road 1140, Green Ridge, Deschutes National Forest (Sisters Ranger District), OR

contentHtml:
The Olallie Lake Guard Station is a rustic cabin built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1991. It sits near 5,000 feet beside Olallie Lake.

The cabin sleeps eight in four rooms and has propane appliances and a wood stove. A vault toilet is about 75 feet away.

title: Maragas Winery
contentHtml:
Maragas Winery brings Old World winemaking and drinking traditions to the high desert of Central Oregon, growing grapes on its estate vineyard and blending art and science in its wines.

Estate wines include a barrel-fermented Dry Riesling and Legal Zin, a Zinfandel-based red blend now in its 25th year.

title: Coyote's Den
contentHtml:
Coyote's Den is a hard, very hilly 18-hole, par-59 disc golf course (about 8,159 feet) through mature juniper and desert sage with a variety of lengths and slopes. Most of it has been limbed and cleared of brush.

Holes have long and short tees and three pin positions, with bag stands on every hole and benches on half. Established in 2013.

Eagle's Nest is an easy, flat 9-hole disc golf course (par 27, about 1,262 feet) in a public park in Warm Springs, with concrete tees and Black Hole Gravity targets. Established in 2023.

The river is out of bounds on Hole 2, the road on Hole 3, and Holes 5, 6 and 7 have island greens.

contentHtml:
Juniper Hills is a moderate, hilly disc golf course in a Madras public park, with a wide variety of shots, lots of elevation changes and a beautiful view. The main layout has 9 holes, and an 18-hole layout (par 54, 5,425 feet) is also available.

title: Josephine County Historical Society
contentHtml:
The Josephine County Historical Society is a nonprofit that collects, preserves and shares the history of the community through exhibits, events and educational programs. It runs the Schmidt House Museum, a research library and a bookstore at 5th and K streets in Grants Pass.

The Schmidt House Museum holds artifacts from around Southern Oregon, shown on guided tours. The research library holds books, family histories, photos, maps, newspapers, documents and microfilm. Tours of historic downtown Grants Pass are also offered.

title: Kerbyville Museum
contentHtml:
The Kerbyville Museum tells the history of the Illinois Valley: the Takelma people, local gold mining and pioneer settlement.

The grounds center on the 1880s William and Nannie Naucke House, listed on the National Register of Historic Places and the museum's main building since 1959, along with a log schoolhouse, a blacksmith shop, a Native American pit house and a miner's cabin.

title: Siskiyou Smokejumper Base Museum
contentHtml:
The Siskiyou Smokejumper Base Museum, at the base known as the "Gobi," preserves the story of early Forest Service aerial firefighting in Southern Oregon and Northern California. The base opened in 1943, partly in response to wartime Japanese attempts to set western forests on fire, and became one of four primary smokejumper bases before closing in 1981 after 38 years.

Its restored buildings are on the National Register of Historic Places and include what the museum describes as the oldest standing smokejumper parachute loft in North America. Volunteers, many of them former smokejumpers, give tours of the buildings, equipment and jump gear.

title: Oregon Caves National Monument and Preserve
contentHtml:
Oregon Caves National Monument and Preserve protects the "Marble Halls of Oregon," dark, twisting passages deep in the Siskiyou Mountains, formed and decorated over long ages by acidic water seeping into marble. It is one of the few marble cave systems in the United States.

Rangers lead three guided cave tours plus an off-trail caving tour, and the preserve above ground has trails and mountain meadows such as Bigelow Lakes. Caves Creek Campground has 17 first-come, first-served sites.

title: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest
contentHtml:
The Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest covers about 1.8 million acres of southwest Oregon, from the Cascades to the coast, managed through five ranger districts: High Cascades, Siskiyou Mountains, Wild Rivers, Gold Beach and Powers.

Highlights across the forest include the Kalmiopsis, Siskiyou and Sky Lakes wilderness areas and the Wild and Scenic Illinois and Rogue rivers. In Josephine County the Wild Rivers Ranger District, with an office in Cave Junction, manages the Illinois River country, campgrounds such as Grayback and Bolan Lake, and much of the Kalmiopsis Wilderness.

title: Kalmiopsis Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Kalmiopsis Wilderness, designated in 1964, covers 180,095 acres of deep canyons, sharp rock ridges and clear, fast streams, including the headwaters of the Chetco and North Fork Smith rivers and part of the Illinois River canyon. Elevations run from 500 feet to 5,098 feet at Pearsoll Peak.

Its serpentine soils support many rare plants, including the namesake shrub Kalmiopsis leachiana, found in 1930 in the Gold Basin area. Trailheads include Babyfoot Lake, Vulcan Lake/Johnson Butte, Chetco Divide/Vulcan Peak, Upper Chetco, Tincup, Illinois River and Kalmiopsis Rim.

note: No drinking water: treat surface water. Trails damaged by past fires are being repaired; watch for dead trees, high winds and fast-changing weather. Overnight groups limited to 12 people and 9 pack animals. Boating permits required. No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles. No caching of equipment or supplies; no hay or unprocessed grain.

title: Red Buttes Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Red Buttes Wilderness straddles the crest of the Siskiyou Mountains, named for the reddish-orange peridotite and serpentine of its peaks. Designated in 1984, it is about 13 miles long and 6 wide, with 3,400 acres in Oregon and 16,500 in California, rising from about 2,800 feet in Butte Fork Canyon to 6,739 feet on Red Buttes.

Dense forest, meadows and glacier-carved lake basins, including 20-acre Azalea Lake, are home to black bears, cougars, deer and peregrine falcons. Trails include about 35 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail, Trail 957 across the core, the Steve Fork Trail from Sucker Creek Gap and the Boundary Trail along the crest.
excerpt: The Red Buttes Wilderness straddles the crest of the Siskiyou Mountains, named for the reddish-orange peridotite and serpentine of its peaks. Designated in 1984
note: No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles. No camping within 100 feet of lakes. Carry plenty of water on the south-facing Boundary Trail. High country is usually snow-covered November to May.

title: Golden State Heritage Site
contentHtml:
Golden State Heritage Site preserves a 19th-century gold mining town, now a ghost town. An 1850s mining camp gave way to a town around 1890 that peaked at about 100 residents; unusually, it had no saloons, two active churches and a large orchard planted by its founding families.

Four buildings remain: a church, a former residence, a shed and the old post office and store. The whole property is on the National Register of Historic Places, and it is the only former mining community owned by Oregon State Parks.

address: Golden, near Wolf Creek and Glendale, OR

title: Illinois River Forks State Park
contentHtml:
Illinois River Forks State Park is a day-use park where the east and west forks of the Illinois River meet, a handy stop for travelers heading to or from the coast and the redwoods on Highway 199. The Illinois Valley is geologically unique, with many rare plants.

The park has picnic tables, a reservable picnic shelter for up to 50, a short walking trail, a 9-hole disc golf course and a life jacket loaner station at Heritage Landing. Horse trails in the West Forks Trail system are about 3 miles away near Kerby.

note: Currents can be swift with hidden obstructions; check Oregon State Marine Board obstruction reports. Pets on leash.
address: Confluence of the East and West Forks of the Illinois River, off US 199 near Cave Junction, OR

title: Wolf Creek Inn State Heritage Site
imageAlt: Wolf Creek Tavern sign above the entrance

banner.alt: Wolf Creek Tavern sign above the entrance

contentHtml:
Wolf Creek Inn State Heritage Site preserves a stop on the Applegate Trail built around 1883 for merchant Henry Smith, which served miners and stage travelers between Roseburg and Redding until the railroad opened in 1887. It claims to be the oldest continuously operated hotel in the Pacific Northwest and is on the National Register of Historic Places.

Jack London finished Valley of the Moon here, and guests have included Clark Gable, Carole Lombard and Orson Welles. Restored by the state in 1975-1979, it still offers nine rooms with private baths and a restaurant serving breakfast, lunch and dinner to the public. Interpretive panels describe life on the Applegate Trail.

title: Bolan Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Bolan Lake Campground has 14 sites on the shore of 12-acre Bolan Lake, high above the Illinois Valley, with big conifers for summer shade and wildflowers in early summer.

Bolan Lake Trail #1245 climbs to the old fire lookout on Bolan Peak; Bolan Mountain Lookout is available to rent.

title: Chinquapin Group Campground

gallery.alt: Picnic table and vault toilet in the pine forest

contentHtml:
Chinquapin Group Campground occupies the site of Camp Oregon Caves, a Civilian Conservation Corps camp that housed more than 200 men from 1933 to 1941. The CCC-built Grayback Ranger Station (about 1936) next door is the camp's only remaining structure, and a Port-Orford cedar by the parking area is an Oregon State Heritage Tree.

A large meadow suits reunions, church camps, school trips and scout events. Grayback Creek offers swimming, and the Grayback Interpretive Trail follows the creek. Oregon Caves National Monument is about 10 miles east.

note: Group site, reservable on Recreation.gov ($75 per night per the client sheet); $5 per extra vehicle. Locked gate: the combination is in your reservation confirmation. contentHtml: Echo Beach is a small, primitive campground on Illinois River Road with three to four tent sites, a pit toilet, picnic tables and fire rings.

title: Grayback Campground
contentHtml:
Grayback Campground has 39 forested sites, several along Sucker Creek, about 5 miles from Oregon Caves National Monument and Preserve. The family-friendly, 1-mile Grayback Interpretive Trail leads to Grayback Creek and the historic Civilian Conservation Corps camp at Cedar Guard Station.

The day-use area has 10 sites, a small amphitheater and a large picnic area with shelters and a fireplace.

title: Little Falls Campground
contentHtml:
Little Falls Campground is a pleasant little campground with three tent sites overlooking the Illinois River and the mountains around the Illinois Valley, near the Little Illinois River Falls, river swimming holes and wildflowers.

It lies in the Eight Dollar Mountain Botanical Area, known for serpentine soils and Darlingtonia (cobra lily), and shares a trailhead with Little Falls Trail #1284, which links to the Jeffrey Pine Loop. An amphitheater has a large fire pit for groups.

contentHtml:
Sam Brown Campground is centered on a large meadow with a history of miners and homesteaders, where deer, elk and many birds gather. Briggs Creek flows through on its way to the Illinois River, and its trailhead starts in the campground.

The campground suits large groups, with two picnic shelters and an amphitheater, and nearby trails for hiking, mountain biking, horseback riding and motorcycles, including Taylor Creek, Onion Way, Secret Way and Dutchy Creek.

It has horse corrals and river access, and connects to the Onion Way, Secret Way, Taylor Creek and Briggs Creek trails.

title: Sixmile Campground
contentHtml:
Sixmile is a small campground with four walk-in sites on the Wild and Scenic Illinois River, known for clear pools and rocky banks. The neighboring Six Mile Day Use Area has deep swimming holes, rock jumping ledges and picnic pavilions.

Serpentine soils, Jeffrey pine and Douglas fir surround the canyon, where bald eagles and river otters can be seen. The Illinois River National Recreation Trail is nearby.

contentHtml:
Spalding Pond is a 3-acre lake ringed by tall conifers, its cool water a relief from hot valley temperatures, with a small pebble beach at the water's edge.

The small primitive campground has three accessible fishing platforms and a surfaced, accessible trail.

title: Store Gulch Campground
contentHtml:
Store Gulch Campground sits on the Wild and Scenic Illinois River among turquoise water, sun-baked boulders, steep canyon walls and a wide sandy beach popular for swimming. Jeffrey pine, Douglas fir and madrone grow on serpentine rock, and river otters and osprey are often seen.

It has six sites (two walk-in). Nearby are the historic 1929 Store Gulch Guard Station, the Swinging Bridge and the Illinois River National Recreation Trail.

title: Bolan Lake
contentHtml:
Bolan Lake is a quiet, 12-acre mountain lake at about 5,300 feet in the Siskiyou Mountains, ringed by tall trees that survived the 2020 Slater Fire. Its sheltered, nonmotorized water suits unhurried shoreline paddling by kayak, canoe or paddleboard.

Boats are carried from Bolan Lake Campground to the shore; there is no ramp. Fishing, paddle-and-camp trips and early-summer wildflowers add to the visit.
excerpt: Bolan Lake is a quiet, 12-acre mountain lake at about 5,300 feet in the Siskiyou Mountains, ringed by tall trees that survived the 2020 Slater Fire. Its shelter
note: Remote forest roads with very limited cell service; download directions first. Access is seasonal and can be affected by snow, fallen trees and fire. No drinking water. Mountain weather changes quickly. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.
address: Bolan Lake Campground, Forest Road 4812-040, above the Illinois Valley, OR

title: Lake Selmac
imageAlt: Lake Selmac County Park disc golf course (area photo)

contentHtml:
Lake Selmac is a small, approachable recreation lake near Selma, good for kayaking, paddleboarding and canoeing, with sailing, fishing and swimming too. Wildlife and birds line its forested and developed shores.

Lake Selmac County Park has boating access, picnic areas, nature trails, disc golf, playgrounds and camping with tent, RV and yurt sites.

note: Day-use parking $10 per vehicle (free on foot or bike). Park open sunup to sundown. Motorboats limited to 10 mph. Wind can make the lake choppy; watch for algae advisories. An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for each paddlecraft (youth 13 and under exempt). Wear a life jacket; clean, drain and dry your boat after use.

title: Grayback Mountain
contentHtml:
Grayback Mountain (7,048 feet) is a non-technical summit on the Siskiyou crest in the Klamath Mountains. From the Upper O'Brien Creek Trailhead, O'Brien Creek Trail #900 climbs to the Boundary Trail #1207, which leads north to Windy Gap, followed by a cross-country finish up the north ridge: about 6.5 miles round trip with some 2,500 feet of gain.

No maintained trail reaches the summit itself. A longer western approach climbs the Grayback Mountain Trail from Williams to the same gap.

note: Public national forest land; no parking pass or trailhead fee. Snow lingers on the summit into early June.

title: Rough and Ready Botanical Wayside
contentHtml:
Rough and Ready Botanical Wayside is a long-standing wildflower viewing area where new plant hybrids are still emerging. Protection began in 1937 with the Illinois Valley Garden Club, and in 1994 1,164 acres around Rough and Ready Creek became an Area of Critical Environmental Concern. The area supports rare plants found only on Siskiyou serpentine soils.

A 0.3-mile accessible interpretive trail of compacted decomposed granite, mostly flat and 5 to 6 feet wide, leads from the parking area and picnic shelter to an overlook above Rough and Ready Creek, with signs on local plants and geology.

note: No fee; day use only. Two van-accessible parking spaces and an accessible portable toilet; no drinking water. Loose surface can be hard for wheelchairs after rain. Stay on the trail. Managed by BLM Medford District.

title: Bolan Mountain Fire Lookout
imageAlt: Bolan Fire Lookout before the fire (courtesy OPB)

banner.alt: Bolan Fire Lookout before the fire (courtesy OPB)

contentHtml:
The Bolan Mountain Fire Lookout ride is a 43-mile loop (5,300 feet of climbing, about 40% gravel) that climbs steadily through dense conifer forest to the rebuilt Bolan Mountain Lookout. On a clear day the views reach the Kalmiopsis, Red Buttes and Siskiyou wildernesses and possibly Mount Shasta.

Around mile 14 the route enters the 2020 Slater Fire burn area, and it briefly crosses into California. It is a development route not yet fully vetted by Dirty Freehub, so go prepared.

note: Large gravel lot at the start. Holland General Merchandise Store near mile 3 is the only listed services stop. Light traffic on paved sections; use a rear light. At mile 18, veer slightly right and climb for the lookout (straight leads to Bolan Lake).

title: Illinois River
contentHtml:
The Illinois River was designated a National Wild and Scenic River on October 19, 1984, for 50.4 miles (28.7 wild, 17.9 scenic, 3.8 recreational) from the Siskiyou National Forest boundary to its meeting with the Rogue River at Agness.

Its 29-mile wild section runs through a steep canyon that is one of the most remote river stretches in the lower 48 states, with whitewater for small rafts and kayaks. The water is a striking blue-green, with 15 feet or more of visibility, and the river is one of the few West Coast salmon and steelhead rivers with no hatchery program. Rare plants such as the California lady's slipper orchid grow on its serpentine soils.

title: North Fork Silver Creek
contentHtml:
North Fork Silver Creek was designated a Wild and Scenic River in 2019 for 6 recreational miles, from its headwaters to the BLM boundary. Its watershed in the Klamath Mountains has diverse geology, unique soils, steep terrain and at least 16 plant communities, including Brewer spruce, and over 90% of it has burned in two major fires in the past 40 years.

Scenic pools, cascades and colorful bedrock make it a remote spot for primitive camping, hunting and swimming. A 30-foot waterfall blocks fish migration, so the designated section holds resident trout, while downstream it is critical coho salmon habitat.

note: Remote, with no developed public access; an adjacent forest road reaches the creek. Managed by the BLM Medford District.
address: Silver Creek watershed, Klamath Mountains, Josephine County, OR (BLM Medford District)

title: River Styx
contentHtml:
The River Styx, the underground stretch of Cave Creek inside Oregon Caves National Monument, is the first and only underground river in the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System, designated in 2014 for 0.4 scenic miles. It flows year-round at about 41°F.

About 220 feet underground, two tributaries join to form the Ghost Styx, which sinks back into the bedrock and rejoins the main river deeper in the cave. The marble cave's river-fed stalagmites are used in climate research, and the cave preserved fossils including an Ice Age jaguar skull.

note: Seen on ranger-led cave tours (see Oregon Caves National Monument and Preserve).

title: Rogue River
contentHtml:
The Rogue River was one of the original eight National Wild and Scenic Rivers named in 1968, from the mouth of the Applegate River to Lobster Creek Bridge. Tributaries added in 2019 bring the total to 203.5 miles (125 wild, 33.2 scenic, 45.3 recreational) in Josephine and Curry counties.

Through the Wild Rogue Wilderness it runs between steep canyon walls, near-vertical cliffs and cascading creeks. Chinook and coho salmon, steelhead, cutthroat trout and green sturgeon live here, and more than half a million visitors a year come for boating, fishing, float trips, camping, hiking and wildlife watching.
excerpt: The Rogue River was one of the original eight National Wild and Scenic Rivers named in 1968, from the mouth of the Applegate River to Lobster Creek Bridge. Trib
note: The upper 47 miles are managed by the BLM Medford District, (541) 618-2200; the rest by the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest, (541) 592-4000.

title: Rogue Valley Food Trail
contentHtml:
The Rogue Valley Food Trail is a self-guided culinary journey through the valley's farmland, open year-round to explore at your own pace for a day or a week. Stops include farm stands, u-pick farms, farm-to-table restaurants, farmers' markets, craft beverage makers, chocolatiers, cheese makers, bakeries and cafes, all committed to sourcing products grown, raised or made in Southern Oregon.

Seasonal highlights include lavender (April to July), pears (July to September), apples (August to November) and year-round farmers' markets. Annual events include the Oregon Chocolate Festival, Oregon Cheese Festival, Rogue Valley Farm Tour and the Brine, Brew & Barrel Fermentation Festival.
excerpt: The Rogue Valley Food Trail is a self-guided culinary journey through the valley's farmland, open year-round to explore at your own pace for a day or a week. St
note: High season is typically April to November; check hours and seasons with each business. A downloadable brochure is available from Travel Southern Oregon.
address: Rogue Valley, Southern Oregon (start anywhere along the trail)

title: Galice-Hellgate Back Country Byway
imageAlt: Hellgate Canyon Viewpoint, Rogue River (photo: Greg Shine, BLM)

banner.alt: Hellgate Canyon Viewpoint, Rogue River (photo: Greg Shine, BLM)

contentHtml:
The Galice-Hellgate Back Country Byway runs about 40 miles one way through Rogue River country, with a deep canyon, tall rock walls and forested slopes. It is the gateway drive to the Wild and Scenic Rogue River, Hellgate Canyon and the old mining and river-running settlement of Galice.

Numerous river access points and recreation sites offer boating, fishing, hiking and wildlife viewing. The Smullin Visitor Center at Rand, about 18 miles in, has information and restrooms, and at Grave Creek the byway meets the Rogue River National Recreation Trail, first developed by the Takelma people.

title: Grave Creek to Marial Back Country Byway
contentHtml:
The Grave Creek to Marial Back Country Byway is a BLM National Back Country Byway that starts and ends along the Rogue Wild and Scenic River. Over 33 miles of paved, gravel and dirt road it winds through the Siskiyou Mountains high above the river canyon, reaching one of the most scenic and remote sections of the Rogue.

Highlights include the Rainie Falls Overlook, access to the Rogue River National Recreation Trail and the historic Rogue River Ranch at Marial. Beyond the ranch the road serves put-ins and trailheads on the wild Rogue.

title: Grave Creek Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Grave Creek Covered Bridge, built in 1920, is a 105-foot Howe truss over Grave Creek that originally carried the Pacific Highway. It is the last covered bridge on that north-south route and the only one left in Josephine County, visible from Interstate 5.

It has six Gothic windows on each side, rounded portals and a shake roof. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, it reopened in 2001 after repairs.

contentHtml: Page Mountain Sno-Park is a winter parking area on Happy Camp Road in the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest, serving snow play and winter recreation in the Siskiyou Mountains above the Illinois Valley.

title: Grants Pass Drive-In
contentHtml: The Grants Pass Drive-In is one of only three drive-in theaters still operating in Oregon, hosting family movie nights, often classic films, on Fridays in season at the Pottsville grounds in Merlin.

title: Oregon Caves National Monument & Preserve
contentHtml:
Oregon Caves National Monument and Preserve protects the "Marble Halls of Oregon," dark, twisting passages deep in the Siskiyou Mountains, formed and decorated over long ages by acidic water seeping into marble. It is one of the few marble cave systems in the United States.

Rangers lead three guided cave tours plus an off-trail caving tour, and the preserve above ground has trails and mountain meadows such as Bigelow Lakes. Caves Creek Campground has 17 first-come, first-served sites.

title: Bolan Mountain Lookout
contentHtml:
Bolan Mountain Lookout is a glass-walled 14-by-14-foot rental lookout at 6,269 feet with views of the Siskiyou Mountains, Bolan Lake, the Red Buttes, Siskiyou and Kalmiopsis wildernesses, Preston Peak and, on clear days, Mount Shasta. The original lookout burned in the 2020 Slater Fire, and the Siskiyou Mountain Club rebuilt it with the Forest Service in 2024.

It sleeps up to four, with a table, two chairs and a bed that folds into two twins; a vault toilet is nearby. Stargazing, hiking and trout-stocked Bolan Lake are close at hand.

Gated Forest Road 535; high clearance and 4WD/AWD recommended. Parking is below 30 to 40 steep steps; not recommended with young children. No smoking.

title: Weekend Beer Company
contentHtml:
Weekend Beer Company brews approachable, award-winning craft beer in Grants Pass around the idea of "living your weekend" every day of the week. The family- and pet-friendly brewery has a large taproom, a walk-up outdoor bar and about 8,000 square feet of outdoor space.

Craft beer, wine, cider and non-alcoholic options are on tap, and resident food trucks serve the taproom.

address: 1863 NW Washington Blvd, Grants Pass, OR 97526

title: Wild River Brewing
contentHtml:
The Cave Junction restaurant is the original Wild River Brewing & Pizza Company, run by the Miller family since 1975. A 7.5-barrel brewery was added in 1990, giving it the longest continuous run of any brewpub in Southern Oregon.

It serves pizza in its signature bite-sized "party cut," plus sandwiches, burgers and ales and lagers brewed on site, with sausage from a local Cave Junction producer. Wild River also has restaurants in Grants Pass, Medford and Brookings-Harbor.
excerpt: The Cave Junction restaurant is the original Wild River Brewing & Pizza Company, run by the Miller family since 1975. A 7.5-barrel brewery was added in 1990, gi
note: Weekday lunch buffet 11:30 a.m.-2 p.m.; open mic Wednesdays 5:30-8:30 p.m.
address: 249 N Redwood Hwy, Cave Junction, OR 97523

title: Cole Family Vineyards
contentHtml: Cole Family Vineyards is a small organic vineyard in Williams, one of the coolest areas of the Rogue Valley, within the Applegate Valley. Its Sauvignon Blanc goes to Weisinger Family Winery, which makes a barrel- fermented Sauvignon Blanc from the fruit.
excerpt: Cole Family Vineyards is a small organic vineyard in Williams, one of the coolest areas of the Rogue Valley, within the Applegate Valley. Its Sauvignon Blanc go
note: Vineyard only; no public tasting room. Look for its wine through Weisinger Family Winery.
address: Williams, OR (Applegate Valley)

title: Plaisance Ranch
contentHtml:
Plaisance Ranch (pronounced "play-zonce," meaning "with great pleasure") has been a working ranch since 1858, in the Williams Valley near Grayback Mountain in the Applegate Valley. Joe and Suzi Ginet's family has ranching and vineyard roots going back to Joseph Ginet, who came from Savoie, France, in 1898.

The ranch farms 210 acres, growing wine grapes for its estate wines and raising USDA Certified Organic grass- fed beef, sold at the ranch and local farmers markets. It offers a tasting room, tours, a picnic area and wedding receptions.
excerpt: Plaisance Ranch (pronounced "play-zonce," meaning "with great pleasure") has been a working ranch since 1858, in the Williams Valley near Grayback Mountain in t
note: Wheelchair accessible; bus and RV parking.
address: 16955 Water Gap Rd, Williams, OR 97544

title: Schmidt Family Vineyards LLC
contentHtml:
Schmidt Family Vineyards is a destination vineyard, winery and tasting room in the Applegate Valley, family owned and operated for over 20 years by three generations of winemakers. Its wines come from the family's estate vineyard.

Visitors can enjoy flights, glasses and bottles, barrel tastings and winery tours, with a full food menu and grounds made for spending an afternoon. The estate Wilderness Red blend was named a 2026 Wine of the Year (USA).

title: Stonefield Vineyards
contentHtml: Stonefield Vineyards is a small estate winery and vineyard in the Illinois Valley near Cave Junction, part of Southern Oregon's Rogue Valley wine region.
excerpt: Stonefield Vineyards is a small estate winery and vineyard in the Illinois Valley near Cave Junction, part of Southern Oregon's Rogue Valley wine region.

title: Illinois River Forks State Park
contentHtml:
The Illinois River Forks course is an 18-hole disc golf layout (about 5,731 feet) in Illinois River Forks State Park, running beside a clean river with swimming holes and hiking trails in the same park. Established in 2015.

It features elevated tees on holes 4 and 8 and an elevated basket on hole 3, with concrete tees and DISCatcher Pro targets.
excerpt: The Illinois River Forks course is an 18-hole disc golf layout (about 5,731 feet) in Illinois River Forks State Park, running beside a clean river with swimming
note: Free to play. Pit toilet; no running water. Signage can be confusing on holes 2-8.
address: Illinois River Forks State Park, off US 199 near Cave Junction, OR

title: Indian Mary County Park
contentHtml: Indian Mary Park has an easy, mostly flat 9-hole disc golf course along the Rogue River in the park's campground (played as 18 holes, par 54, about 3,999 feet). Established in 1996.
excerpt: Indian Mary Park has an easy, mostly flat 9-hole disc golf course along the Rogue River in the park's campground (played as 18 holes, par 54, about 3,999 feet).
note: Listed as free to play (a park day-use fee may apply). Restrooms in the park.
address: Indian Mary Park, Merlin-Galice Road, Merlin, OR

title: Lake Selmac Park
contentHtml: Lake Selmac is a beautiful, very hilly wooded disc golf course of 18 holes (par 55, about 5,431 feet), mid- length and technical, with tight tunnels and elevation changes. It has concrete and dirt tees and Mach V targets. Established in 2005.
excerpt: Lake Selmac is a beautiful, very hilly wooded disc golf course of 18 holes (par 55, about 5,431 feet), mid- length and technical, with tight tunnels and elevati
note: Free to play; day-use parking $10 (annual pass $35 from the park host). Restrooms and drinking water. Dogs allowed. Not recommended for limited mobility.
address: Lake Selmac County Park, Selma, OR

title: Pacifica DGC
contentHtml: Pacifica is a hilly 18-hole disc golf course (par 54, about 5,627 feet on the Red layout) in Williams, with dirt tees and Tone targets, described as a public space open from dawn until dusk. Established in 2015.
excerpt: Pacifica is a hilly 18-hole disc golf course (par 54, about 5,627 feet on the Red layout) in Williams, with dirt tees and Tone targets, described as a public sp
note: Free to play. Restroom; no drinking water. Dogs allowed. A visitor reports the grounds may require check-in before entry; confirm access with pacificagarden.org.
address: Pacifica, Williams, OR

title: Riverside Park
contentHtml: Riverside Park has an easy, flat 9-hole disc golf course (par 27, about 1,777 feet) of short throws in a busy local park, with concrete tees. Established in 1992.
excerpt: Riverside Park has an easy, flat 9-hole disc golf course (par 27, about 1,777 feet) of short throws in a busy local park, with concrete tees. Established in 199
note: Free to play. Restroom; no drinking water. Wheelchair and stroller accessible. Dogs on leash.
address: Riverside Park, Grants Pass, OR

title: Tom Pearce Park
contentHtml:
Tom Pearce Park is a varied 22-hole disc golf course (par 72) on the Rogue River, moving from open grassy fields through tight woods to rocky brambles. Designed by Robert "Papa P" Pina in 1991 and redesigned in 2009, it has concrete tees and DISCatcher Pro and Mach VII targets.

A driving range with three concrete tee pads and baskets at 200, 250 and 300 feet, plus putting baskets, is a highlight. The park also has horseshoe pits, shelters, picnic areas and river trails.
excerpt: Tom Pearce Park is a varied 22-hole disc golf course (par 72) on the Rogue River, moving from open grassy fields through tight woods to rocky brambles. Designed
note: Unlimited free play; parking $10 per car (annual pass $35 from park hosts). Restrooms and drinking water. Dogs allowed. Gate locks at sunset. Not recommended for limited mobility.
address: Tom Pearce Park, Grants Pass, OR

title: Wolf Creek Park
contentHtml: Wolf Creek Park has a short 9-hole disc golf course (par 25, about 1,494 feet) with homemade baskets, played by campers in the park. Established in 1993.
excerpt: Wolf Creek Park has a short 9-hole disc golf course (par 25, about 1,494 feet) with homemade baskets, played by campers in the park. Established in 1993.
note: Free to play. Limited access: there is no bridge to parts of holes 1 and 4 and all of holes 2 and 3, and other fairways are overgrown.

contentHtml: The Baldwin Hotel Museum is one of three public museums owned and run by Klamath County to preserve the history of the Upper Klamath Basin. Housed in a 1906 hotel, it presents early Klamath history exhibits.

title: Favell Museum
contentHtml:
The Favell Museum, founded by Gene and Winifred Favell, holds more than 100,000 artifacts showing the lives of the indigenous peoples of North and South America, mainly Native American tribes, with collections reaching back about 12,000 years: arrowheads, obsidian knives, spear points, stone tools, clothing, beadwork, basketry and pottery.

It also displays contemporary Western art, including Charles M. Russell's oil painting "The Scouts" and works by John Clymer and Frank McCarthy. An annual art show and sale is held each fall, and a banquet room on the Link River hosts events.
excerpt: The Favell Museum, founded by Gene and Winifred Favell, holds more than 100,000 artifacts showing the lives of the indigenous peoples of North and South America
note: Last admission 4 p.m.; allow at least an hour. Email favellmuseum@gmail.com.
address: 125 W Main St, Klamath Falls, OR 97601

title: Klamath County Museum
contentHtml:
The Klamath County Museum is the hub of the county's three public museums, which preserve the history and heritage of the Upper Klamath Basin. It is housed in the 1935 National Guard armory on Main Street.

Its sister museums are the Baldwin Hotel Museum downtown and the seasonal Fort Klamath Museum.
excerpt: The Klamath County Museum is the hub of the county's three public museums, which preserve the history and heritage of the Upper Klamath Basin. It is housed in t
address: 1451 Main St, Klamath Falls, OR 97601

title: Crater Lake National Park
imageAlt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point

banner.alt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point

contentHtml:
Crater Lake fills the caldera left when a tall volcanic peak, Mount Mazama, erupted and collapsed about 7,700 years ago, an event Native Americans witnessed. Fed only by rain and snow, it is the deepest lake in the United States at 1,943 feet and one of the most pristine lakes on Earth, set atop the Cascade Range. The park lies entirely within Klamath County.

Viewpoints around the rim include Discovery Point, looking out to Wizard Island, and Garfield Peak; Mount Scott is the park's highest point. Waterfalls such as Vidae Falls and summer wildflowers add to the scenery.
excerpt: Crater Lake fills the caldera left when a tall volcanic peak, Mount Mazama, erupted and collapsed about 7,700 years ago, an event Native Americans witnessed. Fe
note: The North Entrance is closed in winter. Cleetwood Cove Trail and the marina are closed for a multi- year rehabilitation. The lake is often hidden by clouds: check the webcam and forecast before you go. Cell service is limited. Entrance fee required.
address: Crater Lake National Park, Crater Lake, OR 97604

title: Deschutes National Forest
contentHtml:
The Deschutes National Forest covers nearly 1.6 million acres on the eastern slopes of the Cascades in Central Oregon, with recreation year-round.

Highlights include Newberry National Volcanic Monument (Lava Lands Visitor Center, Lava River Cave, Lava Butte and the Newberry Caldera), the Cascade Lakes, and the Mount Jefferson, Mount Washington and Three Sisters wilderness areas.

In Klamath County the forest's Crescent Ranger District takes in Crescent, Odell and Davis lakes and their campgrounds, along with parts of the Diamond Peak and Mount Thielsen wilderness areas.
excerpt: The Deschutes National Forest covers nearly 1.6 million acres on the eastern slopes of the Cascades in Central Oregon, with recreation year-round.
note: Some sites charge day-use fees. Central Cascades Wilderness permits are required at some trailheads in summer. Lava River Cave needs a timed-entry parking reservation.
address: 63095 Deschutes Market Rd, Bend, OR 97701

title: Fremont-Winema National Forest
contentHtml:
The Fremont-Winema National Forest stretches across southern Oregon to the California border. Its heavily timbered western side borders Crater Lake National Park and the Cascades, while the semi-arid eastern side, part of "Oregon's Outback," includes part of the Warner Mountains, from snow-capped peaks to wide sage basins.

Visitors fish, hunt, boat, ski, snowmobile, camp, bike, ride horses and watch birds. Mule deer, Rocky Mountain elk, pronghorn, black bears, mountain lions and bobcats live here, and geese, ducks and swans pass through in spring and fall.
excerpt: The Fremont-Winema National Forest stretches across southern Oregon to the California border. Its heavily timbered western side borders Crater Lake National Par
address: Supervisor's Office: 1301 S G St, Lakeview, OR 97630

title: Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest
contentHtml:
The Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest covers about 1.8 million acres of southwest Oregon, from the Cascades to the coast, managed through five ranger districts: High Cascades, Siskiyou Mountains, Wild Rivers, Gold Beach and Powers.

Highlights across the forest include Mount McLoughlin and the Kalmiopsis, Siskiyou and Sky Lakes wilderness areas. In Klamath County the forest shares the Sky Lakes Wilderness with the Fremont-Winema National Forest along the Cascade crest.
excerpt: The Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest covers about 1.8 million acres of southwest Oregon, from the Cascades to the coast, managed through five ranger distric
note: Forest headquarters is in Medford.
address: 3040 Biddle Rd, Medford, OR 97504

title: Diamond Peak Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Diamond Peak Wilderness covers 52,337 acres straddling the Cascade crest in the Willamette and Deschutes national forests. Its centerpiece is 8,744-foot Diamond Peak, a shield volcano later carved by glaciers, ringed by dozens of small lakes of 1 to 28 acres.

About 14 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail run along the peak's east slope, and Marie, Divide and Rockpile lakes are popular base camps for climbing it. Mountain hemlock, lodgepole and white pine and true firs shelter deer, elk, black bears, marmots and pikas; huckleberry and wildflowers are common.
excerpt: The Diamond Peak Wilderness covers 52,337 acres straddling the Cascade crest in the Willamette and Deschutes national forests. Its centerpiece is 8,744-foot Dia
note: Wilderness rules apply. Popular for hiking, camping, fishing, hunting, horseback riding, snowshoeing and cross-country skiing.
address: Cascade crest between Willamette Pass and Crescent Lake (Klamath and Lane counties), OR

title: Gearhart Mountain Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Gearhart Mountain Wilderness covers about 22,800 acres around 8,364-foot Gearhart Mountain, which rises above other volcanic domes. High meadows, cirques, U-shaped valleys and rock formations line its ridges, and the summit views reach Steens Mountain, the Cascades, Lassen Peak and the Three Sisters.

Blue Lake is its only lake, and the Wild and Scenic North Fork Sprague River runs along the north edge. The Gearhart Mountain Trail (#100) offers about 13 miles of foot and horse access, plus the 3-mile Boulder Springs Trail. It is named for brothers James and William Gearhart, who ran cattle here in the 1870s.
excerpt: The Gearhart Mountain Wilderness covers about 22,800 acres around 8,364-foot Gearhart Mountain, which rises above other volcanic domes. High meadows, cirques, U
note: Heavy tree mortality from the 2021 Bootleg Fire: Lookout Rock and Deming Creek trailheads are closed, and the North Fork Sprague trail has many downed trees. Group size 10 people and animals combined; no pack animals within 200 feet of Blue Lake or streams. Boil all water. Snow usually late September to early July.
address: Bly Ranger District, Fremont-Winema National Forest, near Bly, OR

title: Mount Thielsen Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mount Thielsen Wilderness covers about 55,000 acres along the Cascade crest just north of Crater Lake, in the Umpqua, Deschutes and Fremont-Winema national forests. Designated in 1984, it rises from 5,000 feet to the 9,182-foot spire of Mount Thielsen, the 'Lightning Rod of the Cascades.'

About 78 miles of trails include 26 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail. The North Umpqua Trail leads to Lake Lucille and Maidu Lake, where the North Umpqua River begins. Alpine wildflowers peak in August.
excerpt: The Mount Thielsen Wilderness covers about 55,000 acres along the Cascade crest just north of Crater Lake, in the Umpqua, Deschutes and Fremont-Winema national
note: Groups up to 20 people, including livestock. The Mount Thielsen summit trail ends in a 200-foot hand- over-hand scramble.
address: Mount Thielsen, north of Crater Lake National Park, OR

title: Mountain Lakes Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mountain Lakes Wilderness is what remains of a 12,000-foot volcano in the southern Cascades whose eruption formed a caldera that glaciers then carved into a scattering of small alpine lakes. Eight peaks of the old caldera rim remain. At 23,071 acres, it is the only wilderness in the nation with a perfectly square boundary.

One of the region's original primitive areas from 1930, it was designated wilderness in 1964. The 8.2-mile Mountain Lakes Loop Trail follows the southern rim and connects the Clover Creek, Mountain Lakes and Varney Creek trails. Rainbow and brook trout live in the lakes.
excerpt: The Mountain Lakes Wilderness is what remains of a 12,000-foot volcano in the southern Cascades whose eruption formed a caldera that glaciers then carved into a
note: No motorized equipment or bicycles. Mosquitoes are abundant from snowmelt to mid-August.
address: Off OR 140 near Lake of the Woods, Fremont-Winema National Forest, OR

title: Sky Lakes Wilderness
imageAlt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin (area photo)

banner.alt: View of Hyatt Lake and Mt. McLoughlin (area photo)

contentHtml:
The Sky Lakes Wilderness covers about 116,300 acres along the southern Oregon Cascades, about 27 miles long and 6 miles wide, from Crater Lake National Park to Highway 140. It was designated in 1984.

More than 200 lakes and pools dot the high country, including 900-acre Fourmile Lake and the pure waters of Alta and Natasha lakes. Elevations run from about 3,800 feet in the Middle Fork Rogue canyon to 9,495-foot Mount McLoughlin, and the Pacific Crest Trail crosses it for about 35 miles.

Elk, black bears, cougars, pine martens, fishers and pikas live here, and hundreds of thousands of migrating birds pass through in October and November.

note: Wilderness rules apply.
address: Along the Cascade crest from Crater Lake National Park to OR 140; Rogue River-Siskiyou and Fremont-Winema national forests, OR

title: Gerber Recreation Area
contentHtml:
Gerber Recreation Area sits on a high desert plateau of mountain ridges and scattered ponderosa pine around Gerber Reservoir, with about 100,000 acres of backcountry for hunting, wildlife viewing and OHV driving.

Gerber North and South campgrounds have 50 developed sites, and a 7-site horse camp has corrals. There are primitive sites, a day-use area, two boat ramps and accessible restrooms; camping, fishing, hiking, riding and mountain biking are popular.
excerpt: Gerber Recreation Area sits on a high desert plateau of mountain ridges and scattered ponderosa pine around Gerber Reservoir, with about 100,000 acres of backco
note: $7 per night; $4 extra vehicle; $2 day use (peak season only). Drinking water, trash and hosts May- September only. 14-day limit. From Klamath Falls take OR 140 east 15 miles to Dairy, OR 70 to Bonanza, East Langell Valley Road 11 miles, then Gerber Road 8.5 miles.
address: Gerber Road, off East Langell Valley Road, about an hour east of Klamath Falls, OR

title: Surveyor Recreation Site
contentHtml: Surveyor Recreation Site is a secluded five-site campground in old-growth Douglas fir forest, valued for its isolation. It is on the Klamath Basin Birding Trail, with abundant wildlife and good bird watching.
excerpt: Surveyor Recreation Site is a secluded five-site campground in old-growth Douglas fir forest, valued for its isolation. It is on the Klamath Basin Birding Trail
note: No fee; first come, first served; 14-day limit. Accessible restroom and a seasonal spring. Keno Access Road is closed in winter.
address: Keno Access Road, about 14 miles from OR 66 west of Keno, OR

title: Topsy Campground
contentHtml:
Topsy Campground sits on the shoreline of the newly restored Klamath River in open ponderosa pine forest, with views of Mount McLoughlin. It is a quiet spot for camping, picnicking, fishing and river boating, and a base for jeep trips into the remote Upper Klamath River canyon.

Its 13 sites have picnic tables, fire rings and tent pads, with accessible restrooms, drinking water, an RV dump station and a campground host.
excerpt: Topsy Campground sits on the shoreline of the newly restored Klamath River in open ponderosa pine forest, with views of Mount McLoughlin. It is a quiet spot for
note: $7 per night; $4 extra vehicle; $2 day use. First come, first served. Pets on leash.
address: Topsy Road, off OR 66 about 20 miles west of Klamath Falls, OR

title: Collier Memorial State Park
contentHtml:
Collier Memorial State Park is known for its outdoor museum of historic logging equipment, with rare and antique pieces dating to the 1880s, a historic cabin village and railroad exhibits. The Williamson River, regionally known for trout fishing, meets Spring Creek in the park.

The first land was given in 1945 by Alfred and Andrew Collier of Klamath Falls in memory of their parents. The campground has full-hookup and standard sites, a two-site horse camp with corrals and a trailhead linking to more than 10 miles of multi-use forest roads.
excerpt: Collier Memorial State Park is known for its outdoor museum of historic logging equipment, with rare and antique pieces dating to the 1880s, a historic cabin vi
note: Logging museum open 8 a.m.-4 p.m. daily, with a self-guided tour brochure. Camping reservations up to 6 months ahead (800-452-5687). Hot showers and flush toilets; dump station $10; firewood $7. Pets on 6-foot leash.
address: US 97, about 30 miles north of Klamath Falls near Chiloquin, OR

title: Jackson F. Kimball State Recreation Site
imageAlt: Spring-fed headwaters of the Wood River

banner.alt: Spring-fed headwaters of the Wood River

gallery.alt: Kayaking the Wood River (photo: Discover Klamath/Larry Turner)

contentHtml:
Jackson F. Kimball State Recreation Site is a secluded park at the headwaters of the Wood River, where the stream flows from lodgepole pine forest into open meadow with quaking aspens in the southern Cascades. A walking trail leads from the campground to a spring-fed source on a rocky hillside.

The primitive campground sits beside a spring-fed lagoon at the start of the river, and the Wood River's fishing can be reached by canoe.
excerpt: Jackson F. Kimball State Recreation Site is a secluded park at the headwaters of the Wood River, where the stream flows from lodgepole pine forest into open mea
note: 10 primitive first-come sites and 2 horse sites, without water. Vault toilet, picnic tables, fire rings and trash service. Forest trails toward Collier State Park are unmaintained and may be unsafe after fire damage.
address: Near Fort Klamath, OR
