title: OC&E Woods Line State Trail
contentHtml:
The OC&E Woods Line State Trail follows the old Oregon, California and Eastern Railroad bed about 100 miles from Klamath Falls east to Bly and north to Sycan Marsh, making it Oregon's longest linear park and one of the country's longest rail-trails. Construction began in 1917, logging traffic ended in 1990, and the railbed was then turned into a trail.

The paved Urban Section (7.6 miles to Olene) is popular with walkers, joggers, skaters and cyclists; beyond it the Gateway Section to Sprague River is gravel, and the Sprague River and Woods Line sections are loose rock through farm, ranch and forest land.
excerpt: The OC&E Woods Line State Trail follows the old Oregon, California and Eastern Railroad bed about 100 miles from Klamath Falls east to Bly and north to Sycan Ma
note: Non-motorized use only. No drinking water on the trail. Toilets at Reeder Road, Wiard Park, Switchbacks, Bly and Horse Glade trailheads. Livestock in farm areas. Closed from Hildebrand Road to Sprague River for fire restoration, and the Woods Line section remains closed after the Bootleg Fire.
address: Western trailhead: Wiard Park and Washburn Way, Klamath Falls; eastern end at Bly, OR

title: Aspen Point Campground
contentHtml:
Aspen Point Campground sits on the northeast shore of Lake of the Woods, about 40 minutes west of Klamath Falls, with a boat launch, docks, beach and a day-use area that connects to the High Lakes Trail to Fish Lake.

Its 58 sites include RV, double, tent-only and a group site for up to 100. Boating, fishing, biking, swimming and hiking are popular, and the nearby resort has lodging, dining and supplies.
excerpt: Aspen Point Campground sits on the northeast shore of Lake of the Woods, about 40 minutes west of Klamath Falls, with a boat launch, docks, beach and a day-use
note: Reserve on Recreation.gov. About $32 single, $64 double, $140 group per night; $10 extra vehicle; day use $8 (rates differ between listings; check Recreation.gov). Flush toilets; camp host. Check current water availability.
address: Forest Road 3704 off OR 140, about 32 miles west of Klamath Falls, OR

title: Boundary Springs Campground
contentHtml: Boundary Springs is a quiet campground under lodgepole and ponderosa pine on the southeast edge of the Crescent Ranger District, bordering Gilchrist State Forest. It is used mainly by ATV riders and hunters.
excerpt: Boundary Springs is a quiet campground under lodgepole and ponderosa pine on the southeast edge of the Crescent Ranger District, bordering Gilchrist State Fores
note: No fee. Vault toilets; No drinking water; bring your own. Maximum spur length 50 feet. From Crescent, drive 2 miles south on US 97, 6 miles on FR 9768, then 1 mile on FR 9768-600.
address: Forest Road 9768-600, about 9 miles south of Crescent off US 97, OR

title: Contorta Flat Campground
contentHtml:
Contorta Flat is an isolated, hidden campground on the far side of Crescent Lake near Willamette Pass, with tent sites right on the lake and larger sites for RVs, 19 in all, many on the water.

Crescent Lake offers boating, fishing and swimming, and the Summit Lake Trail nearby has views of Diamond Peak. Crescent Lake Resort has lodging, a store and rentals.
excerpt: Contorta Flat is an isolated, hidden campground on the far side of Crescent Lake near Willamette Pass, with tent sites right on the lake and larger sites for RV
note: Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day limit. Last few miles are gravel. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From Crescent, drive 12.2 miles west on County Road 61, 3.5 miles north on OR 58, then 9.9 miles on Forest Road 60.
address: Forest Road 60, far side of Crescent Lake, OR

title: Corral Springs Campground
contentHtml:
Corral Springs is a quiet, primitive campground for those seeking solitude, about 15 minutes from Chemult. A narrow spring-fed creek runs through the middle of its five sites among lodgepole pines.

Hunters use it in fall, and it is a relaxing summer stop for picnicking, hiking, mountain biking and wildlife viewing.
excerpt: Corral Springs is a quiet, primitive campground for those seeking solitude, about 15 minutes from Chemult. A narrow spring-fed creek runs through the middle of
note: No fee. Picnic tables, fire rings and two vault toilets. No drinking water; bring your own. Heavy mosquitoes in June and July. Max vehicle length 50 feet.
address: Forest Road 9774-190, about 3 miles north of Chemult off US 97, OR

title: Crescent Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Crescent Creek is a small, fairly quiet campground on Crescent Creek, somewhat apart from other campgrounds, in lodgepole pine forest with mountain hemlock, fir and spruce near Crescent, Odell and Davis lakes. Deer, native fish and migratory birds live here.

Its nine sites fit RVs, trailers and tents, each with a picnic table and fire ring with grill.

note: Vault toilets; no hookups. Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m.
address: County Road 61, about 9 miles west of Crescent, OR

title: Crescent Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Crescent Lake Campground sits on a hill above Crescent Lake, a glacial basin of blue-green water and sandy beaches backed by lodgepole pine. It was the first campground in the Deschutes National Forest to offer yurts.

It has 44 sites and a boat ramp, with a nearby lodge offering a store, restaurant and boat rentals. Boating, fishing, swimming, water skiing, hiking and mountain biking fill the summer, and the Summit Lake Trail has views of Diamond Peak.
excerpt: Crescent Lake Campground sits on a hill above Crescent Lake, a glacial basin of blue-green water and sandy beaches backed by lodgepole pine. It was the first ca
note: Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From Crescent, drive 12.2 miles west on County Road 61, 3.5 miles north on OR 58, then 2.6 miles on FR 60.
address: Forest Road 60, off OR 58 near Crescent Lake, OR

title: Digit Point Campground
contentHtml:
Digit Point Campground lies on the south shore of Miller Lake under hemlock, white pine, white fir and sugar pine, with many lakeshore sites looking out to Mount Thielsen. Ospreys, eagles, loons and grebes live here.

Biking, boating, swimming and fishing for brown, rainbow and brook trout and kokanee (allowed 24 hours) are popular. The 5-mile Miller Lake Trail loop reaches the Mount Thielsen Wilderness and links to the Pacific Crest and Maidu trails.
excerpt: Digit Point Campground lies on the south shore of Miller Lake under hemlock, white pine, white fir and sugar pine, with many lakeshore sites looking out to Moun
note: Listed as closed; check status. $12 per night; $5 extra vehicle. Flush and vault toilets; RV dump station. Heavy mosquitoes in June and July. No bikes in the wilderness.
address: End of Forest Road 9772, Miller Lake, about 35 minutes west of Chemult, OR

title: East Davis Campground
imageAlt: Odell Creek running past East Davis Campground

banner.alt: Odell Creek running past East Davis Campground

contentHtml:
East Davis Campground sits where Odell Creek enters Davis Lake in the eastern Cascades. Davis Lake is known for wildlife, wildflowers, birding and a nearby lava flow, with views of Cascade peaks.

It is a fly-fishing-only lake known for trophy rainbow trout and largemouth bass. The 19 sites fit RVs, trailers and tents.

note: Vault toilets and drinking water; no hookups. Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From Crescent, drive 8.8 miles west on County Road 61, 7.7 miles north on Highway 46, then 2.6 miles on FR 4600-850.
address: Forest Road 4600-850, east end of Davis Lake, OR

title: Fourmile Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Fourmile Lake Campground is a rustic campground and day-use area at the southern end of the Sky Lakes Wilderness, close to the Pacific Crest Trail. Its 22 first-come sites include seven equestrian sites with corrals in the upper loop.

There is a boat ramp on the lake, and winter brings snowmobiling and ice fishing.
excerpt: Fourmile Lake Campground is a rustic campground and day-use area at the southern end of the Sky Lakes Wilderness, close to the Pacific Crest Trail. Its 22 first
note: Day use $10; extra vehicle $10. Hand-pumped water, vault toilets and stock-loading facilities. No electricity or cell service. Dogs on leash.
address: 6 miles north of OR 140 (turnoff near milepost 36), near Lake of the Woods, OR

title: Head of the River Forest Camp
imageAlt: Head of the River Forest Camp
contentHtml:
Head of the River is a rustic five-site forest camp at the headwaters of the Williamson River, where the spring- fed river runs past the campground. There are no official trails, but you can walk down to the riverbank.

It is popular with fly anglers and fall hunters.
excerpt: Head of the River is a rustic five-site forest camp at the headwaters of the Williamson River, where the spring- fed river runs past the campground. There are n
note: No fee. Vault toilet; No drinking water; bring your own. RVs not recommended (small turnarounds). Heavy mosquitoes in June and July. From Chiloquin, drive east on Sprague River Road about 5 miles, then left on Williamson River Road, FS Road 4648 and FS Road 4648-030.
address: End of Forest Road 4648-030, about 50 minutes northeast of Chiloquin, OR

contentHtml: Indian Spring is a Forest Service campground in the Chemult Ranger District of the Fremont-Winema National Forest, off Forest Road 8310 in the Chiloquin area.

title: Jackson Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Jackson Creek is a quiet, secluded 12-site campground under old-growth ponderosa and Jeffrey pines, with aspen and wild roses for color. Willow-lined Jackson Creek, with small brook trout, runs along the south side, and the meadow across the creek blooms with wildflowers all summer.

Deer and badgers live nearby. A rustic cabin by the entrance serves as a winter warming hut for snowmobilers.

title: Odell Lake Resort and Campground
contentHtml:
Odell Lake Lodge & Resort sits on Odell Lake, a 3,562-acre lake about 6 miles long at 4,800 feet in the Deschutes National Forest. It has seven lodge rooms and suites, 14 rustic cabins with full kitchens, and 24 RV and tent campsites.

The marina has a boat launch, moorage, fuel and rentals of boats, personal watercraft, canoes, kayaks, paddleboards and paddle boats, plus guided fishing for kokanee, mackinaw and rainbow trout; the lake holds the state mackinaw record. A family restaurant serves breakfast, lunch and dinner.
excerpt: Odell Lake Lodge & Resort sits on Odell Lake, a 3,562-acre lake about 6 miles long at 4,800 feet in the Deschutes National Forest. It has seven lodge rooms and
note: Front desk 8 a.m.-8 p.m. Fishing season late April to October 31. Winter brings cross-country skiing, snowmobiling and snowshoeing, with downhill skiing at nearby Willamette Pass.
address: 21501 E Odell Rd, Crescent, OR 97733

title: Princess Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Princess Creek Campground sits next to Odell Lake and is a base for fishing, boating, hiking and biking. Odell Lake sits among lakes, streams and peaks, with Diamond Peak, an 8,744-foot shield volcano in the Diamond Peak Wilderness, overlooking it. The forest is Douglas fir, white fir, hemlock and some ponderosa pine; deer, elk, pine martens, ravens and the occasional black bear live here.

Its sites fit RVs, trailers and tents, each with a picnic table and fire ring with grill, and a boat ramp gives access to the lake.

note: Vault toilets; no hookups and no water, so bring your own. Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day stay limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From Crescent, drive 12.2 miles west on County Road 61, then 9.1 miles northwest on OR 58.
address: Off OR 58, north shore of Odell Lake, about 21 miles from Crescent, OR

title: Scott Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Scott Creek is a remote six-site campground about 45 minutes from Chemult, under lodgepole and ponderosa pine and white fir. Scott Creek runs along the north side, where small trout are sometimes visible.

It is popular with hunters in fall.

address: Forest Road 2310-110, off Sun Mountain Road, southwest of Chemult, OR

title: Shelter Cove Resort and Campground
imageAlt: Winter lake sunset at Shelter Cove

banner.alt: Winter lake sunset at Shelter Cove

gallery.alt: Shelter Cove resort entrance in winter

contentHtml:
Shelter Cove Resort & Marina is a private resort on the west shore of Odell Lake in the Crescent Ranger District, with lodges, cabins, cottages and RV sites.

It has a marina, a convenience store and a community fire pit. In winter it is a base for snowshoeing and skiing, with Willamette Pass Ski Resort nearby.
excerpt: Shelter Cove Resort & Marina is a private resort on the west shore of Odell Lake in the Crescent Ranger District, with lodges, cabins, cottages and RV sites.
note: Full hookups; open year-round (per the client sheet).
address: 27600 W Odell Lake Rd, Hwy 58, Crescent Lake, OR 97733

title: Simax Group Camp
contentHtml:
Simax Group Camp is a fully accessible group campground on the northeast end of Crescent Lake, with four group sites and a large picnic pavilion. The lake has blue-green water and sandy beaches, surrounded by lodgepole pine, mountain hemlock, fir and spruce and volcanic features such as cinder cones and lava flows.

An accessible trail links the group sites to day-use areas and beaches. Water skiing, sailing, windsurfing, hiking, mountain biking, horseback riding and fishing for kokanee, mackinaw, rainbow and brown trout and mountain whitefish are popular.
excerpt: Simax Group Camp is a fully accessible group campground on the northeast end of Crescent Lake, with four group sites and a large picnic pavilion. The lake has b
note: Group reservations only. Drinking water, flush toilets, paved roads and spurs. Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day stay limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From OR 58, turn south at Crescent Lake Junction onto FR 60, go 2.2 miles to FR 6005, then about a mile south following signs.
address: Off Forest Road 6005, northeast end of Crescent Lake, OR

title: Spring Campground
contentHtml:
Spring Campground has widely spaced sites in mixed conifer forest with an open, sunny feel, including several lakefront tent-only sites on Crescent Lake. It is rarely full, so it offers more solitude than nearby campgrounds.

There are 56 standard sites, five tent-only sites and a group site for up to about 70 campers. Summer and early fall bring boating, fishing, swimming, canoeing and water skiing; in winter, Crescent Lake Sno-Park is a base for skiing, snowshoeing and snowmobiling. The Summit Lake Trail runs 9 miles one way.
excerpt: Spring Campground has widely spaced sites in mixed conifer forest with an open, sunny feel, including several lakefront tent-only sites on Crescent Lake. It is
note: Drinking water and vault toilets. Some sites reservable, others first-come. Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day stay limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From Crescent, drive 12.2 miles west on Road 61, 3.5 miles north on OR 58, then 8.1 miles west on Road 60.
address: Forest Road 60, southwest shore of Crescent Lake, OR

title: Sunset Campground
contentHtml:
Sunset Campground on Lake of the Woods has 64 sites with a camp host, about 40 minutes west of Klamath Falls. Its day-use area has picnic tables, a boat ramp and a small gravel swimming beach.

Boating, waterskiing, swimming, fishing, hiking and mountain biking fill the summer, with cross-country skiing and snowshoeing in winter. Lake of the Woods Resort nearby has dining, boat rentals and supplies.
excerpt: Sunset Campground on Lake of the Woods has 64 sites with a camp host, about 40 minutes west of Klamath Falls. Its day-use area has picnic tables, a boat ramp an
note: Reserve on Recreation.gov. $30 per night; $10 extra vehicle; day use $10. Half price on single sites with Interagency passes. Renovated flush-toilet restrooms; check current water availability.
address: Dead Indian Memorial Road off OR 140, about 33 miles west of Klamath Falls, OR

title: Sunset Cove Campground
imageAlt: Sunset Cove Campground on Odell Lake

banner.alt: Sunset Cove Campground on Odell Lake

contentHtml:
Sunset Cove Campground sits next to Odell Lake and suits fishing, boating, hiking and biking. Odell Lake sits among lakes, streams and peaks, with Diamond Peak, an 8,744-foot shield volcano in the Diamond Peak Wilderness, overlooking it. The forest is Douglas fir, white fir, hemlock and some ponderosa pine; deer, elk, pine martens, ravens and the occasional black bear live here.

Its 20 sites fit RVs, trailers and tents, with a boat ramp and first-come boat slips on the lake.
excerpt: Sunset Cove Campground sits next to Odell Lake and suits fishing, boating, hiking and biking. Odell Lake sits among lakes, streams and peaks, with Diamond Peak,
note: Drinking water and vault toilets; no hookups. Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day stay limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From Crescent, drive 12.2 miles west on County Road 61, then 6.2 miles north and west on OR 58.
address: Off OR 58, Odell Lake, about 18 miles from Crescent, OR

title: Trapper Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Trapper Creek Campground is a heavily forested campground on a small stream that feeds Odell Lake, with secluded tent and RV sites near the Diamond Peak Wilderness.

Swimming, water skiing, hiking, fishing, boating and mountain biking are popular in spring, summer and fall, and cross-country skiing and snowshoeing in winter. A nearby Odell Lake resort has lodging, a general store and fishing licenses.
excerpt: Trapper Creek Campground is a heavily forested campground on a small stream that feeds Odell Lake, with secluded tent and RV sites near the Diamond Peak Wildern
note: Drinking water and a boat ramp; no hookups. Parking spurs may not be level. Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day stay limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From I-5 exit 188A, drive 62.4 miles east on OR 58, then 1.9 miles south on Road 5810.
address: Forest Road 5810, west end of Odell Lake, OR

title: Whitefish Horse Camp
contentHtml:
Whitefish Horse Camp overlooks Crescent Lake, a high-elevation lake in a glaciated basin with sandy beaches, and is a favorite of horse riders. Snow-capped peaks, scenic rivers and several wilderness areas are nearby.

Its 17 equestrian sites have double or quadruple metal corrals, plus a picnic table, fire ring and trailer parking.

note: For campers with horses; certified weed-seed-free hay required. Drinking water (may end in early October) and vault toilets. Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day stay limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From La Pine, go 17.5 miles south on US 97, 11.9 miles on Crescent Cutoff Road, about 2 miles on OR 58, 2.2 miles on FR 60, 1.2 miles on Crescent Lake Road, then 3.5 miles on FR 60.

title: Williamson River Campground
contentHtml:
Williamson River Campground has 19 sites (one accessible) among ponderosa pine and sagebrush beside the Williamson River, just off Highway 97 north of Chiloquin.

A 1.3-mile walking trail connects to Collier Memorial State Park's logging museum and pioneer village. Fishing, day hikes and mountain biking on forest roads are popular.

title: Windy Group Camp
contentHtml: Windy Group Camp is a rustic, secluded group campground for up to 40 people at the southwest end of Crescent Lake, at the water's edge, with nearby trails and water activities on the lake's blue-green water and sandy beaches.
excerpt: Windy Group Camp is a rustic, secluded group campground for up to 40 people at the southwest end of Crescent Lake, at the water's edge, with nearby trails and w
note: One vault toilet, picnic tables and a barbecue pit; unpaved roads with RV parking. No drinking water; bring your own. No camping within 100 feet of the water. Reserve on Recreation.gov; 14-day stay limit. No generators 10 p.m.-7 a.m. From OR 58 about 8 miles east of Willamette Pass, turn west at Crescent Lake Junction onto FR 60 and go about 7 miles.
address: Forest Road 60, southwest end of Crescent Lake, OR

title: Bear Valley
imageAlt: Old-growth ponderosa pine at Bear Valley

banner.alt: Old-growth ponderosa pine at Bear Valley

contentHtml:
Bear Valley National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1978 to protect a night roost for wintering bald eagles. Its 4,200 acres are mostly old-growth ponderosa pine, incense cedar, and white and Douglas fir on a sheltered slope.

It is among the most heavily used bald eagle wintering sites in the lower 48 states, with as many as 300 eagles in a single night, drawn by waterfowl on nearby refuges. Watch the dawn fly-out from the viewing area on Keno-Worden Road.
excerpt: Bear Valley National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1978 to protect a night roost for wintering bald eagles. Its 4,200 acres are mostly old-growth ponderosa
note: The refuge is closed to public entry except for walk-in deer hunting before November 1. Start at the Klamath Basin refuges visitor center in Tulelake, California, for exhibits and planning help.
address: Klamath Basin NWR Complex Visitor Center: 4064 Hill Road, Tulelake, CA 96134

title: Klamath Marsh
contentHtml:
Klamath Marsh National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1958, protects 40,885 acres at the head of the Williamson River, one of the largest natural marshes in the West. Its wetlands are mostly wet meadows with some open water, kept as feeding habitat for waterfowl and sandhill cranes in fall and spring.

It is a stronghold of the yellow rail and the Oregon spotted frog. All viewing is from the refuge boundary, and a canoe launch on Forest Service Road 690 leads into Wocus Bay in summer.
excerpt: Klamath Marsh National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1958, protects 40,885 acres at the head of the Williamson River, one of the largest natural marshes in th
note: Call ahead; the visitor center is staffed on a limited basis. From Klamath Falls, drive about 45 miles north on US 97, then 9.5 miles east on Silver Lake Road to FS Road 690 (canoe launch 4 miles south on this gravel road); for headquarters, continue on Silver Lake Road to milepost 17.
address: Refuge headquarters at milepost 17, Silver Lake Road, east of US 97, OR

title: Upper Klamath
contentHtml:
Upper Klamath National Wildlife Refuge, set aside by President Calvin Coolidge on April 3, 1928, is one of six refuges protecting what remains of the Klamath Basin's historic wetlands. Its 23,098 acres of marsh and open water lie on the northwest shore of Upper Klamath Lake.

It is key nesting and brood-rearing habitat for waterfowl and colonial birds, including American white pelicans, and important for spring-migrating waterfowl. Most of it is reachable only by boat from Rocky Point and Malone Springs, the launch points for the Upper Klamath Canoe Trail.
excerpt: Upper Klamath National Wildlife Refuge, set aside by President Calvin Coolidge on April 3, 1928, is one of six refuges protecting what remains of the Klamath Ba
address: Klamath Basin NWR Complex Visitor Center: 4064 Hill Road, Tulelake, CA 96134

title: Klamath Wildlife Area
contentHtml:
Klamath Wildlife Area was established in 1958 to protect waterfowl habitat and provide public hunting. Its 3,717 acres in four units are managed for wintering and nesting waterfowl, upland game birds and other wildlife; the main Miller Island Unit lies four miles south of Klamath Falls off US 97.

Bald eagles, American white pelicans, greater sandhill cranes and up to 70,000 spring-migrating geese use the area. Best viewing is February through November, with spring goose numbers peaking late February to early April. Hunting for pheasant, quail, dove, ducks, snipe and geese runs in fall and winter.

note: A Wildlife Area Parking Permit is required ($10 per day, $30 per year). Closed February 1 to April 30 except public roads, parking areas, the birding trail and the dog training area. Boat ramp on the Klamath River, restrooms, picnic areas, trails and a camp host.
address: 1850 Miller Island Road West, Klamath Falls, OR 97603

imageAlt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point (area photo)

banner.alt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point (area photo)

contentHtml:
Annie Falls is one of three named waterfalls in Crater Lake National Park. Annie Creek drops about 53 feet down a sloped step in Annie Creek Canyon, whose walls are petrified volcanic ash from Mount Mazama.

It is viewed from the Annie Falls picnic area, though trees at the canyon bottom block most views.

imageAlt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point (area photo)

banner.alt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point (area photo)

contentHtml: Plaikni Falls is a horsetail waterfall on Sand Creek in Crater Lake National Park, reached by a trail opened in 2011. The gently sloping path is about 2 miles round trip through lush surroundings.
excerpt: Plaikni Falls is a horsetail waterfall on Sand Creek in Crater Lake National Park, reached by a trail opened in 2011. The gently sloping path is about 2 miles r
note: The first three-quarters of the trail is accessible to wheelchair users with assistance; the short final climb to the falls may be too steep.

title: Vidae Falls
imageAlt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point (area photo)

banner.alt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point (area photo)

contentHtml:
Vidae Falls is a spring-fed waterfall about 100 feet tall that tumbles over multiple bluffs above East Rim Drive, which crosses the lower part of the cascade. It is visible from your car, but worth stepping out for a closer look.

A short access road below the falls leads to a picnic area with a trailhead for Crater Peak, a cinder cone.
excerpt: Vidae Falls is a spring-fed waterfall about 100 feet tall that tumbles over multiple bluffs above East Rim Drive, which crosses the lower part of the cascade. I
note: Rim Drive is seasonal; check road status with the park.
address: East Rim Drive, about 2 miles from park headquarters, Crater Lake National Park, OR

title: Lake of the Woods
contentHtml: Lake of the Woods is a mountain lake in the Southern Oregon Cascades with forested shoreline and mountain views, good for kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding and canoeing. Launch from Forest Service campgrounds and day-use areas around the shore or from Lake of the Woods Resort, which runs a marina and has food and services.
excerpt: Lake of the Woods is a mountain lake in the Southern Oregon Cascades with forested shoreline and mountain views, good for kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding and
note: Wind can change conditions quickly on open water, and the water stays cold even in warm weather. Motorboats are allowed: slow-no-wake within 200 feet of any dock or shore, and 20 mph from one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise. Life jackets and an Oregon Waterway Access Permit are required. Check for day-use fees.
address: Lake of the Woods, off OR 140 between Klamath Falls and Medford, OR

title: Upper Klamath Canoe Trail
imageAlt: Upper Klamath National Wildlife Refuge (area photo)

banner.alt: Upper Klamath National Wildlife Refuge (area photo)

contentHtml:
The Upper Klamath Canoe Trail covers 9.5 miles of marsh, open lake and forest in Upper Klamath National Wildlife Refuge, in four segments: Recreation Creek, Crystal Creek, Wocus Cut and Malone Springs. It runs between the Rocky Point and Malone Springs boat launches.

Early morning is best for birds: white pelicans, Canada geese, coots, belted kingfishers, ospreys and bald eagles, with warblers and flycatchers along the shore in spring and early summer. Wocus, the yellow pond lily, is the marsh's most common plant, and river otters often play along the trail.
excerpt: The Upper Klamath Canoe Trail covers 9.5 miles of marsh, open lake and forest in Upper Klamath National Wildlife Refuge, in four segments: Recreation Creek, Cry
note: Wocus Cut is best paddled in spring and early summer and is usually dry by August. Bring a life jacket for each person, an invasive species permit, an extra paddle, sunscreen, insect repellent and a waterproof bag.
address: Klamath Basin NWR Complex Visitor Center: 4064 Hill Road, Tulelake, CA 96134

title: Mount Thielsen
contentHtml:
Mount Thielsen (9,182 ft) is a glacier-carved volcanic spire on the Douglas-Klamath county line north of Crater Lake, nicknamed the 'Lightning Rod of the Cascades.' Its summit is the highest point in the Umpqua National Forest.

Mountain hemlock and whitebark pine give way to steep, treeless rocky slopes. August is usually the best month for alpine wildflowers.
excerpt: Mount Thielsen (9,182 ft) is a glacier-carved volcanic spire on the Douglas-Klamath county line north of Crater Lake, nicknamed the 'Lightning Rod of the Cascad
note: A serious climb, not a hike: the strenuous 5-mile trail (#1456) has no markers above timberline and ends with a difficult 200-foot hand-over-hand scramble; ropes are advised for the summit.
address: Mount Thielsen Trailhead, OR 138 west of Diamond Lake, OR

title: Fremont National Recreation Trail
contentHtml:
The Fremont National Recreation Trail #160, also called the Southern Oregon Intertie Trail, runs about 135 miles through most of the Fremont National Forest. It starts at Yamsay Mountain, crosses Hager Mountain and Winter Rim, and reaches the Warner Mountains, where it meets the Crane Mountain National Recreation Trail.

The northern and middle sections pass near Silver Lake, Summer Lake and Paisley, ending near Lakeview at Cox Pass; the southern section follows the crest of the northern Warner Mountains. It is open to hiking, horseback riding and mountain biking.
excerpt: The Fremont National Recreation Trail #160, also called the Southern Oregon Intertie Trail, runs about 135 miles through most of the Fremont National Forest. It
note: Some sections are very primitive, and past fires and beetle damage near Winter Ridge make parts hard to follow. A gap of about six miles between Cox Pass and Mill Trailhead is bypassed on roads. Treat all water.
address: Fremont-Winema National Forest Supervisor's Office: 1301 South G Street, Lakeview, OR 97630

title: Metolius–Windigo Trail
contentHtml:
The Metolius-Windigo Trail (Trail #99) runs roughly 150 miles through the Deschutes National Forest, from the Metolius Basin near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness west of Sisters south to Windigo Pass near Crescent Lake. Created around 1980 as a lower-elevation alternative to the Pacific Crest Trail, it connects to the PCT at both ends and is popular with horse riders.

Its southern end, Windigo Pass, sits on the Douglas-Klamath county line.
excerpt: The Metolius-Windigo Trail (Trail #99) runs roughly 150 miles through the Deschutes National Forest, from the Metolius Basin near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness
note: Published lengths vary from about 120 to 152 miles.

title: Oregon Timber Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Timber Trail is a 670-mile mountain bike and bikepacking route from the California border near Lakeview north to Hood River on the Columbia, managed by the nonprofit Oregon Timber Trail Alliance. It is split into four tiers: Fremont, Willamette, Deschutes and Hood.

Riders can take on the whole route or ride a shorter piece of any tier.

address: California border near Lakeview to Hood River, OR

title: Pacific Crest Trail
contentHtml:
The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail runs 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada through California, Oregon and Washington, managed by the Forest Service with the Pacific Crest Trail Association. Its roughly 455-mile Oregon section is the shortest and easiest on the trail, from near Siskiyou Summit to the Bridge of the Gods over the Columbia River.

In Klamath County the trail follows the Cascade crest through the Sky Lakes Wilderness (about 35 miles) and the Mount Thielsen Wilderness.

address: Oregon section: California border near Ashland to the Bridge of the Gods, Cascade Locks, OR

title: Pinnacles Trail, Crater Lake
imageAlt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point (area photo)

banner.alt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point (area photo)

contentHtml:
The Pinnacles Trail is a flat, wide path of about a mile one way along an old roadbed of hard-packed dirt and crushed rock, passing volcanic spires and ending at the park's east boundary. It is not a loop.

The park lists it among trails accessible to all-terrain wheelchair users with assistance, with a level 250-foot walk to the first spire overlook.

note: Use caution near cliffs. Pinnacles Road and Rim Drive are seasonal.

title: Destination Milkshake!
imageAlt: High Lakes Trail at Great Meadow trailhead

banner.alt: High Lakes Trail at Great Meadow trailhead

contentHtml:
Destination Milkshake! is an 18-mile out-and-back ride on the High Lakes Trail linking Lake of the Woods and Fish Lake, with a milkshake stop at Fish Lake Resort at the midpoint. It is rated easier, with about 1,100 feet of climbing on a mostly forest-loam path with compacted gravel through a lava field.

Highlights include views of Mt. McLoughlin and Brown Mountain, a fissure over 200 feet long near mile 5.3, the Pacific Crest Trail crossing near mile 8 and more than ten interpretive kiosks on geology, history and wildlife.

note: No facilities at the start. Tires 40 mm or wider. Posts at road crossings narrow the trail to 44 inches; yield to hikers and uphill riders. Ride spring through fall; summer is best.

title: High Lakes - Brown Mountain
imageAlt: Gravel trail through lava flow fields

banner.alt: Gravel trail through lava flow fields

contentHtml:
High Lakes - Brown Mountain is a 25-mile loop around Brown Mountain, a cinder cone in the Cascades. Gravel roads climb through the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest to over 5,700 feet, then descend to Fish Lake for lake views and swimming before finishing on flowing trail through lava fields with views of Mt. McLoughlin.

It has about 1,800 feet of climbing on roughly 85% unpaved surface. Fish Lake Resort's store and cafe (around mile 19.5) is the food and water stop.
excerpt: High Lakes - Brown Mountain is a 25-mile loop around Brown Mountain, a cinder cone in the Cascades. Gravel roads climb through the Rogue River-Siskiyou National
note: Listed as a development route not yet fully vetted; navigation needs attention. Small gravel lot with no services. Free-range cattle in the forest; please do not disturb them.
address: High Lakes Trail West Access, off OR 140 near Fish Lake, OR

title: Klamath Marsh
imageAlt: Riding dirt road near Klamath Marsh

banner.alt: Riding dirt road near Klamath Marsh

contentHtml:
The Klamath Marsh ride is a flat, bird-rich 26-mile lollipop through wetlands and tall ponderosa pine, with wide marsh views backed by Mt. McLoughlin, Mt. Scott, Mt. Bailey and Mt. Thielsen. A signed canoe launch just past mile 4 leads to the water's edge.

The Wocus Loop circles Wocus Butte on double-track and dirt roads, followed by a descent on a wide red cinder road. It is rated moderate, with about 1,000 feet of gentle climbing on 100% dirt and gravel roads.
excerpt: The Klamath Marsh ride is a flat, bird-rich 26-mile lollipop through wetlands and tall ponderosa pine, with wide marsh views backed by Mt. McLoughlin, Mt. Scott
note: No food or water on route. Tires 45 mm or wider (50 mm later in the season). Stay on route, respect seasonal wildlife closures, and leave artifacts undisturbed; the area is important to the Klamath Tribes. Best May through June; birding February through June.
address: Pull-out at Silver Lake Road and NF 690 (Wocus Bay Road), Klamath Marsh NWR, OR

title: OC&E (Yonna Valley Meadows)
imageAlt: The snow dozer at the start

banner.alt: The snow dozer at the start

contentHtml:
OC&E (Yonna Valley Meadows) is a 25-mile out-and-back ride on the old Oregon, California & Eastern railway bed from Olene to Yonna Valley Meadows, on an eight-foot-wide gravel trail with about 700 feet of climbing.

Stops include the 1941 Weyerhaeuser snow dozer at the start, Olene Gap (site of an 1872 Modoc War council), the Olene Flume of the Klamath Reclamation Project and Swede's Cut, a deep cut blasted through basalt. Bald and golden eagles, red-tailed hawks and northern harriers are common.
excerpt: OC&E (Yonna Valley Meadows) is a 25-mile out-and-back ride on the old Oregon, California & Eastern railway bed from Olene to Yonna Valley Meadows, on an eight-f
note: Dirty Freehub no longer recommends this route due to open cattle grazing and limited maintenance. Parking is a dirt lot with no facilities; look for the yellow snow dozer. Can be muddy or rough from frost heaving in April and early May.
address: OC&E Trail parking at Olene, north side of OR 140, OR

title: Oregon Outback (Re-imagined)
contentHtml:
The Oregon Outback (Re-imagined) is a 400-mile point-to-point bikepacking route from Klamath Falls to The Dalles, re-routed by Dirty Freehub to support local towns. Plan 5 to 7 days and about 20,000 feet of climbing.

It passes big skies and high desert along the OC&E Trail, Thompson Reservoir, Silver Lake, Fort Rock State Park, Pine Mountain Observatory and the Cowboy Dinner Tree.
excerpt: The Oregon Outback (Re-imagined) is a 400-mile point-to-point bikepacking route from Klamath Falls to The Dalles, re-routed by Dirty Freehub to support local to
note: Rated demanding and extremely remote; listed as a development route. Water is sparse: carry 5.5 to 7.5 liters and treat all water. Resupply in Klamath Falls, Sprague River (cash), Beatty (limited hours) and Silver Lake. Snow possible into late April and from late October.
address: Starts in Klamath Falls, OR; ends in The Dalles, OR

title: Big Marsh Creek
contentHtml:
Big Marsh Creek is a 15-mile Recreational Wild and Scenic River, designated in 1988, that winds through a rare high-mountain marsh before joining Crescent Creek. The marsh formed from a glacial lake that filled with sediment, and its plant diversity is found nowhere else in the region.

The upper section lies within the Oregon Cascades Recreation Area, with scenic views and wildlife watching.
excerpt: Big Marsh Creek is a 15-mile Recreational Wild and Scenic River, designated in 1988, that winds through a rare high-mountain marsh before joining Crescent Creek
note: Managed by the Deschutes National Forest.
address: Deschutes National Forest, near Crescent Lake, OR

banner.alt: Crescent Creek (photo: Zachary Collier, Northwest Rafting Company)

note: Managed by the Deschutes National Forest. Crescent Creek Campground lies along the designated reach.

title: Klamath River
imageAlt: Klamath River, Oregon (photo: Bob Wick, BLM)

banner.alt: Klamath River, Oregon (photo: Bob Wick, BLM)

contentHtml:
This 11-mile Scenic Wild and Scenic reach of the Klamath River, designated in 1994, runs from the J.C. Boyle Powerhouse to the California border. The Klamath is one of only three rivers that cut through the Cascade Range, and its canyon shifts from high desert to mountain terrain with pine, sagebrush, juniper and basalt outcrops.

It offers a long whitewater season with Class III-IV+ rapids, plus fishing for a distinct wild rainbow trout population, hunting, camping, hiking and four-wheel-drive touring. Native peoples have used the canyon for at least 7,000 years, and the Shasta Nation and the Klamath Tribes consider it sacred.

title: Little Deschutes River
contentHtml:
The upper 12 miles of the Little Deschutes River, from its source, is a Recreational Wild and Scenic River designated in 1988. Its glacial canyon, with moraines and an outwash plain, is the longest and deepest on the east flank of the Oregon Cascades.

Loop meanders, oxbow channels and steep rock walls mark the upper canyon, with lodgepole pine on the terrace and healthy willow and sedge riparian zones that shelter wildlife needing solitude.

title: North Fork Sprague River
imageAlt: North Fork Sprague River (photo: Tim Palmer)

banner.alt: North Fork Sprague River (photo: Tim Palmer)

contentHtml:
The North Fork Sprague River is a 15-mile Scenic Wild and Scenic River, designated in 1988. It leaves the Gearhart Mountain Wilderness through high meadows bordered by lodgepole pine, then drops into a steep, V-shaped basalt canyon with springs flowing from its walls.

Fishing, hiking, hunting, horseback riding, camping, picnicking and floating at high water are popular, with wildflowers and fall color and plenty of solitude.

title: Sycan River
contentHtml:
The Sycan River is a 59-mile Wild and Scenic River (Recreational and Scenic), designated in 1988. Its scenery ranges from a narrow basalt canyon with large water-sculpted boulders to broad meadows, with old-growth ponderosa pine, lodgepole flats and riparian willows.

Sycan Marsh holds rare plant communities and wetland habitat for sandhill cranes, bald eagles and waterfowl, and the river supports redband trout.

title: Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway
imageAlt: Sparks Lake, a favorite of photographer Ray Atkeson

banner.alt: Sparks Lake, a favorite of photographer Ray Atkeson

contentHtml:
The Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway is a 66-mile National Scenic Byway from Bend past Mt. Bachelor and a chain of mountain lakes to Highway 58 near Crescent Lake. Stop at Sparks Lake for views of South Sister and Broken Top and the Ray Atkeson loop trail, shallow Devils Lake, crystal-clear Elk Lake and Hosmer Lake, Lava and Little Lava lakes with Three Sisters views, and Davis Lake's lava formations and fly fishing.

Hike-in lakes such as Green Lakes, Doris Lake and Lucky Lake, and the riverside Deschutes River Trail with two waterfalls, are along the way. Only the southern end crosses into Klamath County.

note: Check TripCheck.com for road conditions and wildfire alerts before you go.

title: Volcanic Legacy Scenic Byway
contentHtml:
The Volcanic Legacy Scenic Byway is a 140-mile volcano-to-volcano drive through Southern Oregon, past cinder cones, pumice plains and Crater Lake, the deepest lake in the U.S. Allow 5 to 7 hours.

From Diamond Lake Junction, OR 138 leads to Crater Lake's North Entrance and the 33-mile Rim Drive. The route continues past Fort Klamath and its museum, along Upper Klamath Lake and its refuge (with the Upper Klamath Canoe Trail near Rocky Point), to Klamath Falls' Link River trails, Baldwin Hotel, Ross Ragland Theater and Favell Museum, then south past Bear Valley and Lower Klamath refuges.

note: Best June through October; Crater Lake's North Entrance is usually open only about June to October, while the South Entrance (OR 62) is open year-round.
address: Diamond Lake Junction (US 97 / OR 138) to the California border via Crater Lake and Klamath Falls, OR

title: Willamette Pass Resort

gallery.alt: Group lessons at Willamette Pass (photo: Eric Berry)

contentHtml:
Willamette Pass Resort sits on the Cascade crest at Willamette Pass on OR 58 and is the closest skiing to Eugene. It has 555 acres, 29 runs and six lifts, including Oregon's first six-person high-speed detachable chairlift, with 1,563 feet of vertical.

Average snowfall is about 430 inches, backed by expanded snowmaking, and the resort offers rentals, demo equipment and group lessons.

title: Crater Lake
imageAlt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point

banner.alt: Crater Lake and Wizard Island from Discovery Point

contentHtml:
Crater Lake fills the caldera left when a tall volcanic peak, Mount Mazama, erupted and collapsed about 7,700 years ago, an event Native Americans witnessed. Fed only by rain and snow, it is the deepest lake in the United States at 1,943 feet and one of the most pristine lakes on Earth, set atop the Cascade Range. The park lies entirely within Klamath County.

Viewpoints around the rim include Discovery Point, looking out to Wizard Island, and Garfield Peak; Mount Scott is the park's highest point. Waterfalls such as Vidae Falls and summer wildflowers add to the scenery.

note: The North Entrance is closed in winter. Cleetwood Cove Trail and the marina are closed for a multi- year rehabilitation. The lake is often hidden by clouds: check the webcam and forecast before you go. Cell service is limited. Entrance fee required.
address: Crater Lake National Park, Crater Lake, OR 97604

title: Train Mountain Railroad
contentHtml:
Train Mountain is recognized by Guinness World Records as the world's longest rideable miniature hobby railway, with more than 32 miles of 7.5-inch-gauge track across 2,200 acres about 25 miles north of Klamath Falls. Its museum holds over 50 full-sized rail cars and maintenance-of-way equipment.

Free volunteer-led rail tours on 1/8-scale trains run in summer, about 30 minutes each, and a self-guided walking tour is available. On summer Saturdays the neighboring Klamath & Western Railroad gives rides and runs a small lunch stand.

note: Free admission, parking and rail tours; donations welcome. Rail tours run Sunday-Friday, 10 a.m. - 2:30 p.m., in summer (no tours on Saturdays or in winter). Closed July 4. Large groups should call ahead. From US 97, turn west on South Chiloquin Road near milepost 249; the entrance is on the left after 0.85 miles.

title: Downtown Klamath Falls
imageAlt: Actor James LeGros runs down Main Street in Klamath Falls during filming of Phoenix, Oregon (2018)

banner.alt: Actor James LeGros runs down Main Street in Klamath Falls during filming of Phoenix, Oregon (2018)

contentHtml:
Downtown Klamath Falls has one of the West's finest historic Main Streets, a hub of shopping, dining and cultural history in Oregon's City of Sunshine.

It doubled as the title town in Gary Lundgren's Phoenix, Oregon (2019), a comedy about two friends who revive a shuttered bowling alley, filmed here in 2018 with locations including Hanscam's Bowling Alley and The Daily Bagel. An Oregon Film Trail sign marks the spot at 7th and Main.
excerpt: Downtown Klamath Falls has one of the West's finest historic Main Streets, a hub of shopping, dining and cultural history in Oregon's City of Sunshine.
address: Oregon Film Trail sign: corner of 7th and Main Streets (outside The Daily Bagel, 636 Main St), Klamath Falls, OR

title: Mia and Pia's
contentHtml:
Mia & Pia's Pizzeria & Brewhouse is the Klamath area's first microbrewery and pizzeria and a local hangout for entertainment, house beers and hand-crafted pizza. About 13 house beers are on tap, kegged fresh.

It has games, a casual brewpub setting and an outdoor patio for warm-weather dining.
excerpt: Mia & Pia's Pizzeria & Brewhouse is the Klamath area's first microbrewery and pizzeria and a local hangout for entertainment, house beers and hand-crafted pizza
address: 3545 Summers Ln, Klamath Falls, OR 97603

title: Skyline Brewing
contentHtml:
Skyline Brewing Company is a family-run farm brewery just south of Klamath Falls, in a renovated milking parlor about 100 years old. Spent grain feeds the farm's cattle, and used hops and yeast become fertilizer.

Beers include the flagship Red Blooded American Ale, an India Pale Ale, Munich Helles Lager, Liquid Vacation Double IPA, Raspberry Wheat (50 cents a pint goes to the American Cancer Society's Harvest for Hope) and Chocolate Raspberry Porter.
excerpt: Skyline Brewing Company is a family-run farm brewery just south of Klamath Falls, in a renovated milking parlor about 100 years old. Spent grain feeds the farm'
address: 927 Old Midland Rd, Klamath Falls, OR

imageAlt: Homestead-era church and windmill at Fort Rock

banner.alt: Homestead-era church and windmill at Fort Rock

contentHtml:
Fort Rock Homestead Village Museum is an open-air village run by the Fort Rock Valley Historical Society, formed in 1984 to preserve the history of the homestead era, which peaked in 1912. Opened in 1988, it gathers homestead-era buildings moved from around the Fort Rock Valley and restored with period furnishings, including cabins, St. Rose's Church, the Sunset School and Dr. Thom's office.

It sits just west of the town of Fort Rock, about a mile from the Fort Rock tuff ring.

title: Deschutes National Forest
contentHtml:
The Deschutes National Forest covers nearly 1.6 million acres on the eastern slopes of the Cascades in Central Oregon, with recreation year-round.

Highlights include Newberry National Volcanic Monument (Lava Lands Visitor Center, Lava River Cave, Lava Butte and the Newberry Caldera), the Cascade Lakes, and the Mount Jefferson, Mount Washington and Three Sisters wilderness areas.
excerpt: The Deschutes National Forest covers nearly 1.6 million acres on the eastern slopes of the Cascades in Central Oregon, with recreation year-round.
note: Some sites charge day-use fees. Central Cascades Wilderness permits are required at some trailheads in summer. Lava River Cave needs a timed-entry parking reservation.
address: 63095 Deschutes Market Rd, Bend, OR 97701

title: Fremont-Winema National Forest
contentHtml:
The Fremont-Winema National Forest stretches across southern Oregon to the California border. Its heavily timbered western side borders Crater Lake National Park and the Cascades, while the semi-arid eastern side, part of "Oregon's Outback," includes part of the Warner Mountains, from snow-capped peaks to wide sage basins.

Visitors fish, hunt, boat, ski, snowmobile, camp, bike, ride horses and watch birds. Mule deer, Rocky Mountain elk, pronghorn, black bears, mountain lions and bobcats live here, and geese, ducks and swans pass through in spring and fall.
excerpt: The Fremont-Winema National Forest stretches across southern Oregon to the California border. Its heavily timbered western side borders Crater Lake National Par
address: Supervisor's Office: 1301 S G St, Lakeview, OR 97630

title: Gearhart Mountain Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Gearhart Mountain Wilderness covers about 22,800 acres around 8,364-foot Gearhart Mountain, which rises above other volcanic domes. High meadows, cirques, U-shaped valleys and rock formations line its ridges, and the summit views reach Steens Mountain, the Cascades, Lassen Peak and the Three Sisters.

Blue Lake is its only lake, and the Wild and Scenic North Fork Sprague River runs along the north edge. The Gearhart Mountain Trail (#100) offers about 13 miles of foot and horse access, plus the 3-mile Boulder Springs Trail. It is named for brothers James and William Gearhart, who ran cattle here in the 1870s.
excerpt: The Gearhart Mountain Wilderness covers about 22,800 acres around 8,364-foot Gearhart Mountain, which rises above other volcanic domes. High meadows, cirques, U
note: Heavy tree mortality from the 2021 Bootleg Fire: Lookout Rock and Deming Creek trailheads are closed, and the North Fork Sprague trail has many downed trees. Group size 10 people and animals combined; no pack animals within 200 feet of Blue Lake or streams. Boil all water. Snow usually late September to early July.
address: Bly Ranger District, Fremont-Winema National Forest, near Bly, OR

title: Duncan Reservoir Campground

gallery.alt: Pronghorn on the snowy rangelands near Duncan Reservoir (photo: Greg Shine, BLM)

contentHtml:
Duncan Reservoir Campground sits in sagebrush rangeland west of Silver Lake's dry lake bed, good for picnicking, canoeing, camping and fishing for stocked rainbow trout, with ice fishing in winter if the reservoir freezes.

Four single campsites line the west side of the reservoir, with a group site at the north end below the dam, plus a boat ramp and covered picnic area.
excerpt: Duncan Reservoir Campground sits in sagebrush rangeland west of Silver Lake's dry lake bed, good for picnicking, canoeing, camping and fishing for stocked rainb
note: No fee; first come, first served. Vault toilet; No drinking water; bring your own. Nearest services in Silver Lake, Fort Rock and Summer Lake. From Silver Lake, drive 5 miles east on OR 31, then 5 miles south on County Road 4-14 (rough gravel; watch for livestock).
address: County Road 4-14, about 10 miles southeast of Silver Lake, OR

title: Green Mountain Campground
imageAlt: Green Mountain Campground (photo: Lisa McNee, BLM)

banner.alt: Green Mountain Campground (photo: Lisa McNee, BLM)

gallery.alt: Green Mountain Fire Lookout from the campground (photo: Greg Shine, BLM)

contentHtml:
Green Mountain Campground is a remote, primitive campground in the Fort Rock and Christmas Valley area with views of lava flows, cinder cones and desert, good for photography, solitude and stargazing. It is a base for nearby Crack-in-the-Ground and the Four Craters Lava Field.

Its six primitive sites have picnic tables and fire grates, and the fire lookout on Green Mountain is staffed June through October.
excerpt: Green Mountain Campground is a remote, primitive campground in the Fort Rock and Christmas Valley area with views of lava flows, cinder cones and desert, good f
note: No fee; first come, first served. Vault toilet; No drinking water; bring your own. Rough dirt roads may be impassable at times; four-wheel drive recommended. From Christmas Valley, go east about 2 miles, north about 5 miles on Crack-in-the-Ground Road, then follow Lava Craters Road past Crack-in-the- Ground about 7 miles onto Green Mountain Road.
address: Green Mountain Road (BLM Road 6109-00), north of Christmas Valley, OR

title: Booth State Scenic Corridor
contentHtml:
Booth State Scenic Corridor is a wayside on OR 140 where you can picnic under old-growth ponderosa pines. The mixed forest through the area locals call Drew's Gap is especially colorful in fall with quaking aspen. Mule deer, coyotes and cougars are occasionally seen.

The land began as a 50-acre gift from Robert A. Booth, and the wayside was developed during the Depression with help from the Civilian Conservation Corps.
excerpt: Booth State Scenic Corridor is a wayside on OR 140 where you can picnic under old-growth ponderosa pines. The mixed forest through the area locals call Drew's G
note: Picnic tables and a vault toilet. No fee listed.
address: OR 140 between Klamath Falls and Lakeview (Drew's Gap), near Lakeview, OR

title: Fort Rock Cave (near Fort Rock State Natural Area)
contentHtml:
Fort Rock Cave is the site where archaeologist Luther Cressman found sagebrush sandals in 1938, about 9,350 to 10,500 years old and then the oldest human artifacts found in North America. The sandals lay under ash from the eruption of Mount Mazama, which formed Crater Lake.

Named a National Historic Landmark in 1961, the cave was donated by ranchers Reuben and Norma Long in 1962. The Fort Rock Basin has long been important to Native American communities.

note: The cave can be visited only on a state park guided tour; reservations required. Tour dates are released in two rounds starting in January. No photography at the cave.
address: Near Fort Rock State Natural Area, Fort Rock, OR (location not public)

title: Fort Rock State Natural Area
contentHtml:
Fort Rock State Natural Area is a National Natural Landmark rising from Oregon's high desert. Its jagged rock walls form a near-circle that resembles a fort; it is an old tuff ring formed in what was once a shallow sea, and it is larger than it looks once you hike around it.

Sandals found in a nearby cave are among the oldest ever discovered. A trail circles inside the formation, and the day-use area is open for stargazing with a permit.

note: Display a printed Stargazing Permit on your dash after hours. Drones prohibited through August 15, 2028 to protect nesting eagles and falcons.

title: Goose Lake State Recreation Area
contentHtml:
Goose Lake State Recreation Area is a shaded, green oasis beside Goose Lake with mature trees, irrigated lawns and mountain views. Migratory waterfowl peak in spring and early summer, sandhill cranes and bald eagles are seen into fall, and mule deer feed on apples from an old homesteader's orchard in the campground.

The campground has 26 electric sites with water and 19 tent sites, plus flush toilets and hot showers. The park is a designated International Dark Sky Place.

note: Reservations 800-452-5687. RV dump $10; firewood $7 a bundle. Dogs on 6-foot leash except in the off-leash pet area. Fuel, groceries and restaurants in Lakeview.
address: On the Oregon-California border, about 15 miles south of Lakeview, OR

Horseback riding, hiking, mountain biking and photography are popular.

title: Campbell Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Campbell Lake Campground sits on a high mountain lake with grassy and pebbly shores, stocked with rainbow trout for fishing, swimming and boating. It has 18 campsites, a day-use picnic area and a boat ramp.

The Lakes Trail System loops between Campbell and Dead Horse lakes for hiking, horseback riding and mountain biking.

contentHtml: Can Springs is a primitive three-site forest camp shaded by large ponderosa pines, with a creek that starts at Can Springs flowing through camp. Picnicking, wildlife watching, day hikes, horseback riding and mountain biking are popular.

Fishing for rainbow and brook trout is popular.

Its six sites are used by hunters in season.

title: Cottonwood (Meadows Lake) Campground
contentHtml:
Cottonwood is one of the busiest campgrounds in the southeast Fremont-Winema, beside Cottonwood Meadows Lake, which is stocked with rainbow and brook trout. Western white pine and white fir give shade, aspens turn gold in fall, and deer and occasionally black bears pass through.

It has 18 standard sites, four walk-in tent sites and a horse site with its own corral, plus a boat ramp, two day- use areas and a trailhead. Fishing, non-motorized and electric boating, hiking, mountain biking, horseback riding and birding are popular, with the Gearhart Mountain Wilderness nearby.

Its four sites share a four-stall corral built by the Back Country Horsemen and a historic Civilian Conservation Corps trough for watering horses.

contentHtml:

title: Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge
imageAlt: Seven pronghorn at Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge

banner.alt: Seven pronghorn at Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge

contentHtml:
Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, established in 1936, covers about 278,000 acres on a fault-block ridge rising nearly three-quarters of a mile above Warner Valley, topped by 8,017-foot Warner Peak. It is one of the largest wildlife habitats in the arid West free of domestic livestock and Oregon's largest refuge.

Set aside for pronghorn, it also shelters California bighorn sheep, mule deer, greater sage-grouse, American pika and redband trout, among more than 300 species. Visitors hunt, fish, watch wildlife, camp, hike, ride, backpack and bike; Camp Hart Mountain and Hot Springs campgrounds lie near aspen groves on the east side.
excerpt: Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, established in 1936, covers about 278,000 acres on a fault-block ridge rising nearly three-quarters of a mile above Warn
note: Free entry. The visitor center is open intermittently Memorial Day to Labor Day. Most secondary roads close December 1 to June 15; check current conditions. No cell service in most areas; carry extra water, a shovel and chains. From Lakeview, take OR 140 east 15.6 miles, Plush Cutoff 19.6 miles to Plush, then Hart Mountain Road 23 miles.
address: 38782 Hart Mountain Road, Plush, OR 97637

title: Summer Lake Wildlife Area
contentHtml:
Summer Lake Wildlife Area, established in 1944 as Oregon's first wildlife area, covers 18,941 acres of marsh and high-desert upland on the Ana River at the north end of Summer Lake. It is one of the best places in Oregon to see migrating waterfowl and shorebirds on the Pacific Flyway.

Swans, geese, ducks, avocets, stilts, phalaropes, sandhill cranes, pelicans, white-faced ibis and bald eagles are seen. An 8.3-mile tour route crosses the area, with two viewing blinds, four primitive campgrounds and hiking on dikes closed to vehicles.
excerpt: Summer Lake Wildlife Area, established in 1944 as Oregon's first wildlife area, covers 18,941 acres of marsh and high-desert upland on the Ana River at the nort
note: Wildlife Area Parking Permit required. The tour route is closed early October to late January for hunting season. Best March-April for waterfowl and April-May for shorebirds and songbirds. Headquarters has restrooms, maps and bird checklists.
address: 53447 Hwy 31, Summer Lake, OR 97640

title: Campbell Lake
contentHtml: Campbell Lake is a quiet high-country lake in the Fremont-Winema National Forest, good for kayaking, stand- up paddleboarding and canoeing, launching from Campbell Lake Campground. Its grassy and pebbly shores and stocked rainbow trout draw anglers too.
excerpt: Campbell Lake is a quiet high-country lake in the Fremont-Winema National Forest, good for kayaking, stand- up paddleboarding and canoeing, launching from Campb
note: Electric motors only. Weather changes quickly and the water stays cold. Carry an Oregon Waterway Access Permit and life jackets, and clean, drain and dry gear. Bring your own food and water; fuel up in Paisley.
address: Campbell Lake Campground, Fremont-Winema National Forest, a little over an hour from Paisley, OR

title: Dog Lake
contentHtml: Dog Lake is a mountain lake in the Fremont-Winema National Forest for kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding and canoeing, launching from the developed ramp at Dog Lake Campground. Pelicans, geese and ducks are often on the water.
excerpt: Dog Lake is a mountain lake in the Fremont-Winema National Forest for kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding and canoeing, launching from the developed ramp at Dog L
note: Electric-motor boats share the lake (5 mph). Aquatic plants increase as summer goes on. Oregon requires a Waterway Access Permit for kayaks, canoes and SUPs. Cell service is unreliable; bring fuel, food and water from Lakeview.
address: Dog Lake Campground, about 40 minutes southwest of Lakeview, OR

title: Crane Mountain
contentHtml: Crane Mountain, at 8,456 feet, is the highest point in Lake County, a summit in the Warner Mountains of the northwest Great Basin ranges. The Crane Mountain National Recreation Trail runs along the range, reached from trailheads such as Walker and Rogger Meadow near Mud Creek and Twin Springs campgrounds.
excerpt: Crane Mountain, at 8,456 feet, is the highest point in Lake County, a summit in the Warner Mountains of the northwest Great Basin ranges. The Crane Mountain Nat
address: Warner Mountains, east of Lakeview, Fremont-Winema National Forest, OR

title: Fremont National Recreation Trail
contentHtml:
The Fremont National Recreation Trail #160, also called the Southern Oregon Intertie Trail, runs about 135 miles through most of the Fremont National Forest. It starts at Yamsay Mountain, crosses Hager Mountain and Winter Rim, and reaches the Warner Mountains, where it meets the Crane Mountain National Recreation Trail.

The northern and middle sections pass near Silver Lake, Summer Lake and Paisley, ending near Lakeview at Cox Pass; the southern section follows the crest of the northern Warner Mountains. It is open to hiking, horseback riding and mountain biking.
excerpt: The Fremont National Recreation Trail #160, also called the Southern Oregon Intertie Trail, runs about 135 miles through most of the Fremont National Forest. It
note: Some sections are very primitive, and past fires and beetle damage near Winter Ridge make parts hard to follow. A gap of about six miles between Cox Pass and Mill Trailhead is bypassed on roads. Treat all water.
address: Fremont-Winema National Forest Supervisor's Office: 1301 South G Street, Lakeview, OR 97630

title: Oregon Desert Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Desert Trail is a 750-mile route across Oregon's high desert, created and managed by the Oregon Natural Desert Association (ONDA). It starts in the Oregon Badlands Wilderness outside Bend and ends at Lake Owyhee State Park near the Idaho border, linking Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, Steens Mountain, the Pueblo and Trout Creek mountains and the Owyhee Canyonlands.

It strings together hiking trails, old jeep tracks and wagon roads with long cross-country stretches. All of it is open to hiking, and some sections suit horseback, boat, bike or skis.
excerpt: The Oregon Desert Trail is a 750-mile route across Oregon's high desert, created and managed by the Oregon Natural Desert Association (ONDA). It starts in the O
note: Some sections are easy, marked walks; many need GPS navigation, real backcountry experience and careful planning, because water can be very limited. ONDA offers maps, a guidebook and GPS waypoints.
address: Crosses Lake County, including Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, OR

title: Oregon Timber Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Timber Trail is a 670-mile mountain bike and bikepacking route from the California border near Lakeview north to Hood River on the Columbia, managed by the nonprofit Oregon Timber Trail Alliance. It is split into four tiers: Fremont, Willamette, Deschutes and Hood.

Riders can take on the whole route or ride a shorter piece of any tier.
