address: California border near Lakeview to Hood River, OR

title: Barnhardy
contentHtml:
Barnhardy is a rugged, 27-mile gravel lollipop on the backroads of Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, with steep rocky climbs, 3,200 feet of gain and wide-open views of Warner Peak, Steens Mountain, Beatys Butte and the Warner Mountains. It is rated very demanding.

Watch for pronghorn, deer and sage-grouse, aspen and willow stands, fall color along Guano Creek and the graves of two soldiers from historic Camp Warner, then soak in the hot springs at the trailhead.
excerpt: Barnhardy is a rugged, 27-mile gravel lollipop on the backroads of Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, with steep rocky climbs, 3,200 feet of gain and wide-
note: No food or water on route; weather changes quickly at 6,000-7,000 feet. The Barnhardy road segment is open only August 1 to December 1; best late September to mid-October. Fall is hunting season, so wear hi-viz. Use very low gearing and tires over 50 mm. The 14-mile gravel drive from Plush can be badly washboarded.
address: Hot Springs Campground, Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, OR

title: Bull Prairie
contentHtml:
Bull Prairie is a 30-mile gravel and paved ride through open prairie, forest and high meadows near Lakeview, rated easier, with about 2,500 feet of climbing on red cinder roads and pavement and a long descent to finish.

Highlights include ponderosa pines draped in wolf lichen, an old-growth juniper stand, a quaking aspen grove, a North Warner viewpoint and an overlook above Goose Lake Valley with views of Crane Mountain. Shorter (18-mile) and longer (41-mile, with Drake Peak Lookout) options exist.
excerpt: Bull Prairie is a 30-mile gravel and paved ride through open prairie, forest and high meadows near Lakeview, rated easier, with about 2,500 feet of climbing on
note: Restroom at the start. Deep potholes on the paved descent; free-range cattle (don't yell at them). Tires 40 mm or wider. Best in spring for wildflowers and in fall for aspen color.
address: Camas Sno-Park, OR 140, about 20 minutes northeast of Lakeview, OR

title: Coffee Pot
imageAlt: Leading out from the parking area

banner.alt: Leading out from the parking area

contentHtml:
Coffee Pot is a 45-mile loop that starts with a long gravel climb (about 2,700 feet in the first 11 miles), rolls through the Fremont National Forest and burn areas, and finishes with a fast paved descent along the Chewaucan River. It is rated demanding, with 4,300 feet of gain.

Along the way are views of the Paisley valley, the ruins of a failed geothermal plant, creeks, aspens and meadows in the Coffee Pot sector and a new Oregon Timber Trail bridge.
excerpt: Coffee Pot is a 45-mile loop that starts with a long gravel climb (about 2,700 feet in the first 11 miles), rolls through the Fremont National Forest and burn a
note: No food or water on route; Paisley has a tavern, diner, coffee stand and small grocery. Limited cell service. The route reaches about 7,000 feet, so check snow. Best late spring through early fall. Tires 40 mm.
address: Paved pullout on the 331 Road, Chewaucan River canyon, near Paisley, OR

title: Drake Peak Lookout
imageAlt: Riding old paved road near Lakeview

banner.alt: Riding old paved road near Lakeview

contentHtml:
Drake Peak Lookout is a 24-mile out-and-back on gravel and pavement to a 1948 fire lookout on the west summit of Light Peak, at about 8,100 feet, with views into Oregon, Nevada and California. It is rated moderate, with 3,000 feet of climbing.

The ride passes Bull Prairie and its aspen stand, old-growth juniper and ponderosa forest, with Mt. Shasta, Hart Lake and Hart Mountain visible on clear days.
excerpt: Drake Peak Lookout is a 24-mile out-and-back on gravel and pavement to a 1948 fire lookout on the west summit of Light Peak, at about 8,100 feet, with views int
note: The final pitch reaches about 12%. Deep potholes on FS Road 3615; watch for cattle. Vault toilet and picnic table at the lookout, no water. Tires 40 mm or wider. Best in spring and fall.
address: Camas Sno-Park, OR 140, about 20 minutes northeast of Lakeview, OR

title: Ft Bidwell
contentHtml:
Ft Bidwell is a 73-mile lollipop through Oregon and California that climbs Mount Bidwell and passes historic Fort Bidwell, a California Historical Landmark founded in 1863. It is rated demanding, with 5,500 feet of gain, including a 3,100-foot climb up the High Grade, on about 70% gravel.

Highlights include the Warner Wetlands, Surprise Valley, the Mount Vida Vista viewpoint and Basque sheepherder tree carvings at Dismal Swamp. Shorter 46-mile and 40-mile options exist.
excerpt: Ft Bidwell is a 73-mile lollipop through Oregon and California that climbs Mount Bidwell and passes historic Fort Bidwell, a California Historical Landmark foun
note: The second half is much harder than the first. The only food stop is the Fort Bidwell Hotel and Restaurant (about mile 33). Very remote: carry a satellite communicator and a rear light. Best early summer through fall; tops out at 7,600 feet. Tires 45 mm or wider.
address: Warner Highway (OR 140) and Twenty-Mile Road, Adel, OR

title: Glass House
imageAlt: Leading out on the Glass House route

banner.alt: Leading out on the Glass House route

contentHtml:
Glass House is a 16-mile out-and-back on dirt roads through Warner Valley, past pothole lakes below Hart Mountain, to a remote, abandoned below-grade glass house built in the early 1990s (locked; view from outside). It is rated moderate, with about 500 feet of gain.

Along the way are Hart Lake and the Warner Wetlands for birding, petroglyphs at the base of the escarpment and a soldier's headstone near Hart Lake, all within the Oregon Outback Dark Sky Sanctuary.
excerpt: Glass House is a 16-mile out-and-back on dirt roads through Warner Valley, past pothole lakes below Hart Mountain, to a remote, abandoned below-grade glass hous
note: Fully exposed, with no shade, possible strong winds and no cell service. Do not touch petroglyphs or remove artifacts. Best mid-March and October for birding. Tires 45 mm or wider. A 28-mile option starts at the Hart Mountain Store in Plush.
address: Warner Wetlands parking area, Hart Bar area, east shore of Hart Lake, OR

title: Guano Creek
imageAlt: Green grasses in June at Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge

banner.alt: Green grasses in June at Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge

contentHtml:
Guano Creek is a remote 55-mile loop through the southern Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, with about 2,200 feet of gain and a stop at historic Shirk Ranch, a homestead of about fourteen buildings. Pronghorn and wide high-desert views are the draw.

Only Blue Sky Road is true gravel; the rest is dirt road and jeep track.
excerpt: Guano Creek is a remote 55-mile loop through the southern Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, with about 2,200 feet of gain and a stop at historic Shirk Ran
note: Listed as a development route not fully vetted. Extremely remote, with no food or water; navigation needs attention. The refuge limits access to June 15 through December 1; best early to mid-summer. Tires 50 mm recommended. At the ranch, watch for missing floorboards and unstable stairs.
address: Lookout Point, via Blue Sky Road (16 miles of gravel from Plush), Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, OR

title: Milk & Honey
contentHtml:
Milk & Honey is a 47-mile loop near Paisley through creeks, meadows, pine and ponderosa forest and ridge- line views, with about 3,100 feet of mostly rolling climbing on 85% gravel and dirt. It is rated moderate and has bail-out points at miles 15, 22 and 32, so it suits mixed-ability groups.

Highlights include Chewaucan River crossings, Coffee Pot Flat, Shoestring and Dairy creeks, basalt outcrops, views of the 2021 Bootleg Fire burn and a flowy serpentine section from miles 23 to 32.
excerpt: Milk & Honey is a 47-mile loop near Paisley through creeks, meadows, pine and ponderosa forest and ridge- line views, with about 3,100 feet of mostly rolling cl
note: Limit groups to four riders for wildlife. Open cattle grazing; slow down near animals. Miles 0-5 are the roughest; the last 7 miles are rough single-lane pavement. No food or water. Tires 40 mm or wider.
address: Gravel pullout on the west side of the road near Paisley, OR

title: OC&E Woods Line State Trail
contentHtml:
The OC&E Woods Line State Trail follows the old Oregon, California and Eastern Railroad bed about 100 miles from Klamath Falls east to Bly and north to Sycan Marsh, making it Oregon's longest linear park and one of the country's longest rail-trails. Construction began in 1917, logging traffic ended in 1990, and the railbed was then turned into a trail.

The paved Urban Section (7.6 miles to Olene) is popular with walkers, joggers, skaters and cyclists; beyond it the Gateway Section to Sprague River is gravel, and the Sprague River and Woods Line sections are loose rock through farm, ranch and forest land.
excerpt: The OC&E Woods Line State Trail follows the old Oregon, California and Eastern Railroad bed about 100 miles from Klamath Falls east to Bly and north to Sycan Ma
note: Non-motorized use only. No drinking water on the trail. Toilets at Reeder Road, Wiard Park, Switchbacks, Bly and Horse Glade trailheads. Livestock in farm areas. Closed from Hildebrand Road to Sprague River for fire restoration, and the Woods Line section remains closed after the Bootleg Fire.
address: Western trailhead: Wiard Park and Washburn Way, Klamath Falls; eastern end at Bly, OR

title: Oregon Outback Scenic Bikeway
imageAlt: Oregon Outback Scenic Bikeway (photo: Russ Roca)

banner.alt: Oregon Outback Scenic Bikeway (photo: Russ Roca)

contentHtml:
The Oregon Outback Scenic Bikeway is an 89-mile road loop from Lakeview through the Warner Mountains, where the Cascades meet the high desert, designated in 2016 and rated extreme. It climbs OR 140 over Warner Pass, descends about 1,300 feet to the desert outpost of Plush, runs to Adel and returns past Hart Lake, Crump Lake and Deep Creek Falls.

Watch for pronghorn, bighorn sheep, sage-grouse, sandhill cranes and wetland birds, with cliff swallows, eagles and falcons above Deep Creek Falls.
excerpt: The Oregon Outback Scenic Bikeway is an 89-mile road loop from Lakeview through the Warner Mountains, where the Cascades meet the high desert, designated in 201
note: Food, lodging and camping in Lakeview; camping and lodging in Plush; Forest Service campgrounds along the route. Best in spring (full lakes, birds, wildflowers) and fall (aspen color, wildlife). Check TripCheck.com for road conditions.
address: Lake County Fairgrounds, Lakeview, OR (start and finish)

title: Schoolhouse Skunk
contentHtml:
Schoolhouse Skunk is a 31-mile loop from Paisley through open rangeland with views of the Coyote Hills and Hart Mountain, grasslands looking toward Lake Abert, and ponderosa, juniper and aspen forest. It is rated very demanding, with 2,600 feet of gain.

It includes old-school single track on the Oregon Timber Trail above the Chewaucan River valley, then a quiet paved descent along the river with a swimming hole near mile 29. An optional detour climbs to Morgan Butte Lookout.
excerpt: Schoolhouse Skunk is a 31-mile loop from Paisley through open rangeland with views of the Coyote Hills and Hart Mountain, grasslands looking toward Lake Abert,
note: Fallen trees from wildfire remain on the single-track section. OR 31 has no shoulder; ride single file with a rear light. No food or water on route; Paisley has a tavern, diner, coffee stand and grocery. Best late spring or fall. Tires 50 mm or wider. Flush toilets at the start.
address: Paisley City Park, next to City Hall, Paisley, OR

title: Shirk Ranch
imageAlt: Riding gravel in the high desert

banner.alt: Riding gravel in the high desert

contentHtml:
Shirk Ranch is an easy 24-mile out-and-back on a flat BLM dirt road through Guano Valley to the historic Shirk Ranch homestead, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2009. It has only about 250 feet of gain.

Look for pronghorn on their migration corridor between Hart Mountain and Sheldon refuges, the Doherty Slide escarpment and unusually tall sagebrush north of the ranch.
excerpt: Shirk Ranch is an easy 24-mile out-and-back on a flat BLM dirt road through Guano Valley to the historic Shirk Ranch homestead, listed on the National Register
note: Extremely remote, with no food, water or cell service. Avoid when wet. Do not enter the ranch buildings. Very exposed in summer; best in spring or fall. Tires 40 mm or wider.
address: Pullout on BLM Road 6106 off OR 140, Guano Valley, about 12 miles south of Shirk Ranch, OR

title: Tall Town
imageAlt: Leading out on the Tall Town route

banner.alt: Leading out on the Tall Town route

contentHtml:
Tall Town is a gravel lollipop from Lakeview that climbs through Bullard Canyon, crosses the Fremont-Winema National Forest and drops into Camas Valley, with views of the Warner Range and Drake Peak, before a long, fast descent back to town. It is rated moderate, with about 3,200 feet of gain on 85% gravel.

It starts past historic Lakeview landmarks such as the Heryford Brothers Building and the Lake County and Schminck museums.
excerpt: Tall Town is a gravel lollipop from Lakeview that climbs through Bullard Canyon, crosses the Fremont-Winema National Forest and drops into Camas Valley, with vi
note: Quads and 4WD vehicles use Bullard Canyon; carry a red light. Open range with cattle. One rough, rutted section on the descent. No food or water. Best spring through fall. A 16-mile option starts at Camas Sno-Park.
address: Swimming Pool City Park, North D Street, Lakeview, OR

title: Winter & Summer
contentHtml: Winter & Summer is a very demanding 44-mile loop with 5,000 feet of gain, starting with a sustained 8.5-mile, 2,500-foot climb up Winter Ridge. It crosses the Wild and Scenic Sycan River, rugged double-track through burned forest and meadows, a 6-mile descent with views of Paisley and a hidden lake.
excerpt: Winter & Summer is a very demanding 44-mile loop with 5,000 feet of gain, starting with a sustained 8.5-mile, 2,500-foot climb up Winter Ridge. It crosses the W
note: No food or water. Open grazing; watch for cattle on blind corners. Large burned areas with active salvage logging. Navigation needs attention. Ride June through October; earlier, boggy sections may be impassable. Tires 40 mm or wider.
address: Dirt pull-out on NF-3313 off OR 31, near Summer Lake, OR

title: Sycan River
contentHtml:
The Sycan River is a 59-mile Wild and Scenic River (Recreational and Scenic), designated in 1988. Its scenery ranges from a narrow basalt canyon with large water-sculpted boulders to broad meadows, with old-growth ponderosa pine, lodgepole flats and riparian willows.

Sycan Marsh holds rare plant communities and wetland habitat for sandhill cranes, bald eagles and waterfowl, and the river supports redband trout.
excerpt: The Sycan River is a 59-mile Wild and Scenic River (Recreational and Scenic), designated in 1988. Its scenery ranges from a narrow basalt canyon with large wate
note: Managed by the Fremont-Winema National Forest.
address: Sycan Marsh area to Coyote Bucket, Fremont-Winema National Forest, OR

title: Oregon Outback Scenic Byway
contentHtml:
The Oregon Outback Scenic Byway runs 171 miles southeast from near La Pine on Highway 31, then south on US 395, a 4-to-6-hour drive across the high desert. Highlights include Fort Rock, a 325-foot volcanic crater with a state park and homestead museum; the Summer Lake Wildlife Area, with nearly 250 bird species; Paisley and its hot springs; Abert Rim, a 30-mile fault scarp popular for hang gliding; and Lakeview, Oregon's 'tallest town' at 4,800 feet.

Most of the route is in Lake County.
excerpt: The Oregon Outback Scenic Byway runs 171 miles southeast from near La Pine on Highway 31, then south on US 395, a 4-to-6-hour drive across the high desert. High
note: Services are far apart: full services in Paisley and Lakeview. Expect occasional winter snow and summer heat in the 90s.
address: OR 31 from US 97 near La Pine, OR, to New Pine Creek at the California border

title: Christmas Valley Back Country Byway
contentHtml:
The Christmas Valley Back Country Byway is a 93-mile, roughly 3-hour loop through high desert out of the Fort Rock and Silver Lake country, past an isolated pine forest called the Lost Forest and a sparkling lake.

Stops include Green Mountain Fire Lookout, Fossil Lake (with remains of creatures that lived here over 10,000 years ago) and the Fossil Lake sand dunes, which rise over 60 feet. Fort Rock State Natural Area lies just off its west end.
excerpt: The Christmas Valley Back Country Byway is a 93-mile, roughly 3-hour loop through high desert out of the Fort Rock and Silver Lake country, past an isolated pin
note: No fees. Managed by the BLM Lakeview District.
address: Loop from OR 31 near Fort Rock and Silver Lake via Christmas Valley, OR

title: Lakeview to Steens Mountain Back Country Byway
imageAlt: A paved stretch of the byway

banner.alt: A paved stretch of the byway

contentHtml:
The Lakeview to Steens Back Country Byway runs about 90 miles from OR 140 north of Lakeview across the Warner Mountains, Warner Valley and Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge to OR 205 south of Frenchglen. About 40 miles are paved and 50 graveled, suitable for passenger cars.

Highlights include waterfowl in the Warner Wetlands, rare lunate sand dunes, pronghorn, bighorn sheep, mule deer and golden eagles on Hart Mountain, and views east to Steens Mountain.
excerpt: The Lakeview to Steens Back Country Byway runs about 90 miles from OR 140 north of Lakeview across the Warner Mountains, Warner Valley and Hart Mountain Nationa
note: No fees; dispersed camping, 14-day limit. Winter storms can close the road briefly; refuge roads are primitive. Fuel and food only in Lakeview and Adel.
address: OR 140 north of Lakeview to OR 205 south of Frenchglen, via Plush, OR

title: Camas
contentHtml: Camas Sno-Park sits on OR 140 in the Fremont-Winema National Forest northeast of Lakeview, a winter access point to the Warner Mountains. In the snow-free months it is the start of the Bull Prairie and Drake Peak Lookout gravel rides, with a large parking area and restroom.

address: OR 140, 13 miles east of Lakeview, OR

title: Warner Canyon Ski Area
contentHtml:
Warner Canyon Ski Area is a compact, volunteer-run ski hill tucked into the Warner Mountains, suited to beginner and intermediate skiers and snowboarders. Its single lift was bought from another resort and given a second life in Lakeview.

The lodge is heated with solar and woody biomass from the property, food is served daily by The Pourhorse, and the lodge can be rented for events.

note: Opens when there is enough snow; check the website. Passes and day passes are also sold at Tall Town Bike and Camp.

title: Fisher Hot Springs
imageAlt: Soaking tub at Fisher Hot Springs

banner.alt: Soaking tub at Fisher Hot Springs

contentHtml: Fisher Hot Springs is a remote, primitive soaking spot on the eastern edge of Warner Valley near Crump Lake, one of seven hot springs in the Crump Geyser geothermal area. Water from a hillside source at about 154 F is piped by hose to a tub that fits about four people.
excerpt: Fisher Hot Springs is a remote, primitive soaking spot on the eastern edge of Warner Valley near Crump Lake, one of seven hot springs in the Crump Geyser geothe
note: The current listing says the owner does not allow access (the tank and parking area are private); check before going. No camping, amenities or fee; clothing optional. High-clearance vehicle recommended; the road can be impassable when wet.
address: Eastern edge of Warner Valley, about 14 miles northeast of Adel, OR

title: Hart Mountain Hot Springs (Antelope Hot Springs)
imageAlt: Seven pronghorn at Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge (area photo)

banner.alt: Seven pronghorn at Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge (area photo)

contentHtml: Hart Mountain Hot Springs (Antelope Hot Springs) is a natural hot spring at the eastern base of Warner Peak, beside the refuge's Hot Springs Campground. It is a soothing stop after a day in the high desert and the start of the Barnhardy gravel ride.
excerpt: Hart Mountain Hot Springs (Antelope Hot Springs) is a natural hot spring at the eastern base of Warner Peak, beside the refuge's Hot Springs Campground. It is a
note: Free. Camping is first come, first served with limited parking. Hot Springs Campground Road is currently closed and sites are walk-in only; refuge secondary roads close December 1 to June 15. No cell service.
address: Hot Springs Campground, eastern base of Warner Peak, Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge, OR

title: Hunter's Hot Springs

gallery.alt: Northern lights over the pond at Hunters Hot Springs

contentHtml:
Hunters Hot Springs Resort in Lakeview has an outdoor natural mineral pool kept at about 104 F, 12 deluxe rooms (some pet-friendly), The Geyser Room restaurant and bar, and pond and mountain views under dark Southern Oregon skies.

Old Perpetual Geyser is a short walk from the lodge.
excerpt: Hunters Hot Springs Resort in Lakeview has an outdoor natural mineral pool kept at about 104 F, 12 deluxe rooms (some pet-friendly), The Geyser Room restaurant
note: Day passes sold on site during public hours. Hotel guests can soak at all hours except Monday.
address: 18088 US-395, Lakeview, OR 97630

title: Summer Lake Hot Springs

gallery.alt: Summer Lake Hot Springs outdoor pools

contentHtml:
Summer Lake Hot Springs is a remote 145-acre retreat in the Oregon Outback, six miles west of Paisley, built around ancient artesian hot springs with 360-degree views of desert, forest and sky. The property also has petroglyphs, a bird sanctuary, a wildlife pond and nature trails.

Soak in the 98 F indoor pool in the historic bathhouse or the 104 F outdoor rock pools. Stay in 10 geothermally heated cabins, two three-bedroom houses, RV sites with full hookups or a tent field.
excerpt: Summer Lake Hot Springs is a remote 145-acre retreat in the Oregon Outback, six miles west of Paisley, built around ancient artesian hot springs with 360-degree
note: Reservations required; no day use. Two-night minimum for cabins and houses; bring your own linens and towels. Check-in 3 p.m., check-out 11 a.m. No soaking 9 p.m.-8 a.m. on cleaning nights (Thursday and Sunday). No TV or Wi-Fi.
address: 41777 Highway 31, Paisley, OR 97636

title: Old Perpetual
contentHtml: Old Perpetual is a geyser on the grounds of Hunters Hot Springs Resort just north of Lakeview, a landmark visitors can see on a short walk from the lodge.
excerpt: Old Perpetual is a geyser on the grounds of Hunters Hot Springs Resort just north of Lakeview, a landmark visitors can see on a short walk from the lodge.
address: Hunters Hot Springs Resort, 18088 US-395, Lakeview, OR 97630

title: Crack-in-the-Ground
contentHtml:
Crack-in-the-Ground is an ancient volcanic fissure more than 2 miles long and up to 70 feet deep. The dry climate has left it largely unfilled, so it looks much as it did when it formed thousands of years ago.

A 2-mile trail runs along its sand-and-rock floor, where it can be up to 20 degrees cooler than the surface.
excerpt: Crack-in-the-Ground is an ancient volcanic fissure more than 2 miles long and up to 70 feet deep. The dry climate has left it largely unfilled, so it looks much
note: No fee; foot travel only. Restroom; no drinking water. Rough dirt roads may be impassable; four- wheel drive highly recommended. From Christmas Valley, go east about 1 mile, north about 7 miles on Crack-in-the-Ground Road, then follow signs on Lava Craters Road. Primitive camping at nearby Green Mountain.
address: Lava Craters Road, about 8 miles north of Christmas Valley, OR

title: Oregon Sunstone Public Collection Area
imageAlt: Visitors hunt for sunstones (photo: Greg Shine, BLM)

banner.alt: Visitors hunt for sunstones (photo: Greg Shine, BLM)

contentHtml:
The Oregon Sunstone Public Collection Area in remote Rabbit Basin lets visitors collect sunstones, the state gemstone, in their natural setting. These feldspar crystals formed in lava from a Steens Mountain eruption 13 to 14 million years ago and were exposed as a later lake dried and the ground weathered.

Camping is allowed anywhere in the area, and the dark skies are good for stargazing.
excerpt: The Oregon Sunstone Public Collection Area in remote Rabbit Basin lets visitors collect sunstones, the state gemstone, in their natural setting. These feldspar
note: No fee; no commercial collecting. Stay within the orange boundary posts: private mining claims surround and lie within the area. Only a pit toilet, picnic tables and a shade structure; come well prepared. From Plush, take Hogback Road (County Road 3-10) about 10 miles, County Road 3-11, then BLM roads 6155, 6115 and 6195.
address: BLM Road 6195, Rabbit Basin, north of Plush, OR

title: Derrick Cave
contentHtml: Derrick Cave is a lava tube about 30 feet high, 50 feet wide and a quarter mile long, named for pioneer rancher H.E. Derrick. It formed just south of the main vent of the Devils Garden lava flows, and in the 1960s it was stocked as a nuclear fallout shelter.
excerpt: Derrick Cave is a lava tube about 30 feet high, 50 feet wide and a quarter mile long, named for pioneer rancher H.E. Derrick. It formed just south of the main v
note: No fee or facilities. Bring a jacket and reliable lights. No camping, fires, pets or removing cave resources. The unpaved road usually suits high-clearance 2WD but may need 4WD when wet and can be impassable in winter. From Fort Rock, take Cabin Lake Road to NF-23, then NF-2325.
address: End of NF-2325, Devils Garden area, north of Fort Rock, OR

title: Oregon Outback
imageAlt: Stargazing at the Warner Valley Overlook (photo: Joey Hamilton)

banner.alt: Stargazing at the Warner Valley Overlook (photo: Joey Hamilton)

contentHtml:
The Oregon Outback International Dark Sky Sanctuary, designated in 2024, covers much of eastern Lake County, among the darkest regions in the world and the world's largest Dark Sky Sanctuary. Its high-desert skies stretch over sage rangeland, mountains, large lakes, playas, Abert Rim and several hot springs.

It is home to the Northern Paiute people, ancient petroglyphs, pronghorn, bighorn sheep and sage-grouse. Nearly 90% of the land is public, open for stargazing, wildlife watching, photography, hiking, camping and biking.
excerpt: The Oregon Outback International Dark Sky Sanctuary, designated in 2024, covers much of eastern Lake County, among the darkest regions in the world and the worl
note: Lodges, cabins, RV parks and hotels are available; guide services offer remote trips. Check the weather near Lakeview before you go.
address: Eastern Lake County, OR (Lake County Chamber of Commerce: 126 North E Street, Lakeview, OR 97630)

title: Bald Butte Lookout
contentHtml:
Bald Butte Lookout sits atop the windy summit of Bald Butte with wide views over forested hills. Built in 1931 from an Aladdin L4 kit packed in by horse, it served as a fire lookout for more than 50 years and is one of only two such lookouts left in Oregon.

The 14-by-14-foot rental has two cots, a table, a propane heater, cook stove and lights, with an outdoor picnic table and accessible vault toilet. Pets are welcome.
excerpt: Bald Butte Lookout sits atop the windy summit of Bald Butte with wide views over forested hills. Built in 1931 from an Aladdin L4 kit packed in by horse, it ser
note: Reserve on Recreation.gov. No water on site. Bring water, bedding, cooking gear, lights and a first aid kit; pack out all trash and food. Entry by combination lock from your reservation. Check with the ranger district for fire, road and weather restrictions. The last 2 miles of FR 450 are steep and rough; large RVs not recommended.
address: Summit of Bald Butte, end of Forest Road 450 off FS Road 3411, Paisley Ranger District, OR

title: Drake Peak Lookout
contentHtml:
Drake Peak Lookout stands at 8,222 feet on the crest of the Warner Mountains, a fire detection site since 1948 with views into Oregon, California and Nevada. The 14-by-14-foot cabin sleeps up to four, with folding cots, a table and chairs and a wood stove.

Hike to Drake Peak's summit, stargaze and watch for wildlife. Pets are welcome.
excerpt: Drake Peak Lookout stands at 8,222 feet on the crest of the Warner Mountains, a fire detection site since 1948 with views into Oregon, California and Nevada. Th
note: Reserve on Recreation.gov. No water on site (fill up at Mud Creek Campground, about 6 miles away). Bring firewood. Bring water, bedding, cooking gear, lights and a first aid kit; pack out all trash and food. Entry by combination lock from your reservation. Check with the ranger district for fire, road and weather restrictions.
address: End of Forest Road 019 off FS Road 3615, Warner Mountains, northeast of Lakeview, OR

title: Hager Mountain Lookout
contentHtml:
Hager Mountain Lookout sits at 7,195 feet on bald cap rocks formed by eruptions about 8 million years ago, one of the few Oregon lookouts still staffed every fire season. On clear days the view reaches Mount Hood and Mount Shasta.

In winter it is a rental for up to four, with a wood stove, propane stove and firewood provided, reached only by a strenuous 4-mile hike, ski or snowshoe.

note: Reserve on Recreation.gov. No water on site; bring all food, bedding and gear. Winter travel requires experience; expect wind. Check snow conditions with the Silver Lake Ranger District.

title: Fremont Point Cabin

gallery.alt: View of Summer Lake from the cabin

contentHtml:
Fremont Point Cabin sits on Winter Rim almost 3,000 feet above Summer Lake, built in 2015 on the site of a lookout lost to a 2002 fire, with a large two-sided deck. It has bunk beds and a queen bed, an LP range, refrigerator and lamps, and a wood stove.

The Fremont National Recreation Trail and Oregon Timber Trail pass nearby.

note: Reserve on Recreation.gov. Bring drinking water, bedding and cookware; clean up and pack out trash. Summer access on gravel roads (FS Road 034 may need 4WD when wet); winter access by a 10-mile ski or snowshoe or 15-mile snowmobile route. Cell service usually available.
address: Off FS Road 034, Winter Rim, north-central Lake County, OR

title: Goose Landing
contentHtml: Goose Landing is a flat 9-hole, par 29 disc golf course on the peninsula in Christmas Valley Lake, established in 2023, with paver tees and Axiom baskets. It is still being developed but is playable, and suits carts and strollers.

note: Free to play. No dogs, water or restrooms. Park east of the red maintenance shed south of the course.
address: Peninsula at Christmas Valley Lake, Christmas Valley, OR

title: Soroptimist Fitness Park
contentHtml: The Sopo disc golf course at Soroptimist Fitness Park in Lakeview, established in 2017, is a flat, grassy course with two baskets on every hole, an easier homemade basket and a tougher Mach II, playable as an 18-hole, par 57 layout. A gravel path runs through the park, and it is cane-accessible.

note: Free to play. Dogs allowed. Bring water: no facilities or shade.

title: Lane County History Museum
contentHtml:
The Lane County History Museum is run by the Lane County Historical Society, founded in 1951, on the Lane County Fairgrounds in Eugene. Its exhibits cover the Oregon Trail, the county courthouse and historic vehicles, and its collection holds more than 300,000 photographs.

The museum also has a public research library, an online photo and manuscript collection, K-12 programs and History Pub talks.
excerpt: The Lane County History Museum is run by the Lane County Historical Society, founded in 1951, on the Lane County Fairgrounds in Eugene. Its exhibits cover the O
note: Admission is free; donations appreciated. Research library by appointment. Closed November 26-28 and December 24-26.
address: 740 W 13th Ave, Eugene, OR (Lane County Fairgrounds)

title: Applegate Pioneer Museum
contentHtml:
The Applegate Pioneer Museum tells the pioneer history of west Lane County in the relocated one-room Pine Grove School. The museum was founded at Crow in 1975 and moved to Veneta in 2000.

The Applegate Trail, the southern route of the Oregon Trail, passed through Veneta.
excerpt: The Applegate Pioneer Museum tells the pioneer history of west Lane County in the relocated one-room Pine Grove School. The museum was founded at Crow in 1975 a
note: Open 1:00 - 4:00 PM on a few weekend afternoons a month (first and third weekends in season, fewer in winter) and by appointment.

title: Bohemia Gold Mining Museum
imageAlt: Bohemia Gold Mining Museum, Cottage Grove

banner.alt: Bohemia Gold Mining Museum, Cottage Grove

contentHtml:
The Bohemia Gold Mining Museum is a living and expanding memorial to the miners and gold mining history of the Bohemia Mining District. Its photographs, tools, ore samples and other artifacts come largely from the collection of long-time area miner Guy Leabo, to whom the museum is dedicated.

Exhibits include a 70-inch wood carving by Floyd Davis, made from a California redwood stump over three and a half years. Tours are available by calling or emailing.

note: Admission $2 per person. Email: Bohemiagoldminingmuseum@gmail.com

title: Cottage Grove Museum
contentHtml:
The Cottage Grove Museum is housed in an octagonal building that opened in 1897 as Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church, modeled on a small church in Germany. Its stained glass windows are original, and the building is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The city bought it for a museum after the parish moved out in 1961.

The Museum Annex shows early Cottage Grove life, with a blacksmith shop, general store, kitchen and parlor, plus the permanent 'She Survived the Titanic' exhibit about local resident Marion Wright Woolcott. Other exhibits cover mid-century fashion, a 1923 oil derrick and the Village Green hotel.
excerpt: The Cottage Grove Museum is housed in an octagonal building that opened in 1897 as Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church, modeled on a small church in Germ
note: Admission is free; donations accepted. Also open by special arrangement. Email: museumcottagegrove@gmail.com
address: 147 N H St, Cottage Grove, OR (mail: PO Box 142, Cottage Grove, OR 97424)

title: Creswell Historical Museum
contentHtml:
The Creswell Historical Museum, run by the Creswell Area Historical Society, opened in 1975 in a former Methodist-Episcopal Church built in 1889.

Its exhibits, displays and photographs trace the area's history from the Kalapuya people and early settlers to the present. Guided tours and genealogical files are available.
excerpt: The Creswell Historical Museum, run by the Creswell Area Historical Society, opened in 1975 in a former Methodist-Episcopal Church built in 1889.
note: Open Saturdays 11:00 AM - 2:00 PM in season; closed November through the off-season.
address: 55 S 5th St, Creswell, OR 97426

title: Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art
imageAlt: Visitor viewing a Jeffrey Gibson work

banner.alt: Visitor viewing a Jeffrey Gibson work

contentHtml:
The Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art is the University of Oregon's art museum, opened in 1933 in a building by Ellis F. Lawrence that is listed on the National Register. It is Oregon's only academic art museum accredited by the American Alliance of Museums, with especially strong Asian art collections.

Changing exhibitions run alongside public events, studio programs and Art Heals programs.

note: Email: jsma@uoregon.edu

title: Junction City Historical Society Museums
contentHtml:
The Junction City Historical Society runs two house museums. The Dr. Norman L. Lee House, the 1872 home and office of the town's first doctor, is Junction City's only building on the National Register of Historic Places, with displays from the town's railroad beginnings.

The Mary E. Pitney House continues the timeline; teacher, artist and poet Mary Pitney was born there in 1891 and left it to the Society. Next door is the town's first jail, a one-room 10 by 14 foot building from 1873 furnished to look as it did in the 1870s.

title: Museum of Natural and Cultural History
contentHtml:
The Museum of Natural and Cultural History is the University of Oregon's museum of science, culture and sustainability, and the state's official repository for Oregon cultural and paleontological materials, with hundreds of thousands of archaeological and ethnographic objects, fossils and geological specimens.

The exhibit 'Oregon: Where Past Is Present' covers 15,000 years of Oregon human history, including the 10,000-year-old Fort Rock sandals.

title: Oakridge Museum
contentHtml:
The Oakridge Museum, run by the Upper Willamette Pioneer Association and long known as the Oakridge- Westfir Pioneer Museum, covers the farming, logging, railroading and Forest Service history of the upper Willamette.

A caboose stands outside.

title: Oregon Air and Space Museum
contentHtml: The Oregon Air and Space Museum opened in 1991 in hangars by Eugene Airport. It displays full-size World War I and World War II aircraft and jets, flight suits, a space-program timeline and a large collection of scale models.

title: Oregon Aviation Historical Society & Museum
imageAlt: At the Oregon Aviation Historical Society museum

banner.alt: At the Oregon Aviation Historical Society museum

contentHtml:
The Oregon Aviation Historical Society & Museum, by Cottage Grove State Airport, is the only museum devoted to Oregon aviation history. Since 1983 the society has preserved the state's aviation heritage, telling the story of ordinary people who achieved extraordinary things.

Visitors can see vintage Oregon-built aircraft, a restoration hangar and a climate-controlled aviation archive.

title: Shelton McMurphey Johnson House
contentHtml:
The Shelton McMurphey Johnson House is Eugene's only Victorian house museum: the 1888 Queen Anne 'Castle on the Hill' on the south slope of Skinner Butte, listed on the National Register and named for the three families who lived there.

No advance tickets are needed for tours. The museum also hosts tea service, game nights, a book club and day camps, and offers a self-guided walking tour of the Skinner Butte neighborhood.

title: Siuslaw Pioneer Museum
contentHtml:
The Siuslaw Pioneer Museum in Old Town Florence preserves the history of Florence and the Siuslaw region from before white settlement through the 1950s.

Highlights include a dugout canoe, first peoples' tools and clothing, pioneer household items, early logging and fishing equipment, a drawbridge operator's control panel, an early telephone switchboard, and lace and quilt work. The museum also offers a historic walking tour of Old Town Florence.
excerpt: The Siuslaw Pioneer Museum in Old Town Florence preserves the history of Florence and the Siuslaw region from before white settlement through the 1950s.
note: Admission $7 for adults 16 and over; free for children 15 and under with an adult, and for members. Groups of 10 or more call to reserve. Kyle Research Library open Tuesday and Thursday 10:00 AM - 4:00 PM. Email: library@spmuseum.org

title: Springfield History Museum
contentHtml:
The Springfield History Museum is Springfield's official history museum, run by the Springfield Public Library in the 1911 Oregon Power Company substation. Its collection of more than 12,000 artifacts covers Springfield and the rural communities of east Lane County.

Changing exhibits run alongside ILLUMINATION, the museum's ongoing story and public history project, and an online collection.
excerpt: The Springfield History Museum is Springfield's official history museum, run by the Springfield Public Library in the 1911 Oregon Power Company substation. Its
note: Admission is free.

title: Siuslaw National Forest
contentHtml:
The Siuslaw National Forest covers more than 630,000 acres of the Oregon coast and Coast Range, and is one of only two national forests in the lower 48 states with oceanfront land. Its landscapes run from mossy coastal mountain forests to sand dunes and Pacific beaches.

Highlights include Cape Perpetua Scenic Area with its rocky headlands, Cascade Head with native prairie and rare wildflowers, the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, and Marys Peak, the highest point in the Coast Range, just west of Corvallis. Visitors come for old-growth forest, waterfalls, camping and off-highway vehicle riding on the dunes.

title: Umpqua National Forest
contentHtml:
The Umpqua National Forest covers about 983,000 acres on the western slopes of the Oregon Cascades in Douglas, Lane and Jackson counties. Its landscape was shaped by high Cascade glaciers, volcanic activity and whitewater rivers, and it is known for its biodiversity, recreation and scenery.

It is managed through four ranger districts: Cottage Grove, Diamond Lake, North Umpqua and Tiller. Highlights include Toketee Falls and the waterfalls of the North Umpqua corridor, Diamond Lake, and the Boulder Creek, Mount Thielsen and Rogue-Umpqua Divide wilderness areas.

title: Willamette National Forest
contentHtml:
The Willamette National Forest runs about 110 miles along the western slopes of the Oregon Cascades and covers 1,675,407 acres of high mountains, narrow canyons, fast streams and wooded slopes. About 61% of it lies in Lane County, with large areas in Linn, Marion and Douglas counties.

It holds eight wilderness areas and seven major volcanic peaks, and offers year-round hiking, backpacking, camping, fishing, waterfalls and skiing.

address: Supervisor's Office: 3106 Pierce Parkway, Suite D, Springfield, OR 97477

title: Cummins Creek Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Cummins Creek Wilderness, designated in 1984, covers 9,173 acres of the Oregon Coast Range and holds the only old-growth Sitka spruce forest in Oregon's wilderness system, with some trees about nine feet across. Cummins and Bob creeks flow west through the rainforest to the Pacific, and salmon, steelhead and cutthroat trout spawn in them.

Cummins Ridge, topping out near 2,000 feet, divides the forest. Summers are wet and foggy, with yellow monkey flower, purple aster, white candy flower and red foxglove, and winters bring no snow. The Cummins Ridge Trail, about 6.5 miles, is the only trail in the wilderness.

note: No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles. Practice Leave No Trace. Stock animals are not allowed because of fragile soils.

title: Diamond Peak Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Diamond Peak Wilderness covers 52,337 acres straddling the Cascade crest in the Willamette and Deschutes national forests. Its centerpiece is 8,744-foot Diamond Peak, a shield volcano later carved by glaciers, ringed by dozens of small lakes of 1 to 28 acres.

About 14 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail run along the peak's east slope, and Marie, Divide and Rockpile lakes are popular base camps for climbing it. Mountain hemlock, lodgepole and white pine and true firs shelter deer, elk, black bears, marmots and pikas; huckleberry and wildflowers are common.

note: Wilderness rules apply. Popular for hiking, camping, fishing, hunting, horseback riding, snowshoeing and cross-country skiing.

title: Mount Washington Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mount Washington Wilderness is a volcanic landscape of jagged peaks and rugged lava, next to the Three Sisters Wilderness across Highway 242. From 7,794-foot Mount Washington, a dissected volcano, the view takes in about 75 miles of lava-strewn plains; 6,872-foot Belknap Crater is a cinder and ash cone.

Lodgepole pine and mountain hemlock forest surrounds 28 lakes, and short trails reach Tenas, Benson and Patjens lakes. The Pacific Crest Trail crosses the wilderness for 16.6 miles.

title: Oregon Islands Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Oregon Islands Wilderness covers the rocks, reefs and islands of Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, some 1,853 of them strung along about 320 miles of coastline from Tillamook Head near Seaside to the California border.

The islands are breeding and resting grounds for most of Oregon's estimated 1.2 million nesting seabirds, including tufted puffins and cormorants, and for seals and sea lions that haul out and give birth there.

The islands are closed to public entry; bring binoculars or a spotting scope and watch from shore.

note: All rocks and islands are closed to the public. Email: Oregoncoast@fws.gov

title: Rock Creek Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Rock Creek Wilderness, one of three small wildernesses created on the Siuslaw National Forest in 1984, covers 7,486 acres of rainforest canyons where clear water runs into Rock Creek and Big Creek and on to the Pacific. Old-growth Sitka spruce near the coast, some nine feet across, gives way to Douglas fir inland.

Pink rhododendron blooms in May, and salmon, steelhead and cutthroat trout migrate up the creeks to spawn. The ridge between Rock and Big creeks is home to the Oregon silverspot butterfly, found in only two other places on Earth. The Forest Service maintains no trails here.

title: Three Sisters Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Three Sisters Wilderness covers about 281,190 acres of the Cascades, crowned by North, Middle and South Sister, all over 10,000 feet, and Broken Top. Collier Glacier is the largest glacier in Oregon, and volcanic features include Rock Mesa, Collier Cone and Yapoah Crater.

About 260 miles of trail, including 40 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail, wind through alpine meadows, waterfalls, lava fields and glacial lakes, starting in Douglas-fir forest on the west side and ponderosa pine on the east.

note: A Central Cascades Wilderness Permit is required from the first Friday after Memorial Day through the last Friday in September. No facilities inside the wilderness.

title: Waldo Lake Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Waldo Lake Wilderness covers 36,572 acres, about 98 percent forested, on the north and west sides of Waldo Lake. Steep slopes, lake basins, meadows and rock outcrops hold the Six Lakes Basin, Eddeeleo Lakes and Quinn Lakes, reached by about 84 miles of trail.

Waldo Lake itself, just outside the eastern boundary, covers about 10 square miles and reaches 420 feet deep. It is one of the purest lakes in the world, and on a clear day you can see about 100 feet down. The 22- mile Waldo Lake Trail loops around it.

imageAlt: Siuslaw River access from the campground

banner.alt: Siuslaw River access from the campground

contentHtml:
Clay Creek is a quiet, family-oriented BLM site in the Coast Range where Clay Creek meets the Siuslaw River. It has 21 campsites for RVs (up to 32 feet), trailers or tents, a summer swimming area, a children's play area, horseshoe pits, a volleyball area and a ball field, plus large group shelters that can be reserved.

The Clay Creek Trail climbs a ridge to a remnant stand of old-growth timber. Salmon can be seen spawning in fall and winter.

title: Sharps Creek Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Sharps Creek is a small family campground and day-use area in the Cascade foothills, tied to the historic Bohemia Mining District. A natural swimming hole sits among rounded boulders below an overlook above the creek; swim with caution.

The 12-site campground is a short walk from the day-use swimming area, and gold panning is a popular activity.

note: Vault toilets and running water. No cell service. Reserve on Recreation.gov, or pay for non-reserved sites with the Recreation.gov mobile app (download it before you arrive; no cell service). title: Whittaker Creek Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Whittaker Creek is a BLM campground and day-use area on Whittaker Creek near the Siuslaw River, with 30 tent-only campsites, a swimming beach, a horseshoe pit and a children's play area. The 2.5-mile Old Growth Ridge National Recreation Trail climbs about 1,000 feet into the Coast Range.

In fall and winter spawning salmon and trout can be watched in the creek. A paved boat ramp gives drift boats and canoes access to a 6.5-mile run of the Siuslaw River with Class II-III rapids.

title: Carl G. Washburne Memorial State Park
contentHtml:
Carl G. Washburne Memorial State Park sits east of Highway 101, buffered from the road by native trees. Trails lead from the campground to the beach, wildlife viewing areas and second-growth forest, and a path runs under the highway to a five-mile sandy beach for whale watching, agate hunting and beachcombing. Another trail connects to the Heceta Head trail and lighthouse.

The campground has about 50 full-hookup sites, electrical sites, seven walk-in tent sites, a hiker/biker camp and two yurts, with flush toilets and hot showers. Elk sometimes visit, and wild rhododendrons bloom in spring.

note: Campsites are first come, first served except the two yurts (one pet-friendly), which can be reserved. Walk-in tent sites close October-April. RV dump station; firewood for sale.
address: East of US 101, Florence, OR

title: Darlingtonia State Natural Site
contentHtml:
Darlingtonia State Natural Site is an 18-acre botanical park, the only Oregon state park dedicated to protecting a single plant species: the carnivorous cobra lily, Darlingtonia californica.

A boardwalk leads into a fen where the plants trap insects and absorb nutrients from them, among rhododendron, spruce, cedar and shore pine. The flowers bloom in spring.

note: Parking area and small picnic area. Collecting plants is illegal.
address: Florence, OR

title: Dexter State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Dexter State Recreation Site sits on the western edge of Dexter Reservoir, with a picnic area overlooking the lake and an 18-hole disc golf course in oak and Douglas fir woods.

Docks and a two-lane boat ramp serve the lake, and trails connect to nearby Elijah Bristow State Park along the Middle Fork of the Willamette River.

note: Picnic area with barbecue stands and fire rings.
address: Western edge of Dexter Reservoir, Dexter, OR

title: Elijah Bristow State Park

gallery.alt: Horseback riding on a forest trail

contentHtml:
Elijah Bristow State Park covers 847 acres of meadows, woodlands and wetlands on the Middle Fork of the Willamette River and is named for an early Lane County pioneer. Salmon and steelhead runs draw anglers, and Channel Lake, a landlocked river channel, supports osprey, great blue herons, bald eagles and beavers, along with threatened western pond turtles and Oregon chub.

More than 10 miles of trails serve hikers, mountain bikers and riders, including part of the Eugene to Pacific Crest Trail, and an equestrian staging area has a shelter, water and restroom. A river access trail for kayaks and canoes marks the start of the Willamette River Water Trail.
excerpt: Elijah Bristow State Park covers 847 acres of meadows, woodlands and wetlands on the Middle Fork of the Willamette River and is named for an early Lane County p
note: Two group picnic areas can be reserved; other picnic sites are first come, first served.
address: Off Highway 58 on the Middle Fork of the Willamette River, southeast of Eugene, OR

title: Fall Creek State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Fall Creek State Recreation Area takes in six parks on Fall Creek Reservoir: the Free Meadow, Lakeside 1 and 2 and North Shore day-use areas on the north side, Winberry on the south side, and Cascara Campground. The lake was completed in 1965 for flood control and is drawn down each winter.

Winberry has a two-lane boat ramp, swim dock and beach, and picnic areas; North Shore has high- and low- water ramps. Cascara Campground has 39 first-come, first-served sites among Douglas firs, and Fisherman's Point Group Camp holds up to 64 people by reservation.
excerpt: Fall Creek State Recreation Area takes in six parks on Fall Creek Reservoir: the Free Meadow, Lakeside 1 and 2 and North Shore day-use areas on the north side,
note: Day-use parking permit required (1-day permits sold on site). Life jacket loaner stations at North Shore and Winberry. Reservations: 800-452-5687.
address: Fall Creek Reservoir, near Eugene, OR
