title: Westmoreland Park
contentHtml:
Westmoreland is a short 9-hole park course established in 1988, 2,367 feet at par 27 with holes from 229 to 322 feet; a round takes about 45 minutes. It is open with some trees and slight elevation changes.

Tees are concrete, with Mach III baskets. It is dog, cart and stroller friendly; there are no restrooms or drinking water.
excerpt: Westmoreland is a short 9-hole park course established in 1988, 2,367 feet at par 27 with holes from 229 to 322 feet; a round takes about 45 minutes. It is open
note: 9 holes · Par 27 · Free to play
address: Westmoreland Park, Eugene, OR (closest parking by the Boys & Girls Club)

title: Burrows House Museum

gallery.alt: The Burrows House in its early years

contentHtml:
The Burrows House Museum is the Lincoln County Historical Society's county-history museum in Newport, in a house built in 1895 for newlyweds Susan and John Burrows. Standing between the Bayfront and Nye Beach, it was nicknamed "The Half-Way House"; it later served as the Sea View Rooms boarding house and, from 1933, as a funeral parlor.

The house was donated to the Historical Society in 1976, moved beside the Log Cabin Museum and opened as a museum in 1978. Its exhibits, updated in 2023, cover the Siletz Tribe and the towns and communities of Lincoln County, plus the Gadget Graveyard, a display on composer Ernest Bloch and a Parlor Room.
excerpt: The Burrows House Museum is the Lincoln County Historical Society's county-history museum in Newport, in a house built in 1895 for newlyweds Susan and John Burr
note: Admission: adults $5, ages 13-17 $3; free for children 12 and under, Lincoln County residents, members and active-duty military. Research Library by appointment. Onsite parking; wheelchair accessible.
address: 545 SW 9th Street, Newport, OR 97365

title: Pacific Maritime Heritage Center
contentHtml:
The Pacific Maritime Heritage Center is the Lincoln County Historical Society's museum and interactive center on Newport's working Bayfront wharf, covering maritime history, art, local culture, commerce and ocean research, with a focus on people who live and work where the sea meets the land.

The building began as the 1925 home of General Ulysses Grant McAlexander, later became the Smuggler's Cove restaurant and nightclub, and was bought by the Historical Society in 2004. It also houses the Doerfler Family Theater and a museum store.
excerpt: The Pacific Maritime Heritage Center is the Lincoln County Historical Society's museum and interactive center on Newport's working Bayfront wharf, covering mari
note: Admission: adults $10, ages 13-17 $5, under 12 free; members and active-duty military free. Park in the driveway marked "Smuggler's Cove"; wheelchair accessible.
address: 333 SE Bay Blvd, Newport, OR 97365

title: Hatfield Marine Science Center Visitor Center
imageAlt: Giant Pacific octopus at the Visitor Center

banner.alt: Giant Pacific octopus at the Visitor Center

contentHtml:
The Visitor Center at Oregon State University's Hatfield Marine Science Center, on the south shore of Yaquina Bay, is run by Oregon Sea Grant. Hands-on exhibits include a tidepool touch tank, a research-vessel simulator, a coastal fog simulator, tsunami and wave energy tanks, and a live giant Pacific octopus on the OctoCam.

A marine mammal skeleton collection includes a gray whale calf and sperm whale calf, and a 70-foot blue whale skeleton is on display through OSU's Marine Mammal Institute.
excerpt: The Visitor Center at Oregon State University's Hatfield Marine Science Center, on the south shore of Yaquina Bay, is run by Oregon Sea Grant. Hands-on exhibits
note: Admission $5 for ages 5 and up, bought on arrival. Summer hours (Memorial Day to Labor Day): daily 10:00 AM - 5:00 PM. Closed Thanksgiving, December 25 and January 1. Email: hmsc_visitorcenter@oregonstate.edu
address: 2030 SE Marine Science Drive, Newport, OR 97365

title: Siuslaw National Forest
contentHtml:
The Siuslaw National Forest covers more than 630,000 acres of the Oregon coast and Coast Range, and is one of only two national forests in the lower 48 states with oceanfront land. Its landscapes run from mossy coastal mountain forests to sand dunes and Pacific beaches.

Highlights include Cape Perpetua Scenic Area with its rocky headlands, Cascade Head with native prairie and rare wildflowers, the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area, and Marys Peak, the highest point in the Coast Range, just west of Corvallis. Visitors come for old-growth forest, waterfalls, camping and off-highway vehicle riding on the dunes.
excerpt: The Siuslaw National Forest covers more than 630,000 acres of the Oregon coast and Coast Range, and is one of only two national forests in the lower 48 states w
note: Forest headquarters is in Corvallis
address: 3200 SW Jefferson Way, Corvallis, OR 97331
photoCredit: USDA Forest Service, Siuslaw National Forest

title: Drift Creek Wilderness
contentHtml:
Drift Creek Wilderness is a 5,798-acre rainforest in the Oregon Coast Range, about seven miles north of Waldport and south of Newport, holding the Coast Range's largest stand of old-growth Sitka spruce and western hemlock. It gets about 120 inches of rain a year.

Roosevelt elk, black bears and northern spotted owls live here, and Chinook and coho salmon, steelhead and cutthroat trout spawn in the creek in fall. Two trails enter it: Harris Ranch Trail #1347 from the south (off Highway 34 east of Waldport) and Horse Creek Trail #1362 from the Horse Creek North Trailhead.
excerpt: Drift Creek Wilderness is a 5,798-acre rainforest in the Oregon Coast Range, about seven miles north of Waldport and south of Newport, holding the Coast Range's
note: No bikes, motor vehicles, drones, horses or stock. Camp at least 100 feet from flowing water. No restrooms, water or picnic tables.
address: Central Coast Ranger District: 1130 Forestry Lane, Waldport, OR 97394

title: Oregon Islands Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Oregon Islands Wilderness covers the rocks, reefs and islands of Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, some 1,853 of them strung along about 320 miles of coastline from Tillamook Head near Seaside to the California border.

The islands are breeding and resting grounds for most of Oregon's estimated 1.2 million nesting seabirds, including tufted puffins and cormorants, and for seals and sea lions that haul out and give birth there.

The islands are closed to public entry; bring binoculars or a spotting scope and watch from shore.
excerpt: The Oregon Islands Wilderness covers the rocks, reefs and islands of Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, some 1,853 of them strung along about 320 miles of
note: All rocks and islands are closed to the public. Email: Oregoncoast@fws.gov
address: Offshore rocks and islands along the Oregon coast

title: Agate Beach State Recreation Site

gallery.alt: Agate Beach with Yaquina Head Lighthouse

contentHtml:
Agate Beach State Recreation Site is a favorite of clam diggers on the north side of Newport, popular for razor clamming and surfing. It sits between new and old Highway 101, and a tunnel under the old highway leads to a large sandy beach.

It makes a good picnic stop on the way to the Oregon Coast Aquarium or Hatfield Marine Science Center.
excerpt: Agate Beach State Recreation Site is a favorite of clam diggers on the north side of Newport, popular for razor clamming and surfing. It sits between new and ol
note: Day-use parking permit required (1-day permit sold on site). Large parking lot with trailer parking.
address: Off Highway 101, north Newport, OR

title: Beachside State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Beachside State Recreation Site is a small destination campground beside a wide, sandy beach between Waldport and Yachats, good for kite flying and whale watching. Every campsite is close to the shore for storm and sunset watching.

The campground has about 30 electrical sites with water, more than 40 tent sites, two yurts (one pet- friendly), a hiker/biker camp, flush toilets and hot showers. Two sites and both yurts are accessible.
excerpt: Beachside State Recreation Site is a small destination campground beside a wide, sandy beach between Waldport and Yachats, good for kite flying and whale watchi
note: Seasonal: open March 15 to November 1, weather permitting. Off-season questions: South Beach office, 541-867-7451.
address: Highway 101 between Waldport and Yachats, OR

title: Beverly Beach State Park
contentHtml:
Beverly Beach State Park sits a few steps from the ocean north of Newport. A walkway under the highway leads to a long sandy beach running from Yaquina Head, with its lighthouse in view, to the Otter Rock headlands; surfers head north and fossil hunters head south.

The forest-sheltered campground along Spencer Creek has about 53 full-hookup sites, about 75 electrical sites, more than 125 tent sites, 21 yurts (10 pet-friendly), group tent areas and a hiker/biker camp. There is a visitor information center, a playground and a grassy day-use area with a yurt meeting hall.
excerpt: Beverly Beach State Park sits a few steps from the ocean north of Newport. A walkway under the highway leads to a long sandy beach running from Yaquina Head, wi
note: Flush toilets, hot showers, RV dump station and firewood for sale. Seasonal Mobi-Mat beach access.
address: Highway 101, north of Newport, OR

title: Brian Booth State Park
imageAlt: The beach at Brian Booth State Park

banner.alt: The beach at Brian Booth State Park

contentHtml:
Brian Booth State Park, also known as Ona Beach, was renamed in 2013 to honor the first chair of the Oregon State Parks and Recreation Commission. The forested ocean flat south of Newport is developed for day use, with easy beachcombing access and picnic areas for large gatherings.

From the boat ramp on the east side of the highway, paddlers can kayak up Beaver Creek into the Beaver Creek wetland. Ona Beach is also the western end of the Corvallis-to-the-Sea Trail.
excerpt: Brian Booth State Park, also known as Ona Beach, was renamed in 2013 to honor the first chair of the Oregon State Parks and Recreation Commission. The forested
address: Highway 101 near Seal Rock, south of Newport, OR

title: D River State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
D River State Recreation Site sits at the mouth of the D River, billed as the shortest river in the world, flowing a very short distance from Devils Lake to the ocean in central Lincoln City.

Its windy beach hosts two large kite festivals each year, in June and October. From mid-October to Memorial Day, Lincoln City's Finders Keepers program hides handmade glass floats on the beach, and D River is a popular place to search.
excerpt: D River State Recreation Site sits at the mouth of the D River, billed as the shortest river in the world, flowing a very short distance from Devils Lake to the
note: Paved parking, flush restrooms and easy beach access. Seasonal Mobi-Mat beach access.
address: Just west of Highway 101 (101 SE Highway 101), central Lincoln City, OR

title: Devils Lake State Recreation Area
contentHtml:
Devils Lake State Recreation Area has two parks on opposite sides of the 685-acre lake: a campground on the west shore, close to downtown Lincoln City and a short walk from the beach, and East Devils Lake, a day-use park with a boat launch around the lake's southern end.

Sheltered from coastal winds, the lake is popular with paddlers, anglers and boaters, and holds rainbow trout, yellow perch, catfish, crappie, largemouth bass and bluegill. Its wetland is a major wintering area for migrating geese and ducks, with osprey and bald eagle nests nearby.
excerpt: Devils Lake State Recreation Area has two parks on opposite sides of the 685-acre lake: a campground on the west shore, close to downtown Lincoln City and a sho
note: Campground: 28 full-hookup sites, 5 electrical sites, 54 tent sites, 10 yurts (5 pet-friendly), hiker/biker camp, flush toilets, hot showers and 12 reservable boat moorage slips (no launch ramp in the campground). Two accessible sites and two accessible yurts.
address: Campground on the west shore of Devils Lake, Lincoln City, OR

title: Devils Punch Bowl State Natural Area

gallery.alt: Exploring the rocks at Otter Rock

contentHtml:
Devils Punch Bowl State Natural Area at Otter Rock is a hollow, bowl-shaped rock formation, likely formed when the roofs of two sea caves collapsed. During winter storms, waves crash into the bowl with a roar and churn the water into foam.

It is a popular spot for surfers and surf watchers, whale watching and picnics on the rocky shoreline, with tide pools to explore on the north side of the bowl.
excerpt: Devils Punch Bowl State Natural Area at Otter Rock is a hollow, bowl-shaped rock formation, likely formed when the roofs of two sea caves collapsed. During wint
address: Otter Rock, OR (off Highway 101 north of Newport)

title: Driftwood Beach State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Driftwood Beach State Recreation Site gives access to the ocean, with picnic facilities scattered among the shore pine.

The wide, flat, sandy beach is good for beachcombing and watching sunsets.
excerpt: Driftwood Beach State Recreation Site gives access to the ocean, with picnic facilities scattered among the shore pine.
address: Highway 101, north of Waldport, OR

title: Fogarty Creek State Recreation Area
contentHtml:
Fogarty Creek State Recreation Area is where a creek meets the ocean in a scenic cove rimmed by cliffs, north of Depoe Bay.

Wooden footbridges cross the creek through a forest of Sitka spruce, western hemlock, shore pine and alder to wind-sheltered picnic areas and a covered picnic shelter. It is a good place for birdwatching and tidepooling.
excerpt: Fogarty Creek State Recreation Area is where a creek meets the ocean in a scenic cove rimmed by cliffs, north of Depoe Bay.
address: Highway 101, north of Depoe Bay, OR

title: Gleneden Beach State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
At Gleneden Beach State Recreation Site, a short paved trail runs from the parking and picnic area through shore pine forest to a soft sand beach below crumbling orange sandstone bluffs. Seals are sometimes seen in the surf, and surfers often ride the morning waves.

Walk north along the beach for views of the Cascade Head headland. Visitors who go as far as the tip of the four-mile Salishan Spit are asked not to disturb the sea lions there.
excerpt: At Gleneden Beach State Recreation Site, a short paved trail runs from the parking and picnic area through shore pine forest to a soft sand beach below crumblin
address: Gleneden Beach, OR (west of Highway 101)

title: Governor Patterson Memorial State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Governor Patterson Memorial State Recreation Site is a beachcomber's delight, with miles of flat, sandy beach a short walk from the mouth of Alsea Bay.

Visitors windsurf, crab and watch seals, and it is a good spot for whale and storm watching and sunsets.
excerpt: Governor Patterson Memorial State Recreation Site is a beachcomber's delight, with miles of flat, sandy beach a short walk from the mouth of Alsea Bay.
address: Highway 101, just south of Waldport, OR

title: H. B. Van Duzer Forest State Scenic Corridor
imageAlt: The Salmon River through the forest

banner.alt: The Salmon River through the forest

gallery.alt: Van Duzer Forest Corridor entrance sign

contentHtml:
H.B. Van Duzer Forest State Scenic Corridor protects an ancient forest along Highway 18 and the Salmon River, with a roadside pull-off to stretch your legs and picnic among old-growth Douglas-fir. Weekdays are the quietest time to visit.

Watch for salmon, deer and Roosevelt elk. One mile east of the park entrance, a pull-out has a short trail to a swimming hole under more ancient trees.
excerpt: H.B. Van Duzer Forest State Scenic Corridor protects an ancient forest along Highway 18 and the Salmon River, with a roadside pull-off to stretch your legs and
note: The 12-mile corridor spans Lincoln, Polk and Tillamook counties.
address: Highway 18 along the Salmon River, between Grand Ronde and Otis, OR

title: Lost Creek State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Lost Creek State Recreation Site, about seven miles south of Newport, is developed for picnicking and beach access.

It is a good spot for beachcombing, whale watching and sunsets.
excerpt: Lost Creek State Recreation Site, about seven miles south of Newport, is developed for picnicking and beach access.
address: Highway 101, about seven miles south of Newport, OR

title: Ocean Shore State Recreation Area
contentHtml:
The Ocean Shore State Recreation Area is Oregon's whole public shoreline, from the Columbia River south to the California border and from the vegetation line down to extreme low tide, taking in sandy beaches, rocky shores and tall headlands.

In 1913 Governor Oswald West signed a law declaring the shore a public highway that would "forever remain open" to the public. The legislature made it a recreation area in 1947, and the 1967 Beach Bill, backed by Governor Tom McCall, gave the public a recreation easement over the dry sand up to the vegetation line, administered by Oregon Parks and Recreation Department.
excerpt: The Ocean Shore State Recreation Area is Oregon's whole public shoreline, from the Columbia River south to the California border and from the vegetation line do
note: General information: 800-551-6949
address: The entire Oregon coast; Lincoln County beach accesses include Nye Beach, Newport

title: Ona Beach State Park
imageAlt: The beach at Brian Booth State Park

banner.alt: The beach at Brian Booth State Park

contentHtml:
Brian Booth State Park, also known as Ona Beach, was renamed in 2013 to honor the first chair of the Oregon State Parks and Recreation Commission. The forested ocean flat south of Newport is developed for day use, with easy beachcombing access and picnic areas for large gatherings.

From the boat ramp on the east side of the highway, paddlers can kayak up Beaver Creek into the Beaver Creek wetland. Ona Beach is also the western end of the Corvallis-to-the-Sea Trail.
excerpt: Brian Booth State Park, also known as Ona Beach, was renamed in 2013 to honor the first chair of the Oregon State Parks and Recreation Commission. The forested
note: Ona Beach is the day-use portion of Brian Booth State Park.
address: Ona Beach day-use area, Highway 101 near Seal Rock, south of Newport, OR

title: Roads End State Recreation Site

gallery.alt: Roads End State Recreation Site sign

contentHtml:
Roads End State Recreation Site is a sheltered, quieter alternative to Lincoln City's busier beaches. A short path leads down to a pebbly beach at a small creek mouth, with tidepools, offshore lava-rock islands where cormorants roost, and a headland with a hidden cove. Sailboarders visit often.

At low tide you can scramble around Roads End Point to the secluded cove, but leave before the tide returns. From mid-October to Memorial Day, Finders Keepers glass floats are placed along 7.5 miles of beach from Roads End to Siletz Bay.
excerpt: Roads End State Recreation Site is a sheltered, quieter alternative to Lincoln City's busier beaches. A short path leads down to a pebbly beach at a small creek
address: Roads End, north end of Lincoln City, OR

title: Seal Rock State Recreation Site

gallery.alt: A brown pelican on the beach

contentHtml:
Seal Rock State Recreation Site is known for large offshore rock formations that are home to seals, sea lions, seabirds and other marine life.

Developed for day use, it has tidepools, a sandy beach, ocean viewpoints with benches and a picnic area among shore pine, spruce and salal.
excerpt: Seal Rock State Recreation Site is known for large offshore rock formations that are home to seals, sea lions, seabirds and other marine life.
address: Highway 101, Seal Rock, OR (between Newport and Waldport)

title: Smelt Sands State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Smelt Sands State Recreation Site in Yachats is an excellent whale-watching and photography viewpoint on a rocky shore, known for tidepooling, rock fishing and its yearly run of smelt, small silvery relatives of salmon.

The historic 804 Trail runs about 0.75 mile one way along the shore, with benches along the way.
excerpt: Smelt Sands State Recreation Site in Yachats is an excellent whale-watching and photography viewpoint on a rocky shore, known for tidepooling, rock fishing and
address: Lemwick Lane at the 804 Trail, north Yachats, OR

title: South Beach State Park
contentHtml:
South Beach State Park sits beside the Yaquina Bay Bridge at the south end of Newport and runs several miles along the coast, with broad sandy beach and trails for walking and biking, including the paved Jetty Trail and an equestrian trail from the South Jetty trailhead to the beach.

Near the campground are a playground, horseshoe pits and a 9-hole disc golf course; the Hospitality Center has maps, camp supplies and free discs and horseshoes to borrow. About 7 miles south, Beaver Creek Natural Area has a freshwater marsh, five miles of trails and about 3 miles of marsh to paddle, with guided tours July through Labor Day.
excerpt: South Beach State Park sits beside the Yaquina Bay Bridge at the south end of Newport and runs several miles along the coast, with broad sandy beach and trails
note: Camping: 227 electrical sites, 60 tent sites, 27 yurts, 3 group tent camps and a hiker/biker camp; reserve up to 6 months ahead. Flush toilets, showers, RV dump station.
address: Highway 101, south of the Yaquina Bay Bridge, South Beach (Newport), OR

title: South Jetty (South Beach)
contentHtml:
The South Jetty is the beach access at the south jetty of Yaquina Bay, part of South Beach State Park, adjacent to South Beach State Park.

The South Jetty trailhead serves the paved Jetty Trail for jogging and cycling and an equestrian trail to the beach. Fishing, crabbing, surfing and beachcombing are popular.
excerpt: The South Jetty is the beach access at the south jetty of Yaquina Bay, part of South Beach State Park, adjacent to South Beach State Park.
note: Covered by the South Beach State Park page.
address: South jetty of Yaquina Bay, at South Beach State Park, Newport, OR

title: W. B. Nelson State Recreation Site

gallery.alt: W. B. Nelson State Park sign

contentHtml:
W.B. Nelson State Recreation Site has a small freshwater lake with a fishing dock, where bass and stocked pan-sized trout are the most common catch.

It is known for abundant waterfowl, with a scenic wetland beside the Alsea River.
excerpt: W.B. Nelson State Recreation Site has a small freshwater lake with a fishing dock, where bass and stocked pan-sized trout are the most common catch.
note: Day use only.
address: Waldport, OR (near the Alsea River)

title: Yachats Ocean Road State Natural Site

gallery.alt: View of the Yachats River and town

contentHtml:
Yachats Ocean Road State Natural Site is a one-mile loop road just south of Yachats with views of Yachats Bay and the Pacific.

Park along the loop to reach the beach, tidepools and blowholes. It is a favorite for summer sunsets and whale watching.
excerpt: Yachats Ocean Road State Natural Site is a one-mile loop road just south of Yachats with views of Yachats Bay and the Pacific.
address: Yachats Ocean Road, just south of Yachats, OR

title: Yachats State Recreation Area
contentHtml:
Yachats State Recreation Area is in central Yachats, where the road west on 2nd Street loops past the mouth of the Yachats River at the Pacific.

Visitors watch the surf and the gray whale migration, fish for rockfish and salmon and explore tidepools. Benches and picnic tables are available.
excerpt: Yachats State Recreation Area is in central Yachats, where the road west on 2nd Street loops past the mouth of the Yachats River at the Pacific.
address: West end of 2nd Street, central Yachats, OR

title: Yaquina Bay State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
Yaquina Bay State Recreation Site is in Newport at the north end of Yaquina Bay, near its outlet to the Pacific, on a bluff forested with spruce and pine.

Its main draw is the historic Yaquina Bay Lighthouse, later used as a Coast Guard lifeboat station and now restored and open to the public. The historic Bayfront, Hatfield Marine Science Center and Oregon Coast Aquarium are nearby.
excerpt: Yaquina Bay State Recreation Site is in Newport at the north end of Yaquina Bay, near its outlet to the Pacific, on a bluff forested with spruce and pine.
address: North end of the Yaquina Bay Bridge, Newport, OR

title: Big Elk Campground
contentHtml:
Big Elk Campground is a small, primitive campground on Big Elk Creek near Harlan, popular for fishing and hiking. It is run by the Harlan Community Development Corporation under a Forest Service special-use permit.

There are ten primitive sites and one hiker/biker site, all first come, first served, with picnic tables. It is the starting point of the Dichotomy gravel-bike route.
excerpt: Big Elk Campground is a small, primitive campground on Big Elk Creek near Harlan, popular for fishing and hiking. It is run by the Harlan Community Development
note: $10 per night; additional vehicle $5; day use $5 per vehicle. No drinking water; pack out trash. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals. Email: bigelkcampgroundharlan@gmail.com
address: Big Elk Creek near Harlan, Siuslaw National Forest, OR (Central Coast Ranger Station: 1130 Forestry Lane, Waldport, OR 97394, (541) 563-8400)

title: Blackberry Campground
contentHtml:
Blackberry Campground sits on a wooded bluff among cedars and Douglas fir above the Alsea River, with some sites overlooking the river and others facing a large grassy field. It has 32 sites, each with a picnic table and fire ring, paved parking spurs, vault toilets, drinking water and an on-site boat ramp.

It is popular for drift boating, fishing for coho and Chinook salmon and steelhead, crawfishing and summer swimming, and makes a good base camp for elk hunting.
excerpt: Blackberry Campground sits on a wooded bluff among cedars and Douglas fir above the Alsea River, with some sites overlooking the river and others facing a large
note: $36 per night; additional vehicle $12; day use $9 per vehicle. Reserve at recreation.gov (some sites first come, first served). No hookups; nearest dump station in Waldport. 8-person limit per site. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals.
address: Highway 34, about 18 miles east of Waldport, OR

title: Canal Creek Group Campground
contentHtml:
Canal Creek Group Campground has two group sites shaded by Douglas fir and spruce, divided by Canal Creek. The Canal Creek site holds up to 100 people and 20 vehicles in a large open field with a picnic shelter (reached by crossing the creek; RVs not recommended). The Alsea site holds up to 50 people and 10 vehicles in ten campsites around a central dining area, and RVs are welcome.

Nearby are fishing, crawfishing, hiking, tubing and swimming.

note: Alsea Group Site $210 per night; Canal Creek Group Site $300 per night. Reserve at recreation.gov. Vault toilets; no drinking water or hookups. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals.
address: Canal Creek Road, 4 miles off Highway 34 (7 miles east of Waldport), OR

title: Cape Perpetua Campground
contentHtml:
Cape Perpetua Campground sits along Cape Creek in the Cape Perpetua Scenic Area, among Sitka spruce, Douglas fir and alder, 3 miles south of Yachats. Sites have a picnic table and fire ring, with flush toilets and drinking water.

A 23-mile trail system runs from the campground through old-growth forest to the Giant Spruce, the Visitor Center, tidepools and the St. Perpetua viewpoint, one of the best views on the Oregon coast.

note: $39 per night. Reserve at recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777; some sites first come, first served. 8- person limit per site. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals.
address: East side of Highway 101, Cape Perpetua Scenic Area, 3 miles south of Yachats, OR (Visitor Center: 2400 Highway 101, Yachats, OR 97498)

title: Cape Perpetua Group Campground
contentHtml:
Cape Perpetua Group Campground is the single group site within Cape Perpetua Campground, holding up to 50 people along Cape Creek in a forest of Sitka spruce, Douglas fir and alder.

Trails lead from the campground to the Giant Spruce, the Cape Perpetua Visitor Center, tidepools and the St. Perpetua viewpoint.

note: $220 per night. Reserve through the Cape Perpetua Campground page on recreation.gov. Flush toilets and drinking water. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals.
address: Cape Perpetua Campground, east side of Highway 101, 3 miles south of Yachats, OR

title: River Edge Group Campground
contentHtml:
River Edge Group Campground is an accessible group campground on the Alsea River for up to 100 guests, shaded by Sitka spruce, Douglas fir and alder. It has a large shelter with picnic tables, fire rings and grills, drinking water, electricity, four vault toilets and an open play field.

A boat ramp and day-use area are next door, for river fishing, canoeing and swimming.
excerpt: River Edge Group Campground is an accessible group campground on the Alsea River for up to 100 guests, shaded by Sitka spruce, Douglas fir and alder. It has a l
note: $300 per night; day use $10 per vehicle. Firewood sold on site.
address: Highway 34, 22 miles east of Waldport, OR

title: Tillicum Beach Campground
contentHtml:
Tillicum Beach Campground is known for its beachfront sites: 61 sites, most with ocean views, with flush toilets, drinking water and a picnic table and fire ring at each site. Some sites have electric and water hookups (these are not on the waterfront).

Surfing, swimming, sand play and whale watching are the main activities, and Cape Perpetua's old-growth Sitka spruce, tide pools and guided hikes are about 6 miles south.
excerpt: Tillicum Beach Campground is known for its beachfront sites: 61 sites, most with ocean views, with flush toilets, drinking water and a picnic table and fire rin
note: Non-electric site $39 per night; electric site $51; additional vehicle $12; day use $10 per vehicle. Reserve at recreation.gov (reservations advised; some sites first come, first served). No showers. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals.
address: Highway 101, 4 miles south of Waldport, OR

title: Oregon Islands

gallery.alt: Refuge staff with a puffin decoy on an offshore rock

contentHtml:
Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1935, is not one place but 1,853 rocks, reefs and islands plus two headlands, running from Tillamook Head near Seaside to the California border.

Most of Oregon's estimated 1.2 million nesting seabirds raise their young here, and seals and sea lions haul out and give birth on the rocks. All the rocks and islands except 1-acre Tillamook Rock are designated wilderness.

The islands are closed to entry, so watch from shore with binoculars or a spotting scope.
excerpt: Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1935, is not one place but 1,853 rocks, reefs and islands plus two headlands, running from Tillamook Hea
note: Email: Oregoncoast@fws.gov
address: Offshore rocks and islands along the whole Oregon coast

title: Siletz Bay

gallery.alt: Kayakers on Siletz Bay (photo: Radford Bean)

contentHtml:
Siletz Bay National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1991, protects salt marsh, mudflats, sloughs and conifer- hardwood forest where the Siletz River meets the bay, south of Lincoln City. Former diked dairy pasture is being restored to tidal marsh, used by shorebirds, ducks, wading birds and young coho and Chinook salmon. Bald eagles and red-tailed hawks roost on snags, and great blue herons and great egrets forage in the tidal waters.

The easy 0.6-mile Alder Island Nature Trail, opened in 2017, winds along the Siletz River and Millport Slough. The bay and sloughs are good for kayaking and canoeing, and bank fishing for salmon is allowed.
excerpt: Siletz Bay National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1991, protects salt marsh, mudflats, sloughs and conifer- hardwood forest where the Siletz River meets the b
note: Free. No pets on the refuge; no overnight parking. Waterfowl hunting allowed seasonally in designated areas. Email: oregoncoast@fws.gov
address: Millport Slough Lane, Lincoln City, OR 97411 (east side of Highway 101, just south of the Highway 229 junction)

title: Drift Creek Falls
imageAlt: Drift Creek Falls from the suspension bridge (photo: Bryan Swan)

banner.alt: Drift Creek Falls from the suspension bridge (photo: Bryan Swan)

gallery.alt: Drift Creek Falls before the 2010 rockfall (photo: Bryan Swan)

contentHtml:
Drift Creek Falls is a 66-foot plunge where the North Fork of Drift Creek runs through a short bedrock sluice and drops off a gorge wall into Drift Creek. A large section of the cliff collapsed in August 2010, changing its look.

An easy trail of about 1.5 miles through the Siuslaw National Forest leads to a 250-foot suspension bridge across the gorge beside the falls, with access to the far side and the base of the falls.
excerpt: Drift Creek Falls is a 66-foot plunge where the North Fork of Drift Creek runs through a short bedrock sluice and drops off a gorge wall into Drift Creek. A lar
note: Day use $5 per vehicle (no cash; buy a digital pass on recreation.gov); Northwest Forest Pass, Oregon Pacific Coast Passport and interagency passes accepted. Vault toilets and picnic tables; no drinking water. Dogs on a 6-foot leash. From Highway 18, take Bear Creek Road, then FS Road 17; from Highway 101 south of Lincoln City, take Drift Creek Road.
address: Drift Creek Falls Trailhead, Forest Service Road 17, east of Lincoln City, OR

title: Alsea River Water Trail
contentHtml:
The Alsea River Water Trail (also called the Alsea Bay Water Trail) is a designated 10-mile network on the lower Alsea River and tidal Alsea Bay at Waldport, including the arms of Drift Creek and Lint Slough. It starts from the Port of Alsea boat launch in Old Town Waldport.

It is flatwater tidal estuary paddling, easy to moderate with no whitewater, but plan around strong tides and mudflats at low tide. The port's ADA-accessible kayak dock and launch was completed in November 2021.
excerpt: The Alsea River Water Trail (also called the Alsea Bay Water Trail) is a designated 10-mile network on the lower Alsea River and tidal Alsea Bay at Waldport, in
note: Managed by the Port of Alsea. Annual launch passes available from the port.
address: Port of Alsea boat launch, 365 NE Port St, Old Town Waldport, OR 97394

title: Alsea River — Don Lindly Park
contentHtml:
Don Lindly Park is a largely undeveloped Lincoln County riverfront park on the lower Alsea River at about river mile 8.2, with mature forest and wetland. It offers rustic, walk-in paddle access for kayaks, canoes and SUPs, with no developed boat ramp.

It has a picnic table and fire ring but no restrooms or drinking water. The park is in a floodplain, so wet-season conditions can affect the site.

Wind can make the open sections harder, and expect motorboat traffic near the launch.

Only electric motors are allowed, so it suits kayaks, stand-up paddleboards and canoes.

Being tidal, depth, current and access to the smaller channels change with the tide, so check tides and coastal wind before launching. Expect motorboats near the launch and main channel.

title: Unnamed Lincoln Co. High Point
contentHtml:
Lincoln County's high point is an unnamed 3,408-foot (1,039 m) summit in the Oregon Coast Range. The summit itself is a forested walk-up; all of the difficulty is in reaching it, through a patchwork of BLM public land and Weyerhaeuser private timberland in the Black Rock logging area.

The practical approach is from the east: from OR-22 at Buell, take Mill Creek Road past the BLM Mill Creek Recreation Site and through the white Weyerhaeuser gate, then follow logging roads, about 49 miles round trip, to a parking area just below the summit. No recreation permit is needed on this route.

title: Corvallis-to-the-Sea Trail

gallery.alt: Hiker and goat on the trail
C2C trail marker on Old Peak Road

contentHtml:
The Corvallis-to-the-Sea Trail (C2C) runs about 60 miles from downtown Corvallis, over the Coast Range, to Ona Beach on the Pacific. It is one of 15 Oregon Signature Trails and is open to hikers and cyclists.

Much of the route crosses public forest and private timberland. Hikers need a free permit for three sections, including a current-year Starker Forests permit, and should sign in at each of the 11 trail kiosks.

Camping is allowed only on U.S. Forest Service land, and campfires only in public campgrounds.

title: Oregon Coast Trail
imageAlt: Oregon Coast Trail sign along a forested trail

banner.alt: Oregon Coast Trail sign along a forested trail

contentHtml:
The Oregon Coast Trail follows Oregon's coastline from the Columbia River to the California border, about 382 miles by the official guide and about 425 miles if no ferries are used around the estuaries. It passes through 28 coastal towns.

Most of the route is on the beach, with other sections through state parks and public lands, on private land under trail easements, and on road shoulders. In Lincoln County the route passes Cape Perpetua, an 800-foot headland south of Yachats, where the visitor center is a trailhead for Oregon Coast Trail #1308.

Hiker/biker tent sites, first-come first-served, are at nearly every coastal state park. Check tide times, as some areas are passable only at low tide. During western snowy plover nesting season (March 15 to September 15), walk on wet sand in protected areas, where dogs, camping and beach fires are not allowed.

note: Trail conditions change quickly; check Oregon State Parks notices and Trailkeepers of Oregon alerts before you go.

title: Cannibal 5
contentHtml:
Cannibal 5 is a 61-mile gravel lollipop through the Siuslaw National Forest, named for Cannibal Mountain and its five major climbs, with high points of about 1,100 to 1,700 feet and some 7,500 feet of climbing. It is about 60% gravel, from smooth hardpack to rugged forest road, and 40% often-rough pavement, mostly under Douglas-fir, Sitka spruce and hemlock.

Rated moderate, in a remote area that needs attention to navigation; 40 mm or wider tires suggested. It adapts Mudslinger Events' Oregon Coast Gravel Epic route to start and finish at Tillicum Beach.

contentHtml:
Dichotomy is a very demanding 31-mile gravel loop from Big Elk Campground with about 3,800 to 3,900 feet of climbing: about 65% gravel, 10% single track and 25% pavement. The steep, technical first half includes a 1,500-foot climb over 3.5 miles, rough Weyerhaeuser roads and narrow, grassy single track on the Corvallis- to-the-Sea Trail.

The second half is mostly smooth gravel, with a sweeping 4-mile descent. Wear long socks and sleeves for thick brush and nettles, and ride in the mapped direction.

title: Drift Creek Falls
contentHtml:
The Drift Creek Falls route is an easier 30-mile all-road lollipop from Taft, about 80% paved and 20% hard- packed gravel, with about 2,900 feet of climbing. A skinny, single-lane Forest Service road climbs to a summit and rolls to the trailhead, where a wide trail of about 1.5 miles leads to the suspension bridge above Drift Creek Falls (bring a lock).

On the way back, wooden fish weirs in Schooner Creek help salmon and trout upstream, and the finish at Taft Waterfront Park has flat sand, a dock and views of the Four Brothers rocks.

title: Lands of the Yachats

gallery.alt: Elk refuge along the Yachats River

contentHtml:
Lands of the Yachats is a 34-mile lollipop of about 40% gravel and 60% pavement with about 3,900 feet of climbing, rated moderate. It follows the Yachats River past farmland, then climbs about 1,400 feet in 5 miles on a narrow gravel road and makes a second, paved climb into the Coast Range forests.

Near mile 28.5 it passes an elk refuge managed by the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife as winter forage for Roosevelt elk. The area was the ancestral home of the Yachats and Alsea peoples.

title: Marys Peak to Pacific Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Alsea Falls, a stop on the byway

contentHtml:
The Marys Peak to Pacific Scenic Byway is a 72-mile Oregon State Scenic Byway from the farmland near Tangent, through Corvallis and Philomath, over the Coast Range on OR-34 and down the Alsea River valley to Waldport on the coast. Allow 3 to 5 hours.

Stops include William L. Finley National Wildlife Refuge, the Philomath Museum in its 1867 college building, Marys Peak (4,097 ft), Alsea Falls, the Hayden Covered Bridge, the Oregon Hatchery Research Center, the Alsea Bay estuary and Seal Rock State Recreation Site.

title: Pacific Coast Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway
Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway
Along the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway

contentHtml:
The Pacific Coast Scenic Byway, an All-American Road, follows US 101 for 363 miles along the whole Oregon coast, from Astoria at the Washington border to Brookings at the California border.

In Lincoln County the byway passes the Cape Perpetua Visitor Center (2400 Highway 101 S, Yachats), a signature viewpoint and interpretive center. Farther along the coast, highlights include clamming on Tillamook Bay, kayaking Alsea Bay, the dramatic rocks and islands of the south coast and jet boat trips up the Rogue River at Gold Beach.

EV charging stations are spaced along the route, making an electric road trip from Astoria to Brookings possible.

title: Central Coast Food Trail
contentHtml:
The Central Coast Food Trail is a self-guided, year-round route of 35 stops along Oregon's central coast: seafood, farms, bakeries, breweries, distilleries and wineries from Lincoln City through Gleneden Beach, Depoe Bay, Otter Rock, Newport, Toledo, Siletz, Waldport and Yachats to Florence in Lane County.

Most of the stops are in Lincoln County. On Newport's historic Bayfront, Local Ocean Seafoods is a dock-to- dish restaurant and market featured in the trail's own itineraries.

title: Chitwood Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Chitwood Covered Bridge was built in 1926 by Otis Hamer beside Highway 20 at Chitwood, a former railway town, and carries Chitwood Road over the Yaquina River. The 96-foot Howe truss bridge has flared sides, semi-elliptical portal arches and the barn-red color typical of Lincoln County's bridges.

It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979 and rebuilt to its original truss design in 1983- 84. It is still open to traffic.

title: Drift Creek Covered Bridge
imageAlt: Drift Creek Bridge in its new location

banner.alt: Drift Creek Bridge in its new location

contentHtml:
Drift Creek Covered Bridge was built in 1914 over Drift Creek south of Lincoln City and was once billed as Oregon's oldest covered bridge. The 66-foot bridge was condemned for safety in fall 1997 after coastal weather rotted its timbers.

Volunteers formed the nonprofit Save the Covered Bridge to rescue it, and it was rebuilt in 2000-2001 over Bear Creek on the property of Laura and Kerry Sweitz in Otis. It still belongs to Lincoln County but is privately maintained, and a public easement allows visitors onto the site.

title: Fisher School Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Fisher School Covered Bridge, also called Five Rivers Bridge, was built in 1919 by George Melvin with local farmers in the remote Five Rivers valley, and is named for the former Fisher Elementary School nearby. The 72-foot Howe truss bridge has a shingled gabled roof and board-and-batten siding.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, it was rehabilitated in 2001 and rededicated in 2005. It is now closed to vehicles and crossed on foot.

address: Off Five Rivers Road, south of Highway 34, Five Rivers valley, OR

title: North Fork Yachats Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
The North Fork Yachats Covered Bridge was built in 1938, the last covered bridge by Otis Hamer. At 42 feet, the queenpost truss bridge is one of the shortest in Oregon, with flared sides and ribbon openings under the roofline that light the center.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, it was rebuilt and rededicated in 1989. It remains open to light traffic, but not to RVs or large trucks.
excerpt: The North Fork Yachats Covered Bridge was built in 1938, the last covered bridge by Otis Hamer. At 42 feet, the queenpost truss bridge is one of the shortest in
note: Surrounded by private property with little or no room to turn around.

title: Yaquina Bay Lighthouse
contentHtml:
The Yaquina Bay Lighthouse, built in 1871, is the second-oldest standing lighthouse on the Oregon coast. It served only until 1874, when the brighter Yaquina Head light replaced it, and was later used as a Coast Guard lifeboat station.

Restored and re-lit in 1996 as a privately maintained aid to navigation, its light is 161 feet above the ocean. Free self-guided tours show its antique period furniture, and there is a gift shop in the basement.
excerpt: The Yaquina Bay Lighthouse, built in 1871, is the second-oldest standing lighthouse on the Oregon coast. It served only until 1874, when the brighter Yaquina He
note: Free. October and March - May: daily 12:00 - 4:00 PM. June - September: daily, from 11:00 AM.

title: Yaquina Head Lighthouse
contentHtml:
Yaquina Head Lighthouse, first lit in 1873 and still an active aid to navigation, is Oregon's tallest lighthouse: a 93-foot tower standing 162 feet above the sea on the westernmost point of a basalt headland at the north end of Newport.

It is in the BLM's Yaquina Head Outstanding Natural Area, whose interpretive center offers shelter from winter storms and summer wind. A limited number of visitors can tour the lighthouse with a guide; tours are free, and reservations are strongly recommended (recreation.gov).

note: Site amenity fee required. Interpretive center open daily 10:00 AM - 4:00 PM. Lighthouse tours daily in July and August.
address: Yaquina Head Outstanding Natural Area, Lighthouse Drive, north Newport, OR (off Highway 101)

title: Depoe Bay Harbor
imageAlt: Whale tail off Depoe Bay (area photo)

banner.alt: Whale tail off Depoe Bay (area photo)

gallery.alt: Whale Watching Center above the ocean at Depoe Bay (area photo)

contentHtml:
The City of Depoe Bay bills its six-acre harbor as the world's smallest navigable harbor. Boats thread a narrow channel beneath the Highway 101 bridge to reach the Pacific.

Whale-watching boats leave from the harbor dock in season. Nearby on the seawall, the Oregon State Parks Whale Watching Center (119 SW Hwy 101, 541-765-3304) has a large viewing deck, binoculars, displays and volunteers who help spot gray whales and other marine life.

address: Depoe Bay harbor, Highway 101, Depoe Bay, OR 97341

contentHtml:
Oregon's tallest lighthouse is the 93-foot tower at Yaquina Head, first lit in 1873 and still an active aid to navigation.

It is in the BLM's Yaquina Head Outstanding Natural Area, whose interpretive center offers shelter from winter storms and summer wind. A limited number of visitors can tour the lighthouse with a guide; tours are free, and reservations are strongly recommended (recreation.gov).

title: Gleneden Beach State Recreation Site
contentHtml:
This Oregon Film Trail marker at Gleneden Beach State Recreation Site honors Sometimes a Great Notion (1971), Paul Newman's film of Ken Kesey's logging novel, which was filmed along the nearby Siletz River at Kernville, where the Stamper family house still stands at the water's edge.

The trail currently lists this marker as unavailable.

note: Marker currently not available.

title: Main Street, Toledo
contentHtml:
Toledo's Main Street Oregon Film Trail marker celebrates the town's role in Sometimes a Great Notion (1971), Paul Newman's film of Ken Kesey's logging novel.

The film was also shot at Kernville on the Siletz River and in Newport.
excerpt: Toledo's Main Street Oregon Film Trail marker celebrates the town's role in Sometimes a Great Notion (1971), Paul Newman's film of Ken Kesey's logging novel.
address: Main Street, Toledo, OR

title: Beachcrest Brewing Company
contentHtml:
Beachcrest Brewing Company is an independent neighborhood brewery and wood-fired pizzeria in the Salishan Marketplace, with a taproom and a beer garden on the back nine of the Salishan golf course. Its beers include Finders Keepers IPA and Siletz Bay Hazy IPA.

All ages are welcome, dogs are allowed in the beer garden, and there is free live music every weekend in the Tsunami Room.

note: Closed Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. Email: info@beachcrestbrewing.com
address: Salishan Marketplace, 7755 N Highway 101, Gleneden Beach, OR

title: Bier One Brewing
contentHtml:
Bier One Brewing is a small mom-and-pop brewpub in Newport's Nye Beach district.

Since Rogue's Newport closure in November 2025, it is Newport's only remaining brewery.
excerpt: Bier One Brewing is a small mom-and-pop brewpub in Newport's Nye Beach district.
address: 255 SW 9th St, Nye Beach, Newport, OR

title: Depoe Bay Brewing and Horn Public House
imageAlt: Depoe Bay Brewing and Horn Public House
contentHtml:
The Horn Public House is a brewpub overlooking the Depoe Bay harbor, pouring Depoe Bay Brewing Co. beers such as King Tide IPA.

The menu features fresh seafood and handcrafted pizzas, with harbor views. Takeout is available.
excerpt: The Horn Public House is a brewpub overlooking the Depoe Bay harbor, pouring Depoe Bay Brewing Co. beers such as King Tide IPA.
address: 110 SE Highway 101, Depoe Bay, OR

title: Rusty Truck Brewing Company
contentHtml:
Rusty Truck Brewing Company is a roadhouse-style brewpub in Lincoln City's Taft district, in the former Roadhouse 101. Beers include Road Wrecker IPA and Chamomellow, a chamomile Kölsch.

Weekend brunch with a Bloody Mary bar runs Saturday and Sunday from 9:00 AM to noon.
excerpt: Rusty Truck Brewing Company is a roadhouse-style brewpub in Lincoln City's Taft district, in the former Roadhouse 101. Beers include Road Wrecker IPA and Chamom
note: Email: rusty@rustytruckbrewing.com
address: 4649 SW Highway 101, Lincoln City, OR 97367 (Taft district)

title: Red Dog DGC
imageAlt: Looking up the path from hole 1

banner.alt: Looking up the path from hole 1

contentHtml:
Red Dog is a short, highly technical 9-hole course in Toledo, established in 2014, on very hilly ground with ferns, ivy, brush and a tree tunnel. A round takes about an hour.

Tees are concrete. There are no restrooms or drinking water; dogs are allowed.

note: 9 holes · Free to play. Reviews report overgrown fairways and missing baskets; check conditions before you go.

title: Red River DGC

gallery.alt: Side view of the Elephant tree

contentHtml:
Red River is a wooded, technical 18-hole course in Waldport, established in 2019, set on extremely hilly ridges in dense Sitka spruce forest with big cedars and old-growth trees. The main layout is par 54 and about 3,400 feet; seven holes have both amateur and pro baskets.

Tees are concrete, with Mach X baskets. Restrooms and drinking water are available, and dogs are allowed. The Woodland Trail runs through the park.

note: 18 holes · Par 54 · Free to play. Not cart or stroller friendly.
address: Crestline Park area, Waldport, OR

title: Twisted Pine DGC
contentHtml:
Twisted Pine is a family-friendly course in South Beach State Park, established in 2020 among coastal dunes and shore pines, with 27 holes; the 18-hole layout is par 54 and about 4,243 feet, with pro and amateur basket positions. It is beginner-friendly but has tight gaps and technical lines, and even a basket hanging in a tree.

Tees are concrete, dirt and turf. Restrooms are in the day-use area; there is no drinking water. Holes 12 and 14 have views of the Yaquina Bay Bridge and Yaquina Bay Lighthouse.
excerpt: Twisted Pine is a family-friendly course in South Beach State Park, established in 2020 among coastal dunes and shore pines, with 27 holes; the 18-hole layout i
note: 18 baskets (27-hole option) · Par 54 · Free to play; State Park day-use fee or annual pass required. Dogs on leash. The middle nine are mostly sand walkways.
address: South Beach State Park, Newport, OR

title: Wilder DGC
contentHtml:
Wilder is a hilly, technical 19-hole course in Newport, near South Beach State Park on the east side of Highway 101, opened in 2018. The short-target layout is par 59 and about 5,525 feet, with several mandos; hole 1 crosses a ravine and hole 7 has a 90-degree dogleg.

Tees are concrete and dirt. There are no restrooms or drinking water; dogs are allowed. The terrain is rugged, so wear hiking boots and use spotters.

note: 19 holes · Par 59 · Free, but a permit is required: email a photo ID to permits@eenw.com before playing. No smoking; pack out trash.
address: Harbarton St (40th St at the top of the hill), South Beach, Newport, OR

title: Linn County Historical Museum
contentHtml:
The Linn County Historical Museum, opened in 1962, fills Brownsville's original railroad depot and six Southern Pacific railroad cars. Its collections cover Native peoples, Oregon Trail immigrants, Black and White pioneer settlers and early Linn County communities, along with the Brownsville Mill Race, the Brownsville Woolen Mill and regional mining.

Highlights include the covered wagon that carried the Drinkard family across the Oregon Trail in 1865, a 29- seat Boxcar Theatre with seats from Brownsville's old Linn Theatre, a genealogy section and displays on the filming of Stand by Me in Brownsville.
excerpt: The Linn County Historical Museum, opened in 1962, fills Brownsville's original railroad depot and six Southern Pacific railroad cars. Its collections cover Nat
note: Free. Email: lchm@co.linn.or.us
address: 101 Park Avenue, Brownsville, OR 97327

title: Moyer House
contentHtml:
The Moyer House is an elegant Italianate mansion built in 1881 in Brownsville, once described as "the most artistically arranged residence in the state."

Operated with the Linn County Historical Museum, it is staged as it originally was, with period furnishings and elaborate paintings and stenciling.
excerpt: The Moyer House is an elegant Italianate mansion built in 1881 in Brownsville, once described as "the most artistically arranged residence in the state."
note: Tours on weekends when volunteers are on duty, and by appointment.
address: 204 N Main St, Brownsville, OR 97327 (about a block from the Linn County Historical Museum)
photoCredit: Travel Oregon; Brownsville Chamber of Commerce

title: Albany Regional Museum
contentHtml:
The Albany Regional Museum, founded in 1980, is in an 1887 Italianate building in Albany's Downtown Historic District. Its exhibits follow Albany from its founding in the early 1850s through its prosperous timber decades, including the Timber Carnival, with its colorful characters, booming industry and explosive events.

There is a hands-on children's area.
excerpt: The Albany Regional Museum, founded in 1980, is in an 1887 Italianate building in Albany's Downtown Historic District. Its exhibits follow Albany from its found
note: Admission: adults and teens $5, seniors $3; free for members, children under 13, active military and veterans, and SNAP EBT cardholders plus up to 3 guests. Email: info@armuseum.com
address: 136 Lyon Street SW, Albany, OR 97321

title: Monteith House
imageAlt: Summer home tour at the Monteith House

banner.alt: Summer home tour at the Monteith House

contentHtml:
The Monteith House is Albany's first frame house, built in 1849 by the city's founders, Thomas and Walter Monteith, astride the line between their two land claims.

Listed on the National Register in 1975 and a museum since 1982, it is considered the most authentically restored pioneer-era home in Oregon.
excerpt: The Monteith House is Albany's first frame house, built in 1849 by the city's founders, Thomas and Walter Monteith, astride the line between their two land clai
note: Also by appointment.
address: 518 Second Ave SW, Albany, OR 97321

title: East Linn Museum
contentHtml:
The East Linn Museum is a small, free, volunteer-run museum in a former church on the edge of Sweet Home, run by volunteers since 1973. It holds more than 3,000 artifacts, photos, documents and records of east Linn County dating to 1852.

Walk through period rooms such as a pioneer kitchen, parlor and bedroom, see antique cameras, telephones and regional firearms, and outdoor displays of logging, mining and farming equipment. Its photo and document files are used for genealogy research with the Sweet Home Genealogical Society.
excerpt: The East Linn Museum is a small, free, volunteer-run museum in a former church on the edge of Sweet Home, run by volunteers since 1973. It holds more than 3,000
note: Free. Group tours by advance arrangement.
address: 746 Long St, Sweet Home, OR 97386

title: Willamette National Forest
contentHtml:
The Willamette National Forest runs about 110 miles along the western slopes of the Oregon Cascades and covers 1,675,407 acres of high mountains, narrow canyons, fast streams and wooded slopes. About 61% of it lies in Lane County, with large areas in Linn, Marion and Douglas counties.

It holds eight wilderness areas and seven major volcanic peaks, and offers year-round hiking, backpacking, camping, fishing, waterfalls and skiing.

address: Supervisor's Office: 3106 Pierce Parkway, Suite D, Springfield, OR 97477

title: Menagerie Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Menagerie Wilderness is a low-elevation wilderness (around 3,900 feet) of rock pinnacles in the Middle Santiam country, named by climbers for their barnyard shapes. Rooster Rock is the best known, and Northwest mountaineers use the spires and cliffs to practice technical climbing.

It can be visited year-round, in second-growth Douglas-fir, western hemlock and western red cedar forest. Trout Creek Trail #3405 starts at milepost 48.8 on Highway 20 near Trout Creek Campground, and Rooster Rock Trail #3399 at milepost 51.5 near Fernview Campground.
excerpt: The Menagerie Wilderness is a low-elevation wilderness (around 3,900 feet) of rock pinnacles in the Middle Santiam country, named by climbers for their barnyard
note: Free self-issue wilderness permit required June 15 to October 15. The north end is closed January 15 to July 31 to protect wildlife. Recreation pass required at the Trout Creek Trailhead. No restrooms or water.
address: Off Highway 20 east of Sweet Home, OR (trailheads at mileposts 48.8 and 51.5); Sweet Home Ranger Station: 4431 Highway 20, Sweet Home, OR 97386

title: Middle Santiam Wilderness
contentHtml:
The 7,500-acre Middle Santiam Wilderness, designated in 1984, protects intact low-elevation old-growth rainforest along the Middle Santiam River near Donaca Lake. Some Douglas fir, western red cedar and western hemlock are estimated at 450 years old and more than 200 feet tall, with true firs higher up.

Elevations run from about 1,600 feet to 5,022 feet; the most prominent feature is Chimney Peak (4,965 feet), a lava plug. Four seldom-hiked trails enter it: McQuade Creek, Chimney Peak, Gordan Peak and Swamp Peak. Chinook salmon spawn in the river in season.
excerpt: The 7,500-acre Middle Santiam Wilderness, designated in 1984, protects intact low-elevation old-growth rainforest along the Middle Santiam River near Donaca Lak
note: No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles.
address: Middle Santiam River country, Willamette National Forest, east of Sweet Home, OR; Sweet Home Ranger Station: 4431 Highway 20, Sweet Home, OR 97386

title: Mount Jefferson Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mount Jefferson Wilderness, established in 1968, protects 111,177 acres in Linn, Jefferson and Marion counties and is Oregon's second most visited wilderness. At its heart is Mount Jefferson, 10,497 feet, the state's second-tallest peak, a stratovolcano with five glaciers; Three Fingered Jack (7,841 feet) anchors the south end.

More than 150 lakes, including Marion, Duffy, Santiam and Wasco lakes, dot the forests and alpine meadows, and about 190 miles of trails include 40 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail. Visitors hike, backpack, camp, ski and climb among Douglas-fir, mountain hemlock, rhododendron, bear grass and lupine, with deer, black bear and bald eagles.
excerpt: The Mount Jefferson Wilderness, established in 1968, protects 111,177 acres in Linn, Jefferson and Marion counties and is Oregon's second most visited wildernes
note: Central Cascades Wilderness permits apply at some trailheads in summer. No motorized equipment or bicycles.

title: Mount Washington Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mount Washington Wilderness is a volcanic landscape of jagged peaks and rugged lava, next to the Three Sisters Wilderness across Highway 242. From 7,794-foot Mount Washington, a dissected volcano, the view takes in about 75 miles of lava-strewn plains; 6,872-foot Belknap Crater is a cinder and ash cone.

Lodgepole pine and mountain hemlock forest surrounds 28 lakes, and short trails reach Tenas, Benson and Patjens lakes. The Pacific Crest Trail crosses the wilderness for 16.6 miles.
excerpt: The Mount Washington Wilderness is a volcanic landscape of jagged peaks and rugged lava, next to the Three Sisters Wilderness across Highway 242. From 7,794-foo
note: No motorized equipment or mechanical transport, including bicycles. Central Cascades Wilderness permits are required at some trailheads in summer.

title: Fishermen's Bend Recreation Site
imageAlt: North Santiam River at Fishermen's Bend

banner.alt: North Santiam River at Fishermen's Bend

contentHtml:
Fishermen's Bend Recreation Site is a BLM riverside area on the North Santiam River, 29 miles east of Salem. The former 50-unit campground with cabins and group areas is now open for day use only, on the River Loop, until further notice.

Day visitors have seven first-come, first-served picnic sites with tables and grills, the reservable Cottonwoods group shelter, trails around the River Loop and to a fishing overlook, and a boat launch and river access. North Santiam State Park is next door.

note: No camping or dump station until further notice. Day use $5 per passenger vehicle; Northwest Oregon District annual day pass $30; interagency passes accepted. Cottonwoods Shelter $110 per day.
address: 27300 N. Santiam Hwy, Mill City, OR 97360 (Highway 22, 1.5 miles west of Mill City)

title: Old Miner's Meadow Group Use Area
contentHtml:
Old Miner's Meadow is a two-acre, fenced BLM group site in an open meadow surrounded by forest along the Quartzville Creek Wild and Scenic River, upstream from Green Peter Reservoir. It holds up to 50 people, by reservation only.

It has picnic tables, campfire rings, a group fire ring and grill, horseshoe pits and vault toilets. Nearby are gold panning, fishing, kayaking, swimming and hiking.

note: $100 per night for up to 50 people ($2 per additional person). Bring your own drinking water and firewood. Unstaffed. Email: Fish_Bend@blm.gov
address: Quartzville Access Road, about 25 miles from US 20 (1 mile past Yellowbottom Recreation Site), east of Sweet Home, OR

title: Thompson's Mills State Heritage Site
contentHtml:
Thompson's Mills State Heritage Site is the last water-powered mill in Oregon, a survivor that chronicles 150 years of rural Oregon life. A water right that predates statehood still powers its milling machinery for demonstrations.

Guided tours show the turbines in action, and the main tour is ADA accessible. It is a stop on the Willamette Valley Scenic Bikeway and the Mid-Willamette Valley Food Trail.

note: Closed Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and New Year's Day.

title: Big Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Big Lake Campground has 49 tent and RV sites on the shore of Big Lake at the top of Santiam Pass, among alpine fir, hemlock and lodgepole pine, with views of Mount Washington. It is busiest in summer.

It has vault toilets, drinking water, picnic tables and a boat ramp. Visitors fish, boat, swim and waterski, and the Patjens Lakes Trail leads into the Mount Washington Wilderness. The Santiam Pass OHV area is next door.
excerpt: Big Lake Campground has 49 tent and RV sites on the shore of Big Lake at the top of Santiam Pass, among alpine fir, hemlock and lodgepole pine, with views of Mo
note: Closed for the 2026 season; reopening summer 2027. $28 per night; additional vehicle $10; day use $10. Reserve at recreation.gov (some sites first come, first served). Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals. 14-day stay limit. Chainsaws prohibited.

title: Big Lake West Campground
contentHtml:
Big Lake West is a small, tent-only lakeside campground of 11 sites just west of Big Lake Campground at the top of Santiam Pass, framed by Mount Washington and surrounded by alpine fir, hemlock and lodgepole pine.

Each site has a picnic table and fire ring, with vault toilets, drinking water, a boat ramp and a swimming area. Ice and firewood are sold. Visitors boat, swim, waterski, fish and hike the Patjens Lakes Trail into the Mount Washington Wilderness.
excerpt: Big Lake West is a small, tent-only lakeside campground of 11 sites just west of Big Lake Campground at the top of Santiam Pass, framed by Mount Washington and
note: Fees per recreation.gov (the Forest Service page lists two schedules: single sites $28 or $55 per night). More than half the sites reservable at recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777. Dogs leashed at all times. 14- day stay limit. Chainsaws prohibited.
address: West shore of Big Lake, Big Lake Road (FS Road 2690) off Highway 126 at Santiam Pass, OR (McKenzie River Ranger Station: 57600 McKenzie Highway, McKenzie Bridge, OR 97413)

title: Big Meadows Horse Camp
contentHtml:
Big Meadows Horse Camp is an equestrian campground near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness with 9 sites, each with corrals or highlines, for trailers up to 36 feet. It has vault toilets, drinking water, picnic tables and fire rings.

Riders and hikers set out on the Duffy Lake Trail #3427, Big Meadows Loop Trail #3456 and Big Meadows Tie Trail #3434, which loop for several miles through the surrounding forest. It is run by Linn County Parks & Recreation under agreement with the Forest Service.
excerpt: Big Meadows Horse Camp is an equestrian campground near the Mount Jefferson Wilderness with 9 sites, each with corrals or highlines, for trailers up to 36 feet.
note: $25 per night; additional vehicle $9. 6 sites reservable at recreation.gov, 3 first come, first served. Check-in 2 p.m., check-out 1 p.m. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). 14-day stay limit. Chainsaws prohibited. Forest roads are not maintained for snow or ice.

title: Cold Water Cove Campground
contentHtml:
Cold Water Cove Campground sits at the south end of Clear Lake among maple, alder and Douglas fir, with views of the turquoise lake, 3,000-year-old lava fields and, on clear days, the Three Sisters and Mount Washington. It has 34 sites (two accessible), each with a picnic table and fire ring, plus vault toilets and drinking water.

Visitors fish, paddle (non-motorized boats only), swim and hike the Clear Lake Loop Trail and McKenzie River National Recreation Trail, near Sahalie and Koosah falls. The resort next door has a general store and restaurant.
excerpt: Cold Water Cove Campground sits at the south end of Clear Lake among maple, alder and Douglas fir, with views of the turquoise lake, 3,000-year-old lava fields
note: Closed for the 2026 season; reopening summer 2027. $25 per night; additional vehicle $10; day use $10 or Northwest Forest Pass. Reserve at recreation.gov. No hookups. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals. 14-day stay limit. Chainsaws prohibited.
address: Forest Road 770, off Highway 126 at the south end of Clear Lake (18 miles east of McKenzie Bridge), OR (McKenzie River Ranger Station: 57600 McKenzie Highway, McKenzie Bridge, OR 97413)

title: Cove Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Cove Creek is the largest National Forest campground on Detroit Lake, with 63 single and double sites in wooded and open settings at about 1,600 feet, plus an accessible group site for up to 70 people.

It has drinking water, restrooms, coin-operated showers and a boat launch and dock next door. Visitors boat, waterski, swim and fish for rainbow trout, kokanee and catfish, and the Stahlman Point Trail starts near the entrance road.

title: Fernview Group Site
contentHtml:
Fernview is a former campground converted to a group site, with 11 sites for up to 75 people on a bench above the South Santiam River at 1,360 feet. It has a hand-pump for drinking water, a vault toilet and picnic tables.

The Rooster Rock Trail (across the highway) and the Trout Creek Trail lead into the Menagerie Wilderness, the Santiam Wagon Road is about 10 minutes away, and Iron Mountain, about 10 miles east, has more than 300 wildflower species, best in early July. It is run by Linn County Parks & Recreation (541-967-3917).

title: Hoover Campground
contentHtml:
Hoover Campground sits on the shore of Detroit Lake at about 1,600 feet, with a fire ring and picnic table at each site, flush toilets, drinking water and a neighboring group site.

A boat ramp and a day-use area with about 1,000 feet of shoreline are next door. Visitors fish for catfish, rainbow trout and kokanee, boat, waterski and swim, and hike the Stahlman Point Trail or the short, accessible Hoover Nature Trail with its viewing and fishing platform.

note: Single $28, double $56 per night; additional vehicle $9; day use $9. Reserve at recreation.gov. Firewood sold on site. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals. 14-day stay limit. Chainsaws prohibited.

title: House Rock Campground
imageAlt: Bridge from the campground to House Rock Falls

banner.alt: Bridge from the campground to House Rock Falls

contentHtml:
House Rock Campground lies in an old-growth grove where Sheep Creek meets the South Santiam River, across the Sheep Creek bridge. Many of its 17 sites have river frontage with shallow swimming areas, and each has a picnic table, fire ring and grill.

The House Rock Trail starts at the day-use area and follows part of the historic Santiam Wagon Road. Anglers fish for native cutthroat trout. It is run by Linn County Parks & Recreation (541-967-3917).

title: Ice Cap Campground
contentHtml:
Ice Cap Campground sits in Douglas fir, cedar and hemlock on a bluff above the McKenzie River and Carmen Reservoir, with Ice Cap Creek along its eastern edge. It has 22 sites, including 9 walk-in tent sites, each with a fire ring and picnic table.

The McKenzie River National Recreation Trail and the Waterfalls Loop Trail to Koosah and Sahalie falls are close by, for hiking, mountain biking, fishing and swimming.

title: Longbow Organization Camp
contentHtml:
Longbow Organization Camp was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s on 10 acres along the South Santiam River. It has six sleeping shelters for 48 people, a covered cooking area with a fireplace, an amphitheater for 75, vault toilets and drinking water.

Groups fish, wade and swim in the river and hike the historic Santiam Wagon Road, once used to drive livestock east across the Cascades. It is run by Linn County Parks & Recreation (541-967-3917).

title: Lost Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Lost Lake Campground sits on the west shore of shallow Lost Lake near the summit of Santiam Pass, with vault toilets and picnic tables. The lake level drops in summer, when willows crowd the marshy shallows.

It is popular in fishing and hunting seasons, and the Santiam Pass motorized recreation area, Sand Mountain Lookout, Mount Washington Wilderness and Pacific Crest Trail are nearby.

Trailers not recommended. Use caution where the lake drains; the ground may be unstable. Quiet hours 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). 14-day stay limit. Chainsaws prohibited.

title: Lost Prairie Group Site
contentHtml:
Lost Prairie is a former campground converted to a group site for up to 75 people, at about 3,600 feet along the Over the Rivers and Through the Woods Scenic Byway. It has 10 campsites with picnic tables and fire pits, paved parking for up to 6 RVs, vault toilets and a hand-pump well.

The Santiam Wagon Road Trail starts from the campground, and the meadow by Hackleman Creek is where a lost scouting party once climbed a tall tree to spot Sand Mountain. The McKenzie River National Recreation Trail and Clear Lake are about 15 minutes away. It is run by Linn County Parks & Recreation (541-967-3917).

note: Closed for the 2026 season; reopening spring 2027. Group site $225 per night; day use free. Reservation only at recreation.gov. Check-in 2 p.m., check-out noon. Gated parking. No firearms or fireworks. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less).

title: Marion Forks Campground
contentHtml:
Marion Forks Campground sits behind the Marion Forks Fish Hatchery on Marion Creek, with 15 single and double sites (one pull-through), each with a picnic table, and vault toilets.

A paved loop of about a quarter mile follows Marion Creek past the picnic area and the hatchery, with signs about spring Chinook salmon and local history. Visitors fish the creek and picnic in the day-use area.

address: Highway 22, 16 miles southeast of Detroit at Marion Forks (turn at the Marion Forks Fish Hatchery sign), OR (Detroit Ranger Station: 44125 North Santiam Highway SE, Detroit, OR 97342)

title: Olallie Campground
contentHtml:
Olallie Campground has 16 sites where Olallie Creek meets the McKenzie River: the lower loop overlooks the river and creek, and the upper loop is more wooded. It has picnic tables, vault toilets, drinking water and a camp host.

Visitors fish, raft and swim in the river, near the McKenzie Pass area and the Mount Washington Wilderness.

title: Riverside at Detroit Campground
contentHtml:
Riverside at Detroit has 32 sites on two loops along the North Santiam River: the upriver loop has more secluded sites on a bluff over the river, and the downriver loop is more open with partial shade. Every site has a picnic table and fire ring, with drinking water spigots and vault toilets, among cedar, Douglas fir, hemlock, rhododendron and ferns.

Visitors fish for rainbow trout, hike the Minto Mountain Trail and the Coffin Mountain area, and visit the Marion Forks Fish Hatchery about 2.3 miles away. It is run by Linn County Parks & Recreation under agreement with the Forest Service.

title: Southshore Campground
contentHtml:
Southshore Campground lies on Detroit Lake southwest of Piety Knob Island, a bit away from the busiest parts of the lake, with 25 single and 5 double sites, shaded and open. It has vault toilets, drinking water and a picnic table at every site.

A boat ramp, dock and day-use area with about 1,000 feet of shoreline are next door. Visitors fish for rainbow trout, kokanee and catfish, swim, boat, waterski and hike on the 9-mile-long, 3,500-acre lake.

title: Trail Bridge Campground
contentHtml:
Trail Bridge Campground sits on the shore of Trail Bridge Reservoir, with sites under big old-growth Douglas fir or in an open grassy meadow: 29 tent sites, 12 RV pull-through sites and a group site. It has vault and flush toilets, drinking water, a boat ramp and a day-use area with a pavilion and interpretive area.

Visitors fish, boat (10 mph limit) and hike onto the McKenzie River National Recreation Trail, near Ice Cap and Olallie campgrounds and the Mount Washington Wilderness.

note: Tent $25, RV pull-through $30, group $225 per night; day use/boat launch $10 or pass. Reservable at recreation.gov; fully reservable after May 15 (some sites first come, first served). Trailers up to 45 feet. Quiet hours 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). No horses or pack animals. 14-day stay limit.

title: Trout Creek Campground
imageAlt: South Santiam River at Trout Creek Campground

banner.alt: South Santiam River at Trout Creek Campground

contentHtml:
Trout Creek Campground was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s on the South Santiam River, with 24 sites, many riverside, shaded by Douglas-fir and hemlock. It has a day-use shelter with a fireplace, vault toilets and drinking water.

Visitors wade and fish in the river and hike the 2.8-mile Trout Creek Trail into the Menagerie Wilderness, the short Walton Ranch Interpretive Trail, or the Rooster Rock Trail across the road to a popular 5.4 climbing pinnacle. It is run by Linn County Parks & Recreation (541-967-3917).

title: Deer Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Deer Creek Falls drops about 92 feet over a volcanic cliff in an impressive canyon: the water free-falls from a small lip, plunges over an undercut cliff, then veils down a rounded outcrop in a rough V into the pool. Big boulders fill the grotto below, and tall trees keep it shaded much of the day.

The creek drains about 13 square miles and should flow year-round, strongest in winter and spring and down to a small flow by late September.

note: No developed access; reaching it means off-trail scrambling in steep, dangerous terrain and is not recommended. High winter and spring flows may require deep wading.

title: Koosah Falls
contentHtml:
Koosah Falls is the middle of three major waterfalls on the McKenzie River near Clear Lake. The river drops 74 feet over a broad, undercut basalt shelf into a large pool, with springs seeping from the cliff around it. In spring and early summer it can form a solid wall of water about 75 feet wide; by late summer it splits into two parallel streams.

Koosah is a Chinook Jargon word meaning 'sky,' and the falls were once called Middle Falls. Viewpoints are a short walk from the parking area near the restrooms, and the Waterfalls Loop Trail links it with Sahalie Falls.

imageAlt: Lower Soda Falls in early November

banner.alt: Lower Soda Falls in early November

contentHtml:
Lower Soda Falls, signed in the park as Soda Creek Falls, drops 134 feet in three tiers down a narrow recess in a large basalt cliff in Cascadia State Park. The top tier meets the lower two at a right angle and is hard to see from below.

An easy trail of about three-quarters of a mile leads from the day-use area, where the road to the east picnic area crosses Soda Creek, to the base of the falls.

title: Marion Falls
imageAlt: The upper two tiers of Marion Falls from the main viewpoint

banner.alt: The upper two tiers of Marion Falls from the main viewpoint

gallery.alt: The upper tier of Marion Falls
The lowermost tier of Marion Falls

contentHtml:
Marion Falls is one of the largest and most impressive waterfalls in the central Oregon Cascades, dropping about 250 feet in three tiers on Marion Creek half a mile below Marion Lake: a narrow 72-foot plunge into a pool, a curtain up to about 85 feet wide falling 75 feet, and a less visible lower cascade.

Snowmelt and springs from the slopes of Three Fingered Jack keep it flowing year-round. From the Marion Lake Trailhead, an easy to moderate trail of about 1.6 miles passes Lake Ann; take the right fork at an unsigned junction for about a quarter mile to the top of the falls, then a moderately steep path to viewpoints.

note: Reaching the base of the falls is dangerous and not recommended.
