title: Pinnacle Peak Falls
imageAlt: Pinnacle Peak Falls in early November

banner.alt: Pinnacle Peak Falls in early November

contentHtml:
Pinnacle Peak Falls is a free-falling plunge of about 145 feet on a seasonal tributary of Lost Creek, near the divide between the North and Middle Santiam rivers. At peak flow it is a narrow plume of spray landing in an alcove beside the road, with smaller falls forming a 'weeping wall' along the canyon.

Take Straight Creek Road just over 6 miles from Highway 22 to a five-way junction, then gravel Lost Creek Road just under 3 miles to the Lost Creek bridge. The falls are on the cliff just west of the bridge; a scramble of about 100 feet up the draw gives a clear view.

note: Seasonal: thins by late spring and likely dries up in summer.

title: Puzzle Creek Falls
contentHtml: Puzzle Creek Falls is a 54-foot curtain about 45 feet wide that spills over a slightly undercut volcanic cliff near Marion Forks. Its spray keeps the canyon below coated in thick moss, and several spring-fed tributaries join the creek just downstream.

title: Royal Terrace Falls
imageAlt: Royal Terrace Falls in early November

banner.alt: Royal Terrace Falls in early November

contentHtml:
Royal Terrace Falls is a 119-foot, stair-step, fountain-like waterfall where Fall Creek drops over the valley wall in McDowell Creek Falls County Park, and the best of the park's four waterfalls.

From the main parking lot, the trail crosses McDowell Creek beside Lower McDowell Creek Falls and runs about a quarter mile to a footbridge below the falls. A spur trail climbs the right side for close views of the upper tier.

title: Sahalie Falls
imageAlt: Sahalie Falls during moderately high flow

banner.alt: Sahalie Falls during moderately high flow

contentHtml:
Sahalie Falls is the uppermost of the McKenzie River's three major falls, a 73-foot plunge over an overhanging basalt ledge into a large basin. Its mist is whipped into a strong wind aimed at the viewpoints just downstream, and at higher flows it splits into two segments.

Sahalie is a Chinook Jargon word meaning 'high'; it was once called Upper Falls. The viewpoint is about 200 feet along a paved trail from the parking area, and the falls appeared in the Disney film Homeward Bound.

title: Soda Fork Falls
contentHtml: Soda Fork Falls drops about 225 feet on the Soda Fork of the South Santiam River in the Willamette National Forest.

title: Tamolitch Falls
imageAlt: Tamolitch Falls flowing with the full force of the McKenzie River

banner.alt: Tamolitch Falls flowing with the full force of the McKenzie River

gallery.alt: A wider view of Tamolitch Falls and the blue pool at its base

contentHtml:
Tamolitch Falls is a 49-foot plunge on the McKenzie River above Tamolitch Pool, better known as Blue Pool. Usually the falls are dry: the river flows underground through porous lava from the Belknap Crater flow and re-emerges as a full-size river from a spring at the base, filling the bright blue pool.

'Tamolitch' means 'bucket' in Chinook, for the pool's shape. From the Blue Pool parking area, hike the McKenzie River Trail upstream about 2 miles, moderately easy but rocky, to viewpoints over the pool.

note: The falls flow only when the river exceeds the capacity of the upstream Carmen Reservoir diversion, which is rare.

title: Clear Lake
contentHtml:
Clear Lake is a spring-fed mountain lake at the headwaters of the McKenzie River, formed when volcanic activity blocked the ancestral river. Its very cold, exceptionally clear water preserves ancient submerged trees that paddlers can see below, depending on light and conditions.

Kayaks, canoes and stand-up paddleboards launch from Clear Lake Resort, which has food, lodging and boating facilities, or from Coldwater Cove, with paved parking and a paved boat slide for non-motorized craft.

note: Oregon Waterway Access Permit required for every paddlecraft (children 13 and under exempt). Life jacket for each person and a sound-producing device; children 12 and under must wear a life jacket. Very cold water. Summer weekends are busy; start early for quiet water. The Willamette River Water Trail follows 187 miles of the mainstem Willamette River, from the Eugene and Springfield area north to Portland. It passes forests, meadows, parks, farms and cities, and it is open to canoes, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, rafts and drift boats.

Designated Water Trail campsites along the river let paddlers plan multi-day trips.

title: Mount Jefferson
imageAlt: Mt. Jefferson from the high desert near Haystack Reservoir

banner.alt: Mt. Jefferson from the high desert near Haystack Reservoir

contentHtml:
At 10,497 feet, Mount Jefferson is the second-highest mountain in Oregon after Mount Hood. It is a heavily glaciated stratovolcano of the Cascade Volcanic Arc, one of the most eroded in the state, whose last eruptive activity was about a thousand years ago.

Known as Seekseekqua to Native peoples, it was named for President Thomas Jefferson after Lewis and Clark saw it from the mouth of the Willamette River in 1806. It rises within the 111,177-acre Mount Jefferson Wilderness, which has more than 150 lakes and 190 miles of trails, including 40 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail; the eastern side lies within the Warm Springs Indian Reservation, so public access is limited to the western flanks.

note: The summit is a technical climb recommended only for experienced climbers; the first ascent was in 1888 via the south ridge.

title: Oregon Timber Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Timber Trail is a 670-mile mountain bike and bikepacking route from the California border near Lakeview north to Hood River on the Columbia, managed by the nonprofit Oregon Timber Trail Alliance. It is split into four tiers: Fremont, Willamette, Deschutes and Hood.

Riders can take on the whole route or ride a shorter piece.

title: Pacific Crest Trail
contentHtml:
The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail runs 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada through California, Oregon and Washington, managed by the Forest Service with the Pacific Crest Trail Association. Its roughly 455-mile Oregon section is the shortest and easiest on the trail, from near Siskiyou Summit to the Bridge of the Gods over the Columbia River.

In Linn County the trail runs along the Cascade crest through the Mount Jefferson Wilderness, which holds 40 miles of the PCT, and the Mount Washington Wilderness, which it crosses for 16.6 miles.

title: Blue Wolf
imageAlt: Bridge on the McKenzie River Trail at Clear Lake

banner.alt: Bridge on the McKenzie River Trail at Clear Lake

contentHtml:
Blue Wolf is a 50-mile, point-to-point gravel ride (60% gravel, 5% single-track, 35% paved) with about 3,700 feet of climbing and a net drop of about 5,400 feet. It opens on single-track along Clear Lake through old- growth forest, climbs forest roads for roughly 8 miles, then finishes flat on pavement along Blue River Lake and the McKenzie River.

Along the way are mountain views, two lakes, a powerful river, a hidden waterfall, ancient trees, seasonal bear grass and wild rhododendrons, and Wolf Rock, Oregon's largest monolith. It is an easier alternative to the Tidbits route.

note: Moderate; remote; tires 45 mm or wider. Shuttle recommended: Horse Creek Lodge offers one (with an end-of-ride shower), or finish at the Lookout Boat Launch on Blue River Lake. Water and food at Clear Lake Lodge (about mile 2.4); no facilities at the trailhead. The GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; auto-generated directions are often inaccurate.

title: Brickhouse

gallery.alt: North Santiam River at the start

contentHtml:
Brickhouse is a 33-mile gravel lollipop (half gravel, half paved) with about 4,300 feet of climbing, part of the Detroit-area Motown series for riders who like steep climbs. It opens with a climb of about 1,300 feet in 4 miles through ponderosa pine, ferns and rhododendrons, rolls for 6 miles with views north, then drops about 2,400 feet in 8 miles before a final 2,000-foot climb and a paved return.

Highlights include basalt cliffs and the Needles basalt towers, views of Mount Hood and Mount Jefferson, the seasonal Pinnacle Peak Falls, the North Santiam River and the area of the 2021 Bruler Fire.

title: Bunchgrass
contentHtml:
Bunchgrass is a 38-mile gravel lollipop (about 70% gravel, 5% single-track, 25% paved) with about 4,100 feet of climbing around Bunchgrass Mountain, which is covered in beargrass. Quiet roads, big old trees and ridgeline views take in the Three Sisters, Mount Washington, Three Fingered Jack and Mount Jefferson.

It starts on the historic Santiam Wagon Road and passes The Husband viewpoint, Deer Creek's salmon and trout habitat restoration, about 2.5 miles of the McKenzie River Trail, Trail Bridge Reservoir (a good midway break) and Wolf Rock, a volcanic plug about 900 feet tall and Oregon's largest monolith.

title: McKenzie Pass Scenic Bikeway

gallery.alt: Reaching the top of the pass

contentHtml:
The McKenzie Pass Scenic Bikeway is an epic one-way road ride of about 35 miles from Sisters west over McKenzie Pass on Highway 242, which follows an 1860s wagon route. After an easy first 8 miles, a climb of about 5 miles starts at McGregor's Curve and passes Windy Point, with views of Mt. Washington, and lava- rock walls to the summit.

At the top, a lava 'moonscape' surrounds the Dee Wright Observatory, whose windows frame 360-degree views. The 25-mile descent drops about 4,000 feet through switchbacks into the wetter McKenzie River forests to Highway 126.
excerpt: The McKenzie Pass Scenic Bikeway is an epic one-way road ride of about 35 miles from Sisters west over McKenzie Pass on Highway 242, which follows an 1860s wago
note: Rated extreme; requires top fitness. Restrooms and water at Village Green Park, the summit and the McKenzie General Store. Highway 242 closes seasonally: check TripCheck.com or ODOT District 10 in Bend (541-388-6169) for conditions. Published lengths range from 35 to 38 miles.
address: Start: Village Green Park, Sisters, OR

title: Motown
contentHtml:
Motown is a 40-mile lollipop (40% gravel, 60% paved) with about 3,900 feet of climbing. The first seven miles follow Detroit Lake on pavement, then gravel leads to the main climb of about 2,600 feet, with steep, soft sections, past basalt cliffs to a ridge with views of Mount Jefferson and Mount Hood, before a loose descent back to the lake.

Points of interest include Detroit Lake (created by Detroit Dam in 1953), Coffin Mountain, welded volcanic tuff at Blowout Creek, an aspen grove, the Needles basalt towers and a red alder grove. Detroit, damaged by the 2020 fires, is still rebuilding, and riders are encouraged to eat and shop locally.
excerpt: Motown is a 40-mile lollipop (40% gravel, 60% paved) with about 3,900 feet of climbing. The first seven miles follow Detroit Lake on pavement, then gravel leads
note: Moderate; remote; tires 45 mm or wider. No services at the start; Hoover Campground nearby has pit toilets, water and parking. No food or water on the route. Not recommended in bad weather. The GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; auto-generated directions are often inaccurate.
address: Start: dirt pullout kiosk on Blowout Road, about 0.25 miles before Hoover Campground, near Detroit, OR

title: The Pyramids
contentHtml:
The Pyramids is a 25-mile gravel lollipop (70% gravel, 10% single-track, 20% paved) with about 2,600 feet of climbing in extremely remote country. It rolls through old-growth forest with ferns and big ponderosa pines, logged openings full of wildflowers, technical forest single-track, a decommissioned logging road and the Santiam Wagon Road back to Fish Lake.

There are no long climbs, but short pitches of 10 to 15% and walking sections on the single-track make it hard; the middle third, from about mile 9 to mile 15, is the toughest. Views take in Three Fingered Jack, Mount Washington and the Three Sisters.
excerpt: The Pyramids is a 25-mile gravel lollipop (70% gravel, 10% single-track, 20% paved) with about 2,600 feet of climbing in extremely remote country. It rolls thro
note: Demanding; navigation needs attention; tires 45 mm or wider. No food or water on the route. Pit toilets at both starts. Many unmarked roads: carry a backup navigation device. Tree fall possible around miles 12 to 14. Shorter options: NF 572 at about mile 11.7 skips most single-track; starting at Lava Lake Sno-Park cuts 3 miles. The GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; auto-generated directions are often inaccurate.
address: Start: Fish Lake Day Use Area, north side of Highway 126 (alternate: Lava Lake Sno-Park, Highway 20), OR

title: Tidbits
imageAlt: Bridge on the McKenzie River Trail at Clear Lake

banner.alt: Bridge on the McKenzie River Trail at Clear Lake

contentHtml:
Tidbits is a beautiful but demanding 57-mile point-to-point ride (70% gravel, 5% single-track, 25% paved) with about 4,600 feet of climbing and 6,400 feet of descent. It starts on the McKenzie River Trail through old- growth Douglas fir, hemlock and cedar past lava-formed Clear Lake, with its submerged trees, then climbs to a high point near mile 18.5 and traverses ridges with short, steep climbs.

A 2,700-foot descent over about 9 miles passes a hidden waterfall on Tidbits Creek, and the flat finish runs along Blue River Lake and the McKenzie River past the HJ Andrews Experimental Forest, the Holiday Farm Fire burn area and the Belknap Covered Bridge. Views include the Three Sisters and Three Fingered Jack, with bear grass and rhododendrons in bloom.

note: Demanding; remote with limited cell reception; tires 40 mm or wider (50 mm preferred for the long descent). Water and food only at Clear Lake Lodge (about mile 2.4). Horse Creek Lodge & Outfitters runs the shuttle (reserve ahead) and has an outdoor shower. The GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; auto-generated directions are often inaccurate.
address: Start: McKenzie River Trail near Clear Lake (shuttle from Horse Creek Lodge); finish at Horse Creek Lodge or the Lookout Boat Launch on Blue River Lake, OR

title: Tom Rock
contentHtml:
Tom Rock is a 31-mile gravel lollipop (80% gravel, 20% paved) with about 3,700 feet of climbing through the Santiam State Forest. The first 15.5 miles are mostly gravel climbing at 7 to 9%, easing to 4 to 6%, with early ridge viewpoints over the 2020 Labor Day fire damage.

Tom Rock, at about mile 15.4, is a 360-degree viewpoint with views of the Three Sisters, Mount Washington and Three Fingered Jack. The long descent includes a short, rugged, technical stretch, then crosses Weyerhaeuser land to a steep final pitch and a paved cooldown.

Avoid wet conditions. Wear bright colors in fall (hunting season). An alternate version skips the technical descent (adds 3.2 miles). The GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; auto-generated directions are often inaccurate.

title: Tombstone Pass
contentHtml:
Tombstone Pass is a 28-mile gravel loop (about 75% gravel, 10% single-track, 15% paved) with about 2,400 feet of climbing. It climbs steep pavement and gravel to Tombstone Pass, named for an 1871 tragedy on the Santiam Wagon Road, then follows the old wagon road through old-growth forest past historic Fish Lake.

It finishes around the west side of Clear Lake on part of the McKenzie River Trail and returns to Clear Lake Resort, whose lakeside restaurant is a good end to the ride. The first half is mostly uphill but not technical; the second half is mostly downhill and more technical.

Parking pass required at Clear Lake (Northwest Forest Pass, America the Beautiful or day pass sold on site); Fish Lake parking is free with pit toilets. Tree fall is common. Expect hikers around Clear Lake on busy weekends. The GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; auto-generated directions are often inaccurate.

title: Willamette Valley Scenic Bikeway

gallery.alt: On the Willamette Valley Scenic Bikeway

contentHtml:
The Willamette Valley Scenic Bikeway, the first official Scenic Bikeway in the United States, runs 135 paved miles one way along the Willamette River between the Coast Range and the Cascades. In Linn County it passes Albany, Thompson's Mills and Brownsville.

The moderate route passes hop fields, vineyards and small towns, Champoeg State Heritage Area, Keizer and the Capitol in Salem, Ankeny National Wildlife Refuge and Thompson's Mills State Heritage Site, with side trips to the Wheatland and Buena Vista ferries. Its high point is 740 feet, after Brownsville.
excerpt: The Willamette Valley Scenic Bikeway, the first official Scenic Bikeway in the United States, runs 135 paved miles one way along the Willamette River between th
note: Rideable year-round; bring rain gear in winter. April through November brings sunshine, flowers and farmers markets.
address: Armitage County Park, Coburg (south end) to Champoeg State Heritage Area (north end), OR

title: McKenzie River
contentHtml:
The McKenzie River rises at Clear Lake in the central Oregon Cascades and flows south and west through the Willamette National Forest. On October 28, 1988, 12.7 miles from Clear Creek to Scott Creek were designated a recreational Wild and Scenic River, not including the Carmen and Trail Bridge reservoir dams.

Lava flows shaped its pools, waterfalls and whitewater: lava from Belknap Crater dammed the river to create Sahalie and Koosah falls. Known as the "Blue McKenzie" for its clear, cold water, it has wild rainbow, bull and cutthroat trout and spring chinook, challenging whitewater, and the 26-mile McKenzie River National Recreation Trail.

note: Managed by the Willamette National Forest. The designated reach crosses Linn and Lane counties.
address: Willamette National Forest, along OR 126 between Clear Lake and Trail Bridge, OR
photoCredit: National Wild and Scenic Rivers System

title: Quartzville Creek

gallery.alt: Trail to Quartzville Creek at Yellowbottom Recreation Site

contentHtml:
Quartzville Creek begins in the Oregon Cascades and flows into Green Peter Reservoir near Sweet Home. Its 12 miles from the Willamette National Forest boundary to the reservoir were designated a recreational Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988.

It is named for a gemstone mined in the area and a ghost town that was the center of two brief gold rushes (1863 to 1892). Visitors pan for gold, fish for small stream trout, camp and picnic along the Quartzville Back Country Byway, and skilled kayakers run Class IV whitewater at high flows, among old-growth forest, rocky outcrops and clear, cascading water.

note: Managed by the Bureau of Land Management, Northwest Oregon District (blm_or_no_mail@blm.gov). Camping at Yellowbottom Recreation Site is closed indefinitely because of hazardous trees; day use remains open.
address: Quartzville Road Back Country Byway, from the Willamette National Forest boundary to Green Peter Reservoir, near Sweet Home, OR

title: Marys Peak to Pacific Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Alsea Falls, a stop on the byway

contentHtml:
The Marys Peak to Pacific Scenic Byway is a 72-mile Oregon State Scenic Byway from the farmland near Tangent, through Corvallis and Philomath, over the Coast Range on OR-34 and down the Alsea River valley to Waldport on the coast. Allow 3 to 5 hours.

Stops include William L. Finley National Wildlife Refuge, the Philomath Museum in its 1867 college building, Marys Peak (4,097 ft), Alsea Falls, the Hayden Covered Bridge, the Oregon Hatchery Research Center, the Alsea Bay estuary and Seal Rock State Recreation Site.

note: 72 miles · 3 to 5 hours
address: Tangent (near I-5) to Waldport (US-101), via Corvallis, Philomath and OR-34
photoCredit: Travel Oregon, Oregon.com, Benton County Historical Society

title: McKenzie Pass-Santiam Pass Scenic Byway
imageAlt: Lava flow and peaks from Dee Wright Observatory

banner.alt: Lava flow and peaks from Dee Wright Observatory

contentHtml:
The McKenzie Pass-Santiam Pass Scenic Byway is an 82-mile loop from Sisters over two Cascade passes: Santiam Pass (4,817 feet), where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses, and McKenzie Pass (5,335 feet), crowned by the lava-rock Dee Wright Observatory with views over an ancient lava flow to 11 peaks.

Along the way are Suttle Lake, Scott Lake, Clear Lake Resort, the wild and scenic McKenzie River and historic stretches of the Santiam Wagon Road. Back in Sisters, browse downtown boutiques and galleries.
excerpt: The McKenzie Pass-Santiam Pass Scenic Byway is an 82-mile loop from Sisters over two Cascade passes: Santiam Pass (4,817 feet), where the Pacific Crest Trail cr
note: The McKenzie Pass section (OR 242) is closed to cars part of the year; check TripCheck.com before you go.
address: Loop from Sisters, OR, via US 20/OR 126 and OR 242

title: Over the Rivers and Through the Woods Scenic Byway
contentHtml:
The Over the Rivers and Through the Woods Scenic Byway is a 66-mile drive of 2 to 3 hours that climbs through five ecosystems from the Willamette Valley to the West Cascades. It follows OR 228 through Brownsville (Oregon's third-oldest town, founded in 1846, and the setting of Stand by Me), Crawfordsville and Holley, then US 20 through Sweet Home and Cascadia, generally tracing the historic Santiam Wagon Road.

Stops include the Linn County Historical Museum, the 1932 Crawfordsville Covered Bridge, Foster and Green Peter reservoirs, Cascadia's swimming holes and Soda Creek Falls trail, the accessible Walton Ranch elk- viewing trail, the Menagerie Wilderness, the Hackleman Old Growth Trail and Tombstone Pass, the byway's high point at 4,236 feet. It ends where the West Cascades and McKenzie Pass-Santiam Pass byways begin.
excerpt: The Over the Rivers and Through the Woods Scenic Byway is a 66-mile drive of 2 to 3 hours that climbs through five ecosystems from the Willamette Valley to the
note: Open year-round. In winter, tundra swans and bald eagles gather in the fields near Brownsville, and elk often graze the meadows at Walton Ranch. Stand by Me Day is celebrated in Brownsville each July.
address: Start: I-5 exit 216 on OR 228; ends at the US 20 / OR 22 / OR 126 junction at Santiam Junction, OR
photoCredit: Dennis Frates / Alamy Stock (Travel Oregon); TripCheck

title: West Cascades Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Along the West Cascades Scenic Byway

contentHtml:
The West Cascades Scenic Byway is a 220-mile National Scenic Byway along the northern half of Oregon's Cascade Range, from Estacada, about 25 miles from Portland, south to Westfir near Oakridge.

From Estacada it follows the Clackamas River on OR-224 and Forest Road 46 to Detroit Lake, then the McKenzie River past Clear Lake and 100-foot Sahalie Falls, ending on the Aufderheide road (Forest Road 19) at the Office Covered Bridge, Oregon's longest at 180 feet.

Along the way are old-growth groves such as the Delta Old Growth Trail, three National Recreation Trails, Olallie Lakes and the PGE powerhouse at Estacada. The full drive takes 7 to 9 hours, or sections can be driven on their own.
excerpt: The West Cascades Scenic Byway is a 220-mile National Scenic Byway along the northern half of Oregon's Cascade Range, from Estacada, about 25 miles from Portlan
note: Forest Roads 19 and 46 are generally closed November 15 to April 30 because of snow.
address: Estacada (OR-224) to Westfir near Oakridge (OR-58), via Forest Road 46, Detroit, OR-22, OR-126 and Forest Road 19

title: Mid-Willamette Valley Food Trail

gallery.alt: Child biting an apple in an orchard (Allison Smith)
Brewery balcony along the trail (Allison Smith)
Lavender bundles at Lumos Wine Co. (Reed Lane Photography)

contentHtml:
The Mid-Willamette Valley Food Trail is a self-guided route through more than 50 farms, eateries, bakeries, farmers markets, wineries, breweries and distilleries in Albany, Corvallis, Philomath, Lebanon, Sweet Home, Brownsville, Monroe and Alsea.

It is arranged as four themed routes: Family Fun For All, A Taster's Tour, Makers and Innovators, and Flora and Fauna. Stops include Lumos Wine Co., Thompson's Mills State Heritage Site, the Alsea Trout Hatchery, Sky High Brewing and Midway Farms, a celiac-safe farm with a red-barn farm market.

A free Digital Passport offers deals and free tastings at selected stops.

note: Self-guided; no set mileage. Phone is the Albany Visitors Association.
address: Linn and Benton counties. Lead farm: Midway Farms, 6980 NW Hwy 20, Albany

title: South Willamette Valley Food Trail
imageAlt: Barrel-aged beer and charcuterie at Alesong Brewing & Blending

banner.alt: Barrel-aged beer and charcuterie at Alesong Brewing & Blending

gallery.alt: Mountain bikers at the Office Bridge in Westfir

contentHtml:
The South Willamette Valley Food Trail is a self-guided journey of 53 stops through Oregon's agricultural heartland: bakeries, restaurants, farms, growers markets, breweries, wineries and food-focused lodges.

It centers on Eugene and Springfield and reaches Veneta, Junction City, Coburg, Creswell, Cottage Grove, the McKenzie River and Oakridge, with stops across the county line in Monroe and Harrisburg.

Highlights include King Estate Winery, North America's largest Demeter-certified Biodynamic vineyard, Alesong Brewing & Blending, the Lane County Farmers Market and seasonal berry, lavender, apple and truffle harvests.

note: 53 stops; self-guided, no set mileage
address: Eugene, Springfield and surrounding towns. Mapped at King Estate Winery, 80854 Territorial Hwy, Eugene

title: Quartzville Road Back Country Byway

gallery.alt: Loop road at Yellowbottom Recreation Site

contentHtml:
The Quartzville Road Back Country Byway is a 50-mile BLM Back Country Byway of paved and gravel road that follows the Quartzville Creek Wild and Scenic River past Green Peter Reservoir and through the Willamette National Forest, a drive of 1 to 2 hours.

It runs through old gold country, where recreational gold panning still goes on in the creek, past old-growth forest, rocky outcrops and blue-green reservoir views. Visitors fish, kayak, camp and pick huckleberries in summer, when wildflowers bloom; autumn brings red and gold foliage. Yellowbottom Recreation Site, midway, has a swimming hole and a one-mile trail linking to the Rhododendron Trail.
excerpt: The Quartzville Road Back Country Byway is a 50-mile BLM Back Country Byway of paved and gravel road that follows the Quartzville Creek Wild and Scenic River pa
note: Route: Quartzville Drive for about 25 miles, then Forest Road 11 for about 23.7 miles to OR 22. Yellowbottom camping is closed indefinitely because of hazardous trees; day use is open.
address: Start: US 20 at Quartzville Drive by Foster Lake; ends at OR 22 and Forest Road 11 (south of Marion Forks), OR

title: Crawfordsville Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1932, the Crawfordsville Covered Bridge is a 105-foot Howe truss span over the Calapooia River at the west end of Crawfordsville, with a narrow slit window on each side. Bypassed in 1963, it is now a pedestrian bridge in a Linn County Parks wayside and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Crawfordsville is named for settler Philemon Crawford. In 1976 the crew filming the TV movie The Flood painted the bridge, and volunteers and an Oregon Covered Bridge Program grant have since restored it after the 1996 flood. A small picnic area sits at the southwest corner of the bridge.
excerpt: Built in 1932, the Crawfordsville Covered Bridge is a 105-foot Howe truss span over the Calapooia River at the west end of Crawfordsville, with a narrow slit wi
note: Open year-round. Take Highway 228 east from I-5 exit 216 through Brownsville.
address: 38300 Courtney Creek Dr., Crawfordsville, OR 97336 (beside Highway 228)

title: Gilkey Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1939, the 120-foot Gilkey Covered Bridge is a Howe truss span carrying Goar Road over Thomas Creek at the site of Gilkey, a farm shipping point that grew up when the railroad arrived in 1880. Until 1960 a covered railroad bridge stood beside it; today little remains of the town except the bridge and a faded sign.

It still carries traffic, was repaired and reopened in 1998 after an overloaded vehicle damaged it, and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. In summer, swimmers use a rope tied to the bridge framework.

address: Goar Road over Thomas Creek, southwest of Scio, OR (3 miles west of Highway 226 on Gilkey Road, then 0.5 mile north on Goar Road)

title: Hannah Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1936, the 105-foot Hannah Covered Bridge is a Howe truss span over Thomas Creek, named for pioneer John Joseph Hannah, who arrived by wagon train in 1853 and built one of the area's first sawmills. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

The bridge is 1.5 miles from Jordan, and several TV commercials have been filmed here. In summer it is a popular swimming spot over a deep pool.

note: From Scio, follow Highway 226 about six miles to Camp Morrison Drive and turn south.
address: Camp Morrison Drive over Thomas Creek, off Highway 226 east of Scio (near Jordan), OR

title: Hoffman Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1936 by Lee Hoffman, the 90-foot Hoffman Covered Bridge is a Howe truss span over Crabtree Creek. Its Gothic-style windows set it apart from the usual open Linn County design, and its upper chord timbers still show hand-adze marks from a time when most bridge crews did not yet use power tools.

Crabtree and its creek are named for John Crabtree, who settled here in 1845. The bridge's portal, once rounded, was later squared to fit larger loads. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

address: Hungry Hill Drive over Crabtree Creek, about 1 mile northeast of Crabtree, OR

title: Larwood Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1939, the 105-foot Larwood Covered Bridge is a Howe truss span with partly exposed trusses, a white- washed interior and rounded portals, crossing Crabtree Creek where Roaring River joins it, a meeting of a river flowing into a creek once featured in Ripley's Believe It or Not.

The town of Larwood, founded by William Larwood in 1888, is gone, but a rebuilt water-powered mill and the bridge remain. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the adjacent Larwood Wayside Park is popular for picnicking, fishing and swimming.
excerpt: Built in 1939, the 105-foot Larwood Covered Bridge is a Howe truss span with partly exposed trusses, a white- washed interior and rounded portals, crossing Crab
note: From Highway 226 east of Crabtree, take Fish Hatchery Road about 6 miles.
address: Fish Hatchery Road over Crabtree Creek at Larwood Wayside Park, about 3 miles north of Lacomb, OR

title: Shimanek Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1966, the red, 130-foot Shimanek Covered Bridge is Linn County's longest and newest covered bridge, a fully enclosed Howe truss span with rounded portals, louvered windows and a white interior. Each compression joint has four truss rods instead of the usual three.

It is the fifth covered bridge at this crossing, which dates to at least 1891; earlier spans were lost to floods and the 1962 Columbus Day Storm. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
excerpt: Built in 1966, the red, 130-foot Shimanek Covered Bridge is Linn County's longest and newest covered bridge, a fully enclosed Howe truss span with rounded porta
address: Richardson Gap Road over Thomas Creek, off Highway 226 two miles east of Scio, OR

title: Short Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1945, the 105-foot Short Covered Bridge is a Howe truss span and the only remaining covered bridge over the South Santiam River. Linn County's easternmost covered bridge, it was first called the Whiskey Butte Bridge and later renamed for longtime resident Gordon Short.

It is one of the few covered bridges in the county with a wooden shingle roof and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Ducks, deer and other wildlife are often seen nearby, and in summer anglers fish from on and under the bridge.
excerpt: Built in 1945, the 105-foot Short Covered Bridge is a Howe truss span and the only remaining covered bridge over the South Santiam River. Linn County's easternm
address: High Deck Road over the South Santiam River, just west of Cascadia off US 20, OR

title: Weddle Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
Built in 1937, the 120-foot Weddle Covered Bridge is a typical open-sided Linn County Howe truss span that crossed Thomas Creek near Scio for about 50 years. Bypassed in 1980 and pulled apart for demolition in 1987, it was saved by protesting enthusiasts, whose campaign with state Senator Mae Yih led to the Oregon Covered Bridge Program.

It was the program's first project, rebuilt in 1989 over Ames Creek in Sweet Home's Sankey Park, where it now serves walkers and hosts weddings and community events.

note: In Sweet Home, turn south on 12th Avenue, east on Kalmia Street, then south on 14th Avenue for two blocks.
address: Sankey Park, 14th Avenue, Sweet Home, OR (over Ames Creek)

title: Big Springs
contentHtml: Big Springs Sno-Park has cross-country ski and snowshoe trails, from easy to more difficult, that wind through large old-growth trees; one route shares about a mile with snowmobiles. It has a large paved parking area and vault toilets.
excerpt: Big Springs Sno-Park has cross-country ski and snowshoe trails, from easy to more difficult, that wind through large old-growth trees; one route shares about a
note: An Oregon Sno-Park permit is required November 1 to April 30 (daily $4, 3-day $9, annual $25; sold at DMV offices, resorts and outdoor shops, and annual permits online at DMV2U.Oregon.gov). Roads may be plowed periodically but can stay difficult; check TripCheck.com. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). Day use only, sunrise to sunset. Watch for tree wells and stump holes. No drinking water.
address: Highway 22, 3 miles west of Santiam Junction (29 miles east of Detroit), Willamette National Forest, OR

title: Ikenick
contentHtml: Ikenick Sno-Park serves cross-country skiers, snowshoers and snowmobilers on a mix of roads and forest trails. Heading north brings views of Three Fingered Jack and Mount Washington; heading south, the route passes through second-growth and older forest.
excerpt: Ikenick Sno-Park serves cross-country skiers, snowshoers and snowmobilers on a mix of roads and forest trails. Heading north brings views of Three Fingered Jack
note: An Oregon Sno-Park permit is required November 1 to April 30 (daily $4, 3-day $9, annual $25; sold at DMV offices, resorts and outdoor shops, and annual permits online at DMV2U.Oregon.gov). Roads may be plowed periodically but can stay difficult; check TripCheck.com. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). At a lower elevation, so conditions depend on low-elevation snowfall. No restrooms or drinking water. Contact: Willamette National Forest Supervisor's Office.
address: Forest Road 2672 off Highway 126 near Clear Lake (19 miles northeast of McKenzie Bridge), Willamette National Forest, OR

title: Lava Lake
contentHtml: Lava Lake Sno-Park, at about 3,500 feet, is lightly used, with three mostly easy loop routes for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, some shared with snowmobile trails. One loop leads down to Lava Lake.
excerpt: Lava Lake Sno-Park, at about 3,500 feet, is lightly used, with three mostly easy loop routes for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, some shared with snowmobi
note: An Oregon Sno-Park permit is required November 1 to April 30 (daily $4, 3-day $9, annual $25; sold at DMV offices, resorts and outdoor shops, and annual permits online at DMV2U.Oregon.gov). Roads may be plowed periodically but can stay difficult; check TripCheck.com. Dogs must be leashed (6 feet or less). Day use only, sunrise to sunset. Vault toilets; no drinking water.
address: Lava Lake Road (FS Road 2067) off Highway 20, about 4 miles west of Santiam Junction (44 miles east of Sweet Home), OR

title: Little Nash
contentHtml: Little Nash Sno-Park serves snowmobilers and cross-country skiers. A snowmobile route links to Ray Benson Sno-Park via the Santiam Wagon Road and the Santiam Air Strip Trail, and a novice-friendly ski trail connects with the Potato Hill trails.

title: Maxwell Butte
contentHtml:
Maxwell Sno-Park, at 3,800 feet, has about 25 miles of cross-country ski and snowshoe trails, from easy to more difficult, some through old-growth forest and some with views of Maxwell Butte, Three Fingered Jack, Duffy Butte and Mount Jefferson.

Several trails reach the Mountain View Shelter, with views on clear days of Mount Washington, North Sister and Three Fingered Jack. The lot has restrooms and hitching posts.

title: Ray Benson
contentHtml:
Ray Benson Sno-Park is the hub of Santiam Pass winter trails, with separate blue-blazed ski and snowshoe trails and orange-blazed snowmobile trails that cross into the Deschutes National Forest to the Brandenburg Butte, Island Junction and North Blowout warming shelters.

It has two vault toilets, a warming hut, picnic tables and orientation maps, and Hoodoo Ski Area next door has food and a phone. After the snow melts it becomes the Santiam Pass OHV area.

title: Santiam Pass
contentHtml: Santiam Pass Sno-Park offers cross-country skiing, sledding and snow play, with access to the Pacific Crest Trail. It has one of only two tubing hills on the forest and the only recommended tubing and sledding hill in the Santiam Pass area, plus a restroom and a winter orientation sign.

contentHtml: Tombstone Sno-Park, at the Tombstone Pass/Cone Peak Trailhead, is a cross-country ski and snowshoe area with a large paved lot and vault toilets. Trails include the Tombstone Nature Trail, the Tombstone Prairie Trail and the Fish Lake and Hackleman and Sevenmile sections of the Santiam Wagon Road.

title: Hoodoo Ski Area
imageAlt: Deep snow on the summit of Hoodoo

banner.alt: Deep snow on the summit of Hoodoo

contentHtml:
Hoodoo Ski Area sits at the top of Santiam Pass with 806 acres, five lifts and 34 runs (30% beginner, 30% intermediate, 40% expert), the longest about 3 miles, over a 1,035-foot vertical drop from 5,703 feet. It averages 450 inches of snow a year and offers Central Oregon's only night skiing.

The Autobahn Tube Hill is very popular, there is a terrain park off the Blue Valley run, and Nordic skiers have 7.5 km of groomed track plus 8.3 km on the Skyliner trail (groomed weekends and holidays). The Ski & Ride School offers lessons, with rentals on site.

note: Email: customerservice@hoodoo.com. Check hoodoo.com for the 2026-27 opening date and lift hours.

title: Albany Historic Carousel & Museum
contentHtml:
The Albany Historic Carousel & Museum is a one-of-a-kind carousel in downtown Albany, opened in 2017 after a community effort of more than 15 years. Its menagerie animals were hand-carved and hand-painted entirely by volunteers and ride on a 1909 Dentzel mechanism, donated by Bill Dentzel, great-grandson of founder Gustav Dentzel, that volunteers spent more than ten years restoring.

It is a living museum: visitors can ride, watch carvers and painters at work in the studios, take a docent-led tour of the displays, and visit the volunteer-run gift shop and Carousel Cafe.

title: Brownsville City Hall
contentHtml:
An Oregon Film Trail sign outside Brownsville City Hall marks a spot where six Stand by Me filming locations are visible, including the street where Vern finds his penny; a penny is still embedded in the Main Street crosswalk on the south side of Park Avenue.

Brownsville doubled as Castle Rock in Rob Reiner's 1986 film Stand by Me, adapted from Stephen King's novella The Body and starring Wil Wheaton, River Phoenix, Corey Feldman and Jerry O'Connell. A walking tour covers more than a dozen movie spots within a few blocks.

note: Stand By Me Day is held every July 23, sponsored by the Linn County Historical Museum (541-466- 3390), with walking tours, a fan forum, blueberry pie, music, a cruise-in and fifties games in the park. From I-5 exit 216, take Highway 228 east 4 miles and turn left at the green 'Downtown' sign onto Main Street.

title: Linn County Historical Museum, Brownsville
imageAlt: Oregon Film Trail Stand by Me marker

banner.alt: Oregon Film Trail Stand by Me marker

gallery.alt: Oregon Film Trail Stand by Me marker

contentHtml:
The Oregon Film Trail's Stand by Me sign, erected in 2019, is on the wall of the Linn County Historical Museum. The museum is not a filming location, but it anchors Brownsville's annual Stand by Me Day and is where fans get film information, souvenirs and the walking-tour map of the film's locations around town.

The sign notes that the four young actors were fascinated by a mounted two-headed calf at the Brownsville meat lockers and often spent their breaks there.

title: Pioneer Park, Brownsville
contentHtml:
Stand by Me's blueberry pie-eating contest, Lardass Hogan's revenge, was filmed in Pioneer Park with nearly 100 Brownsville residents as extras, and the production company donated picnic tables to the park afterward.

In use since the 1840s, the 26-acre park is bordered on two sides by the Calapooia River, with ball fields, basketball courts, horseshoe pits, a covered dining pavilion with a kitchen, a covered amphitheater and summer swimming.

title: Santiam Excursion Trains
contentHtml:
Santiam Excursion Trains, operated by the Albany & Eastern Railroad, run from Santiam Station in Lebanon over 17-plus miles of the Sweet Home Branch toward Sweet Home, along the South Santiam River and US 20 past farmland and forest. Trains depart from and return to the same depot.

Rides include all-ages excursions and 21-and-over beer tasting trains, with beer, wine and cocktails from the bar car, a former Great Northern ranch car. Riders sit in a 1947 Pullman coach or on open-top flat cars, and the restored 1924 Baldwin steam locomotive Santa Maria Valley 205 brought steam back to the line for the first time since the 1950s.

contentHtml:
Barsideous Brewing is a brewpub in Lebanon's historic Gem Theater, built around 1910 as the Kuhn Theatre, where brewer Bill Bartman makes experimental, boundary-pushing beers.

House beers include Hazed & Confused Hazy IPA, Steven Bourbon Barrel Aged Stout (11%), Goldilocks Belgian Strong Blonde and Red Hag Mother Irish red ale, served alongside handcrafted meals.

contentHtml:
Calapooia Brewing was founded in 1993 as Oregon Trader Brewing and renamed in 2006. Since November 2019 it has been owned by the makers of Vivacity Fine Spirits, which now distills on site, and it is known for its chili beer.

The family- and pet-friendly brewpub pours house craft beers and Vivacity cocktails with burgers and pub food, with live music, darts and events, and indoor and covered outdoor seating year-round.

Bryant Park's 18-hole course, established in 2007, is free to play and rated hard, with a par-58 main layout of 6,826 feet over hilly terrain. Holes 3 and 6 through 15 wind through heavy vegetation, and the rest are on grass.

It has concrete tees and Mach VII baskets, with two baskets on most of the wooded par 4s, plus a restroom; it is cart-friendly and dogs are allowed. A round takes about 2 hours 15 minutes.

The park is busy with dog walkers, children and sports, and a round takes about an hour.

title: Waterloo County Park
contentHtml:
Waterloo County Park's 18-hole, par-54 course, established in 2007, is cut mainly from dense underbrush beneath large firs and maples, with tight fairways and heavy rough of ferns, berry bushes and thick brush on hilly ground. It is free to play and rated moderate, with concrete tees and DGA DISCatcher Pro 24 baskets.

The park has restrooms and camping, most holes are accessible, and dogs are allowed on leash. A round takes about 1 hour 45 minutes; the practice basket and hole 1 tee are by the kiosk near the fenced dog park.

title: Four Rivers Cultural Center & Museum
imageAlt: Mounted musk ox in a museum exhibit

banner.alt: Mounted musk ox in a museum exhibit

contentHtml:
Four Rivers Cultural Center & Museum is a nonprofit cultural center in Ontario whose 13,000-square-foot diorama museum tells the story of the region's Northern Paiute, Basque, Hispanic and Japanese heritage, with exhibits on Oregon Trail-era settlement, handmade baskets, arrowheads and flint tools.

The Harano Gallery rotates local and national exhibits year-round, and Hikaru Mizu, its Japanese garden, is described as the only Japanese garden within 400 miles. The center also has a 645-seat performing arts theater, a gift shop and a conference center.

title: Rinehart Stone House Museum
contentHtml:
Rinehart Stone House was built of sandstone in 1872 by Louis and Amanda Rinehart, the first permanent building in Malheur County. It replaced Jonathan Keeney's log house as a wayside inn and stagecoach stop for Oregon Trail travelers into the early 1900s, sheltered settlers during the 1878 Bannock Paiute uprising and served as field headquarters for General O.O. Howard.

Now a restored museum listed on the National Register of Historic Places, it displays period relics and photographs and interpretive exhibits on the Oregon Trail.

title: Malheur National Forest
contentHtml:
The Malheur National Forest covers 1.7 million acres of the Blue Mountains in eastern Oregon, from high desert grasslands of sage and juniper to pine and fir forests, hidden alpine lakes and meadows. Elevations run from 4,000 feet to 9,038 feet at Strawberry Mountain, whose range runs through the center of the forest.

The forest holds 88,350 acres of wilderness and the headwaters of the John Day River, the only tributary of the Columbia with no dams. The Malheur and Silvies rivers have Wild and Scenic stretches, and four former guard stations and a lookout can be rented for overnight stays.

title: Wallowa-Whitman National Forest
contentHtml:
The Wallowa-Whitman National Forest covers about 2.4 million acres of northeastern Oregon and western Idaho, from 9,843 feet in the Elkhorn, Wallowa and Seven Devils mountains down to 875 feet along the Snake River. It holds four wilderness areas, ten Wild and Scenic Rivers and the 652,488-acre Hells Canyon National Recreation Area.

Visitors come for hiking, fly fishing, camping and cabin rentals, ATV riding and snowmobiling.

title: Birch Creek Historic Ranch

gallery.alt: Birch Creek Historic Ranch, Owyhee Wild and Scenic River

contentHtml:
Birch Creek Historic Ranch was established in the early 1900s by a Basque sheepherder and a West Virginia cattle rancher on the Owyhee Wild and Scenic River. Basque-style stone walls still climb the mesa, remnants of a waterwheel mark the old alfalfa fields, and 19 buildings and structures make it a historic rural landscape on the National Register of Historic Places.

A five-unit, no-fee campground sits inside the ranch, with one water source and a restroom. Visitors fish, swim, paddle, hike, ride, climb, picnic and watch wildlife.

title: Chukar Park Campground
imageAlt: Campsite along the North Fork Malheur River

banner.alt: Campsite along the North Fork Malheur River

contentHtml:
Chukar Park Campground has 19 primitive sites on the North Fork of the Malheur River, seven of them in shaded riverside vegetation and the rest in partial shade or full sun. It has drinking water and vault toilets, and campsite 1 and the nearby toilets are accessible.

It is a popular base camp for birders, hunters and anglers, and for travelers on nearby Highway 20.

note: $5 per night; first come, first served; 14-day stay limit. Camp host late April through November. No showers, hookups or dump station; no cell coverage. Mosquitoes can be heavy in spring, and puncture vine (goatheads) grows in places, so watch pets. Email: BLM_OR_VL_Mail@blm.gov

title: Slocum Creek Campground
contentHtml:
Slocum Creek Campground sits in a side canyon near the mouth of Leslie Gulch, a base for exploring the gulch's hiking in the Leslie Gulch Area of Critical Environmental Concern and for swimming and paddling on Lake Owyhee. Rock outcrops in the neighboring Slocum Creek Wilderness Study Area glow in early morning and evening light.

Its nine no-fee sites have shade structures, and eight have accessible features, along with accessible vault toilets.
excerpt: Slocum Creek Campground sits in a side canyon near the mouth of Leslie Gulch, a base for exploring the gulch's hiking in the Leslie Gulch Area of Critical Envir
note: No fee; 14-day stay limit. No drinking water. Camping and fires only in the campground; no overnight backpacking or horses in the Leslie Gulch ACEC. No collecting plants, rocks or firewood. Flash floods, wet roads or winter conditions can close the road; high clearance recommended, large RVs not. From US 95 in Idaho, take McBride Creek Road 8 miles to Rockville, then Leslie Gulch Road 15 miles west. Email: BLM_OR_VL_Mail@blm.gov

title: Three Forks Recreation Site
imageAlt: Afternoon view into the canyon at Three Forks

banner.alt: Afternoon view into the canyon at Three Forks

gallery.alt: Afternoon view into the canyon at Three Forks

contentHtml:
Three Forks Recreation Site lies in the canyon where the North Fork, Middle Fork and main Owyhee rivers meet, among the most remote camping in Oregon. It has five designated primitive campsites, a boat launch, parking and vault toilets, with fishing, swimming, rafting and hiking on old wagon and ranch roads.

Pronghorn roam the rangeland above, mule deer and elk winter in the canyon, California bighorn sheep live along the river year-round, and remnants of a historic military road zigzag up the canyon's west face. The Owyhee Canyon Overlook is 22 miles from the highway.
excerpt: Three Forks Recreation Site lies in the canyon where the North Fork, Middle Fork and main Owyhee rivers meet, among the most remote camping in Oregon. It has fi
note: No fee; first come, first served; 14-day stay limit. High-clearance four-wheel drive strongly recommended. The last two miles drop steeply into the canyon on a rocky, unmaintained road: check it from the rim, or park and hike down. Impassable when wet. Watch for cattle on the road and for rattlesnakes. Email: BLM_OR_VL_Mail@blm.gov
address: Three Forks Road, 36 miles south of US 95 near Danner (about 16 miles west of Jordan Valley), OR (Vale District Office: 100 Oregon Street, Vale, OR 97918)

title: Lake Owyhee State Park
contentHtml:
Lake Owyhee State Park sits on the shore of Owyhee Reservoir, a 53-mile-long lake formed in 1932 by an irrigation dam on the Owyhee River in a deep desert canyon. Boaters explore geology seen only from the water, and anglers catch largemouth bass, white and black crappie and catfish, with occasional rainbow trout stocking.

Golden eagles, pronghorn, mule deer and wild horses live here, and bighorn sheep or mountain lions may be seen. Birders find chukar, rock and canyon wrens and Lazuli buntings, and migrants in the riparian thickets. McCormack Campground has 29 electric sites, 9 tent sites, hot showers, flush toilets, a dump station and a boat ramp; Indian Creek Campground has 22 electric sites and 2 cabins; the Gordon Gulch day-use area has picnic tables and a boat ramp.
excerpt: Lake Owyhee State Park sits on the shore of Owyhee Reservoir, a 53-mile-long lake formed in 1932 by an irrigation dam on the Owyhee River in a deep desert canyo
note: Reservations up to 6 months ahead at oregonstateparks.reserveamerica.com or 800-452-5687. Day- use parking permit required. Water may be off before April 15 and after October 15; docks may be out of the water in summer depending on reservoir levels. No cell service or pay phone; nearest emergency services in Nyssa. Narrow, steep access road. Rattlesnakes present.
address: 1298 Lake Owyhee Dam Road, Adrian, OR (on Owyhee Reservoir, 33 miles from Nyssa)

title: Ontario State Recreation Site
imageAlt: Paddle boarding at Ontario State Recreation Site

banner.alt: Paddle boarding at Ontario State Recreation Site

contentHtml:
Ontario State Recreation Site is a day-use park on the west bank of the Snake River, with grassy picnic grounds shaded by cottonwoods, sumac and junipers, a boat ramp and river access for boating, paddling, fishing and swimming.

Blue herons, Canada geese, river otters and muskrats live along the shoreline, and deer are sometimes seen on a nearby island in the early morning. Birders walk the gravel path from the west end of the parking lot for migrant songbirds, black-crowned night-herons, ospreys and cormorants.

note: Day use and boat ramp open year-round. Free Wi-Fi. Restroom may be closed in the off-season, with portable toilets on site.
address: West bank of the Snake River, about 1 mile north of Ontario (I-84 exit 374, then east on US 30/OR 201), OR

title: Succor Creek State Natural Area
contentHtml:
Succor Creek State Natural Area lies in a deep, rocky canyon, a remote haven for rock hounds and wildlife watchers. Its name may come from the Spanish socorro, 'help,' for the fresh water that saved early travelers.

Primitive, first-come, first-served campsites sit on both sides of the creek (4 west and 14 east), with a vault toilet and primitive day-use areas. Rock hounds may collect up to 1 gallon per person per day and 3 gallons per year.
excerpt: Succor Creek State Natural Area lies in a deep, rocky canyon, a remote haven for rock hounds and wildlife watchers. Its name may come from the Spanish socorro,
note: No water, pay phone or cell service, and no staff on site: come prepared. The Succor Creek Bridge is open to vehicles only for the east-side campsites; the road north of the bridge is not safe for vehicles.
address: Succor Creek Road, about 15 miles of rough dirt road off OR 201 (about 30 miles south of Nyssa), OR

title: Riverside Wildlife Area
contentHtml:
Riverside Wildlife Area's 3,798 acres in the Malheur River canyon near the old railroad community of Riverside give public fishing, hunting and wildlife-viewing access to a remote stretch of river otherwise surrounded by private land. ODFW bought the Riverside Tract from the Blaylock family in 1976.

Bighorn sheep, pronghorn, mule deer, elk, chukar, California quail, sage-grouse, osprey and bald and golden eagles live here, with beavers and river otters occasionally seen. The river has good rainbow trout fishing and is floatable mid-spring through mid-summer, about 12 river miles to the nearest take-out on BLM land.
excerpt: Riverside Wildlife Area's 3,798 acres in the Malheur River canyon near the old railroad community of Riverside give public fishing, hunting and wildlife-viewing
note: Open year-round; no parking permit required. Camping and open fires are prohibited. Very remote with no cell reception; prepare for harsh weather, and expect little wildlife movement at midday in summer heat. Directions: from Juntura, take Riverside Road 16 miles south, pass the BLM campsite, go 3/4 mile to the first two-track road on the left and follow it 1.5 miles to the orange gate.
address: Riverside Road, 16 miles south of US 20 near Juntura, OR (ODFW: 237 S. Hines Boulevard, Hines, OR 97738)

title: Stevenson Benchmark
contentHtml: Stevenson Benchmark is an 8,027-foot (2,447 m) summit in the Oregon Canyon Mountains and a non- technical walk-up, reached from the east off US 95 north of McDermitt.

title: Jordan Valley Tour
imageAlt: Skinner Toll Road outside Jordan Valley

banner.alt: Skinner Toll Road outside Jordan Valley

gallery.alt: St. Bernard's Catholic Church, Jordan Valley

contentHtml:
The Jordan Valley Tour is an easy 18-mile loop (about 45% gravel, 55% paved) with about 800 feet of climbing on quiet roads with wide views across Owyhee Country. It passes old-growth sagebrush taller than riders, crosses Jordan Creek twice and rolls past working ranches toward views of the Owyhee Canyonlands.

It traces the history of the Skinner Toll Road, the 1863 gold strike on Jordan Creek and the Basque settlers who shaped the valley, passing St. Bernard's Catholic Church (built in 1914 of local stone), Pharmacy Hill and Oregon's last remaining Basque pelota court.

note: Easier; tires 45 mm or wider. Flush toilets and shade at the city park; snacks and drinks in Jordan Valley. At about mile 15, take the gravel road around Pharmacy Hill to avoid the 55-mph highway. Cattle graze open range: pass calmly. A red blinking light and rear radar are recommended. The GPX file has no turn-by-turn directions; auto-generated directions are often inaccurate.

title: Owyhees Tour
contentHtml:
The Owyhees Tour is a 225-mile, four-day bikepacking loop (about 75% gravel and dirt) with about 14,000 feet of climbing across the Owyhee Mountains, Owyhee Desert and Owyhee River canyon, much of it in Owyhee County, Idaho.

Day 1 climbs through the Owyhee Mountains past the ghost town of Silver City to Grand View; day 2 climbs about 4,000 feet to dispersed camping at Deep Creek; day 3 crosses the North Fork Owyhee and drops steeply to Three Forks; day 4 returns past Owyhee canyon overlooks, Danner and Inskip Station to Jordan Valley. Wild antelope and the Shoofly Oolite site are along the way.

Watch for ticks, rattlesnakes, Mormon crickets and goatheads. Three Forks Warm Springs and its riverbank are private land; access is not guaranteed. title: Skinner Toll Road
contentHtml:
The Skinner Toll Road ride is a very demanding 58-mile gravel lollipop (about 88% gravel) with about 4,600 feet of climbing into Idaho's Owyhee Mountains, topping out near 6,800 to 6,900 feet. It follows the route Silas Skinner hand-built from 1865 to haul freight between Silver City and Chico, California, after the 1863 gold strike on Jordan Creek.

Highlights include the basalt cliffs of the Long Ridge traverse, Jordan Creek canyons with old mining structures, the preserved mining town of Silver City and its Chinese cemetery, the ghost town of Dewey, the rugged Razr Loop OHV section with pitches near 15%, fall-colored aspen groves and the Split Rock viewpoint.

note: Very demanding; remote; tires 50 mm or wider. Flush toilets at the start; food and water in Silver City (about mile 25.5). Silver City is busy on summer weekends. The Idaho Hotel in Silver City allows a two- day trip. Shorter option: start at Slaughterhouse Gulch for a 26-mile ride. Stay on public streets in Silver City. Cattle on the road. title: North Fork Owyhee River
contentHtml:
The North Fork Owyhee River begins on the east flank of Idaho's Owyhee Mountains and flows southwest through a deep, basalt-rimmed canyon to meet the main Owyhee at Three Forks. Its 9.6 Oregon miles were designated Wild on October 28, 1988.

The 12 miles from North Fork Crossing to Three Forks offer excellent early-season kayaking for experts and fine backpacking, among juniper stands, colorful rock strata, steep canyon walls and side canyons. Mule deer migrate through the canyon, and cougar, pronghorn, raptors and sage grouse live here.

note: Managed by the Bureau of Land Management, Vale District Office (BLM_OR_VL_Mail@blm.gov). Three Forks Recreation Site, at the confluence, has primitive camping and a boat launch.

title: Owyhee River

gallery.alt: Birch Creek Historic Ranch on the Owyhee Wild and Scenic River

contentHtml:
The Owyhee River rises in Nevada and flows through southwestern Idaho into Oregon's remote, arid southeast corner. 120 Oregon miles, from the Idaho border to Owyhee Reservoir (Three Forks to China Gulch, Crooked Creek to the reservoir, plus the South Fork), are designated Wild, all in Malheur County.

Canyon walls rise up to 1,000 feet, with spires, side canyons and cliffs dropping into the river, and it is a nationally known early-season whitewater run for rafts, drift boats and kayaks. About 100 prehistoric campsites have been recorded between Rome and Burnt Creek Ranch, including the 'Hole in the Ground' petroglyph site, and Chalk Basin shows striking dark and chalky deposits. More than 200 wildlife species live here, including bighorn sheep, mule deer, pronghorn, cougars and bobcats.

note: Managed by the Bureau of Land Management, Vale District Office (BLM_OR_VL_Mail@blm.gov).
address: Rome Launch Site, just upstream of US 95 at Rome, OR (designated reach from the Idaho border to Owyhee Reservoir)
photoCredit: Bob Wick, BLM; Bureau of Land Management

title: West Little Owyhee River
contentHtml:
The West Little Owyhee River rises at 6,508 feet near the Nevada border by McDermitt and flows east past Deer Flat into Louse Canyon, then turns north near Twin Buttes through the Owyhee Desert to the Owyhee River. All 57.6 miles were designated Wild on October 28, 1988, and the Oregon Desert Trail follows the river.

Its inner canyon of cool, secluded pools between sheer rock walls contrasts starkly with the flat sagebrush plateau above. There are no developed sites: visitors backpack off-trail, day hike, take on a challenging swim- and-hike route, hunt and camp, among raptors, chukar, prairie falcons, sage grouse and California bighorn sheep.

title: East Steens Tour Route
contentHtml:
The East Steens Tour Route is a 143-mile drive of 4 to 7 hours from Fields, with its stone roadhouse dating to 1881, north past the Alvord Desert playa below Steens Mountain to Alvord Hot Springs, Mann Lake and Ten Cent Lake, then west on OR 78 past Crystal Crane Hot Springs to Burns.

Pronghorn are often seen, and Crane Union High School is one of the few public boarding schools in the Lower 48. Combine it with the High Desert Discovery Scenic Byway for a loop.

title: Four Rivers Farm and Garden Trail
contentHtml:
The Four Rivers Farm and Garden Trail is a self-guided driving tour of the Four Rivers area around Ontario, Vale and Nyssa, where the Payette, Malheur and Owyhee rivers join the Snake and irrigation supports rich, varied farmland. Visitors see irrigation and modern farming, meet local producers and learn how farming has changed.

Its 25 stops cross into Fruitland and Payette, Idaho, and include farms, produce stands, nurseries, the Ontario Saturday Market, Browns Buffalo Ranch, the Kenney Pass and Utter Starvation Camp kiosks and Andrews Seed Company, a century-old seed company known for heirloom seeds. It can be driven in sections or over a full day.

title: Snake River–Mormon Basin Back Country Byway
imageAlt: Entering Public Lands sign along the byway

banner.alt: Entering Public Lands sign along the byway

gallery.alt: Pair of chukars crossing the byway

contentHtml:
The Snake River-Mormon Basin Back Country Byway is a 150-mile drive on paved, gravel and dirt roads through the ranch and canyon country of Baker and Malheur counties, between Baker City and Huntington. Allow at least five hours of driving, not counting stops; the route suits high-clearance two-wheel-drive vehicles.

It follows the Snake River above Brownlee Reservoir, past colorful basalt cliffs and spring wildflowers, then climbs into Mormon Basin, where gold diggings, homesteads and old mines date from the 1860s. Along the way are fishing and boating on Brownlee Reservoir, the Spring Recreation Site near Huntington, and stories of outlaws, moonshiners and counterfeiters. Services are sparse, so carry what you need.
excerpt: The Snake River-Mormon Basin Back Country Byway is a 150-mile drive on paved, gravel and dirt roads through the ranch and canyon country of Baker and Malheur co
note: No fee; take care after storms and in winter
address: Baker Field Office, 3100 H Street, Baker City, OR 97814

title: Leslie Gulch–Succor Creek Back Country Byway
contentHtml:
The Leslie Gulch-Succor Creek Back Country Byway is a 50-mile, all-gravel BLM Back Country Byway through the Succor Creek canyon, with a spur down Leslie Gulch to Lake Owyhee. Leslie Gulch's 11,000 acres of towering, desert-colored cliffs and honeycombed volcanic rock are formed mostly of Leslie Gulch Tuff.

More than 200 California bighorn sheep, reintroduced in 1965, roam the gulch with mule deer, elk, chukar and raptors, and its soils hold rare plants, two found only in the Leslie Gulch drainage. Succor Creek State Natural Area and Slocum Creek Campground are along the way.
excerpt: The Leslie Gulch-Succor Creek Back Country Byway is a 50-mile, all-gravel BLM Back Country Byway through the Succor Creek canyon, with a spur down Leslie Gulch
note: Generally passable mid-April through October; not maintained in winter. Steep (up to 11% grade on Leslie Gulch Road), narrow and rough: high-clearance vehicles recommended, large RVs and trailers discouraged. Summer storms and flash floods can make roads impassable, and summer heat can top 100°F. No services or drinking water. Camping and fires only at Slocum Creek Campground (and Succor Creek State Natural Area). Email: BLM_OR_VL_Mail@blm.gov
address: Succor Creek Road between OR 201 and US 95, with the Leslie Gulch Road spur west to Lake Owyhee, OR

title: Owyhee Uplands Back Country Byway
imageAlt: Aerial view of a canyon and river at sunset

banner.alt: Aerial view of a canyon and river at sunset

contentHtml:
The Owyhee Uplands Back Country Byway is a 103-mile BLM Back Country Byway from Jordan Valley, Oregon, southeast to Grand View, Idaho, almost all of it through Idaho's Owyhee canyonlands on a mix of gravel and paved roads.

It crosses sagebrush steppe among volcanic plateaus, cliffs and canyons formed more than 8 million years ago, with more than 180 bird and mammal species, including bighorn sheep, coyotes and badgers, and plenty of remote solitude.

title: Juntura Hot Springs
contentHtml:
Juntura Hot Springs is a natural, unimproved pool on an island and gravel bar in the Malheur River, on public BLM land at about 3,000 feet in the high desert. The main pool usually runs 105 to 115°F, and soakers cool it with river water.

It is primitive, with no restrooms, picnic areas or on-site camping, though dispersed camping is allowed nearby. It is clothing-optional.
excerpt: Juntura Hot Springs is a natural, unimproved pool on an island and gravel bar in the Malheur River, on public BLM land at about 3,000 feet in the high desert. T
note: No fee. Reaching the pool requires fording the river, which is impassable during most of spring runoff; the access road is rough and muddy in rain, and 4x4 is recommended most of the year (4x4 and chains in winter). No soap or shampoo, no glass; pack out all trash. Not family- or pet-friendly.
address: Horseshoe Bend of the Malheur River near Juntura, OR (BLM land)

title: Snively Hot Springs
imageAlt: Steam rises from Snively Hot Springs

banner.alt: Steam rises from Snively Hot Springs

gallery.alt: Steam rises from Snively Hot Springs

contentHtml:
Snively Hot Springs is an undeveloped BLM site on the banks of the Lower Owyhee River, where a spring emerges at about 190°F and river rocks form soaking pools cooled by the Owyhee's water.

It has day-use parking and a vault toilet.
excerpt: Snively Hot Springs is an undeveloped BLM site on the banks of the Lower Owyhee River, where a spring emerges at about 190°F and river rocks form soaking pools
note: No fee. Day use only; camping is not allowed and the rule is strictly enforced. Littering, underage drinking and drug use (including marijuana) violate federal law and risk the site's closure. No accessible facilities. Email: BLM_OR_VL_Mail@blm.gov
address: Owyhee Lake Road, on the Lower Owyhee River south of Adrian, OR (via OR 201, Mendiola, Kurtz and Overstreet roads)

title: Jordan Craters
contentHtml:
Jordan Craters is a 27-square-mile olivine basalt lava field north of Jordan Valley, among the youngest in Oregon, with craters, lava tubes, aligned spatter cones and ropy pahoehoe lava. The Coffee Pot Crater flow erupted about 3,200 years ago and dammed Cow Creek into the Cow Lakes.

Coffee Pot Crater, a well-preserved, steep-sided crater covering about two-thirds of a square mile, is the only feature with vehicle access.
excerpt: Jordan Craters is a 27-square-mile olivine basalt lava field north of Jordan Valley, among the youngest in Oregon, with craters, lava tubes, aligned spatter con
note: No fee. No trails: sharp lava and open pits are dangerous, and lava surfaces can top 120°F in summer, so bring plenty of water. Roads are nearly impassable when wet and difficult in winter; high-clearance four-wheel drive recommended. Email: BLM_OR_VL_Mail@blm.gov
address: Cow Creek Road, 25 miles west of US 95 (turn 8 miles north of Jordan Valley at the Jordan Craters sign), OR

title: Pillars of Rome
contentHtml:
The Pillars of Rome, officially Rome Cliffs, are a five-mile wall of pale, fossil-bearing clay bluffs about 100 feet tall rising from the sagebrush above the Owyhee River valley. Oregon Trail emigrants took them for the ruins of a Roman city, which named both the formation and the town.

They are tan and white lakebed sediments and volcanic ash capped by tougher basalt and welded tuff, carved by water and wind about 2.5 to 5.3 million years ago, and the light changes their look through the day and seasons. There are no formal trails, but visitors walk the open land for views and photography.
excerpt: The Pillars of Rome, officially Rome Cliffs, are a five-mile wall of pale, fossil-bearing clay bluffs about 100 feet tall rising from the sagebrush above the Ow
note: BLM land; no fee and no amenities. A well-maintained gravel road suits passenger cars. Climbing the pillars is risky and damages them. Rome has few services; the free, first-come Rome Launch campground is 4 miles east.
address: Kiger Road off Old Ion Highway, about 4 miles northwest of Rome (off US 95), OR

title: Sunset Valley Vineyards
contentHtml:
Sunset Valley Vineyards is Jesse Watson's estate vineyard of about 40 acres on a south-facing bench in the Sunset Valley southwest of Nyssa, on the Snake River plain, on the Strickland family homestead.

Malheur County approved its wine processing plant, shop and tasting room in January 2025. Wine and wine- club sales run through its website.

note: Public tasting-room hours are not yet published: call ahead.

title: Willamette Heritage Center

gallery.alt: Thomas Kay Woolen Mill (photo: Ron Cooper)

contentHtml:
The Willamette Heritage Center is a five-acre campus in Salem with fourteen historic structures, formed in 2010 when the Marion County Historical Society and Mission Mill Museum merged. Highlights include the Thomas Kay Woolen Mill of 1895-1896, a National Park Service-designated American Treasure with two floors of exhibits on industrial history, and the 1841 Jason Lee House and Methodist Parsonage, among the oldest standing wooden frame houses in the Pacific Northwest.

Oregon Trail immigrants built the John D. Boon House (1847) and Pleasant Grove Church (1858) on the grounds. Permanent and changing exhibits include the story of the Kalapuya people, and the campus also has a textile learning center, a research library and archives, shops and artist studios.

note: Admission: adults $15, 65 and over $13, students with ID and ages 6-17 $11; children 5 and under, military with ID, educators and members free. Museums for All: free with Oregon Trail, OHP, SNAP and EBT cards. The research library and archives are open by appointment only.

title: Hallie Ford Museum of Art
contentHtml:
Willamette University's Hallie Ford Museum of Art, across from the Oregon State Capitol, opened in 1998 and is the only liberal arts college art museum in the Northwest. It is known for its research on Northwest art and its significant collection of Northwest works.

Six galleries also hold Native American, ancient, European, American and Asian art, alongside changing exhibitions.

note: Admission: general $8, seniors (55+) $5; free every day for ages 0-17, students and educators with ID and members, and free for everyone on Tuesdays. Closed Independence Day, Thanksgiving Thursday and Friday, and over Willamette University's winter break. Accessible parking on Cottage Street near State Street.
address: 700 State St, Salem, OR 97301
photoCredit: Travel Salem; Hallie Ford Museum of Art

title: Bush House Museum
contentHtml:
Asahel Bush, founding editor of the Oregon Statesman and co-founder of the Ladd & Bush Bank, built this two-story Italianate home in 1878 in what is now Salem's Bush's Pasture Park. Listed on the National Register and owned by the City of Salem, it is run by the Salem Art Association and has offered guided tours since 1953.

The house keeps many original furnishings, wallpapers and fixtures, including Salem's first indoor bathroom, and the museum explores the Bush family, the park, Salem's cultural diversity and early Oregon. The renovated Servants' Quarters are open for tours.

title: Deepwood Museum & Gardens
contentHtml:
Deepwood is the 1894 Queen Anne Victorian home of Dr. Luke A. Port, listed on the National Register and owned by the City of Salem, with Eastern Golden Oak woodwork and Povey stained glass windows. The Friends of Deepwood, a nonprofit, maintains the house and grounds in partnership with the city.

About five acres of formal gardens were designed by Lord & Schryver, the Pacific Northwest's first firm of women landscape architects, and the grounds and nature trails are free to wander.

title: Gilbert House Children's Museum
contentHtml:
Gilbert House Children's Museum (A.C. Gilbert's Discovery Village) is a hands-on children's museum spread through three historic Victorian houses in Salem's Riverfront Park, named for Salem-born inventor A.C. Gilbert of Erector Set fame.

More than 20 interactive exhibits teach through creative play, and the 20,000-square-foot Outdoor Discovery Area holds the world's largest Erector Set tower at 52 feet. There are daily crafts, science programs, a cafe, classes, field trips and summer camps.

note: Admission: general $16, seniors (60+) and military/veterans $14, infants under 1 and members free. Gates close at 4:30 PM. Closed Easter, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and New Year's Day. Email: info@acgilbert.org

title: Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health
imageAlt: Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health

banner.alt: Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health

gallery.alt: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest cast and director accepting an award (museum display)

contentHtml:
The Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health occupies about 2,500 square feet in the oldest building on the Oregon State Hospital campus, the Kirkbride-plan hospital of 1883 (formerly the Oregon Insane Asylum), the last of its kind still operating on the West Coast.

Exhibits trace a century and a half of mental-health care in Oregon and the people who lived and worked there, with a memorial to the unclaimed cremains. The hospital was the filming location for One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest in 1975, with real patients and staff among the cast, and the museum keeps an exhibit of props and stories from the production; it is a stop on the Oregon Film Trail.

title: Silverton Country Historical Society Museum
contentHtml:
The Silverton Country Historical Society's museum is housed in the Ames/Warnock/Burch house, built by Louis Ames in 1908 and moved to this site in 1975; the house is itself an exhibit.

Each room has period displays on about 150 years of life in Silverton country, from Homer Davenport and June Drake to logging and the Silverton Red Sox, drawn almost entirely from donations by descendants of pioneer families.

title: The Gordon House
contentHtml:
The Gordon House is Frank Lloyd Wright's only built design in Oregon, a Usonian house he designed in 1957 for Conrad and Evelyn Gordon and completed in 1963. Saved from demolition, it was moved from Wilsonville to the Oregon Garden grounds in Silverton in 2001 and reopened as a museum in 2002.

It is the only publicly accessible Frank Lloyd Wright home in the Pacific Northwest, seen on guided tours.

title: Old Aurora Colony Museum
contentHtml:
The Old Aurora Colony Museum tells the story of the Aurora Colony (1856-1883), Oregon's first communal society, a German and Swiss Christian community of nearly 600 people, at the heart of Oregon's first National Historic District.

The complex includes the Ox Barn (about 1860), which sheltered oxen that pulled Oregon Trail wagons and became a museum in 1966, the board-and-batten George Kraus House, the 1876 George Steinbach Log Cabin, the Will family Wash House and a Tie Shed with shoemaker, woodworker, blacksmith and wheelwright workspaces, with the colony's quilts, crafts and furnishings.

title: Newell Pioneer Village
contentHtml:
Newell Pioneer Village is a living-history village next to Champoeg State Heritage Area, centered on the 1852 Robert Newell House. Newell was Champoeg's leading citizen and the first speaker of the House in Oregon's provisional government.

The village also has the Pioneer Mothers Memorial Cabin, the Butteville Academy schoolhouse and the old Butteville Jail, kept by the Daughters of the American Revolution.

title: Mount Hood National Forest
contentHtml:
Mt. Hood National Forest covers about 1.1 million acres just 50 miles east of Portland, stretching more than 60 miles south from the Columbia River Gorge to the Olallie Scenic Area near Mt. Jefferson.

It has about 80 campgrounds, 20 sno-parks, part of the Pacific Crest Trail and several ski areas, including historic Timberline Lodge. About a third of the forest is designated wilderness, and the forest supplies about a third of Oregon's drinking and irrigation water.

The forest is managed through four ranger districts: Barlow, Clackamas River, Hood River and Zigzag.

title: Willamette National Forest
contentHtml:
The Willamette National Forest runs about 110 miles along the western slopes of the Oregon Cascades and covers 1,675,407 acres of high mountains, narrow canyons, fast streams and wooded slopes. About 61% of it lies in Lane County, with large areas in Linn, Marion and Douglas counties.

It holds eight wilderness areas and seven major volcanic peaks, and offers year-round hiking, backpacking, camping, fishing, waterfalls and skiing.

title: Bull of the Woods Wilderness
imageAlt: Mt. Jefferson from Bull of the Woods Mountain

banner.alt: Mt. Jefferson from Bull of the Woods Mountain

contentHtml:
Bull of the Woods Wilderness was designated by Congress in 1984 and enlarged in 2009. It is a remote, roadless basin of old-growth Douglas fir and western hemlock that feeds the Collawash, Breitenbush and Little North Santiam rivers, and it is home to the northern spotted owl.

About a dozen trout-filled lakes sit between high ridges, and a 68-mile trail system includes several loops. Bull of the Woods Peak (5,523 ft) has a historic fire lookout with views to Mt. Jefferson; the Pansy Lake Trail is an easy 1.2 miles to Pansy Lake, and the Hot Springs Trail leads 1.5 miles to Bagby Hot Springs.

Old mine shafts and equipment remain from early mining days. Twin Lakes and Elk Lake are the most popular spots.

title: Mount Jefferson Wilderness
contentHtml:
The Mount Jefferson Wilderness, established in 1968, protects 111,177 acres in Linn, Jefferson and Marion counties and is Oregon's second most visited wilderness. At its heart is Mount Jefferson, 10,497 feet, the state's second-tallest peak, a stratovolcano with five glaciers; Three Fingered Jack (7,841 feet) anchors the south end.

More than 150 lakes, including Marion, Duffy, Santiam and Wasco lakes, dot the forests and alpine meadows, and about 190 miles of trails include 40 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail. Visitors hike, backpack, camp, ski and climb among Douglas-fir, mountain hemlock, rhododendron, bear grass and lupine, with deer, black bear and bald eagles.
