title: Opal Creek Wilderness
imageAlt: Opal Creek cascades through old-growth forest

banner.alt: Opal Creek cascades through old-growth forest

gallery.alt: Hiker on a forest trail at Opal Creek

contentHtml:
Opal Creek Wilderness protects 20,454 acres around the largest uncut watershed in Oregon. Congress designated it, with the adjoining Scenic Recreation Area, in 1996, after decades of mining ended and the land passed to conservation.

Battle Axe and Opal creeks join here to form the Little North Santiam River, flowing through ancient Douglas fir, western hemlock and western red cedar. Jawbone Flats, a 1929 mining camp of about two dozen rustic buildings, is run by the Opal Creek Ancient Forest Center. Eight trails total 36 miles.

Much of the valley burned in the 2020 Beachie Creek Fire, and access has been limited since. Check current closures with the Detroit Ranger Station before you go.

title: Table Rock Wilderness
contentHtml:
Table Rock Wilderness is an unusual BLM-managed wilderness of more than 5,700 acres in the western Cascade foothills, designated by Congress in 1984. Its namesake, Table Rock, is a columnar-basalt remnant of an ancient lava flow rising to 4,881 feet.

Steep slopes hold Douglas fir, western hemlock, noble fir and rhododendron, and two rare plants, Oregon sullivantia and Gorman's aster, bloom here. Deer and elk winter in the area.

Recent fires damaged parts of the trail system; trails start from the Old Bridge and Table Rock trailheads. Turn back if a trail becomes hard to follow.

Portal sign for Elkhorn Valley Recreation Site (photo: Steve Baldwin, BLM)

contentHtml:
Elkhorn Valley Recreation Site lies on the Little North Santiam River among deep emerald pools, cliffs, waterfalls and old-growth forest, with swimming in the river. The campground has 23 sites.

Downstream, the Canyon Creek Recreation Site is open for swimming, fishing and picnicking.

title: Champoeg State Heritage Area

gallery.alt: Champoeg State Heritage Area RV park

contentHtml:
Champoeg State Heritage Area spreads forests, fields and wetlands along the Willamette River south of Newberg. It is the site of the 1843 vote that formed Oregon's first provisional government, and of the town that grew up there and was washed away by a flood in 1861; it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

A visitor center has historical exhibits and guided walks. Visitors walk or bike paved trails, including 4 miles to Butteville, play the 18-hole disc golf course, picnic, and fish or kayak from the river dock, and more than 130 bird species have been seen in the park.

The campground has 20 full-hookup sites, 54 electric sites with water, 6 tent sites, 6 yurts, 6 cabins and a hiker/biker camp, with flush toilets and hot showers. There is also an off-leash dog park and the Pioneer Memorial Building and Pavilion for events.
excerpt: Champoeg State Heritage Area spreads forests, fields and wetlands along the Willamette River south of Newberg. It is the site of the 1843 vote that formed Orego
note: Day-use parking permit required (buy on site). B Loop, yurts and cabins are open year-round; A Loop closes seasonally; group picnic and tent sites May 1 - Oct 31. Reservations up to 6 months ahead at 800-452-5687. No swimming from the boat dock (strong currents); no drones or metal detectors. Firewood: emerald ash borer quarantine, so buy local or certified heat-treated wood.

title: Detroit Lake State Recreation Area

gallery.alt: Detroit Lake with snow-capped Mount Jefferson
Detroit Lake and a small island

contentHtml:
Detroit Lake State Recreation Area sits on the shore of a nine-mile-long canyon reservoir in the Cascade Mountains, surrounded by forest, with snow-capped Mount Jefferson in the distance. The lake is popular for fishing, boating and water sports.

Nearly 300 campsites include 107 full-hookup sites, 68 electrical sites with water, 96 tent sites and 6 mini cabins, with flush toilets, hot showers and swimming areas. The park has two courtesy boat ramps, two reservable moorages, a fishing dock, horseshoe pits, a basketball court, a volleyball area, a playground and a visitor center selling gifts, ice, firewood and souvenirs.
excerpt: Detroit Lake State Recreation Area sits on the shore of a nine-mile-long canyon reservoir in the Cascade Mountains, surrounded by forest, with snow-capped Mount
note: Reservations up to 6 months ahead at 800-452-5687. Two vehicles per campsite (second vehicle $10/night); no dump station and no generators. Campers can rent kayaks and paddleboards May- September. Lake levels drop for the winter drawdown (check U.S. Army Corps of Engineers water levels); blue-green algae blooms can occur April-September. The surrounding area was heavily damaged in the 2020 Santiam Canyon wildfires.
address: North shore of Detroit Lake off OR-22, 2 miles west of Detroit, OR

title: Mongold Day-Use Area

gallery.alt: Detroit Lake with snow-capped Mount Jefferson (area photo)

contentHtml:
Mongold Day-Use Area, 1.5 miles west of Detroit Lake State Recreation Area, has the only public boat launch on Detroit Lake, with parking for 120 vehicles and trailers.

It also has a swimming area, a grass beach, picnic facilities, restrooms and a life jacket loaner station. Oregon State Parks manages it under a lease with the U.S. Forest Service.

note: Day-use parking permit required (buy on site). Swimming is unsupervised: wear a life jacket. Check water levels with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and watch for underwater obstructions.

title: Silver Falls State Park
contentHtml:
Silver Falls State Park, often called the crown jewel of Oregon State Parks, covers more than 9,000 acres of Cascade foothill forest less than an hour east of Salem. Its best-known feature is the Trail of Ten Falls, a 7.2- mile moderate loop and National Recreation Trail with about 800 feet of elevation change, which passes behind 177-foot South Falls.

More than 35 miles of backcountry trails are open to hiking, mountain biking and horseback riding, and the one-mile accessible North Rim Trail has a North Falls viewpoint. The South Falls day-use area has lawns, picnic shelters, a playground and an off-leash dog area, and the historic South Falls Lodge has a cafe and nature store.

Camping includes 48 electrical sites with water, 43 tent sites, 14 cabins and the Howard Creek Horse Camp, and Smith Creek Village offers cabins, group lodges and the Bigleaf Market & Grill.

note: Day-use parking permit: $10 Oregon residents, $12 out-of-state (machines give no change; Northwest Forest and National Park passes not valid). Pets and bikes are not allowed on the Canyon Trail. Black bears and cougars live in remote areas. Cell coverage is limited. Park office 503-873-8681 (Mon-Fri 8:30 AM - 4:30 PM); reservations 800-452-5687.

title: State Capitol State Park
contentHtml:
State Capitol State Park is the more than 20 acres of Willson Park, Capitol Park and the Capitol Mall around the Oregon State Capitol, cared for by Oregon State Parks since 2008. Rhododendrons, camellias and cherry trees line the mall, planted for color from spring through summer.

Stone plaques on the mall sidewalks mark each county's seat and founding date, and a ring of flags from every U.S. state stands near the Moon Tree, a Douglas-fir grown from a seed Apollo 14 astronaut Stuart Roosa carried to the moon in 1971. The Waite Fountain, the Capitol Fountain and the Wall of Water along Court Street (the only fountain open to public use) run seasonally.

note: Free entry and no state park parking permit needed; metered street parking. Fountains typically run Memorial Day - Labor Day, 10 AM - 7 PM. No public drinking fountains; two single-user restrooms on the east side of the mall. Pets on leash; events need an approved reservation.

title: Willamette Mission State Park
imageAlt: Pond in Willamette Mission State Park

banner.alt: Pond in Willamette Mission State Park

contentHtml:
Willamette Mission State Park covers 1,300 acres of woodland, wetland, meadows and farmland on the Willamette River. It marks the site of the Willamette Mission, founded by Jason Lee in 1834 as the first Methodist mission on the West Coast; a flood destroyed its remaining buildings in 1861.

Beside Mission Lake stands the nation's largest black cottonwood, about 270 years old, over 28 feet around and more than 155 feet tall. The park has 5 miles of bike paths, 6 miles of horse trails, a 2.5-mile self-guided education trail, an 18-hole disc golf course in a hazelnut grove, a boat ramp, three picnic shelters, fishing in Mission and Goose lakes, a four-site horse camp and the Beaver Island Group Camp for up to 75 tent campers.
excerpt: Willamette Mission State Park covers 1,300 acres of woodland, wetland, meadows and farmland on the Willamette River. It marks the site of the Willamette Mission
note: Day-use parking permit required (buy on site). No showers. Trails can flood in winter and spring. E- bikes not allowed on equestrian trails or the Vision Trail. Reservations 800-452-5687.
address: Wheatland Rd NE, about 8 miles north of Salem, OR (next to the Wheatland Ferry)

title: Breitenbush Campground
contentHtml:
Breitenbush Campground has 26 sites along the Breitenbush River in the Willamette National Forest, with plant screening between sites and river views from most of them. Every site has a picnic table and grill, with vault toilets.

Anglers commonly catch rainbow trout in the river, and nearby Detroit Lake offers boating, water skiing and kayaking.

note: Closed for the 2026 season; reopening spring 2027. No drinking water: the water system was damaged in the Beachie Creek and Lionshead fires. Some sites first come, first served; others reserved at recreation.gov. Single site $21, multiple sites $40 per night; extra vehicle $9; day use $9. Senior and Access pass holders get 50% off the single-site fee. Check-in 2:00 PM, check-out 1:00 PM; 14-day stay limit. Chainsaws prohibited. Dogs on a 6-foot leash. No horses or pack animals.

title: Cleator Bend Group Campground
contentHtml:
Cleator Bend Group Campground is a single group site for up to 45 people on the north bank of a bend in the Breitenbush River, with 8 campfire rings, 8 picnic tables, a vault toilet and trash receptacles.

The river is popular for wading, swimming and rainbow trout fishing, and the South Breitenbush Gorge Trail is about three miles away. Linn County Parks & Recreation manages it under agreement with the Forest Service.

title: Elk Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Elk Lake Campground has 17 tent-only sites at the west end of Elk Lake, beside the Bull of the Woods and Opal Creek wildernesses. Its meadows bloom with wildflowers around July, and the quiet, non-motorized lake suits swimming and paddling.

Nearby trails include Elk Lake Creek #559, Bagby Hot Springs #544, Battle Ax Creek #3339 and Beachie #3341. Sites have picnic tables and vault toilets.

note: Closed for the 2026 season; reopening spring 2027. All sites first come, first served. Single $12, multiple $22 per night; extra vehicle $6. No drinking water. No camping within 500 feet of the lake; no motorized boats. Horses and pack animals allowed. title: Fox Creek Group Campground
contentHtml:
Fox Creek Group Campground is a single group site for up to 75 guests in a large, open clearing surrounded by dense forest where Fox Creek meets the Breitenbush River, at 1,700 feet. It suits tent campers and RVs or trailers of any size, with ample parking, picnic tables and vault toilets.

A short walk leads to the river, fed by snowmelt from the Mount Jefferson Wilderness, for fishing (mainly rainbow trout) and swimming.
excerpt: Fox Creek Group Campground is a single group site for up to 75 guests in a large, open clearing surrounded by dense forest where Fox Creek meets the Breitenbush
note: Closed for the 2026 season; reopening spring 2027. $65 per night; no passes honored. Reservation required at recreation.gov. No drinking water. No horses or pack animals. Forest roads are not maintained for snow and ice.

title: Humbug Campground
contentHtml:
Humbug Campground has 22 sites, most with river views, in old-growth forest on the Breitenbush River. Rhododendrons bloom in shades of pink from May through July.

Visitors walk among the old growth, wade and fish; rainbow trout is the most common catch. It has vault toilets, drinking water and picnic tables.

note: Closed for the 2026 season; reopening spring 2027. Reserve at recreation.gov; some sites first come, first served. Trailers up to 30 feet. Chainsaws prohibited. Dogs on a 6-foot leash. No horses or pack animals.
address: Forest Road 46 (Breitenbush Road), 4.6 miles northeast of Detroit, OR (Detroit Ranger Station: 44125 North Santiam Highway SE, Detroit, OR 97342)

title: Lower Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Lower Lake Campground sits beside Lower Lake in the Olallie Lake Scenic Area, just west of the Warm Springs Reservation border. The lake covers about 14 acres and is quite deep, with several small lakes nearby to explore.

Visitors hike, fish and paddle non-motorized boats.

note: Closed: the campground suffered extensive damage in the Lionshead Fire and repairs are ongoing. When open: $20 per night, extra vehicle $10; day use $10. First come, first served. No restrooms or drinking water. Vehicles up to 16 feet. Roads close in winter for snow. Directions: from Estacada take OR-224 south (it becomes Forest Road 46), turn east on FR 4690 for about 6 miles paved and 3 miles gravel to FR 4220.

title: Olallie Meadows Campground
contentHtml:
Olallie Meadow Campground offers views and solitude in a rustic setting just north of Mount Jefferson, with single and premium double sites.

Visitors picnic, day hike, backpack, paddle non-motorized boats and fish the area's lakes and ponds.
excerpt: Olallie Meadow Campground offers views and solitude in a rustic setting just north of Mount Jefferson, with single and premium double sites.
note: Closed. When open: single $15, premium double $30 per night; extra vehicle $5. First come, first served. No drinking water; the Forest Service lists no restroom. Roads close in winter. Directions: from Estacada take OR-224 south (it becomes Forest Road 46), turn east on FR 4690 for about 6 miles paved and 3 miles gravel to FR 4220.
address: FR 4220, just over 1 mile south of the FR 4690 junction, Olallie Lake Scenic Area, Mt. Hood National Forest (Clackamas River Ranger District: 16400 Champion Way, Sandy, OR 97055)

title: Piety Island Campground
imageAlt: Detroit Lake and a small island (area photo)

banner.alt: Detroit Lake and a small island (area photo)

gallery.alt: Detroit Lake and Mount Jefferson (area photo)

contentHtml:
Piety Island Campground sits on an island in the northern part of Detroit Lake, and all of its campsites have views of the lake. While water levels are high it is reached only by boat, landing on the island's north side.

Campers fish, swim, picnic, day hike, boat and waterski. Sites have picnic tables, with vault toilets.
excerpt: Piety Island Campground sits on an island in the northern part of Detroit Lake, and all of its campsites have views of the lake. While water levels are high it
note: All sites first come, first served. Single $12, multiple $22 per night; extra vehicle $6. Pay on site with the Recreation.gov app (no cash or checks). No drinking water. Don't tie boats to live vegetation. In winter, when the island can be reached on foot, park at Detroit Flats Day Use Area. 14-day stay limit.
address: Piety Island, northern Detroit Lake, OR (boat access; winter walk-in from Detroit Flats Day Use Area) (Detroit Ranger Station: 44125 North Santiam Highway SE, Detroit, OR 97342)

title: Santiam Flats Campground
contentHtml:
Santiam Flats Campground has 32 sites (27 single, 5 multiple), most with lake views, where the North Santiam River meets the shore of Detroit Lake, a 3,500-acre reservoir in the Cascades.

Campers fish, swim, boat and waterski, and the nearby Stahlman Point Trail looks over Detroit Lake. Sites have picnic tables and grills, with vault toilets and drinking water spigots.
excerpt: Santiam Flats Campground has 32 sites (27 single, 5 multiple), most with lake views, where the North Santiam River meets the shore of Detroit Lake, a 3,500-acre
note: Reserve at recreation.gov; some sites first come, first served. Trailers up to 30 feet. Single site $21, multiple sites $40 per night; extra vehicle $9; day use $9. Senior and Access pass holders get 50% off the single-site fee. Check-in 2:00 PM, check-out 1:00 PM; 14-day stay limit. Chainsaws prohibited. Dogs on a 6-foot leash. No horses or pack animals.
address: Forest Road 10 (Blowout Road) off Highway 22, about 2.6 miles east of Detroit, OR (Detroit Ranger Station: 44125 North Santiam Highway SE, Detroit, OR 97342)

title: Shady Cove Campground
contentHtml:
Shady Cove is a primitive campground on the Little North Fork of the Santiam River in the Opal Creek Scenic Recreation Area, near trails with mountain views and waterfalls and the Three Pools Day Use Area.

Sites have picnic tables, with vault toilets and garbage collection.

note: Closed because of the Beachie Creek Fire. When open: first come, first served; single $12, multiple $22 per night; extra vehicle $6; no drinking water; limited parking. Directions: OR-22 to Mehama, north on Little North Fork Road 15.3 miles, FR 2209 1.3 miles, right on FR 2207 1.9 miles.
address: Forest Road 2207, Opal Creek Scenic Recreation Area, about 18.5 miles northeast of Mehama, OR (Detroit Ranger Station: 44125 North Santiam Highway SE, Detroit, OR 97342)

title: Triangle Lake Horse Camp
contentHtml:
Triangle Lake Horse Camp is a quiet horse camp at the south end of Triangle Lake in the Olallie Scenic Area, with sites among lodgepole pine and mountain hemlock and long gravel pads for camp vehicles and horse trailers.

Riders have a variety of trails, and campers fish and hike; the lake is a short walk or ride downhill. It has vault toilets.
excerpt: Triangle Lake Horse Camp is a quiet horse camp at the south end of Triangle Lake in the Olallie Scenic Area, with sites among lodgepole pine and mountain hemloc
note: Closed. When open: single $15, premium double $30 per night; extra vehicle $5. First come, first served. No drinking water. Vehicles up to 30 feet. Directions: OR-224 east 30.5 miles to FR 46, 14.8 miles to FR 42 (Skyline Road), left 4.3 miles to FR 4220, right 9 miles to FR 4220-155.
address: FR 4220-155 off FR 4220, south end of Triangle Lake, Olallie Lake Scenic Area, Mt. Hood National Forest (Clackamas River Ranger District: 16400 Champion Way, Sandy, OR 97055)

title: Whispering Falls Campground
contentHtml:
Whispering Falls Campground has 15 sites along the North Santiam River at 2,000 feet, among tall conifers, hemlock, rhododendron and ferns, with river views from most sites. The Forest Service describes it as a retreat for campers wanting a remote experience.

Campers fish the river and day hike. It has drinking water, vault toilets and picnic tables.

note: Closed for the 2026 season; reopening spring 2027. Nine sites reservable at recreation.gov; the rest first come, first served. Trailers up to 30 feet. title: Ankeny
imageAlt: Rainbow over an Ankeny wetland (photo: Larry Clack)

banner.alt: Rainbow over an Ankeny wetland (photo: Larry Clack)

gallery.alt: Boardwalk to the Pintail Marsh blind
Prairie wildflowers at Ankeny Hill Nature Center

contentHtml:
Ankeny National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1965, protects 2,796 acres of Willamette Valley wetlands, cropland and riparian forest kept as a winter home for dusky Canada geese. It is off I-5 at the Ankeny Hill exit (243), about 12 miles south of Salem.

Year-round boardwalks lead to observation blinds: the Pintail-Egret Marsh Boardwalk follows Bashaw Creek, and the Rail Trail Boardwalk winds through flooded ash woodland to a blind over Wood Duck Pond. Visitors see bald eagles, white pelicans, tundra swans, great egrets, osprey, many ducks and red-legged frogs, and the free Ankeny Hill Nature Center has trail loops and a pollinator patch.
excerpt: Ankeny National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1965, protects 2,796 acres of Willamette Valley wetlands, cropland and riparian forest kept as a winter home for
note: No entrance fee. Interior trails and dikes (including the 2.31-mile Eagle Marsh Trail) are open April 1 - September 30, while the interior rests for geese the rest of the year; boardwalks and viewpoints stay open year-round. No pets on trails or roads. No overnight parking. Cell reception is very limited.
address: 2301 Wintel Rd, Jefferson, OR 97352

title: Abiqua Falls
contentHtml: Abiqua Falls is a near-perfect 92-foot free-fall plunge on Abiqua Creek into a basalt amphitheater with striking columnar jointing, one wall stained orange-red by moss and lichen. It once held a claim as the tallest waterfall ever run by kayak.
excerpt: Abiqua Falls is a near-perfect 92-foot free-fall plunge on Abiqua Creek into a basalt amphitheater with striking columnar jointing, one wall stained orange-red
note: The falls are on land owned by Mount Angel Abbey, which has allowed public access (it closed the land for a time in 2010 over liability concerns). Pack out your trash and respect the land. Directions are not published because the falls have no developed or officially sanctioned access.
address: Abiqua Creek, Mount Angel Abbey land, east of Scotts Mills, Marion County, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan (Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest)

title: Ayers Creek Falls
contentHtml: Ayers Creek Falls is a 79-foot plunge over the basalt ledge common to the area, larger than nearby Horseshoe Falls. Ayers Creek is the smallest tributary of Stout Creek in the canyon above Mehama.
excerpt: Ayers Creek Falls is a 79-foot plunge over the basalt ledge common to the area, larger than nearby Horseshoe Falls. Ayers Creek is the smallest tributary of Sto
note: With a small drainage, the falls typically run dry or nearly dry by about May. A tree partly blocks the view from the canyon rim. Directions are not published because the falls have no developed or officially sanctioned access.
address: Ayers Creek, about 100 feet above Stout Creek, in the canyon above Mehama, OR
photoCredit: Bryan Swan (Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest)

title: Butte Creek Falls
contentHtml:
Butte Creek Falls is a 78-foot horsetail on Butte Creek, seen from a rocky promontory about 150 feet above the creek, which curves around it. Flowering trees in the basin frame the falls in spring.

A trail continues down a ledge, precarious in places, to the base of the falls and the smaller Lower Butte Creek Falls below the plunge pool.

note: Directions: from Scotts Mills take Maple Grove Road about 7.2 miles, turn right on Sawtell Road and go just over 5 miles to a fork; bear left on unsigned gravel South Family Camp Road and follow Butte Creek Falls signs 5.8 miles to the trailhead. Stay left at trail junctions; the viewpoint is about 1/3 mile. The falls can no longer be reached via Crooked Finger Road.

photoCredit: Bryan Swan (Waterfalls of the Pacific Northwest)

title: Dome Rock Falls
contentHtml: Dome Rock Falls drops about 250 feet in tiered horsetails from a small basin on the north side of Dome Rock, one of more than a dozen major waterfalls in the upper French Creek drainage north of Detroit Lake.
excerpt: Dome Rock Falls drops about 250 feet in tiered horsetails from a small basin on the north side of Dome Rock, one of more than a dozen major waterfalls in the up
note: Directions: from Salem take OR-22 east about 49 miles to French Creek Road, just west of the Breitenbush River bridge in Detroit, and turn left; go just over 4 miles and turn right on FR 2207 after the pavement ends. The falls are visible across the valley about 3/4 mile up the road. Closer views require a bushwhack of nearly 1/2 mile. The small basin may run dry in summer.
address: Forest Road 2207 off French Creek Road, west side of Detroit, OR

title: Double Falls
contentHtml:
Double Falls is the tallest waterfall in Silver Falls State Park, dropping 184 feet in two tiers (43 and 141 feet) on Hullt Creek just above its meeting with North Silver Creek. It is considered the best of the tributary falls along the Trail of Ten Falls.

Local photographer June Drake discovered and named the Silver Falls waterfalls in the late 1880s.

note: From the Winter Falls trailhead, hike the Winter Creek Trail past Winter Falls to the Canyon Trail (about 0.5 mile), bear left past Middle North Falls and Drake Falls to the Hullt Creek bridge (about 0.5 mile), then take the short spur to the base. Flows about 9 months a year and drops to a trickle in summer. In Silver Falls State Park: day-use parking permit $10 Oregon residents, $12 out-of-state. Pets and bikes are not allowed on the Canyon Trail. Stairs and trails can be slick when wet or icy.
address: Winter Falls trailhead, OR-214, Silver Falls State Park, Sublimity, OR

title: Henline Falls
imageAlt: Henline Falls from the end of the trail

banner.alt: Henline Falls from the end of the trail

contentHtml:
Henline Falls is a 126-foot curtain on Henline Creek, about 50 feet wide, the largest and most accessible of several falls on the creek. At lower water it splits into distinct sheets spraying into its alcove.

The Silver King Mine adit is just right of the base, and remnants of its tramway are visible near the trail.
excerpt: Henline Falls is a 126-foot curtain on Henline Creek, about 50 feet wide, the largest and most accessible of several falls on the creek. At lower water it split
note: About 1 mile one way: follow an old road about 0.5 mile, bear left where the road continues right, and reach the base in another 0.5 mile. Directions: from Salem take OR-22 east 27 miles, turn left on North Fork Road for 17 miles, bear left on FR 2209 (signed for Jawbone Flats and Opal Creek) and go 0.2 mile to parking on the left. Don't enter the mine alone, without lights or through flooded areas. High-water spray makes crossing the creek hazardous. Flows year-round.

title: Horseshoe Falls

note: Sometimes called Stout Creek Falls, a name also used for a different fall about half a mile upstream. Directions are not published because the falls have no developed or officially sanctioned access.

title: Lower South Falls

contentHtml:
Lower South Falls is a 93-foot curtain on South Silver Creek, the fifth tallest waterfall in Silver Falls State Park. The water spreads across a broad basalt ledge, so it stays wide for most of the year.

The Canyon Trail passes behind the falls through a cramped overhang bordered by a stone wall; it is one of four park waterfalls with a trail behind the water.

note: From the parking lots, walk to the base of South Falls (just under half a mile), then about 3/4 mile downstream on the Canyon Trail. The stairs can be slick when wet. In Silver Falls State Park: day-use parking permit $10 Oregon residents, $12 out-of-state. Pets and bikes are not allowed on the Canyon Trail. Stairs and trails can be slick when wet or icy.

title: South Falls

South Falls, a 177-foot plunge on South Silver Creek, is the highlight of Silver Falls State Park and one of Oregon's most visited waterfalls. It is the park's most powerful fall at high water.

A trail passes behind the falls beneath a very tall overhang, where skylights in the rock mark spots where lava once enveloped trees.

contentHtml: Detroit Lake is a large reservoir in the Santiam Canyon, ringed by forested slopes and Cascade foothill scenery, with snow-capped Mount Jefferson in the distance. Paddlers (kayak, SUP, canoe) launch at the Mongold Day-Use Area, which has a paved boat ramp, a seasonal courtesy dock, a low-water ramp, restrooms, picnic facilities, a swimming area and a life jacket loaner station.
excerpt: Detroit Lake is a large reservoir in the Santiam Canyon, ringed by forested slopes and Cascade foothill scenery, with snow-capped Mount Jefferson in the distanc
note: Day-use parking permit required at Mongold. Motorboats share the lake and can be busy; slow-no- wake within 200 feet of shore. Wind can make open-water crossings hard, the water is cold, and rocks and stumps appear as levels change: check reservoir levels before you go. Blue-green algae blooms can occur April-September. Oregon Waterway Access Permit required for paddle craft 10 ft and longer.
address: Mongold Day-Use Area, north shore of Detroit Lake off OR-22, about 3.5 miles west of Detroit, OR

title: Turner Lake
contentHtml:
Turner Lake is a small freshwater lake just southeast of Salem in a former gravel quarry (Riverbend Quarry) that filled with groundwater. The City of Turner opened Turner Lake Park in 2020, with a boat ramp and docks, restrooms and a picnic shelter, and paddlers launch from the North Turner Lake Boat Ramp.

In summer Turn-n-Paddle rents kayaks ($10/hour) and paddleboards ($20/hour), 11 AM - 8 PM daily through September, weather permitting. Fishing is allowed from boats or the bank with an Oregon license.

note: Electric motors only; the whole lake is no-wake with a 5 mph limit and a 14-foot boat limit. Launch only from the boat ramp or city beaches. Parking $10 (collected 9 AM - 8 PM, late May to early September). No lifeguard; no alcohol. Oregon Waterway Access Permit required for paddle craft 10 ft and longer. Phone is for rentals; general questions: general@turneroregon.gov
address: Turner Lake Park, 5203 Holly St, Turner, OR

title: Walter Wirth Lake
contentHtml:
Walter Wirth Lake is a compact, flatwater urban lake of about 20 acres in Salem's 100-acre Cascades Gateway Park, open only to non-motorized boats such as kayaks, canoes, rafts and SUPs. Paddlers launch from a small boat slide on the west side, carrying or rolling their craft from the parking area.

It is a popular fishing lake with accessible bank fishing, and the park has a fenced dog park and a disc golf course.

title: Willamette River Water Trail
imageAlt: Paddlers on the Willamette River Water Trail

banner.alt: Paddlers on the Willamette River Water Trail

gallery.alt: River camp on the Water Trail

contentHtml:
The Willamette River Water Trail follows 187 miles of the mainstem Willamette River, from the Eugene and Springfield area north to Portland. It passes forests, meadows, parks, farms and cities, and it is open to canoes, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, rafts and drift boats.

Mostly flatwater with Class I riffles; the upper reach is faster and shallower, Willamette Falls (about 40 ft) must be portaged, and the river below the falls is deep and tidal to the Columbia. Designated Water Trail campsites let paddlers plan multi-day trips.

title: Mount Jefferson
imageAlt: Mt. Jefferson from the high desert near Haystack Reservoir

banner.alt: Mt. Jefferson from the high desert near Haystack Reservoir

contentHtml:
At 10,497 feet, Mount Jefferson is the second-highest mountain in Oregon after Mount Hood. It is a heavily glaciated stratovolcano of the Cascade Volcanic Arc, one of the most eroded in the state, whose last eruptive activity was about a thousand years ago.

Known as Seekseekqua to Native peoples, it was named for President Thomas Jefferson after Lewis and Clark saw it from the mouth of the Willamette River in 1806. It rises within the 111,177-acre Mount Jefferson Wilderness, which has more than 150 lakes and 190 miles of trails, including 40 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail; the eastern side lies within the Warm Springs Indian Reservation, so public access is limited to the western flanks.
excerpt: At 10,497 feet, Mount Jefferson is the second-highest mountain in Oregon after Mount Hood. It is a heavily glaciated stratovolcano of the Cascade Volcanic Arc,
note: The summit is a technical climb for experienced climbers only. Marion County's own high point is an unnamed spot of about 9,020 ft where the Marion-Linn county line crosses Mount Jefferson's north ridge: reached via Jefferson Park and then off-trail up the north ridge, about 14 miles and 5,000 ft of gain round trip, a serious alpine scramble on snow and loose rock. Central Cascades Wilderness permits apply June 15 - October 15 (Whitewater Trailhead is limited-entry, permit through Recreation.gov), and a federal recreation pass is required for trailhead parking.
address: Central Oregon Cascades, Mount Jefferson Wilderness (Jefferson, Linn and Marion counties), OR

title: Oregon Timber Trail
contentHtml:
The Oregon Timber Trail is a 670-mile mountain bike and bikepacking route from the California border near Lakeview north to Hood River on the Columbia, managed by the nonprofit Oregon Timber Trail Alliance. It is split into four tiers: Fremont, Willamette, Deschutes and Hood.

Riders can take on the whole route or ride a shorter piece.

title: Pacific Crest Trail
contentHtml:
The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail runs 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada through California, Oregon and Washington, managed by the Forest Service with the Pacific Crest Trail Association. Its roughly 455-mile Oregon section is the shortest and easiest on the trail, from near Siskiyou Summit to the Bridge of the Gods over the Columbia River.

In Marion County the trail follows the Cascade crest through the Mount Jefferson Wilderness, which holds 40 miles of the PCT.

note: Central Cascades Wilderness permits apply at some trailheads in summer.

title: Cascading Rivers Scenic Bikeway
imageAlt: Cyclists on a forest road beside the river

banner.alt: Cyclists on a forest road beside the river

gallery.alt: Cyclists on a riverside road through dense forest
Bikes leaning against a tree at camp

contentHtml:
The Cascading Rivers Scenic Bikeway is a 70-mile, one-way road ride from Estacada to Detroit that follows the Wild and Scenic Clackamas River and then the Breitenbush River through ancient forest on quiet, remote roads. It was designated an Oregon Scenic Bikeway in 2014.

Riders get views of Mount Hood and Mount Jefferson, salmon and steelhead runs, elk and grouse, hot springs and swimming holes along the way. Ripplebrook, about 26 miles from Estacada, is the only community on the route, with restrooms, water, a camp store and a campground.

The ride is rated challenging, climbing about 3,125 feet from Estacada (1,985 feet from Detroit), and can be ridden in either direction. Camping is at Milo McIver State Park, with hiker-biker sites, and Detroit Lake State Recreation Area.

title: Scorpion Ridge
contentHtml:
Scorpion Ridge is a 41-mile gravel lollipop loop (about 45% gravel, 55% paved) with about 4,000 feet of climbing around Scorpion Mountain in classic west Cascades forest, topping out near 4,600 feet. It opens into a large burn area with big views of Mount Jefferson and finishes with a long paved descent to the Breitenbush River.

A shorter 33-mile option (about 3,700 feet of climbing) starts at a dirt parking area on Forest Road 4696. Rated moderate, with straightforward navigation in a remote area; tires of 45 mm or more are suggested.

title: Sublimity Hills
imageAlt: Leading out, just before the first gravel sector

banner.alt: Leading out, just before the first gravel sector

contentHtml:
Sublimity Hills is a 28-mile gravel loop (about 45% gravel, 55% paved) with 2,100 feet of climbing over rolling hills rarely steeper than 6%, with a few short 8-9% pitches. Rated moderate with straightforward navigation; 40 mm tires suggested.

Highlights include Lone Fir Pioneer Cemetery (established 1850), views from Union Hill Pioneer Cemetery across the Willamette Valley to Marys Peak and the Silver Falls hills, a Christmas tree farm, Coon Hollow's Mill Creek canyon, Basl Hill, the Fern Ridge overlook above the Santiam Canyon and a mostly downhill gravel run along Mill Creek on Spenner Road.

title: Willamette Valley Scenic Bikeway

gallery.alt: On the Willamette Valley Scenic Bikeway

contentHtml:
The Willamette Valley Scenic Bikeway, the first official Scenic Bikeway in the United States, runs 135 paved miles one way along the Willamette River between the Coast Range and the Cascades. In Marion County it passes Champoeg State Heritage Area, Willamette Mission State Park, Keizer and Salem.

The moderate route passes hop fields, vineyards and small towns, Champoeg State Heritage Area, Keizer and the Capitol in Salem, Ankeny National Wildlife Refuge and Thompson's Mills State Heritage Site, with side trips to the Wheatland and Buena Vista ferries. Its high point is 740 feet, after Brownsville.

note: Rideable year-round; bring rain gear in winter. April through November brings sunshine, flowers and farmers markets.

title: Elkhorn Creek
imageAlt: Elkhorn Creek, Oregon (photo: Greg Shine, BLM)

banner.alt: Elkhorn Creek, Oregon (photo: Greg Shine, BLM)

contentHtml:
Elkhorn Creek was designated a Wild and Scenic River on September 30, 1996: 5.8 miles are classified wild and 0.6 mile scenic, from the Willamette National Forest down through BLM land to its confluence with the Little North Santiam River. It is a low-elevation, pristine stream with limited road access, flowing through rugged, forested foothills on the west side of the Cascades.

Its outstandingly remarkable values are fish and scenery: native cutthroat and rainbow trout, with threatened Upper Willamette winter steelhead and spring Chinook salmon in the lower creek, and a meandering corridor of vertical rock outcrops and dense, mature forest of big-leaf maple, red alder, Douglas-fir, western hemlock and western red cedar. The adjacent forests support the Oregon slender salamander, the only amphibian found only in Oregon.

note: No developed access on the creek itself. Managed by the BLM Northwest Oregon District (blm_or_no_mail@blm.gov) and the Willamette National Forest, (541) 782-2283.
address: Elkhorn Creek, joining the Little North Santiam River in the Opal Creek Scenic Recreation Area, Marion County, OR

title: Silver Falls Tour Route
imageAlt: South Falls at Silver Falls State Park

banner.alt: South Falls at Silver Falls State Park

gallery.alt: South Falls in winter (Silver Falls State Park)

contentHtml:
The Silver Falls Tour Route is a 55-mile Oregon Tour Route, entirely in Marion County, that takes 2 to 3 hours to drive without stops. It links Woodburn's farms and historic Jesse Settlemier home, Bavarian-style Mt. Angel with its glockenspiel and the Northwest's largest Oktoberfest each September, and Silverton, with the Gallon House Covered Bridge, the 80-acre Oregon Garden and Frank Lloyd Wright's Gordon House.

The route climbs past Silverton Reservoir and Christmas tree farms into Silver Falls State Park, Oregon's largest state park, where the Trail of Ten Falls passes above, below and behind its waterfalls, then returns through farmland on the Cascade Highway via Sublimity, Aumsville and Turner.

note: Drivable year-round. Silver Falls State Park requires a day-use parking permit.

title: West Cascades Scenic Byway

gallery.alt: Along the West Cascades Scenic Byway

contentHtml:
The West Cascades Scenic Byway is a 220-mile National Scenic Byway along the northern half of Oregon's Cascade Range, from Estacada, about 25 miles from Portland, south to Westfir near Oakridge.

From Estacada it follows the Clackamas River on OR-224 and Forest Road 46 to Detroit Lake, then the McKenzie River past Clear Lake and 100-foot Sahalie Falls, ending on the Aufderheide road (Forest Road 19) at the Office Covered Bridge, Oregon's longest at 180 feet.

Along the way are old-growth groves such as the Delta Old Growth Trail, three National Recreation Trails, Olallie Lakes and the PGE powerhouse at Estacada. The full drive takes 7 to 9 hours, or sections can be driven on their own.

note: Forest Roads 19 and 46 are generally closed November 15 to April 30 because of snow.
address: Estacada (OR-224) to Westfir near Oakridge (OR-58), via Forest Road 46, Detroit, OR-22, OR-126 and Forest Road 19

title: Farmlandia Farm Loop

gallery.alt: Rogerson Clematis Garden at Luscher Farm

contentHtml:
The Farmlandia Farm Loop is a self-guided farm trail of about 17 stops at the northern edge of the Willamette Valley, from Milwaukie and Oregon City through Stafford, West Linn and Wilsonville and out toward Boring. It is part of the Oregon Farm Loop program.

More than a dozen stops are working farms, joined by vineyards, nurseries, farm stores, farmers markets and a farm-to-table restaurant. Favorites include Lee Farms, a seventh-generation farm since 1869 with a store and bakery; Barn Owl Nursery's nearly 100 lavender varieties; Frog Pond Farm's animals and pumpkin patch; Triskelee Farm; Tollen Farm's miniature donkeys; and Terra Vina Wines.

Lavender peaks in June and July, fall brings pumpkins, and the holidays bring Christmas trees.

title: Great Oaks Food Trail

gallery.alt: Independent Ice Cream Shop (photo: Joshua Rainey Photography)
The Independence Hotel on the Willamette River (photo: Joshua Rainey Photography)

contentHtml:
The Great Oaks Food Trail is a self-guided, year-round tour of 44 farms, wineries, breweries, bakeries and historic towns, mostly in Polk County, built around the restoration of the native white oak savanna and the working family farms that care for it. It has three themed routes: Rooted in Tradition (Dallas to Monmouth), Scenic Sips & Local Bounty (West Salem to Amity) and Paddle, Parks & Pints (Dallas to Independence).

Its one Marion County stop is Ankeny Vineyard, south of Salem, which pours wine with wood-fired pizza, small bites, live music and views, open May through September, Thursday to Sunday. Cherries and blueberries come June-August, hops July-October, apples August-October and the wine grape harvest in fall.

title: Marion Farm Loop
contentHtml:
The Marion Farm Loop is a self-guided farm trail of 22 stops entirely within Marion County, from the Willamette River in the north to the edge of the Cascade foothills, through Aurora, Woodburn, Silverton, Salem and Keizer, Stayton, Sublimity, Aumsville and Jefferson. Visit as many stops as you like, in any order.

Stops include E.Z. Orchards Farm Market (family-owned since 1929, with a May-September shortcake stand and an October HarvestFest), Bauman's Farm & Garden (produce, bakery, cider and nursery), Minto Island Growers' tea garden, Honeywood Winery (Oregon's oldest), TopWire Hop Project's seasonal beer garden near Woodburn, Willamette Valley Pie Co. and Flying Bee Ranch, Oregon's only honey tasting room.

title: Gallon House Covered Bridge
imageAlt: Gallon House Covered Bridge (photo: Taylor Higgins)

banner.alt: Gallon House Covered Bridge (photo: Taylor Higgins)

contentHtml:
The Gallon House Bridge is an 84-foot Howe truss covered bridge over Abiqua Creek, built in 1916-17 and the last of Marion County's original covered bridges; it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Its name recalls Prohibition days, when Silverton was dry and Mt. Angel was not, and whiskey was sold by the gallon at a house near its north entrance.

Damaged in the 1964 Christmas Flood, it was repaired and kept as a historic landmark, repaired again in 1985 and rehabilitated in 1990.

note: Directions: from Silverton take OR-214 north to Hobart Road, turn west 0.5 mile to Gallon House Road, then north to the bridge. Check with Marion County for current vehicle limits.

title: Stayton-Jordan Covered Bridge
contentHtml:
The Stayton-Jordan Covered Bridge is a 90-foot Howe truss footbridge over the Salem Power Canal, joining two parks in Stayton. It is patterned after the Jordan Bridge, which stood over Thomas Creek east of Scio in Linn County until Stayton residents took it over; volunteers and Marine Corps reservists rebuilt it here, dedicating it in June 1988.

Christmas lights set the roof on fire on December 20, 1994, and volunteers built the present bridge with glue- laminated members in 1997-98, dedicating it in September 1998. It is open year-round for sightseeing, picnics and weddings.

title: Breitenbush Hot Springs
contentHtml:
Breitenbush Hot Springs is a worker-owned retreat on the Breitenbush River near Detroit, with seven hot pools of about 100-110°F and a steam sauna. Damaged in the 2020 Santiam Fire, it reopened in 2021.

Day visitors soak 9 AM - 6 PM by advance booking, with optional vegetarian lunch. Overnight retreats include vegetarian meals and 24-hour access to the pools and sauna.

title: Enchanted Forest
contentHtml:
Enchanted Forest is a 20-acre storybook park beside I-5 at Turner that one man built by hand: Roger Tofte bought the wooded hillside in 1964 and spent seven years mixing concrete in a wheelbarrow to raise Storybook Lane's fairy-tale scenes, opening on August 8, 1971.

The Tofte family still runs it. Hand-built attractions include the Western town of Tofteville, the Haunted House, the Ice Mountain Bobsleds and the Big Timber Log Ride.

title: Buena Vista Ferry
contentHtml:
The Buena Vista Ferry is one of only three car ferries still crossing the Willamette River. Marion County's cable ferry crosses about 720 feet of river six miles south of Independence, where Reason B. Hall started Hall's Ferry about 1850.

The current six-vehicle boat entered service in 2011 and runs year-round, seven days a week.

note: Currently closed for dredging and its five-year Coast Guard haul-out inspection, with no reopening date posted: check the county's operating status page before going. Fares: pedestrians free, bicycles $1, motorcycles $2, cars $3 (cash, check or county ferry toll card; no credit cards). Closed Thanksgiving and Christmas Day; closes when the river reaches about 15 feet. Ferry information line (24/7): (503) 588-7979.

title: Wheatland Ferry
contentHtml:
The Wheatland Ferry is one of only three car ferries still crossing the Willamette River and Oregon's oldest ferry crossing, running since Daniel Matheny established it in 1844. The cable ferry crosses about 580 feet of river and is a joint Marion-Yamhill operation staffed by Marion County.

Every replacement boat has carried the founder's name; the current Daniel Matheny V, launched in 2002, carries nine vehicles on its own diesel-electric power, with the overhead cable bracing and steering it against the current.

note: Low summer water and high winter water can stop the ferry; check the county's operating status page before going. Fares: pedestrians free, bicycles $1, motorcycles $2, cars $3 (cash, check or county ferry toll card; no credit cards). Closed Thanksgiving and Christmas Day; closes when the river reaches about 15 feet. Ferry information line (24/7): (503) 588-7979.

title: Gold Butte Lookout
contentHtml:
Gold Butte Lookout is a restored 1934 L-4 ground cabin on the 4,618-foot summit of Gold Butte, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps and used as a World War II aircraft warning station. Windows on all sides and an outside catwalk look out to Battle Ax, Mount Jefferson, Three Fingered Jack, Mount Hood and the Three Sisters.

The Bull of the Woods and Opal Creek wildernesses are next door, and Elk Lake below offers canoeing, fishing and swimming. Wildflowers and wild huckleberries grow nearby.
excerpt: Gold Butte Lookout is a restored 1934 L-4 ground cabin on the 4,618-foot summit of Gold Butte, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps and used as a World War
note: Summer rental by reservation at recreation.gov; sleeps 4 (a twin bed and three cots). Provided: wood stove and firewood, propane cookstove, dishes, outhouse. Bring all water, bedding, lights and a cooler (no water, electricity or refrigeration). The last 2 miles are rough with a 10% grade: high clearance recommended. Park at the second green gate and walk about half a mile; lock the gates behind you. When the cabin isn't rented the hike to the viewpoint stays open.

title: Oregon Museum of Mental Health, Salem
imageAlt: Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health

banner.alt: Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health

gallery.alt: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest cast and director accepting an award (museum display)

contentHtml:
The Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health occupies about 2,500 square feet in the oldest building on the Oregon State Hospital campus, the Kirkbride-plan hospital of 1883 (formerly the Oregon Insane Asylum), the last of its kind still operating on the West Coast.

Exhibits trace a century and a half of mental-health care in Oregon and the people who lived and worked there, with a memorial to the unclaimed cremains. The hospital was the filming location for One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest in 1975, with real patients and staff among the cast, and the museum keeps an exhibit of props and stories from the production; it is a stop on the Oregon Film Trail.
excerpt: The Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health occupies about 2,500 square feet in the oldest building on the Oregon State Hospital campus, the Kirkbride-pla
note: A stop on the Oregon Film Trail (One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, 1975).
address: 2600 Center St NE, Salem, OR 97301

title: Oregon State Hospital Dome Building, Salem
imageAlt: Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health

banner.alt: Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health

contentHtml:
The Dome Building stands on the campus of the Oregon State Hospital, the Kirkbride-plan hospital of 1883 and the last of its kind still operating on the West Coast. In the opening of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, the five-Oscar classic filmed chiefly at the hospital in 1975, McMurphy is dropped off outside this building.

The Oregon State Hospital Museum of Mental Health on the same campus keeps an exhibit of props and stories from the production.

note: A stop on the Oregon Film Trail. The hospital still operates; visit through the museum.
address: Oregon State Hospital, 2600 Center St NE, Salem, OR 97301

title: Silver Falls State Park
contentHtml:
The opening deer-hunt scene of Twilight (2008) was filmed in the forests of Silver Falls State Park, and The Hunted and the horror film Just Before Dawn also filmed among its waterfalls. It is a stop on the Oregon Film Trail.

Silver Falls State Park, often called the crown jewel of Oregon State Parks, covers more than 9,000 acres of Cascade foothill forest less than an hour east of Salem. Its best-known feature is the Trail of Ten Falls, a 7.2- mile moderate loop and National Recreation Trail with about 800 feet of elevation change, which passes behind 177-foot South Falls.

More than 35 miles of backcountry trails are open to hiking, mountain biking and horseback riding, and the one-mile accessible North Rim Trail has a North Falls viewpoint. The South Falls day-use area has lawns, picnic shelters, a playground and an off-leash dog area, and the historic South Falls Lodge has a cafe and nature store.

note: Day-use parking permit: $10 Oregon residents, $12 out-of-state (machines give no change; Northwest Forest and National Park passes not valid). Pets and bikes are not allowed on the Canyon Trail. Black bears and cougars live in remote areas. Cell coverage is limited. Park office 503-873-8681 (Mon-Fri 8:30 AM - 4:30 PM); reservations 800-452-5687.
address: 20024 Silver Falls Hwy SE, Sublimity, OR 97385

title: Benedictine Brewery
contentHtml:
Benedictine Brewery is run by the monks of Mount Angel Abbey, one of only a handful of breweries in the U.S. owned and run by monks. Opened in 2018, it brews on abbey grounds with hops grown on abbey land and water from the abbey's well, as part of a monastic life of work and prayer.

The flagship is Black Habit, a dark, malty ale, alongside Belgian- and German-style and barrel-aged ales. St. Michael's Taproom serves them with locally sourced charcuterie and small bites.

title: For Tomorrow We Die
contentHtml:
For Tomorrow We Die Brewing launched in 2022 in southeast Salem's brewing district. Core beers include a full-bodied stout, a citrus-tinged pale ale, a caramel-toned red ale and Kiss The Girl IPA, with more stouts and porters in winter and lagers in spring and summer.

The taproom has pinball machines and a tree growing through the center of a table, and an on-site food outpost inspired by downtown Salem's Taproot Lounge & Cafe.

title: Ratchet Brewery
contentHtml: Ratchet Brewery opened to the public in 2017 in southeast Salem, with a tasting room pouring many traditional and nontraditional beers. Drink pints on site or take home growlers or cans.
excerpt: Ratchet Brewery opened to the public in 2017 in southeast Salem, with a tasting room pouring many traditional and nontraditional beers. Drink pints on site or t

title: Santiam Brewing
contentHtml:
Santiam Brewing is a British-style brewpub founded by Salem homebrewers, pouring since 2012 from an industrial park at Salem's southeastern edge. It specializes in cask-conditioned real ales, usually with four house and guest casks on at once, among more than a dozen house beers and ciders made from Pacific Northwest apples; its JFK lager won gold at the 2026 Oregon Beer Awards.

The kitchen serves fish and chips, British pub pies and classic burgers, and a separate event venue hosts live music, trivia, comedy and open mic nights. A covered, heated patio is open year-round.

title: Shades of Brew
contentHtml:
Shades of Brew grew out of Bine Valley Brewing (2017-2022) when a former co-owner teamed with a local taphouse co-owner, launching its first beer in 2022. House beers run from tropical IPA to imperial stout, with guest taps from regional brewers and cider makers.

The Northeast Salem taphouse has nearly 30 taps, and a second taproom sits at the South Salem brewery. Expect food carts and pizza, patio seating, live music, trivia and bingo.

title: Silver Falls Brewery
contentHtml:
Silver Falls Brewery is a downtown Silverton ale house that moved to Jersey Street in spring 2021, upgrading from a 2- to a 10-barrel system. It pours nearly two dozen of its own traditional ales and lagers, from a pilsner and Mexican lager to a floral IPA, raspberry wheat and chocolate-tinged stout.

The kitchen makes burgers, sandwiches and salads from scratch, with vegetarian options. There is a spacious taproom, a ground-level patio with gas fire pits and a second-floor brew deck.

title: Snow Peak Brewing
contentHtml:
Snow Peak Brewing became Stayton's first brewery in 2019, opened by a group of friends in an old brick building downtown with plenty of natural light, and a canal-side patio. It brews small batches on a 150-gallon system, pouring ales and lagers such as a smoked IPA, a smoked chocolate porter and Haybox Amber, plus guest taps from regional breweries and cider makers.

Food carts are sometimes on site, and the calendar includes paint-and-sip nights, trivia, bingo fundraisers, live music and stand-up comedy.

note: No standalone website: check Facebook for hours.

title: Xicha Brewing
contentHtml:
Xicha Brewing is a Latine brewery founded in West Salem in 2017, building community around fresh Latin American fusion food and house-brewed European-style ales and lagers. It is known for its Guava Golden Ale and the September Xicha Fest.

Brewing is now consolidated at the North Salem taproom; there is also a Eugene location (747 E 32nd Ave), and the original West Salem taproom has closed.

note: Check the website for current hours.

title: Blue Heron Farm
contentHtml: Blue Heron Farm is a family-owned, regeneratively farmed Chardonnay vineyard in the South Salem Hills of the Willamette Valley, supplying the Morgen Long and Porcelina wineries.
excerpt: Blue Heron Farm is a family-owned, regeneratively farmed Chardonnay vineyard in the South Salem Hills of the Willamette Valley, supplying the Morgen Long and Po

title: Coria Estate Wines
contentHtml:
Coria Estates is a Mexican-American family-owned vineyard, winery and tasting room in the rolling South Salem Hills of the Willamette Valley AVA, where the family has farmed its 94-acre estate vineyard for 25 years. A mother-and-daughter team makes the wine with minimal intervention, and the father grows the grapes.

Pinot Noir is the focus, alongside Pinot Gris, sparkling rose, Chardonnay, Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Tempranillo, poured by the flight, glass or bottle with light bites on a patio overlooking the vineyard and valley.

note: Last reservation 4:30 PM. Email: info@coriaestates.com

title: La Chouette Vineyard
contentHtml:
La Chouette Vineyard is a small 15-acre estate vineyard and winery in the Willamette Valley AVA, making about 600 cases per harvest. Its upper vineyard was planted in 2007 and its lower in 2020, on a southwest- facing slope at 250 to 500 feet with views of the Coast Range and the Ankeny area.

La Chouette is French for "the owl" and slang for "cool."

title: Lady Hill Winery
contentHtml: Lady Hill Winery is an estate winery on the family's historic farm across from Champoeg State Heritage Area in the Willamette Valley AVA, making terroir-driven wines with warm hospitality amid Oregon farmland.

contentHtml: Paradis Vineyards is a family-owned and operated farm winery started by fourth-generation farmers in the Cascade Foothills of the Willamette Valley AVA. The family staffs the Silverton tasting room and loves talking about grapes.

contentHtml: Pudding River Wine Cellars is a boutique winery, vineyard and tasting room in the east Willamette Valley foothills, also offering custom crush winemaking. Owner and winemaker Sean Allen planted the vineyard in 2004, with the first vintage in 2006.

title: Sass Winery
contentHtml:
Sass Winery is Jerry Sass's winery and vineyard in the South Salem Hills. Its Wild Winds (Jory soil) and Walnut Ridge (Bellpine soil) vineyards were first planted in 1989 with dry-farmed, own-rooted vines, and the winery was built in 1995; it makes about 3,500 cases a year.

Wines include estate Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and a rose of Gamay Noir.

title: Scenic Valley Farms
contentHtml:
Scenic Valley Farms is a multi-generation family farm and winery in Gervais, first planted in the 1940s and started as a farm in 1970, now run by the third generation. It released its first wine in 2014 from dry-farmed estate grapes, including Pinot, Gamay, Dolcetto and Tempranillo, made with native ferments and Oregon oak.

The farm also grows hazelnuts, garlic, pumpkins, grass seed, wheat, clover and hops, and is LIVE certified, Salmon Safe and a member of the Deep Roots Coalition.

contentHtml: Sineann is a small winery in St. Paul in the Willamette Valley AVA, where winemaker Peter Rosback is known for single-vineyard bottlings from top Pacific Northwest vineyards.

title: St. Innocent Winery
contentHtml:
St. Innocent Winery was founded in 1988 by Mark Vlossak and makes wines from Willamette Valley vineyards. Its estate Enchanted Way Vineyard was planted in 2018 on a 47-acre South Salem Hills property, and the tasting room, a few minutes from I-5 south of Salem, overlooks the vines.

Visitors book wine flights and pair them with seasonal bites; The Cabin hosts private events indoors and out.

title: Sunnyside Vineyard Inc.
contentHtml: Sunnyside Vineyard was established in 1970-71 and has been farmed by Tom Owen and Luci Wisniewski since 1980. Its own-rooted Pinot Noir, Riesling, Gewurztraminer and Dolcetto grow on volcanic Jory and Nekia soils in the Willamette Valley AVA, supplying client wineries.

note: Vineyard only: no public tasting and no website.

title: The Farm on Golden Hill
contentHtml:
The Farm on Golden Hill is a six-generation, 40-acre family farm near Silverton where two sisters turned childhood dreams into a winery and event destination. The vineyard, introduced in 2018, grows Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling, with over a dozen other varieties and styles, and the tasting room opened around 2023.

Guests taste flights and seasonal menus with vineyard and countryside views, and the farm hosts weddings, retreats, fundraisers and workshops; the old milk house, where the family pressed apples into cider each fall, and the barn loft are part of its story.
excerpt: The Farm on Golden Hill is a six-generation, 40-acre family farm near Silverton where two sisters turned childhood dreams into a winery and event destination. T
note: Tasting room hours are limited: check availability on the website before visiting.

title: Vitis Ridge
contentHtml: Vitis Ridge is a small boutique estate winery founded in 2005, making about 4,000 cases a year. Its tasting room sits on the LIVE-certified Meridian Estate Vineyard just north of Silverton in the Cascade Foothills, with new varietal releases through the year.

note: Also open Memorial Day and Labor Day Mondays and the Friday after Thanksgiving. Closed January and February except by appointment.

title: Willamette Valley Vineyards
contentHtml:
Willamette Valley Vineyards was founded in 1983 by Jim Bernau to make world-class Pinot Noir and is one of Oregon's largest and best-known wineries; Wine Enthusiast called it one of America's great Pinot Noir producers. Its estate in the Salem Hills has fireplaces, a patio, a courtyard, lawns and a 65-foot lookout tower.

Seasonal flights ($25) and elevated tastings ($30) come with daily food pairings, and guests can book private winery tours, a chef's counter, a Pinot Noir clonal blending experience, library tastings and horseback rides through the vineyard.

note: Reservations recommended for indoor tableside tastings (walk-ins welcome for open seating); flight fee waived with a two-bottle purchase. Wine shop 11 AM - 5 PM daily. Dogs welcome on the Pinot Decks and lawns, not in the tasting room.

title: Aurora City Park
contentHtml: Aurora City Park has a flat 9-hole, par-27 disc golf course established in 2020, with holes of 175 to 241 feet, grass tees and Black Hole Portal targets in a mixed-use public park.
excerpt: Aurora City Park has a flat 9-hole, par-27 disc golf course established in 2020, with holes of 175 to 241 feet, grass tees and Black Hole Portal targets in a mi
note: Free to play. Restrooms and a drinking fountain (with a dog basin) during park hours; dogs allowed.
address: Aurora City Park, Aurora, OR (first tee by the baseball backstop next to the parking area)

title: Cascades Gateway Park
contentHtml:
Cascades Gateway has a flat, open 18-hole, par-54 course (5,705 feet) established in 2008 and maintained by the Capital City Disc Golf Club, good for players of all levels. It has concrete tees and DISCatcher Pro targets; only hole 10 has an elevated basket.

The park around Walter Wirth Lake also has a fenced dog park and fishing.

note: Free to play. Rounds take about 1.5 to 2.5 hours. Cart, stroller and wheelchair friendly; dogs allowed. No drinking water. Park restrooms on the east side are closed for repairs; the west side, including the course, is open.

title: Champoeg State Park
contentHtml: Champoeg State Park's disc golf course is a flat, remodeled course among tall oak trees, with concrete tees, new baskets and signage, a mix of shot types, a couple of long holes and a fair amount of out-of-bounds. The full 23-hole layout is about 8,300 feet, par 73.

note: Free to play with a state park parking permit ($10 day pass, paid at the course). Restrooms, drinking water and a store near the main entrance that sells discs; dogs allowed.

title: Chemeketa Community College
contentHtml: Chemeketa Community College has an 18-hole, par-54 course (5,693 feet) established in 2023 in the wooded west side of campus, with concrete tees and Meadowlark targets. It is mostly flat but uneven underfoot throughout, rated moderate to hard.
excerpt: Chemeketa Community College has an 18-hole, par-54 course (5,693 feet) established in 2023 in the wooded west side of campus, with concrete tees and Meadowlark
note: Free to play. 90-minute parking with no permit across from the first tee. No drinking water or course restroom (restrooms in most college buildings). No drinking or smoking anywhere on college property. Dogs allowed.

title: Church Park
contentHtml: Church Park has an easy, flat 9-hole course (holes of 104 to 304 feet; par 54 played twice around) that starts in the trees, opens up for a couple of holes and returns to the woods; most holes are in mature woods with mowed grass. It has concrete tees and DISCatcher Pro targets.

note: Free to play. Restrooms and drinking water; cart, stroller and wheelchair friendly when dry, but wet fields are hard going. Dogs allowed. Church Park is also the start of the Sublimity Hills gravel bike loop.

title: Corban College
contentHtml: Corban University (formerly Western Baptist College) has a hilly 9-hole, par-27 course of about 2,180 feet, established in 2014, wandering the hillside north of the soccer and baseball fields, with grass tees.
excerpt: Corban University (formerly Western Baptist College) has a hilly 9-hole, par-27 course of about 2,180 feet, established in 2014, wandering the hillside north of
note: Limited access: open only to Corban students, staff and alumni with ID. Be very careful of cars and pedestrians during school hours; hole 8 is closed during soccer games. No water or restroom.

title: Jefferson School District
contentHtml: Jefferson School District has a flat, open 12-hole, par-36 course (about 3,450 feet) established in 2015 on school grounds, with grass tees and Mach III targets, open year-round.
excerpt: Jefferson School District has a flat, open 12-hole, par-36 course (about 3,450 feet) established in 2015 on school grounds, with grass tees and Mach III targets
note: Free to play. Recent visitors report some missing baskets and tee markers.

title: Keizer Rapids Park
contentHtml: Keizer Rapids has a wooded 18-hole course with some open holes and two water holes over a pond, established in 2009. The main layout is par 55 over 5,182 feet with concrete tees and DISCatcher Pro baskets, rated moderate to hard; a round takes about two hours.
excerpt: Keizer Rapids has a wooded 18-hole course with some open holes and two water holes over a pond, established in 2009. The main layout is par 55 over 5,182 feet w
note: Free to play. Watch out for poison oak. No drinking water or restrooms. Dogs on leash only. Some holes may be unplayable in December and January rains.
address: Keizer Rapids Park, Keizer, OR

title: Pioneer Park
contentHtml: Pioneer Park has an easy 9-hole pitch-and-putt course established in 2014 (holes of 110 to 206 feet; par 54 played twice around), mostly flat with wide-open fairways, concrete tees and DISCatcher Pro targets. The park is also home to the Stayton-Jordan Covered Bridge.
excerpt: Pioneer Park has an easy 9-hole pitch-and-putt course established in 2014 (holes of 110 to 206 feet; par 54 played twice around), mostly flat with wide-open fai
note: Free to play. Restrooms and drinking water; cart, stroller and wheelchair friendly; ground stays stable most of the wet season. Dogs allowed.

title: Wheatland DGC
contentHtml: Wheatland DGC is a flat, hard 18-hole, par-60 course (about 6,800 feet) in a hazelnut grove at Willamette Mission State Park, mixing wooded and open holes and meadows, with concrete tees and DISCatcher Pro baskets, established in 2014. Hole 12 plays through "the tunnel."
excerpt: Wheatland DGC is a flat, hard 18-hole, par-60 course (about 6,800 feet) in a hazelnut grove at Willamette Mission State Park, mixing wooded and open holes and m
note: Free to play with a state park parking permit or $10 day pass. Restrooms and drinking water; dogs allowed. Thick brush off the fairways eats discs. Occasionally closed in winter when high water covers the road.

title: Woodmansee Park
contentHtml: Woodmansee Park has a hilly 9-basket course with 20 tee pads (played as an 18-hole, par-54 layout of about 5,045 feet), run by the Capital City Disc Golf club. Most holes are tree-lined with a clear fairway, a couple thread tight lines through trees, and some throw up or down a big hill.
excerpt: Woodmansee Park has a hilly 9-basket course with 20 tee pads (played as an 18-hole, par-54 layout of about 5,045 feet), run by the Capital City Disc Golf club.
note: Free to play. Restrooms; no drinking water. Dogs on leash only. Steep sections and trip hazards: not recommended for limited mobility.
address: Woodmansee Park, Salem, OR

title: Morrow County Museum
contentHtml:
The Morrow County Museum is the county's main history museum, in Heppner. Artifacts and murals recreate the lives and activities of Heppner's settlers, and the museum covers the 1903 Heppner flood, Oregon's deadliest natural disaster.

It is also an agricultural resource museum focused on rural history and heritage, with a farm museum holding a collection of antique farm equipment, and is a stop on the River to Hills Farm Trail.
excerpt: The Morrow County Museum is the county's main history museum, in Heppner. Artifacts and murals recreate the lives and activities of Heppner's settlers, and the
address: 444 N Main St, Heppner, OR 97836

title: SAGE Center
imageAlt: Kinetic sculpture at the SAGE Center

banner.alt: Kinetic sculpture at the SAGE Center

contentHtml:
The SAGE Center (Sustainable Agriculture and Energy Center) in Boardman, developed by the Port of Morrow, tells the region's story of agriculture, irrigation, energy, industry and river transportation through hands-on, interactive exhibits. The signature exhibit follows a potato on its journey into curly fries, and highlights include a tractor simulator, the Key Ingredient Theater and the Amazon Racers.

A film in the 200-seat theater tells how the original town of Boardman moved when the John Day Dam pool rose. The building also holds the SAGE Makers Market, a Travel Oregon Welcome Center, the Amazon Think Big Space with hands-on STEAM activities (open to the public on Fridays) and a 15,000-square-foot event center.
excerpt: The SAGE Center (Sustainable Agriculture and Energy Center) in Boardman, developed by the Port of Morrow, tells the region's story of agriculture, irrigation, e
note: Email: sagec@portofmorrow.com
address: 101 Olson Rd, Boardman, OR 97818

title: Umatilla National Forest
contentHtml:
The Umatilla National Forest covers 1.4 million acres of the Blue Mountains in northeast Oregon and southeast Washington, at elevations from 1,600 to 8,000 feet. Its landscape is mostly V-shaped valleys between narrow ridges and plateaus, with timbered slopes, grassland benches and basalt outcrops.

More than 2,000 miles of forest roads and more than 20 campgrounds open it up for camping, hiking, fishing, hunting, and mushroom and huckleberry picking. In Morrow County, the Heppner Ranger District covers the forest south of Heppner along the Blue Mountain Scenic Byway.
excerpt: The Umatilla National Forest covers 1.4 million acres of the Blue Mountains in northeast Oregon and southeast Washington, at elevations from 1,600 to 8,000 feet
note: Some day-use sites charge a fee, covered by certain passes. Permits may be required for mushroom and huckleberry picking.
address: Supervisor's Office: 72510 Coyote Rd, Pendleton, OR 97801

title: Coalmine Hill Campground
contentHtml:
Coalmine Hill Campground is a small, free campground in the Umatilla National Forest just off the paved Blue Mountain Scenic Byway, with one larger site near the entrance and five along the tree edges of a large parking area. It is the trailhead for the Bald Mountain, Hells Half Acre and Willow Creek trails, a 7.5-mile loop for hikers and horse riders.

The Bald Mountain trail leads 1.25 miles to Gibson Cave, a shallow overhanging shelter with an interpretive sign, then climbs to a viewpoint over the drainages between Coalmine Hill and Little Bald Mountain. Penland Lake, about five miles southwest, offers fishing and non-motorized boating.
excerpt: Coalmine Hill Campground is a small, free campground in the Umatilla National Forest just off the paved Blue Mountain Scenic Byway, with one larger site near th
note: No fee. Vault toilet and picnic tables; no drinking water or garbage service, so pack out all trash. Maintained Memorial Day to mid-November; in winter it doubles as a snow park reached only by snowmobile once snow blocks the road.
address: Willow Creek Rd (FS Road 53), about 22 miles south of Heppner, OR (top of Coalmine Hill)

title: Penland Lake Campground
contentHtml:
Penland Lake Campground sits on the shore of Penland Lake in the Umatilla National Forest, popular on summer weekends for fishing, boating and swimming. The National Forest side has seven first-come, first- served campsites and two vault toilets, with more campsites on adjoining Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife land.

There is a boat ramp, a fishing dock and benches on the dam. Gas motors are not allowed on the lake, so boats use electric motors only.

note: No fee. No drinking water, garbage service or host: pack out all trash. Parts of the shoreline are private property. Maintained Memorial Day to mid-November; in winter, access is by snowmobile only once the road is impassable.
address: FS Road 2103-030 off FS Road 21, south of Heppner, OR

title: Umatilla

gallery.alt: Coot with chicks in a wetland
Painted turtle sunning on a log

contentHtml:
Umatilla National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1969 to replace habitat flooded by the John Day Dam. It covers about 23,500 acres of Columbia River waters, islands, shores and uplands, where natural and managed wetlands mix with native shrub-steppe; the Oregon side is the McCormack and Boardman units.

It is a Pacific Flyway wintering and stopover site for geese, ducks and bald eagles, known for waterfowl hunting, and draws birdwatchers and visitors looking for mule deer. Visitors also fish, hike open roads, ride horses, paddle and drive the auto tour route on the McCormack Unit.
excerpt: Umatilla National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1969 to replace habitat flooded by the John Day Dam. It covers about 23,500 acres of Columbia River waters,
note: Self-guided: no visitor center. The only restroom is at the McCormack Unit hunter check station. No camping or overnight parking, no drones, dogs on leash. Most islands are closed to public entry year- round. Email: mcriver@fws.gov
address: 72650 Riverview Lane, Irrigon, OR 97844

title: Coyote Springs Wildlife Area
imageAlt: A dog with her first duck of the season (photo: Aaron Light)

banner.alt: A dog with her first duck of the season (photo: Aaron Light)

contentHtml:
Coyote Springs is a 160-acre Columbia Basin wildlife area east of Boardman with grassland, sagebrush-steppe and seasonal wetlands. Brief flooding in fall and spring draws waterfowl, wading birds and shorebirds, and songbirds and upland birds such as California quail are there most of the year.

It is one of four ODFW Columbia Basin wildlife areas, with Irrigon, Power City and Willow Creek, managed on federal land to protect habitat in a heavily developed landscape. Hunting is allowed in authorized seasons except for big game.

note: ODFW Wildlife Area Parking Permit required ($10/day, $30/year). Walk-in access only; no overnight camping.
address: Off Rippee Rd, east of Boardman, OR (I-84 Exit 165, north on Laurel Rd, east on Columbia Ave)

title: Irrigon Wildlife Area
contentHtml:
Irrigon Wildlife Area is a strip of Columbia River shoreline between Highway 730 and the river east of Irrigon, part of ODFW's 1,885-acre Columbia Basin wildlife areas. It is known for its pothole ponds, painted turtles (best seen on summer mornings), curlews from March, waterfowl and upland birds such as pheasant and California quail.

Visitors hunt, fish, walk the trails and use an ADA-accessible viewpoint. It gets heavy hunting pressure during upland bird and waterfowl seasons.

note: ODFW Wildlife Area Parking Permit required ($10/day, $30/year). No overnight camping.
address: Between Hwy 730 and the Columbia River, from just east of Irrigon to the Umatilla River (I-84 Exit 168)

title: Northwest Discovery Water Trail
imageAlt: Earl Snell Memorial Park on the Columbia in Arlington (area photo)

banner.alt: Earl Snell Memorial Park on the Columbia in Arlington (area photo)

contentHtml:
The Northwest Discovery Water Trail is a 367-mile boating route from Canoe Camp on the Clearwater River in Idaho, down the Snake River and the Columbia to Bonneville Dam in the Columbia River Gorge. More than 150 sites along the way are for launching, picnicking or camping, for motorboats, canoes, sailboats and kayaks.

In Oregon it follows the Columbia's south shore through Umatilla, Morrow, Gilliam, Sherman, Wasco, Hood River and Multnomah counties. Much of it is flatwater behind eight dams, with locks to pass through or portage around.
excerpt: The Northwest Discovery Water Trail is a 367-mile boating route from Canoe Camp on the Clearwater River in Idaho, down the Snake River and the Columbia to Bonne
note: Always wear a life jacket. Check forecasts for high winds and storms, yield to commercial barges and their wakes, and watch for submerged stumps and debris. Plan each dam lock-through or portage before you go.
address: Columbia River south shore, including Arlington, OR

title: Willow Creek Reservoir
imageAlt: Willow Creek Reservoir (Willow Creek Park & Recreation District)

banner.alt: Willow Creek Reservoir (Willow Creek Park & Recreation District)

contentHtml:
Willow Creek Reservoir is a high-desert reservoir just outside Heppner, with open water and rolling Eastern Oregon scenery, good for kayaks, canoes and stand-up paddleboards. Willow Creek Dam was completed in 1983, mainly for flood control and irrigation.

Paddlers launch from the Turner Day Park boat ramp and dock, built for changing water levels. Calm, flat water makes it suitable for first-time paddlers, and anglers fish for rainbow trout.
excerpt: Willow Creek Reservoir is a high-desert reservoir just outside Heppner, with open water and rolling Eastern Oregon scenery, good for kayaks, canoes and stand-up
note: An Oregon Waterway Access Permit is required for paddlecraft. Water levels vary a lot and the ramp may not reach the water when low; watch for wind, submerged stumps and posted dam restricted zones, and check Oregon Health Authority advisories for algae blooms. Clean, drain and dry your boat.
address: Turner Day Park boat ramp, about 2 miles southeast of Heppner, OR

title: Black Mountain
contentHtml: Black Mountain (5,932 feet) in the Blue Mountains is Morrow County's highest point, and a walk-up rather than a technical climb. From Heppner, drive about 25 miles up Willow Creek Road (NF-53) into the Umatilla National Forest, then walk the gated NF-030 summit maintenance road about 2 miles, with roughly 1,000 feet of gain, to the communications towers at the top.
excerpt: Black Mountain (5,932 feet) in the Blue Mountains is Morrow County's highest point, and a walk-up rather than a technical climb. From Heppner, drive about 25 mi
note: Public national forest land throughout; no permit required. Go in the dry season.
address: Umatilla National Forest, about 25 miles south of Heppner via Willow Creek Rd (NF-53)

title: Blue Mountain Century Scenic Bikeway
contentHtml:
The Blue Mountain Century Scenic Bikeway, designated in 2011, is a 108-mile paved loop from Heppner with about 8,000 feet of climbing, rated extreme. It follows the Blue Mountain Scenic Byway past Cutsforth Park and up to Arbuckle Summit (5,319 feet), then descends about 15 miles to Highway 395 near Ukiah, the halfway town.

The route heads north on 395 past Battle Mountain State Park, moving from forest to rangeland over several moderate climbs, then turns west on Highway 74 through rolling hills back to Heppner. Despite the name, most riders plan two days.

note: Lodging is scarce, so plan ahead; Ukiah has overnight accommodations, a grocery store and a cafe. Check road conditions on TripCheck.
address: Start and finish: Main St and May St, Heppner, OR

title: Blue Mountain Scenic Byway
imageAlt: Blue Mountain Scenic Byway (photo: Vince Warren)

banner.alt: Blue Mountain Scenic Byway (photo: Vince Warren)

contentHtml:
The Blue Mountain Scenic Byway runs about 130 miles from I-84 through ranching country into the forests of the Blue Mountains, passing the Willow Creek Wildlife Area, the Wells Springs Oregon Trail wagon ruts (a side trip), and Ione and Lexington, former 1800s sheep stations with frontier architecture.

Heppner, the "Gateway to the Blues," has a historic downtown walking tour, the 1902 bluestone courthouse and the Morrow County Museum. Beyond, the road winds through the Umatilla National Forest past Cutsforth Park and the Potamus Point side trip over the Wild and Scenic North Fork John Day River, through the Ukiah basin, to an overlook of the North Fork John Day Wilderness and the byway's end at North Fork John Day Campground.
excerpt: The Blue Mountain Scenic Byway runs about 130 miles from I-84 through ranching country into the forests of the Blue Mountains, passing the Willow Creek Wildlife
note: Allow 3-4 hours. No fuel between Heppner and Granite. Best in spring and fall; winter snow closes the high-elevation section. Also crosses Umatilla County.
address: OR-74 from I-84 (Exit 147, Heppner Junction) through Ione, Lexington and Heppner to the North Fork John Day Campground

title: Burnt Field Brewing
contentHtml:
Burnt Field Brewing & Pizza is a family-friendly craft beer and pizza restaurant that began in 2018 in Boardman's renovated 1916 train depot, saved from the town's "Old Town." It is known for brick-oven pizza made from scratch with fresh ingredients and house ales.

The name blends the founders' surnames: Brandt ("burnt" in German) and Mayfield. The patio overlooks the Columbia River and the historic tugboat Captain Al James.

note: Call ahead for takeout or reservations.
address: 1 E Marine Dr (at the Depot), Boardman, OR 97818

title: Sailboard Beach
contentHtml:
Sailboard Beach is a mostly flat, moderate 18-hole, par-56 course (5,594 feet) on the Boardman riverfront, established in 2021, with turf tees, Veteran targets, a sandy beach area and open fairways where wind is a big factor. Holes 1-5 run east of the parking area, 6-9 are open holes across the road, and the back nine follows the walking path west of the Main Street overpass before returning to the lot.

A rail line runs through the middle of the course and roads come into play; hole 16 has a mando between two trees.

note: Free to play. Rounds take about 1.5 hours. Park at Sailboard Beach.
address: Sailboard Beach, Boardman, OR
